President William Ruto's directive targeting foreigners in small-scale businesses was set to be implemented on Monday. Ruto had set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5x.title: Nepal cracks down on online abuse of flood survivors
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5x.text:
Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah warning that authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering.

Some have taken to social media to appeal for information about their loved ones and to urge officials to step up search efforts, only to be hit by hostile comments.

"People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals," Shah wrote in a Facebook post.

Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments have originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers.

A woman, whose brother has been missing since the floods hit two weeks ago, had earlier told the BBC that search and rescue operations were too slow.

"If the government had mobilised experts and equipment for rescue in time, would we have known the condition of our family members sooner?

"We still hope we can find him alive."

Days later, she wrote back saying she had "received many nasty comments" in response to her criticism of the search efforts.

"We are already suffering so much and this has only added to our pain," she said.

In a separate case, a young woman had expressed her anger at what she perceived as authorities' "lack of urgency" in searching for her husband.

"My husband is missing now, if the government cannot find him, can it at least show me his body?" she said in a video clip that has gone viral online – and attracted its fair share of insults.

One comment, for instance, urged her to "jump into the river" and help with the search, while another read, "not everything happens just by you putting the blame on the government".

But others have called out the insensitive remarks. "The victim should be consoled at this time, not cursed," one of them read.

Nepali police say they have convened a 10-member committee to look into these online comments.

Under the country's Electronic Transactions Act, those who use social media to defame or harass others could be jailed for up to five years and fined up to 100,000 rupees ($662; £490), or both.

Dovan Rai, the executive director of Body & Data, a Nepal-based non-profit organisation that advocates for a safe digital space, says some of the insensitive comments could have come from social media users who engage in "rage baiting" – that is, those who produce negative content as a "bait" to trigger outrage, or force people to click on or share their posts.

They could also have come from "staunch supporters of the government".

"There is also extremism that is very sympathetic to the government and condemns those who question it. That has further polarized the dialogue on social media," she told the BBC.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5x.summary: Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods. Prime Minister Balendra Shah warns authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering. Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9x.title: North Korea and Russia open first road bridge linking both countries
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9x.text:
The first road bridge linking Russia and North Korea has opened, allowing the two countries to more easily move cargo and passengers between their border across the Tumen river.

Pyongyang state media said the bridge will be used for "personnel exchanges, tourism and trade".

But Ukrainian investigative organisation Truth Hounds said the bridge is intended "primarily to establish a covert military logistics corridor" to support Russia in the Ukraine war.

It comes amid stronger ties between the countries since the start of the Ukraine war, with Russia's Putin and North Korea's Kim Jong Un previously pledging that they would help each other in the event of "aggression" against either country.

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin described the bridge as a "new symbol of friendship", while North Korea's Prime Minister Pak Thae Song said it was a "historical event".

Up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people can cross the bridge daily, Russian state news TASS reports.

Satellite imagery reported by the BBC in May this year showed the kilometre-long bridge alongside several new access roads, a border checkpoint, support infrastructure and parking facilities.

There are existing air links, as well as the rail link between the two countries, but until now the only road link was a makeshift solution where, by special arrangement, wooden planks were placed on the rail bridge to allow cars to travel over it, according to Reuters.

The Russian government said the bridge will initially be used to transport cargo, Reuters reported, before opening to passenger traffic later this year.

The bridge would provide, a "powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," said Mishustin.

Appearing at the opening ceremony via video link, he described ties between Moscow and Pyongyang as being "at an unprecedented high level."

The most immediate impact may be increased export of weapons to Russia.

Researchers at South Korea's spy agency estimates that North Korea has already transferred $7 to 14 billion dollars' worth of rockets, missiles, artillery shells using ships. An estimated 11,000 North Korean troops are actively fighting Ukrainians in Russia.

Truth Hounds said in a recent statement that given the strategic partnership treaty between the two countries in 2024 - the bridge could be used to transport North Korean military personnel, construction workers and senior military officials directly to Russia.

It would also enable the flow of Russian technology and resources in the opposite direction".

Construction started in 2025, after the agreement to build the bridge was made during Putin's 2024 visit to North Korea, his first trip to the state in 24 years, which resulted in the partnership treaty. The bridge took 495 days to complete, after delays.

Russian tourists have trickled into North Korea since they were allowed in in 2024. North Korea has been hosting them in capital Pyongyang and the beach resorts of Wonsan-Kalma, while continuing to block those from other countries.

The road is also expected to transport North Korean labourers to Russia.

Around 10,000 North Koreans are working in Russia's construction sites and logging camps, according to a South Korean estimate. Although the UN bans countries from using North Korean labour, many enter Russia under the guise of student visas.

"The speed of construction is a reflection of the volume of trade activity between the two sides," Victor Cha from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank, told BBC Verify in May this year.

"This is spurred largely by North Korea's provision of troops, weapons, munitions, and labourers for Putin's war in Ukraine," he said.

"It is fair to say that this connection, prior to the war in Ukraine, was one of the sleepiest links between North Korea and its two neighbours."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9x.summary: North Korea and Russia have agreed to build a bridge to link their border. The bridge will be used to transport cargo and passengers between the two countries. It is expected to be used for "personnel exchanges, tourism and trade" But Ukrainian investigative organisation Truth Hounds says it is intended to support Russia in the Ukraine war.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj.text:
President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank'."

The move came amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs were imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) of US goods.

In a statement, Bombardier said it employed thousands of American workers and that it valued its partnerships with US companies.

The BBC has reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney's office for comment.

It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.

The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.

It also operates sites in Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, DC and New Jersey.

About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

In a statement on Monday, Bombardier did not address Trump's threat directly, but said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs through the company's growing American footprint".

"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," its statement said. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country."

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.

The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.

It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.

In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".

She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.

On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."

"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj.summary: Bombardier says it employs thousands of American workers and valued its partnerships with US companies. The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours. Canadian retaliatory tariffs were imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) of US goods on Monday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.

This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.

Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.

Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".

Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods.

"As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."

West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.

At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".

With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.

In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.

Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".

Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.

In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".

As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories".

"I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."

Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley.

"These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.

Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.

Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank.

Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs.

Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.

The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.

This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.

Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth.

"Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says.

"They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."

Israeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.

Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.

Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.

There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.

Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.

There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.

A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.

However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned.

"A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says.

"I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."

Israel's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October.

He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip.

"The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned.

Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.

Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.

Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.summary: Israel announces series of counter measures against settlements in the West Bank. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in West Bank, not including East Jerusalem. There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.text:
The images are hard to ignore.

Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.

One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.

At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.

Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.

"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.

The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.

Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.

But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.

"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.

Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.

But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.

The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.

Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.

And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.

By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.

Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.

"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".

Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.

The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.

However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.

Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.

His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.

The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".

The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?

Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.

For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.

"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.

He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."

The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.

Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.

But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.

"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.

The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.

For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.

"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.summary: Mumbai's Tukaram Mundhe has banned newspapers and synthetic dyes from wrapping food. He has also banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools. Mundhe says he is not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m3.title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m3.text:
The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.

Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.

Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.

However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.

Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.

Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.

Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.

"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.

"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.

Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.

He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.

"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.

"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."

In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.

"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."

Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.

He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.

Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.

This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.

There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.

He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.

"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."

But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.

"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."

As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.

But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots in a very large way. He said the future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4v.title: New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4v.text:
The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals.

The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy.

Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs.

The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before.

The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania.

Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence.

This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside.

Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody.

The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted.

He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment.

After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden.

BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years.

Our investigation also found:

Omar al-Bayoumi arrived in San Diego from Saudi Arabia in 1994. He claimed to be studying English, but court records show that within a few years he had, in effect, abandoned his studies. He was more usually found organising religious events, often with a camcorder pressed to his eye.

One video Bayoumi filmed, from 1997 or early 1998, shows men, including Anwar al-Awlaki, paintballing. Filmed near San Diego, the group engages in urban combat scenes and target practice, many wearing military fatigues.

At one point, some of the men charge into battle, shouting "Allahu Akbar". A visiting Saudi sheikh is with the group and Bayoumi can also be heard addressing Anwar al-Awlaki with the honorific "Sheikh Anwar".

Paintballing emerged as a subject of interest in the FBI's post-9/11 counter-terrorism investigations, and the DOJ used paintball evidence in a number of terrorism prosecutions.

Omar al-Bayoumi and Anwar al-Awlaki were involved in paintball sessions in San Diego for at least three years in the late 1990s and very early 2000s. When the FBI investigated after 9/11, agents were told some of the participants were taking part to train for jihad.

Though Awlaki's extremist preaching would come into sharper focus after 9/11, at the time the paintballing video was recorded he already had connections to al-Qaeda operatives and was shortly to be investigated by the FBI. He was killed in a CIA drone strike in 2011.

Saudi Arabia has stated that the paintball video does not reveal who "made" or "took" it. When he was questioned remotely in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in 2021, Bayoumi insisted he had not met Awlaki. The video evidence contradicting his claim was only made available, confidentially, to the court a year later - and placed on the public docket on 4 September this year.

Another previously unreported clip shows Bayoumi embracing Awlaki in January 1998. Further footage records Bayoumi's many meetings with officials and preachers from Riyadh's Ministry of Islamic Affairs. He appears in a video with two ministry officials, one wielding a clipboard, at SeaWorld. Bayoumi passes the camera to his son and bounds into shot to record his presence with them.

The Ministry of Islamic Affairs, created in 1993, was seen as dominated by clerics who espoused a radical view of Sunni Islam and exported it around the world. It spent hundreds of millions of dollars worldwide building mosques, and sent dozens of officials to the US, some of whom oversaw a network of preachers with hard-line views.

After the 9/11 attacks, Omar al-Bayoumi emerged as an early suspect in the FBI's investigation.

His name had been found on an apartment rental agreement signed by the first two hijackers to arrive in the United States, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, who were part of a five man hijacking team that crashed a plane into the Pentagon.

The FBI traced Bayoumi to Birmingham, UK, where he had moved with his family before 9/11.

On 21 September 2001, officers from the Met Police's Anti-Terror Branch Special Operations team arrested Bayoumi at one of his properties.

He was blue-lighted down to Paddington Green Police Station in London, where detectives began questioning him. Under UK law at the time, officers could only hold him for seven days without charge.

The following morning, in Birmingham, officers began the meticulous process of logging and bagging up evidence in his properties - a cache of many thousands of pages of documents, hundreds of photographs, flight ticket stubs, phone cards, and carrier bags and boxes containing at least 80 videotapes.

Within hours of the search starting, several items of documentary evidence - categorised as the highest priority at the direction of the FBI - were taken by police directly to Paddington Green, where the FBI had stationed an agent.

This evidence included a phone book containing more than two dozen names of Saudi government officials in the US and Saudi Arabia; flight simulator software; tickets and travel documents; and the yellow lined page of a notebook with the sketch of a plane, which an officer had marked: "contains handwritten notes mathematical calculations re height of planes".

Eighteen years later, the FBI would hand the notebook page to the court in the 9/11 families' lawsuit, following a subpoena. The page was made public in 2022.

"It's the mathematical calculation of the crash," Jodi Westbrook Flowers, a member of the 9/11 families' legal team, told the BBC. "When we figured out what it was, we knew that it was the smoking gun that we'd been looking for."

The equation, written in Omar al-Bayoumi's handwriting, indicates the height and distance required for a pilot to guide an aeroplane to a given object on the ground. Underneath it is a small drawing of a plane and a series of numbers.

Last year, the federal judge in the families' lawsuit found the notebook page, on the face of it, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks".

In 2021, when questioned about it in court, Bayoumi said he had the diagram because he liked finding equations and could not remember when he had written it.

By the evening of 22 September 2001, copies of the plane diagram were in London in the hands of both the FBI and UK counter-terror police - and just metres from the custody suite where Omar al-Bayoumi was being questioned. Records show they passed through at least three further FBI agents in the following two days.

But here, the mystery begins. The FBI briefed the Met officers to question Bayoumi about the other high-priority exhibits, but the detectives in the custody suite were never given, or briefed about, the plane diagram.

Many FBI agents have told us the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was a round-the-clock frenzy. But it is hard to understand how a piece of evidence of this importance, in a case being handled with considerable urgency, was not put into the hands of the interviewing detectives.

The FBI declined to respond to our questions. The Metropolitan Police told us it could not comment because of the ongoing legal case.

Soon after the plane diagram was couriered to Paddington Green, all Bayoumi's videos, including the footage of the paintballing, were taken from Birmingham to New Scotland Yard for copying.

By 24 September, the custody suite a mile or so away at Paddington Green had access to the video cassettes. The detectives brought the bags of tapes into the room where Bayoumi was being questioned - and some of the footage was played to him.

He was asked about two tapes featuring a gathering, but the British officers were not briefed by the FBI to ask him about the video of the paintballing session - nor about his association with Anwar al-Awlaki.

On the day he would need to be charged or released, the Met detectives joined a conference call with several senior officials from the US Department of Justice and FBI.

Panorama and Radio 4 have spoken to two participants at the meeting. One recalls the British detectives setting out the evidence they believed met the threshold for the Americans to extradite Bayoumi to face charges in the US.

The response from the DOJ officials was that no extradition would be sought because there was insufficient evidence.

On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.

But, at that point, the FBI had not shipped all of the evidence found in Birmingham back to the US, let alone exhaustively analysed it.

One memorandum from the FBI's legal attache in London, sent two weeks later, noted there were a "number of videos, floppy disks and documentation still to be viewed".

After Omar al-Bayoumi's release, agents continued analysing the evidence against him.

The BBC understands the plane diagram was couriered from London for analysis at the New York Field Office, which was in overall charge of the 9/11 investigation.

But we have not been able to trace any records of this analysis or its conclusions. A 2021 Presidential order required the FBI to declassify files relating to its 9/11 investigations, including into Bayoumi.

However, of the files released, the FBI has only produced one document referring to the diagram, despite its evidential significance, and this was only created 11 years after the diagram's initial discovery in 2001.

The diagram seems to have fallen into a black hole.

It was not passed on to San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the USA and where the FBI Field Office was also investigating him.

In fact, San Diego - where agents were interviewing his associates, searching his mosque, analysing his telephone records and bank statements - received almost none of the large volume of evidence seized by the Met Police in Birmingham.

Rick Lambert, who ran the FBI's investigation there, told the BBC his office made repeated requests to New York to send copies of all the evidence. "Their position was, we're in charge of the case; we'll send it to you when we're finished analysing."

Lambert said New York did not comply his office's requests. "I believe there is the potential that had we received that evidence and analysed it, that we would have been able to put the pieces of the puzzle together much more quickly."

Documents show that, in spring 2002, the San Diego office was ultimately able to get copies of a handful of videos by obtaining them not from New York, but from the FBI liaison in London.

What happened to the paintballing video is equally curious.

A copy of the tape was sent to the FBI office in New York, where it was viewed, one agent told us. But it was not included in the office's summaries documenting Bayoumi's extremist connections.

FBI and DOJ memos from 2002, viewed by the BBC, discussed materials seized from Bayoumi's homes in Birmingham that could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs" and writings by Bayoumi himself that "can be interpreted as jihadist".

But there was no mention of the paintballing video or Bayoumi's connection to Anwar al-Awlaki.

Jeffrey Breinholt, then the deputy director of counter-terrorism at the Department of Justice who oversaw prosecutors working on terrorism charges after 9/11, told the BBC that Bayoumi's name had come up "as one of the hot possibilities for charges".

But he said the New York Attorney's Office never sent charges to him or his colleagues for approval. If they had, the plane diagram would have been significant evidence against Bayoumi, he said. "We've convicted people for less."

The paintballing video, Breinholt told us, is another "very telling bit of evidence" with the presence of Anwar al-Awlaki being "pretty damn significant".

"As a manager who reviewed a lot of proposed terrorism cases over the years, I can tell you that that would have jumped out. I think it would be a material support charge against Bayoumi."

There were no charges brought against Bayoumi.

Agents who tried to investigate Omar al-Bayoumi encountered other roadblocks.

In October 2001 in San Diego, Lambert and colleagues wanted to interview a number of Saudi officials in the US - many connected to the Ministry of Islamic Affairs - who they suspected had co-ordinated the help Bayoumi gave to two of the hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.

Because diplomats have a special protected status, the agents needed permission from FBI headquarters and the State Department.

"The answer came back, 'no, you're not going to do that'," Lambert, who is now a consultant for the 9/11 families in their lawsuit, told us.

Agents in Los Angeles experienced a similar outcome the following year, when they applied to interview a Saudi religious diplomat Bayoumi had met immediately after his first encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar in the city.

"We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns," said Steve Moore, who oversaw the FBI's 9/11 investigation in LA. Moore says his team made repeated requests to interview the official, but permission never came.

Like the FBI, the State Department declined to comment.

In October 2003, the 9/11 Commission - set up by Congress to provide a "full and complete" account of the attacks - interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi in Riyadh. He had returned to Saudi Arabia in the months after his release by British police.

The interview was conducted, in the presence of Saudi secret police, by the Commission's executive director Philip Zelikow, a former advisor to President George W Bush, along with a senior staffer and an agent from FBI headquarters.

The Commission's notes from the time record that Bayoumi was given a remarkable degree of reassurance during the interview. He "was told that no-one believes he knowingly helped the hijackers carry out their terrorist mission".

Bayoumi indignantly said he was a peace-lover who had become "a victim of the victims". During the interview, the delegation broke away for a multi-course dinner hosted by the Mabahith, the secret police, without Bayoumi.

After the interview concluded, the Mabahith told the American delegation they "would like to see him cleared". The Americans responded that no exoneration would be possible before their report was published.

When the 9/11 Commission Report was published in July 2004, Bayoumi was, in effect, cleared. It described him as "obliging and gregarious" and stated there was no evidence he had extremist views.

But some staff on the Commission were not convinced of Bayoumi's innocence, and thought it likely he knew Hazmi and Mihdhar were al Qaeda operatives.

The BBC can reveal that those staff objected to a line in the report concluding that he was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists".

In the end, a compromise was agreed, and this conclusion was attributed to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background".

The line was written based on the four and a half hours the Commission delegation had spent with Bayoumi, which included the interruption for dinner.

The Commission never saw the plane diagram, the paintballing video, written evidence of Bayoumi's alleged extremism, or much of the rest of the evidence the Met Police had seized.

Philip Zelikow did not answer the specific questions we asked him. He told the BBC the 9/11 Commission's findings had been subject to two government reviews, in 2015 and 2021, and the Commission had been "open about our suspicions and uncertainties. We were careful about whom to accuse of complicity in mass murder."

The Department of Justice told us it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.

The head of the FBI's 9/11 investigation, Mary Galligan, has previously stated the Commission had "access to everything".

We tried to contact Omar al-Bayoumi through the Saudi government, but he did not respond. He has previously denied knowing Hazmi and Mihdhar were hijackers, that he was a Saudi spy, and that he had any involvement in 9/11.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia did not respond to our request for comment. It has previously said any allegation that Saudi Arabia or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4v.summary: Video shows Omar al-Bayoumi paintballing with al-Qaeda's future leaders. Footage is part of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families. Video is partof 9/9/11 Families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia Omar al. al- Bayoumi.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986.title: How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986.text:
"Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".

This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?

Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7 million out of 59 million eligible voters nationwide.

How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?

The answer: Very significant.

First and foremost, at home in Germany.

The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.

These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.

The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.

The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist.

The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.

Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?

Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too.

None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.

The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".

Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.

Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.

What interest might Russia have in German regional elections, you might ask, and what was Dmitriev's dig at the UK all about?

The German government is the largest single donor to Ukraine and the UK is known to have provided Kyiv with missiles used to strike inside Russian territory. This has deeply angered Moscow.

The AfD, by comparison, is pretty pro-Russia. It wants to stop sending military aid to Ukraine, halt sanctions against Moscow and start buying much cheaper Russian energy again. Energy-hungry German industry suffered a huge economic blow after the country halted Russian energy imports, following Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The AfD's softly-softly approach to Russia has another appeal in Germany's east, which remains far poorer than the west. This, despite Germany spending between 2.3 and 3tn (£2tn-£2.6tn) - depending on reports and whether inflation is taken into account - to help integrate the former Communist part of the country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.

Saxony-Anhalt is Germany's poorest region and there, as in much of east Germany, you often encounter what's known as "Ostalgie" amongst voters; essentially "nostalgia in the east" for comparatively more stable times under Communism.

Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union.

The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.

The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".

By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany".

Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.

Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.

Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.

Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.

Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.

The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too.

And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".

Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist.

The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjw5.title: Scammers demand ransoms from Instagram users over fake copyright claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjw5.text:
Instagram creators say they have lost thousands of pounds after their accounts were suspended or taken down due to fake copyright claims.

Extorters have filed bogus claims to the Meta-owned social media platform, then asked for ransoms to withdraw them - knowing repeated claims can lead to account bans.

One Instagram user, who has 1.5 million followers, told the BBC he paid a scammer $50 (£37) to get his account back, claiming Meta's appeal process would take weeks, which had previously cost him thousands in lost income.

"We understand this can be frustrating for those impacted, and our systems are designed to protect people from this happening in the first place," a Meta spokesperson said.

"Following our review, we have restored the affected content and added additional protections to safeguard accounts against further attempts of this kind."

However, content creators the BBC has spoken to say Meta is poor at identifying obviously spurious cases, and say its appeals process is slow to respond unless you pay a monthly fee.

The Lost in Time History Instagram account posts historical pictures to its more than 1.5 million followers.

Its creator Olly, who did not share his last name, told the BBC he posts pictures in the public domain or where he has permission from the rights holder.

Yet he has received dozens of "obviously fake" copyright complaints so far in 2026.

Meta does not check the authenticity of complaints when they are made, so if someone is hit repeatedly, their account can be temporarily taken down.

Olly says he often gets struck for multiple posts at a time, all from the same email address.

He then gets contacted by the person asking to go on to the private messaging app Telegram.

"They'll demand a certain amount of money," he said - usually amounting to a few hundred dollars - to withdraw the claim.

The BBC has seen messages from the claimants where they demand money or threaten future copyright strikes.

Olly ultimately agreed to pay an extorter $50 in cryptocurrency to restore his account, which had been temporarily taken down by Instagram.

Law enforcement organisations tell extortion victims not to pay ransoms as it fuels the criminal ecosystem.

Olly said he paid as a "last resort" because it was quicker than going through Meta, which could take weeks.

But he was hit by more copyright strikes immediately after he paid.

"That's the worst part," he said.

"Having to pay the person who's actively put you through all of that anguish only for it to happen straight away again."

As a result of the number of times he has been hit by copyright claims, Olly's account was demonetised, meaning he could not earn money from Instagram for high-performing posts.

"There's no investigation into abuse, or system detection [from Meta] that it could be abuse," he said.

Other Instagram users have shared similar experiences.

"Meta was not helpful throughout the entire process, forcing you to pay for support to talk, even as they claim to be here for the creator," said Abin Tom Sebastian, who is behind the Morbid Kuriosity account.

Meta charges a £9.99 monthly fee to be Verified on Instagram, which gives users 24/7 access to support via a live chat.

"I lost irrecoverable and crucial, brand contracts that unfortunately moved ahead with another creator, and no reassurance or support from Meta saying this will not happen again," Sebastian said.

Instagram says only copyright holders, or an authorised representative, can report copyright infringement, and it advises affected users to contacted rights holders directly.

After the BBC contacted Meta with examples from Olly and other account holders, Meta said it had applied additional protections to their accounts, which it said would prevent similar issues happening in the future.

It said it fought against deceptive behaviour to scam or defraud people and businesses.

The BBC has spoken to three people who file copyright strikes against Instagram users, despite not being the copyright holders.

All three appear to be based in India, or in countries nearby.

They deny they are holding accounts to ransom - instead saying they file legitimate claims on behalf of copyright holders.

But the BBC has seen messages from one where they ask for $900 (£668) to withdraw a strike.

They claimed this was their payment for the service, and confirmed they kept all the money.

Two others denied they made any money at all.

One said they are sent accounts to target and investigate the claim.

"If I find that they are using someone else's content, I issue copyright strikes for the benefit of everyone," they said.

The other said they are sent accounts or posts via an account holder or another representative.

Legitimate agencies do exist which are paid to file copyright strikes on behalf of clients.

But Olly - who has dealt with these before when he has mistakenly posted copyrighted material - says they are usually easy to deal with, and "you can easily tell the difference".

"They're established companies with millions of followers, so it's very different," he said.

These kinds of copyright scams are not new, with a version of the crime dating back to the early days of the internet, said Andres Guadamuz, reader in intellectual property law of the University of Sussex and an expert on digital copyright.

Previously, they were emails or letters sent to website owners claiming they owned the copyright to photos used online, and asking for money to avoid legal action.

Similar strikes have been used against YouTube users too.

But the recent increase in this method may be because AI has made it easier to do this on a larger scale.

"It's a numbers game," Guadamuz told the BBC.

"Pretty much anyone can now deploy [AI] that is going to automate all of this in some way," he said.

It is also harder for the platforms - with billions of users - to police the racket, and distinguish the real copyright claims from the fake ones.

"The system was almost built with the assumption that the person that was making a copyright strike claim was legitimate," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e.title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e.text:
Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.

The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.

The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.

According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.

Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.

The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September.

"While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.

The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.

The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.

It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.

People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.

Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.

She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".

Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.

The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.

It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.

Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.

It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.

The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community".

"Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: OpenAI chief scientist warns no-one is prepared for consequences of AI
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has called for "extreme caution" over AI's runaway progress and warned more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".

"I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," he wrote in a blog post entitled "An Alien Mind".

The post comes only a few days after the ChatGPT-maker released its latest model GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

OpenAI and other AI firms like Anthropic shared reports of their AI agents acting autonomously and carrying out real-world cyber-attacks on other companies.

In July, OpenAI called an incident in which its AI agents - AI systems which can operate alone after human instruction - hacked the tech platform Hugging Face "unprecedented".

Meanwhile in September a report claimed months earlier AI agents from the firm had also hijacked a German website.

"We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity," Pachocki wrote in the latest blog post.

He said OpenAI would continue to "build defensive systems" and seek technical solutions to alignment - a term used to describe ensuring a machine's actions and goals perfectly match human intent and safety guardrails.

Pachocki added one of the firm's main priorities moving forward would be to build an "automated AI researcher" to keep pace with AI progress while ensuring ways that human researchers could remain part of the process.

"Instead of better AI guardrails, regulations, or assurance to keep people safe, they propose developing internal AI agents to research these problems," said Professor Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge.

"Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough."

Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agreed with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI model development - but he claimed OpenAI was unwilling to be transparent, and said this meant warnings risked being dismissed as "just self-interested hype".

"If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," he wrote on X.

Global regulations are struggling to keep up with the pace of AI development.

The European Union's AI Act came into force on 2 August, which requires AI giants like OpenAI to prove their most powerful models cannot autonomously launch cyber-attacks or evade human control before they are allowed to be sold in Europe.

But because the law's jurisdiction is confined to Europe, it cannot stop a rogue AI developed elsewhere from threatening the continent.

In his blog post, Pachocki called for legally or internationally required minimum safety thresholds which could be enforced by a "network of third-party auditors" or "government agencies".

AI labs would need to meet these thresholds, he said, before they were allowed to continue scaling or deploy advanced models.

He added he hoped "voluntary slow downs" - a self-imposed pause by companies in AI development - would become commonplace until shared guardrails were established.

In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.title: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx.text:
Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.

Tributes to the late country legend have appeared online and at locations including the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, after Parton died on 25 August at the age of 80.

Writing on Instagram, Stella Parton thanked those who had shown "genuine support" for the star and her family - but said a "tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted" had been "challenging to absorb".

Her request for people to show "more compassion" in how they respond to Parton's death follows similar pleas from families of late celebrities over AI tributes.

In October, Robin Williams' daughter asked fans to stop sending fake AI-generated videos of her father.

Zelda Williams' plea was shared by Dr Martin Luther King Jr's daughter Bernice A King, who asked fans to "please stop" in a post on Instagram.

Little over a month later, Robert Redford's daughter Amy spoke out over AI content created to pay tribute to the American actor following his death last September.

"Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different," wrote Parton in her Instagram post on Friday.

"Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."

She said there had been a tide of AI and "garbage" posts, adding: "As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move onto the next stampede of endless misinformation."

Parton also asked that people look to her sister's life as "an example for tolerance" and mutual respect.

"It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she said.

With an abundance of AI tools able to quickly generate text, images, video or audio, many have used them to craft tribute posts for departed stars.

Since Parton's death in late August, dozens of AI-generated songs, images and videos have appeared online.

US President Donald Trump was among those to share such material - posting an AI-generated image of himself and Parton, arm in arm, on his platform Truth Social.

Another image criticised as an AI fake, shared on Instagram and X, depicted the late country singer without any make-up or a wig.

One X user described it as "incredibly weird", while another called it a "violation".

On YouTube, a "heartfelt fan-made tribute by Miley Cyrus" to her godmother Dolly Parton and sung in the style of the Wrecking Ball singer has had more than 1.5 million views.

It has an AI label and disclaimer in the description to say it is not an "official release by Miley Cyrus or Dolly Parton's representatives".

But scores of comments have been left on the video thanking Cyrus for the "perfect tribute".

Other AI-generated tributes in the style of singers Pink and Celine Dion have also been widely-viewed online.

And Dolly Parton herself appeared to have been concerned about the potential impact of AI on artists.

She told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023 that while she thought AI was "going to be great for a lot of things, like science and medicine", the idea of it replacing humans "scares me".

"That's like the mark of the beast. It's like you can't remake a person," she said.

"I want to just leave a body of work behind. I think all this stuff can be great, used in the right way.

"But not to replace voices and writings and not to replace a human being that belongs to God."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg7.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website before Hugging Face hack, report claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg7.text:
A new report claims a swarm of AI agents, developed by OpenAI, hijacked a German website - months before the firm revealed its AI had hacked tech platform Hugging Face.

The targeted website, DseWiki, is a Wikipedia-style site for programmers that its community can all contribute to.

The report is from a group called Nightingale Collective and claims that in May OpenAI's agents started using DseWiki as their own message board, shared tips on how to avoid being detected and made 15,000 edits to it.

OpenAI said it could not "meaningfully respond" to Nightingale Collective's findings because it hadn't been allowed to review the report, which was first shared with news agency Reuters.

An email to the address on the Nightingale Collective website bounced back when the BBC contacted it.

The report claims that when DseWiki's editors started deleting pages, the AI agents shared code designed to retrieve them.

Hugging Face's systems were separately hacked by OpenAI agents in July, with the incident described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

The agents involved had also set up a secret message board in order to share information between them.

OpenAI said it had already publicly stated its discovery of some agents learning how to use message boards prior to the Hugging Face attack.

In its report into that incident, it noted "rare cases in which agents without multi-agent tools found ways to collaborate via side channels during training".

Yesterday, OpenAI unveiled a new AI model called GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

The firm's president, Greg Brockman, described Astra as the closest so far to artificial general intelligence (AGI) - a significant future milestone for the AI industry.

AGI doesn't have a specific definition but is broadly said to mean AI which is as good as humans, or better than them, on multiple tasks.

OpenAI claims Astra can do tax returns, and take three minutes to carry out a task which would take a human five hours.

The firm intends to list itself on the stock exchange later this year.
