https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.title: Ancient cave art discovery suggests first known humans in Ireland walked over from Wales
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.text:
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.

During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.

According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.

Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project alongside Genevieve von Petzinger and Barbara Oosterwijk, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.

With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.

Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.

This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Abu Dhabi, Wales and Portugal.

"Up until now the earliest evidence archaeologists had found - through accidental discovery - was from around 10,500 years ago, but everyone - not just me - knew that simply couldn't have been correct.

"We just weren't looking hard enough, and not in the right places. The principle we worked on was 'absence of proof isn't proof of absence'."

He said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) had been a game-changer.

"With the help of caving specialist Shane Diffily and digital mapping consultant Darren Lee, we were able to fill a computer algorithm with everything we knew about the characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales and set it to work searching for similar sites in Ireland, without us trudging blindly around the countryside, hoping to bump into something which looked promising."

What their computer model spat out was 28 potential caves in south-west Ireland which the team investigated.

Eight of them were found to have cave art which they believe dates from at least 15,000 years ago and possibly much earlier, and around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

The team are currently unwilling to be more precise about the location of the caves, for fear that they may be vandalised or looted.

"We know that modern day south Wales was settled from around 35,000 to 40,000 years ago, by intrepid early modern humans from southern England, France and Spain, crossing the then dried-up land bridges of the English and Bristol Channels - seasonally settling in caves along the inhabitable strip of land stretching from Chepstow to St Davids," said Nash.

"Over 20,000 years their art progressed from primitive line drawings which may have been early tally charts, to more figurative and representative depictions of the world around them, and what we've found in Ireland is yet another progression from that."

The rock art which the Lost Land Bridge Project has uncovered includes engravings on the cave walls, paintings in ochre and charcoal and line sketches indented into clay and earth by fingertips.

Nash believes the growing population put pressure on humans to move ever more west and northwards.

"There were around 100 human-inhabited caves on The Gower Peninsula for example, in a time when the technology didn't yet exist for human groups to create their own free-standing dwellings."

Nash said the caves would have been "quite a cosy place to live, especially compared with the -20°C outside".

"Competition for these caves would have been intense," he added.

"As family networks grew, knowledge of how to survive by following animal migration routes improved and they must have become bolder."

The Lost Land Bridge Project team believe the potential for more future discoveries is high.

"The sites we've currently explored are in south-west Ireland, but it's illogical to presume that early humans just bypassed Wexford, Waterford and Cork, and ploughed on west," said Nash.

"There must be more, and even earlier places which are just waiting for us to find them. This project is now pushing the boundaries of what we consider to be the final vestiges of a north-west European frontier. It's all very exciting."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.summary: Scientists believe first known humans to set foot on Ireland were most likely from Wales. They believe the first known human settlement was in Wales, around 5,000 years ago. The Lost Land Bridge Project has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000-years ago.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cde0.title: At least 37 killed by toxic fumes during alleged petrol theft in Nigeria, reports say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cde0.text:
At least 37 people have died after inhaling toxic fumes while allegedly stealing petrol from a pipeline in Nigeria's Rivers State, an environmental group in the oil-rich region says.

Many are still missing after more than 100 people descended on Okari Jetty in Okrika in small boats to collect the refined fuel under cover of darkness, according to the Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC).

The police told the BBC an investigation was ongoing to determine the figures of those affected after people reportedly collapsed - with local reports saying some fell into the Bonny River while others were taken to hospital.

Theft from pipelines has been a problem for decades in Nigeria's oil hub.

Rivers is one of several states that make up the southern Niger Delta region, a vast area of swamps and wetlands with huge reserves of oil and gas along Nigeria's coast.

For years, criminal groups have tapped pipelines and siphon crude oil or other petroleum products into boats and storage tanks, to be sold on the black market or taken to illegal refineries.

The YEAC said its network of volunteers and human rights defenders had reported that people in Okrika had died after inhaling what it locally known as "Indorama fuel", which is a form of refined petrol known as PMS (Premium Motor Spirit).

Nigeria's Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) has urged the public and media to rely on verified information as they work with other security agencies to establish what happened in the early hours of Thursday morning.

It condemned illegal tapping and siphoning, warning that such activities put lives, the environment and the economy at risk.

Similarly, many campaigners have also blamed the practice for contributing to environmental damage.

The government has stepped up operations against oil theft in recent years.

On Thursday, the director of navel information, Capt Abiodun Folorunsho, warned thieves there was "no hiding place" from the navy, which patrols the waterways and coastal areas of the Niger Delta.

"Their days are numbered, and if we catch you, of course, we'll ensure that you face the law," he said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Channels TV.

While the Nigerian navy has increased maritime security operations, the military and other security agencies have carried out operations against oil thieves, who often hid out in the area's dense mangrove forests.

Nigeria is trying to increase oil production after years of problems caused by theft, insecurity and underinvestment.

The country aims to raise production to about three million barrels per day by 2030 and is relying on better security and reforms to attract new investment.

Police say they are investigating the deaths of 37 people who died after inhaling toxic fumes. Rivers is one of several states that make up the southern Niger Delta region.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly4.title: Is a whale fossil the leftovers of a Bronze Age Sunday roast?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly4.text:
The head of a whale, believed to date back to the Bronze Age, has been discovered buried on a beach in Islandmagee.

A 10-year-old boy was out looking for fossils along the shore when he spotted the back of the skull protruding from a bank of earth - but could the fossil be the remnants of a prehistoric Sunday roast?

The find has been described as a totally unique, with geologists and marine specialists trying to establish the fossil's story and the Natural History Museum in London helping to identify it.

It was found on the same beach where Ireland's only dinosaur bones were discovered in the late 19th Century and the 1980s.

Ten-year-old George was out on a walk at Portmuck Harbour with his parents when he spotted something unusual.

"It was just the weird patterns on it," he told BBC News NI.

"The bits that stuck out, it just didn't look like a rock. I thought it was a bone, but I just wasn't too sure. So I asked my dad and he said it was definitely a fossil."

This fossilised hunk of whale bone has lain hidden in the earth on Portmuck Beach for possibly millennia.

Only the back of the head was visible to George, invisible for centuries was the beak, which was about a foot long when excavated.

Katy McMonagle, one of the archaeologists who dug the whale head out, said the fossil was difficult to move and very heavy.

She said it was now in a warehouse in Belfast and there could be a week of cleaning work involved.

"There will be painstaking work in cleaning the fossil and preparing it for a marine specialist who will be able to find out more about the creature."

The process of discovering exactly how old it is may take some time, but flint tools, excavated with the fossil, suggest it could have been buried in Islandmagee as many as 3,000 years ago.

George said it had been overwhelming.

"Yeah, that's really hard to imagine. To think about what it looked like, what it was, what it sounded like. We have a bit of an idea, but we're not 100% sure yet.

"It's been so cool, it shows you what you can find and then to see what happens after you find something - what the experts do with it, how they figure it out, how they do that."

There are secrets and stories held within the remains of this majestic creature.

Geologist Ian Enlander works with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group.

When he got the call to go down to the beach and see the fossil before it was moved he said he was very excited.

"I think it is going to turn out to be unique, a once in a lifetime thing."

Enlander took images of a well preserved part of the whale's ear, which may also be useful for carbon dating, and sent photographs to the Natural History Museum in London.

"The keeper of Mammalian Zoology there was very gracious and kind enough to get back to me the following day. They confirmed that it is a beaked whale, and the likelihood is that it's a species called Cuvier's beaked whale.

"So to put that into some sort of context, all the beaked whales are deep water, offshore species, by and large. If they do come inshore, it's usually because they're ill or already dead."

Enlander said finding "a buried skull, without any other bone present" presented a problem in trying to discern what happened.

"I've seen beaked whales in the Azores. I've seen them at the Bay of Biscay. I've never seen them around Ireland. They've never been recorded in this area. So how did it get here?"

Enlander added that the fossil "could be 3000 years old".

"It looks as if it has been handled, perhaps deliberately buried. I suppose the great wish would be that the archaeologists examine the skull and find evidence of butcher marks, that Bronze Age people have been there, trying to decapitate it and utilising the rest of the body perhaps as Sunday roast.

"And then for whatever reason, preserving the skull."

With the Natural History Museum now involved it's hoped this find will be of huge value.

For George, it's been quite the experience, and he has some advice for other budding archaeologists.

"Just keep your eyes open and see, you might find something good as well. Be curious. You never know what might happen."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3r.title: Renewable energy in NI reaches record level
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3r.text:
More than half (53%) of Northern Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in the year to June – beating the level previously set in 2022.

And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January.

Even when imported electricity was taken into account, the amount of renewables equalled the previous record of 50%, set in 2022/23.

The Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the increasing level of renewable energy would help Northern Ireland "move away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices" .

Almost three-quarters (74%) of renewable electricity came from wind. Bioenergy – anaerobic digestion, incineration and fermentation – provided just under one-fifth (18%).

Solar energy provided 6%, landfill gas provided 1%, and hydro/tidal generation provided 1%.

Northern Ireland has a target of generating 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030.

The increase to 53% to June 2026 follows several years of reduced renewable generation.

Lower levels can be due to weather conditions.

There is also a high rate of dispatch down in Northern Ireland – when turbines are switched off because there is not enough demand for the power being generated.

That is to protect the grid which has a limit on the amount of renewable energy it can carry due to fluctuations.

But moving to more renewable energy is a critical part of the journey to net zero and the transition from fossil fuels.

The minister said the rising cost of fossil fuels globally was "impacting negatively" on both businesses and households, particularly those with lower incomes.

She added that increased levels of renewable electricity "move us away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices for the electricity we use".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyj.title: From 'dog fruit' to darling: India's avocado boom
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyj.text:
Fifteen years ago there was almost no market for avocados in India, remembers Madhu Bopaiah.

Ripe fruit would fall off trees and be eaten by dogs, earning avocados the unappetising name dog fruit, he says.

Bopaiah has been working in India's plantation industry for 26 years, he's currently group manager at Cottanad Plantations, which grows cocoa, rubber, coffee, spices and fruits, including avocado, in the hills of Wayanad in the southern Indian state of Kerala.

"We never planted avocado as our main crop. We introduced it as a shade tree for coffee plantations, and only later realised it could become a profitable business," he says.

He says the turning point was around 2011 when Bollywood star Shilpa Shetty said she used avocado for skincare.

"Overnight, prices doubled and then kept rising," he says.

Cottanad has responded to that demand by planting avocado trees on 40 acres. Last year they harvested between 10 and 15 tonnes of fruit. In three of four years time they hope to raise that to 40 to 50 tonnes.

There's been a lot to learn.

"We completely changed the way we grow avocados after learning from South African experts. Today we use raised beds, wider spacing and different planting methods because avocado roots are highly vulnerable to diseases," Bopaiah says.

There's plenty of scope for Indian farmers to step-up production.

"When we studied the market, we found a huge gap between demand and supply. India imports around 15,000 tonnes of avocados every year, while domestic production is only about 8,000–9,000 tonnes," says Manilal Palliyath who helps promote India's avocado industry.

He sees a big opportunity for farmers, particularly as traditional crops have suffered.

"Coffee and pepper have suffered because of changing climatic conditions, making diversification essential for farmers."

While demand is growing in India, it's not always for locally grown fruit.

"Indian-grown avocados are improving and there are some great farmers working with local varieties, but the quality and availability can vary significantly depending on the season and region," says Hussain Shahzad, the executive chef at Hunger Inc. Hospitality.

The group owns four restaurants in Mumbai, including Veronica's and The Bombay Canteen.

"We have explored different varieties of avocados available in India, but the imported ones currently offer the consistency we need in terms of flavour, texture, size, and ripening," he says

But like many in the catering industry, he would like to source ingredients locally.

"We are always interested in exploring better local produce as it evolves. Supporting Indian agriculture and working with indigenous ingredients is central to how we approach food."

Matching the quality and consistency of imported fruit is the goal of some Indian entrepreneurs.

Harshit Godha is the founder of Indo-Israel Avocado Nursery in Bhopal, in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh.

He founded the nursery business in 2021, after spending a month in Israel learning about the industry.

Since then, business has been brisk. Over the last five years Godha has supplied around 18,000 avocado plants to farmers across India.

All of the saplings are international varieties like Hass and Pinkerton.

"Israel grows avocados on approximately 13,000 hectares - a small country with almost no rainfall for eight months of the year. This is precisely why Israeli avocado technology is the most advanced in the world," Godha says.

Getting a commercial orchard up and running is not easy. It is a very different operation from the traditional way of cultivating avocados in India, where they were planted among other crops for shade.

For a start, you can't just grow a tree from seed. A commercial tree comprises a rootstock, chosen for its tolerance to local conditions, grafted to the upper half which determines what sort of fruit is produced.

Once that's done the trees need a lot of attention.

"When you put in a professional orchard, you have to know the techniques of pruning. A tree can grow up to 25 feet within six to seven years, and harvesting at 25 feet is next to impossible," Godha says.

"Aggressive" pruning is needed to keep the harvest at a height that's convenient for workers.

On top of that an avocado tree cannot easily pollinate itself. To get fruit two different varieties of avocado trees have to be planted right next to each other. One variety needs to be open as a female at the exact same time the other variety is releasing pollen as a male."

"If a farmer gets this planting ratio wrong, the trees will fail to produce fruit, no matter how advanced the irrigation tech is. This single botanical detail is what separates a highly profitable, high-yielding orchard from one that looks great on paper but fails in reality," says Godha.

Using popular foreign varieties is one way of modernising India's avocado industry. Another is improving trees that have in India for generations.

"The biggest issue with the avocado trees in India are that every backyard tree is genetically different," says Dr Ganeshan Karunakaran, the principal scientist at the ICAR-Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru.

"That is why Indian markets are flooded with mixed fruit of varying quality. Standard varieties are essential if we want a reliable commercial market."

For 25 years he has been working on a breeding project which has released two varieties, based on local trees.

"Our objective is to provide farmers with uniform, high-yielding, good-quality planting material rather than thousands of different unnamed trees," Karunakaran says.

He is also concerned about unregulated nurseries selling unidentified, or diseased plants.

"Farmers may unknowingly buy diseased plants. The trees may look healthy initially, but after five or seven years they can suddenly die, causing huge financial losses," he says.

Despite the challenges, farmers see the potential in switching to avocado cultivation.

Shiju Sebastian was an early adopter. Eight years ago he dedicated two acres of his farm in Wayanad Kerala, to the crop.

"Farmers are willing to grow avocados, but they need proper guidance and assured markets," he says.

This year he's harvesting 3,500kg of the fruit, all of which is sold in the city of Bengalaru.

"Avocado will never fail you. It's such a loving and lovable fruit. I have fallen in love with this fruit now. I'm planning to plant another three acres — only avocado."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crer.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing spotted back above Scottish coast
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crer.text:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".

The bird, affectionately nicknamed Kinky because of the kink in its broken wing, was nursed back to health by its two, unusually caring parents.

In an unprecedented display of extended parenting, the two white-tailed parents skipped a year's breeding season to continue to tend to their year-old offspring.

This latest sighting, though, reveals that the bird survived his first winter alone.

The bird was photographed flying over Loch Spelve, a sea loch on the south-east coast of Mull.

Dave Sexton said: "I'm in awe of this bird!"

But the next phase of its life - which he described as a "sub-adult" could be dangerous.

"He'll no longer be tolerated as an immature by established adult pairs and might well come in for some 'you're not welcome here' behaviour, which can be pretty severe sometimes.

"But Kinky's a born survivor; I'm keeping everything crossed for him," he said.

Sea eagles, also known as white tailed eagles, were hunted to extinction in the UK and the UK's last native white-tailed eagle was shot in Shetland back in 1918, according to the charity.

A reintroduction project was started in Scotland in 1975 and the birds have now become established as a self-sustaining population. They returned to the Isle of Mull in the 1980s.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36l.title: 'River is flowing better than it has for 25 years'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36l.text:
A river is flowing better than it has for a quarter of a century after a major restoration but the next stage of works will be "really critical", according to a parish councillor.

Water levels in the River Deben in Suffolk dropped by more than a metre after heavy rain caused a weir structure at Ufford, near Woodbridge, to fall away and a bridge to partially collapse.

While they are still to be fixed, water in the river is again running freely after a multi-agency and community effort saw vital excavations and tree removal take place.

Councillor David Finley, river warden at Ufford Parish Council, said it was a "really exciting moment to actually see the water flowing" again.

"This section of the river used to be cleaned out every five to 10 years, so it's not been like this for 25 years," he said.

"Now, you can see gravel bits and silt bits, and so it's actually creating a really potentially dynamic river."

The collapse in April caused a water-filled crater known as Ufford Hole to drain on to surrounding land, including on a side channel towards the East Suffolk railway line.

It happened after tree roots grew into the weir, which subsequently "fell to pieces", Finley said, resulting in "all the water" rushing towards the Hawkeswade/Lower Ufford Bridge which "cracked" it.

The Essex & Suffolk Rivers Trust said it caused "significant damage to habitats along a large stretch of the river".

A wooden walkway next to the bridge, which allows people to follow a footpath on the river bank, had to be closed off and it is still awaiting repair.

Trevor Gill, from the Lower Deben Riparian Owners Group, said the collapse had a detrimental effect on biodiversity.

"It had a really big impact on nature, but also on people who love this, people who've been fishing and swimming here for decades," he said.

"People were worried about fish dying, which did happen, and it was pretty barren.

"What we've done so far shows people that we are here to get behind this problem and fix it."

After the incident, councils and a consortium of landowners and farmers worked with the Environment Agency and others to form an action plan.

The first phase of that focused on clearing the dried-out channel from Old Melton Mill to Ufford Hole to allow water to flow back to the mill.

Now that has been achieved, attention has turned to repairing the weir before the "winter flood" and also the footpath to restore access.

"The really critical bit is getting this weir sorted out so the water doesn't just accelerate the channel and create real problems further down the river," Finley said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.title: Site investigated over medical waste dumping claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text:
Land that borders a protected nature site is being investigated over claims it is being used as an illegal site to dump medical waste.

The Environment Agency (EA) said it was investigating the site off Mill Lane, near Wadborough, in Worcestershire. The land is near Great Blaythorn Meadow, which is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI).

A resident in the area, who asked not to be named, told the BBC a muck spreader, which are normally used to distribute farmyard manure, had been used to spread medical waste.

The EA said it was investigating alongside West Mercia Police, Wychavon District Council and Worcestershire County Council.

An EA spokesperson said: "Waste crime scars communities and the environment and, in line with our 10-point plan, we're acting quickly to tackle illegal activity."

The resident said they were concerned by how close the site was in relation to Great Blaythorn Meadow, which Natural England lists as an SSSI.

Natural England considers the land special for its biological interest, specifically wanting to protect its rare lowland meadow and grassland habitat.

The resident claimed "local residents of Wadborough and Drakes Broughton had identified some of the spread waste as medical in origin" and "estimated that 300 tonnes of contaminated waste has been spread on the field".

However, the EA has not confirmed the nature of the waste or how much waste has been dumped.

Photos said to be taken at the scene show small scraps of metal and plastic scattered across the area which is under investigation.

In December 2025, the BBC revealed a site off Mill Lane was under investigation for illegal waste dumping.

At the time, it became the third site in Worcestershire being investigated for illegal waste dumping.

The others sites were Stone Arrow Farm, Peopleton and Haselor Lane, Evesham.

The EA said it was "pulling every lever available" to "disrupt those who profit from the harm illegal waste sites cause".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.title: Wildlife and access boost planned for city park
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.text:
Work is due to start improving access and habitats for wildlife at a nature park in Coventry.

Longford Nature Park is a small reserve which the city council has designated as being of high importance to the city.

The improvements will include a new boardwalk across muddy parts of the park, litter-picking and the creation of shallow wetland habitats.

The work is being funded through Section 106 money, paid by developers to councils for major development projects in the area.

Councillor Patricia Hetherton said the improvements would help protect the biodiversity already at the park and make it easier for people to get closer to nature.

"Green spaces like Longford Park play an important role in supporting our health and wellbeing," she added.

Longford Park, as well as being a nature reserve, also acts as a public path, connecting the Coventry Building Society Arena and the Coventry Canal.

The project will be delivered by the council's urban ranger team, working with volunteers from the Friends of Longfofd Park.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c770.title: Study to reveal more about Guernsey's wild ferrets
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c770.text:
The results of a year-long research project are expected to reveal more about Guernsey's wild ferret population than ever, project leaders have said.

Using money from the government's Strategy for Nature fund, La Société Guernesiaise has been tracking the animals by using specialist camera equipment.

The conservation charity said it plotted where devices should be located in areas where ferrets had been known to attack different wildlife, such as La Claire Mare Nature Reserve in St Peters, had taken thousands of photos and the pictures were now being examined.

La Société said it had been aware of the feral ferret population for some time, but "didn't know anything about them".

The charity was one of 11 local projects to be given funding from the Strategy for Nature last year, and applied for cash to buy 15 camera traps.

The traps were motion-activated and used to take photos or videos of wildlife and people without anyone having to be there to operate them, project leaders said.

Leah Cottell, who has been leading the study, said the process had been "incredibly time-consuming" but she had learned a lot.

"I knew that we had ferrets on the island, but we didn't really know anything about them," she told BBC Guernsey.

"They seem to like being around water sites because they like eating things like eggs, and so they'll go for the nests of ground-nesting birds."

However, despite the numbers, ferrets were not native to Guernsey, she added.

"They are an invasive species, and the feeling is that it's probably due to releases from domestic ferrets.

"They look like their polecat wild counterparts, so they have been out there for a very long time; or ferret owners in the 1980s might have let some go and over time it's expanded."

Cottell added it would take "months and months" to sift through all the photos, but the charity would write up a report of its findings.

The next round of Strategy for Nature funding is open, and people wishing to apply for money had until 25 October, fund bosses said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3eq.title: Hot summer helps group clear 'buckets' of lake litter
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3eq.text:
Volunteers in a north Shropshire town have been able to litter pick inside a prominent lake because its water levels have dropped due to the recent hot weather.

With this summer being the hottest and one of the driest on record, lakes and rivers across the country have been running low.

It has meant Ellesmere park ranger, Lee Fraser, has been able to go into the Mere with volunteers and pick out litter, such as bricks, pottery and mobile phones.

He said the team have already collected "five big bucket loads" of litter which he said "covered half the distance" of the town's promenade.

Fraser said this year they decided to collect litter by standing in the water, as it was easier to see what was in the water.

"We tried it last year from a boat, which when you stand on the bank, you can see all the bricks.

"Once in the water, on the boat, even if you are next to them and someone's shouting that it's right next to you, you cannot find it.

"There are quite a lot of bricks out on the side now already and we have only been at it less than an hour", he said.

He added that he thought it would take some time for the level of The Mere to recover.

"It will be quite a while [for it to recover] even with the heavy rains we have had," Fraser said.

"It is slightly deeper than it was the other week but not significantly, and over the surface of the Mere it takes quite a lot for it to get [back to normal.]

The Mere is also cared for by volunteers like local resident, Wendy Salter.

She has been part of the team for three years and said she has enjoyed volunteering to help her community.

"A lot of this rubbish comes from such a big area. [What we find] varies a lot. I also found a mobile phone last week", Salter added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: Shetland spaceport project secures £30m of UK government investment
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
The UK government has announced investment of £30m in SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland as part of a new national space strategy.

A spaceport spokesperson said the funding was a "hugely significant" vote of confidence and would unlock a further £30m of private investment.

Several companies hope to use SaxaVord in Unst, the northernmost point in the UK, as a launch site for small commercial rockets.

A government spokesperson said space was "an increasingly important domain" for keeping the country safe.

SaxaVord is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

The company said the £60m public-private investment package would be used to design and build a second hangar and two more launchpads.

Chief executive officer Scott Hammond said the funding would take the company to the next stage of its development.

"We are building the spaceport for the thousandth as much as the first launch," he said.

"We're trying to create a successful, safe and sustainable business. This is direct investment into Shetland."

Two German companies have signed launch agreements with the spaceport.

Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) is working towards its first vertical orbital test flight from UK soil. In August, SaxaVord paused plans for a test launch after RFA said it had "encountered an issue".

A five-week "launch window" had been due to begin, with temporary traffic restrictions introduced in the event of a flight attempt.

A second company, HyImpulse Technologies GmbH (HyImpulse), plans the second flight of its SR75 suborbital launch vehicle from Shetland this year.

The German firm recently secured investment of more than €50m (£43m).

Derek Harris, head of programmes at Space Scotland, said he was not concerned about the timescale of the launch, adding that the £30m investment was a "good starter".

"The technology is difficult to master but you would prefer it to be there and be reliable so if the timescale slips into next year, I do not see that as a failure," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

"I see that as a very well-maintained programme to make sure health and safety and reliability are at the forefront."

Harris said rain and storms could also impact the process and it was important to remain open minded.

He added: "It will take time and a lot of money but once it launches, the benefits it unlocks for Scotland and the UK will be amazing."

SaxaVord Spaceport has confirmed that it is in discussions with other companies.

The UK government said the new space strategy would "drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life".

Ministers said they wanted to create jobs and help Britain and its partners launch satellites without relying on countries "further afield".

The money for the Shetland project is part of a £148m investment across Europe which ministers said would help UK space technology firms secure more work.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said: "Scotland already builds more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and with a £30m UK government investment boost, SaxaVord is now poised to deliver up to three-quarters of the continent's orbital launch slots."

He added that defence, security and economic growth were at the heart of the plan.

Lise Kaae, chief executive of Heartland, which has a majority stake in SaxaVord Spaceport through its investment arm Wild Ventures, said: "We are very pleased to welcome the UK government as an investor and partner."

The investment is subject to due diligence and final sign-off.

Saxa Vord is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: Manx space group urges election candidates to back treaty
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
Candidates standing in the Isle of Man's general election have been sent letters asking them to back the island signing up to an international space treaty.

The Manx chapter of the Mars Society wants the island to become a signatory to the Artemis Accords, the framework for peaceful, transparent space exploration now backed by more than 70 nations, including the UK as a founding member.

The accords, launched by Nasa in 2020, are non-binding and require no parliamentary ratification, membership fee or financial contribution to sign.

Chapter leader Stuart Mullan said it was a "low-risk, high-visibility way" for the island to show ambition around space projects.

"Signing the Artemis Accords costs nothing and commits us to nothing beyond principles we already stand for," said Mullan.

"Joining the accords would put us on the map internationally and gives a real boost to the case for developing more STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] projects on the island."

The Isle of Man's Space Registry handles satellite filings for some major space operators.

"Nobody is suggesting the Isle of Man starts launching rockets," Mullan continued.

"All we ask is that candidates consider promoting the Isle of Man as an attractive base for STEM companies and businesses, the kind that bring skilled, well-paid jobs the Island badly needs right now.

"The space sector globally needs the same things the Island already provides for aircraft and shipping.

"Finance, legal services, tax expertise, insurance, and regulatory know-how. It would be a strange decision not to look seriously at whether the Isle of Man can capture a share of an industry that's growing this fast. We think it can."

Elon Musk's Space X company operates a satellite ground station on the island while satellite giants including SES, Inmarsat, Avanti and Telesat have all registered spacecraft through the Isle of Man's filing system.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: Scientists may have found first hint of dark matter
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
Scientists believe they may be one step closer to detecting dark matter for the first time, but the findings have not been verified by independent researchers.

Scientists from the University of Bristol were part of a two-year study to try and measure the invisible substance thought to make up over 85% of the universe.

Using a sensitive detector in an an underground laboratory in the US, the researchers saw an atom and mystery particle colliding.

Lead researcher physicist Dr Sam Eriksen said it could be "the first step in understanding dark matter as a particle", but further research could also reveal that the particle is not related to dark matter.

"Following a huge amount of scientific effort, this is incredibly exciting," the University of Bristol senior research associate added.

Although scientists have long been certain of the existence of dark matter, because it is invisible as it reflects no light.

While it is thought to make up the majority of mass in the universe, it has never been directly detected.

For two years, 250 scientists and engineers from 39 institutions spanning six countries, including two universities from the UK, have rigorously scrutinised data from one of the world's most sensitive dark matter detectors called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ).

It is managed by the US Department of Energy's Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota - the deepest laboratory in the US at nearly a mile beneath the ground.

To search for dark matter, LZ uses extremely sensitive light detectors to capture particle interactions.

The study found one particle interaction which could potentially have been caused by a Weakly Interacting Massive Particle, (WIMP), which scientists believe make up dark matter.

But there is currently low statistical evidence in it being a true breakthrough.

The findings were revealed at a conference in Japan on Tuesday, but the research has yet to undergo peer-review by other scientists.

The findings have been rated 2.6 sigma, which is the system that marks the statistical significance of discoveries. The normal threshold is five.

"With only one event, we don't want to get ahead of ourselves," said Professor Rick Gaitskell from Brown University.

"We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input."

Professor Henning Flaecher, an experimental particle physicist at the University of Bristol, said a "huge amount" of work had been carried out over "countless hours" to investigate any previously known reasons researchers might have observed the unusual reaction.

"To date none provide a convincing explanation," he said.

"It's an incredibly exciting time, the kind of event every astro-particle physicist dreams of, and we can't wait to analyse more data to see if additional candidate events appear."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyq.title: Toxic wildfire haze spreads across South East Asia as 'super' El Niño intensifies
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyq.text:
A blanket of toxic haze is enveloping parts of Indonesia and spreading into Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, as weeks-long wildfires continue to burn.

Millions of people across large swathes of South East Asia have been exposed to the smog, which in some areas has fuelled "acutely unhealthy" pollution more than 15 times the World Health Organization's recommended level.

Many of the ongoing fires have been burning across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo since mid-July – underpinned by a so-called Super El Niño that is exacerbating drought conditions.

Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires.

More than 12,000 of those cases are of children under the age of five.

Rizma Nur Fatimah, a 19-year-old teaching assistant at a school in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan, told the BBC that the smog in her classroom had become so thick "you couldn't even see your own feet".

"Even inside the house, with everything closed, the haze still got in," she said. "We've been living with this since I was born. It's the same every year, so we've almost become resigned to it. But this year is worse."

Misbah, a 23-year-old mother from nearby Pengayuan village, said her three-year-old daughter had developed "a cough, a sore throat and a runny nose" during the haze.

Some 1,300 kilometres away, in the Philippine island province of Palawan, residents reported similar symptoms, including itchy eyes, nose and throat.

"We are now experiencing mild headaches," said Dr Precious Bañas-Melad. "My cousin who isn't allergic to anything started developing allergies. My husband is the first one who had itchy eyes and throat."

Malaysia, meanwhile, has reported rising cases of asthma and conjunctivitis amid worsening air quality nationwide as smoke continues to drift across the border.

Indonesia's forest and peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.

Today, large-scale fires are often associated with the expansion of industrial plantations and other commercial land use. Environmental groups, researchers, and government investigations have repeatedly alleged that some companies use fire as a cheap and effective way to clear vast areas of land.

Some point out that while drought and El Niño conditions help fires spread, the severity of the haze is also linked to human activity. Drained peatlands, industrial timber estates and oil palm plantations can leave landscapes more vulnerable to burning, with fires often recurring in the same areas.

Unlike traditional practices, which are small-scale, community-managed, and closely monitored, fires linked to large-scale land development can be far more difficult to control and can cause environmental and public health impacts on a much larger scale.

What makes Indonesian Borneo's wildfires particularly worrying is that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.

Under normal conditions, these peatlands serve as gigantic carbon reservoirs. But under abnormal conditions, such as those currently hitting the region, they can become carbon "bombs".

"Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara.

"But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere."

Others have warned that as the current Super El Niño continues to escalate over the coming months, the fires could significantly worsen.

Last year, without El Niño, forest fires in Indonesia torched a 359,000-hectare area, says Professor Bambang Hero Saharjo, a forest fire forensics expert from Institut Pertanian Bogor University.

Citing research reports, Prof Bambang told the BBC that this year's El Niño could burn an area as large as 11 million hectares – putting it on par with one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons, which happened from 1997 to 1998.

Earlier this week, Indonesia's forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni told reporters that the battle to extinguish the current wildfires was entering a critical phase.

"Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño," he said earlier this week. "September is the main fight for us."

Many of the ongoing fires have been burning across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo since mid-July. The haze is blamed on a so-called Super El Niño that is exacerbating drought conditions.

The quest for Dark Matter just got interesting. Researchers on an international project called the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) Dark Matter Experiment reported they may have discovered the signature of a bit of Dark Matter passing through an underground mine in South Dakota. Kimberly Palladino, professor of physics at Oxford and a member of that LZ collaboration, speaks to Roland Pease to explain how dark matter is being detected.

Probiotics have long been all the rage in health advice, but this week we discovered they may also be good for corals. Microbiologist turned ecologist Erika Santoro has been testing a probiotic treatment on reefs in the Red Sea and joins us to divulge her findings.

We’re continuing with a tone of optimism with this week’s shortlisted book for the Royal Society’s coveted Trivedi Science Book Prize. Despite it All: A Handbook for Climate Hopefuls by veteran environmental journalist Fred Pearce, focuses on the progress humanity has made in protecting the planet.

Plus, mathematician Kit Yates is back, bringing us some of the week’s most exciting science news, including how we might use the earth's magnetic field to authenticate artefacts and a puzzling ten-sided cloud structure on Saturn's south pole.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.title: First dinosaur bone from Antarctica found in a drawer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.text:
An unassuming-looking fossil that spent 40 years lying forgotten in a drawer has turned out to be the first dinosaur bone ever found in Antarctica.

The specimen was unearthed in 1985, but the team that discovered it was not sure what it was - so it was stored away in the geology collection of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) in Cambridge.

Now the fossil has been studied by palaeontologists who have confirmed that it is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur - this group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.

The discovery helps to reveal more about how these beasts lived in a part of the world where the fossil record is sparse.

Dr Mark Evans, the collections manager at BAS, recently spotted the fossil amongst thousands of specimens brought back from expeditions to Antarctica over the decades.

"It's only when you start thinking 'what's in this drawer', that sometimes you come across something and you think, 'Ah, this looks interesting'," he said.

The specimen was originally collected on James Ross Island and its discovery was recorded in a field notebook kept by geologist Dr Mike Thomson.

Alongside a tiny, neat sketch of the fossil dated 9 December 1985 he has written "vertebra of large reptile", noting it was about 10cm wide.

Evans says the team that found it probably thought the fossil belonged to a marine reptile.

But as soon as he saw it, Evans realised the vertebra looked very dinosaur-like. And the date of its discovery meant it would have been the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent.

He called in Prof Paul Barrett from the Natural History Museum (NHM) to confirm his discovery.

"Although it's not too much to look at, it actually has a really distinctive shape," Barrett told us, holding the fossil in his hands.

He pointed to a hollow on one end of the fossil and then turned it over to reveal a rounded bump at the other. The vertebrae line up to create a series of ball-and-socket joints running from head to tail.

"As soon as I saw it, I knew what we were dealing with… it was a dead cert we were dealing with a Titanosaur," he said. "This is a combination of features that's completely unique to these types of dinosaurs."

More than 100 species of Titanosaur have now been identified around the world.

All are four-legged plant eaters, with very long necks that helped them reach up into trees and long counter-balancing tails. The very biggest Titanosaurs were more than 115ft (35m) long and weighed about 60 tonnes.

From the size of this tail bone, the scientists estimate the Antarctic Titanosaur was about 23ft (7m) in length.

"Maybe it was a juvenile dinosaur, or maybe it was a genuinely small one - one that was actually bucking the trend for the rest of the group as a smaller adult," explained Barrett.

This dinosaur would have lived 82 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period when Antarctica was very different from how it is today. It would have been covered in lush forest, providing ample food for the plant-eating beast.

The long-forgotten fossil now holds an important place in the history of exploration in Antarctica. Other dinosaur fossils have been found in this remote part of the world in the years after 1985 - but not very many.

Antarctica is a challenging place for palaeontologists to work and the ice conceals the prehistoric record in the rock beneath.

"It shows that an area that we now think is really uninhabitable was once actually very habitable and had this huge cast of characters living on it," explained Barrett.

"It's helping us to work out how they fitted into these broader ecosystems at the very bottom of the world about 80 million years ago."

A paper on the discovery has been published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.

This group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.text:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gr.title: Public opposed to disability benefit cuts, major survey suggests
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gr.text:
A survey suggests the public does not support cutting payments for disability benefits.

Research by the British Social Attitudes survey found 7% of respondents were in favour of reducing benefits for disabled people who cannot work.

Almost half of those who took part, 49%, said they supported more being spent on disability benefits, even if it led to higher taxes.

The authors noted that the timing of the interviews, just after the Starmer government had failed to reform PIP, meant it was "possible that people were particularly supportive of disability benefits at the time".

They cautioned that public attitudes to disability benefits "crucially depend on which disabled people are in the public's mind", referencing previous research which showed that "some types of disabled people are seen as 'deserving' by the public".

The findings come despite the proportion of those who support increasing welfare spending for the poor being at a near record low.

Labour, the Conservative party and Reform UK have all said there is a need to reduce the amount of money being spent on health and disability benefits, while the Liberal Democrats, Greens and SNP oppose reductions.

Efforts by Sir Keir Starmer to introduce cuts last year were opposed by many in his own party, forcing a government climbdown.

The proportion of GDP the UK spends on all welfare benefits for those of working age has remained broadly flat over the past 40 years, at just under 5%.

It has occasionally increased to over 5%, including in the 1990s, after the financial crisis in 2008, and during the Covid pandemic.

Despite that, the survey found that support for increasing welfare payments to help the poor was close to the lowest level the researchers have ever recorded.

Asked if "the government should spend more money on welfare benefits for the poor, even if it leads to higher taxes," 27% replied they should while 42% were opposed.

While wider welfare spending has, proportionately, remained stable, payments for disability benefits have taken up an increasing share of the total.

The latest figures show four million people in England and Wales are currently in receipt of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit.

Annual spending has increased sharply from £16.3bn in 2019/20 to £27.3bn in 2024/25, and is forecast to rise to more than £41bn by 2030.

But around half of those polled for the survey supported higher spending on disability benefits overall, while a majority also strongly backed extra payments for the costs of having a disability.

Around 83% of respondents supported additional payments to help with cooking, 80% for budgeting, and 78% for washing.

Just 3% replied that "nobody should get any additional money" for all three tasks.

Respondents were not asked if they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits.

"Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong," said Dr Robert de Vries from the University of Kent, who was one of the report's co-authors.

"Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum."

Proposals to reform PIP are due to be unveiled by the government in the autumn after an interim report published in the summer found the benefit was not fit for purpose.

Around 57% of Labour voters polled for the survey favoured more spending on disability benefits.

But there was broad political consensus that cuts would be wrong – just 5% of Labour voters, 7% of Conservatives and 11% of Reform UK backers said they supported cuts to those payments.

The British Social Attitudes survey, carried out by the National Centre for Social Research, has been gauging public opinion since 1983.

Its latest survey saw 4,656 interviews gathered between August and October 2025.

Almost half of those who took part said they supported more spending on disability benefits. But just 3% said they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlw.title: A&E did not get the basics right - my son's life was ruined at 32
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlw.text:
In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness.

He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis.

Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments.

Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history.

Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time.

Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him.

"The hospital didn't get the basics right and my son has paid a terrible price – it's ruined his life. It was an awful error. He trusted the health service and believed it was there to help him, not destroy him."

He says Oli's body is now twisted and paralysed and he has no ability to move around. His breathing, feeding and toileting are all done through tubes at the neurological rehabilitation centre where he is being cared for. He can only communicate through blinking, but Stephen believes he understands everything going on around him.

"There is no worse space for a human to occupy – it's a permanent living nightmare."

North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it.

In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused."

An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life.

"Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families."

She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures.

"There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A&E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death."

A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21.

It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550m last year.

Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed.

And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling.

But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts.

The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted.

The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years.

Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged.

RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering".

"This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing."

But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances.

NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes.

Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses.

NHS England said claim numbers were not a good measure of current safety because of the lag between the incident happening and claims being logged, adding there were signs A&E waiting times had started improving.

Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short".

For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying about his son.

"I know staff are under pressure," he says, "but this is about doing the basics right. They failed Oli."

Additional reporting Nat Wright
