https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.title: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, The World Today presenter was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

In a few cases, PV can develop into another type of blood cancer called myelofibrosis, and even more rarely can develop into a type of leukaemia called acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), according to charity Blood Cancer UK which funds research into blood cancers.

The mother-of-three said she has had to adjust to life with her condition, sometimes not being able to attend family occasions or play with her children because she is exhausted.

"It's the kind of fatigue that is not like I'm just tired and I didn't get a good night's sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference," she explains.

"Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don't know how I'm going to be in six months, one year, two years.

"People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it's something I always have to be aware of and make sure I mitigate."

Despite the fatigue, Moshiri has continued to travel across the world covering the biggest stories over the last two years for the BBC, anchoring from Qatar at the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, covering the selection of the new Pope from the Vatican and travelling to Greenland for Vice-President JD Vance's visit.

She credits her "supportive and helpful" husband Jonathan, management at the BBC and her children Iris, 13, Vivienne, 11 and Caspian, 9.

"It took me a long time to be able to tell them about this illness, because I don't want to worry them, but they have been so understanding. When I say things like 'mummy is too tired to play with you', they get it and they don't push it," she said.

Helen Rowntree, chief executive of Blood Cancer UK, said: "We're so grateful to Maryam for bravely sharing her story. When public figures speak openly about their diagnosis, it cuts through the silence that so often surrounds blood cancer – the UK's fifth most common cancer and third biggest cancer killer."

Rowntree said blood cancer can feel like a "silent" cancer as patients can present with vague, hard to spot symptoms, and highlighted that many with the disease manage their illness, treatment and side-effects alongside work and family life.

"We urgently need continued public and government support to fund the next generation of kinder, more effective treatments with fewer side-effects – so that more people with blood cancer can live well, spend less time dealing with the impact of treatment and be there for the moments that matter," she added.

"There is a lot of research going into blood cancer and scientific advancement to look forward to. Hopefully they'll be some sort of advancement that will help even more than these medications I've been given," Moshiri added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: How hunger for a new weight-loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.

But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.

The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.

But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.

Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.

Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street.

"The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe.

"It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."

One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.

Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.

The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy.

Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.

And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.

Eli Lilly's website carries a strong warning "no one should take anything claiming to be retatrutide outside of a Lilly-sponsored clinical trial".

"Illicit retatrutide products may contain unknown ingredients, harmful contaminants and impurities. These products may also have too much or too little active ingredient, or the wrong ingredient entirely".

Despite this, it seems there are plenty of people willing to take that gamble.

"Young fit patients are coming into hospital with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, in some cases kidney failure," says endocrinologist, Prof Donal O'Shea.

He says some personal trainers are not only supplying their clients with the drug, they are also injecting them with it.

"The patients have no idea how much they have been taking, or even what they've been injected with."

Tom Davies says he nearly ended up in hospital after accidentally overdosing on a fake version of retatrutide. He ordered it from a Chinese supplier after friends at his gym recommended it.

"It was horrendous," says the 20-year-old from Brighton. "My body felt so under pressure, I was so bloated, it was like someone had dropped a 20kg weight on my stomach.

"For 72 hours I had really bad diarrhoea and nausea. I thought, if this continues I'm going to end up in A&E."

Tom later realised he had given himself eight times the recommended dose. Depending on what is ordered, copycat retatrutide can arrive needing to be mixed with sterile, bacteriostatic water which requires various calculations.

Dr Nas Khattak, a research doctor based in Chester, has been screening patients for one of Eli Lilly's Phase III clinical trials. He says those sourcing fake versions are in effect behaving as lab rats without any medical oversight.

"If users who buy it online become their own doctor, they're taking a huge risk," he warns.

He says trial participants need to meet strict criteria before they are given the green light to start taking the real drug or a placebo.

"We request their GP record, we make sure that they're emotionally well. They'll have suicide, self-harm, mental health assessments - and this is all done by doctors.

"Then we come back and have a look at the blood tests, have a look at everything, and then we think whether they're suitable or not."

Tom decided to do more research into dosing and, despite the nasty side effects he'd previously experienced, decided to give his fake version of retatrutide another go. After nine months of taking it in cycles, he says his cravings for sugar and junk food have gone.

Pharmacist Shahid warns that just because a fake version of reta works for one person, does not mean it will "work for the next".

The obesity drugs currently on the market - the likes of semaglutide (marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy), and tirzepatide (marketed as Mounjaro) - target just one or two hormone receptors. But, if approved, retatrutide will become the first weight loss medication in the world to act on three, giving it the nickname the "triple G".

The three hormones it mimics are:

Lisa King has been taking a fake version of retatrutide since July and at one stage, while she was also going to the gym and eating healthily, she was losing 3kg (6lb) a week.

It's also, she believes, helping her manage some of the symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). GLP-1s help regulate blood sugar, and some studies suggest these weight-loss drugs can help with some of the problems caused by PMOS, which can bring about extreme tiredness, kidney problems and high blood pressure.

"I'm not sure if it's due to reta," Lisa says, "but my sugar cravings have gone down, my periods have regulated and I've got a lot more energy."

But retatrutide is still in trials. Does this bother her?

"No," she says, "not at all. There are many things that have not been approved.

"If I start to experience any negative side effects I'll just come straight off it."

Other users taking counterfeit versions of retatrutide have reported a range of issues including brain fog, nausea, diarrhoea, a loss of libido and no longer being able to feel any happiness or joy.

Doctors are becoming increasingly worried about the side effects they are seeing amongst users of these counterfeit weight-loss drugs.

Dr Sahira Dar, a GP and chair of the British Islamic Medical Association, says healthcare professionals should ask about black market products "without judgement", so patients feel able to "disclose what they have taken".

Eli Lilly has been developing retatrutide for nearly 10 years. It is now fighting to protect its product and curb the illegal sales which are taking place across the world.

It's taking action against peptide companies, influencers, compound pharmacies which manufacture the fake medication, and wellness clinics. It has reported more than 14,000 websites, advertisements and social media posts it says are illegally marketing the medication.

Eli Lilly says it "continues to work with law enforcement and regulatory authorities to combat black market drugs".

A spokesperson told the BBC: "Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."

The UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has carried out raids and made several seizures of "products claiming to contain retatrutide" over the past year.

It says there are a number of different routes these products enter the UK and it is working to "disrupt illegal importation and distribution".

But the sales continue.

Prof O'Shea says while we need to "shine a light on the dangers of such black market drugs", we should not "trash this family of medications".

"GLP-1s are a major advance in managing obesity, a major advance in our insight into how the brain regulates cravings and appetite.

"That," he says, "is huge".

For now, there is still a long way to go before retatrutide gets approval anywhere.

Eli Lilly plans to submit its application for US FDA approval early next year. It can take up to a year to carry out a review, so retatrutide would not be legally available in the US until the end of 2027 at the earliest.

In the UK, depending on the approval of the MHRA, it could be on the market by 2028.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c305.title: Transplanted pig kidney works in US man's body for record 271 days
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c305.text:
A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.

Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.

The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.

But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.

Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.

In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.

Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.

"I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.

But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".

"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

Pigs are seen as the ideal animal for xenotransplantation. Their organs are roughly the right size and there have been years of experience farming them.

But you cannot just pop down to the farm and take a kidney from a pig and put it into a person. The human body would immediately identify the organ as foreign and launch a devastating immune assault that would destroy the kidney. It would turn black in minutes as holes are ripped in every cell and the organ clots from the inside.

So researchers have developed Yucatan miniature pigs that have gone through 69 genomic modifications to "humanise" their organs.

These modifications strip out some features of pig cells that our immune system spots and attacks; add some human DNA that acts like camouflage netting to help hide the pig tissue from the immune system and further tweaks disable viruses that hide inside pig DNA to prevent infection.

Andrews had end stage kidney disease as a result of type 2 diabetes and his kidneys were failing.

He was 66 years old when he had the xenotransplant on January 25, 2025.

The transplanted pig kidney worked immediately, according to details just published in the Lancet medical journal.

The kidney continued to function for 271 days until it was removed in October that year. Tim then needed dialysis for 82 days until he had an organ from a donor in January of this year. That organ has been working well.

Dr Leonardo Riella, from the centre for transplantation sciences at Mass General Brigham said the shortage of organs available for transplant meant " we are in a crisis".

"We are working really hard to bring hope and we truly feel that xenotransplantation can be an alternative for patients who don't have a living donor where we could potentially bypass dialysis and get them to a transplant," he said.

There were early signs Andrews' organ was being rejected by the immune system, but that was successfully treated by adjusting his medication.

However, after around six months the blood vessels in the kidney started to become damaged and the organ inflamed and then it started to fail.

It is not clear exactly why as there were no signs of antibodies attacking the pig kidney.

In their Lancet write-up the doctors state: "This case illustrates both the promise and the remaining challenges of clinical kidney xenotransplantation."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5d.title: Children as young as six going to A&E in mental health crisis
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5d.text:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people - some as young as six - attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis - based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England - found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police - some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

Nicholas, a father-of-two, is someone who has seen the impact of this. His 10-year-old son has autism and suffers from mental health issues. It has caused a safety risk - he has attacked others and tried to jump out of windows.

He told BBC Your Voice: "There is no support when in crisis. GP won't prescribe anything. We are stuck on a children's mental health waiting list which is the only service who can provide interventions. The system is broken.

"When at A&E, half the time we don't see a doctor because you have to wait so long. Once my son calms down, it's best to go home rather than have him escalate again while waiting."

RCPCH officer for mental health Dr Sam Jones said there was a lack of support, particularly for those in crisis, in many parts of the country.

"Behind every one of these figures is a child or young person in distress and a family who didn't know where else to turn.

"Emergency departments are a vital safety net, but they were never designed to be a place where children in mental health crisis wait for days at time.

"This is a national crisis that will only get worse without urgent intervention."

She said alongside greater investment in children's mental health services, staff from key agencies across health, social care and education needed better training in helping children who are struggling with their mental health.

Gemma Byrne, of the mental health charity Mind, said: "A&E can be a frightening environment for anyone in mental health crisis, let alone a child. Making them spend more than 12 hours there is simply unacceptable.

"The current system, where many mental health services only provide support when young people are considered 'unwell enough' to qualify, clearly isn't working."

She said expanding the network of young future hubs, which bring together a range of support covering mental health, employment, sports and volunteering, was a crucial step.

The government is planning to publish a new mental health strategy later in the summer.

But a Department of Health and Social Care spokesman said improvements were already being made with investment in mental health teams for schools and more than 150 new mental health hubs in community locations such as banks and libraries.

"No child should have to reach crisis point before getting the support they need," he added.

Dr Mark Buchanan, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, said children and young people facing a mental health crisis were ending up in A&E by "default".

"They deserve care within systems and settings that are designed to meet their needs."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d3.title: Flu vaccine rollout begins as NHS regroups from 'busiest summer'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d3.text:
This winter's flu vaccine has been updated to protect against last year's subclade-K strain, with the first doses being given to schoolchildren and pregnant women.

Flu hit early last winter, with a new mutated version of the virus circulating

Schoolchildren are being prioritised - and like pregnant women can get the jab from Tuesday - because they can catch and spread flu easily. Protecting them also helps others, including baby brothers or sisters and grandparents.

Other eligible groups, including people aged 65 and over, can get a free NHS flu shot from October and should receive an invite by phone or post.

Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual with the new strain that some were calling Super flu.

Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.

Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.

This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.

It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.

Their flu season peaks in July or August. Australia has had fewer cases than last year, but New Zealand has seen high numbers.

Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious.

"Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said.

"With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever – and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."

Everyone is at risk of catching flu. It does not matter how fit and healthy you are, or your age.

Dr Doyle said: "Flu can really knock you for six, and for some children and pregnant women it can mean becoming seriously ill or ending up in hospital."

The vaccine cannot give you flu. Instead, it helps your body know how to fight the virus.

Children, from the age of two upwards, get a nasal spray version, while adults have an injection. A single dose is all that is needed to offer protection ahead of winter.

High Street pharmacies are offering NHS flu vaccines, along with GPs and schools. People who do not qualify for a free jab can pay about £10 to £20 for one.

Schoolchildren and pregnant women can get a free NHS flu vaccine from September onwards. You can get a free one from October if you:

More adults are also being offered another vaccine this winter to protect against RSV or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, which attacks the lungs.

From this September, adults will be invited to have the vaccine when they are 65, rather than waiting until 75, if they have certain pre-existing health conditions, such as chronic lung disease.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: Families hit by long waits for dementia diagnosis
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
Hundreds of families say they have had to wait months or even years for a dementia diagnosis for a loved one.

Such long delays have an impact on their own work, finances and mental health, a survey for the Alzheimer's Society charity reveals.

The charity is calling for a national standard that would mean someone with dementia would receive an accurate diagnosis within 18 weeks of being seen and referred by a GP.

That would put dementia on a similar footing as other major health conditions, including cancer.

Michael Fethon says his dad, Jim, waited 18 months from their initial appointment with a GP before being diagnosed.

It was a delay that took its toll on Jim - and on Michael, who eventually had to give up his job to care for his dad.

"I think my dad felt beside himself because he was experiencing symptoms. It wasn't just memory loss."

Michael says his father struggled to drive, shop and, eventually, even to walk.

"It almost spiralled in that 18 months of his condition, gradually getting worse.

"If we'd have had a diagnosis sooner, he could have started medication sooner, and whilst the medication doesn't cure dementia, it acts to sort of slow it down and eliminate the severity of it."

In the survey, more than a thousand families and carers of people living with dementia revealed that nearly half of them waited for more than six months for an accurate diagnosis after their first visit to a GP.

Michelle Dyson CB, of the Alzheimer's Society, says a diagnosis can really help families access support and plan for the future.

"Too many families spend months, and sometimes years, waiting for answers while their dementia progresses.

"It is like trying to plan a journey without knowing where you are going or when you will arrive.

"You would never accept someone being diagnosed with cancer and then left to work out the next steps on their own."

Dementia does not wait, and neither should diagnosis, she added.

Keith and Sue Andrews first met when they were 15, and they've been married for 57 years.

Sue's condition has deteriorated so much that she now lives in a home.

Keith says they had to wait almost a year for a diagnosis, which was difficult.

He says life became more maneagable, once they knew for sure.

"I won't say it's easy, but you know where you're going, and you know where you're heading and you feel a lot more confident in what you're doing.

"Because you know you're doing the right thing, but before that diagnosis, you don't know if you're doing the right thing or what to do even.

"And it's a horrible time, a horrible time."

Like Keith, 9 out of 10 families surveyed said that a formal diagnosis made at least one aspect of life easier.

That included understanding symptoms and behaviour, supporting the person living with dementia, accessing information or speaking to healthcare professionals.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said:

"This Government is determined to strengthen the support that is available both to individuals affected by dementia, and the family members who look after them.

"We are bringing forward the timetable for Baroness Casey's commission on reform of the social care system, and we are appointing a new dementia tsar to help lead our work in that area, as recommended by Baroness Casey."

"We are also implementing a new action plan for unpaid carers to ensure that they receive the support and recognition they deserve for the selfless work they do."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.summary: Alzheimer's Society survey reveals long delays have impact on families' work, finances and mental health. Charity is calling for a national standard that would mean someone with dementia would receive an accurate diagnosis within 18 weeks of being seen and referred by a GP.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr4.title: Urine test can spot more than nine in 10 bladder cancers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr4.text:
An at-home urine test that the NHS has been trialling can detect more than nine in ten cases of bladder cancer, latest findings show.

The study, published in European Urology Oncology, was led by the University of Birmingham and a diagnostics company Nonacus, and involved nearly 1,000 patients at seven hospitals in England and Scotland.

Researchers hope it could reduce the number of patients needing urgent, more invasive procedures, called cystoscopies, which involve inserting a small camera up the urethra and into the bladder.

If a larger trial is successful, it could mean tens of thousands of patients a year are spared these tests.

More than 300,000 cystoscopies are performed in the UK each year and there are significant waiting lists in some areas.

While the urine test is not a replacement for cystoscopies, it could help doctors identify patients at greater risk who should be prioritised for urgent ones rather than wait.

This NHS trial found that the Galeas urine test identified 92% of bladder cancer cases.

A negative result meant there was more than a 99% chance that the patient did not have bladder cancer.

It checks for any genetic material shed into the urine by bladder cancer and was originally developed by the University of Birmingham with funding from Cancer Research UK (CRUK).

It looks for more than 450 DNA mutations associated with bladder cancer across 23 genes.

Prof Richard Bryan, co-author of the study and from Birmingham University, said after spending years developing and evaluating the science, it was exciting to see "very promising early performance" in a large real-world patient population.

Under a licensing agreement, the test has been commercialised by Nonacus, which pays back part of the revenue to the University and CRUK.

Michelle Mitchell from CRUK said: "Too many people are waiting longer than they should for a bladder cancer diagnosis, and it's essential that we find ways to tackle this problem.

"It's early days for this test and further research is needed, but it's vital that we continue to find faster and less invasive ways to help diagnose or rule out cancer."

Bladder cancer is more common in men over the age of 60 and the main symptom is blood in your urine.

How serious bladder cancer is depends on how big the cancer is and whether it has spread elsewhere in the body.

Early detection and treatment of cancer saves lives.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr4.summary: Study was led by University of Birmingham and a diagnostics company Nonacus. It involved nearly 1,000 patients at seven hospitals in England and Scotland. Researchers hope it could reduce the number of patients needing urgent, more invasive procedures.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99d.title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99d.text:
Sleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield.

Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep.

While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder.

That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn.

So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep?

The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009.

Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.

These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score".

But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London.

"There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers."

Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients.

"I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.

Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds.

"It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it."

One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".

In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims".

"We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added.

Studies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate.

In one study from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score.

The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept.

The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times.

Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake.

This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago.

"I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC.

"I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things."

Her "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept.

"I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says.

The BBC has approached Garmin for comment.

Dr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping.

"The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures."

He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago.

Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says.

"If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99d.summary: Sleepmaxxing is a term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep. Doctors say some patients bring their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced they have a sleep disorder. The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.title: Off to Reading or Leeds? Here's your guide to festival make-up (without the toxins)
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.text:
Festival season is here - with Reading and Leeds taking place this weekend. So now's the time to perfect neon make-up.

Bright graphic eyeliner, vampy lips and holographic highlighter are some of this year's biggest beauty trends for the main stage.

But some of these make-up products, which are being sold by third-party sellers on online marketplaces such as TikTok Shop, can contain a host of toxic chemicals, warns the Chartered Trading Standards Institute.

So here's what to look out for – and how to stay safe while serving festival glam.

How to get the look: Dominic Skinner, make-up artist and judge on the hit BBC show Glow Up, came into the BBC's London offices to show us how to achieve the perfect festival look and make it dance and party-proof.

If you want colours to "pop", he says use a white eye pencil on the skin first and then press bright eyeshadows on top.

"It will make bold colours more intense, and last all night."

What to be aware of: Banned ingredients can cause bad rashes and allergic reactions, so check the label and avoid products that say they're "not for cosmetic use" - even if they say they're for the skin.

Also look out for banned colourants, like Solvent Yellow 172, CI 45161 (Basic Red 1:1) and CI 45174 (Basic Violet 11:1).

Be cautious of cheap products or sellers you've never heard of, says Skinner.

"There are some items that are UV reflective, glow-in-the-dark or neon that are made by cosmetics brands but are quietly labelled as a 'non-cosmetic paint'," he adds.

How to get the look: Fairycore-inspired make-up is in, which means sparkles, face gems and glitter.

Don't go for subtle, says Skinner. "The 'no make-up look' is gone. Clean girl is out!"

There's a child-like quality to festival make-up, he says, so embrace it - think playful colour and crystals.

To stand out, he suggests using glitter in hair partings or your shoulders.

"Personally, I say use gems as they're bigger and more impactful, plus you can peel them off at the end of night and reuse them in the morning."

What to be aware of: Skip near the eyes to avoid nasty scratches on your cornea, says the British Skin Foundation's Dr Emma Wedgeworth, and never use craft glitter.

Use biodegradable, eco-friendly products that are better for the environment and softer on the skin. Safe adhesives, like lash glue, will keep it in place.

How to get the look: Vogue says 2026 is all about juicy and blurred lips that play with texture more than colour. Think "your-lips-but-better", using stains and glosses.

InStyle magazine recommends dramatic, dark red vampy lips as a breakaway from summer-friendly pinks and peaches.

Use a liquid lip product, Skinner says, because it won't budge.

"You can do some drinking, you can do some snogging."

And he says leave that lip liner until last - it'll just "highlight how wonky your drawing skills are". Colour first, liner later.

What to be aware of: Whatever your look, don't share your balm or lipstick. That can spread nasty infections like cold sores.

Cross-contamination is real, and why make-up artists sanitise everything in between clients.

Use high-protection sunscreen - at least SPF 30 - as a base before the make-up and let it soak in like any primer, says Wedgeworth.

Skinner recommends matte or sweat-proof SPF to help your make-up last longer.

Reapply throughout the day, at least every two hours. Don't forget your hairline and any partings to protect your scalp.

Sprays let you layer over make-up, but can be difficult to apply thickly enough, so take shade breaks and bring a big hat for extra protection, says Wedgeworth.

How to get the look: Who, What, Wear says think about accessories - scarfs, crochet beanie caps or eye-catching hair clips, charms or cuffs.

InStyle suggests Mermaid waves or thin Baby Braids if your hair is long enough.

What to be aware of: If you want a colour change with a spray or dye, do a patch test first to check you are not allergic.

Put a small amount behind your ear or on your arm and wait 24 to 48 hours to check for a reaction, says Wedgeworth.

Skinner says you probably already own products that can give you a festival look.

"You just have to think creatively about how to play with it."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.summary: Make-up artist Dominic Skinner, judge on BBC show Glow Up, shows us how to get the look. He says you should be careful of cheap products or sellers you've never heard of.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.text:
I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.

A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.

With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.

This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.

Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital.

While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest £299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.

I will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders.

I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.

The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients.

My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.

Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it.

"While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."

However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".

As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.

Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

Mehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis.

"I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."

After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.

She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2.

Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise.

"I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"

But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".

Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one.

"I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."

After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden.

"But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.

Having felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.

As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.

A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.

I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS.

Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal College of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan.

But former health minister Steve Brine, who acts as an advisor to a preventative healthcare company, says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health".

"Change is afoot across the NHS - prevention is a huge policy area," Brine says. "We want to identify people's problems before they become patients, so these scans could well become a part of our future healthcare and primary care needs to adapt."

As for me? I was told my heart age was four years younger than my actual age, and on the whole, I was in tip-top health. But I've also learned a valuable lesson - that I could be more at risk of skin cancer because of my freckles.

So, thanks to my time in the scanner, I am now far more enthusiastic about lathering sunscreen all over my body - rather than only on my face.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.summary: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells. It is an immune system that attacks pancreatic cell cells, but it also shares traits with type 2. The condition can progress slowly and can be managed with diet and exercise.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x.title: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x.text:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

And can anything be done about it?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, in 1993 15% of those aged 16 and over in England were obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.

Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.

This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.

Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.

Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight".

"With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."

Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.

Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.

Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.

Reports estimate obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately £126bn per year, including £12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.

Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.

Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.

Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.

The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.

During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.

Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.

In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.

Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.

Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.

People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.

Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.

A new weight loss pill from Wegovy is now available to buy privately from High Street and online pharmacies in the UK - but is not yet on the NHS.

The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.

It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.

Earlier this year, England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.

He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.

Now the question is what do we want to learn?

Clarification 13 August: The original wording in our article about obesity rates amongst adults mirrored that used by the NHS and King's Fund. We changed this section to make it clearer to readers that the figures related to those aged 16 and over.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x.summary: In 2024, obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese. In 1993 15% of those aged 16 and over in England were obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyw.title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyw.text:
As temperatures exceed 30C (86F) in some parts of the UK this week, the last thing people want to do is turn on the oven.

Not only can cooking in hot weather feel like a chore, but many of us find ourselves feeling less hungry altogether.

So when the heat gets too much, should we consider changing our diet?

Here are three things to think about next time you're hot and hungry.

"There's no need for more protein in a heatwave," says Aisling Daly, senior lecturer in nutrition at Oxford Brookes University.

But if you fancy it, some of the most common proteins will need cooking (like meat, chicken and fish) and that can be off-putting in the heat. Even an outdoor BBQ can be too hot to handle.

Enter the air fryer. Cooking a chicken leg in the worktop device uses less than half the energy of a conventional oven, according to Radio 4's Sliced Bread. And because they are smaller and speedier, they also pump less heat into your kitchen.

But experts say don't forget about your slightly less fashionable slow cooker - likely buried in the back of your cupboard. Even though they run for longer, they're typically more energy efficient and release even less heat than the air fryer.

The reality, though, is that simply by eating and digesting protein, our bodies produce more heat than other food groups.

That's due to the energy needed by the stomach, intestines and liver to break down and absorb these complex molecules.

So that steak you crave will only bring you out in a sweat.

But you can also get your protein from lentils, nuts, milk, tofu and cheese too.

To reduce body heat while still getting your protein fix, Dr Daly recommends focusing on things like bean salads, eggs, pre-cooked meats and plenty of Greek yoghurt (frozen too).

Making a smoothie by blending up fruit, veg and yogurt (while adding in peanut butter for protein) can provide a balanced, nutritious meal in an easy way.

And it might also be time to turn to some lighter fish, such as tuna, salmon or prawns.

When it's hot, we lose water when we sweat, so we need to replace it or we become dehydrated.

Six to eight glasses of fluid a day is normally recommended by the NHS, and in a heatwave you could need a lot more.

"There is no single amount that suits everyone, because how much fluid your body needs depends on lots of factors like your age, body size, activity levels and health status," says Dr Charlotte Mills, food and nutrition scientist at the University of Reading.

World Cup footballers aren't the only ones who benefit from hydration breaks: other athletes and pregnant and breastfeeding women are among those who need to drink more.

But rehydrating doesn't just mean refilling your water bottle every couple of hours.

"We need to eat our water as well as drink it," says Dr Daly, "80-90% of fruit and vegetables are full of water."

Cucumber, tomatoes, lettuce, celery, watermelon and strawberries all have very high water content, above 90%.

Apples, carrots, cooked broccoli and pears contain 80% to 89% water, as do oranges, grapes and pineapple.

In comparison, boiled eggs are 75% water, with digestive biscuits only 2.8% water. Even a cheese and tomato pizza is 38% water, with takeaway chips containing as much as 51%.

If your mouth has dried up just reading this, try some of these water-rich recipes.

A useful way to check if you're hydrated is to check the colour of your urine.

Pale yellow is what you're after.

If it's orangey or dark brown, that's a sign that your kidneys - which filter waste products and produce urine - are holding onto water because there isn't enough in the body.

That means you're dehydrated and need to drink more.

We know some people love a cuppa, even when it's sweltering, and that actually makes scientific sense.

Warm or room-temperature drinks are just as good as cold ones for cooling you down, says Dr Daly.

Research suggests your body sweats more quickly to get rid of the excess heat after a hot drink. After a cold drink, your body sweats more slowly. Your body is trying to keep your core temperature steady at about 37 degrees celsius.

So hot tea won't necessarily help you cool down more quickly - the key thing is to stay hydrated no matter the temperature of the liquid.

You don't need to shun your favourite coffee either just because it's hot - although too much caffeine can make the body produce more urine, and leave you dehydrated.

For matcha fans, the drink contains more caffeine than a cup of tea but less than a regular coffee.

Dr Daly says one or two coffees a day should make little difference to your hydration levels - but five or six will start to have an effect. Bear in mind that drinking alcohol also dehydrates.

You could structure your day differently too, and take a southern European approach to eating. Have an early breakfast, an afternoon siesta while it's very hot and then a late dinner. Bon appetit.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.title: New mums 'left to get on with it' as C-section numbers hit record high
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.text:
Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support" as the number of babies being born via caesarean reaches its highest rate on record.

A caesarean, or C-section, is a major operation to deliver a baby through a cut in the abdomen, usually just below the bikini line.

Carys Louise Brandon, from Swansea, had an emergency C-section to deliver her first child in 2022 and said she was completely unprepared for what came afterwards.

The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to her needs.

Latest figures show 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, with just over half of those operations being emergencies.

Carys' first baby was born in 2022.

After needing an emergency C-section, Carys, a content creator, said she had many unanswered questions about her recovery.

"I think I was thrown in at the deep end and I really didn't know how to deal with it," she said.

It was almost three weeks before the 29-year-old said she felt physically able to leave the house.

"And even then, I only walked up to the top of the street and back," she added.

Carys has since had two more caesareans and said each experience was very different.

Both times, she said the care she received in hospital and from her community midwife was good. But after getting home, she was left with questions about how her body should be recovering.

"You're thrown so into the deep end and there's no sort of, 'Oh, this is how your scar should look. This is quite normal for this sort of time'."

She recalled taking the dressing off her wound and fainting in the shower.

"I didn't know - should my scar be recovering in a certain way, should I really be feeling like this?

"There's just no support around the fact that after it, you're looking after a baby and recovering from major surgery, and everyone's recovery looks totally different."

She has shared her own experiences online in the hopes of helping other women, and said expectant mums often contact her for advice.

"I wish I'd had more stories that I could read to be a bit more informed before I gave birth that way."

The latest figures from the Welsh government showed that 42% of births in Wales were by caesarean section in 2025 - the highest rate on record - while in England around 45% of babies are delivered in this way.

According to the NHS, a caesarean may be recommended as a planned procedure or carried out in an emergency if a vaginal birth is considered to be too risky. Some women also choose to have a caesarean for non-medical reasons.

The health service's website states that most women can go home from hospital one or two days after a C-section, but that recovery is normally slower than from a vaginal birth.

A Welsh government report published in February highlighted the rapid increase in caesarean sections and inductions, saying the consequences for women, their families and the NHS had not been evaluated.

The report raised concerns about staffing and support across maternity services and said postnatal care was inadequately staffed and supported.

The Welsh government has committed to a three-year programme of improvements, but the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said maternity services had not kept pace with the changing picture.

Julie Richards, director of the RCM in Wales, said postnatal care for C-sections should include support with pain relief, wound care and surgical recovery, alongside help with feeding and caring for a new baby.

She said the rise in caesareans had changed the demands being placed on services.

"What we may not have had is the developments in maternity care to respond to the change in landscape for maternity services."

Ceri Ann Roberts, 29, from Gwynedd, said the care she received at Ysbyty Gwynedd after giving birth to her second child in 2025 had left her "traumatised".

Ceri Ann had an emergency C-section and her daughter, Ania, was taken to neonatal intensive care because she was not breathing.

Ceri Ann said she was then left alone on the recovery ward, unable to move.

"I just wanted to see my baby but I couldn't, and the staff told me there was no-one available to take me up to see her."

She said it was seven hours until she held her baby for the first time, and that was when her husband arrived back at the hospital and took her to the unit himself.

"It was awful, I just cried and cried," she said.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board said while it could not comment on individual cases, women recovering from C-sections while their babies are in special care are supported by midwives who provide updates on their baby's wellbeing and help to facilitate visits to see their babies as soon as they are medically able to do so.

It acknowledged that being separated from a baby following birth could be distressing and said its teams worked to facilitate contact "at the earliest safe opportunity".

Nicola Rous-Morgan is a pregnancy and postnatal yoga teacher and a trained midwife, who works with women recovering after childbirth, including those who have had C-sections.

She said women often tell her they feel left alone to manage their recovery by themselves.

"I think one of the biggest take-homes is they felt that once they had been discharged from hospital, upon coming home, that they were just left to get on with it."

She added: "The focus is on women who are recovering from vaginal delivery. It's not geared towards women who are recovering from major abdominal surgery."

Nicola said women should not have to rely on private services or social media to find basic recovery information.

"These things shouldn't be things that women have to pay for privately. What happens to the women that can't afford that luxury?"

The RCM said staffing pressures were one factor affecting the care available.

Richards said: "Our midwives are stretched, and quite often that is often impacted into the postnatal care, into the community settings."

The RCM surveyed its members in Wales in July, and 94% of respondents said they were not able to give the care they would like to give.

The organisation said midwives were working extra shifts and being moved to cover shortages elsewhere in maternity services.

Richards said more investment and a workforce plan was needed.

The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to their needs.

A spokesperson added: "Maternity teams provide postnatal assessment, advice and support following birth, and where required, women can be referred to specialist services including obstetric physiotherapy.

"Referrals are determined by individual clinical need to ensure women receive the most appropriate care to support their recovery and wellbeing.

"Recovery after birth matters, and where women tell us they have not felt listened to, supported or involved in decisions about their care, we expect services to learn from that feedback and act on it."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.summary: Welsh government says every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to her needs. 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, the highest rate on record.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjrx.title: Powerlifter wins golds despite endometriosis pain
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjrx.text:
A teenage powerlifter managed to win double golds at a world championship despite her endometriosis flaring up to leave her in excruciating pain just before the competition.

Lhamo Weston, from Redditch, also landed second on the podium with a silver and a bronze medal, across three events in the World Sub-Junior & Junior Powerlifting Championships, in South Africa last month.

The 18-year-old only took up the sport three years ago, after being inspired by her brother to give it a go.

Weston now uses social media to speak openly about having endometriosis and being a young woman in the sport of powerlifting, in the hope of empowering others.

Lhamo told the BBC she loves competing in the sport because of its inclusivity.

"I love how inclusive it is and how we're like a community," she said.

"Everyone knows each other and are really supportive of each other, and I just think it's an amazing sport that really brings people together."

She stood on the podium in the Under 57kg category at the championship after getting two golds in squat and deadlift, and a bronze in the bench event.

"It felt incredible to be completely honest, I went into it with expectations of potentially reaching podium. I didn't initially expect to place second or even have a chance at placing first," she said.

But a flare up of her endometriosis, a condition which sees tissue similar to the lining of the womb grow outside of it, meant she was competing in difficult conditions:

"That led to excruciating amounts of pain and a lot of issues again with making weight, which really affected me leading into comp," Lhamo continued.

"It can affect my training with the pain, I get quite tired and I also get back pain which can feel the same as a back injury. It was difficult but we managed to do it."

Endometriosis affects one in 10 women in the UK, but she says many people don't know about it.

"There's not enough awareness about it and how it actually impacts women and girls," she continued.

"I've been dealing with endometriosis since I was 12, and I only got diagnosed last year. It was a very long journey and I just think there needs to be more awareness so we can try and find solutions to help other people.

"As for powerlifting, if you want to do it, go for it. At the end of the day, there's nothing holding you back."

The teenager trains at Elite Fitness gym in Redditch and, despite recently moving to Worcester, still travels the 45 minutes to get there.

Sam Pope, who works there, says Lhamo is an inspiration.

"For other young people of her age, it just shows that actually if you put the effort in, the reward is there," he said.

"We take pride knowing we house her here as a member because we are very much like a family.

"To have her as a role model is very important because it does allow others to think 'I can do this as well' and I think that's very important not just at our gym but every gym as well."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjrx.summary: Lhamo Weston, 18, won double golds at a world powerlifting championship. She was diagnosed with endometriosis last year and has been in pain for years. The teenager now uses social media to speak openly about her condition.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.text:
A breast cancer survivor says she no longer lives "with the same fear" after a clinical trial enabled her to stop the heart medication she needed following cancer treatment.

Lucy Shepherd, from Hertfordshire, was diagnosed with triple positive breast cancer shortly after her 33rd birthday, but a routine scan revealed that her heart function had declined during care.

A new study, described as "hugely encouraging" for patients, has found the majority of breast cancer survivors whose treatment caused heart problems may not need to be on precautionary medication for life.

"Being part of the trial and having the chance to come off my heart medication has definitely improved my life," Shepherd said.

The trial - funded by the British Heart Foundation - involved 90 women in their 40s and 50s across four UK hospitals, whose hearts had recovered after a specific type of treatment for breast cancer.

Most would have been advised to stay on heart drugs for life over concerns heart function would decline if they stopped.

Researchers found that 98% of patients in the group who stopped taking medication had no change in heart function after one year, with just one woman developing a problem with her heart's pumping ability.

Women who came off drugs also reported, in questionnaires, a better quality of life.

Shepherd, now 39, said: "Living beyond my cancer treatment was difficult because no one could tell me whether I should stop or continue taking my heart medication.

"As I got fitter after my cancer treatment ended doctors gradually reduced my heart medication dosages, but I was still having side effects like a low heart rate and fatigue. I also had the mental burden of remembering to take them and the worry of what would happen if I missed a dose.

"I'm still taking hormone therapy, but I don't live with the same fear I once had. It has helped me to trust my body again - I feel strong and I know I can take on new challenges now."

Prof Charlotte Manisty, head of clinical cardiovascular science at University College London and consultant cardiologist at Barts Heart Centre and University College Hospitals London, led the trial, which is published in the Heart Journal.

"Modern breast cancer treatment is a remarkable success story," she said.

"But the damaging effects of these drugs on the heart leaves survivors and their doctors with difficult questions about ongoing treatment to maintain their heart health.

"Our study provides the first evidence that heart failure therapies can be safely stopped in survivors whose hearts have recovered, with the support of ongoing close monitoring.

"We hope these findings will be encouraging for survivors and their doctors, giving hope for a future free from treatment."

The women in the trial will continue to be followed up over the next five years to monitor their heart health.

But the researchers suggest their findings can start important conversations between survivors and their doctors about whether they need to continue treatment long-term.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, with nearly 60,000 new cases diagnosed each year, according to Cancer UK.

Approximately 15 to 20% of breast cancer cases are HER2-positive, meaning the breast cancer cells have higher than normal levels of a protein called HER2 on their surface.

In about 10% of cases, this treatment causes problems with heart function.

Survivors are currently advised to stay on these drugs for life, even after their cancer treatment ends and their heart recovers.

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, clinical director at the British Heart Foundation and consultant cardiologist, said: "These findings will be hugely encouraging for the thousands of breast cancer survivors whose heart health has been affected by lifesaving cancer treatment.

"The study results give hope that many women will be able to safely stop medicines once their heart has recovered."
