https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c23x.summary: Clothing Coventry provides pre-loved and donated clothing for free to families. Charity CEO Katie Wilson said parents were able to select items they needed. Average cost of a school uniform is estimated at £249.58 per child. More than 2,700 children were helped by the charity to prepare for the new school year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1dl.title: Cost of living on many minds ahead of Manx election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1dl.text:
Residents, businesses, and charities say they are feeling the pinch of rising costs, with many describing the economy as a key priority ahead of the Isle of Man general election.

Several independent shops in Ramsey said custom was down and running costs had become harder to manage, while the island's foodbank said demand for support had doubled in two years.

The Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce warned the Island faced "a very hard five years" ahead, citing a shrinking tax base and the recent loss of many high‑earning jobs.

Candidates have been urged to explain how they will fund their plans, support businesses, and reduce the pressures on working families.

Residents in Douglas said rising prices were affecting everyday life, with several describing the cost of living as their biggest concern ahead of the election.

Sharon Cox, from Douglas, said life was "not affordable.. especially for older people and vulnerable people".

Prices were rising "not just by pennies", but by "25 or 30 pence" each time she visited the shops, she added.

Mum-of-one Caitlin Gibson said she was living with her mum and struggled to save anything while caring for her young daughter.

She said: "I can't really afford to move out. I can't afford to save anything, so everything I earn, which is very little in the first place, is going on my baby."

Another Douglas resident, Andrew Cairns, said rising fuel and energy costs were having "a massive impact".

"Petrol is going up, electric, gas. You've only got to go in a shop a month apart and you can see the prices rising," he added.

He said it was something on his mind ahead of election, adding there was "a lot we can do to cut down our costs".

A number of businesses described the last few years as some of the hardest they had faced.

Tania Dolores, from Tania Dolores Shoes and Accessories, said: "Every day is a struggle. We are not making what we used to make."

She said her takings were "exactly the same amount of money as ten years ago", but that her bills were "much higher".

Amy Salter, from the Brunch cafe, said the cost of supplies and energy had changed how the family business operated.

When the business opened three years ago, it was "a lot easier than it is now", she said, adding that even small price rises in stock were having a big impact.

Linda Murphy, from Oma Sustainable Living, said footfall dropped sharply after government services were removed from the Post Office earlier this year.

She said she wanted to see in charge "somebody who understands and is looking out for small businesses, somebody who understands the value of the community, the high street and what it benefits".

Chairman of the Isle of Man Foodbank David Gawne said the third sector was also seeing the impact, and said the charity had become "something of a barometer" for the island's economic pressures.

"Two years ago, we were giving out 200 parcels a month. We're now giving out 400 parcels a month and we're pushing that boundary now," he said.

He explained that 80% of people it supported were working full time, but "not earning enough now to be able to support themselves or support their family".

Gawne said many families were living on a financial knife-edge.

"A lot of people are just one payday away from relying on the food bank… that is a reality for a lot of people."

He called for the next administration to prioritise the economy.

Business lobby group the Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce said the island was entering "a very hard five years" of economic challenges, warning that pressures on public finances and the loss of high‑earning jobs had created a difficult environment for both households and businesses.

She said that after decades of economic growth, the latest statistics released by government showed the economy had declined by 7.4% in the two years to March 2024.

And she added that in the last year, a thousand jobs had been lost in the export sector, which included financial, insurance, and manufacturing sectors.

She described the figures as "incredibly concerning", with the true impact of artificial intelligence on the workplace yet to be quantified.

Watterson called for an election focus on national issues rather than local.

"What we are voting for in September is our national government… how we are going to grow the Isle of Man economy and set us apart on an international stage," she said.

Read more stories from the Isle of Man on the BBC, watch BBC North West Tonight on BBC iPlayer and follow BBC Isle of Man on Facebook and X.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1dl.summary: Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce warns island faces "a very hard five years" ahead. Residents say rising prices are affecting everyday life and living costs are the biggest concern. Foodbank says demand for support has doubled in two years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e2.title: Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e2.text:
Joel has finally landed his first graduate engineering job after several years of lower‑paid roles. He's in his early 20s, lives with his parents and works in London. But instead of splashing the extra cash, or saving up for holidays or a house deposit, he's decided to squirrel more of it away into his workplace pension.

The reason? He doesn't think he'll get any kind of state pension. Like Joel, around half of Gen Z (those born from 1997–2012) say they don't expect the state pension to exist by the time they retire. It's pretty stark to hear, but growing up with constant headlines about an ageing population, a proportionally smaller working-age population, and the pressure that government finances are under, Joel thinks it's his generation that will suffer.

"I don't believe that I'll be a recipient of a state pension. I know a lot of people my age don't think they're going to be... There just won't be enough money," he says.

Retirement has always felt distant when you're in your 20s - something to think about later. But what's emerging among today's under‑30s is something different: not just distance, but doubt.

"It just mathematically doesn't make sense… There has to get to a point where that state pension is taking up too much of the budget and can't exist in the way that it exists right now," Joel says.

The state pension age is shifting. At the start of April, the age at which you receive it began to gradually creep up, rising from 66 years to 67 years by March 2028. It's due to go up again in 20 years' time to 68, though that might happen earlier as the government has an ongoing independent review.

That's a frustration for 27-year-old retail manager Connor, who got in touch via BBC Your Voice, because he says "the goalpost keeps moving". "At the minute I'll be 68 by the time I can retire, but I do think I'll be probably closer to 75, if I'm honest."

More than 13 million people - 19% of the population - are currently of state pension age. By 2050, even with the state pension age rising to 68, that group is projected to exceed 15 million people, nearly a quarter of the population, with numbers projected to climb towards 17 million by the 2070s. In other words, there will be lots more people qualifying for the state pension, and fewer working people, as a proportion, paying taxes into the pot to cover the bill.

At the same time, almost half of working‑age adults are not paying into a private pension pot. That means many will be relying solely on the state pension for their retirement income - and with relative poverty rates among pensioners now at 14%, we can already see how difficult that can be.

Experts warn that if a whole generation stops believing the state pension will be there, it could push people towards more risky investments, prompt overly restrictive behaviour, or lead others not to save at all.

So, are we heading towards a major pension crisis for many in Gen Z? And if we are, might the Gen Z generation end up redefining what retirement looks like?

For those hitting the state pension milestone today, as long as they've made 35 years of National Insurance contributions, they're entitled to £241.30 a week.

That amount rises each year to help people keep pace with rising living costs. Since 2011, pension increases have been guaranteed by the triple lock - which means the rise will either match the rate of inflation, average earnings or 2.5% - whichever is higher.

But in recent weeks, several organisations have called for the rules to be rewritten.

The centre-left Resolution Foundation think tank has argued for scrapping the triple lock, saying that continuing to prioritise the incomes of pensioners over working-age adults and children would be unfair.

Meanwhile, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI), a think tank set up by the former prime minister, takes things a step further and has called for the whole state pension to be scrapped and replaced with a new "Lifespan Fund". Thomas Smith, director of economic policy at the TBI, argued: "Britain's state pension system was built for a different era. We can't keep pouring money into a system that is increasingly unaffordable."

It suggests scrapping the triple lock and allowing people to access some of their state pension early if they need it because of redundancy and frequent job changes.

That's an idea that might appeal to Connor in Chesterfield. He's facing redundancy from his job at a global cosmetics firm, and the ability to draw down a small amount - effectively a withdrawal from his future state pension - might tide him through.

"There's not that many jobs out there at the minute, unfortunately. I still live at home with my parents luckily, but I pay board to them. I still have a car payment, I still have my insurance to pay."

But former pensions minister Steve Webb argues those changes would be "a huge backward step". He says the benefit of the current system is its simplicity which shouldn't be replaced with "something fiendishly complex and highly intrusive, which would take many decades to implement in full."

The government says it has committed to the triple lock for the rest of this parliament, and that the Pensions Commission, an independent body set up to review the regime for UK private pensions, is examining "how we can ensure secure retirements for tomorrow's pensioners".

It's likely that those in their 20s will not have a triple‑locked pension. That means living on the state pension alone will become more difficult, as its value may rise more slowly than the cost of food, travel, clothing and household bills.

For those who doubt the triple lock will endure, the debate often shifts to how the state pension can be sustained at all. One idea that regularly surfaces is means‑testing. In some ways it already is: very low‑income pensioners can receive an additional benefit called Pension Credit. But 24‑year‑old Joel believes that for the state pension to survive, the choices may need to be more radical.

"I don't think a means-tested state pension is necessarily a bad thing. But it would be a bad thing if it only applies to people in 50 years and not now when we should be saving some of that money."

Engineer Joel is one of life's squirrels. His fear about the future of the state pension means he's doubling-down on his private pension. He contacted BBC Your Voice because he feels that consecutive governments have sheltered current pensioners, leaving the consequences for his generation to face.

"I'm going to have to increase the amount of my paycheck that goes into a private pension, which obviously isn't good with cost of living through the roof," he says.

The scale of what younger workers may need to save adds to that anxiety for some. Investment company Rathbones estimates that a single person retiring today at 65 (with the state pension) may need around £796,000 in savings to fund a "comfortable retirement". If the state pension remains, a 25‑year‑old today would need a pot of around £1.68m to retire comfortably as a single person. Without the state pension, the figure for Gen Z jumps to more than £2.4m.

Against this backdrop, Joel says many of his friends are considering opting out of private and workplace pensions altogether and investing independently instead, mostly in "crypto or index funds and things like that.

"There's a sense, whether it's right or wrong, that that's more secure than putting it in a pension where they're also going to take a chip on top."

It's possible that individual investment choices could earn more than a pension scheme, but it's a big gamble.

Behavioural economics suggests that when people lose trust in a system, they tend to either opt out entirely or over‑compensate. Both can be problematic. Saving extra in a private pension may limit current life options, but opting out can leave many with riskier retirement savings, or indeed none at all.

In central Manchester, 23‑year‑old Ashleigh agrees with Joel that the state pension is unlikely to be coming her way: "At this rate I don't think anyone's ever going to retire, I think everyone will just have to fend for themselves in the end."

But as someone on a lower income, her pension choices are less squirrel‑like. When working for a big retailer, she says that she chose to stop contributing to her employer's auto-enrolment pension.

"I opted out of it. I need the money now." She explains: "I'd rather save for a house and then at least I have something to show for it".

Some experts warn that the gap between rich and poor in retirement could widen significantly for this generation.

Dr Suzy Morrissey, deputy director at the Pensions Policy Institute (PPI), believes that alongside how much Gen Z save privately, another factor will widen the divide: far more of them will be renting.

"Renting in retirement increases your chances of pensioner poverty, and they do face challenges to save, as younger people, that previous generations didn't face when they were at the same age," she says. "If we have people paying rent in retirement who don't have large pension pots to cover those expenses, then that equals higher risk of pensioner poverty."

But Morrissey sees a silver lining: pensions auto-enrollment, the system that automatically puts most employees into a workplace pension unless they opt out. If they've been employees, "they will have spent their working life contributing into a pension pot, and they will be the first generation that will have spent their whole life doing that."

It'll be a backstop for many, but the minimum contribution rate is unlikely to be enough for a comfortable retirement. It's not automatic for the self-employed and people like Ashleigh have opted out because of immediate financial pressures, so it looks like plenty won't see the benefit of that silver lining.

For some, the response to an uncertain future is to focus on the present.

Lauren, from Hull, says: "Money always comes back, time doesn't. The world is so vast, we shouldn't wait till the last 10/20 years of our lives to go out and see it!"

At 24, she's about to take six months off from her job as a business coordinator. She's one of a growing number planning to take regular career breaks, or "grown-up gap years", which many are terming "mini retirement". HSBC's 2025 UK survey found that 63% of Gen Z plan to take at least one mini‑retirement, compared with 32% of Gen X and 13% of Boomers.

"The majority of my friends don't pay into pensions and instead decide to take their whole wage [after taxes] and spend it how they see fit. A large proportion goes on travels or holidays," says Lauren.

"I currently don't pay into a pension, actually I never have. I'd way rather have my money now and use it to live life," she says.

But there's a warning for Gen Z from the experience of the Waspi women - hundreds of thousands born in the 1950s who campaigners say have suffered because of poorly communicated rises in the state pension age. Their financial shock shows that costs may only become clear when it's too late to course-correct.

If Gen Z's suspicions are right, and the state pension becomes a less dependable part of income in later life, then more will have to take a totally different approach to retirement, savings and life choices to navigate the new landscape.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d3.title: Reform UK would ban full-face coverings in public
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d3.text:
Reform UK has said it would ban face coverings in public places, including burkas and balaclavas, if it won power at the next election.

Writing in the Telegraph, party leader Nigel Farage said facial coverings were "not the British way" and undermined the trust needed for a "free and open society".

His comments come after protests over the weekend, described as spontaneous by police, when masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads in Dover.

On Monday, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said police had powers over coverings at protests but added: "When people are going about their daily business, it is absolutely fine to wear them for religious reasons, and that will continue."

In his article, Farage said he was "all for the protest" in Dover but added: "This is not the way to go about it."

Arguing for a wider ban, he wrote: "Around city centres, balaclava-clad youths tear around neighbourhoods on e-bikes and scooters, terrorising residents, making them feel unsafe in their own communities.

"We've some­how accep­ted that see­ing masked people in the streets is just part of mod­ern Bri­tain. It shouldn't be.

"Which is why Reform UK is calling for a ban on all full-face coverings in public spaces. No ifs, no buts. And yes, that includes religious ones too.

"This is not a matter of targeting one group. It's about saying that in a civilised society, people should be identifiable in pub­lic".

Labour's Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month's imprisonment, or both.

The power only only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests at the Dover demonstration and described it as a "spontaneous protest". The force has said "specific statutory requirements" needed to be met for a ban.

In a policy document, Reform said current policing powers on coverings were insufficient and that if elected it would pass legislation to authorise uniformed officers to remove items used to conceal someone's identity.

Failing to remove a face covering when asked by a police officer would be an offence, according to the document, unless the covering was worn for a work-related purpose.

Local councils England and Wales have the power to tackle anti-social behaviour through public spaces protection orders (PSPO) and on Monday, Nottingham Council said it was using an order to implement a face covering ban in the city centre

The Nottingham ban is aimed at people whom police believe are concealing their identity to commit a crime or anti-social behaviour.

It will not apply to face coverings worn for religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

Reform figures have previously expressed support for prohibiting face coverings in public, but it had not previously been adopted as the party's official position.

In February, the party's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said he "personally" supported a ban on "all face coverings in public".

Farage called for a ban on the burka and other face veils as far back as 2010, when he was a member of the European Parliament.

In 2025, he said the debate should be broader than just religious face coverings, and that a wider ban should be considered.

He said events he had attended had been targeted by masked protesters, and that he didn't believe "face coverings in public places make sense".

The burka is a veil worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body, often leaving a mesh screen to see through.

It is more concealing than the niqab, a face veil that leaves the area around the eyes clear, and hijab, a term that describes headscarves that in the West most commonly cover the head and neck but leave the face clear.

Several countries have introduced restrictions on where face coverings can be worn, including France, Denmark, Germany, Norway, Chad and Algeria.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr4.title: Some veterans to be called up to test UK's war resilience
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr4.text:
Some veterans will be mobilised as part of a major exercise next year testing the UK's resilience for war.

The government exercise will challenge the Ministry of Defence (MoD) "on a scale that we haven't seen for a very long time" on its reaction in the event of a conflict, armed forces minister Louise Sandher-Jones said.

The drill will involve an as-yet unspecified number of the British military's strategic reserve, which has an estimated 95,000 retired regular and reserve officers.

It forms part of a plan by the MoD for a "real step change" to use the strategic reserve more, following warnings of a workforce retention crisis.

Sandher-Jones is herself part of the strategic reserve, having previously served in the British Army as an intelligence officer before becoming an MP.

"Certainly when I left the Army and found out I was in the strategic reserve, I just filed it away and never thought about it again," she told the House of Lords national resilience committee on Monday.

"We are definitely no longer in that space - the strategic reserve is a real commitment for those who are in it, and they will be exercised as part of our exercise programme next year."

The exercise in 2027 will "go through measures to call out, to use and equip" procedures to mobilise retired troops at scale should it ever be needed, she added.

It comes after the chief of the defence staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, warned in January there was not an effective system of engaging them.

Earlier this year, ministers raised the age limit for the strategic reserve - which includes the Army, Navy and Royal Air Force - from 55 to 65 and lowered the threshold for them being called into service.

The government is under pressure to raise defence spending to 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of the decade, up from an estimated 2.4% last year, according to Nato figures.

A major government awareness campaign will also take place in the coming months to make the public more prepared for emergencies.

Briefings have suggested this could include stockpiling tinned food and bottled water in the event of extreme weather and cyber attacks.

Sandher-Jones praised Finland for "showing the way ahead" with Europe's largest civil defence exercise since World War Two, which saw more than 2,000 people take part in an underground sports hall earlier this week.

She also said young people would prove essential to the military's readiness for future threats.

She hinted a new military "gap year" for under-25s, announced in December and now recruiting its first 150 students until March 2027, could be scaled up faster if it proves successful.

She added that the military "has a role in combatting Neets", the official term for the one in eight young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training, by expanding cadets in schools.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.title: Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurt
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.text:
Police are seeking to identify protesters after several officers were injured and vehicles damaged in Portsmouth at a demonstration sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones told the House of Commons the disorder on Sunday night was "intimidating and thuggish" and warned "those who cross into illegality" would "face the full force of the law".

The protests followed a large group of masked men holding a demonstration over small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing major disruption.

Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had "serious questions to answer" over the decision to bring the migrants, who had crossed the English Channel from France, to shore in the area.

Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".

Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.

Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.

The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".

Footage shared online appeared to show protesters following the convoy of coaches along a motorway after it had left.

Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent.

In a statement to the House of Commons on Monday, the policing minister said: "Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy and it must be defended. But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference – and there can be no excuse for threatening behaviour or serious disruption."

Sarah Jones added: "Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated and those who cross the line from peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law."

Responding, shadow home secretary Chris Philp condemned the violence in Portsmouth but added: "This should also be a wake-up call for the government because it's not just those protesters in Dover and Portsmouth who feel so angry about large-scale illegal immigration.

"It is millions and millions of people up and down this country who feel angry as well."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country is on the edge of "serious civil disturbance" and called on protests to remain peaceful.

In a video posted to social media, he said: "Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution."

Between 1 January and 7 September 2026, a total of 17,281 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 8 September 2025 to 7 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, who represents Gosport near Portsmouth, accused the Home Office of failing to provide local officials with details of Sunday's protest.

"As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension," she said.

The Labour MP for Portsmouth North, Amanda Martin, said the "emergence" of the route across the Channel taken in Sunday's crossing was "deeply worrying for my city".

Some 625 migrants on eight boats were brought to shore at Dover and Portsmouth on Sunday, according to Home Office figures.

A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September - which is 43% lower than the same period the previous year.

UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012.

This weekend's disruption comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

But while the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

In August, a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

It is thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."

Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."

He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."

Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government.

He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."

Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman Zöe Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."

Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."

A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".

The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.

Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.

In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.

Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.

In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.

The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.

In July – just days before Burnham became prime minister – Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

The 14 areas where local government reorganisation is being paused while a review is carried out are:

The government said decisions had not yet been taken on Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, and West Sussex, with these areas being considered alongside the wider review.

Plans for 14 other areas to be reviewed and paused. Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.title: UK begins talks to rejoin EU security missions
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.text:
The UK is in talks over rejoining EU security missions, in a move that would further widen Labour's "reset" in relations with Europe.

The agreement under negotiation could see British officials and experts take part in civilian crisis management operations for the first time since Brexit.

EU is currently conducting 13 crisis management missions from a permanent HQ based in Brussels, as part of its common foreign and security policy.

They span efforts to train Somalian coastguards in tackling piracy, advise border police in Mali, and help Ukrainian prosecutors investigate war crime allegations.

Cybersecurity support to help countries protect themselves from hacking has been a priority area in recent years, with dedicated operations in Moldova and Armenia.

It is understood formal talks began in recent weeks, after EU ambassadors signed off their negotiating instructions for the EU diplomatic service in late July.

The two sides are already in talks for deals on food standards, electricity trading and a youth visa deal ahead of a delayed summit expected later this year.

The proposed "framework" deal with the UK would set the broad terms of future British participation. Individual operational agreements would be required for the UK to then join specific missions in future.

The deal was requested by the Starmer government in the wake of talks that began last year on how the two sides could best work together in "geographical areas of common interest".

The deal under discussion would not cover EU military crisis management missions, where officials have separately discussed options for co-operation.

The EU has struck framework deals with around 20 countries, although some are yet to contribute personnel to its civilian security missions. However, a deal with the UK would mark the first such agreement with a former EU member.

The agreements typically authorise the sharing of confidential information on missions and set out how countries can contribute towards shared costs.

Although non-EU contributors get a say on day-to-day management of missions, they are usually locked out of the initial political discussions where the overall goals and strategy for operations are decided.

As an EU member, Britain had a hand in developing the EU's common foreign policy but it was long regarded with suspicion by Eurosceptics, who regarded it as a rival to Nato or UN-led co-operation.

According to the European University Institute, the UK tended to contribute up to a few hundred personnel annually to both civilian and defence missions, fewer than larger EU members such as France and Germany.

The Cabinet Office said it would not comment on ongoing UK-EU negotiations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qx.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qx.text:
Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash.

"We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."

He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyk.title: Green Party deputy leader linked to property lets despite opposition to landlords
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyk.text:
The deputy leader of the Green Party, Mothin Ali, is linked to two buy-to-let properties, despite his party's opposition to private landlords.

Ali is the sole director of a company, which he set up and controls, that owns two rental properties in Leeds, bought in June 2022 and March 2025 - although he does not appear to profit from either of them.

The property purchases happened before the Greens adopted a policy committing to phasing out ownership of rental properties by private landlords in October 2025.

The Green Party told the BBC that, at the time Ali had set up the company, and since, he "has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities".

Ali's connection to the rental properties via real estate company MA Holdings, which purchased them with buy-to-let mortgages, was first reported by the Times newspaper.

Records held by Companies House show that Ali is the sole director of MA Holdings, incorporated in December 2021, and he is listed in the records as the sole person with significant control, owning more than 75% of the shares.

The company's business includes "buying and selling of own real estate", "letting and operating of own or leased real estate" and "management of real estate on a fee or contract basis".

The BBC has spoken to the previous owner and resident of the second property, who confirmed that Ali's company had purchased the property and believed it was bought with the intention to be let out.

Asked why MA Holdings owns the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson said: "We have provided deeply personal information to the BBC in confidence which shows that Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities.

"At Councillor Ali's request, we are not going to make this information public to protect his family."

The BBC is not publicising the personal information shared with it, at the request of the Greens, as it relates to private family matters.

In October last year, delegates to the Green Party's annual conference, passed a motion titled "Abolish landlords", headed "the private rental sector has failed, it is a vehicle for wealth extraction, funnelling money from renters to the landlord class".

The motion states: "The effective abolition of private landlordism and the private rented sector, coupled with the mass expansion of council housing, is the only way to end the housing crisis."

This is now official policy for the Green Party of England and Wales, with a plan to increase regulation and taxes on private rentals to make it difficult for landlords to make a profit, while boosting housebuilding by councils.

The policy would use existing Green policies such as imposing rent controls, ending buy-to-let mortgages and giving councils the right to buy a rental property when it is sold at a discounted price.

Asked whether Ali had sought to take any steps since the policy had been adopted to change anything with regard to the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson told the BBC he fully supported the policy.

"The policy does not literally seek to abolish landlords, but rather to put in more regulations and taxes on private rentals through measures such as rent controls and expanded social housing," they said. "All of which Mothin Ali supports."

When the policy was introduced, Green Party MP Carla Denyer told the BBC "while the motion to conference had an eye-catching name, it does not actually 'abolish' landlords".

"It does, however, address the housing crisis, empowers tenants and improves their wellbeing," she added.

"It contains a range of policies which, over time, would reduce the proportion of the housing market that is privately rented, and increase the proportion of socially rented homes."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.title: Protesters block roads in Portsmouth after 140 migrants arrive in boat
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text:
Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday night after around 140 migrants arrived in a single dinghy that had crossed the English Channel.

In the second major anti-migrant protest of the weekend, police faced off with demonstrators as they blocked roads in an effort to stop the people who had arrived on the boat from leaving the city.

Hampshire Police urged people to avoid the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were brought ashore, and said a dispersal order was in place, meaning anyone failing to comply could be arrested.

The government condemned "the intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of the protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore masks.

Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent.

Police carrying riot shields protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic.

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo – an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson – was livestreaming from the scene.

"Roads are all blocked, they are never going to be able to leave here," he said.

A government spokesperson said: "The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder."

"We thank the emergency services who are working to safely manage this situation."

The protest came after a large group of masked men held a demonstration over the small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing a major disruption.

Days earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September - which is 43% lower than the same period the previous year.

UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012.

Conservative MP for Isle of Wight East Joe Robertson said on X it was "extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west", given boats ordinarily land near Dover.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones told the BBC her primary concern was that Portsmouth did not become a "destination of choice for people traffickers".

"The government has invested heavily into Dover - the operation down there... is significant in terms of the holding centre, the processing, UK Border Force," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"We have hundreds of miles of coastline across southern England, and if Dover is no longer the destination of choice and instead there is going to be a spread across southern England, this is a significant issue for the government."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage posted on X: "This week Andy Burnham struck an agreement for 45 more officers on French beaches. Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. This is a joke. Only Reform will send the boats back."

The latest dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles from where they are commonly launched near Calais - making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

Between 1 January and 7 September 2026, a total of 17,281 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 8 September 2025 to 7 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

On Saturday, hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads near the Port of Dover and were heard chanting "stop the boats".

A council boss said police were slow to react to the "exceptionally well organised" protest.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

HOPE not Hate founder Nick Lowles criticised the policing response to the protests, asking: "How can you have 300, 400 people turn up in Dover at 07:00 on a Saturday morning and the police know nothing about it?"

He told the BBC on Monday that the protests had attracted "some of the more aggressive and more violent of the far-right activists from around the country" who had taken part in similar action in recent years, and said the government should go further in condemning them.

"We need to call these people out for their politics, and for the type of Britain that they want to see."

A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."

They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."

A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: "In response to a report on September 6 of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams.

"Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire Police and South Central Ambulance Service were also sent."

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

In August, a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

It is thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.summary: Hundreds of protesters blocked roads near Port of Dover on Saturday. Kent Police are yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cevw.title: Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cevw.text:
Scots should not have to travel further for health care under the government's plans to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two, John Swinney has suggested.

The BBC asked the first minister about the impact of such changes for people who are already travelling long distances - such as women living in the far north who have to travel 100 miles down the A9 to give birth in Inverness.

Swinney said it would "not be my intention" for people to travel further, with initial modelling showing the country divided into two east and west health boards.

He also said he could not put a "specific figure" on NHS job losses, but he had been "open about the fact that public sector employment will fall".

Speaking to BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show, Swinney said he wanted to maximise the number of health care services delivered locally as long as it was done safely.

This is so that there is "equity of access" regardless of where people live, he said.

Swinney added: "The example in Caithness is an issue about the delivery of maternity services in Caithness. And that's driven not by efficiencies, it's not by costs, it's delivered by the question of patient safety.

"What I want to make sure is that by removing health board boundaries we can maximise the number of local services that can be provided as close to home as possible for individuals in different parts of the country."

Patients and health care professionals have raised a number of concerns about the provision of paediatric and maternity care in Scotland.

A nine-month review of all maternity services was scheduled to begin this autumn after NHS staff and experts called for improvements to poor and sometimes deadly care as part of a BBC Disclosure investigation.

Meanwhile, all planned paediatric surgery at Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin was suspended last month because of concerns about patient safety. This could remain the case until December, according to NHS Grampian's chief executive.

The plan to cut health boards from 14 to two was announced in Swinney's programme for government earlier this week.

He said it was the "most significant structural reform in the NHS in the era of devolution".

But questions remain about how these two boards would work in practice and what the consequences would be for those living in the islands.

Work began on the proposal last November and maps the country into east and west, with the chief executives of NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde and NHS Lothian taking the lead.

It has been proposed that health care in the islands would be absorbed by local authorities, though no decisions have been made on this.

It is also unclear whether this new structure will result in financial savings by cutting senior roles or streamlining departments.

The trade union Unite branded the plan to cut health boards a "slash and burn programme for the NHS".

Swinney was asked several times by the BBC how many NHS jobs would be lost as a result of the changes.

He said: "I can't put a specific figure on that today and I simply wouldn't be giving a comprehensive answer if that was the case.

"What we've got to work our way through is a programme of reform to make sure that we put people right at the very centre of the delivery of public services so they can see the enhancement in the provision of those services in their localities."

The first minister would also not be drawn on how he would make savings to cover the potential £5bn shortfall in the public finances by the end of the decade.

He said there were "lots of variables" in public finances and that the SNP had demonstrated they could balance the budget through challenges including Brexit, the Covid pandemic and the financial crash.

Opponents have criticised Swinney's remarks and urged him to be clearer on how the plans would work.

Scottish Labour's acting leader Jackie Baillie said "It's hard to tell whether John Swinney is being evasive or simply has no idea what he is going to do, but either way it's not good enough.

"People's jobs are on the line and our public services could be plunged into chaos – Scotland deserves to know what lies ahead.

"The SNP must come clean about what it is planning, how many jobs are at risk and what it will mean for our public services."

Scottish Conservative finance and social security spokesman Craig Hoy said: "John Swinney was asked a basic question about his own plans and repeatedly refused to answer it.

"He cannot say how many NHS jobs could be lost yet expects Scots to believe he has a grip on the SNP's £5bn budget black hole.

"This is a first minister completely out of his depth, trying to bluff his way through the mounting financial chaos his party has created."

Reform UK Scotland leader Malcolm Offord accused Swinney of trying to dodge the question of job cuts with "word salad" answers.

He told The Sunday Show: "What I'm surprised to hear is that a government that has been in situ for 19 years still cannot put names and numbers around the reorganisation."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgk5.title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgk5.text:
Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election.

Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".

It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.

Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended.

In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.

Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity, and responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".

Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.

On tax measures, Reform estimates that increasing the tax-free threshold by £2,430 would save most taxpayers £500 a year and 2.9 million people would stop paying income tax altogether.

It says the policy would cost £17.7bn in the first year, rising to £21bn by the fifth year and could be paid for through £80bn of public spending cuts the party plans to make.

Jenrick told BBC Breakfast Reform would pay for the policy by "cutting out the waste".

Reform has said its spending cuts would include a £50bn reduction in welfare spending.

Half of the £353bn of welfare spending goes on the state pension, but Reform has said it will not cut this proportion.

The bulk of the funding would come from reducing the cost of welfare, Jenrick said, by not paying benefits to people who are not British citizens and helping people who are off work due to their mental health back into jobs.

Jenrick also said the UK would "stop paying foreign aid to rich countries", adding that "we should be looking after British people first".

"Yes, we'll pay for disaster relief but the vast majority of that budget should be spent on the priorities of our own people," he said.

Reform hopes to raise £10bn by scrapping net-zero programmes and Jenrick said, as the UK only amounted to 1% of the world's emissions, it was not sensible to be trying to decarbonise faster than other countries as that was "just impoverishing our own people".

The party hopes to raise £8bn by reducing the number of civil servants and £7.1bn by capping the foreign aid budget.

The policy was announced at Jenrick's speech on the last day of the party's conference in Birmingham.

"As chancellor, I will wake each morning with one purpose. To make Britain a better place to be a worker than it was the day before," he said.

"1.3 million were dragged into paying tax last year alone. Why? Because the tax-free allowance has been stuck at 12 and a half grand since 2021. And Labour has frozen it until 2031.

"That betrayal costs a full-time worker on the minimum wage more than £750 a year. And now for the first time, the freeze means they're going to be taxing the state pension. What a disgrace."

He said that if he failed to deliver the tax cut in his first Budget he would resign as chancellor.

"No ifs, no buts, I'll be gone."

In its manifesto before the general election in 2024, Reform said it wanted to lift the threshold to £20,000. Jenrick told conference activists this remains his long-term aim.

The personal allowance threshold currently stands at £12,570. Anyone earning more than £100,000 starts to lose their personal allowance. For every £2 earned above the threshold the basic allowance decreases by £1.

Shortly after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham told the Times that the "frustration" of people in his Makerfield constituency about the frozen allowance had "lodged in my mind".

He later said that "all of this would be looked at" in the upcoming Budget but that any change would be "difficult given the financial circumstances".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c780.title: Government begins paying off council's £2bn debt
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c780.text:
The government has officially begun reducing the debt pile of a Surrey local authority.

Officials have started paying down £500m of Woking Borough Council's historic £2bn debt.

The authority will be replaced by the new West Surrey Council in April 2027 following the dissolution of Surrey County Council and its 11 boroughs and districts as part of local government reorganisation.

The new council was forecast to start life with a £4bn financial black hole, largely due to Woking Borough Council's shortfall.

Residents have seen cuts to services, council tax hikes and the sale of public assets and its flagship projects as the local authority has tried to manage its debt.

The first government repayment was completed on 1 September with the settlement of an £8m loan, with a further £492m of loans expected to be repaid by the end of March 2027.

The government is effectively paying itself, as the money owed was from its own Public Works Loans Board, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Woking Borough Council leader Ann-Marie Barker said the financial support would help lessen the costs associated with servicing and reducing the council's debt.

She said: "While this marks important progress, we recognise that Woking's debt is an ongoing concern for residents across Surrey.

"There is still much work to do."

Woking Borough Council declared itself effectively bankrupt in June 2023 following a series of borrowing and investment decisions.

The authority will be replaced by the new West Surrey Council in April 2027. The first government repayment was completed on 1 September with the settlement of an £8m loan.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text:
Nigel Farage has insisted a Reform UK government would deliver where other parties have failed, as he set out his priorities in his annual conference speech.

He said Reform's pledges for its first 100 days in power would include stopping small boat crossings, cutting energy bills by £250 a year and ending the net zero "lunacy".

To eliminate "obstacles" to his plans, Farage said he would declare a "national emergency" and threatened to overhaul the House of Lords and how judges are appointed if they stood in the way.

In a speech interrupted several times by protesters, the Reform leader was also forced to address allegations over donations which emerged in an undercover investigation.

Reform had been hoping to use its annual conference to regain momentum after a difficult summer dominated by questions over the party's finances.

However, the main day of the conference was overshadowed after two senior party officials stepped down and Reform launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report on Thursday evening, which was filmed by Verbatim Investigations, a group founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.

In the undercover filming, the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Farage insisted "the party has done nothing wrong" and "has taken no illegal money", claiming the allegations had been made "because they're scared of us".

In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.
