https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.summary: Nigel Farage says he will declare a "national emergency" and overhaul the House of Lords. He also vows to cut energy bills by £250 a year and end net zero "lunacy" in the UK. The Politics Essential newsletter is a weekly look at the inner workings of Westminster.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gk.title: Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally party
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gk.text:
Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party on returning migrants who attempt to cross the English Channel in small boats, should both parties win power.

It comes after Reform UK last month announced a plan to intercept boats and return migrants to French ports using the Royal Navy.

The proposed agreement with RN states that France would "ordinarily accept" those on board, and then repatriate them to their home country.

It was signed at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.

In a speech in the main conference hall, ahead of the deal being unveiled, Bardella told delegates that an RN government would "do everything in its power to ensure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into the United Kingdom".

Hailing Farage as the UK's next prime minister, Bardella pledged to work with a potential future Reform government to tackle illegal migration.

The "memorandum of understanding" unveiled at the conference is a political document, but could be developed into a legal agreement between two future governments, if both parties win power.

It states: "The United Kingdom will intercept boats which have launched from French shores and entered British territorial waters and will return the persons on board to France.

"France will ordinarily accept these persons, who will be repatriated to their home country in accordance with the law in force in France concerning expulsion."

Illegal migrants who successfully arrive in the UK from France would be immediately detained and deported to their home country, rather than to France, under plans previously outlined by Reform.

Challenged during a news conference over whether the wording "ordinarily" meant some migrants would not be accepted by France, Farage said it was "legalese".

He argued the proposals would mean there was "no incentive" to pay a trafficker to cross the Channel, and "in very, very short order the business model is broken".

Farage said the "historic document" would "stop the boats forever".

Achieving this goal within the first 100 days of a Reform government is one of the party's key pledges.

Last month Emmanuel Macron's government hit out at Reform's proposals to use the Navy to return migrant boats to France, saying this would violate the country's sovereignty and breach international law.

Opposition parties also branded the plan unworkable.

Labour has pointed to increased cooperation with France as contributing to the number of small boat crossings falling.

This includes extra officers being deployed to French beaches, and more funding to help prevent crossings.

Last year Sir Keir Starmer's government also signed a "one in, one out deal", which allows the UK to send some small boat-arrivals back to France, while agreeing to take the same number of people from France believed to have a legitimate claim to come to the UK.

Joining Bardella on the stage after his speech, Farage said the deal marked a "new Entente Cordiale" between France and the UK, in reference to a series of agreements in 1904 that paved the way for greater diplomatic cooperation.

Unveiling the memorandum, the pair signed a large mock-up of the document to cheers from the audience of Reform members, with one shouting "Vive la France!".

Farage has been forging closer ties with Bardella and his party since meeting the politician in London last December.

Previously tipped as a potential candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Le Pen has said she wants to make Bardella prime minister if RN wins power.

It comes after party leader Le Pen announced in July she would run for the presidency following a Paris appeal court ruling which upheld her conviction for misusing EU funds but shortened her sentence, clearing the path for her to stand.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gk.summary: Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party. The deal would allow the UK to intercept boats and return migrants to France using the Royal Navy. It was signed by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3eq.title: Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3eq.text:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has described secretly-recorded comments by his senior aides about donations as "injudicious" and "loose pub talk".

James Orr, the party's head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to Farage, have both stepped down and Reform has launched an internal investigation into the allegations.

It comes after Channel 4 News broadcast undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations, in which the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Farage said his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In the Channel 4 report, which aired on Thursday night, a reporter posing as a potential party donor raises a concern to Farage's aide Dan Jukes that his American father wouldn't be able to directly give money to the party within the law.

Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

At the press conference, Farage said that Channel 4 had opted to bleep the names, rather than broadcast them was because Jukes' claims were "simply not true".

He said those donations "haven't occurred" and "don't exist in our accounts".

Farage said his party took compliance around donations "very seriously".

Responding to the allegations, Jukes said: "This was entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year by foreign-funded climate change activists.

"I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name."

Before stepping down from his position Jukes had been seen as Farage's right hand man.

Reform's head of policy, James Orr, who also appeared in the film, suggested to the undercover reporter that perhaps his American father could pay for opinion polling to aid Reform's campaigning.

In all, Channel 4 News claims three polls were commissioned in this way costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

Orr told Sky News: "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the programme, with which I will cooperate fully."

In response to allegations of "entrapment" from Jukes, a spokesperson for Verbatim Investigations told BBC News the investigation was carried out "to the highest journalistic standards", adding: "As the footage shows, the plots we exposed were proposed by Mr Jukes and Mr Orr, not by our journalists."

Farage acknowledged Jukes' comments were "problematic" but added that they were "loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

"And whilst I'm aware that our people were pushed and pushed and pushed into saying these things, the comments were injudicious at best.

"Neither of these members were authorised to act in that way.

"Accordingly, they've stepped down pending an investigation, and I emphasise again: Reform has broken no law, and we take compliance around donations very, very seriously."

During the film, Farage is introduced to the undercover reporter posing as a party donor and an actor posing as his American father.

In the press conference, Farage said he was "annoyed" that he was introduced to the two men adding: "It should not have happened."

He said his party needed to "do better as we professionalise".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The police said it would assess the matter and any information provided to it.

In a statement on Friday, the Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police."

A Channel 4 News spokesperson said: "We stand by the public interest journalism in this investigation, which has been rigorously verified to ensure accuracy.

"We would encourage people to watch the investigation in full."

Channel 4 says it was not broadcast because of the claims made by Farage aides. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage says his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money" James Orr, head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp93.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp93.text:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

Defra said the report showed food supply risks were becoming more complex and the government was working with farmers and industry to strengthen the UK's resilience.

"While our food businesses and supermarkets have continued to feed the nation through significant disruption, we will carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations as part of our ongoing work to build a more resilient, productive and sustainable food system," a spokesperson said.

In July, the government announced plans to set out the "small but important steps" households can take to prepare for food and water shortages in the event of extreme weather or cyber-attacks.

These will form a strategy to be unveiled by the end of 2026 aimed at bringing the UK closer into line with European countries in terms of emergency preparedness.

Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, the body which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, said Britain was "pretty close to crisis".

He told the BBC's Wake Up to Money programme that the country was being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

He added that El Niño, as well as global shipping disruption and the threat of pandemics, mean you cannot "just rely on the private sector coming through every single time".

Asked whether people should be stocking up in case of disruptions, Pluck added: "Yes, we should.

"There should be some sensible stocking in each household. And the government in the autumn will be telling all of us to do that."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp93.summary: Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle says El Niño will lead to more extreme storms in UK. She says Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and climate crisis. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.title: Burnham and Macron agree to scale up action on small boats
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.text:
Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron have discussed how to "scale up" efforts to tackle illegal migration and move the UK closer to Europe, as the new prime minister hosted his first foreign leader in Downing Street.

In an official readout of their meeting, No 10 said the pair also discussed production of long-range missiles in Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the prime minister raised Israeli plans for new settlements in the West Bank, which he condemned as "unacceptable".

Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".

"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship," Burnham added.

Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."

The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum. He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, No 10 said Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

They also "discussed the UK's drive to get closer to Europe", while Burnham raised concerns about the potential impact of the Made in Europe procurement plan, being drawn up in Brussels to protect EU industries, on British sectors.

Burnham has previously called for closer ties with Europe, as had his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The pair also discussed establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the Scalp long-range missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile.

The leaders also discussed the situation in the Middle East and the need to ensure de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And Burnham raised Israel's move to open up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank, saying it was "unacceptable and only served to undermine the prospect of the two-state solution".

The development in the so-called E1 area would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Plans to build there have long been internationally condemned, with settlements illegal under international law.

The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.

But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.

France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.

And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.

The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".

In a post on X, in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".

Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".

"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.summary: Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron discuss how to "scale up" efforts to tackle illegal migration. The pair also discussed production of long-range missiles in Ukraine. French PM says it is "so fitting" that Macron is his first overseas visitor since becoming PM.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cge4.title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cge4.text:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.

Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.

Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.

In comments to the Camden New Journal on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it."

"It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party," he added.

Polanski has already been out campaigning in the constituency despite there being no decision on who the Green candidate will be until next week.

In an interview with the BBC, he said: "We had a huge surge here in [local elections] in May. This is somewhere we can win."

He said he wanted to be the Greens' sixth MP so he could "challenge Burnham constructively".

In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.

But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.

Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, has appeared to back Polanski's candidacy as he ruled out running himself.

Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."

He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."

A date has not yet been set for the by-election.

The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies.

With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour.

Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top".

The London Assembly, on which Polanski currently sits, is an elected body of 25 representatives who scrutinise the policies of the mayor of London.

Sir Keir had been MP for the area since 2015, but said he was quitting to focus on a role in international affairs.

The former prime minister had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But he said it was the "right time" for him to "pass the baton to a successor".

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

Labour has not decided its candidate to potentially take on Polanski, with applications closing on Friday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxz.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxz.text:
Reform UK has pledged to cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare, net zero policies, overseas aid and the number of civil servants.

Speaking from the party's conference in Birmingham, economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said he would like to cut taxes in Reform's first Budget if it wins power at the next election but would have to "earn the trust" of the markets first.

Reform would be the "party of fiscal responsibility", he said and promised to make "big changes... in a careful way, not a cack-handed way".

Labour said the proposed cuts were "incredibly reckless and could mean vital public services like hospitals, schools and law enforcement are put at risk".

The bulk of Reform's proposed cuts come from its previously announced plans to reduce the welfare budget by £50bn.

£10bn would be saved by cutting net zero programmes while £8bn would come from reducing the civil service and £7.1bn from capping the foreign aid budget.

The party says its immigration policies, including abolishing indefinite leave to remain, would result in further savings.

Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and £45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost £15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a £5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.

It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.

But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.

The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.

A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales.

It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apache helicopters.

This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year.

Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army – such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.

The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis.

Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.

Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.

An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness.

"We are also investing £2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."

On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030.

The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."

The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces.

Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.

The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86x.title: Two Reform officials step down after undercover donations report
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86x.text:
Reform UK says two senior officials have stepped down as the party launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report.

Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of the internal probe, the party said.

The party added the investigation should be "allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice" and it would make no further comment for now.

The row threatens to overshadow Reform's conference in Birmingham, which has its first full day on Friday.

In the Channel 4 report, which aired on Thursday night, undercover filming showed Jukes suggesting a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for the party.

The undercover filming was carried out by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform has denied any wrongdoing and said it had "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police over the allegations. The force said on Thursday it would assess the matter and any information provided to it.

In a statement on Friday, the Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police.

"The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500.

"Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."

Jukes said: "This was entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year", adding that he denied wrongdoing and had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name."

Orr told Sky News: "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully."

Reacting on Friday, Farage told LBC a "couple of our contractors have said things that shouldn't have been said" and had been "removed this morning".

The Reform UK leader added: "The party has broken no laws, the party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever."

In response to allegations of "entrapment" from Jukes, a spokesperson for Verbatim Investigations told BBC News the investigation was carried out "to the highest journalistic standards", adding: "As the footage shows, the plots we exposed were proposed by Mr Jukes and Mr Orr, not by our journalists."

Farage appears to be trying to distance himself Jukes and Orr, with his comments to LBC.

However Jukes is widely seen as Farage's closest aide, who is often at his side, and is judged to have an innate sense of his boss's instincts. Jukes has long been the man you need to call if you want to arrange an interview with the Reform UK leader.

Orr, a Cambridge academic who has stepped down the party's head of policy, could also be considered to be in Farage's inner circle.

Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with a reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor posing as his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Jukes and Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's policy chief, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Channel 4 say the proposed £500,000 donation was never made.

Earlier in the film, the reporter is recorded raising a concern with Jukes that his American father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

Earlier in Channel 4 News's film, prior to the suggested £500,000 donation, Channel 4 says Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps his father could pay for opinion polling to aid Reform's campaigning.

The poll would cost £18,000 plus VAT – and Orr suggests that perhaps the polling company could send the bill to the undercover reporter.

In all, Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

On Friday morning, Reform UK chairman Lee Anderson told Sky News there was "no chance" of Jukes and Orr returning to the party.

This appeared to be contradicted by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told BBC Radio 4's Today programme minutes later that "it's not actually, in the nicest possible way, for any individual to make that determination" as the investigation continues.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crk3.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crk3.text:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push the figure to 3% of GDP by 2030.

Badenoch said a Conservative government would fund the commitment, worth £10bn a year, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.

Pointing to the threat from countries like Russia and Iran, Badenoch told a press conference: "Conflict is coming, we must act now."

So far Andy Burnham's government has only committed to setting out a plan in the spring to meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

Speaking at an event in central London, Badenoch said: "Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass.

"Our enemies are not going to sit around and wait for Labour to find the money to fight them."

Burnham has pointed to his choice of Chancellor, John Healey, who quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, as proof of his commitment to defence investment.

However, Badenoch said the prime minister should call a general election if he is not willing to find the money now, adding that Healey's decision to quit over defence spending appeared to have changed since he became chancellor.

"He resigned because Britain was not on track to reach 3% by 2030 and I praised him at the time for that decision," she said.

"Now that he is chancellor he does not seem to believe that any more and I am concerned he has been bought off with a promotion."

Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving £1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with £37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c783.title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c783.text:
Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immediate cap on donations.

Florence Eshalomi said a new team would be "working at pace to find a solution", as some MPs expressed concerns over the influence of wealthy individuals donating large sums of money.

The Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, but ministers have been pressed to go further by introducing a limit for UK-based donors.

Reform UK's Danny Kruger warned the Representation of the People Bill was a "flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap" the party.

Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.

Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving £1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.

Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers.

Last year he gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.

Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.

One of her proposals called for an immediate £500,000 limit which would reduce to £100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap.

The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.

Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."

The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".

Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.

The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."

The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed.

"But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."

Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".

The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics".

"That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.

"I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."

Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.

It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.

This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested £50,000 a year.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".

In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at £100,000 annually.

Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than £100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.

This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.

The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.

MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.

Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1kx.title: Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1kx.text:
Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.

"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'

Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.

He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".

Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68.title: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68.text:
Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's finances.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".

It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and £5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.

Farage acknowledged his party's poll ratings had taken a hit compared to last year, but said it would rebound and still had "every chance" of winning the next general election.

Reform's annual conference begins in Birmingham on Thursday, with both Farage and the party facing renewed questions over money.

A parliamentary investigation into £5m he received from major Reform donor Christopher Harborne was relaunched following Farage's re-election in Clacton, after a by-election he called in the Essex seat.

The Metropolitan Police is also investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.

The police probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell.

It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

Asked if he knew whether or not money donated by Fiona Cottrell had come from her son George, Farage said he was not "involved in the transactions".

However, he added that he "had been told it's her money". Reform has insisted it has always complied with donations rules.

He added: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society. If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."

He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do".

"There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat.

"There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing.

"So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."

Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour.

"People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything."

Farage said he expected it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed by Parliament's standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg as part of his probe into whether he should have publicly declared the £5m he received from Harborne.

He continued to insist the sum, which he says was a personal gift, did not require registration under Commons rules.

He added he had "no questions" about Greenberg's impartiality, but hit out at the "political composition" of the standards committee that will recommend what action should be taken on his findings.

The 14-member panel includes seven MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats, but none from Reform UK.

He added: "Have you seen who's on the committee? I think we know the outcome already. I'm not going to say anything more than that."

"To be judged by members of Parliament by other political parties who you're fighting against in by-elections or general elections, I think that raises a question, I really do," he added.

Elsewhere in his interview, Farage acknowledged that Reform was "down a bit" in its poll ratings compared to 2025, after failing to win in by-elections this year including Gorton and Denton and Makerfield, which saw Andy Burnham's re-election as an MP ahead of becoming Labour leader.

But he added that "markets don't move in straight lines", adding that the party still had "every chance" of winning the next general election, due by 2029.

He said the party was continuing to look "outside of the political sphere" to fill frontbench positions, following a raft of appointments earlier this year to senior posts within the party.

And he said he continued to hold to his previous prediction there would be an election next spring "forced on the government" by the markets, amid rising costs to public borrowing.

Reform's conference, he said, would be a chance for the party to set out details of the "fundamental changes" it would make within 100 days of winning power.

He added that whilst his and other parties had announced a number of new policies in recent weeks, what most interested voters was who is "actually going to deliver" than the specifics of individual policies.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68.summary: Nigel Farage says he is not involved in donations to Reform UK. He says he has been told it's her money, but he is 'not involved' in the donations. He said he expects it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed by Parliament's standards commissioner.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gd.title: Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gd.text:
Reform UK has been hit by a row over foreign donations as the party's leaders and supporters gather for their annual conference.

The row centres on allegations which surfaced during undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations - founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting - and broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday.

The party denies any wrongdoing and says it is investigating. Robert Jenrick, Reform's economy spokesperson, said the two senior aides in the film had been suspended, telling the BBC's Today programme: "Nigel [Farage] got rid of the two people who did this…he acted swiftly, they've gone."

Both Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police, which says it is assessing the claims but has not launched an investigation. The Electoral Commission says it is "in touch" with the police.

We have looked at each of the three main allegations and where they sit with the law.

In the film, Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggest a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totaled £500,000.

Jukes meets an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based son of a wealthy American financier, who voices concern that his father could not directly donate to Reform within the law.

Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?" According to Channel 4, Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the son's name, even though the money would have come from his American father.

A similar arrangement is also mooted in a meeting with Orr.

Farage is shown saying "it's all above board" and expressing thanks. On Friday, Farage said he was in fact asking whether it was above board.

Channel 4 says the proposed £500,000 donation was never made.

Under electoral law, you must be a UK registered voter or a company registered in the UK to be a "permissable" donor to a UK political party. In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, but his father would not be.

Any donation of more than £500 from an impermissible source must be declared to the Electoral Commission and returned within 30 days.

If the party keeps it beyond that, it is deemed to have accepted the donation - and that could lead to a fine and potential criminal investigation.

Channel 4 says Reform commissioned three opinion polls between January and July 2026, costing £32,500 in total.

One was on the front page of the Telegraph newspaper under the headline "Labour would face wipeout if elections went ahead"; another on the front page of the Times with the headline "Reform vote in unions at same level as Labour".

In the film, Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps the American financier could pay for opinion polling to help with Reform's campaigns.

He is shown saying this would "technically be a donation in kind" but "the reality is we could easily get away with it".

The public was not told who had commissioned and paid for the three polls. Polling firm JL Partners, the Telegraph and the Times have all said this was not known to them either.

Farage said on Friday the polls in question had been commissioned by an independent third party and that Reform had "not done anything wrong".

Any legitimate donations from permissible donors worth more than £11,180 in a calendar year must, by law, be declared to the Electoral Commission. The £32,500 polling payment does not appear to have been declared.

The legal definition for a political party donation includes payments for studies and research.

The Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 specifically outlaws knowingly taking steps to disguise or conceal that a donation has come from an impermissible source.

As part of this, it can be a crime for someone to conceal money spent on expenses incurred directly or indirectly by the party - and to mislead a party on the source of a donation. The maximum sentence is 12 months in prison.

It is in this context that Labour is demanding the police investigate the polling and whether there is evidence of concealing who actually paid for it.

But investigating this and the other claims in the film would be hugely complex - and a 30-minute TV report could not be the sole basis for a prosecution.

The police would almost certainly ask Channel 4 for all the unused filmed material, research notes and plans for the documentary. Detectives would want to interview everyone involved and understand their intentions.

In a statement on Friday, JL Partners said that "sometimes people with a party alignment make suggestions about potential clients who may be interested in commissioning and paying for polling" in the UK and abroad, and that it would not expect to be told the precise relationship between Reform and the US-based company.

Nick Vamos, former head of specialist crime at the Crown Prosecution Service, explained: "It is very common for allegations of electoral offences to be reported to the police, especially by political rivals looking to score points," adding the police would assess the evidence neutrally to decide whether a full investigation is required.

Such offences very rarely lead to prosecution. Between 2011 and 2021, the Electoral Commission referred eight cases to the Met, none of which resulted in charges. Even if there were an investigation, it would take months to get near specialist detectives or prosecutors.

Elsewhere in the film, Jukes appears to list other supporters of Reform UK who have potentially donated to the party through UK residents.

The names, made in the context of discussing the proposed £500,000 arrangement, are bleeped out.

He is shown telling the undercover reporter: "But, you know, serious point, [REDACTED] donates to us, and he donates through his son, the [REDACTED] they donate through their…"

The undercover reporter replies, "Through their kids yeah", to which Jukes responds: "The [REDACTED], [REDACTED], one of the two. [REDACTED]. [REDACTED]. The [REDACTED] are Reform donors. It's the father and it's the son, so that's one of the ways in which we do it."

During a press conference on Friday, Farage referred to this as "loose pub talk" with "a bit of boasting, a bit of jack-the-lad-dery going on there".

"Donations from the names that were mentioned have not occurred, don't exist… in our accounts," he added.

It would be for the Electoral Commission and the police to assess any previous Reform donations and their record of declarations.

Reform and the individuals involved in the investigations have denied any wrongdoing.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.title: What big issues are on the agenda as Stormont returns after summer?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.text:
It's not even the start of a new Stormont term and already there have been leaks.

Albeit it wasn't some big scoop but a rather damp surprise for the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) MLA Colin McGrath, who took to social media saying a water leak over summer had left his assembly office looking worse for wear.

Even the most casual observers of politics here could guess, however, that Stormont's leaky roof problems are outweighed by the ever-slow drip of political activity inside the building - a place the assembly's freshest face will witness for himself from this week.

On Tuesday, Paul Boggs was named Sinn Féin's new West Tyrone MLA after Maoliosa McHugh - who'd already said he wouldn't run in the next election - decided to call it quits.

Boggs brings the number of MLAs who have been co-opted since the last assembly election to 14 and that figure could go up still before the upcoming election next May.

Co-options aside (that's a whole other piece), the backdrop of said looming election means parties are likely to be in fighting form when Stormont sittings resume on Monday.

The newly-appointed Health Minister Robbie Butler will be one of those quick to feel pressure, as the 10-year anniversary of the Bengoa report - a major health reform review - approaches next month.

Pay pressures in his department and the Department of Education also make for another winter of discontent, with the prospect of strike action yet to be ruled out.

We know by now that Butler and other ministers argue that their hands are tied without a budget that can allow them to meet all their outstanding pressures.

Executive parties have been taking part in talks with Treasury officials in a bid to break the deadlock but 36 days since the legal deadline to pass a budget expired, there has so far been little sign of light at the end of this tunnel.

So much so that it prompted SDLP leader of the opposition Matthew O'Toole to issue a call to public bodies across Northern Ireland this week, asking them how the ongoing lack of financial certainty is affecting their services.

Whether point scoring or simply making a wider point about the consequences of not having a budget, others are also talking about the problems being stored up at Stormont.

Think tank Pivotal published a report last week on the issue, noting that several departments are facing massive overspends this year, including deficits of about £800m in health and £250m in education.

Money matters are a major sticking point for this executive but whether this can be resolved rests on what comes out of talks with Treasury and the secretary of state - more of those are expected to happen with the parties this week.

The budget, as big as it is, is only one item on the executive's to-do list before the assembly dissolves in March ahead of the election.

Already ministers have been repeatedly warned by assembly Speaker Edwin Poots that time is running out to pass remaining pieces of legislation through all their hurdles.

It's not uncommon for Stormont to sit into the small hours or hold extra days of sittings as the end of a mandate approaches - this one will be no different but there are serious question marks over some key bills.

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald's so-called "Good Jobs" Bill which aims to massively reform employment laws has yet to get executive agreement, after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said it had no support among business groups.

Other flagship policies including the redevelopment of Casement Park and the A5 road project also remain mothballed due to financial and legal disputes.

The reality is that as the countdown to election day gets closer the harder it will be for the executive to make decisions on major issues, for fear that any misstep could go down badly with their respective bases.

The largest parties - Sinn Féin and the DUP - will be feeling the heat in their own ways.

Sinn Féin, which became the largest party for the first time in the last election, needs to consolidate its support and show that it can deliver - without a legislative win or two in the next few months this may be hard to demonstrate on the doorsteps.

The DUP faces its own challenges of going into its first election since the conviction of former party leader Jeffrey Donaldson in June for child sex abuse offences, which he is appealing.

In July, the party moved to commission an independent review over Donaldson's actions while he was a member of the DUP, but it is not yet clear when the report will be completed or published.

Throw in fresh tensions over Drumcree, continuing rows over Irish language signage and pressure on Alliance's agriculture minister over a controversial cattle cull last month and it all makes for a battle a day.

If this current executive has anything going for it, it's that leaks of information and counter briefings against each other are much more rare than in the last executive.

Often the mood around the table is described as collegiate, even if ministers disagree on an issue.

But as one Stormont source put it recently: "You can't leak anything if there's nothing to leak. This is an executive in a holding pattern."

Sooner rather than later this executive will have to circle back to big issues that can't be ducked forever.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.summary: The number of MLAs who have been co-opted since the last assembly election to 14 could go up still before the upcoming election. Will have to focus on big issues like the economy, the economy and the environment?

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd08.title: Why do ex-MPs join the 'Chiltern Hundreds' list?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd08.text:
Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson have this in common: They both stepped down as Prime Minister before their term was up, and within three years of winning an election.

Their subsequent resignation as a sitting MP means they have also shared the unusual office of "Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern".

Sir Keir is the latest person to pick up the title after resigning as an MP this week.

What is it, and what does it have to do with the Chilterns?

Thanks to a law dating back to 1624, Members of Parliament (MPs) in the UK are not technically permitted to resign.

"Unless they die or are expelled, they must become disqualified if they wish to retire before the end of a Parliament," according to the UK Parliament website.

This is because back in the 17th Century, MPs often accepted the role reluctantly, so leaving the job was not to be encouraged.

A "parliamentary loophole" was created to get around this, according to the History of Parliament blog.

"An MP can do this by requesting, and accepting, office as either the Steward and Bailiff of the Chiltern Hundreds, or Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead," wrote Dr Martin Spychal.

"Both offices (or jobs) are nominal. They exist in name only, have no responsibilities and are unpaid."

Anyone with these titles is disqualified from being an MP – originally in order to prevent royal influence on politics – but later used by parliamentarians who were unhappy with their lot.

The "hundreds" were areas that belonged to the Crown as far back as the 13th Century.

The three Chiltern Hundreds mentioned today refer to Stoke, Desborough and Burnham in Buckinghamshire. The regions include the towns of Amersham, Beaconsfield, High Wycombe, Marlow, Eton and Chesham.

Coincidentally, these are near to the prime minister's countryside residence in Buckinghamshire – Chequers.

Because a steward of the hundreds might be able to benefit financially from the role, or promote the interests of the crown, it was seen as a conflict of interest.

"Resourceful MPs discovered that they could request appointment to these offices, which then disqualified them from sitting in the Commons," wrote Spychal.

The House of Commons Information Office said: "The Stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds is thought to have been used for the first time as a means of resignation from the House of Commons on 17 January 1751 by John Pitt, who wanted to vacate his seat for Wareham and stand for Dorchester."

The Manor of Northstead, in North Yorkshire, is the other remaining office given to resigning MPs. Its most recent recipient was Reform UK's Nigel Farage who resigned in order to stand for re-election in his own constituency.

The titles are given out alternately, in case two MPs wish to step down at the same time, and each new appointment replaces the previous one.

Spychal said there have been calls to reform the system since 1775 - but in 2026, the peculiar British formality lives on.
