https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - emotional documentary glosses over the hard stuff
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.text:
"The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam.

"It's not a power struggle any more."

The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus.

In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009.

Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room".

"The band doesn't exist any more," he announces, sounding more irritated than sad.

According to Scottish singer Amy McDonald, who was also on the line-up, the altercation was seismic. "Liam smashed Noel's guitar, huuuge fight!" she tweeted from backstage.

The film, however, never tells us what was said. Nobody explains the fall-out. We don't find out who instigated the rapprochement, nor do we hear how it affected their family.

Instead, we cut to rehearsals for the comeback tour, with a caption informing us the brothers "didn't speak for 15 years", and an implication that all the wounds have been miraculously healed.

Tantalisingly, the first song they practice is Columbia - a fan favourite that never made the tour's setlist - but there's a tension in the room.

The band, under Noel's instruction, is piecing together the setlist. Liam won't arrive until later in the process, and no-one's sure which Liam they'll get.

When he arrives, he seems fantastically grumpy, complaining about the sound-proofing panels that have been placed in front of Joey Waronker's drums.

"They're already giving me the hump," he huffs.

But when he steps up to the mic, the band relax. Guitarist Bonehead - who's strategically placed between Liam and Noel - beams from ear to ear.

A couple of hours later, still in the middle of a song, Liam waves goodbye and casually strolls out of the rehearsal space.

"I'm not sure whether our kid's enjoying himself," Noel says to his bandmates.

In a voice-over, Liam reveals, enjoying himself wasn't the goal.

"If you're not on it, chaos can ensue," he says, adding that he's given up cigarettes and alcohol (the intoxicants, not the song) for the duration of the tour.

"These songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect."

Liam's newfound professionalism is probably the biggest revelation in the documentary, scripted by Peaky Blinders' creator Steven Knight, and shot by directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace.

To their presumable dismay, there are no scenes of the singer quitting the tour to go house-hunting; throwing snooker balls at Blur; or starting a fight on a cross-channel ferry.

Instead, they complete rehearsals without incident and rock up to Cardiff's Principality Stadium for their public reunion.

As the big moment looms, everyone limbers up in the corridors like middle-aged dads getting ready for a Park Run. But when they hit the stage, it's electric.

Liam grabs Noel's hand and thrusts it into the air, they launch into the opening chords of Hello, and the crowd practically explodes with joy. As the gig continues, they dance and cheer and weep.

During Slide Away, a man sinks to his knees and sings the lyrics, his hands clasped together as if in prayer. When the gig ends, cameras capture a young fan in an awe-struck stupor, unable to tear himself away from his spot on the stadium floor.

This is where the documentary excels - capturing the sheer surge of affection that greeted Oasis's return. We visit shows in Dublin, Manchester, Sao Paolo, Tokyo and New York - and every one has a fan with a personal story to tell.

One woman has named her dog Bonehead. Another is a Haenyeo - a South Korean free-diver - who says Oasis's music helped her out of depression.

Noel, in particular, is blindsided by the impact.

"The gravity hit me of what it meant to people and it took me by surprise," he reflects. "I have to say it actually knocked me back."

Structurally, though, the film has a problem. In a biopic, the triumphant night in Cardiff would have been the final scene - the moment of resolution after 15 years of pain. Here, it comes about 40 minutes into the action. Every subsequent concert just rinses and repeats the same story.

The music is still thrilling. The live mix is impeccable. Liam sounds incredible. But Southern and Lovelace are left flailing around for a story.

In Manchester, they focus on a priest delivering a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. In London, they follow a survivor of the Manchester Arena Bombing, who reflects on the way Don't Look Back In Anger became an anthem of resilience.

But the film sidesteps the fact that Liam spent the mourning period criticising his brother for his failure to appear at charity shows supporting the survivors.

It's not the only omission.

There's no mention of the dynamic pricing row that overshadowed the launch of the tour (although Liam is heard apologising for the lack of "cheap seats" during one of the concerts).

And while Noel praises Bonehead's contribution to the band, calling him "the sound of Oasis," we never hear from the guitarist; and the film never addresses his cancer diagnosis, which forced him to miss the final leg of the tour.

Sometimes, the filmmakers hint at uncovered stories. Noel mentions missing weeks of rehearsals because of a bad back; and its revealed that the Gallagher brothers' kids met for the first time on the tour - but, for some reason, those threads are left un-pulled.

Clearly, a decision was made to concentrate on the music. The cameras don't (or weren't allowed to) follow Liam and Noel off stage.

Their joint interview provides a few highlights. Liam's riff on Mick Jagger's creaking limbs is worth the price of admission alone. But you get the feeling that everyone's on their best behaviour for Disney Plus... unless you count the copious swearing.

That said, if you attended any of the Oasis '25 shows, this is an incredible souvenir of all the tear-soaked euphoria and musical communion that accompanied their comeback.

And, of course, it works as a very effective trailer for the band's much-rumoured return to Knebworth next summer.

Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger is in cinemas from Wednesday 9 September.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.summary: Oasis return to the UK in 2025 after 15 years of hiatus. Film never reveals who instigated the fall-out, nor how it affected their family.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.

Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson .Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.

Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.

The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

The recordings will go out throughout October on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at midday on the pair's new show.

A performance from Stockport-formed band Blossoms on 5 October will kick off the run.

Rock band Nothing But Thieves, US rising star Stella Lefty, Brit-nominated singer Beabadoobee and London-based artist Odeal are also among the artists on the line-up.

Brighton duo Royal Blood will close out this year's sessions on 30 October, but a surprise artist, who will perform just before them, is still to be announced.

West Midlands superstar Jorja Smith will be performing following on from the release of her third album, What Are The Odds.

The Brit Award winner's latest album received largely positive reviews, with Rolling Stone UK describing it as her "best album yet".

Electronic heavyweights Chase & Status will also take to the studio after they headlined Reading and Leeds Festival last month.

And Oscar-winner Sam Smith will be rolling out their vocals following on from the release of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes, last month.

Hedges previously hosted the Live Lounge with fellow presenters Rickie Haywood-Williams and Melvin Odoom, who have since left the station as part of a major schedule shake-up.

In an Instagram post at the time, Hedges said she was "so excited" to host the show alongside Asiamah and sent her support to her former colleagues, saying she would be "cheering them on in their next chapter".

Following the Live Lounge announcement, Asiamah said it is a "privilege" to take on the role and host the upcoming line-up of guests.

"Bring it on. Hope you're ready, because I ain't, it's going to be a surprise and a big vibe," he added.

BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month 2026 full line-up:

Monday 5 October - Blossoms

Wednesday 7 October - Nothing But Thieves

Friday 9 October - Sam Smith

Monday 12 October - Stella Lefty

Wednesday 14 October - Chase & Status

Friday 16 October - Jorja Smith

Monday 19 October – Beabadoobee

Wednesday 21 October - Rachel Chinouriri

Friday 23 October - Odeal

Monday 26 October - Anderson .Paak x Cordae

Wednesday 28 October – To be revealed soon

Friday 30 October - Royal Blood

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.summary: BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month 2026 will be held on October 5. Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith among the artists to take to the studio. Indie band Blossoms, Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson and Nothing But Thieves also on the line-up.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.title: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text:
Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed.

The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles for the feature film, with production starting on Monday.

The Inbetweeners 3 will follow on the story of their characters, Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper.

They originally starred in three seasons of the popular coming-of-age sitcom, which aired on E4 between 2008 and 2010.

It followed their trials and misadventures as suburban teenagers at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life and friendship.

The show has gained new fans over the years due to some of its best bits finding new life on social media, as well as through the film sequels.

The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014.

Alongside the announcement, Netflix released a teaser video which showed Will, Simon, Neil and Jay return to their iconic yellow Fiat.

The friend group all get into the tiny car but Simon struggles to start the engine.

After some encouragement, it gets going and they drive out of what looks like a storage unit.

Production kicks off after months of speculation that there would be another film, but beyond the lead characters returning, the rest of the cast is yet to be confirmed.

Fans will be wondering if English actress Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D'Amato.

However, Netflix has announced The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film.

Beesley and Morris said it has been "super fun" hanging out with friends again.

"We're going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans," they added.

The first film sees the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post sixth form break, but they quickly find more trouble than they bargained for.

The 2014 follow-up reunites Will, Simon, and Neil as they travel to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year - where they find out his travels aren't as lavish as his messages had claimed.

Tensions rise as they clash over whether to chase cultural experiences or a wilder time on their trip.

The first film made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix, while the sequel also broke box office records.

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

The cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles. The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xk.title: Dizzee Rascal spotted at community folk festival
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xk.text:
Music lovers were surprised by the "unexpected" arrival of rapper Dizzee Rascal during a market town's folk festival.

They had been attending the BunkFest weekend in Wallingford, Oxfordshire, on Sunday, when the superstar was seen at The Boat House pub.

Several people rushed over to have their photos taken with the grime and hip hop artist, who has so far had five UK number one singles, including Bonkers, Dance Wiv Me and Holiday.

Festival attendee Charlie Garwood, 23, said: "I love his songs. You don't expect someone like that to be in a little town like Wallingford."

The lab technician from Benson said Dizzee told him he was "just seeing a friend" when he bumped into him in the street.

He believes he then got on a private boat on the River Thames.

Garwood told his parents, who initially did not believe him and assumed the photo was AI.

"It's so unexpected," he told the BBC.

"It's one of those things you just don't believe at first. He's known for his dance anthems, we grew up listening to him... it's just a cool thing."

Ashley Carle, 21, a first year psychology student at the University of Liverpool, said she arrived at The Boat House, where several of her friends work, shortly after Dizzee left.

She heard the musician ordered a burger and told the manager it was so good that he ordered a second one.

Carle, who is a big fan of Dizzee's "typical night-out bangers", said she asked the rapper: "I know a million people have already asked but can I have a picture please?"

"He said: 'Yeah, not a problem'."

She described Dizzee as a "very chilled guy".

BunkFest is one of the UK's largest free festivals, attracting more than 30,000 visitors.

It ran from Friday to Sunday on the banks of the River Thames.

Organised by volunteers, it gets its name from the Bunk Railway line which runs between the south Oxfordshire town and nearby Cholsey.

This year's performers included Dr. Feelgood, tribute band The Delicate Sound of Pink Floyd, and supergroup Blue Water Giants.

A spokesperson said: "If Dizzee was here we hope he enjoyed Wallingford's free family festival, run entirely by volunteers, and proud recipients of the King's Award for Voluntary Service."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xk.summary: Rapper seen at Wallingford's BunkFest weekend in Oxfordshire. Rapper has so far had five UK number one singles, including Bonkers, Dance Wiv Me and Holiday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0j.title: Andrew Scott feels the Pressure as 'unsung hero' in WW2 thriller
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0j.text:
Andrew Scott says he loved the challenge of his latest acting role in the film Pressure, as the meteorologist key to the success of World War Two's D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history.

“Group Captain James Stagg may not have been the most charming person, but I think he had a huge amount of humility in the face of nature. And that's one of the themes I think of the film," Scott tells the BBC.

"He appeared to me to be an extraordinarily interesting cinematic character, as well as an unsung hero from history."

Stagg played a crucial advisory role when US General Dwight D Eisenhower invaded Normandy, laying the foundations for the Allied victory in World War Two.

"It was a wonderful part to play," he says, while painting a mixed picture of Stagg, calling him "very chilly", while also "forthright, direct, obsessed with weather - and not afraid to speak truth to power".

Stagg isn't a traditional war hero, something Scott clearly relished sinking his acting teeth into.

"I really enjoyed the way that Stagg was not interested in ingratiating himself with anybody," he told BBC Culture correspondent David Sillito, calling him "a real fish out of water in this situation".

The actor's other starring roles couldn't be more different, including romantic fantasy film All of Us Strangers, for which he was nominated for a Golden Globe, plus his memorable "hot priest" in TV's Fleabag and the menacing Jim Moriarty in Sherlock, for which he won a Bafta. His award-winning stage roles include Vanya and Present Laughter.

In Pressure, Stagg is thrown into a high-stakes furnace of egos. He has to work with a team of meteorologists who robustly and publicly disagree with each other.

Stagg "wasn't a particularly garrulous character" Scott says, which is partly why he was perhaps an unlikely hero.

"So many of the heroes in our own lives don't have that big swashbuckling moment," he says.

"And you know, a hero comes in all different shapes and sizes.

"I tried not to be afraid of the fact that perhaps, at the beginning, the audience might be like, 'Who is this guy?' And hopefully by the end we understand his motivations and his inner workings."

The actor is speaking to the BBC on board HMS Belfast, which led the opening bombardment for the D-Day landings, when tens of thousands of troops from the UK, the US, Canada and France attacked German forces on the coast of northern France on 6 June 1944.

Eisenhower needed a full moon, low tide, not much cloud or wind and low seas.

"The stakes were so enormously high... they were all locked down, and they couldn't leave the place. Stagg's wife was very heavily pregnant at the time, so it was a very, very difficult time for him," Scott explains.

"It's completely unimaginable, the pressure that they would have been under, not just Stagg, but everybody in the building."

This of course explains the name of the film, which is based on the successful 2014 stage play by actor and writer David Haig.

The film also charts how Eisenhower had the good sense to pay heed to the experts around him.

Scott says although the film is about many things, it's chiefly about "the humility of leadership, and about the difference between power and expertise".

"Real experts have the humility to go, 'I don't know about that, but I am in a position of power, so I'm going to delegate this, and I'm gonna listen to what this person has to say'," he says.

The film's co-writer and director, Anthony Maras, employed his own weather experts for the film, including Martin Young, a former deputy chief of the UK's Met [Meteorology] Office, who'd spent 40 years studying the weather and more than 10 as its chief forecaster.

Young's long career also meant he had first-hand knowledge of processes, data and equipment Stagg would have used.

The film is nearly all set in the planning rooms for D-Day, and you see all of them working around the clock, while living on top of each other.

"There's a huge amount of wit in the film that I really enjoyed," Scott says, while adding: "I love films that are about work.

"These relationships are no less significant because they're work relationships, they're collegiate.

"And at the end of these extraordinary three days they shake hands with each other - he's not a hugger, that probably wasn't part of the culture then.

"But they nevertheless went through something absolutely enormous together, and they had enormous feelings towards each other - whether that was rage, admiration, intimidation or connection."

Scott also managed to use some previous experience of working on a film about D-Day to help with his performance.

"I've been very lucky. As a young actor, I was in the opening sequence of Saving Private Ryan [Steven Spielberg's Oscar-winning film which depicts the horror, fear and brutality facing troops landing at Normandy].

"I was there for that as a 19-year-old on the beach. So, of course, I have no sense of what the horrorism would have been like as a reality, but I certainly had an idea of how it would have looked visually because he stretched the camera for as long as the eye could see."

Scott is delighted that Pressure pays tribute not only to Stagg, but also references another unsung hero, Maureen Sweeney, who lived in Ireland and was the first to confirm any break in the weather, from her lighthouse in County Mayo.

"It's another story in itself actually," Scott adds.

"A big part of my family are from around those parts. So that was wonderful," the Irish actor adds.

Scott ends by saying why he was so drawn to the film, and Stagg in particular.

"I think there's something just very moving about a singular passion someone might get.

"Their imagination might get captured by the weather as a young man, and if you apply yourself to something and you become excellent at something, it serves a place in the world and serves a place in humanity.

"He quietly went back to his life and it's wonderful that we can pay tribute to him in this way all these years later. He's a movie hero."

Pressure is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 September.

You can watch Andrew Scott talking about his role to BBC News here on YouTube.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0j.summary: Andrew Scott played a crucial role in World War Two's D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history. Scott says he was drawn to the film because of his family's connection to Ireland.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3r.title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from socials to Shakespeare
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3r.text:
Comedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.

Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.

It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear.

"I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.

While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon.

"I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.

"We're all phone addicts," Chawawa continues. "The average person's picking up their phone 200 times a day. I'm on a bit of a conscious mission at the moment to reduce that.

"And interestingly, the top comments under all the videos I've been watching are people who were at those raves saying, 'I loved being able to dance, maybe get a little high, maybe get too sweaty for too long, and know there was no record of that.'"

Chawawa was in his teens when social media and smartphones took off, and says he "took for granted" the brief time before any and every fun occasion was recorded and posted for posterity.

If he ventures onto a dance floor now, he admits "my two-step has become a lot stiffer" out of anxiety that a wrong move could be filmed and send him viral.

"So yeah, I do definitely pine for those non-digital, in-person experiences, and I envy my parents for having them."

This is coming from someone who owes his fame to the digital age, after making his name with comic videos as characters like upper-class drill rapper Unknown P and chef Jonny Oliver.

But Chawawa has since branched out from social media - making two Bafta-nominated TV documentaries, starring on Taskmaster and doing stand-up comedy.

"I've been making my short-form satirical videos for almost eight years now, creeping up to a decade," he says. "I have a certain skill set that I've acquired there. It's skyrocketed me to all the places I wanted to go.

"But I suppose the question at the beginning was always - if these sketches do work and they do catapult me into this new stratosphere of entertainment, where am I trying to land?"

The aim, he says, was to land on "something bigger and onto a new challenge" - such as theatre acting.

He's starting by playing Bottom in Shakespeare's romantic caper A Midsummer Night's Dream at Chichester Festival Theatre in West Sussex.

In this 90s version, his character is a member of the Young Conservatives and is "a very political Bottom", he says, while Theseus is a Tory MP who has shut down free raves in the county.

"I take it super seriously and I'm very studious when we're in the room," Chawawa explains of his preparations. "I'm taking notes. I'm learning all of these mad Shakespeare terms like couplets and quatrains and anacreontics and stuff that definitely sounds made up but isn't.

"And I think also it's the perfect time to maybe... jump ship, I think is the right word.

"Social media platforms and their algorithms have very much angled themselves against the creatives at the moment, I think."

He's not jumping ship from social media completely, but says the online battle for eyeballs has "turned into a little bit of a dogfight, where even good stuff, even really consciously thought-out material, is just instantly swiped to the bottom of people's pages".

Chawawa thinks he was lucky to "enjoy the golden era of social media" before it became harder to cut through the noise.

"To be able to experiment, to be able to trial these characters and roll the dice on big ideas was fantastic because you were never getting lost in a sea of content.

"There's some mad statistic about there being tens of millions of videos uploaded a day now - but at the time it was like, 'I'm going to try this Jamie Oliver spoof or a Nigella [Lawson] character or the UK's first posh drill rapper, what do you think?' And it felt like the whole internet would give you feedback on that creative product."

He adds: "I love the fact that social media has allowed me to have a career in stand-up, as a documentarian and now as an actor, so I don't have any sort of resentment to it and how it's changed.

"But what I will say is I was there as the sun was coming up on social media, and it was very fun."

Chawawa fell in love with the theatre when he went to see The Lion King when he was 16 and realised it was like "the best movie you've ever seen, but in real life".

However, returning as an adult, he felt out of place as a black man. "In the shows I was going to, it didn't feel as though they were too welcoming to me being there, just through the small social cues."

He had a lightbulb moment after watching For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy by Ryan Calais Cameron, which "I still think is the best play I've ever seen". Chawawa found himself thinking, "I wish every black boy in the world could watch this play."

So he took a group of teenagers to watch it, which he describes as "the most fulfilling and magical and deeply moving experience".

Inspired by their reactions, Chawawa set up the Black Boys Theatre Club to take groups every month to plays ranging from Dracula to One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest - followed by a post-show discussion in Nando's.

"Every time we go and see a play, it's not about the boys skipping out of it going, 'I want to be the next Billy Elliot'," he says. "It's more just them realising it's a safe space for you. It can be your home if you want it to be. You will thrive on stage or as an audience member, but just know that theatre is a part of your multiverse."

In 2023, 10% of theatre audiences were from black, Asian or ethnically diverse backgrounds, according to Arts Council England data.

Chawawa praises theatres for opening their doors to the Black Boys Theatre Club and other efforts to attract more diverse audiences, but says lower ticket prices and "a societal shift" will make a bigger difference.

Next month, his club will travel to see him in A Midsummer Night's Dream - and he hopes more young minds will be captivated by the "snow globe of human emotion" that is live theatre.

"Really, truly, where else can I go in real life and watch somebody express all emotions without restraint? Sadness, anger, joy, envy. And I can be metres away, sometimes centimetres away from seeing real human emotion - not through a screen of any size, but in the room," he says.

"I believe that as more people do try and back off away from screens and digital experiences, theatre will experience a boom."

A Midsummer Night's Dream is at at Chichester Festival Theatre from 18 September to 17 October.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3r.summary: Munya Chawawa is a comedian and documentary maker. He is a stage actor in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Chawawawa set up the Black Boys Theatre Club to take groups to play plays.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q.title: The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q.text:
James Bond is special. Playing him propels an actor into an exceptionally elite group of performers. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, only six people have ever played him in the official film series.

In the last decade alone the UK has had more prime ministers, and twice as many people have walked on the moon than have played the British secret agent.

The last announcement of a new Bond was 21 years ago in 2005. So it's inevitable for Bond fans to want to have their questions answered about the future of one of cinema's most sought after roles, in one of cinema's biggest franchises.

This is, of course, the big question fans have been talking about for the last six years. And with an announcement edging closer and closer, the speculation has intensified recently.

Many of the same well-known faces have been bandied about for months, if not years. Those names have generally included Henry Cavill, Harris Dickinson, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, James Norton, Jack O'Connell, Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

More recently, other names have also been thrown into the mix.

Earlier this year Variety reported that stage actor Tom Francis had auditioned for the role. And in late August Page Six claimed there will be more auditions this month, and that Gladiator 2 star Paul Mescal and Heartstopper and SAS: Rogue Heroes star Jack Barton are also on the audition list.

The announcement about the next film's producers referred to keeping Bond's spirit alive "as he embarks on his next adventure", seemingly confirming that Bond would remain male.

However, it's never been clear whether the rumoured names have been well-sourced inside information, or merely guesswork and speculation.

Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussie…"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

The audition process is likely to have been carried out in a similar way to previous castings.

The scene that many would-be Bonds have traditionally had to peform is taken from From Russia With Love, where 007 comes out of his bathroom to find Tatiana Romanova in his bed. It's a scene where an actor relies on their physical presence, movement and charisma. No explosions fights or gadgets.

As GoldenEye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell explained to entertainment website Gold Derby: "The word is effortless. You never see Bond fumble, he is very economic, efficient and effortless. That scene covers all the bases, basically."

And for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen. As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past: "Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors."

Generally, the unveiling of a new Bond has taken place at a London press conference in front of the world's media. But for the first time creative control of the franchise is in the hands of a studio like Amazon MGM.

Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond. And they're reported to have paid at least $20m more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.

Having paid such eye-watering amounts, it seems more than possible that Amazon MGM might well wish to drive fans towards their streaming service, with any reveal of the new Bond being exclusively announced on Prime Video.

It would almost certainly see a surge in streaming subscriptions. And such an announcement would still inevitably be covered by the world's press.

Global James Bond Day on 5 October, the 64th anniversary of the release of the first film Dr No, is fast approaching. So this date might be a good day for fans to mark in their diaries for a possible announcement.

We don't yet know what it will be called, or have a confirmed release date. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is currently writing the script, and Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct. They and the team may well already have a title in mind. Or, of course, they may just be calling it Bond 26 for now.

Most of the series have taken titles from the original Ian Fleming stories. Four of those remain unused - The Hildebrand Rarity, Risico, 007 in New York, and The Property of a Lady. Although elements from those stories have already been used in previous Bond films.

Fans have also been busy putting forward their own suggestions for potential titles. Since the accession of King Charles III in 2022, those suggestions have included On His Majesty's Secret Service, and King & Country.

As for a release date, it's been widely reported that the next film is likely to be released in 2028. That means it's almost certain that this will be the biggest ever gap between films, more than the six years and four months between 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

Only the Bond team themselves really know this.

But Amazon MGM do have the financial resources to plan well ahead, and explore various issues, such as how Bond will operate over multiple films; will there be an overriding arc that will cover his journey over the next decade etc; will there be a film every two years, every three years, every four or five?

Additionally, with such a huge investment, AmazonMGM will undoubtedly be keen to learn from Disney's experiences with Star Wars, and Marvel's experiences with its Marvel Cinematic Universe, in how best to use the Bond franchise.

While there might be appetite for multiple Bond spin-offs, eg Young Bond, the Miss Moneypenny adventures etc, they will also be wary that they don't over-saturate the market, and damage the films which are at the core of the Bond franchise.

The below contains spoilers for No Time To Die

Daniel Craig's farewell at the end of No Time To Die saw him on the island lair of the film's villain, Rami Malek's Safin, as it was struck by a volley of air strikes, with the super spy apparently finally meeting his demise.

Rumours have indicated that the next film might well reflect Bond's early years at the start of his MI6 career, in effect a reboot, which means that there won't be any pressure or sense of disappointment that the story won't reflect No Time To Die's conclusion.

And in any case, Bond fans have been reassured by the message that has appeared at the end of almost every Bond film - "James Bond will return".

It looks like soon we'll be finding out who that James Bond will be.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q.summary: Amazon MGM have been planning a new film for the Bond franchise. The next film is likely to be released in 2028, according to reports. Only six people have ever played Bond in the official film series.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.title: TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.text:
Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges.

According to state-owned al-Ahram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them.

They also had illegal firearms and munitions.

Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges.

Nine fellow defendants have been sentenced to life imprisonment, while seven have been acquitted.

Khalifa's lawyer said she would appeal the death sentence.

The verdict was first announced last month.

However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases.

During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them.

Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Ahram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips.

According to the state-run Akhbar al-Yom newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices.

According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of which were carried out..

The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7.summary: Sarah Khalifa and 11 others sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges. Nine others sentenced. Nine others have been sentenced to life imprisonment, seven have been acquitted. They were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them. They also had illegal firearms and munitions.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986.text:
For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.

Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.

Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.

And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do.

"They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.

He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else.

"They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May.

"The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."

Engelsman says they themselves initially had many of the same doubts that viewers will have.

"We've had all the same reactions that the audience has had to every part of this process like, 'Who would do that? What an idiot.'

"We've been through it all and we're just lucky enough to have come out the other side and realised, 'OK, this is actually all stuff that could work.'"

"Now we've filmed it, I'm just excited to show the world," Bourgeois says. "We've done our absolute best and the critics will be critics and I hope that we will prove them wrong."

Holland adds that he hopes people will give the show a chance before judging.

"Have a watch and if you don't like it, you're well within your rights, I can't force anyone to like anything."

For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.

Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.

The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.

That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.

Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different.

"As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.

Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.

By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".

While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen.

"It was the most gradual thing," he says.

He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.

For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.

There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour.

The Independent's three-star review described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".

The Guardian's review agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".

But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".

The FT also awarded the show three-stars and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".

It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".

Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going.

"That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.

Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

Bourgeois may be best known for his ecstatic trainspotting videos but he says his love of cars goes back just as far.

Growing up near Willesden Junction in London, there were plenty of trains to watch, but he was also fascinated by the cars outside his home.

"There was a particular Mitsubishi Legnum VR-4 that was outside my parents' flat window and I just loved it," he tells me. "I suppose with my social media, I'm just showing one of my passions and I have really wanted to let out that car enthusiasm too.

"It's nice that these two sides of my very strong passions are in harmony together and it's been a real pleasure to drive some of the cars on The Grand Tour."

His enthusiasm for transport more generally has already rubbed off on his co-presenters who say they've become "very educated by Francis on many things during long walks and long drives".

Bourgeois is even lobbying for The Grand Tour to devote an episode to another of his interests: power stations. And he has found a surprisingly receptive audience in Clarkson.

When the new trio met their predecessors, Bourgeois says seeing Clarkson in person gave him "a flutter in my tummy" and the pair bonded, inevitably, over trains, before moving on to power stations, and a lengthy discussion about cheeseburgers.

Engelsman says all three former presenters were supportive of their successors and "were very paternal and caring about it".

"They all seemed quite excited for there to be a new iteration," Engelsman says, adding that Clarkson even told them: "We'll look after you".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986.summary: The Grand Tour is a new series of The Grand Tours. James Engelsman and Thomas Holland are the first three to present the show since Top Gear and The Grand tour.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c87v.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c87v.text:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

Things came to a head on tour, where her stage fright went into overdrive and she suffered "just terrible, terrible anxiety".

"I become sensitive to sound, so it feels like you're screaming at me if you're talking normally," she says. "I can't process questions very well. I act twitchy and weird, and it seemed to get worse with perimenopause."

She says her behaviour became a "nightmare" for her team. Pressed for an example, she explains: "If you asked me whether I wanted still or sparkling water, I'd say, 'That's a question, and I can't answer questions right now'.

Well, it's not exactly Mariah Carey demanding baskets of puppies and forbidding eye contact, but Imbruglia was shaken up.

The day after one concert, she told her co-writers David Sneddon and Anu Pillai, "Guys, I think I'm going to have to quit my job because I can't cope with how I'm treating people before the show."

They helped to talk her down, putting her fight-or-flight instincts into context.

"What they helped me realise is that I was trying to stop the behaviour with willpower, and if I just relaxed into it and said to myself, 'You know, you're about to perform in front of a lot of people, it's natural that you're nervous', maybe I wouldn't be resisting it as much."

The impromptu therapy session inspired a new song, Upside Down - but Imbruglia is understandably frustrated that perimenopause isn't more widely understood, saying many women are rejected by their GP when they seek HRT treatment.

"My mum never talked to me about it," she reflects, "but looking back, I know she had a really bad one.

"Her anxiety was off the charts, too, and I have a lot more compassion now, because she had four kids. I've only got one."

As a child in Sydney, Imbruglia was drawn to performing. She'd squeeze lemon on her hair to make it blonder, and put on concerts of Whitney Houston covers for her neighbours.

Before long, she was cast in commercials for Coca-Cola and Twisties, and spent her Christmases singing carols in shopping centres.

"But when you turn 15 or 16, and you're into boys, you're like, 'Oh, that's really naff. I don't want to be doing that any more'," she laughs.

From that point onwards, Imbruglia became "basically unparentable".

"I was sneaking out and sleeping in someone's car on the beach, then getting busted.

"My parents were really strict - and my mum would turn up at parties with my picture, going, 'Have you seen this girl?'

"Socially, it was a disaster."

Music continued to be her solace. Dating a drummer, she switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits and Tori Amos, but the urge to sing remained.

You can see that hunger in a recently rediscovered photograph of a pre-fame Imbruglia, pressed up against the barriers of an INXS concert in 1992.

"It was my first ever concert," she says. "I was 15. I had white, tight jeans on."

In the photo, "everyone else is screaming but I'm looking at (Michael Hutchence) with this determination in my eyes.

"I'm studying him, like, 'How can I be up there too?'"

She got her chance in 1997 after quitting her role as builder's apprentice Beth Brennan in Aussie soap Neighbours.

Moving to London, she signed a deal with RCA Records and immediately scored an international hit with her first single, Torn.

Famously, the song was a cover – a fact journalists never let her forget, even though she co-wrote every other track on her debut album, Left of the Middle (lifetime sales, seven million copies).

"Yeah, I got famous on a song that I didn't write," she says now, "but there's more to what you bring to a song than whether you wrote the lyrics."

She still loves the song – "Torn was a beautiful gift" – but the furore around it fuelled her insecurities.

As a result, she essentially self-sabotaged her career. The lead single from her second album, That Day, was a free-verse stream-of-consciousness that sounded like a manic inner monologue.

"That was my rebellion against Torn," she says. "It doesn't have a chorus.

"That was my way of going, 'Can I get on with my life now? I've just started learning the craft of songwriting, I'm young, I didn't ask for this'."

In the midst of the madness, she auditioned for the lead role of Satine in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge – which counts as one of the stranger experiences of her career.

"The audition was, pretty much, 'Have an orgasm'," she grimaces. "Because I think that happens in the movie." (Indeed, Satine delivers a breathy boudoir monologue as she tries to seduce Ewan McGregor's character, Christian.)

But Imbruglia stresses it wasn't a creepy casting couch situation.

"It's Baz, that doesn't really fit," she says of the soft-hearted director.

"But I remember leaving and feeling really icky. Like, 'Ohhh, that was awful. Where's my mummy?'"

Back in the world of music, Imbruglia returned to more commercial sounds on hits like Wrong Impression (2002) and Shiver (2005). But sales dwindled and her fourth album was shelved by her label.

In the years that followed, she joined the Australian version of The X Factor and appeared in a UK production of Alan Ayckbourn's play Things We Do for Love, before making a tentative return to music with covers album Male (2015); and the more personal, introspective Firebird (2021).

"It was quitting music and coming back to it that gave me an appreciation of my abilities," she says.

"I might not be the best songwriter, even now, but there's only one me, and when I go inside myself and feel the emotion of what I'm writing about and deliver it, that's what my fans resonate with, and that's enough."

She certainly has a lot to say on Algorithm. As well as the frank discussion of mental health, the title track talks about her flirtation with internet conspiracy theories.

She won't say which ones ("I think it's irresponsible") but stresses the danger is omnipresent.

"There's a voice in my head that says, 'You don't want to click on that', and I'll click on it. It's like this compulsion.

"You have to change the settings. Don't allow yourself to be in a situation where your stress relief is scrolling on a phone in bed. It's just not healthy."

Ultimately, however, the album ends on a note of positivity.

Beautiful Love, co-written with Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody, is a soaring hymn to embracing your flaws and making peace with life's highs and lows.

"I've always made the joke that I'll never be a Buddhist because it's a middle path," she smiles.

"I like the pendulum to swing. Whether it's extreme joy or extreme pain, I like to feel the experience of life."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c87v.summary: Natalie Imbruglia's seventh album, Algorithm, is out on September 14. She says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD in midlife. She was diagnosed in mid life and has since switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn45.title: Pulp top the bill at 20th End of the Road Festival
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn45.text:
A sell-out crowd of 15,000 helped celebrate the End Of The Road Festival's 20th birthday this weekend, in one of the final events of the UK summer season.

Britpop luminaries Pulp closed the mainstage on Saturday night at the four-day event, near Blandford Forum, Dorset.

The event's anniversary line-up also included Irish indie-pop singer Cmat, New York art-rockers Geese and Canadian singer-songwriter Mac DeMarco.

More than 140 acts performed across the five music stages which showcased a mix of indie-rock, folk and alternative artists.

The festival was set in rolling countryside on Cranborne Chase – a protected National Landscape - and hosted comedians including Fern Brady and Adam Buxton in its Talking Heads arena.

Sheffield indie-rockers Pulp have never appeared at End Of The Road before but the band's frontman Jarvis Cocker has regularly attended and performed a headline solo Garden Stage set in 2019.

Throughout the set which included classics like Common People, This Is Hardcore, and Underwear, Jarvis treated the crowd to a sermon of Pulp history, with slideshows of artwork, postcards, and visuals from throughout the years.

Jarvis sang Happy Birthday to the festival and toasted to another 20 years before telling fans he will be taking a break for a while.

This year's event comes at the end of the warmest summer in the UK since records began in 1884, according to provisional Met Office figures, during which wildfires have been common across the country.

Issuing guidance ahead of the festival, organisers warned that the ground and vegetation remained "extremely dry" and that barbecues and open fires were "not permitted anywhere on site".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn45.summary: 15,000 crowd of 15,000 helped celebrate End Of The Road Festival's 20th birthday. The four-day event was held in the countryside on Cranborne Chase, Dorset. More than 140 acts performed across the five music stages.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: Recipe for success - the Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube star
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
When someone says "we need to talk", it often means one thing - it's time to break up.

After Amelia Dimoldenberg announced on Thursday her hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date would be turning off the fryers after one last series, some fans were begging for a second chance, while others agreed it was time to move on.

Over more than 10 years and 100 dates, Dimoldenberg's awkward flirting, deadpan silences and willingness to overshare has made her channel an unmissable stop for any celeb, single or not.

Before one last slurp on an orange soda, BBC Newsbeat looks back at some of the talk show's most iconic moments.

Chicken Shop Date grew out of a youth club project and interviews Dimoldenberg conducted with south London grime artists as a teenager for The Cut.

She's spoken about how hard she had to work in the early days to persuade guests to come on the channel.

Nearly five years into her series, in 2020, she bagged her first big name outside the rap scene: Oscar-nominated actor Daniel Kaluuya.

During the date, Dimoldenberg admitted she would turn around when fans shouted "chicken" at her in the street.

Her interview with the Get Out star pulled in five million views - a fraction of the audience she'd go on to attract, but evidence her hard work was clearly starting to pay off.

It laid the foundations for even bigger names to join Dimoldenberg, with Sir Paul McCartney, Lando Norris and Shania Twain among those placing orders.

Forgetting your date's name can be a guarantee that there won't be a second one. But in Dimoldenberg's case it created one of Chicken Shop Date's most memorable moments.

During a 2023 date, she discussed marriage proposals with Jennifer Lawrence.

When Dimoldenberg said she wouldn't know how it felt to be engaged, the Hunger Games star looked the host in the eye, and began:

"Did you just call me Phoebe?" Dimoldenberg responded.

The pair burst out laughing, but it wasn't the only time her date was caught thinking about someone else.

Pop star Sabrina Carpenter, who appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, didn't forget the host's name, but did confuse the show with Hot Ones - the YouTube series where celebrities eat progressively spicy chicken wings.

In a sign of her own rising stardom, Dimoldenberg took on the chilli challenge in the same year.

The spice in this series was reserved for the guests - some more than others.

After a couple of red carpet run-ins where there seemed to be palpable chemistry, actor Andrew Garfield's appearance on Dimoldenberg's show set the internet alight with speculation of genuine romance.

When he appeared on Chicken Shop Date, Garfield conceded it had been "vibey" between them for a while, although for some viewers the encounter didn't live up to expectations.

The following year, Dimoldenberg insisted the pair were just friends.

Garfield wasn't the only guest to seem to really hit it off with the host. Singer Billie Eilish was especially flirty, giggling after complimenting Dimoldenberg's body.

And after rapper Aitch came on the channel, rumours circulated it had kindled a real-life relationship, although neither ever confirmed this.

It was the clash of two interviewing titans - the master of the strategic pause and the queen of the awkward silence.

But when Louis Theroux met Dimoldenberg the big takeaway wasn't a new, personal revelation. It was a viral rap.

During the pair's 2022 date, the Chicken Shop Date host reminded the documentary maker of the time he spat some bars on his BBC series Weird Weekends, when his quest to become "the first white, middle-class gangsta rapper" took him to New Orleans in the US.

Despite the 20-year gap, Theroux was able to recall an impressive amount of Jiggle Jiggle, his rap about his love of red wine and the struggles facing the very tall owner of a compact car.

Music producers Duke & Jones added autotune to a TikTok clip of the moment, turning it into a viral sensation that's had almost 84 million views since it was uploaded.

Theroux eventually teamed up with the duo to record a new version of the song.

Unlucky in love Dimoldenberg hasn't had much success when it comes to second dates - but that doesn't stop her asking.

She's been turned down by artists from Central Cee and Digga D to Rosalía.

"When I was 17, I thought that I might meet the love of my life on a date in a chicken shop," she wrote in her farewell statement. "Since then, I've spent my entire twenties sat across from the most incredible people, people I'd always dreamt of meeting.

"All of them charmed me (some more than others), and I definitely charmed them."

With one final series in the pipeline, there's still hope for some rekindled connections.

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.summary: Amelia Dimoldenberg announced on Thursday her YouTube series Chicken Shop Date would be turning off the fryers after one last series. The show has been a hit for more than 10 years and 100 dates. The host has been dating stars since she was a teenager.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.text:
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.

The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.

The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.

"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.

"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.

The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.

There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her.

Such adulation - and scrutiny - has come quickly for Katseye.

Based in Los Angeles, the multinational girl group were only formed in 2023 as part of the online reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

The contest was created by Hybe, the South Korean entertainment company behind acts like BTS and Le Sserafim, and the US record label Geffen, home to Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones. Of the 120,000 who initially applied for the show, only six made it through.

Trained under the rigorous K-Pop system, they had a breakout year in 2025, first with the hyperactive electro-skronk of their single Gnarly, then with its follow-up, a slinky ballad called Gabriela that highlighted Daniela's Cuban-Venezuelan roots.

In London, their audience skewed young: The queue for pick and mix was longer than the one for the bar.

When Megan asked, "Whose first concert is this?" the air curdled with screams.

Throughout the show, fans shook lightsticks, parroted Katseye's dance moves and, in some cases, spontaneously burst into tears.

Many concert-goers also wore bindis, inspired by Lara, who has proudly incorporated her Asian heritage into her aesthetic.

One individual also came dressed as a courgette, a reference to Internet Girl's so-weird-it-almost-works refrain, "Eat zucchini".

The energy was infectious. And, if you looked closely, the parents were enjoying the show as much as their kids.

Even Spice Girl Melanie C is a fan, hosting a Q&A with the band during their first UK trip last October.

"They're incredible girls," she told the BBC earlier this summer. "They've got great music, they've got a great work ethic, and they're really beautiful, you know?

"Obviously, they've had a little drama, as happens with all bands, but they work so goddamn hard."

The drama began in February, when Manon announced she was taking a hiatus from the band to "focus on her health and wellbeing".

It came after the Swiss-Ghanaian singer told BBC News the band had been subject to racism and death threats; but fans also highlighted Katseye's gruelling schedule, suggesting they were being overworked.

In April, she posted a message to fans saying she was having "positive conversations" with Katseye's management, but not before she removed references to the band from her Instagram biography.

Then, just months after Manon stepped back, Sophia announced she was also going on hiatus to protect her "mental health and wellness".

"You can't pour from an empty cup," she posted on social media. "It's important to care for yourself."

Although it was hoped Sophia would return for the European leg of the Wildworld tour, that's proved impossible.

Her mother assured fans the absence is only temporary.

"Don't worry, this is for her own good," she told ABS-CBN News. "This is what I love about her management. They realise when the girls are tired.

"It's a good thing that she is resting so that she's stronger when she comes back."

It is not unusual for members of K-Pop bands to take a break when the mental or physical demands of the job become overwhelming.

Lia from the girl group Itzy took more than a year off work to seek treatment for "extreme levels of anxiety" in 2023-24; while Moka, a singer from Katseye's labelmates Illit, is currently on extended hiatus, also for anxiety.

In keeping with K-Pop tradition, Katseye honoured Sophia's place in the band during Tuesday's show, retaining her pre-recorded vocals on songs like Mean Girls and Pinky Up.

Manon's lyrics, however, were sung by other members of the band - presumably because her hiatus pre-dated production and rehearsals

Which brings me to a related point. After the tour's opened in Dublin on Tuesday, Katseye were accused of miming throughout their set.

But from what I could tell on Thursday, the member's microphones were live all night, with a backing track doubling their vocals at crucial moments.

On slower songs like Tonight I Might and My Way they proved more than capable as live performers.

Meanwhile, Lara's vocals on the solo showcase unloveu (proudly introduced as "the first Katseye song written by a member of Katseye") mixed power and emotion in a way that suggested the band have potential beyond the ear candy pop that's become their trademark.

Other highlights included Daniela's death-defying dance break, complete with aerial splits, that led into Gabriella; and Megan's technotronic shakedown at the end of Pinky Up.

For Yoonchae, the show's high point was Time Lapse, where she got to sing in her native Korean, while mingling with the crowd. ("Keep your hands to yourselves and don't throw any gifts on the stage for our safety," warned Lara, spoiling the atmosphere just a little).

The show ended on a powerful note, with Iconic By Mistake - the band's defiant response to an online hate campaign - and an extended romp through Gnarly, complete with a leather-studded rock remix.

All told, it was a stunningly confident and self-assured show from a band who could easily been diminished by personnel problems.

"This is not a goodbye," promised Yooncahe as Katseye waved goodbye. "We'll come back."

Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage would be a perfect fit.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.summary: Katseye played their first full concert in the UK on Saturday night. The band were only formed in 2023 as part of the reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e.title: 'Gromit was nearly a cat!': Secrets from 50 years of Aardman
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e.text:
Gromit was almost a cat. Shaun the Sheep was nearly given a voice. And Chicken Run helped change the Oscars forever.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story.

Founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976, Aardman has given us Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, the world's most successful stop-motion film.

But the journey from two teenagers "mucking about with plasticine" to an Oscar-winning animation powerhouse has often hinged on chance decisions, practical compromises and creative instinct.

Few examples are better than Gromit.

Wallace and Gromit became Aardman's most famous characters after animator Nick Park joined the studio in 1985.

But Gromit was not always a dog.

"I had this idea of an English guy who builds a rocket, in the basement of his house," recalled Park.

"I was thinking he may have a pet, probably a cat."

The switch was surprisingly simple.

"I started modelling the cat, and it was just very difficult, so I thought I'd do a dog instead!"

Park was developing A Grand Day Out at the National Film and Television School in London when Lord and Sproxton came to speak to students.

"We met him and thought, 'Oh, he's good'. In fact, he's very good. Now I know him, he's actually a genius," said Lord.

The combination was electric. A Grand Day Out was nominated for an Oscar in 1990, losing only to another Aardman production, Creature Comforts, also directed by Park.

Pointing to a poster of Wallace and Gromit floating over Bristol in a hot-air balloon, Lord reflected on their appeal.

"When they appear on the screen, you laugh before they do anything."

Park later won three more Oscars. Perhaps it was just as well he never mastered Gromit the Cat.

By the mid-1990s, Wallace and Gromit had made Aardman one of the most talked-about names in animation.

That success led to an unlikely meeting with Steven Spielberg.

At dinner with Spielberg and DreamWorks chief executive Jeffrey Katzenberg, they pitched what became Chicken Run.

"We want to do The Great Escape," Lord told Spielberg.

"I had always been a fan of Aardman," Katzenberg said. "And I had this secret ambition that someday there would be a way to work together."

Park remembered Spielberg's response.

"Spielberg said, 'The Great Escape is one of my favourite films, and I have 300 chickens on my ranch!' So it went very well."

No-one had ever made a 90-minute stop-motion feature from modelling clay. The budget was more than £20m, and Aardman insisted every frame would be shot in Bristol.

The gamble paid off. Chicken Run took more than $220m (£165m) worldwide and remains the highest-grossing stop-motion film ever made.

But it did not win an Oscar.

At the time there was no Academy Award for animated features.

"And so because they couldn't give Chicken Run a little golden man, they invented the category," said Radio 1 film critic Ali Plumb.

The Academy introduced the Best Animated Feature Oscar the following year.

"And a couple of years later, Wallace and Gromit won that Oscar for 'The Curse of the Were-Rabbit', so they got their own reward," Plumb said.

If Chicken Run proved Aardman could conquer Hollywood, another character would go on to conquer the world.

Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest global stars.

Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions.

"The beauty of Shaun is it transcends borders and cultures because it doesn't rely on the spoken word," said Aardman's Managing Director Sean Clarke.

"You can literally see Shaun the Sheep here in Bristol and in Outer Mongolia."

Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice.

"When we launched the Shaun the Sheep series, we were told to add voices," Clarke remembered.

The same argument resurfaced when Shaun got his own feature film in 2015.

"They said, 'You can't do 80 minutes without any dialogue'.

"But we stuck to our convictions, and I think it is now one of our most revered films."

Lord insists Shaun was not kept silent to boost international sales, it simply "seemed better that way".

However, the character's global appeal is undeniable. Clarke said Shaun has been sold into 170 countries and is especially popular in Asia.

"Shaun is actually our most valuable character now.

"Wallace and Gromit built the house, but Shaun keeps the lights on."

It is a remarkable journey for a company that started almost by accident.

Lord and Sproxton began while still at school, "playing with Dad's cine camera", as Sproxton remembered.

Their first character was a 'superhero dolt', with a cape and a habit of falling down holes.

They called him "Aard Man" as a joke.

"We just thought 'Aardvark' was a silly word, so we combined it with 'Superman', he explained.

To their surprise, their short cartoon was bought by the BBC Bristol TV programme, 'Vision On'.

"They asked us who to make the cheque out to," recalled Lord with a fond smile.

And so 'Aardman Animations' was born.

If that cheque gave them a company name, their next creation gave them a star.

Lord and Sproxton moved to Bristol to work on Take Hart, the successor to Vision On.

On this show they took what Lord called "a leap into the third dimension".

"Plasticine was cheap", Lord explained.

"The budgets were low, and you can work quickly with it."

Soon he had fashioned Morph, the simple little terracotta brown figure that can change shape into anything, hence his name.

"It was just so easy to squash him up and reform him as a dog, or a submarine, or a bird or anything," Lord said.

Morph became a hit with children and parents alike, and remains a fixture at Aardman's Bristol headquarters.

Back in 1989, Lord told a BBC West documentary The Animators he "hoped Morph will still be around in 30 years or so, and still be loved."

It has been 37 years since he said that, and an Aardman exhibition at Bristol's MShed Museum was recently packed with Morph superfans.

But Lord, now the studio's creative director, still comes into the office and playfully reshapes Morph while chatting.

I asked him what Wallace would make of it all.

"Oh, he'd probably just say 'Cracking careers lads!'" he smiled.
