https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Pjotr Sauer
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine

Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.

The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.

Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs

“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.

The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.

After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.

Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.

Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.

Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.

In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.

Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.

Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.

During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.

Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.

At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.

During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.

“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ben Doherty, Andy Ball and Nick Evershed
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Video credit: The Australian Ministry of Defence

In the near pitch blackness of a wet June morning, a US B-2 Spirit stealth bomber swoops from the sky, touching down on the outskirts of Brisbane to swiftly refuel – engines still running – at one of the US air force’s key allied bases. Before the sun is up, the nuclear-capable warplane is back in the air.

RAAF Base Amberley, about 50km south-west of Brisbane, is a vital staging point for US military operations across the region. But it is hardly alone.

This map shows every military base in Australia, which includes US- and Australian-run bases.

Analysts warn of a “saturation” of the continent by the US military, and argue that Australia’s most important security ally could drag the country unwillingly into war.

Amid the red dirt of Katherine, the runway at RAAF Base Tindal is being expanded to be able to better accommodate massive American B-52 bombers, the so-called “Stratofortresses”. These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask.

On the remote coast of Western Australia, a cluster of highly technological assets – deep space radar, space surveillance telescope, and the Harold Holt naval communication station – provide vital information to enable US submarine and space warfare.

The naval communication station is designed to reach submerged submarines. Its antenna array broadcasts on very low frequency radio.

The US-run Pine Gap, in the centre of the country, is regarded by some as the US military’s most valuable intelligence site outside the continental United States.

The satellite tracking and signals intelligence base detects missile launches, intercepts military communications and provides targeting information for US forces around the world.

Essentially incorruptible – difficult to access, physically or otherwise – in a desert valley in the centre of a massive continent, it downloads and transmits masses of data from powerful US satellites constantly monitoring vast swathes of the globe.

For the US military, Australia represents, in the words of one now-retired general, “location, location, location”.

Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here

US military presence in Australia, mapped – video

Why can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcast

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.

New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.

In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.

“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …

“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”

The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:

Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.

Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.

Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.

Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.

Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.

Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.

Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.

Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.

Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.

Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.

Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.

The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.

Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.

The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.

The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.

Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.

“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.

“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”

Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.

“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.

“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”

There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.

Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.

“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”

At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.

Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.

“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.

Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.

Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.

“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”

Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.

The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.

But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.

The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.

Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.

But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.

A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.

Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.

Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).

Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.

Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).

More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.

This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.

“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”

Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.

“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.

“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”

Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.

“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”

She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.

“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”

Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.

“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.

Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.

“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.

“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”

Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”

The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to 100 facilities across the continent. US military presence will continue to expand from next year.

Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.

A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.

The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.

The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.

The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.

The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.

The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.

“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.

Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities

Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.

Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing. Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.

Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.

The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, according to the airport operator, Angkasa Pura. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.

The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.

“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement. “Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”

Volcanic ash can damage jet engines, baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.

Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000ft) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.

Several ​schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents ​suffered eye irritation, and fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.

The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could ​include cloud-seeding to promote rain.

“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.

More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.

At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.

Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.

Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited from going within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.

With Agence France-Presse

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Flushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escape
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tory Shepherd
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
New research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirus

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Flushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.

And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens.

Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes.

Flinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in the Science of the Total Environment journal.

They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles.

That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols.

The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear.

Despite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet.

“Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said.

“Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure.

“The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.”

Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”.

In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote.

“Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.”

Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised.

She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments.

They are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.”

So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said.

Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet.

His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets.

“As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said.

The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down.

If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”.

Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said.

Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone.

“Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses.

“The less contact you have, the better it is.”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Andrew Messenger
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Pre-inquest conference into Queensland deaths hears witnesses did not hear any smoke alarms during 2023 fire

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A landlord was repeatedly warned about improperly installed smoke alarms before a house fire that killed a father and five children in Queensland in 2023, a coroner has heard.

Deputy state coroner Donald MacKenzie held a pre-inquest conference into the Russell Island deaths on Tuesday.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

No witness recalls hearing the sound of an alarm during the blaze, it heard.

The owner was fined $774 for improper installation in 2024, the maximum possible penalty under Queensland law. A conviction was not recorded.

The fire in the two-storey wooden Queenslander broke out on 6 August 2023. The house had been moved to the island and then renovated in 2013 before being rented privately.

Five children – two brothers aged four and others aged three, 10 and 11 – died in the blaze. Their father, 34, died after running into the fire to rescue them. None can be identified for legal reasons.

The children’s mother and father had fallen asleep in a converted “chill out” area underneath the house.

The father awoke to see thick black smoke and immediately raced upstairs, where the children were sleeping.

His partner also tried to get into the house, but was forced back by the fire. Another adult woman leapt off a balcony to safety and survived.

The Queensland fire department does not have a station on Russell Island, and vehicles must be ferried over in an emergency, a process that takes about 45-60 minutes, the court heard.

As a result, it was a paramedic who first arrived at the scene, arriving within minutes at about 6.26am.

“He recalls that the fire’s heat was so intense that he could feel it through his vehicle window, and could see the flames coming from the roof and smoke in a mushroom formation,” counsel assisting Corinne Leach told the court.

“[The children’s mother] was kneeling on the ground in complete distress with [the other woman] beside her. He asked if anyone else was inside, to which [the mother} replied: her five children, and lost all ability to communicate.”

The paramedic also tried to get into the building but was halted by the intense blaze. He instead focused on evacuating neighbouring homes. Rural firefighters arrived at 6.35am.

The court heard the home had poor wiring, an exposed electrical box and faulty power points, known to short out. It also had an extension cord running from a poorly operating power point in a child’s bedroom, from a double adapter, to the understory area.

The home’s smoke alarms also had not been updated in compliance with 2017 laws that applied to any tenancy renewed after January 2022 imposing additional safety measures for alarms.

The homeowner claimed not to have been aware of the legislative change, the court heard.

“[The mother] says that she raised the issue of non-working smoke alarms with the home’s owner, but nothing was done about it,” Leach told the court.

“No witness recalls hearing a smoke alarm sounding at all prior or during the fire.”

MacKenzie has been tasked with investigating seven issues, including whether legally installed fire alarms might have prevented the deaths, and whether the emergency service response to the fire was adequate.

He will also consider whether the presence of any additional emergency service resources located on the island could have prevented the deaths.

Fire investigators have been unable to identify the cause of the blaze, and could not categorically rule out that it was lit deliberately, the court heard.

The inquest has been listed to sit for 10 days in November, to hear from 16 witnesses.

Draft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder content

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.

Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.

Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.

New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.

They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.

The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.

“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.

Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.

The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.

“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.

“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”

The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.

“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”

The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.

The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.

“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.

“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.

“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”

A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.

“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.

“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”

Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.

“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”

Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.

“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”

Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: New laws will allow users to opt out of powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into their feeds. Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content. Platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today.

Before we say goodnight, let’s look at what made the top headlines:

Former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues.

Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation’s super policy, saying it would have a “minute” impact on inflation. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has savaged the plan, saying it was a threat to the compulsory super rules.

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced two key pieces of legislation will be introduced to parliament this week to tackle corruption in the state.

Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”.

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.

Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”.

Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey.

Guardian Australia and the ABC were once again refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria.

A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences.

About 80 protesters gathered to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance by US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of an international dance act.

Another Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance. There are still 35 Australians missing.

Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning!

An Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance.

There are still 35 Australians who remain unaccounted for in the region.

Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom accuse One Nation of ‘practising censorship’ after shunning reporters from press conference

Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom have criticised One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, for barring reporters from a press conference.

Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave.

AJF’s executive director, Peter Greste, said:

Australia’s strong democracy means journalists have the ability to interrogate politicians on the behalf of the people who hire them – the voters. It isn’t always comfortable, but that freedom is one of the reasons our political system is one of the world’s most stable and effective.

No individual politicians or political party should have the right to choose whether a media outlet can scrutinise them. This is democracy 101, when transparency and accountability are lost, citizens are deprived of their right and ability to know what is going on.

Any politician deciding who gets to scrutinise them is practising censorship, and in a democracy, that’s something we should never accept.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to give us your support. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Following the latest updates in the Alan Jones trial?

Nour Haydar and Amanda Meade will be answering reader questions in an upcoming podcast episode of Alan Jones on Trial.

If there’s a piece of evidence, legal process, or courtroom exchange you would like them to explain, submit your question via email to australia.fullstory@theguardian.com.

Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance of US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of international dance act, Burn the Floor: Luminous.

Striking workers – including ushers, food and beverage attendants, stage managers, ticketing staff and more – will establish a picket line from 3.30pm and hold a rally from 6pm outside Hamer Hall, where Gray is scheduled to perform, on Friday.

The state government-run Arts Centre is Australia’s largest performing arts venue, employing around 900 workers, some 600 of whom are casuals. Hundreds are expected to join the strike.

The Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) Victoria, and the Electrical Trades Union have been bargaining with the Arts Centre on a new enterprise agreement since March.

Pay remains the sticking point. The expired enterprise agreement saw wages increase by 1% every six months, and many of the lowest (Band 1) wages in the expired agreement are now well below the national minimum wage. More than a third of employees are classified as Band 1.

A spokesperson for the Arts Centre said all workers were paid at least the national minimum wage and that they had immediately adjusted the pay of workers whose wages had fallen below national baselines after the Fair Work Commission’s 2026 annual wage review.

The Arts Centre has offered workers a pay rise of 3% annually, the equivalent of the Victorian government wages cap. But workers say they need a 7% annual pay rise to make up for wage stagnation since 2022.

A union petition in support of the workers calling on the state government to increase funding to the arts and arts workers had nearly 3000 signatures at the time of writing.

CPSU Vic Secretary, Jiselle Hanna, said:

The decision to interrupt Macy Gray’s show has not been made lightly – but we are left with no choice until the government funds the Arts Centre properly.

Vicki Ward (Minister for Creative Industries) has the opportunity to sweep in and stop this industrial action by committing to paying workers fairly.

MEAA deputy chief executive, Adam Portelli, said:

Workers are at a point where they simply can’t afford to accept another agreement that leaves them falling behind.

This is about protecting the future of a major cultural institution as much as it is about workers’ pay.

Outside the gates of Israel’s Canberra embassy, a lonely saxophone played as about 80 protesters gathered on Tuesday to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

Frankcom was killed by the Israel Defense Forces in April 2024 alongside other humanitarians while driving to deliver basic aid to the Gaza Strip.

The findings of an Israeli investigation last month suggested there was no suspicion of criminal misconduct surrounding her death despite a previous finding there had been failures in how the attack was carried out. No charges were laid.

A group, dressed in red to symbolise blood, passed between them a white, tightly bound cloth, designed to look like the dead body of a baby, AAP reports.

Mourning the life of his wife’s oldest friend, Karuna Ratna Bajracharya told the crowd:

I’m losing my faith in humanity when there is no justice.

I can see that when our leaders fail us, when justice fails, when international law fails.

The protesters called for the Israeli ambassador, Hillel Newman, to be expelled from Australia. At the time Newman said he felt deep sorrow for Frankcom’s family but refused to apologise for the strikes on aid vehicles.

Protesters say the response did not go far enough. Bajracharya, a lifelong Labor voter, said he was disheartened by the government’s sustained ties with Israel. He said:

They have let me down dramatically. They have let down Zomi Frankcom.

A letter to the minister in late August, understood to have been written by Australians previously onboard a Gaza-bound Global Sumud Flotilla, demanded an independent investigation into the IDF’s actions.

The group had not yet heard back, Jewish pro-Palestinian activist Anny Mokotow told the crowd. Before reading out the letter, Mokotow said:

We have to fight against this as much as possible. We do it for Zomi Frankcom and those who have died senselessly with her – for their bravery, generosity and selflessness.

Federal eSafety commissioner failed to participate in Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes, report reveals

Despite the centrality of apps and social media-type platforms to the incidents that triggered the Victorian government inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes, the federal eSafety commissioner did not participate in it.

Finding 37 of the report said:

The Committee is disappointed that the federal eSafety Commissioner declined to participate in this Inquiry.

The committee found that the community felt social media platforms should take greater responsibility for the “harmful targeting” of LGBTQ+ people on their platforms.

It also recommended the state government advocate to the federal government for “a dedicated inquiry into best practice safety features of dating apps utilised by Australian users”, and to ensure that all apps operated under “an enforceable and strengthened Australian Online Dating Code”.

Grindr and Match Group participated in the inquiry, but other apps did not.

Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes hands down findings

Hate crimes against the LGBTQ+ community are under-reported, often not recognised as hate crimes by police, and frequently committed by “thrillseekers” enabled by “the relative permissibility of homophobic acts in society”, a Victorian government inquiry has found.

A legislative council inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes in Victoria handed down its final report to parliament this afternoon. It included 41 findings and 35 recommendations to the state government to strengthen prevention and policing of hate crime related to gender or sexuality, and to fund LGBTQ+ health and community organisations and legal centres to better support victims and the wider community.

The inquiry found that there was significant mistrust of law enforcement among the LGBTQ+ community, which led to under-reporting of crimes against them.

It also found police often did not recognise or record the prejudicial element of the hate crime when it was reported. The committee recommended practical tools be developed to stop hate crime falling through administrative cracks in law enforcement, and an independent evaluation of Victoria police’s LGBTQ+ awareness training.

The inquiry was established after Guardian Australia reported in 2024 on a spate of more than a dozen, separate cases of gay men being allegedly attacked by people they met through dating apps.

A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences, AAP reports.

Ian Campbell, 56, and his daughter Hannah, 23, died on Monday morning when the aircraft crashed south of Brisbane, sparking a large grass fire.

Tributes to the father and daughter highlighted the family’s support for their local community and Campbell’s contributions to the agricultural sector.

The fourth-generation dairy farmer founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company in Queensland and also ran Manana Pastoral in the Goondiwindi region, producing olive oil, lamb and beef.

Goondiwindi mayor Lawrence Springborg said the family had the support, prayers and goodwill of the community, and the pair would be greatly missed. Campbell founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company with his wife, Jane.

Springborg told the ABC:

We feel their grief deeply and what makes it also so hard is that the Campbell family were so generous in their support of the local community.

The Campbell family had raised more than $70,000 for the Royal Flying Doctor Service and invested in agriculture, Springborg noted.

National Farmers’ Federation president Hamish McIntyre said the loss of the father and daughter was an “absolutely heartbreaking tragedy”.

Campbell was a highly respected figure in Australian agriculture and a longtime friend, he said.

Hannah was a bright young woman with her whole life in front of her.

McIntyre said his thoughts were with the family, their many friends and everyone touched by “this devastating loss’’.

Guardian Australia and the ABC have again been refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria.

One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, is due to address the media over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use.

Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave.

Pickering has rejected his ex-partner’s claims as “false”. According to The Australian, he said in a statement:

They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them.

Reporters from The Australian, who broke the story, were not barred from attending the press conference.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

The opposition started on housing, trying to pressure the government over its building targets, and the impact of its housing tax policies.

They then pivoted to the tobacco excise and tried to wedge the government over some comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns questioning the current excise level.

The health minister, Mark Butler, accused Angus Taylor of playing “follow the leader” with Pauline Hanson – the Coalition has pledged to cut the excise by 80% (a week after One Nation promised a 75% cut).

Independent Dai Le asked the government to review her outer western Sydney electorate’s health priority status to bring in more doctors, but Butler said it was “complicated”.

I’ll be honest, it felt like a pretty long and dry question time to me.

And on that note, I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok for the rest of the afternoon. See you back here bright and early tomorrow!

Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey.

Two-thirds of respondents now expect mortgage rates to rise, the survey showed, reflecting a near consensus among economists that the Reserve Bank will hike again this year and potentially as early as later this month.

Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of forecasting, said fears of higher rates were weighing particularly heavily on the mood of mortgaged homeowners.

As petrol prices push back towards $2.10 a litre, Hassan said “the mortgage belt is tightening up on spending plans”.

Westpac’s gauge of house price expectations dipped but showed more respondents expected prices to be higher over the next 12 months than lower. A little over 32% expect property values to decline over the coming year, with 20% expecting no change and 42% anticipating an increase (6% weren’t sure).

Westpac also today has joined the other major banks in predicting the RBA will hike again, picking the November meeting as the most likely time.

Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, said, the main reasons for changing the call “are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from a datacentre focused investment boom”.

While the housing sector is playing out weaker than earlier forecast, the outlook for overall growth is now firmer and the tech sector is adding new cost pressures not evident previously.

Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”.

The government is required to release an IGR at least every five years under the charter of budget honesty, but can be more frequent (the most recent was in 2023).

In the words of Treasury officials, the reports “examine the long-term sustainability of current policies and how demographic, technological and other structural trends may affect the economy and the budget”.

Artificial intelligence is likely to be a major feature of this year’s report, given its potential to transform the way we work and live over coming years and decades.

That said, Treasury officials have already advised they expect AI will only help productivity growth return to historical levels, rather than unleash a new wave of prosperity.

The IGR will also look at the effects of an ageing population on the economy and the country’s finances. The last IGR highlighted how compulsory super had lightened the burden of paying for aged pensions.

The first IGR was delivered in 2002 under then treasurer Peter Costello, and this year’s report will be the seventh.

After a final dixer to Mark Butler, the PM calls time on QT. Kate Chaney stands up looking annoyed – she was probably due to get the next question.

Liberal MP Garth Hamilton asks Anthony Albanese if he will scrap a $5,000 cap on allied health services for veterans, instead of spending $150m on an “overseas climate talk fest” (the COP climate summit). It’s an issue the opposition pushed heavily last sitting fortnight – and called for the minister responsible to be sacked.

Albanese says the government has increased the fees for allied health workers to stop disincentivising treatment for veterans.

Now the review is after $5,000, that will be more than 12 visits. And then, if further care is required, if there’s a clinical need, then they’ll receive it. Importantly, changes will not impact veterans on the special rate disability pension, on the totally and permanently incapacitated pension, or determined to be catastrophic injured. These changes come into effect on July 27, and the government continues to consult.

Butler refutes claim tobacco policies have ‘led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes’

Take three: Liberal MP Mary Aldred, who was on a Coalition-led parliamentary inquiry that recommended cutting the tobacco excise, has a go now to corner the government over the policy.

She again quotes NSW premier Chris Minns warning on the impact of the excise policy, and asks if the health minister will “admit Labor’s failed tobacco policies have led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes?”

The health minister, Mark Butler, says he begs to differ and that smoking rates have been going down despite the hiked up excise.

I don’t agree with that. The Institute of Health and Welfare, which has been the statutory authority under governments of both political persuasions for many, many years, says otherwise as well.

I think we should all be glad the authoritative body set up under statute, supported at least until today, by both major political parties, have said that smoking rates over the last three years have declined by about half a million on daily adult smoking rates.

Labor fumes over Coalition question on tobacco excise

Nationals frontbencher Anne Webster asks the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, why he is “refusing to protect his own constituents” by supporting an excise cut, after a tobacco store in his electorate was firebombed overnight. Mulino was asked about the firebombing in an interview this morning but wouldn’t provide any details on it.

There’s a bunch of back and forth over whether the question is within standing orders or not. Milton Dick calls part of the question a slur, and the government argues that it doesn’t go to Mulino’s portfolio at all.

Webster has another crack and asks why Mulino is “refusing to protect Australians …” which gets some more groans and Dick once again tells Webster to remove that part of the question completely.

Finally we get to the answer.

Mulino defends himself, saying he did answer the question about the firebombing responsibly, because, “what would’ve been irresponsible is for me to speculate on live TV about what actually happened this morning and what might have driven it.”

Can I quote the illicit tobacco and e-cigarette commissioner: ‘Lowering tax on its own is not likely to resolve the criminal side of the market. It does not remove demand, eliminate supply, or the underlying profit opportunities, they, as the organised criminals, can undercut prices no matter where we see the excise.’ We have said repeatedly a responsible approach is to continue our policy on enforcement.

Angus Taylor gets on to the wedge train and tries to pressure the government over comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns again, this time on the tobacco excise.

This morning Minns (who has publicly questioned the efficacy of the excise remaining high) said: “It’s perversely driving a situation where you’re seeing more people, not less people, smoking because they’ve got access to readily available cheap [black market] cigarettes.

The health minister, Mark Butler, says the government is “not interested in joining the Coalition, in following the leader, that he pathetically appears committed to be playing with the One Nation party”.

We’re not interested in joining the Coalition in a price discounting war with organised crime.

We won’t be joining in a policy plucked out of thin air, with one apparent objective, to go a little bit further than One Nation … And the member for New England [Barnaby Joyce] is pumping his fist. He knows what’s going on here. They know this follow the leader game that he’s playing.

In the middle of his answer, Labor MP Matt Burnell gets kicked out for shouting too much.

Hundreds are expected to join the strike, with some 600 casuals expected to take part. Workers say they need a 7% annual pay rise to make up for wage stagnation since 2022.

Victorian One Nation leader says his actions ‘hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian One Nation leader, Warren Pickering, has admitted he “made mistakes” in his 20s, including using ecstasy, methamphetamines and marijuana, losing his licence multiple times for drink driving and hurting people he loved.

But he has denied claims by his ex-partner, published by The Australian, that he smoked ice – also known as crystal meth – in front of children and said he was considering legal action against the publication at a press conference on Tuesday. Guardian Australia and the ABC were barred from attending the press conference.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Accompanied by James Ashby, One Nation’s national director, and his daughter and stepson, Pickering said he was “no angel” as a young man and used illegal drugs in his 20s.

“Never would I have ever said that I was somebody who was a drug addict. I did use them … as a young man and I’m not proud of that,” Pickering said.

He listed ecstasy, methamphetamine, speed and marijuana, but denied using ice or smoking it while his children were home.

“No, I did not,” Pickering said, when asked directly.

Pressed by a reporter about whether he had used ice, Pickering said “ice is not on that list.”

When the reporter said methamphetamines are ice, Pickering replied: “Well, speed”.

“Look, guys, I’m clearly not as familiar with the terms … as you would like me to be,” he said.

“I wasn’t an experienced drug taker.”

Pickering also confirmed he lost his driver’s licence three times for drink driving.

“I believe I lost my licence for drink driving as an 18-year-old, and again as a 20-year-old, and then probably a decade later, I believe they were low-level drink driving,” he said.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Pickering said his actions “hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever”. But he said he had “changed his life dramatically” for the sake of his daughter and three stepsons, stopped using drugs and joined the Australian Defence Force, which he said gave him a sense of purpose.

“That’s what inspired me to engage in the political sphere to provide service to community in a different way, post-service,” he said.

Ashby also spoke, telling reporters a handwritten note from Pickering published by The Australian, which references “sexual deviance”, was in relation to “behaviour that involved the couple’s open relationship”.

“They opened that relationship to a third person, and at the same time, Mr Pickering was exploring his own sexuality,” Ashby said.

Pickering said he was “working with the lawyers” to get the stories taken down and was receiving advice about possible defamation action.

Reporters from The Australian were able to attend the press conference at Crown Casino. However, reporters from both Guardian Australia and the ABC were asked by Ashby to leave after identifying the media outlet they worked for.

He also confirmed he lost his driver’s licence three times for drink driving.

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

Hungary told 10 Russian diplomats “engaged in activities … unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention” to leave the country, foreign minister Anita Orbán said (11:09), prompting a furious reaction from Moscow threatening Budapest with “harsh and painful” response (12:22).

Hungary’s PM Péter Magyar said the decision was taken to “defend our country’s sovereignty” (16:32).

The EU backed Hungary’s decision, saying it was “an expected reaction” in response to “Russia’s persistent campaign in using hybrid attacks against the EU” (12:51).

US president Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin spoke on the phone, discussing the latest in US-led peace talks after peace envoys Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend (16:32).

A Kremlin aide said the two leaders discussed the state of the Russian aggression on Ukraine, and discussed prospects for a potential broader restoration of US-Russia relations (16:45).

These talks come as Ukraine’s allies met online and urged partners to help Kyiv boost its defences amid expectations of continued Russian attacks over the winter (14:28, 15:29, 15:47).

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested he hoped to meet Trump later this month to discuss missile defence, among other things (10:57).

Several European countries condemned Serbia’s decision to hold a ceremonial funeral for Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić, stressing the incompatibility of the move with the country’s aspirations to join the EU (13:16, 15:23, 15:35).

The European Commission joined in condemnations today, after facing harsh criticism from Bosnia over its comments yesterday (12:48), but said it was “looking into” the issue without suggesting any immediate moves against Serbia (12:32).

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.

City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.

Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.

In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.

“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.

Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.

“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.

The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.

“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, we offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.

BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
