Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.

Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.

The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.

Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.

With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.

The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.

Polish-Belarusian journalist and activist Andrzej Poczobut has returned to Belarus on a visit, a Polish ⁠newspaper reported on Tuesday, nearly five months after he was freed from a Belarusian prison and transferred to Poland ⁠in a prisoner ⁠exchange, Reuters said.

Poczobut, a ​member of Belarus’ Polish minority, was arrested in March 2021 and sentenced in 2023 to eight years in ⁠prison on charges of inciting ethnic hatred and harming Belarusian national security.

Poland said the charges were politically motivated and repeatedly called for ⁠his release. Poczobut was freed and transferred to Poland as part of a ​prisoner exchange in April, but immediately ‌signalled that he wanted ‌to return to Belarus.

“On Tuesday morning, Andrzej Poczobut crossed the Polish-Belarusian border ‌and headed to his hometown of Grodno,” Gazeta Wyborcza, a Polish newspaper with which he has long cooperated, reported.

“He intends to meet his family and colleagues from the Union of Poles in Belarus. The trip is expected to last a week,” it said.

Poczobut was awarded in absentia the European Parliament’s 2025 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, a prestigious human rights award, for his “brave fight for freedom of expression ⁠and the democratic future” of Belarus.

Belarusian exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya responded to Poczobut’s decision in a statement:

“Andrzej Poczobut’s decision to return to Belarus shows extraordinary courage. It doesn’t mean repression has ended. Arrests & intimidation continue. I fully support Andrzej. International attention is vital to his safety. Every Belarusian must be able to come home without fear.”

According to the National Research Council (CNR), the summer of 2026 was the hottest recorded in the Italy since 1950, as the country battled a wave of wildfires and the largest glacier in the Dolomites suffered a record loss of mass.

The CNR said on Monday that temperatures during the summer months even surpassed the previous record set in 2003, an exceptionally hot summer that had long been seen as difficult to repeat.

The average temperature across Italy this summer was 24.3C, measured 2 metres above the ground, compared with 23.6C in 2003, said Lorenzo Arcidiaco of the CNR.

The average temperature in August was 25.6C, beating the previous records of 24.6C in 2024 and 24C in August 2017, Arcidiaco said.

“The data suggest that 2026 will end as the hottest year since 1950.”

Meanwhile, wildfires that have hit Sicily in recent days continued to burn on Monday, forcing thousands of residents and tourists to leave their homes and holiday accommodation.

Firefighters were battling blazes in several parts of the island, days after the death of Salvatore Giglia, 26, who suffered severe burns while trying to fight a fire near his home and land in Ciminna, near Palermo.

In Palermo province, fires broke out in Castronovo di Sicilia and Bolognetta, while in Trapani province flames burned woodland near the Zaffarana dam.

The extreme temperatures have also taken a heavy toll on the Marmolada glacier, the largest in the Dolomites.

The glacier suffered a record loss of mass this summer, according to data presented on Monday by the University of Padua, the Veneto environmental protection agency and the Italian Glaciological Foundation.

The Marmolada retreated by an average of about 23 metres over the summer and its surface area fell from 92 hectares to 83 hectares.

Experts said the only comparable loss was recorded in 2022, when part of the glacier collapsed after a heatwave brought unusually high temperatures, killing 11 people.

Let’s take a quick look at other news from around Europe.

Meanwhile, Romania has issued a air alert to residents in the eastern part of the country amid concerns about a potential drone identified in the neighbouring Moldova, likely flying in from Ukraine.

Prefect of Iași County, Constantin Dolachi-Pelin, told Agerpress news agency that the drone entered Romanian territory from the Republic of Moldova.

Two F-18 fighter jets were also scrambled to respond to the incident, Romanian defence ministry said.

The warning also forced a brief suspension of flights at Iași international airport.

Let’s see if we get a bit more detail on the incident later.

Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone for an hour on Tuesday, days after US envoys travelled to Moscow and Kyiv in a renewed push to revive stalled peace talks over Ukraine.

According to Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, the two leaders discussed the war in Ukraine, with Trump stressing his desire to achieve a breakthrough in peace efforts during his presidency.

Trump’s special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend, but the meetings failed to produce a breakthrough. Russia resumed large-scale attacks on Kyiv on Monday night after a brief lull that coincided with the US visit to the Ukrainian capital.

Ushakov said Putin gave Trump an “objective and detailed assessment” of developments on the battlefield. Putin has repeatedly sought to portray Russian forces as making gains at the front, while at times claiming the capture of Ukrainian territory that remains outside Russian control.

According to Ushakov, Trump argued during the call that ending the war in Ukraine could pave the way for a broader restoration of US-Russia relations.

Ushakov also said Putin stressed to Trump that Russia had “no hostile plans whatsoever” towards Europe.

Trump has in recent days insisted that Putin would not attack Nato territory, playing down concerns in European capitals that Russia could eventually test the alliance with some form of military incursion.

Meanwhile, we have just heard from the Kremlin on a phone call between US president Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

The pair talked about the visit of US peace envoys to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend, and prospects for their bilateral relations.

Kremlin claims that Trump would like to see US-Russia ties restored during his presidency, while Putin assured him that he had no hostile plans towards Europe.

We will bring you more on this shortly.

Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar commented on his government’s decision to expel ten Russian diplomats from the country.

In a very brief statement echoing what his foreign minister, Anita Orbán, announced earlier (11:09), he said:

“The Hungarian government has ordered ten diplomats from the Russian Embassy in Budapest to leave the country. They carried out activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats. We will defend our country’s sovereignty.”

He did not comment on Russia’s response after Moscow threatened with “harsh and painful” actions in retaliation (12:22).

Back to the videoconference on Ukraine (15:29), Germany’s defence minister Boris Pistorius urged partners to help Kyiv prepare for winter as it faces “race against time,” as “we can expect Russian air raids to increase again once temperatures drop and the damage will be even greater.”

A senior Pentagon official Elbridge Colby also warned that allies “must be prepared for a protracted conflict and for Ukraine’s requirements to persist in the months and years ahead.”

“Europe’s greater assumption of responsibility for its own defence is fully consistent with a strong and viable Ukrainian defence, provided that Europe continues to act with requisite seriousness and urgency,” he said.

Colby also said Europe “must not slacken” in its remilitarisation efforts.

“Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security by helping to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken. The United States stands ready to continue supporting this effort.”

Separately, Germany’s Pistorius also warned that Ukraine’s supporters face being “targeted by Russia” with “hybrid means to sow uncertainty in order to erode our social cohesion, democratic our democratic principles and weaken our willingness to support Ukraine.”

He recalled the recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in this context, but insisted Germany was “unwavering” in its support to Ukraine.

“These attempts will not produce the intended outcome,” he said.

The UK has joined the growing chorus of countries criticising Serbia for the pomp and the participation of state officials in yesterday’s funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić.

In a short statement, the UK government said that:

“The UK’s Special Envoy to the Western Balkans, Dame Karen Pierce DCMG, summoned the Serbian Chargé d’Affaires to condemn the involvement of Serbian state and military officials in the funeral of Ratko Mladić.”

Europe minister Lord Wood of Anfield said that Mladić “presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the second world war,” and so “the denial and whitewashing of his crimes is an affront to international law and directly undermines regional stability and trust.”

“The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladić’s victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history. Political leaders and public institutions have a responsibility to look to the future, not to the past, and to act in ways that support regional reconciliation, not to reopen old wounds.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was established by the UN Security Council and Serbia is obliged to respect its judgments.

That is why today we summoned the Serbian Chargé d’Affaires. Glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region.

The UK remains firmly committed to international justice, accountability, and lasting reconciliation across the Western Balkans and will continue to work with partners across the region and internationally in support of peace, justice and a secure and prosperous future for all communities.”

Germany will ⁠deliver Patriot air defence missiles ⁠to ⁠Ukraine from ​its national stocks, defence minister ⁠Boris Pistorius.

“I ⁠decided to ​deliver ‌urgently ‌needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles ‌from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine,” Pistorius said at a videoconference of ‌defence ministers from countries supporting Ukraine, in comments reported by Reuters.

Pistorius ​said Germany would also step up ⁠the provision of air-to-air ​missiles and ​would ​continue to ​deliver ‌drones and long-range ​ammunition ​to Ukraine.

EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas ramped up pressure on Serbia, condemning “the public glorification afforded to a convicted war criminal in Belgrade” after yesterday’s funeral of Ratko Mladić.

Kallas said the ceremony was “an affront to the memory of the victims, their families, and all those who suffered during the conflicts in the Western Balkans.”

“True reconciliation cannot be built on revisionism, the denial of genocide or the honouring of perpetrators.

Serbia’s path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment to fundamental European values and historical truth. There is no place in Europe for the glorification of war criminals.”

Several other EU foreign ministers also condemned the memorial service and put a question mark on Serbia’s accession path, including Austria’s Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Lithuania’s Kęstutis Budrys, and Sweden’s Maria M Stenergard.

Separately, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s foreign minister Elmedin Konaković ordered two Serbian diplomats to leave the country in protest at Serbian government officials taking part in the funeral. Earlier, he also withdrew Bosnian diplomats from Serbia (12:48).

The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK, have issued a statement saying they ⁠would support or consider restrictions ​on trade in goods with Israeli ⁠settlements in the West Bank that are illegal ⁠under international law.

The countries confirmed “their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements which are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and other measures, in accordance with their national procedures,” the nations’ foreign ministers said in a statement.

“The government of Israel must immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers, ensure accountability for settler violence, and investigate allegations against Israeli forces,” it added.

The (relatively new) UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has been speaking in the House of Commons, setting out the government’s position.

Taking a much stronger stance than his predecessor, Yvette Cooper, Miliband said the government would now take the official stance that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, while announcing an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories, among a number of other policies.

You can read more in our UK politics live blog here:

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, has said that Ukraine will ⁠be able to buy crucial ⁠parts for ⁠Patriot ​air defense systems through the ⁠next €3.2bn (£2.7bn; $3.7bn) disbursement ⁠from the EU’s support ​loan.

“Together with Nato secretary general Rutte, I welcome the agreement ‌by Member States on the ​derogation for Ukraine to purchase crucial products for Patriot ⁠air defence systems,” she ​said in ​a statement.

Ukraine heavily relies on advanced air defence systems, mainly US Patriot interceptors, to protect its skies from Russian ballistic missile attacks. But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to strikes.

After a brutal summer of deadly Russian missile and drone attacks, Ukraine last week requested an exemption from Buy European procurement rules to acquire US-made Patriot interceptors using the EU’s €90bn support loan.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Artworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heist
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Jon Henley and Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled

French police are hunting two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum on the French Riviera after breaking in through a hole cut in its garden fence.

Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, about 10 miles west of Nice, said the pair appeared to have been “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, which houses works by the French impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir in his former home.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The theft early on Tuesday is the latest in a string of recent museum heists in France and across Europe, including the brazen break-in at the Louvre in Paris last October, when ⁠thieves stole crown jewellery worth €88m (£75m), including tiaras, a brooch, necklaces and earrings.

Masson told the local broadcaster Ici Azur that the two thieves sliced through the museum garden fence with an electric knife or metal saw, entered the building through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames.

Police arrived about five minutes after the museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am, Masson said, which “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”.

Two of the four works taken were abandoned in the museum gardens during the getaway, the mayor, a member of the far-right National Rally (RN), said. His office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m.

The two stolen paintings were Young Woman ‌at the Well and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano. Both were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, in Paris. “They’re Renoirs … you cannot sell them like that,” Masson said.

The paintings the thieves abandoned were both portraits: Portrait of Madame Pichon, and Coco Reading, a portrayal of Renoir’s young son Claude.

The Renoir Museum was established in 1960 in the mansion where the painter ‌died aged 78 in 1919. It houses about a dozen of his paintings and about 40 sculptures, as well as photos, furniture and objects including his easel and wheelchair.

Masson called for greater security for museums around France. “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art,” the mayor said.

An art theft expert, James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register, said thieves were increasingly targeting valuable artefacts. “Sadly, without further funding to improve museum security, we are likely to see an increase in the number of museum thefts,” he said.

“Each time thefts occur, it draws yet more attention to the perception of these museums as relatively easy targets. That can only encourage some criminals to consider them as straightforward places to steal from,” he told the Associated Press.

Europol, the pan-European police organisation, said last month robberies at European museums were becoming increasingly violent, with some thieves brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives.

The Europol report suggested specialist property crime or art theft gangs, who usually avoid violence, were being replaced by “individuals who often have histories of involvement in other types of crime”, who were recruited through social media.

The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they allegedly grabbed in the seven-minute heist have not been found. Two of the suspects have reportedly told police the mastermind behind the heist was disappointed by the haul and thought “they could have taken more”.

Italian police recently recovered paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m stolen from a museum in March. However, last month four of the most important works by the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Thieves broke in through a hole cut in the garden fence of the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France. Two of the four works taken were abandoned in the museum gardens during the getaway. The thieves are believed to have cut the clips securing the artwork frames. The paintings were both portraits: Portrait

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Organised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Jon Henley, Europe correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports

Europe live – latest updates

The illegal trade in tobacco is booming in the EU, according to a report by the bloc’s financial watchdog, with almost one in 10 cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13bn loss in tax revenue each year.

The European Court of Auditors (ECA) said in a report on Tuesday that the trade had “changed significantly” in recent years as smuggling, while still “a problem”, was overtaken by illicit manufacturing, which has increased dramatically in the bloc.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Organised crime gangs are moving production inside the EU “to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers”, said the ECA’s Petri Sarvamaa. “Illegal production sites have now been detected in almost every EU member state.”

The ECA cited the example of a large-scale illicit cigarette factory in Belgium dismantled by police last year. It operated around the clock, with 50 workers running four production lines, each able to produce 1m cigarettes every hour.

During a raid on the largest illegal facility so far uncovered, in Spain, police seized 3m packs of cigarettes valued at €15m, five tonnes of raw tobacco worth €5m, and made 20 arrests. The factory’s products had been distributed across six EU countries.

“The scale is quite remarkable,” Sarvamaa said. “Last month French authorities dismantled a cross-border operation that had been supplying the city of Lille only since last December but had already made 120 deliveries of 7,500 packs each.”

The ECA report said such illicit cigarette factories, which usually operate for two- to four months, were using sophisticated equipment and employing experienced technicians to set up and maintain their machinery.

The organised crime groups that run them split production across multiple facilities and often locate them in border regions, tailoring their operations by producing specific brands for individual markets and even developing new tobacco products.

The damage goes beyond lost tax revenue. The trade “undermines public health policies by making tobacco products cheaper and more accessible, especially to young people”, Sarvamaa said. It also feeds organised crime and finances other illegal activities.

While, overall, tobacco consumption has continued to fall across the EU, the quantity of illicit tobacco products has risen steadily, reaching about 8.8 % of total cigarette consumption in 2023 (the latest figures available), the report said – although information about the size, structure or economic impact of the trade remains “incomplete and unreliable”.

The report said the EU and many member states had taken steps to combat the trade, but were hampered because European law in the area was not harmonised and member states’ efforts were uneven, leaving enforcement gaps.

National control systems and enforcement have different definitions of offences and of penalties, encouraging criminals to move to the more lax jurisdictions, and information exchanges in the bloc were inconsistent.

“Criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade are succeeding not because Europe lacks legislation but because gaps remain in coordination, information and enforcement,” Sarvamaa said. “Organised crime has a strategy. We need one too.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports. Almost one in ten cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13billion loss in tax revenue each year.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Flight delays and disruption across UK after air traffic control technical issue
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
London airports worst hit and 300 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of UK air traffic system

Flights in and out of the UK have been significantly disrupted due to an air traffic control issue affecting airports including Heathrow and Gatwick, with cancellations and delays continuing into Tuesday evening.

About 300 flights have been cancelled so far, flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Departures from London airports were most severely affected, with few take-offs since a fault was reported early on Tuesday afternoon.

Air traffic control service provider Nats said shortly before 5pm that it had fixed the problem in its system. Airlines renewed calls for the agency to be overhauled after the third major incident in just over three years.

Most flights due to depart Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted and London City airports since 2pm appeared to have been delayed or are yet to take off.

About 90 flights in and out of Heathrow and Gatwick had been cancelled by 4.15pm, according to data by analytics company Cirium.

Flights from other airports around the UK, including Manchester, Edinburgh, Birmingham and Belfast airports, were also affected.

Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed with 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights around Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.

The air traffic control service Nats said at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. Nats later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and at 4.40pm announced it had implemented a fix.

However, it said the system was only “starting to recover”, adding: “We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery. We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”

Heathrow originally said only departures were affected but a later statement confirmed that the Nats issue was “impacting arriving and departing flights across UK airports”.

It added: “We are supporting our local Nats team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. We apologise to those affected by the disruption and advise passengers to check with their airline for the latest flight information and only travel to the airport if their flight is confirmed.”

British Airways said it was experiencing some disruption and was in touch with its customers.

Belfast City airport warned of “some disruption” to flights after the technical issue affecting Nats. “Due to the technical issue referenced below, there may be some disruption to flights due to arrive in and depart from Belfast City airport,” they said in a statement.”

A Birmingham airport spokesperson apologised to customers and advised them to “arrive at Birmingham airport (BHX) in line with their airline’s check-in requirements and to contact their airline directly for the latest flight information and updates”.

Edinburgh airport said it was aware of the issue which “may impact operations”.

The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago which caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.

Airlines have been increasingly critical of Nats after the outages.

Ryanair repeated its calls for Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.

He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.

Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.”

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.”
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: About 300 flights cancelled so far, flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said. Air traffic control service provider Nats said shortly before 5pm that it had fixed the problem in its system. Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed with 50 flights cancelled.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Fourteen men go on trial in Paris over deadliest small-boat Channel crossing
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Sinking of inflatable dinghy in 2021 resulted in 31 people dead or missing, including a seven-year-old child

Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record.

The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.

The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead also included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.

A team on a French fishing boat near British waters off Calais had raised the alarm when they saw several lifeless bodies floating in the water.

According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes – between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England – began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.

Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived the tragedy.

Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.

Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia.

Among the defendants are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the ​smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched.

Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.

Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators.

The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as people who were seeking to make the journey themselves.

However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain.

For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by the French fishing vessel.

A separate investigation is ongoing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel – who have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.

The UK’s Cranston inquiry, in its report released in February, found that systemic failings, missed opportunities and inadequate resourcing undermined the UK’s maritime search and rescue response on the night of the disaster. HM Coastguard was placed in an “intolerable position”, it said, with chronic staff shortages and limited operational capacity contributing directly to the failure to rescue people in the water.

It found the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard.

Families ​of some of the victims will travel from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said.

“Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” the lawyers, Matthieu Chirez, Thomas Ricard and Camille Renouard, said in a statement.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record. The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: British family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordeal
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Geneva Abdul
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017

A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.

The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The father of three, who is the son of Ali Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.

He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-up at the the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.

Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.

Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia and for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.

“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at a campaign launch to bring Naimi home in London on Tuesday.

Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.

“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”

Naimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.

They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.

His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whose assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.

Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.

He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.

His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.

It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.

After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.

“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.

“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.

In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.

“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.

As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointment of a special envoy for Britons detained overseas did not go as far as campaigners, experts and parliamentarians had called for.

Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”

Last month the Guardian reported that X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.

The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Rami Naimi was abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from Australia. He was released the following year after being tortured and released. His family have alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities. He now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia Human

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

UK politics live – latest updates

Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with the tacit backing of the government, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband has said, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.

In the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, Miliband said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, saying such acknowledgment was “the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

After Miliband spoke, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced a suite of measures in response, including the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem. Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.

Miliband said the UK government would enact:

An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.

A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.

A ban on the advertising in the UK of illegal settlement properties.

Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.

A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

The UK is among 12 countries that said on Tuesday they would impose sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. They include Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden.

In further retaliation for the British action, Saar said the UK would no longer be permitted to participate in the US-led Gaza coordination mission. And 11 British pro-Palestine MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Zara Sultana, Diane Abbott and several other Labour and Green MPs, as well as a lawyer who filed Hamas’s challenge to proscription in the UK would be banned from entering Israel.

Miliband said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Miliband said those who financed or facilitated illegal settlements would “face the full force of UK sanctions” and that he expected the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months.

He stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, Miliband said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”

He said the British government had previously described settlements as illegal but had not described the occupation itself as unlawful, and that would now change.

Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust.

“I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

He said to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

Miliband said he felt a “deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community” and said there had been “the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years – death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale”.

The foreign secretary said the action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine; one that not only condemned but took action.

“Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”

He said he believed the majority of the British people would support the ban on trade with illegal settlements. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” he said.

He said the UK would support “full, robust and fair judicial processes” to determine if Israel had committed genocide and said the government would not pre-judge that process.

“This has been the case for all of the genocides since the 1948 genocide convention: Rwanda, Srebrenica, Cambodia, and acts against the Yazidi people. This will remain our policy. It is right that this issue has been brought before the ICJ [international court of justice] and I want to make it clear that we support the court in coming to its determination.”

Speaking in the chamber, Miliband said the UK “should have acted earlier” to formally recognise the illegality of the occupation and appeared to suggest it had been delayed under Keir Starmer. “It has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation, to recognise the degree of public concern,” he told MPs.

The shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but that Miliband was “enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won’t work – but it does know they will harm innocents”.

He said there was a risking of harming Palestinians who worked in the West Bank and that “the economies of Palestine and Israel are too interconnected” for a ban on goods for illegal settlements to work.

But the veteran Conservative MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said.

Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar says UK will not participate in US-led Gaza coordination mission. Miliband says he is taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British people

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Netanyahu was warned of 7 October Hamas attacks, book claims
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Israeli PM says allegation that UAE president alerted him more than a week before major offensive is ‘absolute lie’

Benjamin Netanyahu was personally alerted by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a large-scale offensive against Israel a week before its 7 October 2023 attack, but did not act on the warning, according to a book by Haaretz reporters.

The claim, which comes amid a crucial election campaign, prompted Israeli opposition leaders to describe the prime minister as “unfit” for office, even as Netanyahu denounced the report as an “absolute lie” and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.

Haaretz said the Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing “a terrifying operation” which he described as an “earthquake”.

According to the report, the UAE president, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack, and told him Hamas was planning a major operation.

The allegations, published in Haaretz on Tuesday, pile more pressure on the Israeli prime minister who has already faced heavy criticism for his handling of events before the 7 October attacks.

Hamas militants killed more than 1,200 people and took another 251 people hostage during the offensive. Hundreds of Israelis, mostly soldiers, have been killed in continued fighting from consequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 73,000 Palestinians.

The claims are contained in the book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, which, its authors say, is based on dozens of sources in Israel and worldwide, including very senior officials.

According to Haaretz, bin Zayed communicated frequently with senior Israeli leaders, including Netanyahu and the Israeli president Isaac Herzog, with a UAE diplomat delivering a secure phone to the Israeli prime minister for the conversations.

A week and a half before 7 October, the reporters say, bin Zayed called Netanyahu from the presidential palace in Abu Dhabi and, in a 45-minute call, warned that Sinwar was planning a major operation which the Emirati leader was concerned could destabilise the region.

To bin Zayed’s surprise, Netanyahu reacted calmly to the news, the report said.

In a joint statement on Tuesday, several Israeli opposition party leaders declared their intention to find out what Netanyahu knew and when, and what actions he took, if any.

“Why did he not inform the security establishment, and why did he not act to protect Israeli citizens?” the statement demanded.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival in the October elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to “pathetic” excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack.

“Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for 7 October and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot wrote on X.

Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in the elections, said Netanyahu “bears personal and direct responsibility” for the deaths on 7 October, the deadliest attack in Israeli history. “Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute,” Bennett said.

The leader of the centre-left Democrats party, Yair Golan, accused Netanyahu of “endangering Israel”.

“The stories about ‘no one woke me up’ are over. You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame,” he said, in a video posted on social media.

Many Israelis have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry into the security lapses that failed to prevent Hamas’s attack.

Opposition parties say establishing such a commission, whose members would be appointed by the supreme court, would be their first priority if elected. Netanyahu’s government has rejected the proposal.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Israeli PM says allegation that UAE president alerted him more than a week before major offensive is ‘absolute lie’ Netanyahu denies he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities in significant expansion of Middle East war
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Peter Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Riyadh says it will retaliate after overnight attacks by Iran-backed Yemen group on oil facilities wound more than 70

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war.

Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The country would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”, a foreign ministry statement said, demanding a halt to the Houthi strikes on Saudi territory and oil tankers in the Red Sea.

Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said pro-government forces “will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve”.

The Houthis, who control most ⁠of Yemen’s populated areas including the capital, said ⁠they had launched a broad operation deep ​into Saudi territory using drones and missiles to strike an airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border, and the Aramco facility at Jizan.

Jizan, which is home to one of Saudi Arabia’s biggest refineries, is close to the border with Yemen and was damaged in an attack weeks ago.

Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt. The large numbers of people reportedly wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the US and Israel began their war against Iran in February.

While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been entangled in a long running conflict in Yemen, the US-Israel war against Iran has added a dangerous new regional dimension.

After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2% on Tuesday, above $99 a barrel.

Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the ‌war’s global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.

The Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.

Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade ​just beyond it.

Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon reveal details of a “maritime exclusion zone” that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade through the strait and into the Gulf itself.

Washington fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at US warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack American ships.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council wrote on X: “In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to ⁠the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated.”

Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert at King’s College London, said the Houthi attacks create an “extremely uncomfortable dilemma” for Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler.

After four years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen conflict, “restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation”, Krieg said.

AFP and Reuters contributed to this report
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Saudi Arabia says it will retaliate after overnight attacks by Iran-backed Yemen group on oil facilities. More than 70 people were wounded in the attacks, including women and children. Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move fiercely criticised by US and Israel

Ed Miliband will announce a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

In an intervention which has already drawn fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict, with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to the US president, Donald Trump, on Monday night, a call which No 10 said “stressed the importance of a two-state solution”, but it gave no other details of the conversation.

On Tuesday the US ambassador to Israel said the US could issue its own reprisals against the UK. Mike Huckabee, who had claimed the Labour government is gripped by “Jew hatred”, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme it would “do great damage to any Brits who are doing business in a number of states in the US”.

He said he did not “know what all of the national sanctions or repercussions or retaliations will be from the US, it hasn’t been announced yet … but one of the largest US states, Florida, that has a law that if this action is taken, then Brits will not be able to do business with any company or business in Florida”.

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said on Tuesday that the motivation for the move was the desire to protect the viability of the two-state solution.

“At the heart of the statement is the idea that the UK, along with many other countries, do not want to see the possibility of a two-state solution in Israel and Palestine being erased by changes to the facts on the ground, and the reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months,” he told Sky News.

Plans in the “E1” area could mean the “effective cutting off of the north of the West Bank from the south of the West Bank”, McFadden said. “But I think it’s also important to say that Israel is an important trading partner for the UK. This isn’t intended to be a boycott of all Israeli goods.”

In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza.

The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.

Israel has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid for Gaza. Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, appeared to respond to the reports by saying: “Expel the British ambassador tonight!”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political spectrum favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.

The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.

Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions to be lifted.

His claim that aid was being held back was denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.

Miliband is likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of two key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), which are under attack by the US.

The package is unlikely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.

after newsletter promotion

But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention may help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s election next month.

British sources said that even Israeli military officials had warned their prime minister that the IDF would struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.

Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu over the settlements issue, to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled, saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.

The UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Keir Starmer’s government said it was broadly compliant.

The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and advertising illegal settlements.

The Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products coming from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.

Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.

Goods produced in Israeli settlements have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures will make such investments unlawful.

The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

Labour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens on Palestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.

In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina, not Britain.

He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the islands. He told GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.

The Foreign Office declined to comment when approached by the Guardian.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: UK ban on trade in settlement goods is in line with ICJ advisory opinion in 2024. US has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu over the settlements issue.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: ‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Niha Masih
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

T
here isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.

Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?

Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.

In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.

India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.

“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”

In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.

Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)

Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.

But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.

The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.

The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.

Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.

Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.

That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.

The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

after newsletter promotion

A recommendation from someone with great taste

Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

A number worth knowing

One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.
