https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Kathmandu
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.

In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.

“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”

Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”

For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.

“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”

Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.

Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.

While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”

He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.

The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.

Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.

“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.

He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.

Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.

“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.

“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.

The workers were rescued during an operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s floods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said.

A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been found during the rescue operation, which has yet to be identified. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the search as they had found no more signs of life.

Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.

Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”

Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.”

He said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said.

To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others.

“We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.

Officials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care.

Hirashova Maharjan, Kabir’s wife, said he had been in shock at first and was not talking, but had since said “a few words”. She said he had an injury to his leg and was extremely jaundiced.

“He did not even recognise me initially. He only said: ‘Where am I? What happened to me?’ He did not say anything else,” she said. “He is better now. He said he wanted some water, so I gave him water. Then I asked him if he recognised me, and he said yes. He nodded his head.”

“We had almost lost hope,” she said, adding that when she saw the photos of him being pulled from the tunnel, “I was so happy that I cried.”

Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.

Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.

Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army.

“The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.”

Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.

In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.

Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Pair rescued from Trishuli 3A tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres. They were recovered from a depth of 200 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.

Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.

At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”

“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.

According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

More than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropowers projects. Morethan 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Matthew Pearce
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.

“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”

Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”

The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.

They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”

The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.

Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.title: Israel to close UK consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions against illegal settlements – UK politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Andrew Sparrow
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text:
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, has said his country will retaliate for the sanctions imposed on West Bank settlements.

He has just announced:

The UK consulate in Jerusalem will be shut.

The UK will no longer be allowed to participate in the US-led Gaza coordination mission in Israel.

Twelve Britons are being banned from entering Israel.

In a response, Saar also accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and claimed the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.

UPDATE: There are 12 Britons being banned, not 10 as originally stated. See 4.13pm.

And Israel has also said Britain can no longer train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank under the “British Support Team in Ramallah”.

These are from Anshel Pfeffer, the Economist’s Israel correspondent and author of a biography of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli PM. Pfeffer is sceptical about what the West Bank settlements trade ban will achieve.

Sanctions on Israeli settlements fully justified, but empty gesture unless “comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements” means sanctioning Israeli government and Israeli banks doing just that. Which I doubt

Miliband says he “couldn’t have been more clear in my statement about our friendship with the Israeli people and indeed our wish to have trade with Green Line Israel” but there’s really no way to differentiate. It’s a muddled empty gesture policy which won’t achieve anything

Jeremy Corbyn, the former Labour party leader who is now parliamentary leader of the small, leftwing Your Party, has issued a statement about being banned by Israel. (See 4.13pm.) He says it is “shocking” that Israel does not want the world to know what is happening in Palestine, and he says “Israel’s genocide cannot go unpunished”.

Sir Ephraim Mirvis, the chief rabbi, has issued a damning verdict on the trade ban announced by the government.

In a statement, he said:

This is truly a dark day for British Jews.

Today our government has chosen to ignore the deep concerns expressed by so many of us. The measures announced amount to little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric and those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish State.

These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah and at a time when our community is more vulnerable than ever to the wave of extremism that has been building over recent years, these sanctions do nothing to advance the cause of peace. Nor do they make anyone safer – quite the contrary.

Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, has been asked about the UK government’s decision to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements. As Shrai Popat reports on our US live blog, Rubio said that the US was “not going to do what the UK did”. But he did not comment on the decision in detail.

He also said the US does not “want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region”.

UPDATE: Here is the full quote from Rubio.

Well, they alerted us to it. We don’t have any announcements, obviously, those are decisions that they make, and we – and the president has expressed this in the past – we don’t want to see anything destabilising going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region.

We think it has implications as well on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza and the 20-point plan and the Board of Peace that we’re very committed to. Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now.

Here is the full text of Ed Miliband’s statement to MPs about the ban on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank.

Emma Graham-Harrison is the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent

This is from Michael Sfard, one of Israel’s leading human rights lawyers, on the significance of Ed Miliband saying in his statement earlier (see 1.38pm) that the UK government now believes ethnic cleansing is taking place in the West Bank.

Because ethnic cleansing is a mass atrocity that consists of war crimes and might even consist of crimes against humanity, that recognition puts an obligation on the international community, and on the UK that recognises it, to take every legal measure to pressure Israel to stop it.

And that is very important, because that would dictate many aspects of British policy towards Israel.

The Greens have more MPs sanctioned by Israel today (see 4.13pm) than any other party. Here is their response to the settlement trade ban announcement. It is from Ellie Chowns, their parliamentary leader and foreign affairs spokesperson.

The measures announced today mark a critical and overdue step towards upholding the UK’s obligations under international law – one which the Green party has long fought for and strongly supports.

We additionally welcome the government’s recognition that the occupation is unlawful and that Palestinians face ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Exerting pressure on the Israeli Government over illegal settlements is crucial to protecting the human rights of Palestinians, and Greens are pleased to see action taken to progress this aim.

But Chowns said that the government should have gone further.

Britain’s legal duty to prevent genocide arose when ministers knew, or should have known, of a serious risk. That threshold was crossed long ago. Continuing military and intelligence cooperation with Israel while Palestinians are killed and denied lifesaving aid is a shameful failure to fulfil that duty. Ministers must take further action.

That requires a full two-way arms embargo, wide-ranging sanctions, an end to military and intelligence cooperation, and withdrawal from the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement.

Existing export licenses that sustain the occupation must be ended, and restrictions must cover F-35 components supplied through the international pool.

Britain must also press for unimpeded humanitarian access and independent war crimes investigations to secure accountability and justice.

Aamna Mohdin is a Guardian community affairs correspondent.

While the leading British Jewish communal organisations have expressed “deep regret” at the government’s decision (see 3.21pm and 4.21pm), the response has not been uniform; progressive Jewish groups have welcomed the announcement.

Yachad, a UK Jewish organisation that advocates for a political resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said:

The UK government’s announcement today that it will ban trade in goods with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and expand sanctions beyond violent extremists, to include those responsible for deepening and entrenching the occupation, is an important and necessary development. We believe it should be supported by those that support the rights of the seven million Israelis and seven million Palestinians to live with freedom, dignity and security.

These new policies do not target Israel; they target the occupation. They draw a clear distinction between the legitimacy of the state of Israel and the settlement enterprise which is illegal under international law.

Distinguishing settlements from Israel proper is not a judgement on where a border will ultimately fall, it’s a recognition that unilateral facts on the ground should not be allowed to decide that question in advance.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews has released its response to Ed Miliband’s announcement. Here is an excerpt.

As proud Brits who love our country, and who also have a deep religious, cultural and family ties to Israel, we feel a deep sense of anguish about this breakdown in relations. We are also impacted directly by heightened rhetoric about the conflict, including policies that focus on the actions of the Israeli government, and do not sufficiently address responsibilities of Palestinian leaders and malign actors in the region.

Announcing such measures during an already heated Israeli election – which has the potential to lead to considerable change to the situation in the West Bank and Gaza – risks perverse consequences which go against the UK’s stated objectives. We urge both governments to avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests.

Here is the full list of 12 Britons being banned from Israel by the Israeli government following today’s illegal settlements trade ban. Eleven of them are MPs, and the other person, Fahad Ansari, runs an anti-Zionist legal group.

There are five Green MPs on the list, four Labour MPs and two from Your Party.

Here is the list of all 12 people being banned.

3. Fahad Ansari, Director of Riverway to the Sea

10. John McDonnell MP

11. Richard Burgon MP

This is what Gideon Saar, the Israeli foreign minister, said as he announced the measures his government is taking in response to the ban on trade with West Bank settlements unveiled in London.

Today, with the agreement of Prime Minister Netanyahu, I decided on a series of Israeli countermeasures in response to the series of new sanctions announced today by the British foreign secretary of the Labour government and following a series of anti-Israel decisions by the Labour government.

The accusations made today by the foreign secretary of the Labour government [Ed Miliband] in the British parliament were outrageous lies.

Let me make this clear from the outset: we have nothing against the British people. We know that we have many friends in Britain.

Unfortunately, a hostile Labour government is in office, systematically acting against the state of Israel, and it has left us with no choice but to finally respond to its hostile actions.

The British move is morally distorted and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process.

The attempt by the British Labour government to impose measures in the style of the ‘white paper’ carries echoes of the antisemitic words of British Lieutenant-General Barker, commander of British forces in the Land of Israel during the Mandate, who said: “punish the Jews by striking at their pockets.”

The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel. The connection and right of the Jewish people to this land are documented more extensively than those of any other people in human history.

I say to the Labour government and to every government in the world that thinks it can force Israel to act against our national and security interests: You have no chance of succeeding.

We did not return to our land after 2,000 years only to lose it under pressure from jihadists, Islamists, antisemites, far-leftists and wokes.

Not only will you fail to harm us. You will harm yourselves and your own influence.

The latest decision by the Labour government joins an increasingly escalating series of unilateral measures against Israel adopted by the hostile Labour government since it took office in July 2024.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, has said his country will retaliate for the sanctions imposed on West Bank settlements.

He has just announced:

The UK consulate in Jerusalem will be shut.

The UK will no longer be allowed to participate in the US-led Gaza coordination mission in Israel.

Twelve Britons are being banned from entering Israel.

In a response, Saar also accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and claimed the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.

UPDATE: There are 12 Britons being banned, not 10 as originally stated. See 4.13pm.

And Israel has also said Britain can no longer train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank under the “British Support Team in Ramallah”.

Aamna Mohdin is a Guardian community affairs correspondent.

Ed Miliband’s sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, announced alongside France and Canada, have been hailed as a historic step forward by many in the British Palestinian community – though others have urged the Foreign Office to go much further.

Shaher Saed, general secretary of the Palestine General Federation of Trade Unions (PGFTU), said:

We see this as an important step in the right direction and a clear message that the illegal settlement enterprise cannot continue without accountability and consequences. The continued expansion of settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, accompanied by acts of killing and violence, the burning of property, and the destruction of agricultural land, seriously undermines the prospects for achieving a two-state solution and violates the rights of the Palestinian people.

We encourage the UK government to go further and take stronger and more effective measures to halt settlement expansion, ensure respect for international law, hold those responsible for violations accountable, and protect the rights and livelihoods of Palestinian workers.

The British Palestinian Committee said in a statement:

Today’s announcement by the British foreign secretary indicates a shift in position from the previous Labour administration. It is a necessary and overdue step. Among the announced positions are certain measures which, if implemented and taken further, bring the UK closer to meeting its obligations under international law, and would indicate a shift towards holding Israeli war crimes to account.

Omar Barghouti, co-founder of the BDS movement for Palestinian rights, said:

The announced UK measures against Israel’s settlements are largely performative and ineffective, yet they also reflect the impact of relentless public pressure on the current government. The UK is going after a crime while continuing to be complicit with the serial criminal.

Aside from its shameless, multi-faceted complicity in Israel’s ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza, the UK has an unequivocal obligation, arising from the ICJ advisory opinion of July 2024, to end all military, intelligence, trade, academic and other relations with Israel that enable its regime of illegal occupation and apartheid in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem. Insisting on letting ‘humanitarian aid’ into Gaza does not begin to end UK complicity.

The Jewish Leadership Council, which represents Jewish organisations in Britain, has issued a statement has accused the government of having an “increasingly punitive and unbalanced approach towards Israel”. It also says this risks becoming a “de facto boycott of Israel”.

The Palestinian presidency has issued a statement welcoming Miliband’s announcement. It describes the move as “an important step toward confronting the system of Israeli colonial settlement and its violations against the Palestinian people”.

In the Commons Andrew Murrison (Con) asked who the government would distinguish between goods made in the Israeli settlements and those made in green line Israel.

Miliband said this would be the responsibility of companies importing good from Israel. He said the sanctions rules would probably use postcodes to identify illegal settlements, and companies importing goods would “have to say that the goods that they are bringing in do not come from those areas”.

Ed Miliband said in his statement it could take up to nine months to introduce the ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements. (See 1.50pm.)

The Lib Dems have said the government should act more quickly. Calum Miller, the Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesperson, said:

The settlement trade ban is a long overdue step in the right direction, but ministers now need to move with urgency.

The current extremist Israeli cabinet is racing to establish facts on the ground to prevent a two-state solution. Liberal Democrats are calling on the government to introduce emergency legislation to implement this ban without delay.

In the Commons, when asked if the government would be able to act more quickly, Miliband said this might be possible. He said:

I want to do this as quickly as possible. And I just say this – six to nine months is what I’ve said in the statement, if we can do it quicker, we will.

In the Commons, the first backbench MP to be called to speak was Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs committee. She started with the words: “At last.”

Emma Graham-Harrison is the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent

The former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert has backed Ed Miliband’s announcement. Olmert told the Guardian:

The British government decision became unavoidable as a result of a continuous effort of ethnic cleansing perpetrated by a large group of Jewish terrorists in the West Bank. The crimes of these terrorists are actively assisted by police and military units over a long period of time. The highest levels of government led by minister of defence Katz and prime minister Netanyahu are actively supporting these terrorists and avoid taking the necessary measures to stop it.

Millions of Israelis are appalled by this terror and are actively resisting the terrorists.

Sanctions are directed against the terrorists not against Israel, and as such they are unavoidable.

Miliband quoted Olmert approvingly in his own statement. (See 1.38pm.)

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.author: Charlie Moloney (now) and Graeme Wearden (earlier)

Nats said its flight system is “starting to recover” after a fix was implemented following a technical issue.

In a post on X, it said: “We have implemented a fix and our flight system is starting to recover.

“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery.

“We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”

A look at Heathrow’s live departure board hints at the scale of the disruption. While a number of green flights are still marked as “on time”, there are many that have simply been cancelled, leaving passengers scrambling for solutions.

It’s not just UK airports that have been disrupted either; flights that hoped to land in the country have also faced delays or cancellations.

One social media user earlier wrote: “Venice to Bristol EZY2832, all been dumped off a plane back to the gate with zero communication. Already 3 hours delayed, what’s the plan?”

Passengers have vented their frustrations on social media about the delays to their flights, stating there had been “zero communication” from airlines.

One woman told EasyJet on X: “I appreciate it is difficult, but the lack of communication at Alicante re delays is abysmal”.

Another user said: “Flight from Porto to Gatwick cancelled. No sign of any easyJet staff for those that have gone through security and need to leave the airport”.

Shortly after 4.45pm, one man told the airline: “Stuck on runway at Gatwick still after meant to take off at 2:20pm. At least EasyJet have offered us a snack of up to value £2.80! Can’t even buy any food or beverages and I’m starving”.

Many social media accounts messaged the airline with their flight numbers requesting updates, one account saying: “Venice to Bristol EZY2832, all been dumped off a plane back to the gate with zero communication. Already 3 hours delayed, what’s the plan?”

Some departures from Newcastle Airport have been delayed amid the flight disruption, according to a Newcastle Airport spokesperson.

“We are aware of a technical issue affecting Nats which is impacting some flights at airports across the UK”, the spokesperson said in a statement.

“While some departures from Newcastle are experiencing delays, our operations have not been affected to the same extent as those at some airports in the south of the country.

“Passengers are advised to check with their airline for the latest flight information.”

Nats said its flight system is “starting to recover” after a fix was implemented following a technical issue.

In a post on X, it said: “We have implemented a fix and our flight system is starting to recover.

“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery.

“We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”

Time for a quick recap…

Flights around the UK are facing delays and disruption due to an air traffic control issue which has affected a string of airports including Heathrow and Gatwick, and recovery may take time.

According to aeroplane tracker Flightrader, there have been “nearly 300 cancellations so far this afternoon”, with British Airways and easyJet most affected.

Departures from London airports are most severely affected, with few take-offs since a fault was reported early on Tuesday afternoon.

The air traffic control service Nats said at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”.

Nats added: “Our engineers are on site and we will provide an update as soon as we can. We apologise for the delay this will cause to journeys, passengers should check with their airline on the status of their flight.”

The UK’s biggest airport, Heathrow, said planes were continuing to arrive, although Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely to continue until the evening.

Nats later added that its engineers are “working urgently” to fix the problem, but warned that “recovery will take some time”.

Ryanair has revealed that 65,000 of its passengers have been delayed up to 8 hours, and called for the head of Nats to quit.

Here’s our news story on the disruption:

I’m handing this blog over now to my colleague Charlie Maloney.

Flightrader 24 has posted on X:

Nearly 300 cancellations so far this afternoon as NATs systems return to normal.

Nearly 300 flights have been cancelled as a result of the UK air traffic control issue, FlightRadar24 has said.

The worst affected airports are Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham.

The air tracker found 352 flights to and from Heathrow were delayed out of its daily average of about 1,300.

Meanwhile 281 Gatwick flights were delayed out of its 850 total operations average. This was 249 out of 650 for Manchester, and 101 out of 300 for Birmingham, the Press Association report.

Budget airline Ryanair has blasted “overpaid failing NATS CEO Martin Rolfe” over today’s disruption, and demanded (not for the first time) that he quits his job.

According to Ryanair, over 65,000 of its passengers have been delayed today, with more than 50 flights cancelled, after today’s air traffic control technical problems.

Ryanair COO, Neal McMahon, says:

“How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure NATS CEO, Martin Rolfe, accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns? Over three years after NATS’ catastrophic 2023 system meltdown, it’s clear that nothing has changed, with UK passengers once again suffering avoidable ATC delays of up to 8 hours today due a critical NATS ATC system failing. Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for NATS’ abhorrent failure.

The astonishing part is that NATS continues to charge airlines and passengers more each year while delivering a worse service. Following the 2023 collapse, we were told lessons would be learned. We were told “resilience would improve”. We were told the systems had been fixed. Yet here we are again. This is a pattern of repeated failure with Rolfe in charge getting paid over £1.4m in bonuses p.a. while he delivers failure after failure.

The UK Government, the CAA and the NATS Board must stop making excuses for repeated NATS failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system without repeated failures. Its time for overpaid failure Martin Rolfe to go.”

Back in March, Rolfe argued that the criticism over the 2023 technical meltdown was unfair, as Nats had only suffered four incidents in 12 years.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander has posted on X about the disruption, saying:

I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak.

I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry. Please check with your airline for latest advice.

London City Airport has confirmed it is experiencing disruption to departing flights, following the NATS technical problem today.

A spokesperson for London City Airport said:

“Due to an air traffic control issue affecting airports across London, London City Airport is experiencing disruption to departing flights.

“Passengers should check their flight status with their airline before travelling to the airport.

“We apologise for the inconvenience and thank passengers for their patience.”

Away from today’s flight disruption, a lung disease drug being developed by AstraZeneca for COPD has performed well in late-stage clinical trials, a welcome boost to Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical company following several setbacks recently.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a long-term lung condition that makes breathing harder over time through chronic inflammation of the airways, and can also lead to a chronic cough and excess mucus.

The company’s tozorakimab drug, administered once every four weeks, showed a reduction in moderate and severe COPD exacerbations (which lead to more than 2,500 emergency department visits a day in the US) in former smokers of up to 34%, and in current and former smokers by 30%, compared with a placebo. A total of 2,306 patients were involved.

The drug led to a reduction of 43% in exacerbations in patients with the highest level of of blood eosinophil, a biomarker. The data was presented at the European Respiratory Society Congress in Barcelona.

Frank Sciurba, professor of pulmonary and critical care medicine at the University of Pittsburgh and chief trial investigator, said:

“These unprecedented results, along with its favourable safety profile, underscore tozorakimab’s potential as an innovative treatment for the millions of people living with COPD who remain at risk despite treatment with inhaled standard of care.”

COPD is the third-biggest cause of death worldwide, excluding Covid-19. Only half of COPD patients live more than 3 ½ years after their first severe exacerbation.

AstraZeneca estimates peak annual revenues of $5bn for the treatment, which would make it one of its biggest selling drugs, while analysts at Morgan Stanley have pencilled in $6bn.

Airline Wizz Air have lambasted NATS for today’s technical failure.

Wizz Air says it is “extremely disappointed” by the UK’s air traffic control issue.

The company adds that a critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill, declaring that NATS is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.

Less happily, budget airline easyJet reports that the UK air traffic control system failure is causing delays to flights across Europe, with some flights unable to operate (Reuters reports).

Happily, the impact at Cardiff Airport due to the air traffic technical issue is “currently minimal”.

A spokesperson for Cardiff Airport said:

“A technical issue affecting Nats Air Traffic is causing some disruption to flight departures across parts of the UK.

“The impact at Cardiff Airport is currently minimal though we’d encourage passengers to check directly with their airline or travel operator for the latest information on the status of their flight.”

Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial ratings company Defaqto, has sent over some advice for passengers affected by today’s flight disruption:

“If there is a significant delay to your flight, your airline should be covering the costs of essentials you’ll need during that delay. Such as food and drink, phone calls and if necessary overnight accommodation including transport to the hotel.

Insurers and Airlines could class issues as ‘extraordinary circumstances’, which ultimately means it is a situation beyond their control and could not have been foreseen or avoided. As a result, you may not be entitled to compensation as it is not considered to be the airlines’ ‘fault’ and therefore they are not liable.

That being said, the above refers to ‘compensation’. Transport providers and tour operators do have a responsibility to either provide a reasonable alternative or a full refund should a flight not go ahead as planned. If a replacement flight is offered but is delayed, depending on the distance being travelled, the Civil Aviation Authority do set out under what circumstances you would have a legal right to claim for compensation.

Travel Insurance may also cover you if you cannot claim costs back from the airline, operator, or credit card but that will all depend on whether your policy includes cover for delay, travel disruption, missed connection or abandonment.”

Flightradar24 also shows that a Japan Airlines flight from Toyko to London is being diverted to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport.

The flightradar24 app suggests that a lot of planes at Heathrow Airport in London are pretty much static on the ground right now, with nothing obviously taking off or landing at this moment…

National Air Traffic Services have confirmed that the technical problem scuppering flights today is within its flight processing system.

It says staff are ‘working urgently’ to fix it, but warns that ‘recovery will take some time’.

Posting on X, it says:

We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system. Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise.

Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time. We will provide further updates as soon as possible.

Passengers should check the status of their flight with their airline. We will provide further updates as soon as we have confirmed information, at https://nats.aero and on X at @NATS.

British Airways has confirmed that it is “experiencing some flight disruption” as a result of a technical issue at NATS, and is in touch with customers.

Details passed to Kent police after people heard in pub boasting about going to Dover to ‘attack Muslims’

Police were told the night before far-right agitators blocked roads into Dover that those involved had converged on a village 18 miles away and planned to use it as a launchpad, it has emerged.

People in Preston-next-Wingham told of how hundreds of men had started to arrive in the village of just over 920 residents on Friday afternoon and in effect “took over” the village.

At least one person is understood to have sought to pass on details to counter-terrorism police after people heard the far-right activists boasting in the local pub that they intended to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”.

The information was passed on to police but little or no interest was shown in the tipoff, according to the anti-fascist group Hope Not Hate, who spoke to the person. Others reported careless and illegal parking to the police but no action was said to have been taken.

The claims have raised fresh questions about Kent police’s handling of the protest, in which hundreds descended on Dover at 7am and which the force described as “spontaneous”. No arrests were made during the action, which involved hundreds of black-clad masked men standing in the middle of roads and led to access to the port of Dover being blocked for several hours.

Kent olice admitted on Tuesday that an initial review of its handling of the protests found that the force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the next day.

“This information was not fully assessed. If it was, it may have allowed the force to consider its resourcing,” it said in a statement.

“However, this information would not have prevented the lawful protest from taking place, nor the disruption experienced by the town, port and wider community.”

Roger Gale, the MP for Herne Bay and Sandwich, who lives in Preston-next-Wingham, said the unrest in Dover on Saturday was clearly not “spontaneous”.

He said that the village in Kent was unusually full of cars on Friday night and that a local car park and the recreation ground was still full of vehicles on Saturday morning, prompting him to call 999.

Gale said: “A local councillor took photographs of the number plates and they should be able to work back from those to establish who owns the cars. I called 999 at around 9.30am on Saturday and two officers came over quite quickly.

“I am going to write to the chief constable to ask what they are going to do with this information. There were roughly 50 cars in the car park and the recreation ground and more on the road. [What happened in Dover] was not spontaneous. It was carefully coordinated. Those participating were transported from the village to Dover, most likely in Luton vans.”

Gale was not aware of calls being made to the police on Friday but he added that he knew that conversations among participants in Saturday’s unrest had been overheard in the village pub on Friday night.

The action was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far right activist known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to a blockade in Portsmouth the following day.

One person who lives in Preston-next-Wingham told Hope Not Hate: “There were hundreds of them. They took over the place.

“They were literally parking everywhere. They parked in the recreational ground, in the butcher’s car park, in the primary school, on the roads and even on junctions.”

A fleet of vehicles is understood to have arrived at about 5.30am on Saturday in the village. Video footage later showed men who took part in the protest disembarking from the back of the vehicles in Dover.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
More rapid use of blood products may have raised chance of 19-year-old making it to hospital, though chance was low, says counsel

The death of a 19-year-old student who was killed in the Nottingham attacks in 2023 was “potentially preventable”, a public inquiry into the incident has heard.

Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, both 19, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, a paranoid schizophrenic, on 13 June 2023.

In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.

The inquiry is examining the events leading up to attacks, and has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.

During closing submissions on Tuesday, it heard how a panel of medical professionals had assessed the emergency medical response to the attacks and the “survivability” of victims.

Rachel Langdale KC, counsel to the inquiry, said the assessment had found that “more rapid administration of blood products” could have increased Webber’s chance of getting to hospital and possibly undergoing surgery.

The 19-year-old had a “far less” than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, which was classed as “potentially preventable”, Langdale said. She added that O’Malley-Kumar and Coates’s deaths were “not preventable”.

The assessment, which also acknowledged the efforts of emergency services, found that a more rapid administration of blood to Webber would have to have been coupled with multiple other rapid and meticulous steps “in order for Barnaby to survive to intensive care”.

The inquiry also addressed the emergence of further evidence after hearings had concluded in early June.

At the start of closing arguments, the inquiry’s chair, Deborah Taylor KC, said it was “disappointing”, and that further evidence “ought to have been identified by core participants and disclosed earlier”. She called on them to provide all corrections and omissions by 31 December.

Such evidence included the police discovery of a holdall bag at Calocane’s former address in Nottingham in the days after the attack. The bag contained notebooks that were not disclosed to the inquiry until June this year.

The books contained notes from Calocane in which he described himself as God, and said police had “mind-reading software” and that he had the power to “resurrect people”, the inquiry heard.

Other documents created by Calocane were found in a bin at the property, containing bullet points about explosives, including TNT and nitrate fertiliser. Such notes were not identified or taken into account by police, nor made available to the Crown Prosecution Service or to psychiatric experts, the inquiry heard.

The lawyer representing bereaved families, Tim Moloney KC, said one of the notes appeared to say “Manchester Arena”. Calocane had also searched online for “large venues in Nottingham”, he said.

“Nobody has ever asked [Calocane] why he was researching explosives and large venues, because they couldn’t,” Maloney said. “There was a failure to investigate [Calocane’s] historical behaviour and actions.”

The inquiry was also not told of violent assaults committed by Calocane until after the hearings concluded in early June. One involved an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in 2021, and in another he punched a colleague in Normanton in February 2023.

Evidence presented to the inquiry earlier this year detailed how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, leading to him being sectioned four times in the space of two years.

An arrest warrant was also out for Calocane at the time of the Nottingham attacks, after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer, the inquiry heard previously.

Closing submissions will conclude on Wednesday and a report detailing the inquiry’s findings will be published next year.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Phillip Inman
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
In partnership with DWP, firms such as John Lewis and M&S plan to offer 18- to 24-year-olds placements of two to four weeks

UK retailers aim to create up to 100,000 jobs for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years by giving them a first step on the ladder into work.

In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home, Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.

The move comes after the former health secretary Alan Milburn warned in a recent report that the 1 million Neets in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervened.

Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, welcomed the retailers’ initiative, saying too many young people were stuck in a vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities.

He said: “Six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. Unless we can increase work opportunities, Britain’s Neet crisis will get worse not better.”

Other employers signed up to the scheme include Tesco, New Look, Wickes, Currys and Greggs.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.”

The scheme, known as Opening Shift, follows the appointment earlier this year of the former M&S chief executive, Marc Bolland, to head a taskforce to tackle the growing youth unemployment crisis.

Bolland, who led the retail chain from 2010 to 2016, has secured the support of retailers for the work placement scheme amid warnings that the country risks a “lost generation” without urgent intervention.

Participants will continue to receive universal credit throughout their placement, mainly because of the logistical barriers claimants face when accepting short-term jobs that mean quitting and then rejoining the welfare programme.

The programme was developed with retailers through the British Retail Consortium and the DWP and has 11,305 placements already pledged.

Bolland, who is also a senior non-executive director at the DWP, is understood to have been chosen for the role thanks to his involvement with the charity Movement to Work, which had already helped more than 200,000 unemployed young people find jobs.

He said: “My work as founder and chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what’s possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people.

“Today’s announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain’s biggest industries and I’d encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.”

Each participant will be guaranteed an interview at the end of their placement, which will vary from 16 to 35 hours each week. Retailers will offer each recruit a “buddy” to help them navigate the new role, with the aim of moving as many recruits as possible into a job should one be available, Bolland added.

The DWP said it would use jobcentres to allow Neets to access the scheme.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the Neets crisis, given the industry’s scale and reach touching every corner of the country.

“Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the Neet crisis.”

Democrats are starting to hit back against Donald Trump for his recent social media post suggesting that the state of New Mexico should be changed to “New America”.

The state’s senior senator, Martin Heinrich, shot back on X, blasting the president’s recent efforts to rename bodies of water via executive order.

“Three things I will always call by their actual names,” Heinrich wrote. “The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico.”

His colleague in the Senate, Ben Ray Luján, echoed the sentiment.

“It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” he said, adding that Trump will “always be a sinvergüenza” – a spanish word for “scoundrel” and “corrupt”.

Similarly, Melanie Stansbury, one New Mexico’s Democratic US House representatives, was resolute. “WE ARE NOT CHANGING OUR NAME!” she said in a video, standing on the banks of the Rio Grande, which runs through the state. “New Mexico is New Mexico. We are fiercely proud of our name, our people, and our places, including this river.”

The lawyer of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, has said he hopes Donald Trump will pardon his client after her trial recently ended with a deadlocked jury.

Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, made the appeal on a televised interview on the ABC show Good Morning America today. The plea comes to Trump after a judge on Friday declared a mistrial after the jury in the Clancy case could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty or not guilty, opening the way for another trial.

Reddington said he hoped that the president would “consider a pardon” for Clancy given “the type of person she is” and “what she has been through”.

“Mr President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady,” said Reddington, who also alluded to how Trump on Friday called the case a “tragedy”.

Trump’s pardon powers are applicable in the federal justice system in the US, and Clancy was tried in Massachusetts’ state criminal justice system.

The president was asked about the trial by reporters on Friday, with Trump calling the case “a shame” and a “horrible tragedy”.

“I think the judge has said it’s going to be a mistrial, so there’s going to be another trial,” he said. “It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing.

“Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial.”

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed said they seized an American submarine drone “equipped with the latest technology” in the strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.

“The IRGC naval forces captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines of the US terrorist army at the entrance to the strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action at dawn today,” the Guards said in a statement carried by Iranian state TV. “This submarine has now been captured and images of it will be released in the coming hours.”

The White House did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media.

“The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read.

The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism.

One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions.

“Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded.

US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people.

Marco Rubio said today that US is “not going to do what the UK did” and impose sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, but stopped shy of commenting on the matter while speaking to reporters in Miami. However, the secretary of state said that the US does not “want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region”.

Earlier today, UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband announced the measure, the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, which accused Israel the country of conducting “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank.

The sanctions include an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.

Donald Trump is speaking now in Washington, at an event for first responders at the 9/11 terror attacks.

The president just spoke about how his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, narrowly avoided being at the World Trade Center on 11 September 2001, when he took his son to school instead of being in his office at Cantor Fitzgerald, which occupied several floors of the North Tower.

“This was the first time in years that he wasn’t there early in the morning,” Trump said, noting that Lutnick’s brother, Gary, who also worked at the investment banking firm and 657 other Cantor Fitzgerald employees were killed in the attacks.

Trump added: “[Lutnick’s] got some faults, but overall he’s excellent. He’s a great guy. Now he went through a lot, didn’t he?”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Tuesday that New York City would release 170,000 pages of previously undisclosed documents that show officials at the time knew that the air quality after the 9/11 terror attacks posed health risks, despite assuring the public and first responders that the air quality was safe.

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks, the city has published the documents to a publicly accessible portal, which includes air quality reports and correspondence between New York officials. Mamdani directed $34m of the city’s budget to create the portal for the records. Many documents were stored in 68 boxes in a city office, and many were only discovered last year by officials.

The initial release on the portal includes the document commonly known as the “Harding Memo” sent to then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding in 2001, which provides insight into the City’s consideration of potential legal responses in the aftermath of the attacks, including concerns about the prospect of litigation arising from toxic exposure and the adequacy of safety equipment.

“For too long, information about the aftermath of September 11th has not been provided to the public. For years, families, city workers, and survivors have been crying out for more transparency from their government,” said Stephen Banks, head of the city’s law department, about the release.

While almost 3,000 people were killed in the attacks, in the years since, “thousands more have become devastatingly – often fatally – ill from toxins and debris, though the true magnitude of the attack’s impact has yet to be fully realized,” Banks added.

Greg Hull, the Republican nominee running to replace New Mexico’s term-limited governon, Michelle Lujan Grisham, denounced the president’s suggestion to change the state’s name to “New America”.

“New Mexico does not need a new name,” Hull said in a statement to Santa Fe Public Radio. “This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what it is today. That identity is not up for negotiation.”

Further down the ballot in New Hampshire, the Democratic primary for Chris Pappas’s House seat has drawn eight candidates, with Stefany Shaheen – daughter of the outgoing senator – and Maura Sullivan, a former Obama administration official, leading the field.

The district, long purple, has been reliably blue since 2017. Republicans now see it as flippable, and Donald Trump has endorsed Anthony DiLorenzo, a businessman who owns several car dealerships, in the GOP race.

As voters head to the polls for primary elections in New Hampshire, some Democrats worry the Granite State could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, the now-governor, captured a seat.

Congressman Chris Pappas insists he’s not taking anything for granted in his bid for Senate, and is running like he’s “10 votes behind” at all times – especially in a midterm cycle where progressive challengers have scored surprise primary wins across the country. This, however, hasn’t fazed Pappas who says he is running as a “New Hampshire Democrat” who knows his state.

But Dr Karishma Manzur, Pappas’s main challenger, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said, calling both Pappas and John E Sununu, the frontrunner in the Republican primary race, “corporate politicians”.

“One has a ‘D’ after their name. One has an ‘R’ after their name … neither of them have been able to address the real needs of the people,” Manzur added.

Pappas, for his part, has long backed US aid to Israel but told the Guardian that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister is ousted in the country’s October election. Pappas noted he has rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid.

Pappas says he would support the Democratic nominee if he loses. “We need a big tent and new voices in the party to win tough elections,” he said at last week’s Democratic debate.

Manzur declined to make the same commitment. “I’m focused on winning,” she told the Guardian. “I’m not going to get into these discussions – they’re intentionally distracting from the people’s movement.”
