https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree? | Marina Hyde
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Marina Hyde
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity

B
usy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under the highest diesel prices in its history while his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.

In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.

In the end, you sense, most of the places in the US will go to the chop shop, and either have “America” bolted on the back, or have the Trump name fused on to them as a prefix. See the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC. Or, indeed, the President Donald J Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida. A new class of warship may also be procured for naming privileges.

As for potential rebrand candidates/victims, how your area votes clearly affects the order in which its landmarks – or itself in its entirety – will be slapped with a fun new identity. When proposing the New Mexico renaming, Trump casually noted that it was “one of the great vote-cheating states of all time”. I wouldn’t be feeling all that confident if I were the Georgia state capitol, or the Trump America capitol as it may imminently be known.

Meanwhile, it must be said that all this frenetic activity does feel born of Trump’s conviction that it should surely be possible to shitpost his way out of anything, even a war. After all, the Iran war, which I seem to remember was won on day one, has now been going on for more than six months. This feels confusing. First it was going to be two weeks, then four to five weeks. Four days into Operation Epic Fury, Trump explained that the US was “already substantially ahead of our time projections”, while the secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, added: “It could move up, it could move back.” Having said that, evidence suggests it could only move up, although Trump wrapped up his first week of the conflict back in March by assuring the American people that his campaign continued “to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before”. Two days after that, the conflict was downgraded to “a short excursion”, with non-committal historical allies dismissed with a triumphant: “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” The war was “complete, pretty much”, he said two days later.

And yet, was it? A couple of weeks in, Trump was explaining he’d know when the war should be over because he’d “feel it in my bones”. Alas, he seems to have failed to get the arthritic signal to pull out as late as three weeks in, despite assuring everyone that – contrary to appearances such as still bombing the shit out of things – the war had in fact been over “in two or three days”. Flash forward to a month in, and they were still “way ahead of schedule”, although once the five-week mark was hit Trump was dropping casual asides like “a whole civilization will die tonight”. Six weeks in, things were going “swimmingly”. Although, not to nitpick, but were they?

That was April. In May, a deal with the Iranians could apparently “happen any day”. By the end of the month, it could have potentially happened “over the weekend”. Same thing a weekend later. A whole two months after that, unfortunately, Trump shifted from the war being over to declaring that his notional/imaginary agreements to end the war were in fact the thing that was “over”. He no longer wished to negotiate with Tehran. Jump ahead to the present day, in fact, and he has spent quite a lot of the past week bombing the shit out of things again. Which is very much the behaviour of any state that won a war back in the first days of March. Unhelpfully, the former US defence secretary Leon Panetta estimated at the weekend that the war would drag on for another six months.

All of which suggests there has really never been a better time to rename New Mexico. Those eternal searchers for a so-called Trump doctrine are surely beginning to see that it essentially boils down to wimping out of the big, painful calls that could literally move the dial – for example, boots on the ground – and existing in an eternally figurative zone where you can simply post the problem away. Here, there is no better way to signal that the war is over than to unilaterally rename the strait of Hormuz either the strait of Trump, or the strait of America. As some psychologists like to say: you have to name it to tame it.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living

I
f I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president. A Forbes calculation from March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trump made $2.2bn in 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency and Trump Bibles to offering early access to his (often market-moving) Truth Social posts.

To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday night alongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!”

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s made hundreds of billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US government took a 9.9% stake in Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much.

According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White House released a statement calling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. What is having an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries.

But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According to Trump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stocks had risen by nearly $16m because of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read.

Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings. A 2022 New York Times investigation found that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence.

Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americans support commonsense legislation to stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect is winding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however.

Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance.

But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war is bleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says works
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ezra Levin and Leah Greenberg
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Candidates must focus on two issues: affordability and accountability. They are not competing priorities

A
s the November election approaches with control of the House and Senate on the line, the stakes are high. With so much riding on the outcome, there is no shortage of debate about the message Democrats need to win.

Affordability has emerged as a shared – if often undefined – rallying cry. Working families are struggling with rising costs and looking for answers. But too often, we’ve seen affordability positioned as the beginning and end of the plan. Meanwhile, many see holding the Trump administration accountable for its corruption and harms as at odds with a relentless focus on kitchen-table issues.

In such a moment, what kind of message actually breaks through to voters?

To find out, Indivisible partnered with Lake Research Partners to go directly to the voters Democrats need to win: 2026 battleground voters, key 2028 Senate battleground voters, and voters of color across the south.

What we found challenges the conventional wisdom that affordability and accountability are competing priorities. Affordability is essential, but our polling shows that the case for lowering costs becomes more compelling when paired with a clear commitment to take on corruption and special interests.

The data makes clear why. Seventy-one per cent of 2026 battleground voters are extremely concerned about politicians rigging the system to benefit themselves at the public’s expense, while 69% are extremely concerned about political corruption costing taxpayers money. And 88% strongly agree that we must focus on both lowering costs and addressing corruption. These numbers are astounding – 88% of Americans probably can’t agree what color the sky is, but they agree on these issues.

Most importantly, the combination is far more persuasive than either message alone. Seventy-three per cent of 2026 battleground voters are more likely to support a candidate who both fights to lower costs and takes on corruption and special interests, compared with just 19% who prefer a candidate focused solely on corruption and 5% who prefer one focused solely on lowering costs. The takeaway is clear: voters find the two issues far more compelling when paired together.

The point is not simply that voters care about both affordability and corruption. It is that accountability gives an affordability agenda credibility. When voters believe the system is rigged, a promise to lower costs can sound like another campaign pledge that will never become reality. Showing voters that Democrats are willing to fight against the status quo answers the question lurking behind every campaign economic promise: why should voters believe this time will be different?

That helps explain why anti-establishment outsiders are viewed more favorably than either political party: they are seen as more willing to challenge the system, rather than simply manage it. For Democrats, that is both a warning and an opportunity. Concrete plans to lower costs matter, but they become more credible when Democrats make clear that they are willing to confront the powerful interests that have benefited from the current political order. With Republicans in control of the House, Senate, presidency and supreme court, they can’t credibly claim to be fighting a corrupt regime they themselves control. But Democrats can force them to defend the indefensible.

Trump and his regime have made corruption impossible to ignore, so Democrats should connect the administration’s self-dealing and abuses of power to the economic pressures voters are feeling, showing that the fight against corruption is also a fight against the forces making life more expensive. Then they should pair those attacks with concrete plans to lower costs.

And if Democrats win in November on that message, they must follow through. A mandate to take on corruption and lower costs cannot end on election day. Democrats should use the power voters give them in 2027 to conduct aggressive oversight, expose politicians and corporate actors lining their pockets at the public’s expense, and hold the powerful accountable. That follow-through is essential to rebuilding a credible opposition party and a Democratic brand that too many Americans see as part of the problem.

The path to November is clear: run on affordability, but make the case for why Democrats can actually deliver it by pairing concrete plans to lower costs with a commitment to take on corruption and special interests. Voters do not just want to hear that Democrats understand the affordability crisis. They need to believe Democrats are willing to fight the people and interests standing in the way of solving it.

Affordability and accountability, together, offer Democrats the strongest case to voters – and a mandate to govern after winning.

Ezra Levin and Leah Greenberg are co-executive directors of Indivisible

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Donald Trump’s midterm strategy? Make it all about him | Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The president apparently plans to focus on the person he most admires – himself – even if Republicans would rather he didn’t

W
ith the midterm races officially beginning this week, a big question hanging over the Republican party is how Trump will allocate his giant stash of Super Pac money. As of 31 July, Maga Inc had more than $400m on hand, larger than the cash reserves of any of the major party committees.

But he’s barely spent any of it yet. Why not?

Is he waiting to see where his stash can do the most good for Republicans during the peak campaign season, starting in a few weeks? On Friday, he said he would personally weigh where to direct support, including toward Republican candidates he believes can win competitive races.

But this seems doubtful. He’s already missed the chance to lock in airtime at lower, advance rates and define candidates before attitudes harden.

Is he using his stash as a means of silencing criticism in the Republican ranks, or holding back support until a candidate lavishes praise on him?

Also doubtful. Republican candidates who believe they need to criticize his war or his economic policies to stay viable won’t restrain themselves because of his possible campaign cash.

Maybe he’s conserving the money to discipline Republican candidates in the 2028 primaries and general election, when he’ll use the stash to penalize disloyalty and reward loyalty?

Possibly, but he’s already practically a lame duck.

Is he conserving the cash to pass it on to his chosen presidential successor – either Vance or Rubio or a third selection as yet unknown?

Probably not. That’s a long way off.

None of these theories holds water because they don’t figure in Trump’s giant, towering, malignant narcissism.

It seems he’ll be putting money behind his favorite politician – the person he most admires, who represents everything he believes in, who he considers the single most important and talented living person in the entire flaming firmament of the known universe.

He’s going to use campaign cash to make himself look good, or at least far better than he looks now. Multiple polls show Trump’s approval rating now mired in the mid-30% range – at or near historic lows for a president facing a midterm election.

So he’ll launch a campaign to regain the adulation he’s lost, to recast himself as the hero he believes he is, to reclaim the mantle of savior to which he thinks he’s entitled.

In other words, it will be a campaign to promote, glorify and exalt Donald J Trump.

The non-profit arm of Trump’s political operation, Securing American Greatness, has already spent about $1m on its first midterm ads set to air nationwide, featuring video clips of Trump talking about tax breaks in his domestic spending legislation and lower prices for eggs and prescription drugs.

In early August, according to the Atlantic, Trump told advisers that they should follow the same strategy as the Democrats: making the election about him.

But as Karl Rove, who was senior adviser and deputy chief of staff for George W Bush, notes in the Wall Street Journal, given Trump’s unpopularity, making the election even more about him only helps the Democrats.

Trump also plans to travel all over the country, holding rallies like he did during his presidential elections. As Rove notes, Fox News’s senior White House correspondent, Peter Doocy, reports hearing “whispers of a ton of Trump travel in October, possibly as much as a Trump rally a day” in competitive states and districts.

But Rove also warns: “Trump is never disciplined. He’ll have no script, saying whatever comes to mind. His crazy comments will dominate the news, locally and nationally. Republican candidates will constantly have to fend off questions about whether they agree with his latest insult or half-baked idea. The narrative won’t be on anything positive about them or the GOP.”

Presumably this is why some battleground Republicans told Trump’s staff that they would prefer he not visit their districts ahead of November, according to four Republican operatives involved in the conversations, as reported by Politico. Meanwhile, Republican pollsters have told candidates in tight races to limit their references to him.

“We’ve told them he cannot come,” one senior Republican, involved in a district where Trump won by double digits in the last election, told Politico. “Candidly, he would not be helpful here … I do not believe they would send him without our OK. And if they did, we probably wouldn’t campaign with him.”

Rove and other Republican functionaries are urging Trump to “act more presidential” by using his Super Pacs’ $403m to support Republican candidates rather than support a campaign about himself.

But they’re yelling into the wind of Trump’s ballroom-sized ego.

The truth is, Trump doesn’t give a damn about the midterm elections except insofar as Republican losses make him look bad. He probably figures if he backs a candidate with his Pac money and they lose, he’ll look even worse.

So better to spend it on boosting himself.

As almost everyone in the world knows by now, Trump cares only about himself. That’s been his MO for ever.

Bad news for Republicans in the midterms and good news for Democrats.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan Llerena
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan Llerena
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The breach won’t be the last – or the most dangerous – of its kind. We need an agency capable of full investigations into AI incidents

W
hen OpenAI first revealed that its AI agents had autonomously hacked a major real-world company, Hugging Face, many assumed only one or two agents were involved. The truth, a new report reveals, is far stranger: the incident involved about 1,200 AI agents, 700 of which directly participated in the attack.

OpenAI invited researchers from METR, along with an expert from Redwood Research, to produce the new report, alongside the company’s own investigation. The findings shocked the experts.

The agents were highly coordinated, constructing complex message boards in the nooks and crannies of their shared artefact repository. All told, agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages in less than a week. Even more concerning, the agents took steps to hide their behavior – spoofing tool calls and attempting to tamper with their own logs.

Initial reporting assumed that the agents had attacked Hugging Face in search of an answer key to a difficult test. In reality, investigators found that the agents had figured out a way to derive the answers within the first few hours. The days of work that followed focused on another goal: concerned that the automated scoring system might identify the agents’ cheating, they aimed to learn more about the scorer. The goal wasn’t just to cheat, but to hide it.

These details are startling, and they’re a warning sign about the current trajectory of AI development. But just as concerning is how limited the investigation was and how much we still don’t know.

We work at a thinktank that analyzes AI-related legislation, and we’ve been worried for a while that legal requirements for reporting incidents like these are insufficient.

These reports make that clear: they’re informative enough to tell us something went wrong, but not detailed enough to tell us why.

This shouldn’t surprise us. These investigations are entirely voluntary, and their findings are limited to what the company is willing to disclose. METR’s independent investigation was highly constrained by an agreement with OpenAI. For example, the investigators were not given access to the underlying model that created the majority of the misbehaving agents. And despite indications that message boards had formed as early as May and that coordinated agent activity persisted after 13 July, METR was only permitted to investigate the period from 26 June to 13 July.

And that was the good part. METR was given close to nothing about OpenAI’s safety and security practices. If OpenAI ignored warning signs – as several data points suggest – violated its own safety procedures, or failed to implement fixes that would prevent future events, these all fell outside the scope of METR’s investigation. The expert investigators themselves were left with many questions and continued concerns.

Concerns about the limits aren’t hypothetical. On Friday, Reuters reported that another swarm of OpenAI agents had broken out this spring, hijacking a German website and using it as another message board. According to the report, OpenAI knew about this incident but said nothing, and it was entirely absent from METR’s report.

Clearly, this kind of investigation – however well-executed – leaves a lot to be desired.

When planes crash, trains derail or chemical plants explode, expert government investigators arrive with legal authority to compel evidence, preserve records, and tell the public what happened. Hugging Face reported this incident to law enforcement, and multiple attorneys general have expressed interest in looking into it.

But no government agency has both the mandate and expertise to investigate the technical facts of the incident and OpenAI’s conduct. As far as we know, the only people to examine this incident did so at OpenAI’s discretion and with its consent.

And while the Hugging Face breach is not as severe as a plane crash, it was a serious and costly attack. It’s unlikely to be the last, or the most severe.

Existing laws don’t fill this gap. While some attorneys general have tried to use existing investigatory powers, these offices aren’t built for technical fact-finding, and the laws they rely on are limited to questions of consumer deception, not public risk. Despite significant AI laws passed in California, New York and Illinois, none create the investigative authority demanded by these incidents. As we’ve written elsewhere, existing incident reporting laws probably don’t cover the Hugging Face attack, and even if they did, OpenAI might share little more than the date and a short summary.

What we need is a federal body equipped to conduct expert investigations of serious AI incidents – with the authority to compel documents and testimony, resources and personnel to examine the systems involved, and the ability to partner with third-party experts like METR.

Reports should be published, subject to appropriate redactions, to ensure the public learns from the incident. And reporting should also extend to near-miss events, which may reveal warnings before major harms occur.

This structure would not be unusual. In aviation, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates accidents with subpoena and wide-ranging investigative powers. Aircraft operators must preserve wreckage and records; and the NTSB may confer with employees and contract external experts.

Congress can build a similar system for AI incidents, while protecting AI developers’ legitimate interests. Investigations should open only upon clear triggers and be bound to the incident. Certain confidential information can receive statutory protection. And investigations can be limited to one agency with priority to avoid duplicative investigations.

The need and urgency is real. Subsequent reports have revealed that the Hugging Face breach was not an isolated incident and that autonomous agents from Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have hacked third parties in separate incidents. We’ve been lucky so far – the harms have been limited. But luck is no substitute for the law.

Mackenzie Arnold is the managing director of US law & policy at the Institute for Law & AI, where he provides analysis and advice to ensure that advances in AI benefit the public at large

Stephan Llerena is a research scholar at the Institute for Law & AI. His research focuses on US law and policy regarding frontier AI governance

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Lindsay Clancy’s case is a rorschach test | Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Clancy’s case became a referendum on mothers, healthcare and the status of women

M
ost family annihilators are men. It’s a grim fact that such incidents are common enough to have a discernible pattern. The massacre is carried out by a husband and father, often one who is on the verge of bankruptcy or divorce; typically, it forms the finale of a long reign of domestic violence terror.

About half the time, the perpetrator kills himself after slaughtering his family. Gun use is common – a large number of what are termed “mass shootings” in the United States are in fact family annihilation killings, in which a man turns his weapon on his family members. Other times, the killer uses knives, or fires.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

This kind of killing does not always make the news. When it does, news organizations often run family photos, in which the killer smiles on a beach or beside the Grand Canyon with his arm around the wife and children he will later shoot or strangle.

In this context of pervasive and normalized male domestic violence against women and children, the Lindsay Clancy case was always going to attract outside attention. Because in that case, when three Massachusetts children were strangled of their family home in January of 2023 – Cora, who was five, Dawson, who was three, and Callan, who was just eight months old – the killer was their mom.

As is fairly common for family annihilators, Clancy attempted suicide after killing her children. But Clancy survived. Injuries left her paralyzed below the waist. At her murder trial, which lasted an unusually long six weeks and concluded in a hung jury on Friday, she rolled to the defense table each morning in a wheelchair.

The mistrial means that Clancy – along with her children’s father, their grandparents, and everyone else who loved them, to say nothing of the state – will now face the possibility of being subjected to a second trial. All because of a hung jury.

Eleven of the 12 jurors accepted the argument put forward by Clancy’s defense, that Clancy, who does not contest that she killed her children, was suffering from an acute case of postpartum psychosis, and hence could not be held legally responsible for their deaths. But according to notes that the forewoman of the jury sent to the judge, one juror, a man, expressed “reasonable doubt” about Clancy’s culpability under the law, but refused to apply that doubt as is legally required.

That this lone juror who wanted to convict Clancy was male is relevant, because the Clancy case itself became, in the distorting ways that such stories tend to when they are witnessed en masse through social media, a referendum on motherhood, mental healthcare, and the status of women.

Some mothers have expressed deep sympathy for Clancy’s postpartum mental health crises, citing resonances with their own experiences and a hope that the case can bring greater attention to the rare but acute and debilitating kind of postpartum mental suffering that Clancy seems to have experienced; others say that medical neglect of the condition, and of the experiences of postpartum women more broadly, create the conditions for tragedies like that of the Clancy family.

Some on the misogynist right, meanwhile, have seized upon Clancy’s actions and the support she has received as evidence that women are congenitally evil, disposed to violence, untrustworthy and unfit for public life.

Your opinion on the Clancy case will probably largely depend on whether you believe her defense team’s claim that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that was severe enough that she experienced the kind of delusions, hallucinations, paranoia, rapid shifts in mood, and other departures from reality that would render her not responsible for her own actions. In other words, do you think she was really ill, or do you think that she killed her children in cold blood, and is lying?

The facts suggest that she isn’t. Clancy had a history of postpartum psychological distress following the births of her first two children, in 2017 and 2019. She was prescribed medication after those births, and seems to have been a loving and attentive mother to them for years.

But following the birth of her third child, a little boy named Callan, in 2022, reports suggest that Clancy began to experience something different, and much more serious, than her previous bouts with postpartum anxiety.

She couldn’t sleep, wasn’t eating, and would experience bouts of sudden, acute terror. Going back to her job as a nurse in a labor and delivery unit seemed impossible; she could barely function. She sought help again and was diagnosed with anxiety.

Later, she would speak to other mental health practitioners, too. A series of providers issued her a stunning array of psychiatric medications. As her sleeplessness continued, Clancy was prescribed increasingly powerful tranquilizers.

More than a month before she killed her children, Clancy reported that she had begun to hallucinate. She kept seeking help, saying that she was thinking of killing herself; she told both her mother and her husband that she feared she would harm her children, though she had never mistreated them before.

Clancy briefly checked herself in to inpatient treatment, but left after just a few nights. The Clancys seem to have thought that longer-term hospitalization was out of the question. After all, she had kids to take care of. Soon, she was hearing voices.

Those who are most outraged by the Clancy case, and by the sympathy that a homicidal mother has received, are disturbed by the unnaturalness of a woman killing her children, disturbed by what they fear is a secret core of hate and depravity in women that could be unleashed at any time.

But if I were a psychoanalyst, I might say that the right wing that imagines all women as potential Lindsay Clancys is projecting their own guilt: on some level, they know that what our culture asks mothers to do is unsustainable, cruel, and often quite literally maddening.

Because to me, what is most haunting about the Clancy case is how ordinary and unsurprising all the failures were that led to her break.

She was failed in ordinary ways by providers who saw a woman living in relative comfort and assumed her suffering could not be very serious; she was failed in ordinary ways by a community that understands motherhood to be a state of variously mild and acute suffering, and has so normalized women’s disappearance into the family that they can barely see the mother for the baby.

She was failed by the expectation that women will persevere through their own suffering, even their most disturbing and agonizing moments, to care for their children; she was failed by the trivialization of women’s lives, and by the blithe assumption that the so-called “baby blues” were mere neurotic episodes, not psychotic breaks requiring serious clinical interventions. Her children were failed, too.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.title: For baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhere
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.author: Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.text:
From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness

O
ver the last several years, simultaneously lauded and paralyzed by its ironclad traditions, baseball has undergone various forays into reinvention, trying to free itself from its unwritten rules of retaliation, its seeming aversion to joy, its demand that every generation of player of every culture and background play the game with the grimness of a Dust Bowl farmer.

The sport even attempted to change those customs by promoting a cultural shift with an industry-wide motto: Let the Kids Play. But in a time of intense division within the aggressive backdrop of Trumpism, the result is a racial clash that is actually a generational and cultural one that predates current politics by a century.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

On Saturday night, Braves superstar Ronald Acuña Jr hit a third-inning home run off Zack Wheeler of the Phillies and floated around the bases, arms wide, imitating an airplane, Euro-stepping past third base as if he were Manu Ginobili, and infuriating Wheeler and his manager Don Mattingly with his apparent disregard for the accepted customs of the game.

A week before, in the midst of what would be a 16-1 rout, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm swiped two meaningless bases in a blowout win over the Red Sox when the defense had conceded his presence – according to a 150-year-old custom, runners are expected to respect this courtesy by not advancing. Chisholm’s breach of protocol prompted Red Sox radio announcer Will Flemming to suggest on the air that a Yankee player drill one of Chisholm’s teammates for his insolence.

For the trifecta, during a Colorado-St Louis series this weekend, neither the Cardinals nor the Rockies had a problem with each other – but umpire Doug Eddings did, stopping the game to tell Cardinals rookie Hancel Rincon to adjust his hat. Eddings determined the rookie’s hat was too crooked (despite his later admission that Rincon had not violated any official rules) and Rincon would not disrespect his game on his field. Eddings then issued a time violation to the Cardinals when manager Oli Marmol complained, then ejected Marmol, and then missed an obvious call at the plate against the Cardinals.

In each of the incidents, the offended – Eddings, Wheeler (and to a lesser extent Mattingly), and Flemming – were white, while the alleged offenders – Acuña, Chisholm, Rincon, and Marmol – were Black or Latino. Periodically this season, baseball has found its way into the repellent culture wars, first during the World Baseball Classic earlier this year when the Americans soured the proceedings with their militia-like grimness when the rest of the world was having fun. Maybe war is all America has to offer these days.

In June, when participation was optional, several players decided to exercise their religious freedoms by crashing Pride Night by writing Bible passages on their hats. When the players were warned over the incident, the Department of Justice threatened to investigate whether baseball was discriminating against Christians.

If, however, it appears that baseball is an extension of Maga – and it very well may be – what Eddings and company have really resurfaced over the past is not exactly Trumpism per se, but what Trumpism tacitly demands: an incessant imposition of whiteness on American institutions, and an aggressiveness that emboldens the gatekeepers like Eddings to put the coloreds in their place.

No league forces its historical whiteness on its players like Major League Baseball. That whiteness is also known as “tradition,” of playing the game the right way. That tradition is practiced by players Black, white and Latino, who were raised in the old-school American baseball tradition with its ethnic, Depression-era seriousness. Other sports adjust to the new generations of players who enter the game. The NBA’s Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are not expected to play like George Mikan and John Havlicek. In baseball, Bob Gibson and Pedro Martínez are proudly the spiritual extensions of Rube Waddell and Walter Johnson.

Mattingly, wasn’t happy with Acuña, but judging by his postgame comments his conflicts were not racial, or racist, but instead resigned to a baseball becoming unrecognizable to him – a carnival of bat flips and unprofessionalism masquerading as fun. Mattingly has been in the game nearly 50 years. He was teammates with the ultimate showman, Rickey Henderson, whose on-field expressions were loathed, but Mattingly knew Henderson was no clown. He also managed Yasiel Puig, who was electric but whose respect for his craft wavered. Mattingly knows the difference between being professional and not, joy and disrespect, and seemed to be lamenting the desperate blurring of the two at the encouragement of the people who run the sport.

In better times, when it didn’t appear umpires were looking for a fight, and when baseball especially did not appear to enlist itself in harassing players of color – Eddings might have been shrugged off as another power-tripping umpire having a bad day and taking it out on a kid making his big-league debut and the manager telling him to “fucking grow up,” as Marmol did.

These are not better times. Eddings looked small and petty, and baseball’s strain of “playing the right way” is usually code for its eternal conflicts with how Black and Latino players express themselves in competition, how they dress, celebrate, emote. Even in 2026, somewhere in baseball – as evidence by Flemming’s comments and subsequent apology – it is always 1926.

What, it should be asked, is this all about? It is an example of just how frayed the nerves of the country are, and what abuses of authority look like, especially as baseball in the backdrop of a Maga country feels like a hostile place. The Cardinals responded by protecting their player, and thumbing their nose at Eddings by tilting their hats as a team in solidarity. The small moments can provide the kind of kindling that can bring a team together (after five months of mediocrity, the Cardinals are trying to snag an 11th-hour playoff spot.)

As for Eddings, who later apologized, he resembled the doomed, peacocking general surrounded by enemy forces. Umpires have few friends these days. The humorous YouTube channel Jomboy, once an innocuous value-add for Yankee fans for its clever lip-reading of on-field incidents, became a viral sensation, and MLB, desperate to attract a younger audience, realized the telegraph isn’t going to make a comeback and bought an equity stake in the company, transforming Jomboy from a clever fan site to an arm of MLB, which is not so innocuously trying to rid the game of human umpiring. In addition to Jomboy, numerous unofficial social media users virally spread umpires’ worst calls, intensifying the drumbeat that umpiring in its current form needs to go the way of the flannel uniform.

Eddings spent this Labor Day weekend making another case for the robots, contributing simultaneously to baseball’s 100-year culture war and to the umpires’ digging of their own graves.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He writes at Substack.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question | Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Our three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measures

This summer, mayors met in London during the heatwave that ironically threatened to derail London Climate Action Week.

As temperatures broke records across the UK and Europe, leading some climate talks to be suspended or cancelled, we found ourselves seeking shelter and comparing how our cities prepare for extreme heat: how we protect vulnerable residents, communicate risk, and redesign neighbourhoods for hotter summers.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

At the same time, Paris was overseeing the city’s crisis response as another intense heatwave swept across France. Across Europe, more than 14,000 people lost their lives due to the heat.

As mayors, we are confronting the same question: how do you protect millions of people when extreme heat is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly familiar part of summer?

For Phoenix, that question has shaped city government for decades. For Paris and Milan, it is now becoming one of the defining challenges of urban leadership.

It may strike some people as unusual that two of Europe’s oldest and most prestigious cities are looking to a city in the Arizona desert for ideas. But rising temperatures are now a global challenge, and we don’t have time for each city to figure out what works on its own.

Phoenix has learned, sometimes the hard way, that extreme heat cannot be treated as simply a weather event. It shapes decisions about transport, housing, public health, public space, and emergency planning. Preparing for summer begins long before temperatures start to rise.

Phoenix established one of the world’s first city offices dedicated to heat response and mitigation, reflecting an approach that focuses on both immediate relief from extreme heat, especially for those most vulnerable, and building resilience in the medium-long-term by implementing cooling solutions to make the city safer and more comfortable.

The city’s shade plans require 75% shade coverage in new development in areas with high pedestrian activity, and programs that support schools, transit users, and those most vulnerable. To further reduce the urban heat island effect, Phoenix is applying cool surface treatment to buildings and roadways, including on more than 300 kilometers of neighborhood streets.

The city leads its region in heat response, including providing a 24-hour cooling center with wraparound support to connect people with resources such as housing, medical services, and even job placement. Landlords are required by law to maintain a safe indoor temperature (28C/82F or lower), and companies that contract with the city must implement heat safety plans to keep workers healthy and comfortable. These measures save lives: during the summer of 2024, which was the hottest on record in Phoenix, the city’s coordinated heat response measures contributed to a 20% year-over-year decline in heat-related 911 calls.

Paris and Milan bring different expertise as well as unique challenges.

Both are historic European cities where streets, buildings and public spaces were designed for a different time and a different climate. Today, both cities are adapting.

Every Parisian now lives within a seven-minute walk of a cool spot. The city now has more than 1,400 of these spaces where people can cool down during a heatwave, including parks, gardens and other public facilities. The city also extends opening hours for parks, swimming pools, and public baths during high temperatures. The city has mobilised a network of 27,000 climate volunteers to raise awareness within their communities of the climate crisis and heatwave adaptation strategies, alongside preventive actions.

The city is also planning for a future that would have been inconceivable to Parisians just a few decades ago: “Paris at 50°C” was organised in October 2023 to test the responsiveness of the municipality and its partners, as well as improve planning and coordination for future heat emergency responses. This involved the whole community, utilities, media and schools and directly inspired Barcelona to carry out the same exercise in 2027.

No city can simply import another’s model. Geography, history and politics are different everywhere. But every mayor owes it to their residents to gather the best ideas from cities around the world; and through the C40 Cities network, nearly 100 of the world’s biggest cities are sharing climate solutions for our residents and businesses. Cities have always learned from one another. We have adapted successful transport systems, housing policies and public health measures for generations. Heat adaptation should be no different.

If one city discovers a better way to protect outdoor workers, cool public spaces or communicate risk to residents, others should not spend years reinventing it. Good ideas should travel.

Inspired by Barcelona and Paris cool spaces initiatives, Milan is expanding its Piazze Aperte (Open Squares) and School Streets programme to integrate cool spaces by planting trees, replacing hard surfaces with permeable green space and creating shaded areas. The Municipality also provides a helpline and support services for the elderly and vulnerable residents through Milano Aiuta (Milano Helps). Milan’s Air and Climate Plan outlines a binding goal to limit local temperature increases to 2C by 2050; they are one of the only cities in the world that has set a temperature-related target, which is very ambitious.

Extreme heat already claims more than half a million lives every year, making it the deadliest climate hazard. Cities are particularly exposed because buildings, roads and pavements absorb heat during the day and release it long into the night, meaning residents get no respite and struggle to cool down properly. Older residents, young children, outdoor workers and lower-income communities often face the greatest risks.

Planting trees, cooling schools, redesigning streets, improving buildings, and expanding early warning systems are often described as climate policies. They are also public health measures, investments in local economies, and practical improvements that make cities more livable throughout the year.

Meanwhile, heating and cooling account for nearly half of all energy use in Europe, with about 70% of heating still generated by fossil fuels. Cities have the power to lead a fair transition to clean heat. By investing in renewable energy and cleaner heating systems, they can cut emissions, improve air quality, and create local jobs, ensuring the benefits reach those who need it most.

Cities are often the first to experience climate impacts but the last to receive the powers, funding and flexibility needed to respond. National governments should work with cities to develop more effective adaptation strategies, expand early warning systems, and make it easier for local leaders to access the finance needed to protect residents. Those investments can save lives, strengthen economies and reduce future costs across the entire country.

This summer has given Europe a glimpse of what those living in desert climates feel so often, and what we can all expect to become our norm in the age of climate crisis.

Extreme heat is not an individual burden; it is an existential challenge we must all rise to. The responsibility cannot fall on the shoulders of an isolated pensioner, a vulnerable child or a construction worker. Heat is a political crisis that demands bold political action.

We must prepare and fight back. The climate crisis is redefining what our definition of “normal” is at a rapid rate. Our ability to learn from one another must move even faster.

Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego are the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: US Open 2026 quarter-finals: Aryna Sabalenka v Linda Noskova – live
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Katy Murrells (now) and Taha Hashim (later)
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
Sabalenka has such a fine record in tie-breaks, though, and Sabalenka surges 1-0, 2-0, 3-0 ahead as she ups the ante with some heavy hitting. And then 4-0, when Noskova nets her return. And 5-0, when Noskova can’t deal with the body serve and hits beyond the baseline. So Noskova has two must-win points on serve … but she loses the first with an errant backhand, and they change ends at 6-0 …

First set: Sabalenka* 6-6 Noskova (*denotes next server)

Credit to Noskova for the way she’s come back at Sabalenka, after admitting her last-16 win over Marta Kostyuk, when she recovered from missing double match point in the second set to eventually prevail on her sixth MP in the third, took a lot out of her emotionally. But she looks sharp and focused here, pushing Sabalenka into a tie-break when she dismissively holds to love.

First set: Sabalenka 6-5 Noskova* (*denotes next server)

It’s one-way for Sabalenka at 40-0 … until Noskova hits an improbable backhand return winner at full stretch for 40-15! That’s one for the highlights reel, perhaps the shot of the match so far. But Sabalenka holds from there, stopping the run of games against her, and Noskova must serve to stay in the set for the third time.

First set: Sabalenka* 5-5 Noskova (*denotes next server)

Noskova, perhaps a little over-excited after winning two successive games, pushes a forehand long on the opening point. But she wins the next two, lashing down a fifth ace in the process (Sabalenka has hit three), and then turns 30-15 into 40-30 with another ace. And Noskova makes it three games on the spin when Sabalenka snatches at a backhand! The Czech’s comeback is very much on.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to give us your support. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Noskova breaks: Sabalenka 5-4 Noskova* (*denotes next server)

Sabalenka has lost from several winning positions this summer – and will that be on her mind as she serves for the opener? She wobbles at 15-all with a double fault – cue a huge roar of disgust from the defending champion, it’s a rare blot on her service book in this first set – and then Noskova nails a forehand winner right into the corner! It’s 15-40, the first break points for Noskova .. and Sabalenka smacks a forehand into the net! Perhaps the ghosts of grand slams past this year are still on Sabalenka’s mind.

First set: Sabalenka* 5-3 Noskova (*denotes next server)

A straightforward hold to 15 for Sabalenka leaves Noskova serving to stay in the first set at 5-2 down. Perhaps she can take some inspiration from Zheng’s escape acts from 5-0 behind in the first set against Iga Swiatek in the last 16 – and in the final set against Madison Keys in the third round. But at 15-all, Noskova misses a makeable volley, and Sabalenka then moves within two points of the set at 30-all. Noskova nudges to 40-30, is dragged back to deuce, but lives to fight another game in this set when she takes the next two points.

First set: Sabalenka* 4-2 Noskova (*denotes next server)

The luck is with Sabalenka on the opening point as a mis-hit return makes it 0-15. Which becomes 15-30. So with Noskova 1-4 and 15-30 down, desperate times call for desperate measures … and Noskova opts for the serve-volley, but it doesn’t come off. Sabalenka’s return is too hot for Noskova to handle on the fourth point, creating two break chances for Sabalenka at 15-40 … but her return loses its range and Noskova gamely takes the next four points, sealing the hold with an ace.

First set: Sabalenka 4-1 Noskova* (*denotes next server)

A prolonged rally at 15-all – that’s a rarity in this battle of first-strike hitting – with Sabalenka staying patient, not going for too much, eventually forcing Noskova to go for broke, and the Czech clunks into the tramlines. Undeterred, Noskova manages to get to 30-all for the second successive Sabalenka service game … but doesn’t advance any further. Sabalenka retains her advantage.

First set: Sabalenka* 3-1 Noskova (*denotes next server)

At 30-all, Sabalenka is applying more pressure on Noskova’s serve, but Sabalenka smacks a backhand return into the net and Noskova can breathe a little at 40-30. And the Wimbledon champion gets her side of the scoreboard moving when Sabalenka again errs with her return. The Arthur Ashe crowd – perhaps only about a half full so far – cheer loudly. They’re not against Sabelenka – as they were in the previous round when she played the American Taylor Townsend – but of course they want a close match.

First set: Sabalenka 3-0 Noskova* (*denotes next server)

Sabalenka concedes her first point for 0-15, after a Noskova backhand winner (that’ll help shake off any nerves for the Czech), and it’s soon 15-30. Sabalenka takes a little more time before the next point, blowing on her hand before serving, and it does the job as she batters away a backhand winner, also from the middle of the court. Who needs angles when you’ve got that much pace. And an ace, already her third of the match, brings up 40-30. And after an aborted ball toss, she consolidates the break with an unreturned serve. Sabalenka looks every inch the two-time defending champion right now, rather than the possibly soon-to-be-deposed world No 1 who has had such a shaky summer.

Sabalenka breaks: Sabalenka* 2-0 Noskova (*denotes next server)

Both of these players are big hitters – but they aren’t afraid to come to the net either – and both will be vying to become the frontrunner in the points. Sabalenka does that successfully in a short, sharp opening service game, holding to love, before Noskova drops 0-40 down. It’s quite hard to follow the ball because of the confusing contrast – with Noskova’s half of the court baked in sun, Sabalenka’s entirely in the shade. But it’s Sabalenka who puts Noskova firmly in the shade with an inside-out forehand winner from virtually no angle in the middle of the court on the second break point. It’s been a flawless start from the defending champion.

These two have played each other twice before, with both matches taking place on hard courts, three years ago in Adelaide and this year in the Indian Wells semi-final. Sabalenka won both in straight sets. But Noskova is a grand slam champion now, on an 11-match winning run at majors.

Despite Sabalenka’s struggles this summer, you can’t discount her numbers either: this is her sixth successive US Open quarter-final (she’s emulated Serena with that), she’s the two-time defending champion, and she’son an 18-match winning streak in New York. So something will have to give today.

Walking out into the sunshine on Arthur Ashe is Noskova, closely followed by Sabalenka, who once again is wearing her basketball-inspired orange mesh dress, which is accessorised by several hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of bling. Noskova has opted for a more understated white number, with a blue and red trim.

With Rybakina v Zheng and Gauff v Andreeva to come in the quarter-finals tomorrow, the current holders of the four grand slam titles are all still in contention (Sabalenka, Rybakina, Andreeva and Noskova) - and just to add to the tournament’s finale, the four women who can leave Flushing Meadows with the world No 1 ranking are still in the mix too (Sabalenka, Rybakina, Gauff and Pegula - though if Rybakina defeats Zheng she’ll be guaranteed to become No 1 for the first time in her career). The strength at the top of the women’s game right now is seriously impressive.

Yesterday’s last-16 matches in the women’s draw were stacked with top match-ups, with Elena Rybakina and Coco Gauff making statements of intent with clinical wins over Naomi Osaka and Iva Jovic respectively; Zheng Qinwen coming from 5-0 down for the second match in a row (has that ever happened before?!) to knock out Iga Swiatek in two absorbing sets; and Mirra Andreeva mounting her own comeback to defeat Anastasia Potapova in three.

On the men’s side, Alexander Zverev had a welcome pre-midnight finish for once, Alexander Blockx’s brilliant run continued despite injury and the rejuvenated Russian Karen Khachanov ended American hopes of having four home men in the quarter-finals after defeating Learner Tien from two sets to one down.

Simon Cambers has posted on social media that tickets for tonight’s Alcaraz v Shelton showdown are being sold on resale for a minimum of $500 up in the nosebleed seats to more than $11,0000 courtside. Yikes. Maybe we can blame the influencers for that too.

Aryna Sabalenka (1) v Linda Noskova (Cze, 6)

Men’s singles quarter-final
Frances Tiafoe (US, 11) v Alex Michelsen (US)

7pm New York/midnight BST

Men’s singles quarter-final

Hello and welcome to our coverage of the US Open - day 10!

So here we are, at the quarter-final stage. Gone is the compelling chaos of matches taking place here, there and everywhere in the earlier rounds, and finally we can make do with only one pair of eyes, our gaze both shrinking and intensifying now we’re down to the one singles court.

Being the focus of that gaze is still something new to Linda Noskova, who’d reached only one grand slam quarter-final before her run to this summer’s Wimbledon title, but the 21-year-old Czech seems unfazed by the big stage and is unlikely to be intimidated by the task of facing Aryna Sabalenka today, especially with the defending champion’s aura not what it was. Yes, Sabalenka has reached the last eight with four straight-sets wins, but her prickly exchanges with reporters in the early rounds perhaps betrayed the pressure she is feeling, having not claimed a grand slam this year or a title since March amid several head-scratching defeats to much lower-ranked players. Sabalenka also knows her near two-year stretch as the world No 1 will end if Elena Rybakina wins one more match in New York. If Noskova can reproduce her Wimbledon form today, we’ll get to find out where Sabalenka’s level and head is really at.

They’re first on Arthur Ashe in the day session, before the American derby between Frances Tiafoe – two times a semi-finalist at his most successful major but never a finalist – and the surprise package Alex Michelsen, who’s reached his first slam quarter-final without even dropping a set. Tiafoe, at 28, has far more experience than the 22-year-old Californian but is also carrying heavier baggage; he knows the years of opportunity are passing by, while Michelsen has almost nothing to lose - that’s if you can call a grand slam quarter-final a free shot. Crowd loyalty will be divided but Tiafoe will hope his superior athleticism and momentum from his clutch win over Daniil Medvedev in the last 16 will see him through against a 6ft 5in, big-serving opponent who once compared himself to Obi-Wan Kenobi because of his ability to balance defence and attack.

Away from Arthur Ashe, the doubles continues – the top seeds and Wimbledon champions, Britain’s Henry Patten and Finland’s Harri Heliovaara, are among those in action – while the wheelchair events begin, with the five-time US Open doubles champions Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid among the headliners. And all of this before a blockbuster night session, as Carlos Alcaraz faces off against Ben Shelton and Jessica Pegula plays Emma Navarro, in the second all-American affair of the day.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.title: Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham have been stalked. They’re far from alone in the WNBA
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.author: Stephanie Kaloi
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/s.text:
Players generally welcome interacting with their fans. But as the league’s popularity surges, there are dangers to be aware of

C
aitlin Clark spent most of the 2025 WNBA season sidelined with a series of injuries that forced her to miss more than 30 games. But she also spent part of the season (and the preceding offseason) quietly navigating a tumultuous and scary reality: a 55-year-old man was stalking her, and he was convinced they were in a relationship.

That man, Michael Lewis, was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in prison last July. Lewis sent Clark “hundreds” of messages – many of which were “threats and sexually explicit” – between 12 December 2024 and 11 January 2025. Lewis, who is from Texas, was arrested at a hotel in Indianapolis, where Clark plays for the Indiana Fever. The case took a toll on Clark: she said she feared for her safety and had changed her appearance in public.

Clark isn’t the only player in the WNBA who has had a stalker, and stalking isn’t limited to the pros. In 2024, a 40-year-old man pleaded guilty to stalking Paige Bueckers, who was then playing for the UConn Huskies; former Indiana Fever guard Syd Colson has spoken about her own stalker several times. As a college student at UCLA, Toronto Tempo’s Kiki Rice received “dozens” of messages from a man who believed the pair shared something “magnetic.” In June, a 48-year-old man was arrested for stalking Clark’s teammate Sophie Cunningham.

The problem is not unique to the WNBA: NFL star Aaron Donald was stalked by a woman who falsely claimed they were married. But the league’s rising popularity, the ever-present threat of misogyny and the fact that women are far more likely to be stalked than men mean the problem is one the league is unfortunately becoming more familiar with.

That’s not to say that every fan interaction is negative; in fact, most are great for both parties. Earlier this month, the Portland Fire’s Emily Engstler told reporters that the team gets “recognized a decent amount.”

Portland fans are “super respectful,” she added. That’s something Engstler “really appreciates,” and she likes the fan-athlete relationship to be a two-way street. “I think it’s not hard to be respectful to your fans and give them the time of day,” she added. “So I try to make sure I do it.”

The fan-athlete relationship is parasocial, Dr Shira Gabriel, professor of psychology at SUNY, University of Buffalo, says. But, she points out, parasocial relationships aren’t inherently bad, and we all have them.

Gabriel, whose book Collective Effervescence will be released next year, studies these relationships. While writing her book, she found that researchers examining parasocial bonds “at first were looking for all the bad stuff and trying to find that these are the loneliest, most desperate people,” she says. “And if anything, the opposite is true.”

Forming these bonds “is a part of being a healthy person in the modern world,” Gabriel says. “We have access to information about people that we would never have had when we were developing as a species.”

She went on to point out that nearly all of us have some kind of parasocial bond, whether that’s keeping up with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, or attending WNBA games and following players on social media to find out more about their lives.

Humans seek connection, Gabriel says. “If you’re a big WNBA fan, you can feel connected to the whole fandom, and that’s great,” Gabriel continues. “That’s an important thing for us. Again, we’re a really social species, and we want to have those connections … this is something that healthy people do and that increases the degree to which we can feel connected.”

Those relationships begin to go wrong when “people sort of forget that the person who they have the bond with is an actual living and breathing human being, and you are sort of dehumanizing them” when you forget that, Gabriel says. “They’re just sort of this person online, and that opens up avenues for people to behave in ways or treat people in a way that they wouldn’t in their real life.”

The risk factors that make someone more likely to escalate a parasocial relationship to stalking are similar to those that exist in real relationships, too.

“I think the people who are doing this are people who are probably not particularly stable in other aspects of what they’re doing,” Gabriel says. “You’re not going to find somebody who is doing well in their lives, and is happy, and not suffering from severe mental illness, who mistakes these for real bonds and starts going after someone, just like you’re not going to date somebody who’s actually like a super healthy wonderful person and have them turn into a stalker who completely disrupts your life.

“When that happens, that’s because this person is bringing some kind of real emotional baggage with them, and that’s what we would see with a parasocial bond, too.”

A league source told the Guardian that the WNBA is well aware of all of these dynamics, and player safety is paramount. The league pays attention to safety across the board: at games, of course, but also at hotels, airports, and online. The new Collective Bargaining Agreement contains minimum safety requirements each team must have in place.

There is a three-step process when a threat is reported. First, the league’s Global Security Operations Center, which operates on a 24/7 basis, assesses the validity of the threat and begins an investigation. The league next determines what additional security needs to be deployed to mitigate the threat. The third step includes potentially banning or restricting the threatening individual from arenas and games, or referring the case to local authorities. Every reported incident is investigated.

“We’re going to care about what the prominent people in our society are doing,” Gabriel says. “And that’s good. There’s nothing bad about that. That’s like being an engaged person who cares about the world around them, and all the research that I’ve done and other people have done really suggests that this can be a really healthy part of life in the modern world.”

The WNBA is working to ensure that when those relationships turn unhealthy, the problem is quickly dealt with.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Man City-bound 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan is MLS’s chaotic revelation
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: John Muller
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The Philadelphia Union midfielder has gotten his longest run of game time since turning pro, and the data is tantalizing

There’s a video from a United States U-15 camp three years ago that will make your head spin. It’s a routine training session for the boys on the pitch except one, a head shorter and a year or two younger than the others, who’s practicing with the national team for the first time.

Is the boy nervous? He is not. A pass floats into the box and he checks his run, tries to get under it, but the ball is too high for his 13-year-old head to reach. He doesn’t even jump. As the cross sails over him, he flings himself forward like Superman and flicks a heel up behind his back, catching the ball with a scorpion kick that bounces straight into the path of a teammate for a cartoon assist.

This is Cavan Sullivan: a player whose next move is difficult to predict, probably even for him. Which makes it even more remarkable that the predictions about him keep coming true.

By now, you may have heard about him. Whispered about by scouts since childhood, signed before he had played a single minute as a pro to join Manchester City the day he turns 18, Sullivan became the youngest debutant in Major League Soccer history when he was 14. But raw potential doesn’t mean much at that age: the child star whose record he broke was none other than Freddy Adu, the great cautionary tale of American soccer.

For two tantalizing years after he turned pro, Sullivan remained more a prophecy than a player, growing up on the Philadelphia Union’s bench. This summer, though, he got his shot, and in a recent run of starts he’s been rapidly, visibly maturing into the star who was promised. We finally have actual data on Sullivan and it’s very, very exciting.

Just getting on the pitch is already a promising sign. Of the 10 teenagers who have earned the most playing time in MLS since 2015, eight have made the leap – with varying degrees of success – to Europe’s top five leagues. Sullivan isn’t there yet but he has by far the most minutes of any 16-year-old in that time and runs a close second to Adri Mehmeti, the 17-year-old currently bossing the New York Red Bulls’ midfield, at the next age up.

Another leading indicator is how much his teammates trust him.

“No matter what age you are, when a practice starts and guys give you the ball, that’s the ultimate sign of respect,” Sullivan’s first coach at the Union, Jim Curtin, said. “Within 10 seconds into the first training session, they gave him the ball.”

That’s true in games, too. Sullivan takes 10.3% of his team’s touches, the most of any teenage MLS winger in at least a decade. Second place is Alphonso Davies, now of Bayern Munich, the best homegrown player the league has ever produced.

Then of course there are the highlight numbers – four goals and three assists in MLS this season. Seven and seven in all competitions. Three and three in his last five games alone. Those are noisy stats, but the underlying numbers so far look just as bright: his 0.48 expected goals and assists per 90 minutes rank fourth among MLS teens with at least 1,000 minutes played, one spot below Jhon Duran, who broke the league transfer fee record when he moved to Aston Villa at 19.

Advanced stats go deeper into Sullivan’s game. Player ratings in futi, a soccer stats app I co-created, use a model called possession value to estimate how much every touch of the ball changes teams’ goal probabilities, so that a line-breaking pass in midfield, a goalline clearance or a dribble on the wing can all be added up in terms of their expected impact on the scoreline. The app adjusts these values based on how a player’s team plays with and without him, then scales the rating within his data-derived tactical role.

According to futi ratings, Sullivan’s 2026 is the second-best of any MLS teenager on record, trailing only Gianluca Busio, now the captain of Venezia in Serie A, when he was three years older. The best 16-year-old MLS has ever seen isn’t just getting minutes and goals – he’s helping his team all over the pitch.

When trying to describe a precocious, small, left-footed right-winger who loves to perform tricks, it’s too easy to reach for the most unfair comparison of all time, yet it’s a documented fact that Sullivan modeled his game after Lionel Messi (obligatory note: we’re not saying Sullivan has the same level of ability as the Argentinian). When Sullivan scored his first professional goal by slicing inside and curling a diagonal to an overlapping left-back before finishing a cutback from the penalty spot, it was impossible not to see Messi’s signature combination with Jordi Alba.

Sullivan doesn’t play as centrally as Messi, though. Futi’s player style model classifies him as a “wide playmaker”; an attacker who likes to collect the ball out near the touchline and then break lines and create for teammates. He’s a ball-to-feet type who averages just 6.2 progressive receptions per 90 minutes and ranks in the 19th percentile among wide attackers for the directness of the passes he receives, meaning he’s not doing a lot of running in behind.

What he’s doing instead, mostly, is dribbling. Sullivan’s style on the ball is less a young Messi and more like his other childhood hero, Alexis Sánchez: hips low, elbows out, juking defenders with feints, stutters, stepovers and changes of direction. He mixes in his weak foot to keep tacklers on their toes and applies a variety of touches to the ball, including a kid’s fair share of overly ambitious ones.

The thing that makes his chaotic game hang together is an awareness of what’s going on around him. “I would say the big word is ‘playmaker,’” Sullivan told ESPN when he was 14. “That’s what I try and be every game, every training. I think I’m good on the dribble. My decision making is pretty good, and my vision on the field is one of my qualities.”

Even when he’s squirming past defenders, Sullivan is preternaturally aware of his teammates’ runs and constantly looking to play them into dangerous spots. He averages 5.0 progressive passes per 90 minutes, top five among all MLS wide attackers. One of his trademark moves is dribbling across the defense and then snapping off a perfectly timed ball at an unexpected angle for a runner in the channel; another is trying some crazy lob over the back line, which occasionally comes off.

The downside of this risky style of play is that he makes a lot of turnovers. The Union don’t really mind, though. Sullivan’s 65% pass completion rate is among the lowest in the league but about par for Philadelphia, the most direct team in MLS. It’s anyone’s guess how he might adapt to a totally different game at Man City.

To even get there, he’ll have to answer some hard questions about his size and speed. Only 15 players in the Premier League last season were listed at or below Sullivan’s current 5ft 7in, and just one of them, Enzo Le Fée, was a starter in a similar role. Unlike Christian Pulisic, America’s last phenom to break through on the wing, Sullivan isn’t especially fast, which will be a tough sell in an increasingly physical European game.

Then again, he’s been beating bigger, faster guys his whole life. Go back and watch those old videos of this squib of a kid getting hip-checked by players twice his size, sprawling to the ground and somehow popping up with the ball velcroed to his feet. He is scrappy, relentless. As Bruce Arena once said of Clint Dempsey, Cavan Sullivan tries shit.

Go ahead, just try to predict what he’ll do next.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Grindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV status
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Julia Kollewe
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
US-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK law

Grindr will pay £26m to settle a lawsuit brought by thousands of users in the UK who allege that the US dating app shared highly sensitive personal information, including in some cases their HIV status, with advertising companies.

The settlement brings to an end a two-year legal battle, after the UK law firm Austen Hays filed a claim at the high court of England and Wales in April 2024 on behalf of Grindr users alleging violations of UK privacy laws during a period up to early 2020.
