Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.

“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”

OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours.

Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.”

Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”.

Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts.

Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.

But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences.

On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources.

But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”

He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”

The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals.

The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn.

Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signed a joint letter this summer that warned the companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’S chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’ The San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Hundreds gather to urge Scottish government to pause datacentre boom
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Patrick Greenfield and Aisha Down
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world

Kat Jones may be the closest thing Scotland has to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?” she calls to the crowd.

On Thursday, hundreds travelled to Edinburgh to call for an immediate moratorium on Scotland’s datacentre boom, which includes one project in Auchtertool, Fife, that has been billed as the second largest in the world.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, is spearheading a campaign demanding a pause while the Scottish government produces analysis on the environmental impact of the centres, and clear planning guidance on the definition of a “green” datacentre.

She is a whirr of action: greeting, encouraging, emailing and introducing. Thursday’s protest was the biggest yet.

In John Swinney’s programme for government on Tuesday, Scotland’s equivalent to the king’s speech, the first minister said he would take a strategic approach to datacentres with “expectations around environmental sustainability, resource use, community benefit”, but stopped short of agreeing to a moratorium.

For the campaigners, this is not enough. From Dunbar to Greenock, there is fierce anger at the speed and scale of the projects in the planning pipeline. At least 20 are proposed so far, with more rumoured. Some are planned in the countryside not far from small villages, others next to care homes and residential housing.

Kathleen White, who is campaigning against a proposed £2bn datacentre in Lammermuir hills in the Scottish borders, said the project did not make any sense in her area.

“We are from a small village of about a hundred people. The project is planned about a mile up the road,” she said.

“There’s a reservoir and an angling spot. It’s an upland area with dark skies. The datacentre buildings would cover eight hectares [20 acres] of mostly concrete in a greenfield area. It is going to be a monstrosity.”

The rising public anger about the datacentre buildout that underpins the global AI boom is a growing threat to the UK’s strategy. Keir Starmer’s government leaned heavily on AI as a means to turbocharge a limp economy while he was prime minister.

Crucial to this were “AI growth zones”, which were areas where Britain planned to build massive AI datacentres in the hope that jobs and growth would follow. The Guardian’s investigations have called into question the numbers and reasoning behind this strategy.

The UK’s grid is strained, and proposed datacentres are meeting stiff resistance in London and elsewhere in the south of England.

This spring, British officials pushed would-be AI datacentre developers to look north – suggesting Scotland, with its renewable energy and abundant water resources, is better-equipped to support the country’s efforts to keep up in the AI race. One of the UK’s five AI growth zones will be in Lanarkshire, a rural area outside Glasgow.

Mounting public anger – and a potential moratorium – could jeopardise this pivot. But Jones rejects any suggestion that the moratorium campaign is standing in the way of progress.

“People who are campaigning locally on issues that matter to them a lot get accused of being nimbys. But this is a campaign that has national and international consequences. Datacentres are some of the biggest buildings on the planet, they use so much energy.

“Local campaigners are the most motivated to oppose them because they are a direct existential threat to the places they love, right near their homes, near hospitals, near schools.”

The opposition to large-scale datacentres has also been backed by the Scottish Greens and by Reform UK. Reform has raised concerns about the number of projects, while the Scottish Greens have backed the moratorium – echoing the campaigners’ demands for a national framework.

Ross Greer, co-leader of the Scottish Greens, who was outside Holyrood with protesters, said: “If we want to have the internet, we need datacentres and Scotland already has plenty of them.

“But those proposed would require more energy than all of Scotland needs at its peak at the moment. That is clearly not possible.”

The Scottish government has said that all planning authorities must notify ministers of new datacentre applications exceeding 50MW within a week to help monitor their impact on infrastructure, but underscored that the centres are important for economic growth.

The public finance minister for Scotland, Hannah Mary Goodlad, said: “We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities.

“I am clear that voices of communities that will be affected will be central to any considerations on datacentres.”

But Jones and the campaign want more. She fears that Scotland could be overwhelmed without a formal national strategy. “We are not saying everything needs to stop for ever. But it’s moving so fast. We need a pause.”

This article was amended on 7 September 2026 to remove a quote from Ross Greer that had understated the power that would be needed by the proposed datacentres.
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Campaigners want an immediate moratorium on Scotland's datacentre boom. At least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.title: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.author: Philip Oltermann in Venice
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text:
Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

V
eteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of  civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.summary: Alex Gibney's documentary is one of the most anticipated films at Venice film festival. It is about the richest broligarch on the planet, and is about how he managed to amass so much money and political influence.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greeting
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Status: Under threat of extinction.

That’s ridiculous – we’ve been saying hello to each other for millions of years. Well, that isn’t true. As I just mentioned, the word appeared in print a couple of hundred years ago. But it’s a deviation of “holla”, “hollo”, “halloo” or “hillo”, all of which were used in English as attention-grabbing noises since at least the 16th century.

But we use it all the time now. Only because of the telephone. After the phone’s invention by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, Thomas Edison decided that a new standardised greeting needed to be invented.

Why? Because previously people tended to greet each other with time-based salutations, such as “good morning” or “good evening”. But the telephone could instantly cross time zones, which made these redundant.

But why hello? Because Edison preferred it to Bell’s favoured “Ahoy-hoy”.

Shame. I know. Anyway, forget all that, because nobody says hello any more.

But I like hello. Too late. Technology has marched on again: everyone has a smartphone with caller ID now. Why go through the charade of a “hello?” when you already know who’s calling you?

I don’t know, basic politeness? Tell that to gen Z. The New York Times has reported on the death of hello, stating that young people now prefer to answer the phone with “Hi”, “What’s up?” or “Yeah?”.

This sounds spurious. It isn’t. A survey last year revealed that 40% of 18-24 year-olds feel that it is acceptable to answer the phone without any form of greeting whatsoever.

Isn’t that a bit weird? It sort of makes sense, though. Conversations have become free-form things spread across multiple formats. If you’ve just been texting, or DMing, or emailing with someone, a phone call is just a continuation and arguably doesn’t require anything as formal as a hello.

Still, it’s nice. Only if you love AI scammers.

What the hell? Where did that come from? You didn’t hear about this? Apparently scammers can now replicate your voice with AI, cloning it from your telephone greeting, and use it to beg your loved ones for money. This is a real thing that has been covered by the consumer watchdog Which?, the BBC and the Guardian.

This is genuinely nightmarish. Guess what the best way to beat it is.

I’ll guess rudeness. Correct! If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you are sure that a friendly human being is on the other end of the line. Not saying hello first could save you a whole heap of trouble.

Well, it looks like this is goodbye to hello. Don’t say goodbye. Say au revoir.

Because it’s romantic? No, because the terrifying hordes of robot scammers might clone you into a French person, and your family would be confused.

Do say: “Hello is becoming obsolete.”

Don’t say: “Ahoy-hoy!”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.title: Ninja Artisan electric pizza oven review: so good it might even convert the purists
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.author: Rachel Ogden
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Affordable, fast-heating and with a clever air fryer function, this versatile model is a winner for outdoor cooks who are willing to give up the traditional flame

The best pizza ovens – tested
 Gozney Dome Gen 2 pizza oven review

A
n electric pizza oven with no flame and no need to rotate the pizza may seem sacrilegious to purists, but the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven solves many of the hassles of outdoor pizza making. There’s no lighting or monitoring a flame, no need to keep adjusting the heat, and no need for a turning peel, bulky gas bottle or constant use of an infrared (IR) thermometer (although you may still want one – read on for details).

Equipped with four presets – Artisan, Thin Crust, New York, Pan – plus a custom setting to enable you to bake your pizza exactly how you like it, the Ninja Artisan is as effortless as can be, even next to the simplest plug-and-play gas oven. As you might expect from Ninja, it’s a multipurpose cooker, too, transforming into an outdoor air fryer with a capacity to turn out up to 1.3kg of french fries, or bake six chicken breasts.

Being electric also means fast heat-up – useful if a rain shower is looming. In tests, it reached 370C in 14-15 minutes, and pizzas were perfectly cooked in just two minutes, despite the three-minute preset. At an RRP of £314.99 (but £229.99 at the time of writing), it costs about the same as a compact gas oven but is cheaper to run, using less than 1kWh of electricity after an hour at full temperature.

I tested the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven & air fryer MO201UK in the same way I test all pizza ovens I review for the Filter, although the temperature range here is different.

As well as judging the quality of pizzas cooked with different toppings – cheese and tomato at 370C; a veggie pizza with onion, pepper and tomato at 220C to slowly caramelise the toppings; and a salami pizza at 245C – I rated the oven for ease of assembly, overall usability, temperature control and how easily it could be stored.

I also recorded how long it took the oven to heat up to its maximum temperature of 370C (which is lower than the maximum on gas and wood-fired ovens).

Those with gas or wood-fired ovens are likely to need to plan pizza nights, ensuring they have enough fuel and that the weather will hold out long enough for both the oven heat-up and the cooking time.

With the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven, you can be more spur-of-the-moment. Simply plug it into an outside socket, and heat-up is fast, with a beep to signify it’s ready to use. And because there’s no flame and the heat is evenly distributed, there’s no need to even rotate your pizza mid-cook.

You’ll need to keep a close eye on cooking time, however. I was caught out with my first pizza, so I shortened the cook time for the next. The Artisan’s door also takes some getting used to: unlike standard open-fronted pizza ovens, you’ll need to factor in time to open it to check or remove your pizza before the base or crust starts to char. Every second counts.

Dimensions: 40.31 x 57.2 x 31.39cm (WDH) / mouth 34 x 12cm (WH)
Running cost for one hour on maximum: 25p (£0.25/kWh x 0.989kWh; 15-min heat up, 45mins at 370C)
Maximum capacity: 30 x 31cm pizza stone (working capacity 12in pizza)
Features: four functions: Pizza, Bake, Air Fry & Prove; 30cm sq bake tray, pizza peel, air-fry basket
Fuel: electric, 1,760W
Dishwasher safe: no
Spare parts: replacement stones, base unit, bake tray, air-fry basket
Weight: 13.98kg

Beyond its preset programmes and ability to cook more than pizza, the MO201UK Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven’s standout feature is its rapid heat-up time. It reaches 370C from cold in just 14-15 minutes, giving you just enough time to shape your dough and add your toppings. While it’s faster than a gas pizza oven, it’s worth noting that gas ovens typically cook at a higher temperature of about 430C.

But it’s quick to cook, too. While a thin, lightly topped pizza typically takes about 90 seconds in a gas-powered oven, the Ninja’s Artisan programme is set to three minutes. In my tests, though, I found two minutes was enough. The full three-minute cook burned my pizza, whereas reducing the time produced a well-risen crust with just a slight char on one edge.

For a slower cook, choose the New York setting, which runs for eight minutes. This produced a pizza with browned meat and a reasonable rise, without any burning.

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

The Ninja Artisan’s tightly sealed door helps the oven retain heat (and makes it safe to use), but it can also be a barrier to the best results. I found it stiff and difficult to open single-handed – with my pizza peel at the ready in the other hand – which made it tricky to launch the pizza and resulted in some burning as I struggled to retrieve it once cooked. Hopefully, the door loosens somewhat with use.

A more concerning issue arose when switching from high- to low-temperature cooking. After making pizza at 370C, I selected the 220C Pan setting for a veggie pizza. Although the oven beeped that it was ready, the stone was still far too hot for a 13-minute cook. Because of this, if you’re likely to switch temperatures often, I’d suggest having an IR thermometer to hand so you can check that the stone is at the right temperature before adding your food.

Once at the lower heat, the Artisan appeared to have cooked the veggie pizza well – although on trying to remove it, I found it had stuck to the stone, which reinforces the earlier point of the temperature not being right after all. As such, it might be wise to do your lower-temperature cooking first, and know that the heat is accurate, before ramping up to the hottest settings.

As an outdoor electrical appliance, the Ninja Artisan comes with a shorter warranty than most gas pizza ovens: one year as standard, extended to two years if you register it with Ninja. Spare parts, including the base unit, pizza stone and air-fry basket, are also available.

Note, too, that while Ninja says the Artisan electric pizza oven has been built to withstand outdoor elements, it recommends buying a cover for “extra protection”. There’s also extensive cleaning and care advice for prolonging the oven’s lifespan.

The MO201UK Ninja Artisan pizza oven has plenty going for it compared to other such appliances. It’s relatively affordable, heats up faster than a gas-powered model, allows for spur-of-the-moment pizza making, and is “plug and play” – no gas, wood or charcoal required. From a convenience point of view, it’s hard to beat.

Its ability to bake and air fry foods will also appeal to outdoor cooks. There’s no need to keep popping inside to your kitchen for chips, chicken, nachos or sweet treats; you can do it all in the Ninja Artisan (with recipes for everything from a tart to cookies and granola included).

There are compromises, however. While the pizzas are very good, they lack the blistered finish you’d get from hotter temperatures. The Artisan’s door also creates issues, making it trickier to launch and retrieve pizzas compared with open-mouthed ovens. And while electric power is undeniably practical, I missed the charm of cooking over a live flame.

Whether the MO201UK Ninja Artisan is right for you will depend on what you want from an outdoor oven. If versatility, convenience and cooking a range of dishes for family and friends are top of your list, the Ninja Artisan is an excellent choice. But if you want to master the perfect leopard-spotted crust, manage a live flame and turn out pizzeria-quality margheritas, a traditional gas oven (such as my overall favourite, the Gozney Arc Lite) still has the edge.

Her home has hosted hundreds of appliances while her garden has seen a succession of pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters put through their paces. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models

P
icture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.

These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.

That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.

Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.

“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”

The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.

There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.

He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.

Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.

Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.

Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.

The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.

With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.

Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.

Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.

The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.

OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.

The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.

OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.

“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”

His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”

And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.

He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

Even if the legislation passes, tech companies may still find ways to frustrate its intent and keep Australians hooked on their feed

Social media could become a “choose your own adventure” between the doom-scrolling status quo, or just the feed of the friends you want to see, if the government’s planned digital duty of care legislation passes, and the tech companies don’t muck around on compliance.

For years people have complained about the random videos or posts cluttering their social media feeds as served to them by the tech giants.

It often feels invasive – tracking our activity across websites and apps to serve content and ads – but in many cases, it is also toxic.

Guardian Australia was first reporting these issues back in 2024, conducting experiments with blank phones set up to be young men, with very little other information to go on and to see what the algorithms pushed into our feeds.

The results were shocking – how the default would quickly send someone down a rabbit hole of extreme misogynistic and far right content, and just how sensitive the algorithm is to any minor interaction on an image or video.

Many of the perceived problems teens face on social media are also problems facing adults. While the social media ban was designed to combat the harms faced by under-16s, many of us know relatives who have been radicalised reading Facebook comments, or grandparents scammed out of their retirement money by fake investments they saw on social media.

Outrage bait is rewarded by engagement on platforms, and this has infected politics and public discourse in Australia and elsewhere.

The move, announced by the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, on Tuesday to have a pop-up notification proactively require users to decide whether they want the platform to decide what they see or just want to see the content of the people and groups they’ve chosen to follow – similar to how many of the platforms worked in the early 2010s – could be game-changing.

When Apple introduced a notification in iOS in 2021 that allowed people to opt in or opt out of ad tracking in apps, it cost Meta $10bn in one quarter, with users rushing to opt out of tracking on Facebook and Instagram.

Compare that to when Instagram chief executive, Adam Mosseri, was on the stand in the landmark US court case last month just before Meta agreed to a $18bn settlement with state attorneys general.

One of the company’s safety features for teens, called Take a Break, which was designed to let teens stop using Instagram if they had been scrolling for a while, had a take up rate of 1.8%, the court heard.

The companies love to tout their safety features, but then often bury them within the settings, with little notice to users, and then suggest to regulators that the low take up shows people love their product as is.

The companies may also find ways to make it as clunky an experience as possible when people opt out, to drive them back to the preferred model, depending on how the law is written.

Just look at Europe. In 2023 Meta introduced the option for a no-algorithm feed to comply with EU law, but in 2025 a Dutch court found people were automatically reverted to the Meta algorithm when they closed and reopened the app.

The court ordered the company to provide a direct and simple way for people to opt out of the timeline, to comply with the law. Meta continued to argue it was already in compliance.

Instagram is also expected to sell the benefits hard. It will launch its “Algo Confessions” series in Australia this week, in which celebrities and influencers run through their “For You” feeds, and why what Instagram recommends to people is just so good.

They may find a sympathetic ear among organisations that have benefited from algorithms that reward outrage content with user engagement. It was telling the prime minister pointedly thanked News Corp for its support for the social media ban in Tuesday’s press conference.

It’s not clear whether the “my feed, my way” proposal will enjoy similar levels of full-throated support in the newspapers as the social media youth ban had, particularly as it seems likely that other parts of the proposed law around combating online harms will face opposition from the Coalition and One Nation.

But by framing it as “empowering people” Albanese is hoping it won’t be seen as the big arm of government coming in and determining what people see on social media. Through the pop-up notification every Australian will have a choice.

“If people want to doom scroll … that’s fine, that’s up to them,” Albanese said on Tuesday. “But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them an opportunity.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Thor Benson
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech

Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.

“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”

Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.

Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.

Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.

“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”

Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.

While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.

Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.

“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

The backlash against Flocks is a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Gene Marks
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works

O
ne thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.

The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.

This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many cases squandered – by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.

What works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.

Small businesses are watching. And now doing.

A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.

Big companies have also begun to discover the astronomical computing costs that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companies throw away billons on large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.

But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.

Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.

For months, on earnings calls and investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.

We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring, only to hire those same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.

Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.

Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, recently admitted that their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.

Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.

The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at, says John Sutter. Sutter: Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.title: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.author: Keza MacDonald
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.text:
A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised

T
he Trump White House on Thursday released a horrible little propaganda arcade via its website, a collection of nasty riffs on popular games. Wrapped in the cutesy, nostalgic aesthetic of early-90s pixel art, these mindless fascist diversions are harmless-looking, but their intent is stomach-turning: this is the appropriation of play in service of propaganda. It’s just the latest in a series of attempts from Trump’s administration to use video game memes and imagery to further its messaging.

Having riffed on Halo and Pokémon in social media ads last year, inviting potential ICE recruits to “stop the flood” and “catch ’em all”, this time the administration has ripped off a series of recognisable games. Flappy Bill, perhaps the least gross, is a version of the old mobile hit Flappy Bird, except here you’re an eagle with a scroll in its claws. Supply Line could almost be an educational game about healthy food in schools, where you sort junk food off a conveyor belt destined for school lunches, except for some reason you play as a boxer who becomes more bloodied with every seed-oil containing, ultra-processed food item that you fail to punch into the garbage chute.

Then come the really nasty ones: Build the Wall, which warps Tetris into a game where you must fortify the southern border to keep out “the coming horde”, and an evil little take on Snake where you patrol the Rio Grande, collecting brown people who then follow you around in orange jumpsuits. The final game is Trump Savings Tycoon, where you “fill your kids’ Trump accounts” by catching bills and gold coins in a net. (The algae-beset Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is depicted in the foreground, inaccurately coloured in blue.)

I have played all of them, so that you don’t have to. Build the Wall and Rio Run are actively disgusting, built around the naked dehumanisation of migrants, but mostly these games are just embarrassing. Like most things that come from the Trump White House communications team, they are mean-spirited, unimaginative and lazy. I have a strong suspicion that they are vibe-coded using AI, and I almost hope that they are, because the idea of humans spending their precious time on Earth making these horrid, half-arsed games makes me even sadder than playing them did.

Anyone involved in the creation of the original games that the White House Arcade is ripping off is surely cringeing. Members of the original Halo team were moved to speak out on social media after the White House posted a picture of Trump as Master Chief last year; I wonder if Sega will have anything to say about this trailer, which opens with a digital chorus singing “Magaaaa”, soundtracking the sorry collection with music that sounds a lot like Sonic’s Green Hill Zone.

The leveraging of video games and their imagery for political influence has been under way for some time, beginning perhaps with 2014’s Gamergate, an online harassment movement that was stoked by Steve Bannon and far-right website Breitbart. Trump, alongside other rightwing regimes, has had an enormous head start on this front. “The use of video game content, culture and aesthetics for communication is a feature of Trump’s White House, rather than a bug, because much of the modern political right emerged from toxic game communities,” says George Osborn, author of Power Play: Video Games, Politics and the Battle for Global Influence.

“Activists who shaped the Gamergate movement have become an established part of the political right … Until now, it seemed to be restricted to social media posting. I estimated that video game-coded posts had approximately twice the reach of a regular White House Instagram post, suggesting it was able to simultaneously rile up audiences offended by its post and delight supporters. But the deployment of an arcade on its website marks a change of course … Now, it appears that Trump’s White House is ready to use games to begin to try to win over audiences – escalating from appropriating video game culture to ensnaring the medium itself for its own ends.”

Artists and activists have been using video games to put across political messages for a very long time. I have played games about escaping war-torn countries; about examining the paperwork of desperate people at the border of a fictional eastern bloc country; about running a dictatorship or taking one down. Governments, however, are new players in this space.

These games, in line with the Trump administration’s wider social media and communications strategy, are culture-war shitposting. They are almost entirely valueless, and exist more to rile us up than to actually persuade anyone of anything. If we attach too much outrage to them, we are being drawn into someone else’s game; it is deeply unlikely that a round of Rio Run is about to radicalise anyone who isn’t already fully on board with Trump’s whole schtick. But at a time when the Saudi Arabian wealth fund now co-owns one of the world’s biggest game publishers alongside an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, gaming’s propagandist potential should not be a blind spot.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.title: Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.author: Daniella Lucas
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.text:
As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands

Pokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than 85bn cards printed over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s now almost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.

One card recently sold for an eye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading to a rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.

Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”

The images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.

Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues with Royal Mail items going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.

“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”

Stack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area have mentioned similar problems to him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK use CardMarket to sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.

Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.

With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversary Pokémon card set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.author: Kirk McKeand
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/s.text:
As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet

S
ince 2009’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named after Demon’s Souls and its sequel Dark Souls – is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’s Elden Ring, which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto.

Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Malania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos.

FromSoftware’s in-game universes are filled with clues – enemies, places and scraps of information from item descriptions paint a vague image of the world, and the player fills the blank space. You never fully understand these domains, although countless YouTube video game theorists have tried – as have other developers in awe of his work. “Of all the many things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest,” explains Dishonored director Harvey Smith, who has more than 40 days’ playtime in Elden Ring. “It’s so incredibly hard to do in video games, which are technical systems … But Miyazaki somehow creates an atmosphere of wonder. Even when finishing, you are left ruminating on fun, murky elements that feel half understood. It’s a delicious sense of intrigue.”

Rather than the single-player action game that Miyazaki’s audience craves (fans are desperate for a sequel to his 2015 gothic masterpiece Bloodborne, for instance), his latest project The Duskbloods is a multiplayer Switch 2 exclusive. Eight players face off against ghoulish horrors, fighting each other to avoid being culled at the end of each round. The survivors are whittled down over three phases culminating in a final three-way battle. The Duskbloods is releasing to an audience with shifting tastes and trends, and it is certainly a risk. “I’m very nervous,” Miyazaki says. “With every title we release there is this mounting tension.”

The game opens with an arresting image: one hand reaching out for another. A male character is slumped on a chair, dejected; the shot moves in close to focus on their draped fingers. From below the frame, a pale hand slowly reaches out and caresses them before gently clasping his wrist. Hands are a recurring motif in Miyazaki’s games; in Elden Ring, massive crawling hands burrow up from underground to attack you, and hand-like giants are revered as deities.

“It’s not necessarily something I’m consistently aware of – maybe it’s something subconscious coming through,” Miyazaki says when I ask about this imagery. “Take a look online and there’s a rumour that I have a bit of a thing for feet, but I’m not honestly sure where this comes from. I feel like I’m trying to depict some side of human nature or the human existence that is difficult to describe.” (His games have featured, by my count, at least six barefoot female characters.)

Perhaps all the hands and feet are symbolic of human connection. One hand reaches for another; bare feet connect skin with earth. Miyazaki has been exploring that theme since Demon’s Souls, whose novel, stranger-centric multiplayer was inspired by a time his car slipped on an icy hill and a stranger helped to push him to safety. In Demon’s Souls and the Dark Souls series, players paint runes on the ground, which other players can then use to summon help in a fight, creating moments of spontaneous togetherness before an inevitable parting.

While The Duskbloods primarily puts players in opposition, it also explores temporary alliances and conflicting objectives, buoyed by Miyazaki’s love for tabletop role-playing games and board games. Players can even become betrothed to each other, forming an alliance. “I feel it’s less a traditional romance and more a sense of secure trust with a character in the world, and that’s something I personally yearn for,” he says. “It’s not necessarily a romantic pairing – it’s having someone that you can ultimately rely on. This concept is carried through from characters like the maidens in Elden Ring … it’s a transient, ephemeral love, which is maybe a motif I’m striving for.”

The Duskbloods is preoccupied with ruin and rebirth, a thematic cornerstone of From’s games – much as Godzilla was a product of nuclear paranoia in Japan. Even as Miyazaki and I talk, a deadly magnitude 6.8 earthquake hits the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island, a thousand miles away. If the very ground beneath your feet is unreliable, that can shape your outlook on life, a concept explored extensively in Japanese literature and entertainment, recently on the hit television show Shōgun. “[Ruin and rebirth] is an ongoing theme in a lot of my games, I realise,” Miyazaki says. “That theme on a cosmological scale applies to The Duskbloods as an interesting philosophical area to explore.”

Miyazaki describes himself as a pessimist, a tendency that he believes comes across in his output. That should be obvious to anyone who’s finished any of his games, in which you keep throwing body and blade against seemingly impossible odds, reborn each time you die at a bonfire checkpoint, to try again. Even when you triumph, nothing ultimately seems to change: these games culminate in bleak, morally ambiguous gut-punches, leaving you not as a conquering hero but as the perpetuator of a hopeless cycle. “If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,” Miyazaki says. “[But] if you explore the ruin and the decay in those worlds, it also lets you explore some chance of rebirth, and I think having that tiny pinprick of light or hope can be something beautiful, something fleeting.”

Sekiro, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring are all separate series, but they share the same bones. They’re reborn in different forms, to explore fresh ideas, places and perspectives while still playing, feeling and sounding like a FromSoftware game. While it’s immediately clear The Duskbloods is a Miyazaki game, it too wears a different skin, inspired by extraction shooters like Escape from Tarkov and those tabletop role-playing games the director loves. “There’s no intentional FromSoftware [mantra] – ‘this is the way we make our games’ – because if you start to do that it becomes stale and conservative, and you start having to adhere to a set of rules and philosophies, and it just doesn’t become interesting, you can’t make anything that’s as fun,” Miyazaki says.

“So I feel like at least what’s worked for us philosophically is trying to adhere to what we find interesting first. I think that has created a good throughline through our games, and that’s what we concentrate on to [conceive] a new title.”

Back in his early days at the studio, when he was only a coder on the Armored Core series of games, Miyazaki volunteered to take on a struggling project at From – the game that would become Demon’s Souls. (The game was already in trouble, so he felt he had nothing to lose.) He changed everything about the game, and then the game changed everything about his life, as he climbed from coder to company president. From failure was born a game that changed the landscape of video games. Ruin and rebirth.

But does Miyazaki think he has changed? “I don’t intend to,” he says, a smile curling on his lips. “But I probably have.”

As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining

P
redictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last week was a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to data collated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.

Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.

I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC television has been in decline for years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.

On top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”

The thing is, GTA is a phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.

True, some games have drawn similar levels of media attention. Minecraft and Fortnite receive regular coverage, but almost always because of concerns over children and games addiction, or because of how they intersect with other media: Minecraft through its hit movie, Fortnite through its many collaborations with music artists. And this is the key problem. Mainstream media is still at the stage where every single games story that does make it to TV or radio has to do the job of explaining and justifying the whole industry. It’s time for programme-makers to understand that video games are a mass cultural phenomenon. Enough people play them and understand them so that they don’t have to be re-introduced every time they’re covered. And most importantly, there is life, love, art and brilliance beyond Grand Theft Auto and beyond the coming storm of hype.

It was my birthday a couple of weeks ago, so I set out to find a simple, fun video game that the whole family could enjoy – and I wanted to share my discovery.

Inspired by Dominik Diamond’s recent column on this very subject, I downloaded the party game What The Dub?!, in which players watch old film clips with portions of the sound dubbed out and then enter their own amusing dialogue to fill the gap. The clips are then re-shown with each player’s text added to the soundtrack via a stilted robotic voice – then everyone votes on the funniest entry. It was hilarious, especially because the clips are from weird old public domain films and TV shows, so everything feels stilted and ridiculous. It’s also simple to take part, with each player using their phone to enter their dialogue choices. Apparently, it’s possible to add new clips via the Steam Workshop, the digital store’s user-generated content feature, but we didn’t figure that out. Regardless, What the Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.

EA staff have been speaking anonymously to the industry-news site Game Developer about their concerns after the Saudi-led buyout of Electronic Arts. Some are troubled by the prospect of popular games such as EA Sports FC, Madden and Battlefield being used by Saudi Arabia to distract from its poor human rights record. There are also worries about the company’s culture and job security.

TV producers looking for interesting game stories that don’t involve GTA could check out Eurogamer’s excellent article on the No Man’s Sky’s Galactic Hub project. It’s a community of players exploring and scientifically cataloguing specific regions of the long-running space adventure sim, like a sort of ragtag Starfleet mission. Live long and prosper, lads.

As if making and marketing independent video games isn’t hard enough, several developers have reported thefts at this year’s Gamescom event in Cologne. Posting on X, Mimic creator Ryan Laley said: “Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what’s left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally.” According to VGC, others affected included publisher iam8bit and Tessera Studios.

A question from Richard via email:

“My son, aged 6, is a big fan of aeroplanes and is really interested in flight. What games are there that could be used to entertain him, as a thing to do with me. I have (ridiculously) a PS5 and Xbox Series X – is Flight Simulator right? How about Ace Combat? Anything else?”

I’d definitely recommend Microsoft Flight Simulator, which is available on PS5 and Xbox. It can be controlled with just a joypad and you can switch off all the technical elements for your son so he’s basically just steering the craft like in an arcade game. There are lots of aircraft to fly, from tiny prop planes to passenger jets, and you can choose anywhere on Earth to explore. I love simply zooming over cities and scenic highlights, taking it all in.

If you’re ok with him doing a bit of shooting, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is out in October, promising highly detailed visuals and exciting dogfighting. Fans say it looks to be a highlight for the series. I’d also recommend No Man’s Sky, which is a space exploration game, but the flight feels lovely, whether you’re scorching over the surface of a planet or out in the depths of the cosmos. The controls are extremely intuitive too. If he gets into space flight, the slightly more involved Elite Dangerous is worth a look, and for an accessible combination of space flight and shooting, Everspace: Stellar Edition is a really nice option on PS5.
