“We are very fortunate to have a lot of really knowledgable volunteers alongside our brilliant staff who are managing the land that allows the glowworms to re-establish itself in this landscape after an absence of more than 100 years,” said Warwick. “They are incredibly rare in the region and I can’t tell you how excited the volunteers have been about it.”

This year, helped by glow-getter volunteers at Westbury Wildlife Park Foundation, Cooper has bred another 1,900 glowworm larvae which will be released at Nosterfield later this year.

According to Cooper, they will not be certain that the reserve has a self-sustaining population of glowworms until 2030, when the offspring of this year’s wild adult glowworms will reach maturity and shine their lights.

Ceilidhs for wildlife organised by Cooper and friends have raised enough money to upgrade the breeding facilities at Westbury to ensure it is easier to captive-breed more glowworms, with growing interest from other conservation groups in glowworm translocations and reintroductions. The UK glowworm survey is also helping by collecting sightings of glowworms nationally to help conservationists assess where translocations would be helpful and where hidden populations of glowworms may still endure.

“It will be wonderful to see this project grow bigger than me,” said Cooper.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/s.title: Hawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of genius
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/s.author: Philip Ball
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/s.text:
A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneath

W
hen I wrote an unadoring review of Stephen Hawking’s final book, a collection of essays published posthumously in 2018, New Scientist suppressed some of my criticisms on the grounds that it was “too early” to voice anything other than praise for the physicist who died, aged 76, that March. It was apparently still too early in 2021, when no British publisher would touch Charles Seife’s exposé of Hawking’s bullying and self-aggrandising behaviour, Hawking Hawking.

In this new biography, veteran science writer Graham Farmelo takes a different approach. It is a comprehensive and accessible portrait of a brilliant scientist and an extraordinarily determined man who also possessed deep personal flaws to which the scientific community and the public mostly turned a blind eye. The uncomfortable but unavoidable truth is that Hawking’s overweening ambition and self-promotion, his repeated failure to acknowledge the work of others, his sexism and controlling behaviour were largely ignored because of his disability. I think it is indeed going to take us years to process that.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

As this book was authorised by the Hawking family, and as Farmelo (whose superb biography of Paul Dirac, The Strangest Man, won a Costa award in 2009) is a generous and kind writer, I had feared the warts would be omitted. But instead Farmelo handles them mostly by letting others’ words speak for themselves.

But let’s start with the science, which offers a genuinely inspirational tale. As Farmelo says, while Hawking’s longevity against all odds was surely due in part to the exceptional care and treatment he received, “it was his unconquerable will, resilience and fortitude that did most to make his remarkable career possible”. His scientific achievements would be impressive by any measure; when accomplished in the face of debilitating and ultimately paralysing motor neurone disease, they are extraordinary.

Like many scientists of his calibre, Hawking was a slow and rather lackadaisical starter. But once installed at Cambridge for a PhD under the supervision of astrophysicist Dennis Sciama, his sharp intelligence emerged. It was there in early 1963 that, after a series of falls, he was diagnosed and given less than 10 years to live. Undeterred, and despite steadily declining mobility and speech, he was electrified by the work of physicist Roger Penrose, 10 years his senior, on the gravitational collapse of dead stars into what had become known as black holes.

That process was predicted by Einstein’s 1915 theory of general relativity, but Penrose was the first to show convincingly that it should lead to a “singularity” where all the star’s matter condenses to zero volume: an object with mass but no matter. Hawking had the brilliant insight that this same process, happening in reverse, could explain the big bang, in which the entire universe came into being from “nothing” 13.8bn years (as we now know) ago.

That was his first triumph, described in a 1970 paper with Penrose. The best came four years later, when Hawking proposed that, thanks to the peculiar quantum-mechanical nature of spacetime, black holes are not really black because they should constantly radiate a dim glow of particles – now called Hawking radiation – that will eventually lead to their evaporation. That work was a virtuosic blend of four fundamental ideas in physics: general-relativistic gravity, quantum mechanics, thermodynamics and information theory.

It was the high point of his research career: Hawking’s scientific achievements were largely done by the time he became a global celebrity, appearing on Star Trek and The Simpsons and becoming the subject of the 2014 Oscar-winning biopic The Theory of Everything. It is “as a truly great elucidator of black holes” that he will be remembered, Farmelo rightly judges.

I’m not alone in thinking Hawking’s work on black-hole thermodynamics and the discovery of Hawking radiation were worthy of a Nobel prize. (Hawking became obsessed to an unseemly degree with getting one.) But let’s keep it in proportion. Anyone who compares Hawking to Einstein knows nothing about Einstein or physics. Einstein made wide-ranging contributions to the discipline, but Hawking’s expertise was narrow and his forays outside it were sometimes embarrassing. Even in the closely related field of particle physics he said things that were, as Peter Higgs (of Higgs boson fame) said, “total crap”. “He made pronouncements about things he had no understanding of,” Higgs said – in the confident knowledge that it would make newspaper headlines the next day, uncritically lapped up by reporters.

Which brings us to the problematic stuff. While professional colleagues mostly spoke about Hawking with reverence and affection, it is often those closest to him who speak of another side. His father, Frank, worried that the teenaged Stephen “was developing into a selfish character … like a small boy who took everything but gave little in return”. There was evidently no love lost with his sister Mary, who called him “one of the most self-centred people I’ve ever met”. At Oxford, some friends found him rather lazy and entitled, and at Cambridge “annoyingly haughty”. His youngest son recounted how his father was “hugely competitive” and never let him or his siblings win at board games.

His unsparing ridicule of his first wife Jane’s religious beliefs contributed to their marital tensions, and the sacrifices she made often went unremarked by him. The pressure of going from lover to carer would never have been easy, but Hawking’s “authoritarian” demands and indifference to Jane’s interests added to her isolation. His adoptive brother, Edward, admitted “I’ve never really felt close to Stephen … he seems very cold.” And his mother, Isobel, complained how he would ignore people when it suited him. “I suppose what in other people would just be bad manners is excusable great-mannishness in him,” she wrote bitterly in her diary.

Sometimes the indulgence gets creepy. Who else’s Marilyn Monroe obsession would be pampered by hiring a lookalike to croon “I want to be loved by you” to him in a “whispery voice” on his birthday? What Farmelo calls “flirting” might have been seen as something else if Hawking had not been using a wheelchair. He does not mention the nights at Stringfellows strip club and makes light of the trip to (pre-conviction) Jeffrey Epstein’s island. But we do hear how Hawking’s victory in a scientific bet was celebrated by making his opponents deliver lectures in T-shirts showing scantily clad women. Hilarious.

Hawking was scandalously bad at giving due scientific credit to others, a trait evident from the outset when he failed to indicate his debt to Penrose. Worse was his treatment of physicist Jacob Bekenstein, whose idea about the connection between the area and the entropy of a black hole he mercilessly derided before discovering for himself that Bekenstein was right – and then essentially claiming the idea as his own, which Farmelo says “disappointed some of Stephen’s friends”. Hawking could clearly be a supportive and kind adviser to his own students, but when one discovered an argument for why Hawking was wrong about a conjecture concerning black holes, he tried to get him dismissed from the Cambridge PhD programme.

Some of his colleagues, Farmelo says, “believed that Stephen’s talks were ‘all about him’ and that he rarely gave much public credit to his peers”. Farmelo suspects they rarely grumbled because “such comments would have been interpreted as mean-spirited”. But mean-spiritedness rarely deters academics; what he surely means is mean-spirited about a scientist with a disability. And there’s the problem. If we were to start finally treating Hawking as we do any other scientist, it would be a positive step for disability in science (which is still poorly accommodated). The effect on Hawking’s legacy is another matter.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Alcohol-related cancer deaths in US have more than doubled over three decades
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Study finds just one drink per day could raise risk of disease with impacts extending far beyond liver cancer

Alcohol-related cancer deaths in the US have more than doubled over three decades, with new research showing that just one drink per day could raise cancer risk and that the impacts extend far beyond liver cancer.

Researchers at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, analyzed more than three decades of Global Burden of Disease data. Their study, published in August in the Lancet Regional Health, found that annual cancer deaths attributed to alcohol climbed from 11,361 in 1990 to 23,126 in 2023.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The findings link alcohol consumption to an increased risk of death from breast, prostate, colon, rectal, stomach, pancreatic and liver cancers, along with cancers of the head and neck.

Older men faced the heaviest effects, although researchers found increases across most cancer types, age groups and regions.

Alcohol has long been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, placing it in the same category as tobacco smoke and asbestos.

Research also indicates that even relatively low levels of alcohol consumption can raise cancer risk. Elevated risk has been linked to intake levels of just 5 to 15 grams per day. Given that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines a “standard drink” in the US as containing 0.6 ounces (or 14 grams) of pure alcohol, just one drink per day could increase cancer risk.

According to the National Cancer Institute (NCI), alcohol can contribute to cancer growth in several ways. The NCI said alcohol consumption accounted for about 5% – nearly 100,000 – of the 1.8m cancer cases diagnosed in the US in 2019. It was also responsible for about 4% – nearly 25,000 – of the roughly 600,000 US cancer deaths that year.

Older men saw a particularly sharp impact in the August study. The alcohol-related cancer mortality rate among males aged 55 and older rose nearly 24% during the 33-year period.

Among men, liver cancer deaths had the strongest association with alcohol, followed by esophageal and colorectal cancers. Among women aged 55 and older, breast cancer was the leading alcohol-linked cancer killer, followed by liver and colorectal cancers.

Early last year, the then surgeon general, Vivek Murthy, said alcohol use was the third-leading preventable cause of cancer in the US, behind tobacco and obesity, and called for alcoholic beverages to carry warning labels alerting consumers to cancer risks.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
New Zealand decision follows Australian approval in 2023 of psychedelics to treat PTSD and treatment-resistant depression

Two psychiatrists in New Zealand won approval on Friday to prescribe pharmaceutical-grade MDMA to people with severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

The move by New Zealand’s pharmaceutical regulatory body Medsafe makes the country only the second worldwide to approve the party drug for use in treating PTSD, following Australia in 2023.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“PTSD ruins lives and is difficult to treat,” said the deputy prime minister, David Seymour, who last year backed the approval of magic mushrooms to treat people with severe depression. “MDMA can be very effective at treating it through psychedelic-assisted therapy.”

New Zealand is committed to opening up access to “innovative treatments”, Seymour said.

PTSD is a mental health condition that develops after a person experiences or is threatened by traumatic events such as death, combat or sexual assault.

There are clinical trials in the United States after the Food and Drug Administration rejected legalising MDMA’s medicinal use in 2024, saying there was not enough evidence it was safe or effective.

Pharmaceutical treatment options for PTSD in the US have so far been limited to two antidepressants that require three months of dosing to take effect. Response rates to the medications have been uneven.

A study in Israel last year found that MDMA taken by partygoers at the Nova music festival when hundreds were killed by Hamas in the 7 October attacks had been helpful in cushioning the impact of the trauma they endured.

Wellington’s Ministry of Health said MDMA-assisted treatment would be combined with psychotherapy and stressed that patients would not be supplied drugs to take home.

“Treatment takes place in a controlled clinical setting under the care of an authorised psychiatrist and forms part of a comprehensive treatment plan,” the ministry said.

Any patients would have to be aged 18 or older, it added.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US

A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first.

Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply.

Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system.

The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant.

Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, were published in the Lancet medical journal.

Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said.

Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months, according to the Lancet.

Before the transplant in January 2025, Wilma the pig had received 69 edits to her genome. Some of these were designed to dodge viruses that might pose a risk to humans, while others made the organ more compatible with humans, reducing the odds of immune rejection.

The team behind the transplant at Mass General Brigham, a non-profit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, said Andrews successfully lived with the genetically edited kidney for 271 days before receiving a human kidney from a donor.

His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following pig kidney xenotransplantation in a living human, and the world’s first transition to human kidney transplantation, the team said.

“The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said Dr Leonardo Riella, of the Center for Transplantation Sciences and the Division of Nephrology at Mass General Brigham. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.

“Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap – initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right.”

After roughly six months, damage developed in the pig kidney’s blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the kidney was removed nine months after transplantation.

After several months back on dialysis, Andrews received a kidney from a dead human donor, which worked well during six months of follow-up, according to the Lancet.

There were no new antibodies against human tissue detected, indicating the pig kidney had not made it harder for the human kidney transplant to work successfully. No pig viruses or other pig pathogens were detected at any point.

The team cautioned that this was a single patient with no comparison group, and that the outcome reflected careful patient selection and intensive specialist care that may not be available elsewhere.

Further clinical trials such as the one Andrews participated in will be needed. But the success opens the door to pig kidney transplants as a bridge for other people facing long waits for a human kidney, they said.

“The patients are the true pioneers here,” Riella said. “By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early stage studies, they are advancing the science. Without their trust and courage, we would not be able to do what we do.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
We round up this year’s winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’

It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards.

Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”.

We'll bring you right back here

Not signed in before? Create a free account

On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners.

Are rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days. I didn’t think I’d ever win one,” said Dr Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine.

Piff and his colleagues found that upper-class drivers were more likely to cut other cars off at junctions and ignore pedestrians at crossings. Wealthier people also appeared more willing to lie at work. In one experiment, volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children. When the researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled nearly twice as many candies as lower-class people.

“The general pattern seems to be that with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships,” Piff said. “Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritise one’s own needs over those of others.”

Researchers at Oxford University ensured the UK could hold its head high after winning the biomechanics prize. “The whole team is thrilled,” said Dr Matilda Brindle. She and her colleagues investigated the evolution of kissing and needed a scientific definition of the act. They settled on “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, infraspecific oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”.

Brindle, who is writing a book on non-reproductive sexual behaviour, has also studied the evolution of masturbation, making her a strong contender to become the Marie Curie of Ig Nobels by winning more than once. “We’re so focused on penises, what they do and why they are important, but all these other sexual behaviours are important,” she said.

A team of students led by Kavee Thurairajah at the University of Waterloo in Canada worked out that urinal splash is almost entirely eradicated if the stream strikes the urinal at less than 30 degrees. They went on to design a urinal whose shape ensures minimal splash regardless of the user’s aim. “I am very proud,” said Dr Zhao Pan, who runs the lab.

It is natural to want friends that are kind to us, but our friends interact with others in the world in ways that can affect our lives. Dr Jaimie Krems at the University of California, Los Angeles, showed there’s plenty of room for attack dogs in our friendship groups, as long as they target those we dislike. “Sometimes we want our friends to be more vicious and indifferent when they interact with our enemies,” she said. “I’ve felt, in many instances, incredibly loved when people have carried my hate for me and been willing to have my back.”

Researchers in Brazil donned safety boots to explore what made venomous snakes bite in defence by softly stepping on different parts of their bodies. Pressure on the head triggered most bites, they had found, but the study had been retracted by the Scientific Reports journal as the team did not have ethical approval to step on the creatures.

The chemistry prize went to an international team that found cockroach milk contains three times as much energy as cows’ milk, while the olfaction prize went to scientists who discovered babies smell wonderful to their parents, but teenagers do not. Other researchers landed prizes for turning mosquito proboscises into 3D printing nozzles, clarifying the aerodynamics of nose blowing, and burying underpants to monitor soil quality.

The Ig Nobel awards will be announced in Scandinavia next month.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Space junk punched a new hole in the moon. It’s not ours to abuse | Moriba Jah
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moriba Jah
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The space industry treats the sky as a place to dump what it no longer wants. We must develop a new model of accountability

O
n 5 August, a piece of a derelict SpaceX rocket traveling at 5,400 miles an hour met with the moon and punched a fresh hole into it near Einstein Crater. Astronomers were thrilled. The European Southern Observatory caught sodium and lithium flaring in the debris plume and called it a bonus. The media called it a light show. Nobody was physically hurt, so nobody is responsible, and within a week the story was gone.

I have spent 20 years tracking the junk humanity leaves behind in space for a living, and I want to tell you plainly what that crater actually is: a receipt. It’s what you get when an entire industry treats the sky, and now the moon, as a place to dump what it no longer wants, and calls the dumping “normal operations” or “space exploration”.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Here’s my thesis, and I won’t soften it: we don’t own the moon, but we’re behaving as though we did, and that behavior has a name. It’s the oldest colonial instinct there is, dressed up in aerospace engineering. Take what you want, leave what you don’t, and let someone else, or something else, absorb the cost.

Stewardship asks what we owe a place. Ownership asks what we can extract from it before anyone stops us. Right now, in cislunar space, ownership is winning by default, because nobody with power has bothered to claim the alternative, and power doesn’t reside in controlling outcomes but rather in the ability to make choices. Remember this.

So, let’s start with the plain facts of the object itself. The Falcon 9 upper stage that hit the moon launched in 2025 carrying lunar landers, finished its job, and was simply abandoned in a high orbit that happened to cross the moon’s path. Nobody designed a deliberate end for it. The curvature of spacetime and the sun’s radiation pressure did the steering instead, for months, until a predictable, computable trajectory ended predictably, in a fresh scar.

SpaceX didn’t choose to hit the moon. But it did not prevent the collision, which, in an industry with the money and the trajectory software to do otherwise, is probably a choice all the same. That is my first point, and it is not an isolated one. Companies have the power to not allow their rockets to hit the moon. Moreover, rocket bodies have hit the moon before, in 2022 and earlier still, and are always treated as curiosities rather than as pattern.

The pattern is the second point, and it’s where I stop being generous. Look at what we have already done to low Earth orbit, the space closest to home. Tens of thousands of tracked fragments, and uncountable smaller ones, now circle the planet because for 60 years, operators launched first and asked about disposal never. Abandonment is not disposal, but those with power have chosen it to be so.

Starlink alone accounts for more active satellites than the rest of the world’s operators combined, and its own operators report rising near misses as the constellation grows. We built that congestion through a very specific kind of confidence (AKA hubris): the belief that space is big enough to absorb whatever we throw into it, forever, without a bill ever coming due.

It’s the same hubris a mining company has about a river, or a fleet has about a fishery, right up until the fish are gone. We are simply exporting the same appetite further out, because the moon, unlike the ocean or the atmosphere, has no way to fight back. No air to burn up what we drop on it. No tide to wash away what we leave behind. Whatever debris we send there is, for all practical purposes, permanent. You’ll still find bags of astronaut poop on the lunar surface from the Apollo program.

Which brings me to the third point, the one under all the others: why does this keep happening, when the physics has been understood for decades and the fixes are neither exotic nor expensive?

The honest answer is entitlement. Not carelessness – entitlement. There is a difference between not knowing better and knowing better and doing it anyway because nobody will stop you.

This is the same posture empires have always taken toward frontiers they didn’t build and don’t have to live inside the consequences of. Plant a flag, extract the value, leave the mess for whoever comes next, and call the mess someone else’s problem, or better yet, call it nobody’s problem, because there was never an owner to complain.

That isn’t a metaphor. It’s a fairly literal description of how spacefaring nations and companies currently treat the moon, a place that legally belongs to no one and is treated, in practice, as though it belongs to whoever gets there first with a bigger engine. People love to own the profits without owning the consequences of them left in their wake.

To be sure, I don’t think most of the engineers doing this work are villains, and I don’t think this particular impact was reckless in the way, say, a rocket exploding over the Caribbean and scattering debris over a populated area would be (wink). This piece of debris hit an empty stretch of lunar terrain in daylight, and it genuinely did hand scientists a rare, useful dataset. Some operators are also trying to do better. Companies now design certain missions with deliberate deorbit plans, and there is real, if slow, movement toward international norms for orbital debris mitigation.

I don’t want to pretend none of that exists. But good intentions from a minority don’t change the system’s default setting, and the default setting, according to recent evidence, is still: launch, abandon, hope nothing important gets hit. Isolated best practice is not governance. It is public relations for an industry that still has none.

So no, nobody owns the moon. Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, no nation can claim it, and no company can either, whatever their marketing suggests about future colonies and mined regolith. But ownership was never really the problem. Nobody owned the lands where Native Americans thrived either. The problem is that we are acting out ownership’s oldest habits, extraction without accounting, expansion without consequence, on a body we all agreed, on paper, to hold in common.

A crater near Einstein Crater is a small thing by itself. What it represents is not small at all.

We have a narrow window left in which the moon still looks the way it has looked for billions of years, before the coming decade’s hundred-plus missions turn “who hit it this time” into a monthly headline instead of a rare one. We can spend that window building the tracking, the disposal rules and the accountability that stewardship actually requires. Or we can keep doing what we did on 5 August: witness something we built come out of the dark, watch it hit a place we don’t own as if we did, and call it a light show.

Moriba Jah is a professor of aerospace engineering and engineering mechanics at the University of Texas at Austin and a MacArthur “Genius” fellow

The solution to today’s underwater conundrums

Earlier today I set you the following puzzles. Here they are again with the solutions.

A fish is swimming in a tank that is two metres high, one metre across and one metre deep. The image below shows one path it swam.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Here is the same path shown from the front, the right side and the top.

I gave two examples of a front and side view, and asked you to draw the top view of the shortest path that results in those views.

Start off by looking at the cross section defined by the vertical line of the 1. The diagonal of the 7 has to be on that plane, as does the horizontal part of the 7. The final segment has to be on the area I shaded in above right. The top view is thus:

The bottom half of the path must fall on the shaded cross section above left. Likewise, the top section (excluding the very top and middle of the tank) must fall on the shaded cross section above centre. We want the shortest path, so there is only one way to join the bottom part of the path to the top part, and to link the path on the top cross section, above right. The top view is thus:

I hope you enjoyed these challenges. I’ll be back in two weeks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump order directs officials to consider stripping protections for gray wolves
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Roque Planas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Interior department given three months to decide whether wolves can be removed from endangered species list

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them.

The order gives interior secretary Doug Burgum three months to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican gray wolves have recovered enough for the federal government to de-list them.

But the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a division of the interior department, has already attempted to de-list the gray wolf – a decision that is currently tied up in litigation. A 2022 federal court order has left wolves protected by the ESA across most of their range in the lower 48 states.

The major exception is in the northern Rocky Mountain states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, where states manage wolves. In Minnesota, wolves are classified as “threatened” rather than “endangered”.

The USFWS has not attempted to de-list the Mexican gray wolf, a rare sub-species that was reintroduced to New Mexico and Arizona in 1998.

The current recovery plan for Mexican gray wolves requires a population average of more than 320 animals for four years in a row before federal authorities consider de-listing. Arizona and New Mexico counted a total of 319 animals at the end of 2025, triggering the first year in which officials can start counting to make the case for de-listing.

But Mexican gray wolves also face dire threats from lack of genetic diversity, according to Michael Robinson, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Premature de-listing, he said, would likely invite challenge from environmental groups.

“We’re going to be fighting every step of the way, with information, with science,” Robinson said. “That should be the core of the decision-making process.”

Trump’s order also directs federal authorities to urge states to remove protections for gray wolves and loosen local restrictions on wolf killing.

The order drew sharp criticism from environmental groups.

“Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians.

“Directing federal agencies to pressure states into rolling back their own wildlife protections isn’t just bad policy, it’s an attempt to bypass the very framework Congress built to keep species recovery decisions insulated from political whims.”

The federal government systematically trapped and killed wolves in the US through the late 19th and early 20th centuries, pushing them to the brink of extirpation from the contiguous states, largely to protect livestock from predation.

Ranchers still largely view the animals as a nuisance that threatens their already slim profit margins. Trump’s order was part of a broader series of measures aimed at protecting ranchers and American beef production.

Trump appeared to suggest his order would make it easier to shoot wolves, despite the fact that most of them remain protected.

“You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked at the signing ceremony, referring to Mexican gray wolves while talking with an Arizona rancher.

The comment drew laughter. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins interjected to say that interior secretary Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”.

Gray wolves are protected under the Endangered Species Act across most of their range in the lower 48, making it a federal crime to kill one in most cases, regardless of Trump’s order.

But Trump raised the issue again at the signing ceremony. A rancher told the president that people in his home state of Washington struggle with wolves, noting that in one case a pack of wolves caused a young girl to climb a tree to safety.

“You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump told the rancher.

“If you say so, sir,” he replied.

“We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Razed by wildfire, erased by USPS: Hawaiians fight to restore mail delivery
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Wildfire victims rebuilt their homes in Lahaina only to find USPS had ‘eliminated’ their addresses – while houses that didn’t burn receive mail as normal

T
wo months after a devastating wildfire whipped through Lahaina in August 2023, Pam Reader was allowed back to see what was left of her home. With a heavy heart, she returned to the Hawaiian oceanside town now filled with endless blocks of burned houses. As she rounded her corner, she saw the only thing remaining was her bright turquoise mailbox.

“It was an old crappy mailbox,” Reader said. “It was metal, though, which is why I think it survived.”

She could see many neighbors’ mailboxes also outlasted the flames. There was one shaped like a fish, some built into lava rock walls, and other metal ones. She and her daughters had painted their mailbox when the girls were young, with drawings of fish, butterflies and surfboards.

“Everybody’s house was ash, but their mailboxes were standing,” Reader said.

As fire victims have started to return to Lahaina after going through the process of rebuilding their homes, dozens of these mailboxes have become useless. Residents say they are not getting mail service. They see mail carriers drive by without stopping, only to make deliveries a couple of blocks away – to houses that didn’t burn.

“You never really realize how shitty it is to not get your mail, until it actually happens,” said Calvin Cox, whose home also burned in the 2023 fires. “At first, I was like, ‘It’s just junk mail and I have everything on auto-pay,’ but that’s not the case.”

Residents were initially in the dark as to why the mail carriers were passing them by. When Cox moved back in February, he stopped by the main post office to re-register his Lahaina address. When the postmaster looked up his house, he said the United States Postal Service, USPS, didn’t yet have a neighborhood route re-established because not enough new homes had been completed. He told Cox to check back in a month.

Cox went back several times over several months, and still didn’t get any clarity. In July, he filed a complaint with the agency’s federal headquarters. After a back-and-forth with a customer relations specialist for USPS’s Hawaii district, Cox got an answer.

“All dwellings that were affected by the fires in 2023 that have been rebuilt will no longer receive street delivery,” reads an email from the specialist, seen by the Guardian. Cox was told Lahaina’s reconstruction was being treated as “new development”, and under current USPS policy that means no door-to-door mail service.

Cox said this was shocking, considering Lahaina was a centuries-old town and the first capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom. In 1962, the National Park Service even took the rare step of designating downtown Lahaina as a “national historic landmark”.

“If the fire wouldn’t have happened, then we wouldn’t be a new development,” Cox said. “But, because our houses burned down, we’re a new development.”

Three years after the fire killed more than 100 people and destroyed roughly 2,000 residential buildings, only about 25% of homes have been rebuilt. To get mail, fire victims have to go to the main post office branch, which is more than two miles away. Residents say there’s often only one clerk working, and lines can be out the door. Opening times are limited. The office has PO boxes, but the cheapest ones, which can’t fit packages, are $250 a year.

Downtown Lahaina used to have a post office, but it burned in the fire. In a letter to residents last month, the USPS said it planned to permanently close that branch due to “irreparable damage”.

“Generations of people have lived here,” said Sara Clark, who has lived in Lahaina for nearly 40 years and says this situation is especially hard for the elderly. “You have these kupuna who are used to getting their mail at home and are also used to walking to the store, and now they’re having to catch rides to go get their mail.”

Clark moved back to Lahaina with her husband Gerald in June. She said their mail was initially delivered for six weeks, but then just stopped. They’d see the mail carrier drive by, she said, so didn’t realize anything had changed. Gerald said that led to being late on his car registration, because he didn’t get the DMV (department of motor vehicles) notice.

“Until we found out they were holding [our mail], we just didn’t know,” Gerald said. “They just took it away without notifying anybody.”

Cox said he had two home insurance policies lapse because he didn’t get notices, something that could be disastrous in a place where it’s hard to get insured. He said he also didn’t get his voting ballot for the primaries.

For Kesa Ferguson, not getting mail has been maddening. She was born and raised in Lahaina, her parents live down the street, so does her sister. Now, she’s raising her children there. All of them lost their homes in the fires. Ferguson said she had nearly missed medical prescriptions, tax forms, her social security card and DMV paperwork for her son’s driver’s permit.

She said she first realized she wasn’t getting mail after the county called to ask if she moved. Apparently, her trash bill had been returned. Confused, Ferguson went to the postmaster to ask what was going on.

“His response, literally word for word, was: ‘Your address has been eliminated,’” she said.

The whole situation is Kafkaesque, Ferguson said. “That’s where I pay my property tax. That’s where we live. That’s the address I give out to people … Like, you can’t just delete me out of your system.”

The mail crisis in Lahaina comes as Donald Trump has put the USPS in his crosshairs, calling it a “tremendous loser for this country”. Just weeks after Trump’s 2025 inauguration, the then postmaster general and top Trump donor, Louis DeJoy, signed an agreement with Elon Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge) to help with “efficiency gains” and “cost savings”. Since then, the agency has cut thousands of jobs and closed distribution facilities. Victims of major fires in years past, like those in Colorado and California, didn’t see their mail service terminated.

The USPS is a federal agency but functions like an independent business. It has suffered from drastic budget shortfalls over the past several years as competitors like Amazon, UPS and FedEx have moved in. In March, the agency declared a cash crisis and said it would run out of money if Congress didn’t intervene – this announcement coincided with Lahaina residents losing their mail service.

Residents have repeatedly taken the issue to local authorities and have received some promising results.

Clark sent a letter to Hawaii’s governor and her state and federal representatives, saying: “I watch the mail carrier drive past my house in the historic district on the way to deliver mail to new homes just two blocks away. I have lived in my home for more than 35 years, and it is deeply insulting for the USPS to call our neighborhood a ‘new development’.”

Cox and Ferguson also reached out to their representatives. Initially, they were told that because of the “new development” distinction, the downtown district would get cluster mailboxes dotted throughout the community. The timeline was unclear.

Jill Tokuda, a congresswoman for Hawaii, called this decision “absolutely unacceptable”, and said USPS needed to restore home delivery to these families.

“My staff and I have been pressing USPS on this and are working directly with USPS Hawaii leadership to get it fixed,” Tokuda said. “That’s not how you welcome people home. Lahaina has already lost enough.”

Richard Bissen, the mayor of Maui county, too, is pressuring USPS to make restoring mail delivery to the town a priority. “Families should not lose an essential service simply because their homes were destroyed,” he wrote in a letter to the postmaster general.

A spokesperson for the federal USPS said the agency had received “many mail delivery questions” from Lahaina fire victims and that “local and national postal service representatives are diligently working to evaluate this input and determine next steps”.

“I swear to you, my mom’s favorite part of the day is probably going out to walk to her mailbox and check her mail,” said Ferguson of her 80-year-old mother, who’s been living in a trailer on her property as she and her husband work to rebuild their home. “You lose your house, and then to have that as a cherry on top – it’s kind of a slap in the face.”

Cox, meanwhile, has started a petition asking USPS to immediately reinstate their pre-disaster mail delivery. It already has about 130 signatures.

For Reader, the only remaining artefact she has from when her daughters were young is that bright turquoise blue mailbox. Before the fires, she was planning to buy a new one. Now, she says, there’s no way she’d get rid of it. Instead, she built a sturdier stand and painted it with clear shellac to preserve those paintings of fish and butterflies.

“We lost all of our kids’ little mementos and old drawings and all of these things, and then there’s the mailbox with all of our art on it,” Reader said. “Every little thing matters when you’ve lost everything.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Residents in Lahaina, Hawaii, say they are not getting mail service because of USPS policy. The USPS has been in the spotlight after Donald Trump signed a deal with Elon Musk to help with ‘efficiency gains’ and ‘cost savings’ The agency has cut thousands of jobs and closed distribution facilities.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: The plastic waste overtaking New York – and the people trying to curb it
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Photo essay by Bryan Anselm, words by Dharna Noor
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
From New York to Quebec, photographer Bryan Anselm spent months capturing spaces overrun with plastic and the actions individuals and groups are taking to reduce waste

In New York City, the plastic we discard has a way of remaining in plain sight. There are few alleys to hide residents’ refuse, and the clear recycling bags leave their contents on full display. In a city built on a dense grid, lightweight wrappers, bags and bottles spill from overflowing bins and skitter down sidewalks, collecting in gutters and corners before the wind carries them on.

All that plastic is a layer of the urban landscape, as familiar as subway grates and fire escapes, revealing a messy and unflattering aspect of city life. “Garbage is not what we cast out, but the prime locus of meaning in our lives,” the character Nick Shay says in Don DeLillo’s Underworld.

It was not always this way: plastic production has ballooned in recent decades. In 1950, the world produced just 2m metric tons annually – that amount doubled by 1955. Since then, producers and lobbyists worked to advocate for their interests, steamrolling environmental concerns, research shows. By 2019, the world produced 450m metric tons of plastic, and that number is expected to continue growing rapidly.

All that growth has reshaped industries from shipping to medicine. It has also taken a huge toll on the planet. Every day, the equivalent of 2,000 truckloads of the material is dumped into the world’s water bodies. And even when it is landfilled or incinerated, it spews toxic and planet-heating emissions into the atmosphere. (Less than a tenth of all plastic globally is recycled, and in the US, only about 5% of plastic waste generated by households is recycled.)

What kind of world are we making with all this plastic? What do all these changes mean for our environment, our health and our wellbeing? Are we locked into a future jam-packed with the material, or is there anything we can do to reverse course?

A worker sorts and counts plastic bottles at Sure We Can’s recycling redemption center in Brooklyn on 16 April 2025.

Photographer Bryan Anselm took a look at how plastic is shaping environments in New York City – celebrations, workplaces, research centers, neighborhoods.

“It’s wild to see how after events the plastic, the garbage, can just pile up and pile up,” he told me.

He pursued the photo project because it is “important for all of us to understand what happens to the plastics we use”.

“Since it’s so prevalent and available in our daily lives, most people just toss it in the recycling bin or trash and never think of it again,” he mused. “Chances are the yogurt cup you threw out this morning will outlive you, decomposing in a landfill over several decades.”

Look ahead to see what he found.

In the United States, the average person generated 60lbs of plastic waste per year in 1980. By 2018, that number was up to 218lbs per person, marking a 263% increase, according to federal data. Ordinary people never pushed for that increase, said Judith Enck, a former Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regional administrator who now heads up the anti-plastic advocacy group Beyond Plastics.

“No one voted for more plastic, but we don’t have much choice when we enter a modern American store,” she said.

Plastics are made largely from oil and gas. In the US, the fracking boom created a glut of cheap natural gas, including ethane, a key ingredient in plastic production. As gas prices fell, the plastics industry became a lucrative outlet for the oil and gas sector, helping absorb the oversupply and spurring investment in new plastic manufacturing facilities.

“We’ve seen that increase because this is where fossil fuel companies are making really big investments, aided by enormous taxpayer subsidies,” Enck said. “That’s had a huge effect on how much plastic we consume.”

Department of sanitation workers clean up trash after the Mermaid Parade in Coney Island, Brooklyn, on 21 June 2025.

New York is no exception. About 15% of municipal solid waste in New York is made of the material, data shows. When people gather at street fairs or head to the beach during the summer, they are often sold food, beverages and souvenirs wrapped in plastic. All that packaging tends to overwhelm the city’s trash cans.

Some of those things get a second life when they are picked up by collectors with Sure We Can, the city’s last remaining non-profit waste redemption center. Members of the organization take to the streets to collect garbage, which is then recycled in Brooklyn.

For plastic waste generated at home, New York City also has a mandatory recycling program: the city’s department of sanitation provides free curbside pickup, and residents must sort their trash themselves or risk being fined. Curbside plastics are processed at the Sims Municipal Recycling Facility in Sunset Park, Brooklyn – the largest sorting plant in North America – or at PQ Recycling in Farmingdale, New York, which focuses on converting used bottles into reusable materials.

Despite these efforts, huge masses of plastic waste still end up as litter. Scientists across the country and world are working to better understand the effects of all of it, including researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology who regularly collect waste from storm drains, some of which had been discarded years ago.

Public concern about the plastic crisis is growing. Nearly 90% of Americans, for instance, are worried about microplastics – tiny particles which come from the breakdown of larger plastic – a June survey showed. A 2021 poll also found that more than four in five people globally reported worry about plastic litter in the ocean.

One New York City group working to remove plastic from our ecosystems is the community organization A Tribe Called Earth. On Earth Day in 2025, they hosted a cleanup in Brooklyn’s Coney Island Creek Park, where they collected 287lbs of garbage. But even after volunteers’ all-day efforts, the sand remained stippled with plastic fragments in all different shapes, sizes and colors.

Litter is among the most visible impacts plastic has on our environment, but the material has ecological impacts when it’s disposed of in sanctioned ways, too. When it is burned in garbage incinerators, for instance, it emits toxic compounds such as dioxins and mercury, which damage people’s respiratory health.

Volunteers Sasha Filippova (left) and Mohammad Ghouse Syed (right) clean litter from a beach during a cleanup.

Rochelle Bonner, a resident of Peekskill, New York, believes she has seen those effects first-hand. She lives near the city’s Win Waste trash incinerating plant, the largest toxic polluter in Westchester county. Both she and her daughter have seen their asthma flare due to fumes from the plant, she said. Nearly 80% of all garbage incinerators are located in low-income communities, a 2019 analysis found.

It’s a kind of inequality seen across plastic’s life cycle, said Enck.

“Plastic is largely produced in low-income communities and communities of color in Louisiana, Texas and Appalachia,” said Enck. “Then it ends up in landfills and incinerators which are also disproportionately sited in low-income communities and communities of color.”

What about recycling? New York City is home to the Sunset Park Material Recovery Facility, a recycling facility at the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal in the Sunset Park neighborhood. At the 11-acre facility, workers unload hundreds of tons of recyclable material – metal, glass and plastic – each day to be sorted.

These kinds of scenes – workers handling hulking towers of discarded trash – are common in efforts to take on plastic waste. Hundreds of miles north, photographer Bryan Anselm captured another one at plastic recycling company Ced-Lo in Farnham, Quebec. In the photo, an employee is dealing with a giant mass of plastic “bladder”-style bags from the inside of boxed wine containers. They were collected by TerraCycle, a company that works to recycle plastic garbage that you can’t put in your curbside bin.

But plastic is notoriously expensive and difficult to recycle, because the process requires meticulous sorting since most of the thousands of chemically distinct varieties of the material cannot be recycled together. Plastic also degrades each time it is reused, meaning it can generally only be reused once or twice. Critics say even companies like TerraCycle, which work to process hard-to-recycle plastics, can give companies license to keep producing plastic waste. Real solutions to the plastic waste issue would require cutting production, said Enck.

“I can say after all these years of attempts at plastics recycling that plastics recycling is a dead end,” Enck said. “It’s never gotten to double digits – right now, we have just 5% to 6% recycling rate for plastic in the US. It’s just not a viable solution.”

A worker rearranged pellets of recycled plastic in a box at the Ced-Lo plastic recycling facility in Farnham, Quebec, Canada, on 15 October 2025.

At the aforementioned non-profit Sure We Can’s redemption center in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn, bags of discarded cans and bottles are stacked from floor to ceiling. Founded in 2007, the organization serves canners – people who collect redeemable containers from the streets and exchange them for cash in a practice made possible by New York’s 1982 Returnable Container Act.

In recent years, the organization has also pushed for broader reforms to curb packaging waste, including New York’s Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act. The bill would have required companies to reduce packaging and improve recyclability, but despite passing the state senate, the measure stalled in the state assembly for the third time this year amid intense lobbying from industry groups.

In communities in which plastic waste is processed or disposed of, residents have spent decades battling the health and environmental consequences of the country’s throwaway economy. Among them is Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living, an environmental justice organization in Chester, Pennsylvania, that has long opposed the concentration of waste facilities in the predominantly Black city. Below, they are pictured protesting against a garbage incinerator commonly known as Covanta, though it was rebranded Reworld in 2024.

As workers sort through the plastic waste we create, advocates push to reduce the amount of plastic entering the waste stream, and communities work to check the harms of disposal, scientists are working to understand the scale of the plastic crisis and its effects.

Existing research makes clear that chemicals such as hormone-disrupting phthalates can leach out of plastics and get into people’s bodies through food contact, skin absorption and inhalation, said Katrina Korfmacher, professor of environmental medicine at the University of Rochester Medical Center. “Many of these chemicals are particularly harmful for children and the developing fetus,” she said. But many questions about plastics’ impacts are still open.

Protesters chant and carry signs during a march organized by the Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living protesting against the local incinerator which burns trash from New York in Chester, Pennsylvania, on 3 May 2025.

“There are so many questions remaining about how different plastics get into, move through, and change in the environment and what this means for the amounts, sizes, and types of microplastics in the environment that people might be exposed to,” Korfmacher said. “It’s important to figure out what kinds of micro- and nanoplastics get into the human body and how so we can focus our research on realistic exposures.”

At the University of Rochester, researchers are studying how microplastics move through ecosystems and what they may mean for our bodies and ecosystems. One of those scientists, Dr Jacques Robert, observes frogs to do so.

By examining how microplastic exposure affects the creatures’ immune systems, Robert is hoping to better understand their impacts on humans.

Other researchers are following plastic after it disappears from view. At the Rochester Institute of Technology’s (RIT) Tait Preserve, sustainability PhD candidate Sydney VanWinkle studies how plastics break down in freshwater under different temperatures and pH levels. Her experiments aim to create a better understanding of how long plastics persist and how environmental conditions may influence their spread. Other RIT researchers are tracing another part of the journey, collecting debris from storm drains to investigate how plastics move from streets into waterways and eventually drinking water supplies.

Environmental science student, Alonso Ponce, (left) and RIT research technician, Jayson Kucharek, (right) examine debris collected from a storm drain as part of a study to understand how plastics are entering the water supply at the Rochester Institute of Technology in Rochester, New York, on 7 October 2025.

Some scientists are looking for ways to address the problem after plastics have already entered the environment. At the University of Rochester’s Anne Meyer Lab, researchers are experimenting with engineered bacteria biofilms, using 3D-printed structures to explore whether biological systems could one day help break down plastic waste.

Others are trying to avoid creating the waste in the first place. In Brooklyn, refill shops like Maison Jar are part of a growing movement focused on reuse, allowing customers to bring their own containers and refill household products like dish detergent instead of buying new plastic packaging each time.

The next step for people looking to curb their own plastic consumption is to push for systemic change, said Enck.

“It’s a very, very slow process, but I think the public sees the severity of the problem, and we just need more people getting into the political arena,” she said.

This photo essay was supported by funding from the Center for Contemporary Documentation.

Litter is among the most visible impacts plastic has on our environment. Nearly 80% of all garbage incinerators are located in low-income communities.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President’s order strips nearly 3m acres of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, sacred tribal sites, of safeguards

Patagonia, the outdoor clothing and gear company, has joined a lawsuit challenging Donald Trump’s decision to significantly reduce the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, removing protections from nearly 3m acres.

In July, the president approved the reduction of the sites by 90%, clearing the way to open the land to oil and gas companies. He argued in his proclamations that doing so would allow lands to be “put to a higher-priority use” and that they contained critical minerals important to “resource independence …[and] national security”.

Trump previously targeted the monuments, which are sacred to tribes, in his first term. Joe Biden ultimately overturned it.

Patagonia sued Trump in 2017 when he first sought to downsize the public lands in Utah. His proclamations earlier this year represented an even more dramatic reduction of the monuments than he sought in his first term.

The retailer announced on Wednesday it was joining a lawsuit to put a stop to what it described as illegal orders that “betray Tribal sovereignty”.

“We will not stand idly by while anti-public lands crusaders attempt to exploit these lands for their extractive-industry friends or disrespect tribal nations,” Ryan Gellert, the company’s CEO, said in a statement.

The Antiquities Act allows presidents to establish national monuments, but it does not give the executive the authority to undo them, Gellert wrote. Trump’s move was an effort to “force secession of federal land to the state and allow private companies to extract natural resources from that land”, Gellert said, pointing to mining claims that have already been filed in areas that are no longer part of the monuments.

“Protecting Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante is worth more than any amount of money. The vast majority of Americans agree,” Gellert said.

Barack Obama established Bears Ears in 2016 during his final weeks in office, after years of advocacy by Indigenous American tribes, while Bill Clinton established Grand Staircase-Escalante.

The Natural Resources Defense Council, which filed the federal lawsuit on Wednesday along with several other conservation groups, described Trump’s proclamations as “one of the largest rollbacks of public land protections in US history”.

“These monuments protect places that took millions of years to form. President Trump is trying to destroy them with a stroke of a pen. That cannot stand,” said Christy Goldfuss, the NRDC executive director.

“Once you open these lands to mining and drilling, what gets lost is not coming back – ancient cliff dwellings, dinosaur fossils found nowhere else on Earth and sacred sites tied to the tribal nations.”

The other groups that challenged Trump’s rollback in court include the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and Earthjustice, which represents Grand Canyon Trust, WildEarth Guardians, the Sierra Club, Western Watersheds Project, the Center for Biological Diversity, Great Old Broads for Wilderness and the National Parks Conservation Association.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Temperature check: alarm as prediction markets lean into weather and climate bets
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Climate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperatures

Online prediction markets, saturated by money staked on sport, crypto and politics, have now set their sights on a promising new area of growth: betting on the future livability of the planet itself.

The rise of gamified predictions on the unfolding climate crisis, and shorter-term weather forecasts, has been underscored by a new deal that allows Kalshi, a leading online financial exchange, to access data from the Weather Company, owner of the Weather Channel, to verify weather-related betting outcomes.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The weather is “one of the fastest-growing and most crucial categories” at Kalshi, the company said, with monetized predictions made by people, and bots, on weather and climate events growing 500% in the past year into a $1.1bn market.

“The long-term vision is to financialize everything and create a tradable asset out of any difference in opinion,” Tarek Mansour, co-founder of Kalshi, said of the company’s broader objectives last year.

Startlingly, Kalshi even claims that this gauge of public opinion can not only act as a financial hedge for businesses exposed to extreme weather, but also help shape the weather forecasts themselves. Kalshi’s betting markets will appear on the Weather Channel’s app, which is used by more than 330 million people worldwide.

“Given the severity of the climate crisis, it’s crucial for policymakers and the general public to have well-calibrated forecasting data about future climate impacts,” said a Kalshi spokesperson, citing a company study on how accurate its markets’ predictions are. Asked whether this meant Kalshi saw its weather markets as part of delivering well-calibrated forecasting data, the spokesperson said this was the case.

“Weather is the ultimate equalizer – it fundamentally affects everyone and everything,” the spokesperson said.

People visiting Kalshi or Polymarket, its main rival, can bet on weather predictions such as how hot it will be in certain places on a given day, as well as longer-term bets – from how many climate-fueled disasters the US will have, to whether the world will avoid catastrophic global heating, to how severe the die-off of corals in Hawaii will be.

You can even wager how far Lake Mead, the US’s largest reservoir and a crucial water source for the American west, will drop below its already record-low levels. Last year, amid ruinous wildfires in Los Angeles, there were $1.2m in bets laid on Polymarket on the extent of the fires, with one user posting that “volume so high in this market it cause another fire”.

While Polymarket’s international platform still hosts wildfire bets, US consumers are barred from accessing them. Kalshi meanwhile has never offered wildfire markets, citing “perverse incentives”.

Distinctions can be hard to draw, though – the websites will allow betting on, for example, the severity of heatwaves in Phoenix, Arizona, even though up to 500 deaths in Maricopa county, which includes Phoenix, are being investigated as possibly heat-related. Excessive heat is the biggest killer among extreme weather events in the US.

For scientists and people affected by climate-related disasters, though, it has been troubling to see the painful consequences of an overheating world turned into an online money-making market.

When the Eaton fire swept through Los Angeles county last year, killing at least 19 people and razing thousands of buildings, the home of Kaitlyn Trudeau’s grandfather was among those destroyed.

While he was unhurt, Trudeau, a climate scientist at the non-profit Climate Central, said it “left a bad taste in my mouth imagining people making money off it. People were posting ‘that was fun, until next time!’ I’d be lying if I said it didn’t hurt a bit.

“The dehumanization of these events really concerns me. I worry about the gamification of this because it distances us from the impacts of climate change, it affects our empathy,” said Trudeau, who added that she questioned Kalshi’s blurring of distinction of weather and climate and how such bets are adjudicated.

“I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” she said. “I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides. They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.”

Kalshi’s claims around weather forecasting are “confusing”, Trudeau added. “I’d be curious to know which resolved markets are related to future climate impacts and what sources they used to calibrate them,” she said. “Since calibration is measured by comparing many predictions against many realized outcomes, how can a market be calibrated on impacts that, by definition, haven’t happened yet?”

Placing bets on the weather or the broader climate is harmful “because of all of the perverse incentives this can create, especially among bad actors with malicious intentions”, said Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania who said he worried about the bets fueling conspiracy theories about weather manipulation.

Other critics contend that the public’s understanding of actual weather data could be obscured or even altered by big-money betting. Kalshi, Polymarket and the Weather Company all dismissed concerns of potential improper practices, pointing to company policies and federal regulation deterring insider trading and conflict of interest.

“We view weather data through the lens of decision intelligence and risk management – not gamification,” said a Weather Company spokesperson about the deal with Kalshi. “This partnership elevates weather data into a highly reliable tool, allowing both individuals and mission-critical enterprises to better quantify and manage real-world weather outcomes.”

Polymarket, meanwhile, said it saw itself in grander terms than a mere betting website for people facing the perils of a hurricane, wildfire or heatwave made far fiercer by the burning of fossil fuels.

“When tragedy unfolds, people turn to the news for commentary and they come to Polymarket for information,” said a company spokesperson. “While we are not blind to the risks, removing these markets does not prevent a tragedy but makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most.”

While they are booming in popularity, however, the wagering platforms are under increasing scrutiny from federal lawmakers and several states. Last week, a federal appeals court ruled that states can regulate prediction markets like gambling, after a case brought by Nevada, which had attempted to shut down Kalshi.

This mounting legal and regulatory pressure means that sites that allow wagers on everything from the value of gold to the words mentioned in a Donald Trump speech may find the climate crisis a less politically fraught arena to focus on, even though the topic still only attracts a small fraction of the bets laid online, experts point out.

“They have to convince the courts they aren’t a gambling platform for sports and crypto,” said Jamie Pietruska, an economic historian at Rutgers University. “The weather and climate are seemingly innocuous in comparison. There is a longstanding belief that the weather can’t be controlled so it’s perfect to bet on and different to other categories, such as geopolitics.”

Much like how CNN already includes prediction market outcomes in its political coverage, the Weather Channel could soon feature Kalshi odds amid its own forecasts, Pietruska said, further warping public trust in the National Weather Service, the bedrock federal forecasting agency that has faced deep cuts under the Trump administration.

“Who is the wisdom of the crowds in that situation? There are casual betters, dumb money and weather trading bots,” said Pietruska. “Is that going to produce a forecast better than a meteorologist? Is that just vibes weather?”

What will this all do to the public’s appetite to address global heating? One 2023 study found that participating in a climate prediction market elevated concerns about the climate crisis and even altered the viewpoint of those who denied established climate science.

“The only thing that seems to work in changing minds of climate deniers [is] to let them put their money where their mouth is,” said Moran Cerf, a Columbia University researcher who led the study.

Still, Cerf said, the negatives of wagering on the climate outweigh the positives. “It’s bad, in one word,” he said. “The prediction markets have taken a turn to the dark side by gamifying disasters. The fact it’s unregulated, unlike the stock market, means it is getting worse, too.”

Pietruska shares these misgivings. “I’ve been uncomfortable with this sort of betting for some time. It has serious moral consequences,” she said. “An academic study isn’t the same as the speed and scale of the new casinos that are being set up.

“If I go online and see the perception that the world will pass 2C (3.6F) warming by 2050, it creates a sense of a predetermined future, even though this is an aggregation of public opinion. It’s not a truth machine.”

Listing climate-related disasters next to the timing of Taylor Swift’s next album or the winner of the next Super Bowl “casualizes and trivializes catastrophe and human suffering”, Pietruska said. “The wisdom of crowds isn’t going to encourage the community building and solidarity we need to address the climate crisis. That is not good, to say the least.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Kalshi, Polymarket and Weather Company all dismissed concerns of potential improper practices. The wagering platforms are under increasing scrutiny from federal lawmakers and several states.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: One in 12 golf clubs in England broke water extraction rules in past five years
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Emma Howard
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
More than 140 clubs breached licences, with a third caught taking water illegally, analysis shows – but no fines issued

More than 140 golf clubs in England have breached their water extraction licences in the past five years, according to data analysis by the Guardian.

More than a third of these clubs were caught taking water illegally from the environment, either by taking more than permitted or by removing it outside the permitted period.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In most of the other cases, the breaches were the result of golf clubs that were either not reporting or monitoring their water usage properly, or were not reporting and monitoring it at all.

Although 100 of the golf clubs breached their licences in a way that put the environment at risk, none of the infringements have led to a prosecution or fine.

Amy Fairman, head of campaigns at the campaign group River Action, described the figures as “absolutely unacceptable”. “It suggests that there are no meaningful consequences for breaching licences. Monitoring and enforcement must be significantly strengthened.”

The Environment Agency (EA) told the Guardian that it had increased its ability to monitor and detect breaches of abstraction licences. A spokesperson said: “Our first response is to work with abstractors to bring them back into compliance, however we won’t hesitate to take further action if necessary.”

Over 70% of England is now in drought after a summer of back-to-back heatwaves, which the Met Office has just declared to be the UK’s hottest on record. The previous record was set just last year. Nine major reservoirs are classed as having exceptionally low storage, and farmers have warned that the drought could lead to food shortages.

The Guardian obtained the data, which covers the period from 2021 to 2025, from the EA via an environmental information request (EIR). The overall number of breaches has more than doubled in that time, probably largely because of the digitisation of records and improved monitoring.

Over the five-year period, golf clubs breached their licences 279 times, accounting for about 6% of the total breaches. Of these, 175 were category 2 or 3 breaches meaning that they posed the threat of a “reasonably foreseeable” impact on the environment, human health or quality of life.

Although the figures do not relate to the 2026 drought, they do include breaches that occurred during the droughts of 2022 and 2025.

Fairman said: “As we face increasingly climate stressed conditions, we need to look at who is prioritised to extract our water and that should be essential services, not golf clubs. Demand and competition for water is going to increase so the government needs to take this issue really seriously and put in place a national plan for water resilience.”

In England, the removal of water from rivers, lakes and boreholes in the ground is governed by a system of abstraction licences, held by public water companies, farmers and many other businesses. The licences place conditions on where, when and how much water businesses can remove, as well as how they must monitor and report their usage.

Dr Megan Klaar, an associate professor in hydroecology at the University of Leeds, told the Guardian that breaches of abstraction licences were “bad news for the environment”.

“If the water level gets too low this can increase the temperature, concentrate effluent and other pollutants and dry out the river. There needs to be enough water so that species such as fish have enough habitat to exist in.”

The Environment Agency checks compliance through a mix of inspections and desk-based assessments, including use of satellite data. Where breaches occur, the agency can respond with advice, a warning letter, a fine or a prosecution.
