https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve Rotheram
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Steve Rotheram
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story

Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

O
ne of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage characters shouting abuse at people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.

But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.

And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control, starting in St Helens in Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.

What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.

Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.

Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly with Liverpool John Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.

And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”

That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a £500m fleet of new trains and are working towards bringing Merseyrail services into public ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, the Royal Daffodil – our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.

For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.

When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railways back into public ownership and giving local leaders more power over the essentials that ordinary people depend on.

After decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.

I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?

Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren Edwards
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Lauren Edwards
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers

Lauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood

I
was elected to Westminster two years ago, when the country was crying out for change and looking to parliament to tackle the big issues that had been forgotten for too long. When that change didn’t come fast enough, trust in politics once again started to ebb away. We have one last chance to prove we can deliver on people’s priorities.

Assisted dying didn’t feature in the manifesto I was elected on. Nor should it have done. Matters of conscience such as this are rightly left to individual MPs to decide upon. There will always be a range of views within all political parties. But this issue has been supported by a substantial majority in the country for a very long time. Reputable independent polling has shown support for assisted dying consistently at about 75%. The latest British social attitudes survey from the National Centre for Social Research found that “it is clear we are observing a continued high level of public support for legal change to allow assisted dying in some circumstances”.

Having examined the issue with great care, MPs decided in the last session to support the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill. On the Labour benches there was a clear majority in favour, as there was on the Lib Dems’. The Greens supported it unanimously. It is the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper.

On Friday, I will be asking MPs to send the bill back to the Lords. There they can amend the bill if they choose, just like any legislation, and if the Commons agrees, that’s fine. But they should not be allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time.

I am not reopening divisions in the Labour party or in parliament, as some have claimed. Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions.

The voters put us here to tackle the big issues they care about, not to constantly kick them down the road. After a shaky start, this parliament has the chance to show that it can deliver; that we won’t shirk our responsibilities and will start to restore the public’s faith in our democratic system.

Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial. It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly Toynbee
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Polly Toynbee
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacle

Y
ou might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?

For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.

A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.

Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.

Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.

Leaflets saying only the Greens, or only Labour, can win here are arriving through letterboxes – and it’s true, no one else is likely to. That Polanski is seeking the nomination boosts the Greens. Tot up issues where they challenge Labour, and many resonate with the student population. They oppose nuclear weapons and seem divided over increased defence spending. They back rent controls that Burnham has rejected. They oppose Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea oil and gas drilling, which may both be approved any day now. They want rapid nationalisation of utilities, where Labour hesitates. Locally they campaign on crime, mobile phone thefts and housing.

But it’s Gaza that may shift votes from Labour to Green: in the 2024 election, Starmer’s vote share was slashed and a pro-Palestinian, independent candidate came second with 18.9% of the vote. Arresting thousands for terrorism for silently holding placards supporting Palestine Action is another gift to the Greens. Labour instead points to impossible promises in the party’s £160bn tax, spend and borrowing pledges.

The Green campaign asks: “Why elect just another Labour MP, when a Green MP in parliament will challenge the government?” But this week Labour looks set to select not just “another Labour MP” but Sagal Abdi-Wali, Camden council’s leader and community organiser, popular with her party and a well-known dynamic force locally. Green criticism of Labour over Gaza comes up against a hijab-wearing Muslim woman who has spent years calming racial and religions tensions, and building relationships with many Jewish voters here, too. “If Greens stir up community antagonisms over Gaza,” she says to me, “that would be disgraceful”.

Reform has no foothold here but its attacks on her from afar may galvanise Labour people to come out and vote. Its poisonous home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spits out Reform’s usual ethno-nativist bile, pointing out on X that Abdi-Wali “was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” Georgia Gould MP, former Camden council leader, ripostes on X that she “has dedicated her life to public service” and is “the elected leader of Camden council, a community where she grew up and has lived for 35 years” who “embodies the best of our values … an outstanding example of British success”. Telegraph headlines similarly define her primarily as a “Somali refugee”. All this will remind Labour voters that fighting off the racist right is Labour’s great cause.

On the doorstep with Abdi-Wali, in a social housing estate, I saw how she is known and liked for her community work. She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism. But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will “never vote Labour again”. Not for Abdi-Wali? It’s all about Palestine.

Nonetheless, Polanski takes a big risk here after sliding in the polls. For Labour, the challenge is to show how Burnham’s raft of positive policies can ward off hopeless wishes and still reach the left with his hopefulness.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessness | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change

W
hat links the thuggish masked agitation in southern England this weekend and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland’s (AfD) best-ever result in a German state – where it more than doubled the 21% vote it received five years ago? Several hundred men in balaclavas blocking an A road are not the same as a party winning a landslide election. But both events draw on the idea that the political system has lost control. The extremists in Dover and Portsmouth dramatise this claim; the electoral result in Germany threatens to institutionalise it.

The prospect of Germany’s first far-right-led state government since the second world war carries real consequences. In Saxony-Anhalt it could see power handed to a party hostile to migrants, Islam, LGBTQ+ rights and climate policy. Alarmingly, it has senior figures linked to former neo-Nazi groups. About 170,000 foreign nationals live among 2 million people in Saxony-Anhalt – and roughly a fifth of the state’s doctors were born abroad. The grim paradox is that an AfD government could oversee the very state intelligence service that has classified the party as “rightwing extremist”.

In England, the “Patriot Platform” agitation is far-right vigilantism that claims it will “stop the boats” if the authorities won’t. The AfD is a political party which presents its success as a repudiation of established parties that, it claims, have failed – most notably on immigration. The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are, however, two sides of the same coin: a broader politics in which migration is felt to embody a sense of powerlessness – not just over borders but over state institutions, economic change and national identity.

The AfD polls highest in Germany’s eastern states. These have a post-reunification history of population loss and high unemployment. Britain has its own political geography and history. The small boats are a live political issue. More than 33,000 people arrived by that route in the year to June 2026. Nearly all will claim asylum. But arrivals were 23% lower than the previous year. The street escalation is occurring as numbers are falling.

Across Europe, the far right keeps rising because immigration has become a test of whether states can still govern effectively. Cutting migrant numbers or asylum claims does not lessen the issue’s potency. Studies suggest that, in Germany, political alienation is more important to AfD support than deprivation. That is also why, in Britain, using facts alone – that crossings are falling, or that migrants aren’t responsible for NHS waiting lists or stagnant wages – may have little electoral effect. The reality answers the far right’s argument, but doesn’t dispel the deeper belief that the country is becoming ungovernable.

Borders, in that sense, are a symptom of a bigger problem: voters increasingly distrust democracy to make things happen for them. In Germany, politicians can point to the constitutional settlement and coalition arithmetic and say that their hands are tied. In Britain, they defer to the bond markets and the Bank of England. The language is different, but the message can sound the same: you can vote for change, but the government is limited in what it can achieve. The answer is not to pretend that inflation or legal constraints are irrelevant. It is to show that they do not amount to a permanent veto on democratic choice.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on skin cancer: fear the heat of the sun | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
With melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhere

N
ew climate risks bring with them new health risks. An exceptionally warm and dry summer in Europe meant that outdoor workers, and those who choose to spend leisure time in the sun, were confronted more directly than usual by the need to protect their skin from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, as well as avoid dehydration and overheating. In the UK, the annual total of new melanoma cases was reported to have risen above 20,000 for the first time earlier this year (the two most common forms of skin cancer, basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, are less dangerous).

As with other cancers, the increase in cases reflects an ageing and a growing population. A third of those diagnosed with cancer in the UK are over 75. But with the NHS struggling to cope with the number of those seeking treatment, and melanoma the fifth most common cancer – after prostate, breast, lung and bowel (and excluding other skin cancers) – there are growing calls for behaviour change aligned to stronger public health measures. In May, a group of MPs proposed a ban on advertising sunbeds, which – along with sunburn and tanning – are linked with a raised risk of skin cancer. Last year, a group of experts advocated banning their commercial use altogether, as in Australia and Brazil.

There are lessons to be learned from other countries besides new laws. In Australia, melanoma is the third most common cancer, and strong public health warnings have been the norm for decades. In 1981, a cartoon seagull was the face of a “slip, slop, slap” campaign aimed at persuading people to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. At school, children are expected to follow a “no hat, no play” rule (meaning no games in sunny outdoor spaces for those with bare heads). While some British nurseries and schools have adopted similar policies, awareness of the risks remains far lower. Many people still habitually welcome bright sunshine and high temperatures.

That is partly because these remain much rarer in the UK, especially in northern areas. For good reason, melanoma is less likely to be a priority for health authorities in Scotland than in south-east England. But with global temperatures predicted to keep rising, and given their commitment to shift towards prevention in healthcare, UK ministers and local health bosses should look again at the risks of UV radiation and the factors driving it (the National Cancer Plan has already committed officials in England to seek further evidence on sunbeds). In Australia, doctors have objected to tanning apps promoted by influencers; in the UK there has been an increase in the popularity of tanning among young people, due in part to promotion on social media.

Personalised care for many cancers, in the form of immunotherapy, has led to the present being termed a “golden age” for oncology. Such advances deserve to be celebrated. But there are tensions between the desire to focus on innovation and the need to improve access to more established services, and invest in prevention and public health. Melanoma is one of many diseases in which behaviour has a role (cancers linked to obesity are others). After a tightening of the law on tobacco and vapes, and following this summer’s record high temperatures, there is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun as well as artificial UV light – in time for summer 2027.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby Hinsliff
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Gaby Hinsliff
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity

Nigel Farage didn’t know. He wasn’t told.

Sure, he was right there at the table when the undercover reporter he believed to be a rich American’s son spelled out very clearly how he hoped to channel his father’s money to Reform, in ways that certainly don’t sound too lawful.

But he wasn’t listening, you understand. God forbid that the man who insists his party takes compliance very seriously, and who never stops warning that the establishment is out to get him by any means possible, should actually pay attention to the details of a donation offered bang in the middle of a byelection that was fought over – of all the luck, eh? – some other questionable donations.

Farage’s defence is essentially that he was present but not involved, as Jeremy Corbyn once famously said of attending an event where someone laid a commemorative wreath for members of the terrorist group behind the 1972 Munich Olympics atrocity.

It didn’t work for Corbyn, any more than claiming to have tried cannabis but never inhaling worked an age ago for Bill Clinton, in part because some people just didn’t believe it. But mostly, perhaps, because critics found it revealing even that Corbyn would be at the kind of gathering where such things might happen. Most aspirant prime ministers take good care to avoid moving in circles where someone might end up venerating terrorists, or explaining exactly how they intend to get around the law. For good reason, it turns out.

What we are being asked to accept, in the instance caught on camera, is that at best Farage has been astonishingly sloppy; that he just turned up, tuned out, thanked the guy without even really knowing what for, and then went happily on his way. Take Farage at his own word and he is describing someone curiously semi-detached. Someone who, despite repeatedly claiming his enemies will stop at nothing to stitch him up, puzzlingly doesn’t seem to take such basic precautions against entrapment as noticing what’s actually going on around him. Someone for whom fighting a byelection in which nobody else of note is standing, bar a talking bin, is apparently so all-consuming that he can’t possibly be expected to concentrate on talking to donors as well.

If that degree of walking and chewing gum is a stretch, imagine what a shock running the country might be. No wonder some in Reform are starting to ask themselves if, deep down, that’s what he even wants.

What would Reform look like without Nigel Farage? Once upon a time that would have been a ridiculous question – without him, it would simply fall apart – but the party now is not quite what it used to be. Among the faithful, the fact he doesn’t seem to take the job too seriously is still part of his charm, and many Reform supporters will be nothing but indignant on his behalf at the undercover tactics used to catch him out.

But there are also people in Reform these days who have seen the very real possibility of seizing power to enact an agenda not seen before in Britain, just as Alternative für Deutschland is starting to do in Germany and as the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella (the star turn at Reform’s party conference this year) and Marine Le Pen threaten to do next year in France. They won’t want to let that opportunity slip through their fingers.

Having lost its lead in the polls, Reform finds itself ironically in a version of the dilemma Labour faced a few months ago: torn between those who think recovery depends on tacking left (in this case towards Tory voters who are Reform-curious but worry that it seems too extreme or sleazy) or tacking right (towards Rupert Lowe’s Restore, now consistently taking small but damaging chunks out of them, and other far-right groupings). Events like last weekend’s sinister black-shirted, paramilitary-style show of force in Dover by the little known Patriot Platform group – which even the government took a surprisingly long time to condemn in the decisive terms that chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds eventually did on Monday morning, after what looked like copycat demonstrations in Portsmouth – may now start to push those tensions into the open.

Are these their people, or not? Having ripped open Pandora’s box by saying what others would not on immigration, there would be a grim irony in Reform struggling to deal with the furies unleashed, if only the whole thing wasn’t so frightening for everyone else. Farage ended up calling the Dover mob “disgusting” because of their balaclavas, while suggesting he absolutely shared their anger about small boat crossings (now, of course, down to a seven-year low). But is covering your face at a protest the only line Reform won’t cross?

Some of its supporters clearly do want a leader prepared to say what Farage won’t, a niche that Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, evidently aims to fill. Others more recently arrived from the old Conservative party might prefer a leader who treads a hard line on immigration, welfare and woke, but with some rougher edges sanded off (or so Robert Jenrick clearly hopes). Crucially, some in both camps will see the departure of close aide Dan Jukes – who along with head of policy, James Orr, has taken the rap for this latest donor scandal, though both deny wrongdoing – as an opportunity to replace Farage’s loyal and protective sidekicks with people less tied to him personally.

Historically, anyone daring to fly this close to Farage’s sun has got their wings scorched. But what if that sun doesn’t burn quite so brightly any more? What if the political judgment that always served him so well in the past is now fractionally off-key? For now, the idea that there could be an election any minute – forced, perhaps, by some future bond market crisis – is perhaps imposing a measure of discipline on the party. But what if that imaginary snap election never materialises?

For now, these are all still very much “what ifs”. Given his miraculous capacity for resurrection, it is a mistake to underestimate Farage or count him out when he is down.

But until recently, even the idea of Reform without its leader seemed ridiculous; he was Reform, to the point that without him it would cease to meaningfully exist. In the current climate, that assumption may no longer be safe. Bardella, after all, got his big break when Le Pen was brought down by a financial scandal. It’s time the other parties thought harder about the shape Reform might take without its maker, rather than assuming the battle begins and ends with him.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Painful, unconvincing and boring: welcome to John Healey’s late show | John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Chancellor has the look of a man born to announce the UK is under nuclear attack

M
eet the new chancellor. Same as the old chancellor. Although, on reflection, that might be a little hard on Rachel Reeves. At least Rachel had given the job some thought before she got it. She had had some experience working at the Bank of England and, whether you liked it or not, she had some kind of plan. John Healey? Not so much. No one can remember him ever having given the economy much thought until Andy Burnham offered the job. He was more the strong and silent type.

As defence secretary, Healey had looked like a man of principle. A defender of the armed forces, a guardian of the realm. He had even resigned over Keir Starmer and Reeves’s refusal to guarantee increasing the defence budget to 3% of GDP by 2030.

Now that he’s in charge of the purse strings, he’s remained silent. Though not so strong. It feels as if he doesn’t know what he thinks. Or if he even thinks at all. Almost as if, were he to spend too much time in deliberation, he might have to resign all over again. He doesn’t even come across as a career opportunist. A well-trodden route for cabinet ministers over the years. Instead, he’s just a rabbit caught in the headlights.

There again, for your first major speech as chancellor, you’d probably prefer it if the cost of government borrowing wasn’t at a record high since the financial crash and that Jaguar Land Rover hadn’t chosen that morning to announce 4,000 redundancies. On the plus side, Healey could be guaranteed everyone’s attention. The trickier question to answer was whether he would want it.

Burnham had stayed away from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry because he didn’t want to steal his chancellor’s sun. Amazingly though, Healey somehow managed to eclipse himself. It was like watching a man in negative space. The lights were off and no one was at home. One of those occasions when to have barricaded himself in the Treasury, refusing to come out, would have been a massive improvement all round. With John, less really is more. At least that way there’s the possibility of authority.

You would have hoped Healey’s ability with numbers was rather better than his time-keeping. He was 15 minutes late for his own debut and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the entire Treasury ministerial team were getting decidedly fidgety before his arrival. Perhaps they were wondering whether the chancellor was going to throw a sickie. Had decided he wasn’t the right man for the gig after all. We’d have all understood. It’s a tough job and it isn’t for everyone. I’d hate to do it.

It was a very nervy-looking Healey who eventually appeared. Occasionally having to grab hold of the lectern to make sure he didn’t fall over. Not the most reassuring sight. Less rock. More Northern Rock. Even when you know the news is going to be bad, you want your chancellor to appear strong and coherent. In the same way you want your doctor to tell you she has a plan and you are not going to die, in the same breath as she has said you have a life-threatening illness. A chancellor is someone you need to believe in. Not someone who will agree with you that we are probably all screwed.

Healey started downbeat. The global situation was terrible. The Tories had trashed the economy. Politicians don’t get to choose the time and circumstances in which they are asked to serve. It rather suggested he would have much preferred not to have landed up at the Treasury just now. But hey! We were all in it together so we might as well make the best of it. He would do what he could to make things a bit better, but if it didn’t work out he hoped there would be no bad feelings. You couldn’t help feeling it was the blind leading the blind.

Then came the continuity Rachel stuff. Fiscal discipline was his priority. He would be maintaining his predecessor’s fiscal rules. He would be honest about government spending. Manifesto promises would be honoured. It made you wonder why we had changed prime minister if it was all going to be much the same. Had we been through all that psychodrama just to get someone with a little more personal charm, had twinklier eyes and who looked good in a T-shirt?

Having made all his excuses, Healey turned to the good vibes stuff. The hallmark of Andy’s two months in office so far. Yes everything was terrible. Yes everything was going to stay the same. But not to worry because if we all just sat in a circle, chanted “Om” and had positive thoughts then we could turn this around. We were going all out for growth through devolution. He wanted to bring hope to every postcode. John is one of the few people who can make hope sound like a sexually transmitted disease.

It was all a bit painful. Unconvincing. Boring. You longed for him to stop because the speech was as painful to listen to as it was for him to give. Healey isn’t cut out for all this positivity stuff. It dies on his lips. He was far better off where he had come from. He has the look and the gravitas of a man who had been born to make a television announcement that the UK was under nuclear attack. It was time to hide under the kitchen table with the dog and a can of baked beans and wait to die in half an hour’s time. Thank you and goodbye.

The questions were no more revealing. Everything was either met with a dead bat, “You can’t expect me to comment before the budget” or was brushed aside with mindless waffle as Healey tried to fill the dead air. Still, his speech didn’t cause any extra volatility in the bond markets, so that was something. Then again, as he had spent half an hour saying nothing of interest, it would have been remarkable if the bond markets had moved. Perhaps he had sent the traders to sleep for a thousand years.

They wouldn’t be the only ones. The whole of the government appeared to be in a Healey-induced sense of torpor. There was no sign of the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood. Normally, she would have been quick to crack down on the balaclava protesters in Dover and Portsmouth. But she too had been silenced. Almost as if the government wasn’t quite sure if it was OK to call out the protests.

Strange that, given even Nigel Farage thought they weren’t OK. It was fine to attack migrant women and children, just so long as you did it out in the open. Take a leaf out of the Reform conference where members had been filmed apparently attacking female protesters. That was the Britain we all knew and loved.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Farage still Reform’s best hope as rivals struggle to match appeal to party faithful
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Pippa Crerar and Peter Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Despite series of scandals, members remain loyal to their leader as questions over his successor grow

F
ew British politicians unleash the kind of evangelical zeal among their party faithful as Nigel Farage. Despite being weighed down by weeks of scandal, last weekend’s Reform UK conference showed that – as far as the membership is concerned – the lustre has not come off their man.

So it was notable that Farage felt compelled to reassure his disciples that he wasn’t going anywhere. “I’m only here because of the failure of our political class, and I am determined to lead Reform to victory at the next general election. That is my job,” he told them during his speech.

While support within the party for Farage remains rock solid, the same cannot be said for the wider public. Dogged by financial controversy and with a parliamentary standards investigation hanging over him, as well as the police looking into Reform, it is unsurprising that his ratings have slumped.

The steady drumbeat of speculation over his future has continued. But while he has publicly declared he intends to fight the next general election – and beyond – sources close to Farage have told the Guardian that if Reform UK loses that particular contest, it will be his last.

By 2029, the likely date for the next election, Farage would be 65 years old. That would make him the same age – he tells friends – as Winston Churchill in 1940, the oldest first-time prime minister to take office in the modern era. Another five years at the helm would put Farage well ahead by that measure.

Yet four out of five Reform UK members say they would want Farage to continue as leader even if the party is not in government after the next election, according to a poll of 850 members by Lord Ashcroft in June. Just 13% said he should step down if they don’t win.

There are those inside the party who don’t think Farage will stick around even until the next election. “There are all sorts of reasons why Nigel could throw in the towel before then,” one Reform official said, citing family, security and money. “He’d have an easier life on the outside.”

What almost everybody inside Reform agrees on, however, is that if Farage does decide to stand down, it would be on his own terms. The party base is so fervently behind him it would be virtually impossible for a rival to stage a coup.

Whether Reform UK could carry on making the political weather to the extent it currently does without him at the helm is far from clear. So while any doubt remains over his plans, speculation over a possible successor will continue.

One Reform insider said that if Farage did depart, the race was expected to quickly turn into a battle between Zia Yusuf and whichever “anyone but Zia” candidate seemed best placed to beat him, with the home affairs spokesperson a divisive figure even inside the party.

“Everyone loves Zia when he’s on policy and focused, and when we were polling at 32%, they didn’t mind when he wasn’t,” they said. “But now it’s more like 23%, and every vote counts, there is a concern that he puts off possible switchers, especially from the Conservatives.

“If you lead a party you have to be able to build internal coalitions, and he’s so combative I can’t see that happening.”

Yusuf’s social media outbursts have prompted even party loyalists to urge him to rein it in. Nadine Dorries, the former Tory culture secretary who defected to Reform last year, said at the weekend: “I think Zia’s got a problem with Twitter and someone needs to take his phone off him.”

One close ally of Farage said the party leader was “unimpressed” by some of Yusuf’s comments, which he felt distracted from Reform’s attempts to make itself look ready for government. “Nigel thinks he’s a wanker,” they added.

But when asked unprompted who they would like to see as the next Reform UK leader, party members were most likely to name Yusuf, with the backing of 22%, according to the Ashcroft polling.

Reform insiders believe he wants the top job – the backstory video he launched online at conference looked every bit like a veiled leadership pitch – even though party bosses have to date appeared less than enthusiastic about finding him a seat to stand for parliament.

Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, was almost level, on 21%. Tellingly, just 6% suggested Robert Jenrick, the economy spokesperson, who is viewed with some scepticism among Reform activists because he defected from the Tories after losing that leadership contest, and was also a key member of the last Conservative government.

“My view is there’s an acceptance that it probably can’t be a former Tory MP, and that Richard would have the authenticity to beat Zia,” one Reform insider said. “It doesn’t mean that Robert wouldn’t think about it, but if it was him against Zia, Zia would probably win.”

Tice, who led the party for three years until Farage’s return to frontline politics in spring 2024, probably has greater public appeal than Yusuf, and as a more moderate figure could win more votes from the Conservatives.

Yet neither Yusuf’s provocative outbursts, nor Jenrick’s ruthless ambition, nor Tice’s more mainstream leanings are ever likely to deliver the same level of cut through that their boss has achieved, and so electoral success could end up eluding them.

For now, despite his increasing toxicity with the general public, Farage remains Reform’s best hope.

But sources close to Farage say if Reform UK loses that particular contest Tice's more mainstream leanings are never likely to deliver the same level of cut through that their boss has achieved.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: ‘We can win here’: Zack Polanski presses the flesh in Holborn and St Pancras
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Polanski is confident of taking seat vacated by Keir Starmer, but says he will stay on as Green party leader even if he loses

Zack Polanski has said he will remain as Green party leader even if he loses the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a high-stakes contest for the left of British politics.

Speaking to the Guardian while door knocking in the north London constituency, Polanski calls the Greens underdogs in the race but says he is confident he could beat Labour, which won the seat with a majority of more than 11,000 at the 2024 general election. The seat has been vacated by Keir Starmer, who announced last Tuesday he was leaving parliament having resigned as prime minister in June.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The Greens are confident about their chances, with party activists having already “knocked on thousands of doors”, according to Polanski, but the race comes as the party has fallen in the polls. There have been murmurs that it might have reached its peak in dying days of Starmer’s premiership, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.

Polanski is not yet formally the Green’s candidate for Holborn and St Pancras but local members are likely to select him. The race will test the electoral heft of his eco-populist party and Andy Burnham’s Labour. The byelection will be Labour’s first electoral challenge since Burnham became prime minister six weeks ago.

Some critics saw Starmer’s decision to announce his intention to leave Westminster on Burnham’s first day in the Commons as prime minister as a way to twist the knife against his successor on his way out of parliament.

Polanski joined volunteers in King’s Cross over the weekend to speak to local voters. It was his fourth visit to the constituency in a week. Should he win, Polanski says he will not move to the area but cycle from his flat in Hackney. “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.”

Some political commentators have said the seat is a difficult one for the Greens to win and that his run is a high-risk proposition. “I think it’s nonsense,” Polanski says. “I think people are trying to up the stakes because they want some drama.” Nigel Farage ran for election eight times before he won, Polanski says. If he does fall short of winning, he says he definitely stay on as Green leader.

Polanski appeared popular while canvassing. Members of the public stopped him several times between knocking doors to express enthusiastic support for him. At one point, an eager procession of young men who say they have seen Polanski on TikTok gather around him before shaking his hand one by one, making off to the side in an orderly fashion once done. “I feel like the Queen!” the Green leader says.

Starmer won the seat with a 11,572 majority in 2024. The anti-apartheid activist Andrew Feinstein, who is on the left, came second with 7,312 votes and the Greens were third with 4,030. Even if the vote for Feinstein, who will not run this time and has endorsed Polanski, and the Greens was tallied up, the party would be more than 7,500 votes shy of unseating Labour based on the general election figures. Despite this, Polanski still fancies his chances. “We know we can win here,” he says.

It was slow going on the doorstep at first and not many people answered, but things soon picked up. The first woman who answers the door via her buzzer is a big fan. She has arthritis and is unable to come downstairs but she tells Polanski she loves him. “This is a great response. Thank you. I love you too,” he shouts into the buzzer.

Shortly after, Usman Ayyub stops Polanski in the street and shakes his hand. “He is standing on his principles,” says the 27-year-old section manager, who plans to vote for him. He is unimpressed by Labour, who he says has “completely lost the plot”.

“They don’t know what they’re doing,” Ayyub says. “Sometimes they’re falling towards the far right, sometimes they say they’re for the left or the centre. They are not standing for anything.”

After another door knock, a man who claims he worked with Polanski at an adventure summer camp in 2002 stops him. “I saw you on TV and said: ‘That’s Zack!’. Very well done,” he says.

Polanski says he has spoken to Labour voters who are considering a switch to the Greens. “It’s a very easy conversation to have with people. Even if you support Labour or you want to give Andy Burnham a chance, voting Green in this election still makes sense because it’ll make him be a better Labour prime minister,” he says.

after newsletter promotion

“We’ll make sure that we keep pushing him left rather than listening to Nigel Farage. That argument has been resonating with people.”

Pointing at Scala, a famed nightclub in the constituency, Polanski says he worked the door there years ago. He also says his barber is in the constituency. “I come here every week,” he adds.

Some sources in the party have expressed frustration about Polanski’s social media use, with one saying he is “terminally online”. When asked about that, Polanski says: “I think people really appreciate the fact that I’m accessible. With other politicians you get corporate politicians where every single part of their life is micromanaged.

“Every sentence that comes out of their mouth is focus-grouped and I think people absolutely see it as more of a benefit that they know I’m genuine and authentic.”

The issues of housing, the NHS and local crime come up on the doorstep. Burnham has spoken at length about the north-south divide, but Polanski believes there is stark poverty in London and the constituency he is vying for.

“Regional inequality exists so it is important that we talk about supporting all communities,” he says. “It’s also true though that there’s a sense that London is wealthy, but actually somewhere like Holborn and St Pancras has deep poverty and deprivation and often it lives side by side with huge pockets of wealth.”

As the clock passes 11am, Polanski buzzes on a door across from King’s Cross station as people rush pass with suitcases, hoping to catch their trains. Instead of saying “Hi, this is Zack from the Green party” as he normally would, he has begun using his full name, even though it feels “odd”. It appears to work. The man over the buzzer can’t believe it. “Is this Zack Polanski, seriously?” he says.

“Yes, it’s Zack Polanski seriously,” he hears back.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Polanski is confident of taking Holborn and St Pancras seat in north London. He says he will stay on as Green party leader even if he loses the seat. The seat has been vacated by Keir Starmer, who announced last Tuesday he was leaving parliament.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future

Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double in rush for support

G
eorgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.

Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).

The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.

“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.

Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.

“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”

The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.

But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.

“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”

Simon Essex, the executive head of Thomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.

“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.

“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: G eorgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents 'don't need to fight' for support. Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see secrets of its success.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Helena Horton and Aamna Mohdin
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right

The bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action.

Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

At the weekend, the former home secretary James Cleverly was seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate.

“I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even though London is a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.”

Also standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.”

But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment. A recent poll by Savanta UK for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, put Labour’s candidate in the mayoral race on 33%, the Tories 18%, Reform UK 18%, Green party 17% and Liberal Democrats 9%,.

The Conservatives’ bid to unseat Khan is complicated by the presence of Reform. Laila Cunningham, a former Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, is Reform’s candidate. She has been pounding the streets of London since the beginning of this year trying to drum up support.

“I’m not stepping aside for the Tories,” she told the Guardian. “How many times have they tried to unseat Khan? They have failed.”

Cleverly, she says, is “literally the establishment and he’s gone from one ministerial job from another”. She thinks he will be picked as the Tory mayoral candidate and said: “It will be two Sirs versus a woman. Sir Khan and Sir Cleverly.”

Though the rightwing vote looks evenly divided between Tories and Reform, she is confident she can charm some of Khan’s voters: “It is not a left or right divide either, we won nine seats in Barking and Dagenham in the local elections, where the Tories wouldn’t dream of winning one.”

Cunningham, the daughter of Egyptian immigrants, said she was “not your typical Reform person. People often see me and say they are surprised I am in Reform.”

Akinbusoye is on the licensing committee of Westminster council, which is consulting to restrict “vertical drinking” in pubs – standing and drinking. Cunningham said: “That says it all. The fact they even call it vertical drinking is a joke.”

The Labour MP Dawn Butler hinted at her intention to run this week: a video of herself walking past a sign reading “a new Dawn for London”, captioned: “When London puts up signs saying ‘A New Dawn’ … what else was I supposed to do?”

She first floated her mayoral ambitions in 2023, and has since confirmed to the Guardian that she would run as soon as Khan confirmed he would not seek a fourth term. Khan did not respond to a request for comment.

There are no obvious contenders in sight for the Greens, with the party’s attention focused on its leader Zack Polanksi’s plan to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. A Green party source said: “We do have a number of people who’d be incredible candidates but no firm name. We feel confident after our latest local election results that Londoners will be excited by our vision for London.”

Would Cunningham rather fight Butler or Khan? “[Khan’s] got incumbency. He may do better. It doesn’t make a difference because it’s what the party represents, she seems to think he was a great mayor so she seemingly wants more of the same.”

This article was amended on 6 September 2026. If Sadiq Khan ran in the next election, he would be seeking his fourth term, not his third as an earlier version said.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.title: ‘Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter?’: family seeks answers after care home heatstroke death
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text:
Thousands died because of this summer’s extreme hot weather – caused by the climate crisis. Anita Bazell, taken to hospital during June’s heatwave with a body temperature of 41.2C, was one of them

Anita Bazell had never coped with the heat very well, her family said. So they were worried about her when temperatures across the UK soared to record highs of 35C (95F) in May, and then again in June.

She was living in a nursing home in Southampton near her family, who had struggled to care for her at home due to her declining mobility. Although there were air conditioning units in the communal rooms, there was not one in Anita’s room, which was on the third floor.

“I used to see her every weekend. Heat rises and she was on the top floor, and the windows were open as far as the restrictors would let them go,” said her son, Steve Bazell. “It was hot in there. It was so hot you couldn’t sleep at night around here back then.”

The first phone call came on 25 June – Steve was told his mother was feeling unwell and she was being taken to bed. “I remember it because it was the hottest day on record [for June] that day,” Steve said. It was actually the second of three days that week when the temperature record for June was broken.

The next phone call, just after 9am the following day, was a shock. Paramedics called to say his mother had been found unresponsive and was being taken to Southampton general hospital. The family were urged to get there as soon as possible – medics were not sure she would make it to the hospital.

When they arrived, Anita’s face looked drooped on one side and they thought she had suffered a stroke. Doctors were putting towels soaked in ice water on her, replacing them every few minutes. The family were soon told she had been diagnosed with heatstroke, which had caused a bleed on the brain.

When she arrived in hospital, she had a body temperature of 41.2C – anything above 40C is considered a medical emergency.

“You could see her improving as she was getting cooler but she was still unresponsive,” he said. “We had mixed reactions. I mean, my mum was 88, but she was mentally fine. We couldn’t understand how this had happened – did they check on her?”

Anita was hospitalised on 26 June, which was then the hottest June day on record in the UK with 38C recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk, breaking the previous record of 35.6 degrees set in Southampton 50 years earlier. It was the fifth hottest day in the UK ever.

Steve was told Anita was one of at least seven elderly people taken to Southampton general hospital with heatstroke that day, and some did not make it there before they died.

The day before Anita’s admission, University hospital Southampton NHS foundation trust had declared a critical incident due to the extreme heat, which forced some operations and appointments to be cancelled.

David Higgs, the hospital’s deputy chief medical officer, later said Southampton general came “very close to collapse” during the June heatwave, which was “in many ways almost worse than Covid”.

“There was a huge amount of attendances in our emergency department. Primary care was overflooded. The ambulance service pretty much collapsed,” he told the city’s health and wellbeing board.

Steve said the hospital set up a special “cooling” ward specifically to deal with the influx of patients with heatstroke. Staff ran out of towels to soak in ice water to cool patients down, and resorted to cutting up bed sheets. “I remember I went upstairs to get more towels and help,” said Steve. “The hospital was really good. But they were stretched.”

Anita’s condition improved once her body temperature reduced, but ultimately there was nothing that could be done to save her. Over the next few days, Steve said her eyes would follow family members as they moved around her, and she could gently squeeze a hand when asked, but never regained full consciousness.

Steve and his sister took it in turns maintaining a bedside vigil every day until at least 10pm at night. He said they were a small but close family, and his mother devoted much of her life to supporting them.

As the siblings were growing up, Anita worked as a dinner lady and in their school library, volunteered as a Cub scout leader and supported them in their hobbies of motorbike racing and horse riding. She was married to her late husband, Les, for more than 50 years.

Anita died on 6 July with heatstroke recorded as her cause of death.

She is one of thousands of people believed to have died a heat-related death during the extreme hot weather this year. There were an estimated 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during the May and June heatwaves, nearly double the 1,504 excess deaths recorded for the entire summer of 2025.

With four more heatwaves recorded across July and August, heat-related deaths this summer are expected to be the highest on record.

On 24 June, the Met Office issued a rare red heat weather warning due to the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and predicted increased mortality and hospital admissions due to heat-related illness.

Some deaths may be linked to exertional heatstroke, caused by heavy physical exercise. Sophie Goodyer-Bird, a 35-year-old woman from Birmingham, died of heatstroke after climbing Yr Wyddfa – also known as Snowdon – on 10 July.

But most of the fatalities will be among the elderly population, although heatstroke is rarely recorded on death certificates as extreme heat often acts as an indirect trigger, placing severe strain on pre-existing health conditions that can be fatal.

Care homes for elderly people are on the frontline of dealing with this – during the July 2022 heatwave, nursing home deaths increased by 34.1% and residential care home deaths increased by 13.0%.

This year, many care homes reported using fans, air conditioners, paddling pools, ice lollies and cold fruit to keep residents cool. But research has found many are still underprepared for severe heat caused by the climate crisis.

The Care Quality Commission is investigating a care home in Watford after four residents were taken to hospital during the May heatwave, with one dying and the others “coming to harm”. An inspection report said there were concerns residents were left “at risk of dehydration”.

Anita’s family has written to her nursing home – which they have chosen not to name until investigations are complete – as they have concerns about the care she received in the hours before she collapsed.

After her death they were given the clothes she was wearing when she was brought into hospital, which Steve described as “a short-sleeve woolly jumper and wool trousers”. He said: “Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter? And how long had she been wearing them for?”

Steve said he wanted to raise awareness of the risks of heatstroke, particularly among elderly people in care homes, with more extreme heat on its way next year.

“They’re already saying it’s going to be hotter next year,” he said. “What my mum went through, what we went through as a family, it’s really not a very pleasant experience. I’m not saying it wouldn’t have happened anyway, but I do want to know if anything could have been done differently.”

She is one of at least seven elderly people taken to Southampton general hospital with heatstroke. Sophie Goodyer-Bird, 35, died of heatstroke after climbing Yr Wyddfa – also known as Snowdon

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘Catastrophic’ fears: health staff made lists of concerning cases days after Australia’s aged care funding tool launch
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Melissa Davey Medical editor
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Exclusive: Documents reveal assessors’ grave fears if client needs are underestimated by tool that can’t be overridden

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

State health officials were so alarmed by a controversial federal government aged-care funding tool that they kept a log of hundreds of cases where vulnerable older Australians were severely under-assessed.

It also led to one senior state health official writing to the federal government to warn of “catastrophic” outcomes from its algorithmic tool – used to determine support levels for in-home care – and that her staff were “fielding calls from distraught clients and assessors”.

Documents obtained by Guardian Australia under freedom of information laws show officials from four states and the Northern Territory recorded systemic errors that had occurred since the federal government rolled out the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) last November.

The IAT includes a questionnaire completed by aged care assessors from state and territory health departments. The information is then analysed by an algorithm which determines the level of funding a person receives for support at home packages, as well as their urgency of need.

The documents reveal the algorithm was designed by federal health and ageing staff, led by four assistant secretaries overseeing five departmental data scientists, a principal cost modeller and a director.

Days before the IAT was rolled out, the department barred the IAT’s decisions from being overridden by assessors.

Within days of launch, people were being under-assessed by the algorithm, the documents released by the federal department of health and ageing reveal.

Assessors reported feeling powerless and ethically challenged while clients were left at risk of deteriorating, remaining in hospital, or being forced into aged care, the documents show.

The director general of WA Health, Dr Shirley Bowen, became so concerned that she emailed her federal counterpart with a warning.

“Without a pathway for discretion, a small but vulnerable group of older people might experience catastrophic outcomes while waiting for algorithmically determined access to services,” she wrote on 24 November.

“This also creates risks of further discharge delay, blocking access to acute care for others who need it.”

The documents released to Guardian Australia show departments around the country also emailed their concerns within days and weeks of the tool’s rollout.

In a 7 November email, a staff member with Aged Care Assessment Victoria wrote to the federal health department about feedback it was receiving about “concerning outcomes from the IAT algorithm and the assessors not being able to override the outcome”.

“The assessors are feeling conflicted as they do not agree that the IAT algorithm outcome reflects the clients’ needs,” the email said, providing a list of examples.

On 13 November, less than two weeks after the algorithm was introduced, a representative from NT Health emailed the federal government about “concerns regarding the algorithm and erosion of clinical judgement within the new assessment system”.

“Attached are some examples of clinical assessments conducted in the past week that have resulted in unexpected outcomes,” wrote the NT Health planning system staffer.

“Assessors and delegates are feeling very disheartened that they are no longer able to use their clinical judgement and years of clinical experience to over-ride the IAT recommendations, to achieve optimal consumer outcomes.

“These outcomes have required many difficult conversations with consumers, families, and providers … this combined with the lack of respite in the NT is likely to lead to increased carer stress and increased hospital admissions.”

The email said the algorithm was particularly failing those with “good” physical abilities but have “significant cognitive impairment”.

A day later, WA Health’s strategy and governance department also emailed spreadsheets of issues and complaints about the algorithm to the federal government. It sent a second email – marked with high importance – on 20 November that outlined “numerous concerns across most of our outlets regarding … inappropriate SAH (support at home) classifications”.

“Approving classifications and assessment outcomes that they [aged care assessors] do not agree with does not align with their professional ethics and they are concerned this has possible legal impacts,” the email said.

The WA Health official said there needed to be a way to quickly escalate errors or override decisions. “Keen for any quick advice you can provide on this to avoid negative impacts on older people,” the email said. “Staff attrition is a very real issue for us at the moment.”

In Queensland, a state health staffer sent a spreadsheet listing more than 100 examples of “unexpected IAT outcomes” to the federal government on 18 November.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

In all but a few cases, the algorithm had under-assessed the person’s needs, the member of Queensland Health’s policy and planning division said in the email, and they will “continue to collect examples over the coming months”.

Within a week, a similar spreadsheet was sent by NT Health, while a representative from the Northern NSW health district separately raised a number of issues with the IAT and asked for legislation to be changed to allow for assessors to override wrong algorithm decisions.

In her 24 November email, Bowen, who heads WA Health, said older people who needed commonwealth-funded home support in order to be discharged from hospital previously received an urgent funding package within four weeks.

Hospital staff would arrange discharge to short-term rehabilitation or other services in the interim, she said in the email.

“These same clients are now classified as ‘medium’ priority, with an estimated 8-9 month wait time until support at home services commence. Our hospital teams are at a loss as to how to manage discharge in such circumstances,” she wrote in the email.

On 12 March, NSW Health sent a spreadsheet titled ‘Misaligned IAT outcomes’, recording more than 50 cases where state-employed clinicians found the algorithm’s funding determination failed to match a person’s needs.

Asked to comment on the logs of inadequate assessments and concerns revealed by the documents, a department of health spokesperson said: “We’ve listened to people’s experience of the system, and we’ll deliver a practical, responsible safety net that supports the older people whose circumstances don’t fit neatly into a tool”.

“… the government will legislate a new assessment escalation pathway to ensure decisions can be reviewed and changed when necessary,” the spokesperson said.

The government has stopped short of returning human oversight and the ability for assessors to immediately correct wrong algorithm decisions, despite growing calls from clinicians, advocacy groups and politicians. Instead, the aged care minister, Sam Rae, said in July assessors would have the option to escalate cases to a system governor.

This differs from the existing, lengthy review process, as assessors will be able to escalate cases rather than relying on the older person to start the process. It remains unclear how long the new escalation and review process will take.

The documents released to Guardian Australia separately show a number of aged care advocacy organisations – including Ageing Australia, the Older Persons Advocacy Network (Opan), and Dementia Australia – also sent detailed examples of the algorithm’s failures to the federal government soon after it was launched.

“Delays in assessment, algorithmic misclassification, and inaccessible review processes create a cycle in which urgent needs are not recognised, carers are pushed to exhaustion, older people deteriorate without support, preventable hospitalisations and premature residential aged care entry increase, [and] some individuals die before receiving any assistance,” Opan wrote to senior department staff.

In December, a staff member of Dementia Australia wrote to the department to say the organisation was “very concerned” by feedback about the IAT. The organisation said support services were telling people with dementia not to bother asking for an IAT assessment “as they have seen a number of people with dementia receiving less or no support … even if their care needs are increasing”.

In response, a staff member from the department wrote the algorithm had been designed to consistently determine an older person’s home support classification.

“This approach ensures that people with similar characteristics and functional needs receive the same level of funding to support their aged care needs,” the response said.

Guardian Australia previously revealed the experts consulted to develop the IAT questionnaire were not told the tool would be underpinned by an algorithm being developed internally by the government.

Do you know more? melissa.davey@theguardian.com

It recorded more than 50 cases where state-employed clinicians found the algorithm’s funding determination failed to match a person’'s needs.
