Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs

Devi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies. Such measures can help identify health risks earlier. However, I would take issue with her suggestion that a “health MOT” is “precisely what prevention is all about” (Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see, 2 September).

Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.

In England, people living in the most disadvantaged communities can expect about 19 fewer years of healthy life than those in the least disadvantaged communities. Free testing is welcome, but a genuinely upstream approach would focus not only on identifying risk, but also on tackling the social and economic conditions that make healthy choices possible in the first place.Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

Prof Devi Sridhar is right to emphasise prevention and the importance of identifying cardiovascular risk early. However, screening is only the first step. As a GP in London, I worry that suggesting annual “health MOTs” risks creating expectations that the NHS currently lacks the capacity to meet. Without substantial investment in general practice and community services, what happens after we identify millions more people with pre-diabetes, obesity, mildly raised cholesterol or borderline hypertension?

These patients will understandably seek advice, support and follow-up from their GP. Yet many of these conditions are driven less by a lack of diagnosis than by wider societal factors such as diet, inactivity, housing and poverty. They are not problems that can simply be solved with a prescription, or advice.

Articles advocating routine health checks without this context may also encourage patients to request annual MOTs from their GP when these are not clinically indicated or commissioned. At a time when primary care is already under intense pressure, increasing demand without increasing capacity risks diverting resources from those with established illness and greatest need. Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows.Dr James HibberdBarnet, London

I always appreciate Devi Sridhar’s articles for their straightforward and sensible approach to health. However, could I humbly suggest that she reconsiders the inclusion of a press-ups test? For far too many of us, particularly those with the musculature of an anaemic grasshopper, nightmares of the school gymnasium spring to mind, with those familiar and ignominious collapses on to a sweat-speckled floor. Never to be forgotten.Bob ForsterShipton-under-Wychwood, Oxfordshire

I agree with Devi Sridhar that annual screening tests offer the prospect of improving the health of the nation, starting with NHS cholesterol testing for 40- to 84-year-olds. Alas, I’ve just had my 85th birthday, so I’m presumably fit only for the knacker’s yard.Dr Giles YoungsRetired consultant physician, Drinkstone, Suffolk

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: AI transcriptions are no time-saving measure for doctors | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Dr Mary Gibbs says there are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand, as Debbie Cameron can attest

I am an out-of-hours GP, and I am glad to see a news report on this issue, which has been causing me increasing concern at work (Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns, 31 August). There are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand and contradict itself, which can lead to dangers for the patient, but I will concentrate on the supposed “time-saving” aspect.

Many of the patients I see will have been assessed by someone else first on the phone, and I am used to reading through a triage assessment before I call in the patient. My heart sinks when I see that AI has been used – the consultation is invariably long, with duplications, and sometimes contradictions. Often, any history I take turns out to be significantly different from what is listed. So I can never trust that it is correct – I can state with certainty that I find meaningful errors far more often in AI consultations than in those typed out by colleagues.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

You may blame the original clinician, but anyone who has tried to proofread something they have created, particularly under time pressure, will know how difficult this is. So how can this save time, when the first clinician has to check through a long, repetitive account, and the second clinician can’t trust what is written and has to check it again?

In addition, turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn, as any medical student can tell you. If we do not learn and maintain this skill, we will lose a lot, and so will our patients.Dr Mary GibbsManchester

Re the risks of AI diagnosis and medication being mistranscribed, I have first-hand experience of the problems. A consultant I worked for as a secretary had a week’s trial of voice recognition software. He gave up the idea when “I recommend two weeks on lansoprazole” turned into suggesting a two-week holiday on Lanzarote. A prescription I’m sure the patient would have been more than happy to try.Debbie CameronFormby, Merseyside

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Nakedly political’: US attempts to link trans support to authoritarianism in new health department report
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
HHS releases report linking ‘gender ideology’ to political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a report linking “gender ideology” to leftwing authoritarianism and political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted and “nakedly political”, probably leading to greater politicization of science and health.

It follows attempts by the administration to limit access to gender-affirming care – including, on Friday, an agreement reached between the Department of Justice and a New York hospital to no longer offer pediatric gender-affirming care. Dozens of hospitals stopped offering gender-affirming care after the Trump administration began investigating them for offering the standard of care.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Patients on Medicaid and government insurance plans have also been blocked from accessing care, and a proposed rule would block any health system offering gender-affirming care from receiving federal funding.

The new report, which was not published by a scientific journal and did not undergo peer review, takes aim at medical organizations offering guidelines on gender-affirming care. It also links those who say they support trans individuals with supporting authoritarianism and political violence.

“It was a very poorly done piece of research,” said Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, an epidemiologist from the University of Sydney, who highlighted several methodological failings. “It was nakedly political. I think this is probably the most obviously political study that I’ve come across.”

The report is “quite an abnormal document with a number of oddities,” said Daniel Aaron, an associate professor at the University of Utah’s SJ Quinney College of Law.

“It likely also violates federal law because it’s not peer-reviewed, and it’s essentially quite an influential dissemination of information,” which could mean it violates the Information Quality Bulletin, a federal regulation that requires peer review for influential scientific information from the US government, he said.

HHS did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about whether this report was commissioned by the agency and if it violated federal regulations.

Aaron believes the report would not survive peer review and wondered why a political science report was published by HHS.

“It’s actually not even health-related, so I don’t understand why this is related to HHS’s mission,” Aaron said.

Craig Konnoth, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law who co-authored with Aaron a perspective on gender-affirming care policy for the New England Journal of Medicine, agreed. He sees the report as an attempt to undermine mainstream health and science organizations such as the American Psychological Association, American Psychiatric Association, the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, and the American Academy of Pediatrics, all named in the report.

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

“By that standard, any medical recommendation becomes ‘authoritarian’. Any standard set by any licensing board becomes ‘authoritarian’,” Konnoth said. “What we’re seeing is this broadside attack on the scientific establishment more generally, and trans rights are being used as the vehicle to do this.”

Colin Wright, an author of the report and a fellow at the conservative thinktank Manhattan Institute, said he believed the study was published by HHS quickly because a draft had been leaked to the public. He said the researchers were planning to release more information, including the numbers from the survey, and they are planning to submit the study to an unnamed journal for publication.

“It was kind of a surprise to us that it dropped when it did, and so we didn’t have plans beforehand,” Wright said. “We probably could have tightened the language a little bit more.”

Wright disputed that the study was an attempt to link support for trans people and political authoritarianism and violence, though the report itself says: “These findings suggest that gender ideology is associated with LWA [left-wing authoritarianism] and willingness to justify political violence.” Gender ideology was measured by statements such as: “People should be supported in expressing their transgender identity,” and “Parents should support their children’s transgender exploration.”

Wright suggested that the study was about the guidance offered by medical organizations and “in many ways geared to make people sort of have a more extreme reaction to it, and to kind of fuel somewhat authoritarian tendencies of trying to silence people” on gender-affirming care. He argued that the guidelines appear to push people toward ideological extremes.

“Sort of independently, it increased their willingness, at least correlationally, to their support for political violence,” Wright said. “There’s a lot of ideological content to it.”

In an online survey, 1,208 people ranked statements about support for trans people as well as about political ideology and political violence.

The political ideology questionnaire essentially measured whether someone was a Democrat, said Meyerowitz-Katz, who added: “I don’t think anyone would think this is a good measure of authoritarianism.”

One of the statements was about whether opposition to gay marriage is homophobic; another was a statement about whether the focus on terrorism should shift to the far right. “If you were a rational human being who understood the facts, you would agree with that,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. For instance, approximately 75-80% of deaths from terrorist attacks in the United States come from people on the far right, and rightwing attacks are more lethal than leftwing violence.

Similarly, the questions on political violence focused only on political violence against conservative figures or institutions, he said. If they had included political violence against other actors, “you would almost certainly see the opposite correlation,” making the questionnaire an unreliable predictor of whether someone supports political violence, Meyerowitz-Katz said.

It was also difficult to parse these relationships, because the researchers haven’t yet released any numbers from the survey, Meyerowitz-Katz said: “The only thing they report in that paper is correlations.” But they don’t say, for instance, how many respondents supported actions like arson of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) buildings.

“This is very silly,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. “They’re producing what I would describe as pseudoscience … It’s a bad, poorly done report.”

Konnoth, who studies the link between opposition to LGBTQ+ rights and authoritarianism, noted that the report overlooks significant research in the field. “They don’t cite and engage in the data that goes against that thesis,” he said.

Typically, HHS publishes issue briefs and synthesized information, but this was an “extremely weird” case of the HHS appearing to adopt a study as its own report, Aaron said.

The purpose of the report appears to be an attempt to correlate leftwing people, particularly those who support transgender people, with violence, said Meyerowitz-Katz. “The only possible outcome of this survey was to show a correlation between leftwing beliefs and support for transgender people and ‘political violence’, and so I think that was the aim. I don’t see another possible way to interpret this particular piece of research.”

Aaron said it appears to be “aimed to benefit a political group or demonize an opposing group and build political support,” he said. “It kind of builds this fake evidence base for transgender people as a political issue.”

HHS is tasked with protecting the health and wellbeing of all Americans, he said, noting: “It’s not happening here.” Aaron compared the report to recent actions on vaccines that depart from the scientific evidence and reshape the vaccine infrastructure – influencing those who make decisions on vaccines and fueling the anti-vaccine political movement.

“I think we can draw parallels with this consistent anti-science production of information by the federal government,” he said.

Konnoth called it an “attempt to create an alternate scientific narrative” that affects all Americans.

“There’s a targeting of these mainstream fundamental organizations that put out research that doesn’t just involve trans rights, but involves broader claims about science,” he said. “If we buy into their attempt to discredit the medical establishment, then we are in deep trouble … It’s life-and-death for massive swathes of the American population.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Kevin Rawlinson and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Newscaster says rare but treatable condition polycythaemia vera left her feeling like she ‘had her batteries taken out’

The BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has been diagnosed with a rare form of incurable blood cancer, she has revealed.

Doctors told the broadcaster last November she had polycythaemia vera (PV), which cannot be cured but is treatable. The condition, which affects about 8,000 people in the UK, is associated with an increased risk of the blood clots that can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“When I was first told to have blood tests, I wasn’t worried because I didn’t really have any symptoms,” Moshiri said. “I thought: it can’t happen to me. Even after I was told I had PV, I didn’t really understand what it meant. It was a cruel blow to realise that while I could have treatment, this was a cancer that was incurable.”

She described the symptoms, including headaches, blurred vision, fatigue, night sweats and burning pain in the hands and feet. As well as the waves of fatigue that would hit her after days of working in a demanding role, saying it was “like someone had taken your batteries out”.

Moshiri began taking daily aspirin and having regular venesections to reduce her red blood cell count. The procedure involves a needle being put into a vein in the arm to draw blood out.

The treatments worked, she said, but also left her dealing with the exhaustion. “When you do live news you get a rush of adrenaline, but I was doing long days under pressure while dealing with chronic tiredness. Back home, I would zonk out on the sofa for hours to recover. It really made me reflect on the fact that there are so many misconceptions about blood cancer and the fact it’s a ‘silent or hidden’ cancer.

“People think you have chemotherapy and then you are cancer-free, but for many people like me it is a chronic condition. You have to live with it, the treatments and the side-effects around your everyday life, and that’s hard.”

Moshiri switched to Pegasys, a weekly injection, which she said still caused fatigue but had proved effective. She said she was sharing news of her diagnosis to raise awareness for the charity Blood Cancer UK.

PA Media contributed to this report

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: As assisted dying bill returns to Commons, families recall loved ones’ battle to ‘go out on own terms’
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Caroline Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Elise Burns and Keith Williams appeared in campaign filmed by Rankin this year – both were denied their wishes, but their relatives are picking up the baton

The feeling, said Sarah Burns of her sister’s last days, is one of overwhelming guilt.

“You feel really guilty, and helpless,” she says. “Because we knew what she wanted. We really did know. But we couldn’t do anything.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

When time eventually ran out for Elise Burns, a 52-year-old woman who worked in publishing, the circumstances were “absolutely her worst nightmare”. Initially treated for breast cancer and subsequently diagnosed with terminal secondary cancer, which had spread to her liver, lungs and bones, Elise had campaigned passionately for the assisted dying bill, daring the peers who ensured it ran out of time to “look me in the eye”.

As part of the Dignity in Dying campaign, she was one of eight terminally ill people who appealed directly to MPs in powerful videos, filmed by the world renowned British photographer and director Rankin.

She died on 22 July – the second of the eight terminally ill people who featured in the Rankin videos, which were filmed in May, to go. The first, Keith Williams, a 77-year-old former welder who became a social worker, died of lung cancer on 16 June, having also been denied, according to his son, his desperate wish to “go out on my own terms”.

The controversial bill, reintroduced by Lauren Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, returns to the Commons for a second reading on 11 September. Andy Burnham has already said he will not vote to avoid influencing the emotional debate.

Burns will be at the Commons, carrying the baton for her sister, who was from Faversham, and was one of the last people Edwards heard from before reviving Kim Leadbeater’s private member’s bill, bringing it back to parliament after it foundered under the weight of hundreds of amendments by peers in the Lords.

“I would simply like the chance to put a human dying face to what this debate really means for terminally ill people like me,” Elise Burns wrote to Edwards. “For me this is not about politics or ideology, it’s about dignity, compassion and the possibility of having some choice at the end of life.”

After her secondary cancer diagnosis, Elise wanted to “live life to the full” but also started talking seriously about Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic. “She said all along ‘I do not want a painful death’. And literally every day was painful,” said her sister.

In the end, the speed of events deprived her of that choice. At the beginning of July, just two months after shooting her Rankin video, she developed an infection and was hospitalised. Sixteen days later, she was moved to a hospice, dying two days later.

“The hospice was incredible, trying to make her as comfortable as possible, all the time,” said Burns. “But legally there is only so much they can do. They all knew her wishes.”

The family were left feeling utterly helpless.

More than 100 cross-party peers have written to MPs urging them to send the bill back to the House of Lords so that it can complete its passage through parliament.

The signatories, including the former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell, the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson, said the upper house’s failure to pass the legislation in the previous session had let terminally ill people and their families down and blocked a measure which had public support.

They accused a minority of peers who had opposed the backbench bill of filibustering after hundreds of amendments tabled by just seven opponents meant it ran out of time.

They wrote: “As even opponents of the principle of assisted dying in the Lords have acknowledged, the elected chamber has every right to ask us to do this. The overwhelming majority of the public – who vote for you but do not vote for us – expect the same.

“And the many terminally ill people and their families who are depending on parliament to pass this long overdue change to the law should not be asked to wait any longer than absolutely necessary for us to come to a decision.”

Marc Williams, Keith Williams’ son, has written directly to Burnham, describing the circumstances surrounding the death of his father, who was a committed campaigner for the bill.

“Dad could have chosen to fly to Switzerland to end his life, but he would have needed to go in November to ensure that he was still fit enough to be able to travel and to endure the loneliest journey imaginable,” Williams, a civil servant, told the prime minister. For the “dignified death” he sought, his father “would have been forced to end his life prematurely”.

Keith Williams, who was a canoeing instructor from Tonyrefail, the Rhondda, was diagnosed in 2023 with prostate cancer and undergoing radiotherapy, which left him with distressing long-term side effects. Last October, he was diagnosed with lung cancer and pulmonary fibrosis. He died on 16 June.

“Dad had some red lines. He wanted to die at home. He was: ‘I want to go out on my own terms. I am desperate to go out on my own terms at home.’”

He shot the Rankin video in early May. Within days he was in hospital struggling to breathe. On returning home, his wife, who suffers from arthritis, was now physically unable to care for him, “much as she wanted to”, said Williams. He was moved to a hospice and died the following week.

“He wasn’t just in pain,” his son said. “He was suffocating to death. The pain, they could give him medication for, but no one could breathe for him.”

Four days from death, a physiotherapist gave him a pint of water and two straws, telling him to exercise his lungs by blowing through the straws, said Marc. “He was four days away from dying! It was ridiculous.”

“He didn’t want any of that. He was ready a long time before that to say goodbye and have his peace.” His children and grandchildren could do nothing but sit and watch him deteriorate because “there is nothing you can do”.

His father was “chuffed to bits” about the bill being back. “Because he wanted it for us,” said Williams. “Obviously it was too late for him, but that’s what he wanted all along, for other people.”

Additional reporting by Pippa Crerar
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Elise Burns and Keith Williams were denied their wishes by peers in the Lords. They were one of eight terminally ill people who appealed directly to MPs in powerful videos. The controversial bill, reintroduced by Lauren Edwards, returns to the Commons for a second reading on 11 September.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘I felt robbed’: bereaved parents hope for answers from Sussex maternity review
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Donna Ferguson
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Review led by Donna Ockenden launches after campaign by families and media investigation into deaths at NHS trust

Susan Cacciacarro was almost 37 weeks pregnant with her daughter Chiara when she woke up one morning in 2021, unable to feel her baby kicking.

“My belly just didn’t feel right,” she said. “I didn’t feel any movements.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Chiara, her first child, had been diagnosed with a hole in her heart during a 20-week scan. Since then, Cacciacarro’s pregnancy had been classed as high risk and the growth of her baby had been regularly monitored in hospital.

But when a 34-week scan revealed Chiara had lost weight over the previous two weeks, maternity staff at Worthing hospital in Sussex did not make a plan to expedite her birth, which was planned to take place at 39 weeks.

On the day Cacciacarro woke up and realised Chiara was not moving, she rushed to the hospital, which is run by University hospitals Sussex NHS foundation trust.

Staff were unable to find the baby’s heartbeat and Chiara was delivered stillborn. “I’ve never felt so devastated and so crushed,” Cacciacarro said. “Your world turns upside down and suddenly it’s black.”

She is among the bereaved parents who will give evidence at a major independent review into maternity and neonatal services in Sussex, led by the senior midwife Donna Ockenden.

The review launched on Saturday with a public meeting in Brighton after months of campaigning by bereaved Sussex families. In February, a joint investigation between the New Statesman and the BBC revealed the deaths of at least 55 babies might have been avoidable if they and their mothers had received better care from University hospitals Sussex.

Ockenden, an expert on maternity safety, led the landmark review into maternity care at Shrewsbury and Telford and another into maternity services at Nottingham University hospitals NHS trust. She is also chairing a review into maternity and neonatal services at two Leeds hospitals.

At the meeting on Saturday, Ockenden discussed the review’s terms of reference with the families who will be most affected by it. “We need to get the finer details right to make sure that no family is left behind,” said Cacciacarro, who is now a mother of two. “I felt robbed when we lost Chiara … I’m hoping this review will provide answers to all harmed and bereaved families.”

As well as accountability and transparency, she said what was most important to the families was that the review brought about an improvement in the safety of maternity care services. “We definitely don’t want other families to go through this.”

When her appointment was announced, Ockenden said it was an honour to be asked to chair the review, which is expected to investigate more than 1,000 maternity and neonatal cases dating back to 2018.

Sign up to First Edition

after newsletter promotion

“I am absolutely aware of the responsibility I have to the families and babies across Sussex,” she said. “My priority will be to listen carefully to harmed and bereaved families and to engage comprehensively across communities and with staff ‘on the ground’ here in Sussex.

“We will proactively reach out to ensure that the voices of seldom-heard families are heard through this review. It is vital that the scope of the review now reflects the experiences of families and enables a thorough and meaningful examination of care, so that improvements can be made as the review progresses.”

The bereaved campaigners, who are members of the Truth for Our Babies group (TFOB), are urging other affected families to come forward and participate in the review.

Dr Andy Heeps, the chief executive of University hospitals Sussex, said: “Our thoughts remain first and foremost with the families whose babies have died or who have suffered harm when receiving care in our hospitals.

“We welcome Donna Ockenden’s review and remain committed to fully supporting the process so families can get the answers they need, and we take any possible opportunity to learn and improve. Our overriding priority is always to provide the safest possible care for mothers and babies – that is why our maternity teams have implemented many positive changes in recent years, and why we will work with the review team to find new ways of making our services better, and safer, still.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sympathy are with Susan [Cacciacarro] and all women and families who were failed by maternity services in Sussex.

“Through the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, increased investment in maternity safety, and the wider reforms following the previous Ockenden and Amos reviews, we are working to ensure families receive safer, more compassionate and more consistent care in every part of the NHS.”

She was unable to feel her baby kicking and rushed to hospital where she was delivered stillborn.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Almost 75% of A&E staff in UK face violence or aggression daily or weekly
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Survey finds long waiting times and overcrowding have made abuse ‘routine’ part of working on hospital frontline

Nearly three-quarters of A&E staff experience violence or aggression daily or weekly, according to a survey highlighting the “appalling” abuse of NHS workers.

The Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) said understaffed and overcrowded emergency departments were contributing to increased targeting of medics.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In a survey of more than 2,000 workers in the UK, 63% said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia, while 73% said violence or aggression of all kinds was a daily or weekly occurrence. Almost all (96%) said they had experienced abuse from patients or members of the public.

Dr Ian Higginson, the president of the RCEM, said: “No one should go to work fearing or, worse, expecting to be attacked, intimidated or abused. Nor should they lack confidence that their employers have their backs, or that the judicial system will kick in.

“Yet that’s the reality faced by the majority of my colleagues in EDs [emergency departments] across the country. They often do not feel safe to care for patients. It is an appalling state of affairs which is contributing towards many people seriously considering whether emergency medicine – or even healthcare in general – is for them.”

Senior nurses said in January that abuse of NHS staff had become a national crisis.

In the survey, emergency department workers said long waiting times and overcrowding had made violence and aggression a “routine” part of working on the hospital frontline. Staff shortages and corridor care – patients being treated in non-clinical spaces because of overcrowding – were also cited as main reasons behind the abuse.

One anonymous resident doctor said: “Working in the ED, you brace yourself for a lot, but nothing truly prepares you for direct, hateful verbal abuse, especially when it’s racially charged.”

A senior emergency doctor told the survey they had been kicked in the face by an aggressive patient lying on a trolley.

Ministers have pledged to get key waiting times across the NHS back on track before the end of this parliament in 2029. However, the leaders of professional bodies have called for faster action after a series of targets were missed at the end of the financial year in March.

The NHS was told to ensure 78% of A&E patients were treated within four hours by March. While it came close to that target – 77.6% of patients were treated within four hours that month – the proportion has since slipped.

Higginson called on the government to accelerate its drive to reduce waiting times and overcrowding. “Much has been said by us and other organisations over the years about violence and aggression towards healthcare staff. But the problem seems to be getting worse, not better,” he said.

“It’s time for action, time for governments, employers and organisations stand up for NHS staff, and time to ensure that those who intimidate, abuse or assault those who are trying to care for them face meaningful consequences for their actions.”

The worsening conditions in A&E would have “devastating” consequences for the workforce if they continued, the RCEM added.

Only 4% of those surveyed said they always felt safe working in A&E, while 75% reported short-term stress and anxiety, 40% said they had experienced burnout and 28% long-term stress or anxiety.

In January, data obtained by the Guardian revealed that more than 295,000 incidents of physical violence and aggression by patients against staff had been recorded by 212 NHS trusts in England between 2022 and 2025.

Hospitals records showed the number of violent incidents, which ranged from violent threats to attempted and actual assaults, had risen from 91,175 in 2022-23 to 104,079 in 2024-25. This was equivalent to about 285 cases being reported every day in the most recent year.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Any acts of violence, abuse or harassment towards NHS staff are completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated. Everyone working in our national health service has a fundamental right to be safe at work, and it is deeply concerning that so many emergency department staff continue to experience this behaviour.

“That is why this government recently introduced new NHS staff standards, which set out the steps that every NHS employer across the country must take to prevent and reduce violence and abuse against their staff and help ensure they can do their jobs safely.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they are

T
he numbers are now trickling in: nearly 2,900 dead in the UK, at least 35,000 dead across Europe. That’s how many people are believed to have lost their lives in this year’s early-summer heatwaves – the death tolls for the August heatwaves have yet to be counted. In a sense, these people died in a series of natural disasters, similar to the hundreds who died last month after flooding in Nepal, or during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain. And yet we do not process these events the same way. Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe, but they are rarely framed as such.

There are some obvious reasons for this. Heatwaves by definition unfold over longer periods than other disasters, they are less dramatic, the majority of those who die are elderly or otherwise vulnerable, and their deaths often take weeks or months to be catalogued and reported, all of which make heatwaves seem less immediate and visible. But while heatwaves will probably never provoke the same visceral shock as earthquakes or tornadoes, it should still be possible to shift the way the public thinks about them, which could save lives and lessen their damage.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The first and most obvious change is in the way heatwaves are reported on. The tendency to use images of “fun in the sun” should be balanced by serious examination of disrupted transit and the dangers of living in sweltering buildings. Perhaps the immediate fallout could be made more legible: heatwave deaths might be made more granular with personal detail. Ultimately, governments should report the death tolls and other fallout closer to the actual event – recall that during the Covid-19 pandemic the UK government statistics reporting was tweaked to reflect weekly Covid-specific deaths, which the media and public followed with close interest.

More could also be done to make heatwaves feel like a major collective experience, similar to other disasters. Research shows that over time the British public have come to regard heatwaves as a serious problem, one linked to the climate crisis. But at the same time, most people think that they are personally unlikely to suffer any health consequences. Worryingly, work by the British Red Cross showed that a majority of those aged over 75 did not consider themselves vulnerable to extreme heat.

It would help to better communicate the risks and potential adaptation measures to vulnerable people, but equally good would be fostering a sense of community responsibility. Currently, the UK government has an excellent system to warn specific sectors – such as medical and care services – about extreme heat. This messaging should be expanded, and voluntary and local groups should be further encouraged to help people at risk. Again the pandemic gives a model here – the Scottish and Welsh governments in particular fostered a sense that we were all in this together.

At a society-wide level, a pilot project in Seville, Spain, to name specific heatwaves and give them a categorisation system like hurricanes made early warnings more effective, and also provided an important anchor for news coverage. This simple intervention should be considered in the UK. Changing the way we talk about extreme heat seems a minor thing. But if the public can be helped to recognise heatwaves as the major disasters that they are, lives would be saved and people would be convinced that the difficult work of adapting to the climate crisis is urgent and necessary.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: My dad’s determination to choose life despite his cruel illness has taught me gratitude | Nomi Kaltmann
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nomi Kaltmann
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We can’t control what happens to us – only how we react to it. And when we help others we are reminded that we are more than our suffering

Making sense of it is a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday life

M
y dad, Max, is in his early 60s. More than 15 years ago he was diagnosed with early onset Parkinson’s disease. Since then his illness has progressed, affecting his mobility and making ordinary tasks, like walking, increasingly difficult.

My dad is softly spoken and endlessly kind but beneath his gentle exterior is a steely determination. Perhaps this comes from being the son of a sole survivor of the Holocaust. Growing up he was taught that people don’t get to choose the hardships life places before us but we can choose how we react to these challenges.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Parkinson’s is a cruel degenerative disease. It slowly takes many things away: your independence, your confidence in your own body, your ability to work.

My dad has never pretended his disease is easy. There are days when his body simply refuses to cooperate. Yet when he was diagnosed, he made the decision to not let grief and anger consume him nor let Parkinson’s disease become the defining story of his life.

There is a Yiddish expression that he lives by: Tracht gut, vet zein gut – Think good, and it will be good.

This expression does not mean that optimism changes what happens to us. Rather, it means that with hope and positive thinking we can change how we experience what happens to us and how we respond to it.

My dad is a man of deep faith and believes that nothing in this world is random. He has taught me that every person, regardless of circumstance, still has something good and worthwhile to contribute to the world and the people around them.

Modern psychology has found that one of the most reliable ways a person experiencing illness or adversity can restore a sense of agency is by performing acts of service. When we help another person, we are reminded that we are more than our suffering.

In 2018 my dad set up a charity that established one of Australia’s first non-contact boxing programs for people living with Parkinson’s disease. Twice a week, dozens of men and women gather at a local gym where they punch pads, practise their gait, laugh together and cheer each other on.

On the surface, it looks like a regular exercise class but I know that it is so much more than that. It is a community built around the conviction that even when our bodies become weaker, our capacity to strengthen another person’s spirit does not diminish.

For the duration of the classes, no one is sick or feeling sorry for themselves. They are all fighters who support one another through their difficult neurological illness.

One of my favourite verses in the Torah encapsulates the dogged determination that my dad exemplifies: “I have set before you life and death, a blessing and a curse. Therefore, choose life.”

As humans, we do not choose so many of the things that shape our lives. We do not choose illness or grief or disappointment.

But choosing life is not about choosing our circumstances. It is about choosing our response to them. We choose life when we refuse to surrender to bitterness. We choose life when we build community instead of retreating into isolation. We choose life when we use whatever strength we still possess to make someone else’s burden a little lighter.

Watching my dad has made me grateful for many things that some may take for granted. I am grateful for my legs that carry me where I need to go, I am grateful for the ability to work a day job, even though sometimes work is tiring. I am grateful to be a present mum who can hug my children, run after them in the park and sit with them on the floor and read them books. I know that having a body that works properly is a huge blessing.

More than anything, my dad has taught me that life is not defined only by what happens to us. It is defined by the choices we make in response.

Parkinson’s disease has taken things from my dad but it never took away his kindness, his faith and his desire to help those around him.

Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish community

His son Nomi Kaltmann is a lawyer and journalist from Melbourne. She is proud of her dad's determination to help others around him.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Let your mind wander, don’t retire and stop worrying: surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Guardian staff speak to Dr Norman Swan
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
In his new book The Brain Cliff, Dr Norman Swan outlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive decline

You write that instead of fearing cognitive decline, “changing the way you think about the brain cliff can literally change the way you think and remember”. How?

Dr Norman Swan: There are three things you need to know which are not widely known.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Think cognitive change not cognitive decline: one way people think about our cognitive function is by comparing it to what it was like when we were in our 20s and it’s not a valid comparison. It leads to an assumption that we’ve declined into deficit. That’s not actually what’s happened, especially when we’re in midlife (40s and 50s). Our brains have changed, not deteriorated. Focusing on what that “change” looks like can make the task of maintaining cognitive function and perhaps even improving it, much clearer. Sure, our fluid intelligence – which is about speed and problem-solving – peaks in our 20s, but unless you’re a maths whiz or a gun lab researcher, that is less important than what’s called your crystallised intelligence, which can actually improve with age. It’s the wisdom of knowledge and experience.

Secondly, as the years pass, our thoughts move address.

This is about a phenomenon in the brain called scaffolding. To protect our cognitive abilities and perhaps even enhance them as the years pass, our brains build out networks of nerves which act pretty much like the scaffolding inside a skyscraper. It’s the infrastructure around which the brain works. The more successfully we scaffold, the further away we push the brain cliff. This scaffolding initially moves across the brain then into the frontal lobes – the all-important prefrontal cortex which brings our thoughts and memories together and is involved with judgment, decision-making and emotional control.

The third idea is that we should do as much as possible to encourage the scaffolding and as little as possible to get in its way.

For The Brain Cliff I interviewed seven cognitive super-agers, who are as different as you could imagine – from the illiterate 95-year-old shoemaker to the woman who taught Mick Jagger statistics and the 94-year-old woman who still works in McDonald’s in Kyushu, Japan. But underneath, they’re remarkably similar and they’re all protecting their scaffolding in several ways. One example is how they respond to stress. They get over it. They problem-solve. They don’t ruminate. And where do you think we ruminate? Yes, in our prefrontal cortex. So you’re occupying valuable brain space for cognitive function with unproductive circular thoughts. As we move through life, the prefrontal cortex becomes more and more important and anything that distracts or damages it potentially brings the brain cliff closer. Depression affects the prefrontal cortex. Alcohol does too.

You mention that the time to start helping our brains adapt is in our 40s and 50s. What should you be doing at that age and is it ever too late to start?

It’s never too late to start.

Exercise enhances our brain plasticity, which in turn encourages brain scaffolding. An anti-inflammatory diet – with low amounts of red meat, high diversity of vegetables including leafy greens, fermented foods such as yoghurt and fruits such as berries – can change the microbiome and aid direct absorption of bioactive compounds, both of which support brain scaffolding.

What’s also thought to be part of scaffold building is what’s called the default mode network – what our brain gets up to when it’s supposedly at rest. When the default mode network fires up, parts of the brain that don’t normally talk to each other make connections. How do you know if your default network is at work? Your mind wanders. Mind wandering looks as though it’s good for your brain.

An associated activity is mental time travel: reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future. When you’re in midlife you’re in a good place when it comes to mental time travel. When you’re young, there’s not much past; when you’re much older, the past tends to dominate. Mental time travel and mind wandering seem to encourage our scaffolding.

What was the thing about cognitive super-agers which most surprised you, having interviewed so many of them?

One of the important findings from research has been that genes don’t play a large role in whether we’re on a journey to the brain cliff or when we might reach it. That means the environment and how we live matter hugely and that’s what the cognitive super-agers I interviewed illustrated.

There was only one of them where you could convince yourself that his family history mattered, and even he – a neuropsychiatrist from New Jersey aged 100 – was doing the things that maintain your brain. He had learned a new skill – pencil drawing – and through the classes had made new friends and was well connected with other people beyond his family.

What have you changed in your own life or daily habits since going on this deep dive into cognitive decline?

I’ve become much more aware of when I might be ruminating and how I respond to stress. I work hard at problem solving and “getting over it”. I’ve really cut back my alcohol intake – not that it was ever high. I’m much more assiduous about my coronary risk factors like cholesterol and blood pressure. Leafy greens, berries and yoghurt are more prominent in my diet, and moderate to vigorous exercise is not an optional extra in my life. Oh … and I’ve no intention of retiring. Retirement is bad for your brain. So the ABC will have to sack me.

You say that rumination and stress may accelerate cognitive change. How, and how can people best try to counteract this?

For some people these are disabling and it’s hard to change by yourself. There are variations on cognitive behavioural therapy which can help in the hands of a well-trained clinical psychologist.

You have a chapter titled “Don’t Retire”. Should we all be working until we drop?

Work is mostly good for our brains. The evidence is strong that cognitive decline speeds up after retirement. Now some people with hard physical jobs simply can’t keep them up. The point here is what retirement means. If you move from your job to other work such as volunteering, new leisure activities, learning new and complex skills, then that’s actually not retirement. You’re still at work. Retirement to the couch and Netflix is a bad idea.

The Brain Cliff by Dr Norman Swan (A$34.99, Hachette Australia), is out 8 September

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Our US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff …

I
’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) are calling us Europeans, mocking us for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.

GB news presenter Tom Harwood declared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

There are massive, obvious caveats. GDP is a wholly inadequate proxy for quality of life or even prosperity: the UN’s proposed alternative dashboard of 31 indicators  includes the likes of “respect for the planet” and wealth inequalities, against which the US would surely take a beating. US mortality rates are higher than European ones and life expectancy is lower, so, when a medical diagnosis or accident could bankrupt you, how rich do you really feel?

But, actually, this Europoor stuff is hitting me where it hurts: my New York-based grad student son out-earns me, and his junior nurse girlfriend is paid six figures – that’s more than I made in a city law firm. Quite right – nurses should earn more than corporate lawyers – but it’s hard to imagine them ever choosing to live here in the UK (an NHS nurse’s starting salary is £32,073).

To console myself as I contemplate years of getting even Europoorer, flying long-haul to hug my son, I’ve been counting the ways we’re Eurorich. Sure, healthcare, social protections, holidays, blah blah – but what about the really important stuff?

Cheese“The United States offers over 1,000+ cheese varieties and styles,” the Cheese from the USA website claims, to which I would counter: “But do any of them taste of anything?” I doubt a single Freedom Cheese can clear a train carriage like a ripe époisses.

BikesApparently, Americans buy 130m bicycles a year, but I suspect that’s thanks to a handful of legmaxxing California billionaires. Anyway, 130m also feels like the number of bikes parked outside Amsterdam Centraal station on any given day (in 2019, 41% of Netherlanders said the bike was their main mode of transport).

SaintsThe US has 11 saints – pathetic. I’ve seen the remains of more than 11 saints in a single European mini-break; Ireland alone has an estimated 1,000.

Wholesome foodLet’s take stock of this summer’s US food safety scares. Lettuce, blueberries, jalapenos, fruit bars, granola, eggs, alfalfa sprouts, mangoes, sourdough, tofu … basically anything healthier than Flamin’ Hot Cheetos is a gamble; Gwyneth Paltrow is probably claiming asylum in Puglia as I write.

Weird rulersSure, they have their stable genius, but nothing can match absolute monarchy and centuries of inbreeding for floridly unhinged leadership. Charles VI of France thought he was made of glass; the future Peter III of Russia court-martialled a rat for eating one of his toy soldiers.

Characterful teethThe US has, I read, “entered the age of veneer regret”, with people rueing their decision to drop big money on massive, gleaming, Hollywood teeth. Not over here! We’ve still got teeth Breugel the Elder would recognise (in the UK it’s partly because we can’t access affordable dentistry, but sssh).

Disturbing folkloreScratch the surface of any European country and some weird, sinister custom emerges. At Belgium’s Matî l’Ohê festival they mourn a bone by waving celery; Austria’s demon-chasing Perchten festival involves dressing like a horned haystack; in Wales’s Mari Lwyd, people take a horse skull on a pole from door to door singing for midwinter. In the name of carnival, we throw herring in northern France, execute a pretend mare in Czechia and hunt people dressed as bears all over the place. And really, what’s better – purchasing power or an annual opportunity to wave celery at a bone? I know my answer.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Students are suffering from US colleges’ shaky finances. Trump policies are making everything worse
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Marina Villeneuve in Lynchburg, Virginia
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Many four-year colleges will resort to laying off faculty, cutting services and increasing prices amid financial stress

Nalia Mutz started her freshman year at the University of Lynchburg in 2022 knowing exactly where she wanted to be four years later: right on track toward her dream of becoming a doctor.

When the university eliminated a dozen majors in 2024, the resulting layoffs left fewer professors to teach the science courses she needed to graduate. She began to fear earning her biomedicine degree the way she had planned could take two extra years.

“It was just a lot of cuts all around, and then they just didn’t have enough staff,” Mutz, 21, said.

Higher education has faced fiscal headwinds in recent years as hundreds of institutions grapple with declining enrollment because of demographic trends and growing public skepticism about the value of a college degree. Trump policies targeting international students and cutting federal research funding made the financial situation more dire, as have new caps to graduate student loan borrowing and threats to block undergraduate programs from accepting federal financial aid unless alumni earn more than a typical high school graduate.

As colleges tighten their belts, millions of students like Mutz feel the consequences. Small, private non-profit institutions that rely heavily on tuition – like the University of Lynchburg – are likely to be hit hardest.

While just a small fraction of colleges will end up closing, those that survive may resort to cutting programs and staff, a move that could balance the books but leave students adrift. Experts and students themselves say it is time to pay more attention to the impact of college downsizing.

“The academic literature draws a straight line from student-faculty ratios and advising supports to what that means for students’ likelihood to persist and complete their college degree,” said Justin Ortagus, professor of higher education and public policy at the University of Texas at Austin. “It has a real impact on their ability to graduate.”

A new interactive tool from the Hechinger Report, the College Financial Health Tracker, allows users to research whether a particular college is showing financial warning signs: dropping enrollment, declining revenue, growing deficits and shrinking endowments. The tracker also includes data on faculty layoffs and cuts to academic programs, as well as accreditation decisions.

Hundreds of four-year colleges and universities show clear signs of financial stress, according to Hechinger’s analysis of a decade of federal higher education data for colleges primarily granting bachelor’s degrees.

Roughly 1,100 out of the 1,900 colleges in our dataset experienced enrollment drops in three of the five years from 2019 to 2024, the most recent year for which data is available. About 6.4 million students attended these schools.

About 1,500 colleges saw net revenue from tuition drop from 2019 to 2024.

Roughly 960 institutions, enrolling 5.2 million students, had 75,600 fewer instructional staff in that period.

Nearly 440 colleges and universities reported ending the financial year in the red in three of those five years.

It can be hard for students and families to figure out how a college is doing financially. Small colleges tend to provide limited information about their finances in annual public reports. And unlike public institutions, private non-profits are exempt from public records laws.

Yet the tough choices colleges make to stay afloat directly affect students. Meal plan costs can go up. Library hours may decrease. Staff might not have the time to handle complaints about dorm conditions. Cuts to academic advising staff can increase caseloads, which research links to worse graduation rates.

Faculty make up the largest – and an increasing – portion of college job cuts, federal data shows. Hechinger’s analysis found private non-profit institutions that cut instructional staff tended to do so at a faster rate than their enrollments fell, leading to worse faculty-to-student ratios. Layoffs can mean fewer professors to teach classes, making it harder to graduate on time or in a chosen major. Buyouts can mean fewer classes taught by the most experienced faculty.

And replacing tenured professors with instructors who have fewer job protections could limit academic freedom and hurt the student learning experience, said Tim Gibson, president of the Virginia conference of the American Association of University Professors, which filed a complaint in February 2025 protesting against cuts at the University of Lynchburg.

“Faculty in those positions tend to be very afraid of speaking out on matters of curriculum or governance issues, or pushing back,” said Gibson, an associate professor of communication at George Mason University.

Scores of schools that Hechinger’s analysis flagged with warning signs have cut staff and campus amenities to balance their budgets.

At the University of New Hampshire, officials closed the dining hall on weekends, shut campus pharmacies, raised tuition and laid off dozens of professors and staff members. Students have protested against the state legislature’s votes to further cut funding for higher education.

Students at Meredith College in North Carolina are protesting layoffs they say have led to fewer courses offered and the elimination of four dean positions.

Rhode Island’s Johnson & Wales University cut 91 faculty and staff positions last year. Students have raised concerns about worsening dorm conditions, the rising cost of laundry and meal plans, and a new policy requiring students to live on campus for three years.

And the University of Lynchburg cut, in all, 12 undergraduate majors, 25 minors and five graduate programs, as well as announced 40 staff and 40 faculty reductions.

For most universities, financial troubles start with student enrollment. Declines have been accelerating; in 2019, for instance, about 1,050 colleges and universities – or 53% – had experienced enrollment drops in three of the previous five years. By 2024, that figure rose to about 1,090 institutions – or 58%. And public universities in particular are seeing steeper enrollment declines: One in three public universities saw enrollment decline at least 10% from 2019 to 2024. That’s up nearly 50% from one in four in 2019.

The problem is probably going to get worse.

“Looking at demographic projections, with smaller high school graduating classes coming, it’s going to be harder for them to compete for students and get enough bodies in the door,” said Robert K Toutkoushian, a University of Georgia professor who specializes in economic analysis of higher education issues.

At Lynchburg, enrollment rose to nearly 3,600 in 2020, before dropping to roughly 3,200 in 2024. The university president, Alison Morrison-Shetlar, declined to provide the latest enrollment figures.

The institution’s struggles offer a glimpse of what students at more colleges may soon encounter.

It ended four of the last five fiscal years at a deficit, reporting a $2.1m loss as of mid-2025, according to a financial audit. Graduation rates have slipped: 57% of students seeking bachelor’s degrees graduated within six years as of 2024. That’s down from 66% in 2021, though similar to the 2014 rate, 56%.

An accreditation body placed the university on warning in 2024 and again in 2025 for its failure to meet standards for financial responsibility and student outcomes. Morrison-Shetlar told the accreditors she is confident the university will reach full compliance by December 2026. The accreditor did not respond to emails or phone calls seeking comment.

The university’s board of trustees has shrunk from 36 members in 2020 to 22. Former trustee Michael Gillette said he resigned in 2023 because administrators made key financial decisions without providing board members with budget documents. The university said it follows established governance procedures.

The University of Lynchburg spent at least $1.7m to change its name from Lynchburg College in 2018 to raise the institution’s stature and attract more foreign students, who typically pay full price. Federal data shows the university had 249 international students – about 8% of the student body – in 2024, nearly quadruple the number in 2014.

Appealing to foreign students to subsidize domestic ones is a popular strategy; about 750 public and private not-for-profit colleges have boosted enrollment of international students by at least 10% in the past decade. But those efforts are in jeopardy as the Trump administration pushes to make it harder for international students to get visas.

Recently, the university launched certificate programs like one for cannabis careers, its first PhD program and several three-year bachelor’s degree programs. Morrison-Shetlar is focused on stabilizing the budget, launching a fundraising campaign and “adding programs that are attracting more students towards high-paying jobs, something that families are very, very aware of these days”, she said. “They want to make sure that their kids have a good job to go to and are well prepared for that job. And we do that very, very well at the University of Lynchburg.”

Mutz enrolled there because it was near her home town and offered a better financial aid package than another local university. Her family still took out about $10,000 a year in federal loans, but she hoped that investment would be worth it as she pursued a biomedicine major.

Mutz said officials announced the 2024 cuts in a mass email to students. “They did tell us you can still continue your degree plan,” Mutz said. But she said university officials didn’t acknowledge the cuts meant fewer in-person classes at the university – and she didn’t receive any follow-up after that initial email.

Instead, students often learn new information first through the student newspaper, The Critograph. This year, student journalists reported about a recent and otherwise unpublicized round of university-wide faculty buyouts. The newspaper also revealed that the university is down to just three academic advisers, compared with seven previously.

Morrison-Shetlar has said that students will still receive adequate advising, but some students have already run into problems. Willow Martin, a psychology major, received a surprising message from the advising office this year – that she won’t be able to graduate on time.

Martin, who expected to graduate in May, was told she needed 11 more credits, including courses that she fears the buyouts will affect.

“I’m not really sure who’s going to teach my upper-level psychology classes,” she said. “I’m not really sure what’s going to happen.”

Meanwhile, Lynchburg has moved some undergraduate classes online.

Morrison-Shetlar, who will retire at the end of June, said students can take other classes through a regional consortium.

“All of the students work with their advisers to make sure that they can graduate on time and that the classes that they need are appropriately provided,” she said.

Students said that was not the same as taking all their classes at Lynchburg. Some have started voting with their feet. Thirty per cent of Lynchburg students transferred out in 2024, according to federal data – up from 18% a decade ago.

Mutz tried to make it work at Lynchburg. She returned to campus in fall 2024 for junior year, but “I didn’t really like the environment,” she said. “The financial issues were a huge contributor. We were paying, but we just weren’t getting enough resources or benefits.”

She ended up transferring to Radford University, in south-west Virginia. Even when she learned some of her core courses wouldn’t transfer because they didn’t meet her new university’s standards, she said it was the right choice to leave Lynchburg.

“All my friends that I know that went there transferred,” Mutz said. “I don’t know anyone that graduated from there.”
