https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Australia’s classroom disruption among worst in world, prompting calls for ‘digital detox’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Caitlin Cassidy
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Public school students are the equivalent of two and a half years behind their independent peers, as global report shows decline in reading and maths

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Public school students are more than two years behind their independent counterparts and Australia’s classroom disruption remains among the worst in the world, a global report has found.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results, released on Tuesday by the Australian Council for Educational Research (Acer), tested the literacy of 15-year-olds in 91 countries, including Australia. The tests have run every three years since 2000.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The latest report found Australia’s year 9 students were continuing a long-term national decline in performance, particularly in mathematics and reading, despite maintaining above-average OECD results. It also pointed to continuing gender divides in performance.

Acer’s research director, Dr Jonas Bertling, said Australia remained a “strong international performer” that was placed “well above the OECD average” but the full story was “a little mixed”.

He pointed to “persistent challenges”, including a steadily falling trend in the three Pisa testing areas – mathematics, reading and science – as well as persistent inequalities.

“We see a decline that is different for different genders in reading and in math. And we see that there are uneven outcomes by socioeconomic backgrounds,” he said.

“The disciplinary climate also still needs attention, so we’re not quite where we want to be as a nation. We’re really standing high, but I think we have some strengths to build on.”

Students in government schools recorded a mean score about 50 points lower than independent schools across science, reading and maths – equivalent to two and a half years of study behind. The federal government has reached a deal with states and territories to fully fund public schools for the first time – but not until 2034. Low funding has been blamed for a steady exodus from the sector.

The latest results also found gender differences in performance were persisting, with more female students reaching the proficient standard and exceeding in reading than males and the converse in maths. Performance in science was similar for both genders.

Australia’s disciplinary climate had improved compared with a record low in 2015 but remained poor, ranking behind 68 countries and better than just 11.

Noise and disorder in the classroom was reported by 41% Australian students as occurring often, compared with the global average of 31%, and 39% said their peers got distracted by using digital resources compared with the OECD average of 28%.

Australia is among 58% of countries that have banned smartphones in schools, indicating other tools, such as laptops and tablets, are causing distractions.

The federal education minister, Jason Clare, said Pisa results pointed to the “need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools”. “A bit of a digital detox” was required, he said.

“These results and Pisa over the past show us students who use screens a lot score lower than those who don’t.”

The last Pisa test, undertaken in 2022, saw Australia’s students climb into the top 10 of OECD countries, despite continuing the national dip. Australia’s 2018 results were the nation’s worst performance to date, due to narrowing gaps between its average results and the OECD average, particularly for mathematics.

Australia is now ranked 11th for science and reading and 17th in mathematics, which is largely stable compared with the 2022 results. The OECD gap between Australia and other nations had widened in all domains, with students around a year ahead of average in science and reading and six months ahead in mathematics.

The 2025 tests were the first time Pisa introduced a new category, learning in the digital world, which required students to demonstrate their use of digital tools to solve problems, including generating online models. Australia ranked lower than seven countries and 32 points, or around one and a half years, above the OECD average.

East Asian nations including Singapore, Japan, South Korea and participating Chinese regions performed the best overall globally, while Estonia also ranked highly. Australia scored higher than the US in science, mathematics and reading but below the UK and New Zealand. It also ranked above Canada in reading.

The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, said the results should be a “wake-up call” for the federal government.

“This is the sharpest drop in maths and reading scores in a decade,” he said. “What we need is a rigorous curriculum, effective teaching methods and discipline in the classroom.”
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Public school students are two years behind independent peers, according to new report. Australia's year 9 students are continuing a long-term national decline in performance. The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results were released on Tuesday by the Australian Council for Educational Research (Acer)

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
OECD test sees results dip in almost all member nations and warns of ‘digital distractions’ eroding academic skills

England’s teenagers are outperforming their peers in most countries in maths, reading and science, according to an international survey that warns of “digital distractions” eroding academic skills around the world.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) programme for international student assessment (Pisa), which last year tested 760,000 15-year-olds in 91 countries and regions, found that results dipped in almost all of its members compared with previous years, with the exception of England and a handful of others.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

England’s steady performance helped move the UK into the top 10 international rankings as other countries dropped out, with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland recording results slightly lower than in previous years.

While England’s biggest improvement came in science, it was its performance in reading that stood out, putting it ahead of Australia, the US, Finland and France, and with only the scholastic powerhouses of Singapore, Taiwan and the combined Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang regions in China performing significantly better.

Prof Mary Richardson of University College London, the lead author of the Pisa reports for Wales and Northern Ireland, said: “Despite the international trend of declining performance in reading, we found 15-year-olds in England, Wales and Northern Ireland to be reading just as well as they were in 2022.

“In science and maths, we also saw good performances, particularly for pupils in England and Northern Ireland, where scores were above the international average.”

Georgia Gould, the schools minister for England, said: “We are determined to build on these positive results and go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy. And we want to take on the areas where England performs less well – how far pupils feel like they belong and value school. The next leap forward will come from pupils engaged and excited to be at school.”

Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary for England, said it was “bonkers” for the government to move away from the academic emphasis that was proving to be so successful in England’s schools.

Trott said: “Focusing on academic outcomes increases opportunity. It beggars belief that Labour wants to reduce standards. In doing so, the most disadvantaged will be worst hit as they will lose out on the most opportunity.”

The OECD’s overall analysis was gloomy, saying that “learning outcomes have stagnated or declined in many countries, in some cases for well over a decade”.

It highlighted the international decline in reading scores as “most concerning”, with average scores falling by double digits across OECD members since 2018. The organisation said the results implied that a majority of 15-year-olds in 2025 had performed at a level previously expected of 14-year-olds.

The OECD’s analysts stated: “The long-term declines in performance suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level. These include changing attitudes towards reading, the impact of digital distractions on students and rising levels of absenteeism.

“Overall, the data suggest weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change.”

Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education and skills, said while the negative impact of the Covid pandemic was a common explanation, the downturn in reading skills had emerged before the pandemic.

“We cannot say for sure but declining levels of reading for enjoyment and the shift towards digital reading – skimming social media feeds and rapidly processing information – may be compromising the ability of students to engage with complex texts and data,” Schleicher said.

Schleicher noted that while some uses of digital devices for learning were beneficial, those countries where devices were allowed for leisure at school saw “substantially lower” student performance.

“This raises questions about whether devices such as smartphones – designed to maximise a user’s attention – are compatible with sustained academic attention,” Schleicher said.

A report on Scotland’s performance, produced for the Scottish government, said that the 2025 result “presents a mixed but more positive picture”, with performances in science, mathematics and reading little changed since 2022.

But the report concluded: “Scores remain significantly below those achieved in several previous cycles, and a substantial proportion of pupils, particularly in mathematics, did not reach the OECD baseline proficiency level.”

Màiri McAllan, the education secretary for Scotland, said: “While recognising the positives, these results also underline the need for change in certain areas.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: OECD test sees results dip in almost all member nations and warns of ‘digital distractions’ eroding academic skills. England’s steady performance helped move the UK into the top 10 international rankings. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland recording results slightly lower than in previous years.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision

‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision

Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.

Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.

Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.

School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.

One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.

Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.

“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.

“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”

EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs, according to official data.

The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt.

Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.

During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.

“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.

“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.

after newsletter promotion

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”

Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.

Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”

Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.

Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”

The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.

William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.

Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: ‘Alarm bells were going off’: parents tell of ordeal at Send school closed down after abuse allegations
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Annette and Kevin Maxwell say children with special needs have become moneymaking tool for private companies

A
nnette and Kevin Maxwell were nervous about sending their son Jonah to a residential home for children with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Jonah has severe autism – he is non-verbal, has epilepsy and behavioural problems and needs round-the-clock care.

“It was a huge decision, but we almost had no choice because with Jonah at home, you can’t work and we had two other children to think about. He’s beautiful, but he is very, very complicated,” said Annette. “Outsourcing parenting is just foreign to us and it’s horrible, but we didn’t have another option.”

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

When he first arrived at St Christopher’s in Bristol, Jonah was thriving, receiving different therapies and doing activities such as horse riding. Then, in 2016, the charity that ran the home collapsed and the centre was acquired by the Aurora Group, which runs more than 30 Send schools and is owned by Octopus, an investment management and real estate company.

The Maxwells, who live in Bath, noticed a change almost immediately. They said the food quality went downhill, there were plans – later suspended – for an overnight nursing position to be cut and they began to have concerns about Jonah’s wellbeing. Whenever he came home to visit he seemed very tired.

“Alarm bells were going off. But every time we spoke to management and staff, they would always reassure us that everything was OK,” said Annette.

At this point, the Aurora Group was being paid £292,000 a year by their local authority to care for Jonah. The company was expanding rapidly by acquiring several established providers to become one of the UK’s largest specialist education and care operators.

Then, in 2019, it was announced that St Christopher’s was being closed down by Ofsted after serious allegations of child cruelty came to light. Vulnerable children had to move out at short notice, their belongings hastily packed into black bin bags. They were sent across the country to new placements.

The police began an investigation into alleged child cruelty and safeguarding concerns and this concluded after two years without any criminal charges being brought.

The Maxwells were told by police there had been allegations involving Jonah. In one incident, he was said to have been roughly grabbed and shoved into his room by a staff member. They also found out a carer had allegedly been waking him up every two hours through the night to go to the toilet to avoid having to clean soiled sheets, which police said could be classified as child cruelty.

“I just wish I’d been more pushy at the time and tried harder to get to the bottom of things. I really, really regret that I didn’t do more,” said Annette.

Police later confirmed they were unable to interview the directors of the Aurora Group, who parents believed had questions to answer over cost-cutting that may have contributed to alleged abuse. Child cruelty legislation applies only to those who directly commit an alleged offence.

St Christopher’s was classified as a school, not a care provider, meaning it could not be investigated under legislation that might implicate both a corporation and individuals.

Kevin said: “Our kids have become a moneymaking tool for these companies, and they squeeze it, because they know that, ultimately, they can walk away. There has to be better accountability.”

The couple pursued civil action against Aurora, alleging a breach of Jonah’s human rights. The company agreed to pay £18,600 without admission of any guilt.

The Maxwells are pushing for stricter laws to ensure private Send providers face the same levels of accountability and transparency as other schools.

As part of sweeping Send reforms announced earlier this year, the government promised to “crack down” on private companies running schools, imposing fee caps and minimum standards.

Those in the sector said they had been raising the alarm for years and urged the government to create more state schools in the Send sector to wrest back control from private companies, which charge significantly more.

Darren Northcott, the national officer for education at the NASUWT teaching union, said: “There is a big problem where public money which should be being spent on children, young people and the staff working with them is leaking out of the system in the form of profits and surpluses. That’s not acceptable.”

He said many Send schools, in the state and private sector, had become incredibly challenging places to work because of a lack of staffing or resources to deal with children with complex needs. He said staff were increasingly expected to accept violence from children as “part of the job” and in some cases “the level of care and investment in staff falls short of would reasonably be expected”.

Hayley Harding of the Let Us Learn Too campaign said many parents were frustrated by the lack of Send places in state schools, leaving private providers as the only option for many. “There’s a huge issue with local authority capacity and lack of planning – for so many years they have been firefighting, rather than actually planning for how many children need this,” she said.

“Nobody wants people making profit out of our children. But we want them to be educated, and that’s often the only option available.”

A spokesperson for the Aurora Group said it was the only B Corp accredited provider in the sector. B Corp certification is a private credential for for-profit companies that prove high social and environmental standards through independent evaluation. Aurora also said 96% of its services were rated by Ofsted as good or outstanding.

The spokesperson added: “St Christopher’s was in serious difficulties under different ownership and under close Ofsted scrutiny when we responded to a campaign to keep the school open. We invested substantially in improving staffing, facilities and overall provision.

“We regret that we were ultimately unable to overcome the school’s challenges, and we remain saddened by the circumstances surrounding its eventual closure in 2019. We did all that we could at the time to support the Maxwell family and wish them well.

“The police thoroughly investigated the allegations and agree that we did all we could to support their inquiries. Police took no further action.”

The spokesperson said all the Aurora Group’s profits were reinvested in establishing new schools in partnership with local authorities, bringing “relief to families and making it far easier for children to go to school nearer to home”.
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Annette and Kevin Maxwell say children with special needs have become moneymaking tool. They are pushing for stricter laws to ensure private companies face the Aurora Group. Aurora Group said it was the only B Corp accredited provider in the sector.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: ‘A huge learning curve’: apprentices on the benefits and pitfalls of vocational training
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Jane Clinton and Majidah Chowdhury
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
While many young people have found jobs and built careers, some have struggled to complete their courses

T
he crisis in the youth employment market, with almost a million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the UK, has placed fresh emphasis on ways of getting employees into the workforce.

The government hopes to increase focus on technical and vocational learning in England from the age of 14. In parallel, there is an ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has also announced a new bursary aimed at ensuring families will not be left financially worse off if their teenager starts an apprenticeship.

Research from the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) found that black and mixed-ethnicity learners from poorer backgrounds and those for whom English is an additional language are less likely to complete their apprenticeships.

The Guardian asked people to share their experiences of apprenticeships.

Ellen*, 24, from Worcester, decided an apprenticeship would work better for her than university, although it was “never suggested” as an option at school.

“It was just assumed that uni was going to be the way I went,” she says. “I did my own research on my other options.”

Securing an apprenticeship was not easy, and she experienced “a lot of rejections” before she won a place at a medium-sized MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) consultancy.

Her three-year apprenticeship was four days a week with a day at college for her higher national certificate (HNC) studies. Her HNC course was two years, but the apprenticeship requirement of submitting evidence added an additional year.

Ellen passed, gaining a BTec level 4 HNC as well as a CIBSE (Chartered Institute of Building Services Engineers) Licentiate, and EngTech certification through CIBSE as an end-point assessment organisation and the UK regulatory body, the Engineering Council.

“It was a huge learning curve and I had to ask for extra help from my teachers,” she says. “At 18, being thrown into the deep end, you just want to do well, you just want to try your best to get all the answers right.

“I had a really good experience at the company that took me on as an apprentice and then gave me a job – really supportive managers – but I found it difficult to balance work, study and having a social life. All my friends chose to go to university and were all over the country, and there was no one around my age at work so having any social life was very difficult.”

Ellen says a “lack of female role models” within her industry and office was also “a difficulty”.

“I have since moved into fire sprinkler design, but starting my new career with a construction qualification and four years of industry experience has meant I am progressing faster than my colleagues who have degrees,” she says.

Harry, 26, a machinist, says he feels “gratitude” that he has a job, as he sees friends who went to university now questioning that decision.

“Some have needed uni to get the jobs that they have now, but some of them I don’t think have needed it, and they’re starting to realise that,” he says.

Harry, from Billingshurst, West Sussex, says that, after achieving three A-levels, he briefly flirted with the idea of studying business at university.

“The cost put me off,” he says. “Also, it didn’t sit right with me in my gut to go to university. I just didn’t think I had the mental strength for full-time education while balancing a part-time job and watching my money.”

Instead, he worked two ski seasons as a chaperone in France and was planning a third when the Covid pandemic closed down tourism.

“I was lucky and privileged enough to be able to come back home to stay with my family,” he says. “They obviously wanted me to get a job to pay rent.”

Harry knew about apprenticeships through his father, who had done an electrician’s apprenticeship in the late 1980s, and applied for “about five”. He got a four-year level 3 engineering machine technician work placement, involving a day a week of study. He started his apprenticeship in 2020, but delays due to Covid meant he finished it in 2025.

Harry threw himself into his studies. “While I was at college, I made sure that all the time I was there, I was doing as much work as I could because I was effectively being paid to learn,” he says.

At the end of his apprenticeship, he gained an engineering technician (machinist – advanced manufacturing engineering) level 3 qualification. The apprenticeship had a guaranteed job if he passed. Harry was offered a role, but he decided to go elsewhere for a better wage.

He adds: “I do take gratitude in the fact that I have a job. People are meant to come out of uni and find a career, but I don’t think many of them can.”

Hannah*, a metalworker, says while her apprenticeship was “amazing”, she saw how others struggled and missed out on completing theirs because of a lack of support.

“The work suited me, and I received plenty of affirmation after a long spell of unemployment and low self-confidence,” she says. “The college qualification opened a lot of doors.

“I took maths and English functional skills tests as part of the process, having not taken any exams as a school-refusing teenager, but the course had some shortcomings when it came to material and delivery – my cohort on the course were almost universally disengaged.”

Hannah, who is in her 30s and lives in south-west England, dropped out of school aged 14, only returning sporadically. She was “in that category of Neet for quite a while”, turning to the apprenticeship after periods in college, cleaning part-time and picking up “little bits of work” in her 20s.

While she is encouraged by the government’s plans regarding technical learning and apprenticeships, she sounds a note of caution. Hannah saw several people unable to continue with their apprenticeship and believes more guided support would have helped, adding that some of the cohort “struggled with attendance and emotional regulation”.

“I think apprenticeships can be fantastic, but they aren’t the panacea for joblessness,” she says. “There’s a lot of really good intentions to try and use the apprenticeship programme to get people who might have been a bit like me, though I was also very privileged because I had a supportive family and wasn’t from a really deprived background.

“But I saw some people on the apprenticeship, particularly the younger ones, who were just not ready to come into work. Some of them had quite complex emotional problems or difficult backgrounds as well, which makes it even harder.”

Jotham, 24, from Buckinghamshire, says he regarded his three-year degree apprenticeship as the “safest route” to securing a job.

“I knew before I did my A-levels that I wanted to do an apprenticeship,” he says. “My dad had said it was a good option and I looked at the government list. University was a backup option if it hadn’t worked out.”

He applied for “about 20 to 30 apprenticeships” and chose a scheme with one day a week studying at university in London that meant he could live at home and commute. It started in 2019.

“The company I chose had two apprentices at the same time, so that was an advantage, as you had someone to do it with, and the previous apprentice was also there and would help us,” he says.

He achieved a first in his digital and technology solutions apprenticeship BSc. Although there was no guarantee of a job at the end of his course, Jotham “carried on working at the same place and was offered a job”.

“It’s a very practical option, isn’t it?” he says. “It has all of the advantages of university and none of the disadvantages. Not having any debt is very freeing.”

However, he knew of some apprentices who were not so lucky: one had to stop “a year in” because the firm collapsed.

“Others either had to stop completely or change how they did the course because the company wasn’t able to employ them for the whole three years,” he adds. “That was a lot of bother for them, because there was no backup plan built into the course.”

Jotham is now working in database management.

“In the job market, really what’s wanted is experience, but people coming out of their degree may struggle to get that,” he says. “With an apprenticeship, you get the experience. The degree is almost like a checkbox item.”

*Names have been changed

In parallel, there is an ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships. Almost a million young people not in education, employment or training across the UK.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures | Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The pre-university shop is the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. In my case, none

I
have yet again found my ultimate tribe in a high-street shop, this time Ikea. As far as the eye could see, there were middle-aged women trying to choose kitchen essentials for their late-teenaged sons, for whom the next chapter of life, in which they move to another city and never once use a kitchen, cannot commence fast enough. I don’t know where all the girls were – did they do it all online? Have they been collecting teapots for years, as part of a wistful university trousseau?

The negotiation started with a chopping board, which my son said he absolutely did not need or want. I said, “How are you going to chop vegetables?”, and he said he would cross that bridge when he came to it, and I said: “Oh my God, you’re going to get scurvy.” Behind me a woman and her son were arguing about whether or not he needed a cheese grater, which ended in her saying: “I think you might be about to starve.”

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The household-item shop is a uniquely confronting experience, I realised halfway through, and one I had in no way prepared for. It’s the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. When you get a question like “Can you wash sheets?”, it turns out the answer is: “None.” I remember going round a far larger Ikea with my own mother, when I was in my 30s and my youngest was a baby, and my mum noticing, on the way in, that my daughter had nits. I say “nits” – it was one tiny nit. “Give her a chance,” I said. “She’s barely got any hair.” My mum, taking this as proof that I wasn’t serious enough about hygiene, tried to buy every bath-related item in the shop – at the top of her voice. By the third hour, there was nobody in there who didn’t know about the nit.

Ikea should have a sign at the door, saying: “Parents! If you’re having this conversation now, it’s already too late.” It would probably sound quite melodic in Swedish.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom | Nell Frizzell
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nell Frizzell
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect

Y
ou know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.

That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.

But as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometres back home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.

It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the name the Strokes, and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.

I’m also far from the only person I know hole-punching their way into a new career after decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.

The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years and then went into creative fields – Romesh Ranganathan, Philip Pullman, Joanne Harris, Greg Davies and so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.

I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.

after newsletter promotion

And this time I don’t even need to bring in my PE kit.

Nell Frizzell is a journalist and author

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged

H
ow many of the young people who attended Reading and Leeds festival or a Prom this summer will be picking up a guitar or clarinet when they return to school? New figures suggest not many. The number of students taking A-level music is at a record low: under 5,000, a drop of nearly half from 15 years ago. “We are facing the worst-case scenario prospect of A-level music disappearing from English state schools entirely,” warned Deborah Annetts, the chief executive of the Independent Society of Musicians. Music GCSE entries have also fallen. It has the widest attainment gap for disadvantaged students of any subject. Private violin lessons are beyond the purse strings of most parents.

The statistics for drama are similarly bleak. A-level drama entries have almost halved in 10 years, with by far the biggest drop in state schools. Forty per cent of state schools no longer even offer music or drama GCSEs. Leading universities have been forced to close music departments and arts courses. The number of teachers training in creative subjects has also declined sharply over the past 15 years. It is no coincidence that the Ebacc, which prioritised core academic subjects at the expense of the arts, was introduced by the Conservatives in 2010. No wonder the worlds of music, theatre and television have become so privileged.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“How did British singers get so posh?” asked a recent piece in the New Statesman. Exceptions such as Adele, Raye and Olivia Dean are all alumni of the Brit school, one of the few state-funded vocational schools for the performing arts in the UK. “Learning an instrument and getting up on stage … is now a luxury not every child can afford,” Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year, asking the government to commit £250m of funding for music education. Its 600 signatories included Elton John, Harry Styles and Stormzy. Alison Balsom, the world-class classical trumpeter, has said that her career would not be possible for a state-school pupil now. Julie Walters and Michael Sheen have spoken out about the challenges facing children from working-class backgrounds hoping to become actors.

Sir Keir Starmer was hailed as the most musically accomplished prime minister since Ted Heath, playing four instruments as a child and becoming a junior exhibitioner at the Guildhall School of Music. “To everyone who makes music happen – this government is on your side,” the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has promised. Scrapping the Ebacc last year was a welcome start. Other plans include the National Centre for Arts and Music Education, finally launching this autumn. Andy Burnham, an English graduate and music fan, has already put vocational education on the agenda. Now he must take up the baton for the arts. Mood music is not enough.

Every child should have the right to discover their gifts and fulfil their potential. Music and drama help develop discipline, confidence and social skills, and enhance wellbeing. The creative industries – a source of great economic value and soft power on the world stage – must be accessible to all. Reversing elitism in our recording studios, concert halls and theatres starts at school.

As Femi Koleoso of the jazz quintet Ezra Collective put it in their acceptance speech at last year’s Brit awards, giving a young person a trumpet or a saxophone might be the solution to many of society’s problems: “Because when you do that, you give them a dream, an aspiration and a goal.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Britain’s schools are failing its young people – and 1m Neets are paying the price | Simon Jenkins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Simon Jenkins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Obsessed with exams, devoid of vocational training: there is a total mismatch between schools and life beyond their gates

B
lame the schools. Alan Milburn’s report on Neets, published in May, was one of the most damning comments on the welfare state I have read. It described a new generation of a million mostly poor Britons now encouraged to fare worse, not better, than their parents. This means, said Milburn, that “the great British promise” – the advance of generations – is being broken. A sizeable chunk of the population is going backwards.

The number of young people not in education, employment or training – one in eight of all 16- to 24-year-olds – is rising fast and will be 1.25 million by 2030. More than 80% of them claim to want to find a job, education or training. A third even have “good GCSEs”, but 44% of them are on state benefits, now costing £8.1bn. Many of them suffer from anxiety and other disabilities, according to the NHS. The number of young people with special educational needs has doubled in 10 years. Mental ill-health is bordering on pandemic levels.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The Neets crisis is a gift to politicians. There is always someone else to blame. The most obvious target is Labour’s curiously punitive treatment of small businesses and casual or unskilled jobs. Curbing zero-hours contracts and proposing first-day job security are measures that seem almost targeted at keeping Neets out of work.

But the complaint ringing ever louder from employers is that young people leaving school are unready for work and life in the real world. August’s Department for Work and Pensions survey of employers’ views is an indictment. More than 90% thought the education system should offer more vocational pathways to young people. They pleaded for the young to understand personal motivation, teamwork and time management. They believed schools were too focused on ensuring children and young people passed exams, and lacked anything passing for careers guidance.

Reading these reports leaves an eerie sense of a total mismatch between schools and the social and economic life of the community beyond their gates. They seem like monastic institutions, fixated on their own seasons and periods, and on “subjects” handed down from the past. Above all, they love to measure what they teach, even if it has nothing to do with their pupils’ futures.

If I were an employer I would want new entrants educated in handling money, public affairs, the law, crime and punishment. They should learn about citizenship, the economy and the environment. They should know about public health and their own physical and mental wellbeing. They should be taught elementary ethics and the meaning of morality.

This should be just a beginning. What Neets most clearly lack is self-confidence. The new oracy movement is pleading for practical lessons in getting the young to talk clearly and present themselves to others. They should learn to articulate views and listen to others and learn how to agree and disagree. I cannot imagine a more critical skill, yet it is virtually untaught in schools. The reason, of course, is that authority cannot measure it. There is no league table for confidence.

Here the temperature rises. I used to notice pupils at my local secondary breaking up for the day. They would burst through the gates conversing in twos, threes or larger groups. These groups would merge and dissolve down the street like clouds. I liked to see them as a metaphor for the economy at work.

Today those same groups are quite different, composed of pupils with heads buried in phones and with just a few of them shouting into the air. The American social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation, finds this a universal facet of younger generations on both sides of the Atlantic. Social media is denying them the art of conversation, of intellectual tolerance. It is electronic introversion and there is no GCSE in that – let alone a job interview. These phones must disappear.

Milburn’s Neets report is interim. It poses the problem. We await his solution this autumn. It will doubtless elevate the importance of technical and vocational education alongside the cult of the academic subject. Nothing would aid this more than to end the disastrous merging of universities and technology colleges that took place 30 years ago.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Is it too much to dream that Milburn might look deeper? For more than a century, education’s radicals, such as Rudolf Steiner, Maria Montessori and John Dewey, have sought to bring a fresh relevance to what is taught in schools. Reading, writing and arithmetic remain necessities, but they are primary-stage skills usually acquired before the teens.

Secondary curriculums emerged from the 19th-century academies and have remained little changed ever since. They rank as noble pastimes much to be cherished, but they have scant relevance to the future lives and livelihoods of most pupils. Teaching, the world’s most conservative profession, merely clings to them. Britain’s Neets are the most unjustly treated victims.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.title: Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.text:
One Palestinian student found herself facing permanent expulsion and the revocation of all her academic credits at Zefat Academic College in Israel, after posting a video of a religious preacher praying for the people of Gaza.

Another Palestinian student, at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, was suspended for posting a Quranic verse.

The individual cases reflect a sweeping institutional crackdown documented in a report this week by Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Adalah received more than 130 inquiries from Palestinian students facing disciplinary proceedings across approximately 40 institutions. More than three in four of the targeted students were women.

The report concluded that Israeli academia has established a two-track disciplinary system amounting to apartheid within higher education.

Palestinians go through an “administrative track”, characterised by the suspension of standard procedural protections and the presumption of innocence.

Meanwhile, Jewish Israelis have “constitutional track” protections, grounded in the rule of law.

The report revealed a host of systemic procedural flaws in the monitoring of Palestinian students, notably the reliance on automated software like Google Translate to interpret Arabic texts, prayers, and cultural expressions.

Adi Mansour, an Adalah affiliate attorney, European University Institute PhD researcher and co-author of the report, said this shouldn’t be viewed as a calculated tactic.

“We view it as institutional incompetence, compounded by an unwillingness to both understand the complexity of language and discourse, and to engage with anything that departs from a majority Zionist Israeli Jewish point of view,” he told Al Jazeera.

But the proceedings against students were structured to prevent Palestinians from sharing their perspective or defence.

“Even where defence linguists were brought forward, their opinions were routinely dismissed or disregarded,” Mansour said. “Students’ identity was put on trial so explicitly that one committee even noted a student’s identification with children in Gaza could be ‘interpreted as offensive’, and questioned that student on why they didn’t identify with Israeli children.”

Historically, Article 17 of Israel’s Students’ Rights Law limited disciplinary powers against students to conduct connected to academic studies.  But institutions expanded their jurisdiction over students’ lives after the war on Gaza began. They employed catch-all provisions like “unfitting conduct” and “harm to public peace”, as well as replacing legal thresholds with tests evaluating “public sensibilities”.

“These ‘public sensibilities’ and this ‘reasonable person’ were effectively interpreted by committees and tribunals to mean the Jewish Israeli public and the sentiment of the majority,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.

“By effectively turning emotions into legal authority, used to determine the legality of speech and its meaning, institutions created uncertainty around what type of speech is prohibited.”

According to Mansour, this approach resulted in a state of conditional inclusion for Palestinian students in Israeli universities.

“[Palestinians] remain students only for as long as their expression stays within boundaries set by the comfort of the majority, and the alignment with the broader Jewish-Israeli discourse,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Adalah report documented that Israeli academic institutions ignored widespread calls by Jewish-Israeli students for the annihilation and genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Commenting to the Times Higher Education on Wednesday, the Technion said the report was “part of a broader attempt to discredit Israeli academia and institutions”, and called the accusations “baseless”.

To justify these severe measures, institutions such as the Hebrew University of Jerusalem invoked the 1965 Yardor ruling, a “militant democracy” doctrine originally used during periods of military rule to suspend the protections of the law against perceived internal enemies.

Mansour explained that this legal manoeuvring is part of a broader, deeply entrenched system weighed against Palestinians in Israeli academia.

“We see this less as a testing ground for future expansion than as one expression of an existing system, one that has long treated Palestinian citizens as the ‘other’, a fifth column, an internal enemy, particularly when they express their Palestinian identity, national narrative, or engage in discourse considered illegitimate from a majority Zionist-Jewish-Israeli point of view,” Mansour said.

“[Academia is] one visible, well-evidenced part of a system that already spans multiple sectors in parallel,” he said. “One that continuously defines aspects of language, religion, culture and political symbols such as the Palestinian flag as markers of the enemy”.

Mansour called upon international human rights bodies to hold Israeli universities accountable for breaches of international law.

“We do believe that academic freedom, adherence to international law, and freedom of expression should be an absolute precondition for any academic partnership or collaboration,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.

“Our report clearly finds a structural, institutionalised repression, applied at scale across roughly 40 institutions. These are not isolated incidents – it’s a policy, which we call on these institutions to immediately end”.

That “institutionalised repression” has fundamentally altered the shared academic space in Israel, Mansour said.

“From our direct work with around 100 students, we can say that the impact has been substantial, and it has produced a chilling effect,” he concluded.

“The stakes were not limited to disciplinary proceedings: students were arrested, and in some cases held in detention in harsh conditions. Universities even reported their own students to the police”.

A legal complaint against FIFA has been extended to cover its “abusive conduct” towards the women’s game in Europe.

The complaint by the European Leagues umbrella group, which includes the Premier League and Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL) as members, was first lodged with the European Commission in October 2024.

The complaint states FIFA abused a dominant position under European competition law in allegedly failing to properly consult with leagues over the men’s international match calendar announced in 2023.

European Leagues formally welcomed 14 European women’s leagues to its ranks in June of this year, including the Women’s Super League (WSL) in England and the Scottish Women’s Premier League (SWPL), and has now extended the legal complaint to cover the impact on the women’s international match calendar.

A media release issued by European Leagues on Tuesday said: “European Leagues is extending the scope of its complaint to the European Commission about the international match calendar to include FIFA’s abusive conduct regarding the women’s international match calendar and related women’s football regulatory decisions.

“FIFA’s conduct threatens the growth and financial sustainability of women’s professional leagues, and risks player health and wellbeing.

“The European Commission must now act to ensure that EU law is respected and that the future of women’s professional football is not determined unilaterally by FIFA.”

This season’s league phase of the Champions League kicks off on Tuesday, with Real Madrid vs Inter Milan and Porto vs Man City among the standout games on the first evening.

Two-time defending champions Paris Saint-Germain are looking to make it three in a row and are the team to beat. In last week’s draw, they were handed meetings with Barcelona, Manchester City and Aston Villa, among their eight matches in the league phase of this season’s Champions League.

But several other teams fancy their chances of toppling the Parisians, including last year’s runners-up Arsenal, and Bayern Munich, who pushed PSG hard in the semifinal.

Meanwhile, Barcelona will expect to be among the favourites, while archrivals Real Madrid – now led for the second time by Jose Mourinho – will hope their Galacticos can power them to a final being held in their city, albeit at Atletico Madrid’s Metropolitano Stadium.

Click here to read our main talking points ahead of the new campaign.

When Jose Mourinho left Inter Milan for Real Madrid in the summer of 2010, after leading the Italian outfit to Champions League glory, he was at the peak of his powers.

The Portuguese coach claimed an historic treble with Inter, clinching Serie A in the last week of the season and lifting the Coppa Italia.

Inter beat Bayern 2-0 in the Champions League final at Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu stadium that year, winning the trophy for the first time since 1965 and becoming the first Italian team to win the treble.

The day after the final Mourinho said it was likely his last match in charge and about a week later his appointment at Real Madrid was finalised.

Now 16 years on, and beginning his second stint at Madrid, Mourinho kicks off the record 15-time Champions League winners’s European campaign against Serie A champions Inter.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.title: Maldives asks UK to reopen sovereignty talks over Chagos Islands
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.text:
Maldives ⁠President Mohamed Muizzu has written to UK ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham, asking ⁠him to reopen talks over the sovereignty of the ‌Chagos Islands rather than handing over the islands to Mauritius.

In a statement released on Tuesday by the Maldives’ presidential office, Muizzu emphasised “the importance of meaningful dialogue between the UK and the Maldives on matters concerning the sovereignty of the Chagos archipelago”.

The Maldives government maintains that its own claim to the Chagos Islands is backed by historical ties and geographical proximity, being about 500km (310 miles) away while Mauritius is more than four times that distance.

These islands are home to the key UK-US military base on the island of Diego Garcia. It is the largest island in the archipelago, a strategic location in the middle of the Indian Ocean between Asia and Africa, and home to a military base that the UK leases to the US in a 99-year deal.

In his letter, Muizzu “expressed the Maldives’ concerns regarding the UK’s decision to proceed with the handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius”.

Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, had finalised a deal in May 2025 to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. The multibillion-dollar agreement would allow the UK to maintain control of the strategically important US-UK airbase on Diego Garcia.

However, in his latest letter, Muizzu said he was “deeply disappointed” that the UK did not ⁠consult the Maldives ⁠when Starmer agreed to cede sovereignty ‌of the archipelago to Mauritius, and urged Burnham to “rectify this oversight by your predecessor”.

Muizzu went on to highlight “the shared history and cultural ties between the Maldives and Chagos, as well as the Maldives’ longstanding support for major marine conservation and scientific research expeditions in the region”.

Last April, the UK set aside Starmer’s bill that would return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius due to a lack of support from United States President Donald Trump, as Mauritius promised to “spare no effort” to reclaim the archipelago.

A spokesperson of the UK’s Foreign Office was quoted on Tuesday by the Press Association news agency as saying that “the question of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago is a matter for the UK and Mauritius, which is why the previous government launched negotiations with Mauritius on the issue in 2022, rather than with the Maldives”.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.summary: Maldives president Mohamed Muizzu has written to UK PM Andy Burnham. He has asked him to reopen talks over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands. The Maldives government maintains that its own claim to the Chagas Islands is backed by historical ties and geographical proximity.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats, Moscow promises harsh response
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.text:
Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country, accusing them of “unacceptable” activities that it says are incompatible with their diplomatic status.

Anita Orban, Hungary’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, said on Tuesday that the decision to protect “Hungary’s security and sovereignty” does not mean the country is “breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia”.

Russia promised a “harsh and painful” response, the country’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told Russia’s TASS news agency.

Hungary was one of the few European Union allies to Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Under the previous government, Budapest’s relations with Moscow were warm.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban (not related to current Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orban), who lost the elections last April after 16 years in power, reportedly told Russian President Vladimir Putin: “I am at your service” during last year’s phone call.

Hungary took a “legitimate decision”, EU spokesman Christian Wigand told journalists, adding that the EU “will continue to closely coordinate” the situation.

Many EU member states expelled Russian diplomats following Moscow’s all-out war on Ukraine, but Hungary was not one of them until now.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.summary: Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country. Hungary was one of the few European Union allies to Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.title: What is BAPS, the Hindu group whose demands led to Eiffel Tower closure?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.author: Sarah Shamim
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.text:
The Eiffel Tower was temporarily closed on Monday after workers went on strike to protest the sidelining of female staff during a private visit by a Hindu religious group.

The tower, which has since reopened, shut after members of Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a global socio‑spiritual Hindu denomination, visited the site. Female staff were reportedly asked to give way to male staff for the group’s tour, prompting protests from the workers’ union, outrage from French politicians and an apology from the Hindu group.

Here is more about BAPS and how the controversy unfolded.

The Eiffel Tower closed after staff walked out over the removal of women staff during a weekend visit by BAPS.

The Societe d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, or SETE, which runs the Paris landmark, acknowledged that the group had requested the Saturday visit be organised in a way that limited “interactions with women”, and said “these conditions should not have been accepted”.

The BAPS monks, or sadhus, practise strict celibacy, which requires them to avoid physical contact with women and being alone in their company, and to minimise personal interaction or attention towards the opposite sex.

Wider community members of BAPS are not bound by these celibacy rules. According to news reports, the BAPS delegation visiting the Eiffel Tower comprised both monks and community members.

Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that they condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation.

“Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” the staff union said, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said an investigation would be launched “as soon as possible”. In a post on social media, he said he was aware of the employees’ anger and agreed their dissatisfaction was legitimate.

BAPS was founded in India in 1907 and began expanding internationally from the 1960s. It is a spiritual organisation which works on community building, constructing temples, helping with disaster relief and running medical camps, environmental drives and educational programmes.

It now also runs an extensive network of temples and cultural centres across the world, including more than 100 in the United States and more than 1,000 worldwide, including across Europe, Africa and Asia. BAPS also runs a temple in Paris.

On Tuesday, the BAPS Paris account posted a statement on X responding to the controversy.

“To our knowledge, at no time was access to the Eiffel Tower denied to anyone,” the account wrote, originally in French.

“Nevertheless, we wish to offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation,” it added.

Leaders within France expressed outrage over reports of women being removed from the premises.

Aurore Berge, the minister delegate for gender equality and fight against discrimination in France, wrote in an X post on Monday: “In France, we do not ask women to step aside. No dogma, no religion is superior to the laws of the Republic.”

Yael Braun-Pivet, president of the National Assembly, wrote in a post on social media: “Welcoming others never means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become invisible.”

Former French President Francois Hollande, now an MP, wrote on X on Tuesday: “We do not ask women to step aside to satisfy religious demands.”

He expressed support for the Eiffel Tower staff who walked out.

“Equality between women and men is a fundamental achievement of our Republic. It applies everywhere, to all women and all men, without exception,” Hollande wrote.

Parliamentarian and former PM Michel Barnier wrote on X: “It is therefore utterly unacceptable that an order aimed at making women disappear from this space could have been issued.”

Barnier added that “women are not hidden. They are not erased. They are respected, and their freedom is defended”, demanding an explanation from the SETE.

Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally, wrote on X on Tuesday: “This degrading demand should never have been met. In a free country like France, gender equality is respected, and no religious reason can override women’s dignity.”

Prominent far-right MP and leader of the National Rally (RN), Marine Le Pen wrote in an X post: “In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be ‘limited.'”

BAPS is not officially part of a political party in India, and has long insisted that it is apolitical.

But researchers have long pointed to a close, cooperative relationship with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government.

In fact, the Eiffel Tower closure came just a day after Modi virtually inaugurated the BAPS temple in Paris.

Modi also attended the physical inauguration of the BAPS temple in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2024.

BAPS has faced a series of high-profile controversies in the past.

During a landmark legal battle in 1966, BAPS leaders argued in court that their sect was not part of Hinduism but a distinct religion. They did so in an attempt to avoid the Bombay Harijan Temple Entry Act, which required Hindu temples to open their doors to Dalits, a historically marginalised caste group. The Indian Supreme Court rejected the appeal made by BAPS.

In 2013, two former BAPS monks filed a complaint accusing senior BAPS leaders of sexual assault dating back to the 1970s. BAPS leaders denied the allegations. The complaint did not result in any publicly reported criminal charges.

In 2021, a US federal class‑action lawsuit accused BAPS of exploiting low‑caste labourers from India to work on its temples. The case, brought on behalf of about 200 Indian workers, alleged they were lured from India, coerced into employment agreements, and forced to work more than 12 hours a day with only five days off a year at a temple in Robbinsville Township, New Jersey.

The suit says they were paid as little as $1.20 an hour, far below the US federal minimum wage of $7.25 and New Jersey’s $12 statewide minimum.

A US federal investigation into labour trafficking at the Robbinsville temple has since been closed without criminal charges, but the civil class‑action lawsuit brought by the workers continues.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/8/.summary: Eiffel Tower closed after staff walked out over 'professional instructions' BAPS leaders denied allegations but complaint did not result in any publicly reported criminal charges.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: The shift in British policy on Israel is palpable
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Chris Doyle
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Fifty-nine years after Israel established its first illegal settlement in the occupied Palestinian territory, the United Kingdom has imposed a ban on trade with Israeli settlements. It is not before time, as the settler population numbers more than 750,000 residing in more than 140 formal settlements and more than 390 outposts and farms.

The ban comes as British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has promised a “comprehensive reset” in relations with Israel. This term is loaded – one he repeated multiple times in a meeting with me this week. A reset implies a realignment of the whole relationship, a strong term to choose to define the trajectory.

Is this a divorce, or a temporary separation? Is it just rhetoric or something more substantive? The foreign secretary told me he is determined to lead on this policy and do what he can to deter not just Israel’s settlement frenzy but its unparalleled aggression on the Palestinian people.

Is this seismic? Historically, it has been a close relationship with frequent road bumps but no crashes; a few marital spats but no more. In 1917, Britain authored the Balfour Declaration and presided over a disastrous mandate period in Palestine, leaving with war and ethnic cleansing in its wake.

In recent decades, the UK and Israel have enjoyed cosy relations, intense trade, defence and security cooperation, only interrupted by British statements of concern – occasionally deep concern – over Israel’s treatment of the Palestinian population.

March 2023 marked the high point of the British-Israeli relationship. The two governments signed the 2030 Roadmap for Bilateral Relations, envisioning close collaboration in all sectors, especially tech and security.

Then Prime Minister Rishi Sunak cemented this with fulsome support for Israel following the October 7 Hamas atrocities. Sunak stated: “I am unequivocal. We stand with Israel, not just today, not just tomorrow, but always.”

The UK-Israel relationship started deteriorating when Labour took over in 2024, not least due to the imposition of a partial arms ban. But Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer was reluctant to hold Israel to account. Within the UK, he was largely viewed as a warm friend of Israel and was widely accused within his own party of having done little to nothing to stem the genocide, implementing only partial measures at the last moment. At no point did Starmer ever accuse Israel of violating international law in Gaza.

Yet in Israeli leadership circles, Starmer and his government were viewed as inherently anti-Israel, even as friends of Hamas who echoed the Palestinian group’s talking points. This view became more widespread after the UK’s recognition of the State of Palestine in 2025 and the sanctioning of two Israeli ministers, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Since Andy Burnham took over in late July, the British tone has shifted dramatically. The evasive, hesitant rhetoric of Starmer has vanished, replaced by more strident statements placing the clear blame on Israel for its actions.

Burnham signalled a change even before he took his post. “Labour’s initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry for that,” he wrote on social media in early July. Downing Street has confirmed Burnham has yet to speak to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Foreign Secretary Miliband has been even more forthright. In his statement in response to the Israeli decision to move forward with tenders for E1, he pledged “a comprehensive set of measures to respond to Israeli government policies.” Comprehensive is another powerful term to let loose. Actions against arms sales are not ruled out.

All of this has shocked the Israeli political establishment. The assumption has been for years that European powers like Britain talk loud but would never wield a stick.

Official Israeli responses have framed the British government as anti-Semitic, whose policies are designed to appease the British Muslim vote. Netanyahu led the way by referring to the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain.”

The Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar fumed, “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have tools.” Smotrich demanded the expulsion of the British ambassador to Israel, a measure the UK might reciprocate.

The US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, further fuelled the flames: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.”  Perhaps he did not know that Miliband is Jewish himself and a son of Jewish refugees.

Apart from upping its hostile rhetoric, what can Israel do? It can press the US to punish the UK. It can impose its own sanctions. It can kick the UK out of the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up by the Board of Peace to monitor aid flows into Gaza. But it is highly likely that much of the retaliation will be taken out on Palestinians. There may be announcements of new settlements and other such measures to show Israel will proceed despite British sanctions.

At this point, is there a way back for the UK-Israeli relationship? With Netanyahu in power in Israel, and with a Labour government in charge in London, the answer is a clear no. If Netanyahu is dethroned and replaced by Gadi Eisenkot, a thaw might be possible.

The danger here is that any new Israeli government may be more diplomatic, less brash, but still pursue the same strategic policy towards the Palestinians. It is the policy, not the personnel, that matters.

The British government has to stay the course until Israel abandons its settlement industry. It should not be swayed by vague promises or less abrasive language. The measure of success can only be real change on the ground.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Ban on trade with Israeli settlements in Gaza is not before time as the settler population numbers more than 750,000. British government has to stay the course until Israel abandons its settlement industry.
