https://www.wired.com/story/rei-labor-da.title: The 57 Best Deals From the REI Labor Day Sale
https://www.wired.com/story/rei-labor-da.author: Scott Gilbertson
https://www.wired.com/story/rei-labor-da.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

REI'S ANNUAL LABOR Day Sale ends today—this is your last chance to score some great deals on outdoor gear. Many items are up to 40 percent off, and REI Co-op members can save up to 20 percent on any REI Outlet item.

Many of the best REI deals are on gear from the company's house brand. But there are also good discounts on other brands, like Mountain Hardwear, Nemo Equipment, Big Agnes, and Coleman, among others. I’ve also pulled some deals from competing sales at Backcountry, Fjällräven, and other cottage industry retailers. Below, find the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, sleeping pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more. Be sure to check out our outdoor gear guides, like the Best Tents, Best Sleeping Bags, Best Sleeping Pads, Best Backpacking Tents, Best Merino Wool, and Best Base Layers.

Updated September 7, 2026: We've removed a few sold-out deals and added more deals on merino base layers, backpacks, sleeping bags, socks, rain jackets, and more.

Can’t You Just Put Links to All Your Outdoor Guides Right Here?

Now is a great time to score some new base layers and mid layers ahead of the cooler months, or pick up one of our favorite rain jackets.

Arc'teryx's Beta AR rain jacket is one of the burliest rain jackets I've tested. The Beta AR uses 40D fabric for most of the face, with reinforced 80D patches in high-wear areas, all of it with a Gore-Tex Pro 3L membrane. It's been the only Gore-Tex jacket I've tested that hasn't wetted out yet, and the pit zips provide excellent ventilation. At 1 pound, 0.3 ounces, it's not the lightest jacket, but you'd be hard-pressed to find anything else this durable at this weight.

I have the 2024 version of this jacket and it has proved reliable and waterproof. The taped seams and welded construction keep wind and moisture at bay, and the side zip vents run all the way from the hem to the bicep, offering great ventilation when you're moving (also handy for getting at stuff in the pockets of your mid layers). Only the men's version is on sale.

Patagonia's classic rain jacket is half off. It's only one color and only women's sizing, but this is a great deal if it works for you. The Torrentshell has a two-way adjustable hood, and the cuffs have velcro to give a nice, tight seal against the rain. The only real complaint I have with this jacket is that's it's on the noisier side, but at this price, I can deal with a little extra nylon crinkling.

The Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket, especially when it's on sale. This particular deal, while limited in color options, is the lowest price I've seen in 5 years of covering REI sales. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.

Looking to avoid the sun? REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen. I don't often use a sun hoodie myself, but I have worn this one and it does do a good job of protecting you without feeling too stuffy on a hot day (it's definitely better for protecting against high altitude sun rather than humid, Florida sun).

The Ghost Whisperer Down jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. This is the hoodie version of the same. It weighs just 10.7 ounces for a men's medium, packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. Unfortunately, colors and sizes are very limited.

Darn Tough makes some of our favorite merino wool socks. You can't go wrong with a pair of on your next trip. The Light Hiker Quarter Socks for $16 are nice for anyone who's moved to lightweight trail runners or minimal shoes. Most Darn Toughs are about 60 percent merino, with rest nylon. The nylon does mean you can't wear them as long without washing, I find about 2 days max for blends like this.

This is the quarter zip version of the best midweight base layer we've tested. I find this Smartwool shirt perfect for chilly spring and fall mornings. It's comfortable, though tending to be looser fitting, which is something to keep in mind when layering. The heavy-duty seams (read: sturdier, longer lasting) don't rub, and sit off the shoulder for more comfort when wearing a pack.

Cold temps are coming soon, grab this and keep your neck warm. I live in this Turtle Fur gaiter during the winter, and I also use the lighter, superfine version for hiking at elevation in the summer to keep the sun off my neck without resorting to sunscreen. It's wonderfully soft, not overly tight, and never smells.

Our favorite synthetic base layer, these super soft and stretchy unders are made from Capilene, which is 100 percent recycled polyester (Capilene is Patagonia's proprietary fabric and not the same as polypropylene). The synthetic threads here perform about on par with wool. Capilene is also just about as comfortable, all while being light and quick-drying. Sizes here are very limited since this version has been replaced by an updated, revamp version that we are in the process of testing.

This is an REI Outlet deal because it's been discontinued, which is a shame (hopefully that just means new colors are coming next year). REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides, but if you prefer, the regular top (on sale for $30) is also on sale, as is the base layer bottom (on sale for $30).

Nothing says outdoors like a hatchet loop on your pants. Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers give you that and great ventilation. The Vidda Pro uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere and extras like ventilation zippers, reinforced knees (with openings for pads), and that sweet, sweet hatchet loop on the leg.

The REI Half Dome 2 is the best budget two-person backpacking tent. I’ve toted it on many backpacking trips and found it plenty sturdy, quick to set up, and capable of fitting two people along with their gear. It even comes with a footprint (which I never bother with, but it's nice to have it if you have to deal with pointy rocks).

The Big Agnes Copper Spur series is our top pick among freestanding ultralight tents. This is the bike-packing model, which features shorter pole segments that are easier to haul on a bike, but I really prefer it for the more subdued colors. The Copper Spur is a high-quality, well-designed tent that's lightweight, easy to set up, and roomy enough to be livable in the backcountry. The “awning” design (with trekking poles or sticks) is a nice extra.

Nemo's Dragonfly tents are roomy for the weight. There's a generous amount of mesh at the top, which provides some nice ventilation on warm summer nights and is perfect for falling asleep under the stars when the weather permits. The Osmo fabric is a blend of nylon and polyester that absorbs less water than pure nylon rainflies.

MSR's Groundhog stakes aren't cheap, but they're the best backpacking tent upgrade you can make. They're superstrong—I've never had one bend or pull out on me—and considering their strength, they're pretty lightweight. I suggest carrying a mix of stakes when backpacking—some of these, some carbon fiber pegs, and some shepherd hooks. That way, no matter the terrain, you've got something that'll work.

REI's Base Camp tent is my favorite car camping tent. It's a traditional dome tent design, with two crossed poles and two side poles, that hold up very well in wind. The floor is high-quality 150-denier polyester, which so far has not shown any signs of abrasion, despite quite a few nights on rough ground out West. Inside, there are loads of storage pockets, and the double doors make great vents in warmer weather, with huge windows that ensure you catch any whiffs of breeze on hot nights.

The Marmot Halo is my favorite all-weather four-person family tent. The low-profile design stands up better to wind, while the steep sidewalls maximize interior space. It also has a nearly full-length rain fly, which helps make this a real haven in a storm. The name comes from the unusual pole design. There are two cross poles, like every square, domed tent, but the side poles connect halfway up the tent body instead of at the ground. The only downside is that you can't stand up in it. If you want more room, the six-person version, which, with a 76-inch peak height, may be tall enough for you to stand up in, is also on sale.

My favorite barefoot sandals are 25 percent off right now. I always call these the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust, and I'd still bring Chacos if I were white-water rafting, but for everything else these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale.

The best all-around barefoot shoe, the Prios are your classic sneaker reimagined for barefoot shoe enthusiasts. When you were a kid, you had just one pair of shoes: The Prios are that pair. The toe box is wide enough for my toes to splay out nicely, and the heel cup is snug with no slipping. The ground feel is great too, enough feedback to feel barefoot, but you're not going to wince when you hit a sharp stone.

Altra's Lone Peak shoes have carried countless thru-hikers to the finish line. The Lone Peak first came on the scene in 2011 and quickly built a cult following. They're light (11.5 ounces) and very comfortable in our testing. The reinforced toe and heel offer excellent protection against rough, rocky trails, and while they're much more padded these days than early versions, they're still zero drop.

Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky.

This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is somewhat huge, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works well and has produced some great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example: It's comfortable (it does wobble a little side-to-side when you move) and less than half the price of competitors.

I've noticed that when people try to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter backpack, they struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which smashes anything soft down to about half the size of the same item in a regular stuff sack. This works well with sleeping bags and clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino wool.

The High Coast Rolltop 26L pack from Fjällräven is my favorite waterproof pack. It's the perfect size for a day hike, with room for all my gear, and plenty of kid gear should the family be coming along. It's made of waterproof 400D polyamide, and it's seam taped and fully waterproof, thanks to the rolltop closure. The High Coast has stretchy mesh side pockets that hold water bottles and snacks. There's also a zippered side pocket on the outside of one of those side pockets, which can store small items like wallet and keys (none of the outer pockets are waterproof).

Mountainsmith has been making this lumbar pack for ages and it's stood the test of time. It's by far my most used pack. It can be worn as a lumbar pack (which I do when riding my bike), or as a a shoulder bag around town. I also strap it to the handle bars of my bike (it's amazing what you can do with some voile straps), and to the outside of a Mystery Ranch backpack (to use as a daypack/outside storage). This is an REI Outlet deal, so if you use the code LABORDAY26 you can get an extra 20% off.

A long time WIRED favorite, Peak Design's Everyday pack is a chic and understated, endlessly adaptable, and easy-to-use pack that can go everywhere you go—from the woods, to the office, to the bar. The greatness is in the thoughtful design details. For example, there are quick-release loops on the arm straps to swiftly loosen one just enough to swing the bag around and get your keys or wallet while standing or walking.

Nemo's Resolve is a great little daypack. The Cero fabric is solution dyed to reduce water waste, as is the cushioning, and it uses a system of bungees and pull-tabs, instead of straps or webbing. Over the long term those bungees should be easier to repair and replace making the pack longer lasting. It's also very comfortable. Though technically frameless, it feels like it has some structure, and at just over two pounds, it’s pretty light.

REI’s Big Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

The Flash 22 is one of the best-value day packs on the market, especially on sale. It's surprisingly comfortable despite the lightweight straps and minimal padding. It carries loads up to 15 pounds without straining the shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. Note that this deal is only on the patterned colors.

WIRED staffers have North Face duffels that have been going strong for 25 years, earning a spot in our Buy It for Life guide. They're big ol' bags (this one is 62 liters), capable of swallowing gear like a whale, and unlike all the other identical cases on the luggage carousel, they’re always easy to spot. This version is made of phthalate-free, recycled PVC and recycled nylon that’s treated with a non-PFC water-repellent (DWR) finish.

Our favorite backpacking sleeping bag, the Bishop Pass 15 offers the best warmth-to-weight ratio while packing down small and staying affordable. I have slept in this bag for more than two weeks, with nighttime temps ranging from 28 to 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and, yes, it was too warm in the heat, but on those warmer nights, I unzipped it and used it as a blanket. It isn't perfect, but it's a versatile bag.

REI's Magma line of down gear is some of the best value around. The Magma 15 sleeping bag has long been an affordable option that's perfect for shoulder-season trips when the temperature potentially swings lower than you expect (the comfort rating is 21). There are three lengths and three widths, which makes it easy to find a perfect fit for your body, and the 850-fill-power goose down (Bluesign-approved) packs down nicely and small. If you don't need the shoulder-season coverage, the Magma 30 is also on sale for $262 ($87 off), and it makes a great summer sleeping bag.

This down mummy bag has a spoon-shaped design for side sleepers and extra room in the elbows and knees so you can roll over onto your side without feeling like you're slipping into a straitjacket. It's built for temps down to 30 degrees Fahrenheit and has zippered gills you can open to avoid overheating when it's warmer.

The best budget ultralight quilt, the Magma Trail is a great value for the money. The lower price does mean that this one is a bit heavier (it uses 850-fill-power down), though at 24 ounces for the long, wide version I have, it’s competitive on the scale. The straps for attaching it to your sleep pad aren’t as nice as what you’ll get with something like the Enlightened Equipment's Revelation Quilt, but it’s just as warm and does a respectable job of keeping out drafts. There's even a zippered foot box with a drawstring for cooler nights.

Nemo's Pulse quilt uses RDS-certified, gold-infused 1,000-fill-power ExpeDRY down, which does a good job of shedding moisture from tent condensation and reportedly dries faster than standard down, though I've never figured out a good way to test this. The Karo Step baffle stitching keeps down well distributed, and at 12 ounces for the regular, this one is pretty dang lightweight.

The Zenbivy sleep system uses a clever sheet and quilt combo to deliver the best backcountry sleep I've ever had. It's light at 1 pound, 12 ounces (or 793 grams) for the 25 degree Fahrenheit large version, though Zenbivy does make an ligher, Ultralight Quilt. I find the Light Quilt to be the better value (especially on sale like this). You can read my full review of the Light Bed for more on why I think it's the best way to sleep when backpacking.

This is our favorite ultralight sleeping bag. Quilts are great, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is the best sleeping bag I've tested. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down, and while the zippers are on the small side, they slide well and rarely, if ever, snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

This is our favorite sleeping bag for car camping. The REI Siesta is plenty warm and affordable. It's also not a mummy bag because you're not climbing Denali here. The rectangular cut makes for a much roomier, more comfortable sleeping experience. The 20-degree-Fahrenheit rating makes it warm enough for three seasons, and unlike most rectangular bags, the Siesta has a hood, which helps on those cold nights.

The Kindercamp makes a great car camping bag if you've got young children. Once your kids are about 4 feet tall, an adult sleeping bag works just fine. Prior to that, they'll benefit from a kids' sleeping bag like the Kindercamp, which is cut smaller so your little ones don't have to heat up a huge, adult-size sleeping bag to stay warm.

There are other good sleeping pads out there, but nothing compares to the Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft for comfort. This pad reinvigorated my love of backpacking by ensuring that I get a great night's sleep. It's cushy and comfortable, especially if you're careful not to overinflate it. The R-4.8 insulation keeps you warm down to about freezing, though I've used it in colder conditions by pairing it with a closed-cell foam pad.

The Z-Lite Sol weighs next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), folds up compact enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and will completely change your backpacking experience for the better. I am too old and too soft to sleep on just this anymore, but I use it as a chair, padding for a nap on the rocks, a table, extra padding on cold nights, and more. It's possibly the most versatile piece of gear I own.

If you want to feel like you never left your bed at home, this is the camping pad to get. You really have no idea how comfortable tent camping can be until you sleep on a Megamat. The firm, 4-inch-thick pad is both soft and surprisingly firm thanks to the closed-cell foam inside, which relieves pressure and feels about as close to the mattress in your bedroom as you're going to get in the woods.

Nothing says camping like roasting marshmallows over open flames and burning beans on the camp stove. Check out our guides to the best backpacking stoves and best camping stoves for more picks.

MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe is our top pick for a backpacking stove. It wins the title thanks to its larger burner area, which allows the flame to spread out for faster boil times and better fuel efficiency, especially with larger pots. It also fared better in the wind than smaller burners. The genius of the deluxe model is the small curved lip around the burner, which helps keep wind from getting to the base of the flame. It's a small design element, and one that you certainly want. During long-term testing, I found it more effective at maintaining a simmer in the wind, should you want to do any actual cooking.

You can put together a lighter cooking setup, but Jetboil's Stash is the lightest all-in-one system out there, and it does boil water a bit faster than the rest. The heat diffuser design speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I could only match indoors in still air), but the real appeal is how this kit packs down into itself and how simple it is to use.

Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

While I prefer the larger burner head of the Deluxe model above, the MSR PocketRocket 2 is lighter at 2.6 ounces compared to the Deluxe's 2.9. It still has wide enough arms to support just about any one- or two-person pot. It's simple to use, even while wearing gloves, and it's efficient. At 947-foot elevation, it boiled 1 liter of water in 3 minutes, 47 seconds. You can even get it to simmer, though the flame radius is small, so fancier cooking isn't easy.

MSR's WhisperLite series is probably the most popular backpacking stove ever made. They last forever (mine is over 30 years old and still works great), and this model, the Universal, can use just about any fuel you can imagine—white gas, kerosene, unleaded gasoline, and isobutane-propane canisters, to be precise. The only downside is that it can be fiddly compared to stoves like the Jetboil. But if you're headed out on a long trip, buying fuel as you go, this is the most flexible option out there.

This is by far the most compact two-burner stove I've tested. It's my pick for any situation where space is at a premium—whether that's canoeing or just because you have a small car. The burners are large, and with some practice, I could get a light, simmer-friendly flame. My main gripe is the windscreen, which is not the best. The Basecamp version, with fitted pots, is also on sale for $300 ($100 off).

My favorite stove in Coleman's current lineup, the Coleman Cascade 3-in-1 features heavy-duty cast-iron grates and comes with a cast-iron griddle and grill. It'll comfortably fit a 12-inch pan and a 10-inch pan side by side, and it's significantly sturdier and more robust than other Coleman stoves, making it worth the extra money if you use it often. That said, the much cheaper stove below will get you by if you're only using it a few nights a year.

This stove is ubiquitous at campgrounds for a reason. It's well-built, sturdy on a table, and just works. It's not the most powerful stove, and it lacks frills like push-button ignition, but it's capable of holding a low flame, simmering soups, and cooking scrambled eggs without browning them. It's also incredibly durable.

The MSR Gravity Autoflow filter is a must-have for backpacking with a group. To use this filter, scoop up 10 liters of water in the dirty water bag, attach the hose, connect your water bottle, and sit back and relax. The filter is good enough to keep you safe from all the usual protozoa and bacteria, and the flow rate is a solid 1.5 liters per minute when the filter is clean.

The MSR Guardian is our pick for trips with sketchy water sources because it filters down to 0.02 microns, which will even remove viruses. It is heavy at 22 ounces and may be overkill for trips in the US, but it's a great option for overseas adventures. I really like that it's designed to be self-cleaning, which makes field maintenance incredibly easy, and that it screws right onto a Nalgene bottle. Also, because it's a pump filter, it's very fast. You can crank out a couple of liters in hardly any time at all. The gravity-fed version is also on sale at Backcountry for $232 ($78 off).

If you snap a selfie in the woods and Instagram isn't around to see it, did it happen? You'll never have to answer that question if you've got one of our favorite action cameras or 360 cameras with you.

Insta360's X6 360 camera just launched—our review will be coming soon—but the X5 is still a great option, especially on sale. The twin 1/1.28-inch sensors capture 8K video, which means you can reframe your footage to fit rectangular video formats and still have nearly 4K clips sharp enough to mix with footage shot with your phone. The dynamic range is impressive, and the X5 also has great battery life.

If you're going to turn your action camera on yourself, consider the Ace Pro 2, our top pick for vlogging. It has a great lens and sensor co-engineered with Leica, is capable of recording 8K video at up to 30 frames per second (fps), and has some pretty darn nice color even in the default settings. My guess is that the Ace Pro 3 is coming pretty soon, but this is still a good deal.

Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

https://www.wired.com/story/dark-energy-.title: Two of the Universe's Great Mysteries May Have Their Own Dimension
https://www.wired.com/story/dark-energy-.author: Steve Nadis
https://www.wired.com/story/dark-energy-.text:
THE ORIGINAL VERSION of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For those who see the world as a dark place, the universe seems to offer little solace. According to current estimates, approximately 70 percent of the stuff that makes up the cosmos consists of dark energy, an unknown force that pushes space to expand. And another 25 percent consists of dark matter, a mysterious material that holds galaxies together.

But semantically speaking, dark energy and dark matter are not so much “dark” as they are invisible. They do not emit, reflect, nor absorb light, and they have so far proven impossible to observe directly.

Generally, dark energy and dark matter are regarded as separate entities, their elusiveness their primary link. But recent astronomical observations have spurred scientists to look further into a less popular idea—that the two are in fact physically intertwined.

In 2024, the research team known as DESI, for Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, found evidence that the strength of dark energy, sometimes referred to as the “cosmological constant,” had lost its presumed constancy. A 2025 study based on more than twice as much data also concluded that dark energy was changing over time.

These results indicate that after attaining a maximum value about 2 billion years ago, dark energy may have begun to weaken. But the results also suggested that in an earlier era, dark energy could have grown stronger, in seeming defiance of the law of energy conservation.

Researchers describe this as dark energy entering the “phantom regime.” They liken the situation to a ball rolling uphill. It’s certainly possible, but only if the ball is under the influence of something other than gravity.

A slice of a 3D map produced by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument team shows connected strands of galaxies forming the structure of our universe.

A growing number of theorists are looking into the possibility that what’s influencing dark energy are its ties to dark matter.

Even though scientists have assumed that dark energy and dark matter “don’t have anything to do with each other,” said Tim Tait, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine, “you can imagine a case where one influences the other. And it would not be surprising if [they] were manifestations of a kind of unified theory of the dark universe.”

The idea that dark energy and dark matter interact is not new. For example, Justin Khoury, a physicist at the University of Pennsylvania, investigated the prospect in 2005.

Khoury explained that in that study, he and two coauthors posed a hypothetical question: Could there be a form of dark energy whose energy density increased over time? He and his collaborators found that if dark energy and dark matter could affect one another, they could produce what looked like (but was not) phantom behavior. “It is the most natural, simplest way of achieving this,” Khoury said.

Two decades later came the DESI finding that dark energy might actually be changing over time. The result spurred Khoury and two Pennsylvania colleagues, Meng-Xiang Lin and Mark Trodden, to construct a model of dark interactions based on a dark-sector analogue of quantum chromodynamics, a cornerstone theory of particle physics. In the new model, both the energy density of dark energy and the mass of dark matter change in concert.

Another recent study imagines something similar. According to this model, which was published in January in the journal Physical Review D, dark matter could have transferred a small fraction of its energy to dark energy during a previous era of cosmic history. “Dark matter is the main brake on [the universe’s] expansion,” said one of the authors, Elsa Teixeira, a cosmologist at the University of Montpellier in France, so easing up on that brake would have caused the expansion of the universe to accelerate.

Elsa Teixeira, a cosmologist at the University of Montpellier in France, investigated a cosmological model in which dark energy and dark matter interact.

The appearance of phantom behavior is basically the result of bookkeeping, said David Andriot, a physicist at CNRS, the French National Center for Scientific Research. “Any change or evolution of the mass of dark matter has been put into the box of dark energy,” said Andriot, who presented his own coupled dark energy-dark matter model in May 2025.

Cumrun Vafa, a physicist at Harvard University, agreed. “The notion that you can compute dark energy independently of dark matter is wrong,” he said. “That assumption, often made by cosmologists and also followed by the DESI team, led to the physically unacceptable phantom behavior.”

The DESI findings are not the only reason to consider an association between dark energy and dark matter. Teixeira and colleagues’ recent study shows how allowing the two to interact can, at least in some scenarios, ameliorate one of the most persistent problems in cosmology: the Hubble tension.

At issue is the current expansion rate of the universe, known as the Hubble constant. Its value can be measured by using light from the early universe, which provides a view of how the cosmos was growing in its earliest days. It can also be measured by drawing upon more recent phenomena, such as exploding stars called supernovas, which reveal how the universe is growing now.

Studying the light from supernovas like this one—the flash of light in the bottom right of an image from the Hubble Space Telescope—can tell us about the expansion rate of the universe.

According to the standard model of cosmology, that expansion rate should be the same no matter how you measure it. But in recent years, scientists have found that the expansion rate of the early universe and that of the more recent universe vary by approximately 9 percent.

That discrepancy, or tension, “has provoked heated debates in the cosmology community about whether this difference could be due to systematic errors or whether it is a signal of new physics,” Teixeira and her co-authors wrote. Their model posits that in a world where dark energy and dark matter interact, what seemed to be a crisis caused by disparate expansion rates instead becomes something to be expected.

If dark energy and dark matter do interact, it could mean that they have a common origin, Khoury said.

Ongoing work in string theory—the idea that our universe, at its smallest, most fundamental level, is made up of vibrating strings—suggests a way these concepts might be connected. In 2019, building on the idea in string theory that dark energy is naturally varying, Vafa and two collaborators concluded that the mass of dark matter particles may also vary over time. This led them to propose in 2022 that dark matter and dark energy could share a link with a so-called dark dimension.

String theory posits the existence of six or seven extra dimensions in addition to our familiar three dimensions of space and one of time. All of these dimensions are thought to be as small as physically possible—close to the Planck scale (10-35 meters)—but the researchers proposed that the dark dimension could be significantly bigger than the others—on the order of a micron (10-6 meters).

Gravitons, theoretical particles that impart the force of gravity, could leak into this enlarged dark dimension. If they did, they would pick up mass and become what are called dark gravitons. These massive gravitons would reside in the dark dimension, but their gravitational effects could be felt in other dimensions, allowing them to fulfill the role that is normally ascribed to dark matter.

Cumrun Vafa, a physicist at Harvard University, thinks the mass of dark matter may vary over time.

In this scenario, “there is a very natural coupling between dark energy and dark matter,” said Georges Obied, a physicist at the University of Chicago. Changes in the size of the dark dimension would affect both dark energy and dark matter.

In a July 2025 paper, Obied and Vafa, along with Alek Bedroya of Princeton and David Wu of Harvard, found that the scenario proposed in 2019 was consistent with the DESI data. Their model predicts that the strength of dark energy and the mass of dark matter will decrease over time and that the rate at which dark energy changes will be proportional to its energy density. Because astrophysical measurements tell us that the energy density of dark energy is extraordinarily small, “it won’t change fast,” Vafa said.

“It’s not surprising that we didn’t see it until now,” he said, because the rate of change is so tiny. “We had to wait the entire age of the universe to detect something that small.”

If dark matter is coupled to dark energy, dark matter particles could interact with one another through a new, long-range force that is separate from gravity. The good news, Obied said, is that “there could be astrophysical ways of testing this.”

Coincidentally, two physicists—Marc Kamionkowski, now at Johns Hopkins University, and Michael Kesden, now at the University of Texas at Dallas—have already looked into one such test. In a paper published in 2006, they imagined a sequence of events in which two galaxies come close to each other and the gravity of one galaxy tugs at the other. If dark matter has a stronger gravitational attraction to other dark matter than it does to ordinary matter, a special kind of “tidal tail”—an extended stream of stars, gas, and dust—would form behind one of the galaxies.

Kesden and Kamionkowski looked for this effect and didn’t find it, which enabled them to set an upper bound on the possible strength of the extra attractive force. The upper bound was about 20 times bigger than the number Vafa’s team proposed, so the predicted value fell well within the observational bound. “It is interesting that we are now finding connections between that fairly abstract work and observational and experimental work,” Kamionkowski said.

The fact that a prediction based on calculations from string theory roughly agreed with the astrophysical evidence does not confirm the validity of these “stringy” models. But any correspondence between string theory and experiment is gratifying to Vafa, who has spent the past four decades trying to wrest the theory from the purely conceptual realm to the point of generating testable predictions.

Obied, one of Vafa’s former Ph.D. students, is driven by the same goal. Understanding dark energy and dark matter and the relationship they may share is a daunting problem, he said. “And I think it’s very beneficial to come at this in different ways”—be it from observational cosmology, from particle physics, or from string theory.

“This is how people should do science,” Obied said. “I mean, it’s the job of theoretical physicists to explore everything that’s possible, to get all the possibilities on the table. And eventually, the data will help us decide.

https://www.wired.com/story/astronomers-.title: Astronomers Have Completed the Largest Map of Space. Yes, You Can Play With It
https://www.wired.com/story/astronomers-.author: Ritsuko Kawai
https://www.wired.com/story/astronomers-.text:
THE DRIVING FORCE behind our universe’s accelerated expansion remains one of the greatest mysteries in astronomy. While this force, which scientists refer to as dark energy, pervades our universe, we know almost nothing about it.

Located on a remote mountain in Arizona’s Sonoran Desert, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) has spent the past five years mapping the cosmos with the goal of unraveling this mystery. The result is the largest three-dimensional map of the universe ever created. And now—with the release of the latest version of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, a free online tool for exploring the vast imaging data—you too can poke around the universe.

The new map boasts an overwhelming amount of information: 5.6 trillion pixels containing approximately 4 billion celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, black holes, and asteroids. It covers approximately 75 percent of the entire sky, recording both visible light and near-infrared wavelengths.

Those missing pieces include the deeper parts of space blocked by the stars, space dust, and other matter in our own galaxy, which is a major challenge for astronomy surveys, especially ground-based ones. However, since the Milky Way is splayed out like a fried egg—which is why it appears as a dense band of stars in the night sky—the researchers aim DESI’s 5,000 mechanical eyes out of the top or bottom of our galaxy to capture some of the clearest images of distant space yet.

A galaxy cluster located in the constellation Leo, affectionately known as “Copeland’s Septuplets.”

Though this particular survey lasted five years, it built on another 13 years of groundwork. More than 160 scientists were involved in data collection, and over the course of the project, researchers have already published upwards of 1,800 scientific papers referencing the data.

“It’s part of the fabric of astronomy research now,” David Schlegel, a researcher at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and colead of the Legacy Surveys, said in a press release. “When you’re working with astronomical objects today, you often start by pulling up the Legacy Imaging Viewer to see what you’re looking at.”

Earlier this year, DESI researchers released another map, which projected the distances of 47 million galaxies and quasars. This reconstructed 11 billion years of cosmic history, bringing the effects of dark energy into focus. Dark energy is thought to be responsible for the expansion of our universe, and while the force itself remains ellusive, astronomers can track it by analyzing the rates at which other celestial objects appear to be moving away from us.

Data from the first three years of DESI’s survey—combined with observations of supernovae and the pervasive radiation leftover from the big bang—have hinted that dark energy may not be a constant force but is gradually weakening over time. An analysis of the full five years of data is scheduled to be released in 2027, which scientists believe will paint a picture of the past and present of the universe more vividly than ever before.

Going forward, DESI’s observations will also serve as a reference and comparison point for other cosmic projects, such as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Researchers also plan to train artificial intelligence tools to accelerate analysis of the petabyte-scale astronomical data—within which much remains to be discovered.

“Explorations of our universe always start with images of the night sky,” said Arjun Day, codirector of Legacy Surveys and an astronomer with the National Science Foundation. “These data are fundamental to the investigation of the expansion history of the universe and the formation of our galaxy. But the skies belong to everyone, and this survey gives everyone the chance to marvel at their wonders.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

It covers approximately 75 percent of the entire sky, recording both visible light and near-infrared wavelengths.

https://www.wired.com/story/every-samsun.title: Every Samsung Galaxy Phone Comes With This Unique Add-On
https://www.wired.com/story/every-samsun.author: David Nield
https://www.wired.com/story/every-samsun.text:
IF YOU OPT for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.

Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.

With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.

If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.

You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.

When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).

There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).

The names of these panels give you some idea of what they can do. You can use the Apps panel to access the apps you use the most, without having to hunt for them in the main app drawer or having them clutter up your home screen. You can also jump to your most important people on the Contacts panel in the same way.

The Clipboard panel gives you quick access to the phone clipboard, while Tasks features shortcuts such as taking screenshots, adding new calendar events, adding alarms, and taking a screenshot. Having these shortcuts on the Edge Panel means you don't have to dig through menus or remember key combinations for the same functions.

Tools is actually just a single tool: a compass that tells you your current location and points you north, south, east, or west. Weather is pretty self-explanatory, while Reminder syncs information from the Reminder app that comes preinstalled on Galaxy devices.

The Edge Panel works fine in its default state, but to make the most of it you really need to set it up to suit you and the way you use your phone. From the main Settings menu, choose Display, then tap Edge Panels.

First, select Panels to pick which panes are shown. Put a check next to the panes you want to have available. If you tap the three dots (top right) then Reorder, you're able to choose the order they appear in as well—place the panes you use most often furthest to the left, as they'll be available in fewer swipes.

You can also tap the three dots then Hide on Lock screen if you don't want the Edge Panel to appear before you've unlocked your phone. Bear in mind that you might not want some information—such as the contents of the clipboard or your reminders—being available to anyone who picks up your handset.

With Apps, People, and Tasks, you can customize what's included. Just tap the Edit button underneath the pane. In each case, there are more available options than there are slots on the Edge Panel, so you need to prioritize accordingly.

Back on the Edge Panels screen, there are a couple of other options worth knowing about. If you pick Handle, you can set the properties of the little onscreen strip that Edge Panel is activated through. Pick the size and transparency level of the handle, its color, and which side of the screen it appears on.

Finally, there's the Show in landscape mode toggle switch; disable this if you don't want to see the Edge panel when you're using your phone in its landscape orientation. This mode is mainly used for watching videos and playing games, in which case the Edge Panel and its handle might distract you.

It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcuts. There are seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature.

https://www.wired.com/story/whispering-c.title: Whispering Complaints Into Your Phone May Be the Future of Customer Feedback
https://www.wired.com/story/whispering-c.author: Reece Rogers
https://www.wired.com/story/whispering-c.text:
SOME OF THE hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.

Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.

I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.

“In the last two years, we hit a tipping point,” says Karan Gupta, CEO of Voicebox, a startup designed to collect feedback via voice. “That voice could now be accurate. It could be fast.” His previous startup also relied on voice technology—an app called Alice designed for secure transcription.

Giving feedback through Voicebox is simple. Shoppers can scan a QR code or tap their phone to an NFC chip posted in a store and then say whatever they want. The feedback is automatically transcribed and sent to the company’s dashboard, with a sentiment analysis. Companies can also follow up over email, if needed. Voicebox has partnered with airport terminals so that travelers can give their two bits about bathroom messiness or gate directions.

Gupta wants this type of feedback to extend beyond corporate experiences. Earlier this year, Lena Dunham held an event in San Francisco for her book Famesick and flashed a Voicebox QR code on the screen. Numerous attendees gave feedback, sharing emotional messages about how they empathized with her medical journey. He sees this as an example of the public wanting to share more feedback more easily on topics they feel passionate about.

As part of this larger vision, Voicebox recently launched its “directory,” so feedback can be sent in from anywhere and, in future iterations, users can discover what other people are saying publicly about a specific business. I could give a quick opinion about my haircut on my way out of the barbershop by just whispering into my phone, or share advice for future visitors about navigating some hospital’s parking situation.

The directory expands Voicebox’s potential from a customer-complaint vehicle centered around business needs into something more like Google Maps, with crowd-spoken reviews. This voice-centric approach mirrors other popular software trends, where the future of dictation feels so natural that using your thumbs to tap away on a smartphone may feel cumbersome and outdated.

After chatting with Gupta, I opened the Voicebox directory and searched for, well, Voicebox. It was time for my voice to be heard. Though I’m still waiting for the couple sitting next to me at the airport to leave so I don’t feel awkward about whispering into my phone.
https://www.wired.com/story/whispering-c.summary: Voicebox is a new software that collects feedback via voice. The company has partnered with airport terminals to give travelers feedback on bathroom messiness. The directory expands Voicebox’s potential from a customer-complaint vehicle to a Google Maps vehicle.

https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-watch.title: How to Watch the Apple September Event (2026)
https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-watch.author: Boone Ashworth
https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-watch.text:
ANOTHER APPLE EVENT is almost here, though this one will likely feel a little different than the September events of lore. It’s the first Apple event since CEO Tim Cook’s departure, and might be the first time the public gets a taste of how the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, can slip into those shoes.

The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern). You can watch the stream right here on this page, or on Apple’s website and YouTube channel. Apple will also stream the event on its Apple TV devices and Apple TV+ streaming service. Leaks and rumors have left just about everyone expecting news about Pro-level iPhones and a long-awaited Apple foldable device.

Since the Covid pandemic, Apple has eschewed live presentations, instead inviting media and employees to the Apple campus to watch prerecorded videos of all its product announcements. WIRED will have reporters on the ground—you can follow along with all the action on our live blog, which will go live the morning of the event. WIRED will also have a roundup of everything the company announces for your perusal right after the event.

Thanks to leaks from sources like Bloomberg, the event is widely expected to be the moment Apple finally announces its long-rumored foldable iPhone. It’s bound to be pricey, with rumored estimates sitting around $2,000.

Apple is also expected to focus on premium products, chiefly the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4. That means Apple may push the launch of its base iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027. The move likely stems from increased manufacturing costs and limited product availability due to the ongoing memory crisis. It's also an effort to build hype for Apple’s more premium—and expensive—products, and maybe entice customers to sign up for the company’s new iPhone leasing program. We’ll likely see the mid-tier iPhone 18e at that spring event, alongside a second-gen iPhone Air.

New AirPods may also be on the table, though Apple’s heavily rumored AirPods Pro with cameras—designed to be the “eyes” of Siri for AI-powered visual assistance—could be delayed to later this year or to 2027.

If you’re hoping for new iPads, Macs, or home devices, well, you may have to wait a little longer. Apple announced a new Mac Mini and Mac Studio at the end of August, but the company may debut new home products, a new iPad Mini, and new MacBooks during events in October.

As for snagging devices right after Apple announces them this week, unconfirmed reports suggest the company will open iPhone preorders on September 12, a day later than it usually offers them, out of respect for the victims of 9/11. The following week is likely when the company will drop the final, official versions of its software, like iOS 27 and macOS 27.
https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-watch.summary: The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern) It's the first Apple event since CEO Tim Cook’s departure. The event is widely expected to be the moment Apple finally announces its long-rumored foldable iPhone.

MATTRESS DEALS COME around pretty frequently, which means you can almost always save at least some money. But the very best deals come around Memorial Day, Labor Day, Black Friday, and Cyber Monday. If you're in the market for a new bed, or you need some sleep accessories like bedding, pillows, or blankets, we've found deals on tried-and-tested favorites.

Be sure to check out our related roundups for deals on tools, outdoor gear, tech, and kitchen goods.

Updated September 7: We've added new deals from Naturepedic, Birch, Bryte, Casper, and Purple, and ensured accuracy throughout.

Use code LUXE25 at checkout to save on the best mattress we've ever tried. Out of the hundreds of options we tested, this strikes the best balance between features and price for most sleepers. Individually wrapped springs provide support and pressure relief, and six layers of cushioning mean it's cozy but not overly plush. Make sure you get deep-pocketed sheets to accommodate the 13-inch height.

The best hybrid mattress has a fabric cover that helps to wick away and disperse your body heat. If you're a hot sleeper, it can help alleviate your problems. And it can help with back pain as well, thanks to its different types of coils arranged into three strategic zones. The pillow top can make the mattress feel softer than you might expect, so keep that in mind when you're choosing between the three firmness levels.

The best mattress for side sleepers has been a personal favorite among WIRED reviewers. It offers enough support to keep side sleepers' spines aligned without pushing things out of whack. This bed is bouncy and temperature-neutral, though you can pay a bit more for a cooling pillowtop that will decrease the mattress's firmness.

This affordable mattress is even more accessibly priced for Labor Day. It's a little firm, but offers great contouring and pressure relief, and motion stays isolated. The bed also doesn't get too hot overnight. If you prefer a slightly softer bed, you might want to pair this one with a mattress topper.

We quite like this inexpensive mattress. It's literally cool to the touch and therefore ideal for hot sleepers. And while you might think of cooling beds as being more suited to summer, they can also be nice in winter, since they'll help prevent you from overheating under all those covers. It's available in three firmness levels—we think the softest would be too soft.

Our top firm pick for back pain is still fine for side sleepers. It's very firm, with five layers of foam and coils, so it might be a bit shocking at first. But the support will help prevent and possibly even alleviate sore spots and back pain, and it's a particularly good pick for couples where one person might crave additional support for their spine while sleeping. The phase change material helps keep you cool.

We quite like this organic mattress, particularly for couples due to its modular design that allows for different firmness levels on either side. If you like a soft bed and your partner likes a firm bed, this mattress might be the perfect solution. You can swap out the layers for free for 100 nights to get your firmness level perfectly dialed in.

Birch Luxe Natural Mattress

Our favorite organic mattress overall has a plus pillow top and individually wrapped coils that provide excellent support to any style of sleeper that prefers a medium firmness level. It isn't too stiff or too soft. I don't love the lack of edge support, but I do love the organic wool, latex, and cotton construction.

This smart mattress has 100 adjustable firmness levels that you can tweak on your own or let the bed do it on its own when sensing too much pressure in a certain area. There are also a lot of features to help with sleep, from the mattress rocking you to sleep to silently waking you up in the morning. You can read more about it in our in-depth review.

The Casper Dream Hybrid Mattress is a great option if you know you want memory foam. It'll contour your body and feel softer and warmer than some other beds, but thanks to the hybrid design that has coils inside, this bed won't cause more trouble than it's worth. It isn't exactly cooling, but it doesn't run too warm, and it doesn't have too much motion transfer. Consider it the elevated version of your favorite memory foam bed.

These bamboo sheets are a must-have, per resident sheet expert Nena Farrell. They're silky, soft, and cozy, with a supremely comfortable and lightweight drape. They'll make you feel sleepy right away and get even softer over time. We also like the color selection.

This is my favorite down comforter. I keep it on my bed as soon as it starts getting a little chilly out. It's fluffy and lofty, but still well ventilated, and the construction of the baffle boxes and down-proof fabric means I'm never getting stabbed with a feather in my sleep. It feels very cloud-like and is available in three warmth levels.

Our favorite mattress topper is organic. It's made with cotton and latex, so it's soft but still slightly springy and supportive. It's nice and plush but won't turn your bed into something too squishy or cradling. While it doesn't have straps, it's heavy enough to stay put.

Our favorite pillow is dense but adjustable, so you can make sure it cradles your head exactly how you want it to. This sale comes around relatively often but is still worth checking out, no matter how you like to sleep.
