https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.title: Immigrants with ischemic stroke face longer ICU stays
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.author: Richard Gawel
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Immigrants and long-term residents of Canada, including citizens, with ischemic stroke had similar rates of ICU admissions, but immigrants had longer ICU stays, according to a study published in Neurology.

Higher rates of lifesaving treatments among immigrants may drive these differences in lengths of stay, Manav V. Vyas, MD, PhD, adjunct scientist at the Institute for Clinical and Evaluative Sciences, in Toronto, and colleagues wrote.

“The number of immigrants will increase or has increased over the years because of war, persecution and climate change,” Vyas, who also is a clinician scientist with Unity Health Toronto, told Healio. “We wanted to understand how immigration status acts as a social determinant of health, especially brain health.”

Previously, Vyas and his colleagues found that immigration status did not have an impact on quality of care following a stroke, yet immigrants were leaving hospitals with greater disability.

“ICU care is quite standardized, and we have very clear indications for why people need to go to ICU,” Vyas said. “So, can we study a standardized paradigm of care for patients with stroke and see if that is also associated with immigration status?”

The population-based retrospective cohort study included 85,507 patients with ischemic stroke hospitalized in Ontario between April 1, 2014, and March 31, 2023, including 11,021 (12.9%) who were immigrants, defined by birth outside of Canada and arrival in the country after 1985.

Median ages included 69 years for the immigrant group and 76 years for long-term residents. Percentages of patients with mild stroke included 56.6% of immigrants and 46.7% of long-term residents.

The researchers said immigrants had greater odds for living in neighborhoods with fewer material resources as well as lower or similar odds for risk factors for ischemic stroke except for diabetes.

Rates of thrombolysis or thrombectomy included 17.2% for immigrants and 18% for long-term residents (P < .001). Mechanical ventilation rates included 6.5% for immigrants and 5.3% for long-term residents (P < .001).

Similar rates of other life-prolonging interventions included 0.6% for immigrants and 0.3% for long-term residents (P < .001) for craniectomies and 3% for immigrants and 1.9% for long-term residents for gastric-tube insertions (P < .001).

Other differences in outcomes included 17.5% of immigrants and 19.1% of long-term immigrants (P < .001) experiencing medical complications, 55.1% of immigrants and 49% of long-term residents (P < .001) being discharged home and 7% of immigrants and 9.3% of long-term residents (P < .001) dying during hospitalization.

ICU admission rates included 22% of immigrants and 25.8% of long-term residents (P < .001), but adjustments for covariates yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 0.97 (95% CI, 0.91-1) for ICU admission for immigrants compared with long-term residents, which Vyas and colleagues called similar.

However, immigrants who did not receive reperfusion were less likely to be admitted to the ICU than long-term residents with reperfusion (aOR = 0.92; 95% CI, 0.87-0.99), according to the researchers. Odds for death in the ICU were similar after adjustment for the groups as well (adjusted HR = 0.81-1.08).

Mean lengths of ICU stays in the unadjusted model included 5.6 days for immigrants and 3.8 days for long-term residents (P < .001), but immigrants were more likely to have longer stays after adjustment (adjusted RR = 1.3; 95% CI, 1.1-1.5).

Immigrants continued to have longer ICU stays if they had reperfusion (aRR = 1.34; 95% CI, 1.08-1.65) or if they did not have reperfusion (aRR = 1.27; 95% CI, 1.09-1.49) compared with long-term residents who did or did not have this treatment, respectively.

Odds for ICU admission fell for immigrants who migrated for economic reasons (aOR = 0.83; 95% CI, 0.76-0.91) and for those who were from Africa (aOR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.57-0.98) or Europe or the United States (aOR = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.8-0.98) compared with long-term residents as well.

Immigrants who were refugees had longer ICU stays than long-term residents (aRR = 1.48; 95% CI, 1,25-1.75) but were less likely to be admitted to an ICU (aOR = 0.95; 95% CI, 0.84-1.06).

Finally, ICU stays were longer for immigrants from Africa (aRR = 1.93; 95% CI, 1.13-3.29), East Asia (95% CI, 1.22-1.46) and the Middle East (aRR = 2.11; 95% CI, 1.64-2.72), compared with long-term residents.

Overall, the findings indicate that admission rates between immigrants and long-term residents were similar.

“Immigration status does not influence admissions to the ICU, meaning no one is left behind if they need higher critical care needs,” Vyas said. “The care is equal.”

Yet Vyas called the longer lengths of stay for immigrants “surprising.”

“You would expect that people will have the same amount of time that they would need to stay in an ICU if the reason for going to the ICU were similar,” he said.

Multiple factors may be driving these differences, Vyas said, including younger ages among the immigrant group.

“Many of them received more invasive treatments, lifesaving treatments, perhaps because they were younger,” he said. “That just shows variation in practice.”

Physicians, policymakers, caregivers and the patients themselves in the immigrant population may be more accepting of invasive treatment due to their personal biases, Vyas continued.

“When we compared this based on whether they were in hospitals that saw more immigrants, we saw no difference,” he said. “It’s not the knowledge or ability to care for immigrants that was driving this, so perhaps there’s more to understand.”

Researchers attributed lower rates of ICU admissions and other outcomes among immigrants to lower stroke severity, ineligibility due to delays in arriving at the hospital, and language barriers interfering with obtaining consent.

Language barriers also may drive longer stays for those who do enter the ICU, in addition to health literacy and varied perspectives on end-of-life care, the researchers continued.

Additionally, Vyas noted that these results may differ in the United States, which has private insurance while Canada offers universal healthcare.

“If you don’t have health insurance, you may not be able to afford or willing to have the longer length of stay, which is usually associated with higher costs,” he said.

These differences in care should be investigated, the researchers said, as structural barriers could be addressed via expanded interpreter services, stronger cultural humility training, and structural equity frameworks.

“The next step would be to truly ask people, patients and providers about what it is that they would expect to be the anchor for where interventions can be done,” Vyas said.

“Unlike treatments for many neurological diseases which focus on medications, when you’re dealing with social determinants of health, interventions are much more complex and multi-layered, and they have to influence everyone,” he said. “Talking to people, providers can help identify areas of improvement.”

Healthcare systems and clinicians can do more to mitigate these differences as well, Vyas said.

“From a policy perspective and clinician perspective, it’s important to understand the positionality of where people come from,” he said.

This includes understanding cultural preferences regarding invasive treatment, training in unconscious biases and conversations about the usefulness of treatment, in addition to ensuring that people who need good care receive it.

“If there are patients who need treatments, we should not withhold those treatments,” Vyas told Healio.

For more information:

Manav V. Vyas, MD, PhD, can be reached at ManavV.Vyas@unityhealth.to.

Data derived from Kuczynski AM, et al. Neurology. 2026;doi:10.1212/WNL0000000000218543.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Pulmonary artery denervation may work for HF-related pulmonary hypertension
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — Pulmonary artery denervation greatly lowered clinical worsening at 2 years in patients with left-sided pulmonary hypertension and heart failure, researchers reported at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

The PADN-HF-PH trial, simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine, included 264 patients (median age, 66 years; 51% men) with left-sided pulmonary hypertension and HF regardless of ejection fraction who were randomly assigned to pulmonary artery denervation (PADN system, Pulnovo Medical) plus guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) or GDMT alone, Shao-Ling Chen, MD, director of cardiology at Nanjing First Hospital, Nanjing Medical University, China, said during a presentation.

“Despite contemporary guideline-directed medical therapy, we still lack an effective treatment for patients with heart failure associated with pulmonary hypertension,” Chen said. “With understanding the central role of sympathetic and RAS activation in the heart failure development, so the PADN technology emerges. It was designed to interrupt sympathetic nerves surrounding the pulmonary artery. The consistent findings from prior studies included improvements in hemodynamics and exercise capacity, and many fewer clinical events. Unfortunately, neither of these studies provided definitively very strong power of the clinical benefit. So a large clinical trial was therefore required.”

Median follow-up was 338 days.

The Kaplan-Meier estimated 2-year incidence of the primary outcome of clinical worsening, defined as death, transplantation, HF hospitalization, outpatient worsening HF leading to IV diuresis or decline of 10% or 30 m in 6-minute walk distance, was 25.7% in the pulmonary artery denervation group and 51.1% in the medical therapy group (HR = 0.49; 95% CI, 0.3-0.82; P = .006), according to the researchers.

The secondary outcomes of clinical worsening without decline in 6-minute walk distance (HR = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.27-0.86; P = .01) and outpatient worsening as indicated by oral diuretic intensification (HR = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.3-0.78; P < .001) favored the pulmonary artery denervation group, but there was no difference between the groups in all-cause death, heart or lung transplantation, HF hospitalization, outpatient worsening as indicated by IV diuresis or decline of 10% or 30 m in 6-minute walk distance, Chen said.

The treatment effect was greater in women than in men (P for interaction = .04), which the researchers consider hypothesis-generating, Chen said.

“Also PADN improved the outcomes directly relevant to the patient, including 6-minute walk distance, [Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score] and [N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide],” Chen said during the presentation. “At 6 months of follow-up, echocardiography confirmed the PADN plus GDMT led to significant improvements in left and right heart function, notably [right ventricular] systolic pressure decreased by 13 mm Hg and the ratio of [tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion] to [systolic pulmonary artery pressure] increased by 15 in the PADN plus GDMT group.

“Our trial has several limitations,” Chen said. “No. 1 is the trial was unblinded to the operators, research personnel and patients. Secondly, secondary endpoints were not powered or adjusted for multiplicity. No. 3, we need long-term clinical follow-up, particularly beyond 3 years of follow-up, to identify the real difference in all-cause deaths or rehospitalization between two groups. Finally, all patients were in rural China. However, the generalizability and the impact of blinding are being assessed in the ongoing international sham control trial PULSE-LHD.”

In a discussant presentation, Felix Mahfoud, MD, MA, professor of cardiology at the University of Basel and chairman of the department of cardiology at University Hospital Basel, Switzerland, said the results were “quite impressive,” but “when looking more closely at the primary endpoint, the picture becomes somewhat more nuanced. Only 67 patients experienced the first primary event. There was no significant difference in death, and although the numbers were lower for heart failure hospitalization, the difference was not statistically significant. So indeed, no individual conventional component of this clinical composite was significantly improved with pulmonary denervation. But most important for me, the most relevant limitation of this trial is the lack of sham control. The physicians and patients were aware of treatment allocation. And we have learned from other trials that invasive placebos can be quite powerful.

“We have a compelling efficacy signal, [but] we require further confirmation with sham-controlled, larger trials, international with hard endpoints, and longer follow-up duration with careful phenotype selection before final conclusions can be drawn with respect to pulmonary denervation,” Mahfoud said.

Chen SL, et al. Hot line 6. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

Disclosures: Chen reports receiving speaker fees from Biomed Central, Boston Scientific, Medtronic, Microport Scientific and Pulnovo Medical, having a family member employed at Pulnovo Medical and being named on a patent held by Pulnovo Medical for a multipole synchronous pulmonary artery radiofrequency ablation catheter. Mahfoud reports receiving consultant or speaker fees from Ablative Solutions, AstraZeneca, Inari, Medtronic, Merck, Novartis, Philips and Recor Medical, and that his former institution received research support from Ablative Solutions, Medtronic and Recor Medical. The study was funded by Pulnovo Medical.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Remote option does not increase participation in cardiac rehabilitation after heart attack
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — Remote exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation did not increase participation compared with center-based cardiac rehab in patients with heart attack, according to findings presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

However, patients with the option to use a remote exercise-based program had just as much improvement in physical capacity as those who had to use a center-based program only, according to the results of the Remote Exercise SWEDEHEART study.

“Exercise as part of cardiac rehabilitation supports recovery and improves better long-term health after a heart attack. Yet only around 15% of eligible patients complete supervised center-based exercise programs,” Maria Bäck, PhD, FESC, from Sahlgrenska University Hospital and University of Gothenburg, Sweden, said during a press conference. “And therefore, we thought that remotely delivered exercise may improve access by allowing patients to exercise at home with a real-time support from a physiotherapist. Previous studies within this field are quite small, single-center [randomized controlled] studies. But whether this approach works at scale as part of routine healthcare has remained unclear.”

Bäck and colleagues conducted a cluster randomized trial of 23 Swedish centers that offered cardiac rehab programs to 3,112 patients recovering from MI (mean age, 66 years; 25% women). Centers were assigned to center-based rehabilitation only or an intervention in which patients could choose between remotely delivered exercise, center-based exercise or a combination of both, Bäck said. After 15 months, the centers crossed over to the other option, and the study continued for another 15 months.

When the remote option was available, 38% of sessions were performed remotely, Bäck said during the press conference.

Physical capacity improved by 11% in both groups and there were few serious exercise-related adverse events (center-based exercise, 0.47 per 1,000 patient-hours; remote exercise, 0.17 per 1,000 patient-hours), Bäck said.

There was no difference between the groups in mean number of completed exercise sessions, nor in the percentage of participants who completed the full exercise program (intervention period, 13.8%; control period, 13.6%), she said.

“The take-home message is that remote exercise should be viewed as an additional patient-centered option within cardiac rehabilitation, but not as a standalone solution to low participation rates,” Bäck said during the press conference. “Remotely delivered exercise was indeed used when available. It produced similar improvements in physical capacity, and it was associated with few serious exercise-related adverse events. But it did not increase overall participation. Therefore, cardiac telerehabilitation can be viewed as a more personalized form of cardiac rehabilitation, including the option to exercise remotely from home, which may better meet individual patient needs and preferences.”

Quality of life data were collected and will be reported later, she said.

Bäck M, et al. Hot line 5. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

Disclosures: Bäck reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: FDA adds boxed warning to Injectafer for hypophosphatemia risk
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The FDA added a boxed warning detailing the known risk for symptomatic hypophosphatemia associated with ferric carboxymaltose injection, according to an agency press release.

The boxed warning recommends phosphate monitoring for patients at risk for hypophosphatemia and any patients who receive a repeat course of therapy within 3 months of the prior course. Generic ferric carboxymaltose injection products are also expected to update their labels to reflect the added boxed warning, according to the release.

Ferric carboxymaltose injection (Injectafer, Daiichi Sankyo/American Regent), a prescription iron replacement medicine given intravenously, is approved by the FDA for patients aged 1 year and older who cannot tolerate or do not fully respond to oral iron. It is also approved for adults with chronic kidney disease not on dialysis with iron deficiency and adults with New York Heart Association class II/III heart failure with iron deficiency to improve exercise capacity.

The decision to add the boxed warning stemmed from an assessment of multiple data sources, including the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System and literature reports. Multiple cases of symptomatic hypophosphatemia tied to single and multiple infusions of ferric carboxymaltose injection were reported despite previous labeling revisions in 2020 and 2023 emphasizing the risk, according to the FDA release.

Additionally, data from the FDA’s Sentinel System show serum phosphate testing occurred in fewer than 20% of ferric carboxymaltose injection administration episodes, according to the release.

Hypophosphatemia may manifest differently based on condition severity and duration, with symptoms including muscle weakness or pain, fatigue, tremors, confusion, seizures and cardiac arrhythmias, according to the release. Serious adverse outcomes associated with ferric carboxymaltose injection include hospitalization, a need for prolonged phosphate replacement therapy, osteomalacia and bone fractures.

Clinicians should inform patients about the risk for hypophosphatemia associated with ferric carboxymaltose injection, according to the release. Clinicians should also continue to monitor serum phosphate levels for at-risk patients and consider permanent discontinuation for persistent hypophosphatemia or severe chronic hypophosphatemia, according to the release.

On September 1, 2026, the FDA approved a labeling change to ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) that adds a boxed warning describing the risk for severe symptomatic hypophosphatemia. The warning recommends phosphate monitoring for patients at risk for hypophosphatemia and for any patient who receives a repeat course of therapy within 3 months.

The development of hypophosphatemia has been associated with all IV iron products that employ a carbohydrate iron shell, including iron dextran, ferumoxytol, FCM and ferric derisomaltose, and is attributed to the phosphaturic effects of fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF-23), the synthesis of which is induced by the carbohydrate moiety. Iron sucrose and sodium ferric gluconate, which do not employ a carbohydrate shell, are not associated with hypophosphatemia.

The incidence of hypophosphatemia with FCM is significantly higher than that with other agents, averaging around 40% in clinical trials and observational studies depending on the patient population, dosing and definitions utilized. The majority of serum phosphorus reductions with FCM are small and transient. More severe and prolonged hypophosphatemia may lead to the “6-H syndrome” with high FGF-23 level, hypophosphatemia, hyperphosphaturia, hypovitaminosis D, hypocalcemia and secondary hyperthyroidism. Deteriorating mobility and multiple fractures, akin to tumor-induced osteomalacia, have been reported.

In patients with nondialysis-dependent CKD and iron deficiency who have failed oral iron therapy or have more severe iron deficiency, IV FCM is an attractive therapeutic option since 1,000 mg can be administered in 15 minutes, unlike iron dextran, which requires a 2 to 4-hour infusion to administer 1,000 mg, or iron sucrose, sodium ferric gluconate or ferumoxytol, which require multiple infusions to deliver 1,000 mg. A single, shorter visit is more patient-friendly and preserves veins for future hemodialysis vascular access.

FCM has a lower rate of severe allergic reactions than iron dextran, ferumoxytol or ferric derisomaltose. In patients with nondialysis-dependent CKD who receive FCM, risk factors for the development of hypophosphatemia include pre-existing secondary hyperparathyroidism, significant residual renal function and concomitant therapy with bisphosphonates or diuretics. The recently published Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative commentary on the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes 2026 anemia guideline recommends prompt assessment of serum phosphate levels for patients presenting with progressive fatigue, bone pain or muscular weakness during FCM therapy to minimize complications associated with hypophosphatemia (Jalal DI, et al. Am J Kidney Dis. 2026;doi:10.1053/j.ajkd.2026.03.036). If hypophosphatemia is present, it should be repleted as indicated and additional IV iron, if needed, should be switched to a formulation other than FCM.

The most severe cases of FCM-induced symptomatic hypophosphatemia have been reported in patients requiring multiple, repeated doses of FCM for bleeding due to gynecologic and gastrointestinal disorders, not nondialysis-dependent CKD patients who may require occasional doses of FCM once or twice per year. According to the consensus statement of a multispecialty expert panel, routine serum phosphate level measurement is not recommended for low-risk patients before or after treatment with FCM, and prophylactic oral phosphorus after FCM is unlikely to effectively elevate phosphate and is not recommended for routine clinical practice (Rosano G, et al. J Clin Med. 2025;doi:10.3390/jcm14144861).

Because of its ease of administration and low rate of severe allergic reactions, FCM remains an attractive IV iron supplement despite the new boxed warning from the FDA regarding severe symptomatic hypophosphatemia, which is rare in patients with nondialysis-dependent CKD with occasional use.

https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.title: Can AI address Data bias and integrity?
https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.author: Josh Friedman; Chadi Nabhan, MD, MBA
https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The internet went mainstream less than 40 years ago, yet it is hard to remember the world without it.

Chadi Nabhan, MD, MBA, hematologist, medical oncologist, podcaster and author, believes the same will hold true for AI in the not-so-distant future.

“There’s no way around it. AI is here to stay,” Nabhan told Healio. “Humans who are smart in using AI will advance better and faster in life and in career than humans who do not embrace AI.”

The same holds true in healthcare. Clinicians and institutions that best utilize AI will likely have the greatest impact on patients.

Barriers remain to unlocking AI’s full potential, though.

AI models continue to be trained on biased and inaccurate data, which limits practical application to real-world patients, Nabhan and colleagues discussed at the third Collaboration for Outcomes Using Social Media in Oncology (COSMO) Conference in Chicago.

“If you always believe everything that you’re being told, you’re going to make mistakes,” Nabhan said.

Healio spoke with Nabhan about AI bias and integrity, how it impacts equity and ways to improve it in the future.

Healio: What is AI bias?

Nabhan: The data that are being used in the algorithm to create the output representative of patients with cancer being seen in the real world.

Most oncology datasets, especially datasets being used to train AI algorithms, are not random samples. Most of the datasets represent patients from large academic centers, patients who have undergone genomic testing, possibly patients who are insured, who had access to healthcare. If there were patients on clinical trials, they were healthy enough to get on clinical trials, and patients who have more longitudinal follow-ups.

If we are training AI models on these data, the output may not be representative of all patients with cancer who are seen across community clinics in America.

Let’s say you have a model about managing prostate cancer, but that model was developed based on white men who are 75 years of age, can you realistically apply that model on a Black man who is 45 years old who has the same disease? I argue that you can’t.

Healio: What is the solution?

Nabhan: Before we deploy the model, before we say that this is a great model and could be utilized in making decisions, we should validate it.

There’s a training cohort and a validation cohort. You characterize the model using this training population from the datasets that you have, but then you should validate it, and you should validate it in a cohort that represents patients from the real world. These are patients who are in community practices, could be seen in rural settings. They are different racial and ethnic groups. While many datasets include predominantly Caucasian patients, the U.S. Census suggests that 25% of the U.S. population is underrepresented minorities. That’s very important to understand and take into context.

Healio: What is AI integrity?

Nabhan: Integrity asks the question of whether the data are correct.

Imagine there is a patient in the electronic health records who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS), and that patient is biomarker negative. That’s patient A. In contrast, we have patient B who has never undergone NGS. AI could view these two patients as identically not having an actionable mutation. While this may appear true on the surface, patient A did have NGS, and was biomarker negative, but patient B never had the test done to begin with. The AI reported no actionable mutation on patient B because nothing was recorded in the EHR given the lack of testing . AI can’t really understand that difference. They can only read the fact that these two patients don’t have biomarkers.

Absence of evidence in the medical record is not evidence of absence.

Healio: How can that problem be solved?

Nabhan: AI systems need to be trained to differentiate between unknown vs. negative.

Let’s say a clinical trial is looking for a patient that is biomarker negative. To decide on eligibility, the AI should be able to tell you if the eligibility cannot be determined because required molecular testing has not been performed vs. the patient is not eligible because the patient is indeed biomarker negative. That nuance is important and it does play a role in equity.

Healio: Why would EHRs have inaccurate data?

Nabhan: EHRs are messy. We use a lot of copy, paste and forward. We have a lot of outdated problem lists. A lot of physicians don’t update the problem list on the patient every single time.

I had a patient, who, when they were reviewing their records, noticed that I still said they were a smoker, and they were upset with me. They said, “Doc, you know I quit 5 years ago.” I apologized, but the reality is, for a lot of us in a very busy clinic, we don’t always update this information, so it’s missing. Sometimes there is incorrect staging. Sometimes you have incomplete treatment histories.

Imagine a patient had a particular test done at a different hospital and it’s not linked to the EHR at the current hospital. You don’t have that information integrated into the existing records. Sometimes genomic records are integrated in the EHR. Sometimes they’re coming through PDFs, and the nurse or the doctor forgot to scan it.

If you have AI models trained on EHRs, you are held hostage based on the data that exist in the EHRs even if some were inaccurate. AI doesn’t necessarily correct bad data.

Healio: How can data accuracy be assured?

Nabhan: That’s the million-dollar question. The short answer, unfortunately, it can’t. It’s dependent on what the human enters, unless you have somebody else checking the work.

What AI could be trained to do is detect inconsistencies. For example, if in my note I write that the patient quit smoking and the EHR still shows that he is a smoker, maybe I get something on the screen saying, there’s inconsistency here, please double check.

Healio: How can AI help with health equity?

Nabhan: Expertise in cancer care can be geography dependent. If you live in Chicago, New York, or a large metropolitan area, your access to expertise is much easier than if you live in rural America, where you sometimes have one doctor for 100,000 people.

AI could solve this, because it provides physicians access to state-of-the-art information through large language models.

Healio: Will AI help or hinder equity in healthcare?

Nabhan: It depends how it’s used. Every single technology we have has pluses and minuses. The internet has pluses and minuses.

On balance though, I believe that AI is net positive despite some of the issues and shortcomings we highlighted. Nothing is perfect. If we’re able to refine the algorithms, make sure that the data are getting better with time and represent people that we are seeing in the real world, the output could be very helpful.

If you’ve seen a difficult patient, you often have called your colleague for a consultation. Now, you call ChatGPT for a consultation. These large language models search lots of datasets, databases and so on, and bring you back various opinions that hopefully represent your patient. You are still in charge, but I think it’s going to help you provide better care.

I am an AI enthusiast. I believe it’s helping patients, families, caregivers and physicians.

Healio: How can AI shortcomings be mitigated?

Nabhan: No. 1, human in the middle is very important. This is an ancillary service. Ultimately, the human must interpret the information.

No. 2 is validation. If the data being used to create the model do not represent the people that you are treating in the real world, that output is not going to be very helpful. If it’s going to be implemented to take care of patients, into decision-making, it must be validated.

Healio: How should clinicians view AI long term?

Nabhan: Cautiously optimistic. AI is going to continue to be part of everything that we do. If we were in the year 1999 and you told me, I don’t want to use the internet, I hate the internet, it’s sloppy. Yes, it was sloppy, but how could you live without the internet? It’s the same thing with AI.

Our goal is to train patients, students and fellows to understand AI and utilize it smartly and effectively and be cognizant of its shortcomings. Let’s work together on mitigating some of these issues, because they are going to be mitigated with time.

I think these issues will be addressed in 5 years, I really do. The validation models are already happening. I’m also very optimistic about how AI is going to change the way we do clinical trials.

Healio: How can AI help with clinical trials?

Nabhan: Clinical trials take a long time. Most could take 10 to 12 years to complete, and they are costly. That length could delay patients’ access to [life-saving drugs]. AI could help with that. It could help with clinical trial matching. For example, if you have a clinical trial at your center and you have a patient that you are seeing in clinic that matches available clinical trials at your institution, it could be flagged.

The other way for AI to help with clinical trials is in selecting the proper research sites. Many clinical trials open at sites that are not going to enroll on this particular study. If we’re able to use AI to help select the most appropriate sites for a specific trial, this will expedite that trial.

Healio: Is there anything else you would like to emphasize?

Nabhan: In my book, “AI and Cancer Care,” that is coming out on Dec. 1, I surveyed and spoke to many people from across all sectors; many were not doctors. People at the gym, people at Starbucks, people who are at Walgreens, and so on. I asked them who do you think should govern AI? Nobody wanted the government to govern AI, because they were nervous that the government would be too slow and too bureaucratic to govern this very innovative technology. At the same time, nobody wanted the private sector to govern AI because of the conflict of interest.

On the COSMO panel, we really did not have a solution, but I proposed a combination between the private and the public sector, where you have both sides coordinating the governance and have a lot of guardrails to make sure that this is not getting out of control.

Chadi Nabhan, MD, MBA, can be reached at cnabhan1968@gmail.com.

AI Bias, Data Integrity and Equity in Digital Oncology. Presented at: COSMO Conference; Aug. 7-8, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Nabhan reports being chief medical officer at Ryght AI and an affiliate at the University of South Carolina.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Resolution blocks proposed changes to grantmaking process
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

A continuing resolution that averts a government shutdown also has implications for the federal grantmaking process.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 6500 on Sept. 1, and President Donald Trump signed it into law on Sept. 2. The stopgap funding bill temporarily blocks proposed changes to the federal grantmaking process. The House vote was bipartisan, with 370 “yes” votes and 48 “no” votes. Fourteen members were recorded as not voting.

As Healio previously reported, the Office of Management and Budget proposed what experts called “an unprecedented shift” in the way the federal government determines how to distribute grant funding. It would move away from the peer-review process to a system that allows political appointees to decide what should be funded and federal officials to cancel grant funding at any time.

But the continuing resolution blocks the Office of Management and Budget from finalizing and implementing the changes until Dec. 11.

The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and HIV Medicine Association (HIVMA) released a statement applauding Congress “for its swift and overwhelmingly bipartisan approval” of the resolution.

“The proposed rule would overhaul federal grant processes; replace peer review, scientific merit and patient needs with political alignment; and upend federal support for medical research and public health with devastating consequences that would leave our nation far more vulnerable to infectious diseases and put ending the HIV epidemic further out of reach,” IDSA President Ronald G. Nahass, MD, MHCM, FIDSA, and HIVMA Chair Anna K. Person, MD, FIDSA, wrote. “We call upon Congress to enact a long-term solution to protect the patients, communities, clinicians and researchers who rely on federally funded research to deliver lifesaving prevention and treatment and public health infrastructure to prevent and track serious health threats.”

*Editor’s note: This story was updated after the resolution was signed into law on Sept .2 to reflect that information.

H.R. 6500. https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6500. Accessed Sept. 2, 2026.

Congressional bill H.R. 6500 signed into law. https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2026/09/congressional-bill-h-r-6500-signed-into-law/. Published Sept. 2, 2026. Accessed Sept. 4, 2026.

Disclosures: Nahass is president of the IDSA. Person is chair of the HIVMA.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Wearable ECG monitor boosts arrhythmia detection after syncope
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Katie Kalvaitis
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — Starting 14-day ECG monitoring immediately after ED assessment for unexplained syncope did not result in fewer patient-reported recurrent episodes at 1 year compared with standard care, according to results of the ASPIRED trial.

However, early use of a wearable patch for 14 days more than doubled detection of serious arrhythmias and led to more patients receiving treatment, researchers reported at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

The ASPIRED trial, simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine, included 2,234 patients (mean age, 58.3 years; 52.1% men; 89% white) who visited 45 EDs in the United Kingdom with syncope that remained unexplained after evaluation. Almost 50% had previous syncope, according to the researchers. Researchers randomly assigned patients within 72 hours of the ED visit to 14-day ambulatory ECG monitoring with the BodyGuardian Mini device (Boston Scientific Cardiac Diagnostics) or standard care, which included inpatient telemetry and ambulatory monitoring. Patients wore the device for 14 days during daily activities and were followed for 1 year using text, email and phone calls every 4 weeks.

“Millions of people attend EDs across the world every year with syncope. We find it difficult in the ED to diagnose everybody. Fifty percent are discharged from the ED with an unexplained cause. Many will be benign, but some will have a cardiac cause. ... Our study looked at whether earlier and longer monitoring could improve diagnosis,” Matthew James Reed, MD, an emergency physician with the Usher Institute at the University of Edinburgh and the Emergency Medicine Research Group Edinburgh (EMERGE) at Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, said during a press conference.

For the primary outcome, there was no significant difference in the mean number of patient-reported episodes of syncope at 1 year, at 1.37 in the early monitoring group vs. 1.58 in the standard care group (incidence rate ratio = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.68-1.18; P = .42), Reed said during the presentation.

Recurrence rates were low, Reed said, at 28% in the early ECG monitoring group vs. 28.6% in the standard care group.

Early ECG monitoring identified a clinically significant cardiac arrhythmia in 22% of patients vs. 9% with standard care (OR = 2.95; 95% CI, 2.28-3.81).

Median time to detection was 22 days vs. 54.5 days, according to the results. This included the time it took to get fitted with the device, return the device, interpretation of the data and results sent to the treating physician, Reed said.

The researchers noted that most clinically significant arrhythmias were detected within 7 days.

Early monitoring also picked up more symptomatic cardiac arrhythmias (9.3% vs. 5.9%; OR = 1.66; 95% CI, 1.2-2.31), Reed said.

More patients in the early ECG monitoring group received prompt treatment, including antiarrhythmic therapy (10.8% vs. 7.3%) or pacemaker implantation (6.8% vs. 4.6%).

“We believe this may provide a biologically plausible mechanism for halving of all-cause mortality at 1 year,” Reed said during the presentation.

At 1 year, death from any cause was reported in 1.5% of the early ECG monitoring group vs. 2.9% of the standard care group (OR = 0.5; 95% CI, 0.27-0.93), according to the results.

Fifty-seven adverse events were reported (49 in the early ECG monitoring group) and most were mild, mainly skin irritation due to electrode adhesive.

Reed said patients found the patch easy to use because it could be worn while sleeping, during physical activity and showering.

The researchers noted several limitations of the trial, including its open-label design; possible detection and reporting bias; and a lower-than-anticipated recurrence of syncope overall. Still, they said, the results may be generalizable to other settings, given the trial’s large size and broadly representative population of patients presenting with syncope. The ongoing REMOSYNCED trial will further evaluate this monitoring in different clinical settings, according to the researchers.

“So, we think starting monitoring immediately, soon after the ED attendance ... for unexplained fainting, can diagnose more serious heart rhythms, can diagnose them sooner, allow early treatment and we can potentially save lives. Evidence for heart monitoring such as this should become routine care for patients who present to the ED with unexplained fainting,” Reed said.

During a discussion following the presentation, Michele Brignole, MD, FESC, with the Faint & Fall Research Center at IRCCS Instituto Auxologico Italiano in Milan, said “technically this is a negative trial.

“Nevertheless, the ASPIRED trial provides two very important findings: It allowed a higher detection rate of clinically significant arrhythmias in 22% of cases and reduced all-cause mortality by 50%. However, the direct cause-effect relationship between arrhythmias and all-cause mortality remains uncertain. My alternative plausible biological mechanism is that the reduction in all-cause mortality may reflect more thorough investigations following arrhythmia detection.”

Reed MJ, et al. Hot line 10. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

Disclosures: Brignole reports no relevant financial disclosures. Reed reports being supported by an NHS Research Scotland Career Researcher Clinician award. Boston Scientific Cardiac Diagnostics provided the heart monitor used in this study, but had no other involvement. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/pulmonology/.title: CPAP lowers blood pressure more in patients with OSA and insomnia
https://www.healio.com/news/pulmonology/.author: Isabella Hornick
https://www.healio.com/news/pulmonology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Adults with both obstructive sleep apnea and insomnia vs. only obstructive sleep apnea had larger decreases in 24-hour, daytime and nocturnal systolic blood pressure following 4 weeks of CPAP, according to data published in CHEST.

“These findings underscore the potential for a more personalized management strategy for [blood pressure] management in patients with OSA, where the presence of comorbid insomnia may signal a subgroup with a distinct and favorable hemodynamic response to CPAP therapy,” Shuang Li, MD, of Capital Medical University in China, and colleagues wrote.

In a prospective cohort study, Li and colleagues evaluated 71 adults (mean age, 40.9 years; 93% men) with OSA (median apnea-hypopnea index [AHI], 54.4 events/hour) and elevated blood pressure (BP) who completed 4-week auto-CPAP therapy to determine if the change in 24-hour systolic BP from before to after the therapy differs between patients with comorbid insomnia and patients without this comorbidity.

This cohort included 22 patients with comorbid insomnia and OSA (COMISA; mean age, 39.7 years; 95.5% men; median AHI, 50.6 events/hour) and 49 patients with OSA only (mean age, 41.5 years; 91.8% men; median AHI, 54.4 events/hour).

Twenty-four-hour systolic BP among patients with COMISA fell by 6 mmHg after the CPAP therapy, which was significantly larger than the 0.3 mmHg reduction in patients with OSA only (P = .002). Importantly, the study outlined that a decrease of at least 5 mmHg signaled a clinically meaningful reduction in this BP.

In terms of daytime systolic BP, researchers also found a significantly greater drop in this measure after the CPAP treatment period among those with COMISA vs. OSA only (–5.2 mmHg vs. –0.2 mmHg; P = .013). This was also the case for nocturnal systolic BP (–9.5 mmHg vs. 1 mmHg; P = .001).

Following adjustment for age, sex, BMI and sleepiness, the odds for a clinically meaningful reduction in 24-hour systolic BP were significantly increased among those with insomnia symptoms at baseline (adjusted OR = 5.05; 95% CI, 1.64-15.55). Researchers continued to find this outcome in five other multivariate logistic regression models adjusted for the same four confounders plus:

In the model adjusted for age, sex, BMI, sleepiness, baseline BP, AHI, LSpO2 and CPAP adherence, no significant link was found between insomnia and 24-hour systolic BP reduction (greater than 0 mmHg) or between insomnia and daytime systolic BP reduction.

In contrast, the odds for a reduction in nocturnal systolic BP were significantly higher among those with baseline insomnia symptoms (aOR = 4.76; 95% CI, 1.21-18.72). This link lost significance following Bonferroni correction, according to the study.

Researchers further divided the patients based on good CPAP adherence (n = 40) and poor CPAP adherence (n = 31) and found a nonsignificant greater decrease in 24-hour, daytime and nocturnal systolic BP after 4 weeks of CPAP among those with good vs. poor adherence.

Twenty-four-hour, daytime and nocturnal systolic BP each significantly fell from baseline to after CPAP in the group with good adherence but not in the group with poor adherence.

Among those with good CPAP adherence, 24-hour systolic BP in patients with COMISA fell by 6.8 mmHg after the CPAP therapy, which was significantly larger than the 1.5 mmHg reduction in patients with OSA only (P = .026).

“Good CPAP adherence is critical but challenged by insomnia-induced intolerance,” Li and colleagues wrote. “Future strategies should therefore combine insomnia-targeted interventions with CPAP to improve tolerance and potentially achieve synergistic cardiovascular benefits.”

Li S, et al. CHEST. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.chest.2026.07.5226.

Disclosures: The authors report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.title: Low hydroxychloroquine markers linked to heart risk in lupus
https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.author: Max R. Wursta
https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and sustained low hydroxychloroquine blood levels may be at significantly increased risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, according to data published in Arthritis Care & Research.

“Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of SLE management because it reduces disease activity, prevents flares, limits organ damage accrual and has been associated with cardiovascular protection,” Shivani Garg, MD, PhD, director of the Yale Lupus Program, told Healio. “This study provides hypothesis-generating evidence that optimizing both HCQ blood levels and long-term adherence may influence cardiovascular risk in SLE.”

In a prospective longitudinal study, Garg and colleagues analyzed data from 248 adult patients with SLE who took HCQ and had minimum 1-year follow-up. Their goal was to examine how HCQ blood levels and long-term intake impact atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk at baseline and 1 year.

The researchers assessed patients’ long-term HCQ intake using proportion of days covered (PDC), as well as HCQ blood levels. Low long-term HCQ intake was defined as PDC of less than 80%, while very low HCQ blood level was defined as less than 200 ng/mL.

“Measuring HCQ blood levels provides an objective assessment of recent drug exposure, while refill-based measures capture long-term intake patterns,” Garg said.

Researchers used the PREVENT calculator to assess patients’ 10-year risk for ASCVD.

At baseline, patients with low long-term intake and very low HCQ blood levels demonstrated 2.1% greater risk for ASCVD and a mean predicted risk of 6.6%, according to the researchers. In addition, patients who sustained low HCQ markers, and patients who transitioned from high HCQ markers to low HCQ markers over 1 year, had the greatest predicted risk for ASCVD.

“These findings suggest that both adequate HCQ exposure and sustained adherence over time may be important contributors to reducing cardiovascular risk in SLE,” Garg said.

“Physicians should consider HCQ blood level monitoring and longitudinal adherence measures as complementary tools to support clinical decision-making,” she told Healio. “Together, these measures can help identify patients with inadequate exposure, distinguish nonadherence from pharmacokinetic variability, guide patient counseling and reinforce the long-term benefits of HCQ therapy.”

Shivani Garg, MD, PhD, can be reached at shivani.garg@yale.edu.

Garg S, et al. Arthritis Care Res. 2026;doi:10.1002/acr.80128.

Disclosures: Garg reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.title: Taltz, Zepbound combo yields sustained improvement at 1 year in psoriatic disease, obesity
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.author: Gabrielle M. Grasso
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Adults with moderate to severe psoriatic disease and overweight or obesity saw sustained or continued improvement in disease activity at 1 year with tirzepatide plus ixekizumab vs. ixekizumab monotherapy, according to a Lilly press release.

One-year data from the phase 3b, randomized, double-blind, open-label TOGETHER-PsO and TOGETHER-PsA trials build on the previously reported 36-week findings that showed marked improvement in psoriatic disease outcomes and body weight among people who received combination therapy with ixekizumab (Taltz, Lilly), an IL-17A inhibitor, and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Lilly), a dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide agonist, vs. ixekizumab monotherapy.

“Psoriatic disease is often accompanied by obesity or overweight, which can make treatment goals related to the skin and joints harder to reach,” Joseph F. Merola, MD, MMSc, FAAD, professor and chair of dermatology and professor of internal medicine in the division of rheumatic diseases at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, said in the release. “In psoriatic arthritis, the greater improvements in disease activity seen with Taltz and Zepbound in the first month, before clinically meaningful weight loss occurred, continued through 1 year. In psoriasis, the durability of complete skin clearance at 1 year represents real, lasting progress for patients. Paired with continued metabolic improvements, these findings show what may be possible when treating psoriatic disease and obesity concurrently.”

TOGETHER-PsO enrolled 274 adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis and TOGETHER-PsA enrolled 271 adults with active psoriatic arthritis. In both trials, participants also had obesity or overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbid condition. All participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive ixekizumab plus tirzepatide or ixekizumab monotherapy, and counseled on diet and physical activity.

In both trials, improvement in the primary outcome continued through 52 weeks, according to the release.

In TOGETHER-PsO, 30.6% of participants who received combination therapy vs. 4.4% who received monotherapy achieved the primary multicomponent endpoint of PASI 100 and a 10% or greater reduction in body weight by week 52. More than 40% of participants who received combination therapy achieved complete skin clearance by week 52 vs. 29.1% in the monotherapy group, according to the release.

In TOGETHER-PsA, 39.2% of the combination group vs. 1.7% of the monotherapy group achieved the primary outcome of 50% or greater reduction in psoriatic arthritis disease activity based on American College of Rheumatology 50 plus at least 10% weight loss by week 52. The proportion of participants who achieved a 50% or greater reduction in psoriatic arthritis disease severity without weight loss by week 52 was 43.7% in the combination therapy group and 15.7% in the monotherapy group, according to the release.

Inflammatory and metabolic markers, including high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, BMI, blood pressure, glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides and total cholesterol improved and were sustained through 52 weeks among the combination therapy groups in both trials.

“The 52-week topline data from these trials adds more evidence that in patients who are overweight or obese treating psoriatic disease holistically by adding a GLP-1 agonist to a biologic results in not only better metabolic outcomes, but also better outcomes in the skin and the joints,” Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, professor of dermatology and epidemiology at University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and Healio Dermatology’s Chief Medical Editor, told Healio. “I routinely recommend GLP-1 agonists when indicated to my patients with psoriatic disease with the goal of not just improving their skin and joint disease, but also their overall cardiometabolic health.”

Adverse events among participants treated with ixekizumab plus tirzepatide across the trials at 52 weeks were mild to moderate in severity and were consistent with the known safety profiles of each medication. Adverse events occurring in 5% or more participants who received combination therapy in both trials included nausea, diarrhea, constipation, injection site reactions, vomiting, dizziness and headache.

The 52-week results from TOGETHER-PsO and TOGETHER-PsA will be presented at future medical meetings and published in peer-reviewed journals, the company stated.

Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, is the James J. Leyden Professor of Clinical Investigation and professor of dermatology and epidemiology at University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and Healio Dermatology’s Chief Medical Editor. Gelfand can be reached at dermatology@healio.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Catheter ablation for AF does not improve quality of life vs. sham procedure in new trial
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — In patients with atrial fibrillation, catheter ablation did not improve quality of life at 6 months compared with a sham procedure, according to the PVI-SHAM-AF trial presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

However, fewer patients in the catheter ablation group had recurrent AF at 6 months compared with the sham group.

The results differ from the SHAM-PVI trial presented at the ESC Congress in 2024 and published in JAMA, which found that catheter ablation improved quality of life compared with a sham procedure.

The PVI-SHAM-AF trial, simultaneously published in The Lancet, included 262 patients with symptomatic AF from nine sites in Germany and Poland who were indicated for catheter ablation in accordance with ESC guidelines, Rolf Wachter, MD, professor at the Clinic and Polyclinic for Cardiology at University Hospital Leipzig in Germany, said during a press conference.

“We started with the question, what is the real effect of catheter ablation on quality of life?” Wachter said during the press conference. “To do this, we did a randomized multicenter double-blind trial and we found out that ... catheter ablation did not prove superiority to the sham procedure for improvement in the prespecified [Atrial Fibrillation Effect on the Quality of Life Questionnaire] summary score at 6 months.”

The sham procedure consisted of conscious sedation and two punctures in the groin, but no transeptal puncture or electrophysiological testing in the left atrium, Wachter said. In both groups, any patient who went into AF during the procedure was cardioverted, according to Wachter.

The AFEQT score improved from 61.3 at baseline to 81.1 at 6 months in the catheter ablation group and from 59.2 at baseline to 74.9 at 6 months in the sham group (between-group difference in change from baseline to 6 months = 2.6; 95% CI, 2.7 to 8; P = .36), Wachter said.

“We were surprised,” Wachter said during the press conference. “It probably shows that our sham was pretty good. Two years ago, there was a trial presented here, and they had a similar effect on AFEQT by catheter ablation, but not so much by the sham.”

The percentage of patients with AF at 6 months was 21% in the catheter ablation group and 41% in the sham group (difference, 20.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 32.6 to 7.7), the researchers found.

“We had a symptomatic improvement observed after ablation, but this cannot necessarily be attributed entirely to the ablation procedure, although other sham control trials have reported an incremental quality of life benefit,” Wachter said during the press conference. “Clinical counseling should consider data from sham control trials along the broader evidence base. The main finding is that we have to distinguish objective rhythm control benefits from effects on patient-reported quality of life. As a more general remark, the impact of the technical procedure catheter ablation probably has been overestimated in previous research, and we have underestimated the impact of active human care on these patients. Future research is needed to identify the patients who obtain most symptomatic benefits from catheter ablation.”

When asked by Healio at the press conference whether the results change his opinion on who should receive catheter ablation, Wachter said “if quality of life is the one and only reason [to offer ablation], I think we should look closer than before.”

Wachter R, et al. Hot line 8. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmolog.title: Much preparation needed to become a speaker, key opinion leader
https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmolog.author: Richard L. Lindstrom, MD
https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

See all articles from Lindstrom’s Perspective

Click here to read the Healio Exclusive, “Experience builds confidence when it comes to speaking at meetings.”

I am often asked by residents, fellows and younger ophthalmologists to share the pathway to becoming a key opinion leader in ophthalmology and a regular invited speaker at educational meetings.

In the following paragraphs, I will share a few thoughts gained from my personal journey as a lecturer and a frequent organizer of educational programs today.

Remember, there is no elevator to success or excellence as a key opinion leader (KOL) or speaker — you must take the stairs. The first stair is quality training including, for most, one or more years of post-residency fellowship. I personally completed three fellowships after residency, the first in cornea and external disease at the University of Minnesota, the second in advanced microsurgery at a busy surgical academic private practice in Dallas, and the third in glaucoma at the University of Utah supported by the Heed Ophthalmic Foundation. These fellowships provided extremely valuable clinical training and a strong knowledge base as well as a solid set of credentials supporting expertise.

Next, it is important to build a busy clinical practice. You cannot be a credible educator of other clinicians unless you have strong clinical experience. As you grow your clinical experience, you will become passionate about one or more areas of clinical practice. Focus on these areas of interest and study global literature to become a true expert in your chosen topics. Then, compile and evaluate your own clinical outcomes and compare them with world literature. Collaborating with an industry partner and performing an investigator-initiated clinical trial in your area of interest is a good way to strengthen this process. Once complete, you will have a unique set of personal data and clinical insights useful to others, including your colleagues and industry.

The next step is to get invited to share your thoughts and insights at a meeting. Here, a residency or fellowship mentor, senior partner or industry representative can help.

Finally, when invited to present to your colleagues at an educational event, it is critical to take the time and effort required to deliver an outstanding presentation. It is important to know that once you are at the podium, you will have a critical audience. Your presentation with be critiqued by the meeting organizer, in many cases a panel of expert colleagues, meeting attendees and any industry representatives present.

The lecture you give must end on time, be delivered smoothly with support from high-quality audiovisual PowerPoints and/or video, and be free from commercial bias. If you fail in any of these regards, you are much less likely to be invited to present again. If you succeed, you will find yourself a regular speaker as your reputation as an excellent and honest educator expands by word of mouth among those who have the responsibility to organize quality educational programs for their colleagues. Always present information that is evidence based with references, clinically useful and unbiased, while being presented in the time allotted with a high-quality delivery style.

Once positioned as a quality speaker with useful information to share, you will find yourself in demand to participate in industry-sponsored clinical trials, join medical advisory boards, participate in leadership positions at ophthalmology societies and over time become a meeting organizer yourself. You will be a KOL!

Now, a few thoughts on how to prepare and present a quality medical lecture. An excellent lecture has a central idea and provides information that can be used immediately to improve a colleague’s clinical or business performance when returning to their practice. It is important to know your audience, know your subject matter, prepare your presentation well in advance and practice the talk repeatedly at home.

Every lecture has an architecture. Dress appropriately for the setting. Adjust the microphone before you begin to speak. Speak in an audible, purposeful, paced fashion and make eye contact with the audience right, left, center, front and back. Pause and direct the audience view to the PowerPoint presentation when appropriate to emphasize key points. Start by telling the audience what you are going to teach them, teach with your verbal and audiovisual presentation, and then, when closing, tell them again what you taught them. Case presentations are a powerful and memorable way to illustrate diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic choices and keep listeners engaged by making them think during the presentation.

Just like no one is born a great surgeon, no one is born a great orator. It helps to critically observe other speakers. One can learn from good and bad speaker examples. Adopt a style you find attractive and emulate it through practice. Training courses such as Dale Carnegie and Toastmasters are available as are personal coaches. Many universities, colleges, societies and some companies offer speaker training programs. Ask a few friendly colleagues and mentors to critique your presentations and offer constructive advice. If your presentation is recorded or on video, watch it and learn, just like you would review a video of your surgical procedures.

Like every other skill, practice makes perfect, and your presentation skills will improve over time. Be patient with yourself and do not expect to be perfect at first. Remember that while it is an honor and gratifying to be chosen to teach your colleagues, it is also a significant responsibility. Never forget that what you teach has the potential to impact many patients’ vision, positively or negatively. Integrity and honesty in your presentation are critical to earn the long-term trust of your colleagues and those who put you on the podium.

Richard L. Lindstrom, MD, can be reached at rllindstrom@mneye.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: ‘The case is closed’: Immediate angiography after cardiac arrest does not improve outcomes
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — In patients with cardiac arrest but no ST elevation, immediate coronary angiography did not improve survival or neurological outcomes compared with deferred angiography, according to results of the DISCO study.

“Immediate coronary angiography of the cardiac arrest does not improve survival or neurological outcomes. The case is closed,” Sten Rubertsson, MD, PhD, professor of anesthesiology and intensive care medicine at Uppsala University in Sweden, said during a press conference at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

The DISCO study was the largest to examine whether immediate coronary angiography was better than deferred coronary angiography in patients without ST elevation who were resuscitated after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. It confirms the results of four previous smaller studies and supports ESC guideline recommendations against immediate coronary angiography in this patient population, Rubertsson said.

The researchers randomly assigned 1,006 patients who were successfully resuscitated after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and had no ST elevation on ECG to immediate coronary angiography or deferred coronary angiography. The immediate group received coronary angiography within 2 hours after randomization, and if PCI was performed, revascularization was limited to the acute occlusion in accordance with a predefined protocol, while the deferred group did not have coronary angiography performed within 72 hours unless clinically indicated, and if PCI was performed, revascularization strategy was based on clinical guidelines, Rubertsson said during the press conference.

Rubertsson reported no difference between the groups in the following outcomes:

“The DISCO study provides solid support for the current guideline recommendation against routine immediate coronary angiography in patients successfully resuscitated without ST elevation on ECG after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest,” Rubertsson said during the press conference. “These results may impact the acute care of resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in a crude estimate of about 35,000 to 40,000 people per year in Europe ... if they follow the guidelines. So I think we can say that this question is closed and further studies on how to improve survival in cardiac arrest are warranted.”

The most hope may lie in preventing cardiac arrests from happening in the first place, Ruberttson said during the press conference.

“I am a little bit discouraged by all the larger studies that we have performed lately trying to find a magic bullet in post-resuscitation care,” Rubertsson said. “I think it’s very difficult to find something that will really change the outcome. I think what we need to do is go back to the ... pre-hospital care arena because that’s where we have the chance to do something that might change the outcome in the end.”

Rubertsson S, et al. Hot line 12. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

Disclosures: Rubertsson reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: Some adults with elevated BMI not diagnosed with obesity
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Nearly 30% of adults with an elevated BMI in the U.S. and more than 97% of those with a high BMI in Japan did not receive a diagnosis for obesity, according to findings from the CALOR study published in Obesity.

Deborah B. Horn, DO, MPH, DABOM, MFOMA, medical director at the University of Texas Center for Obesity Medicine and Metabolic Performance and clinical assistant professor in the department of surgery at University of Texas McGovern Medical School in Houston, and colleagues wrote that the shift in recognizing obesity as a chronic disease makes it crucial to understand the prevalence of obesity-related diseases. In a longitudinal study assessing claims data and medical records in the U.S. and Japan, researchers assessed how many adults with a high BMI received an obesity diagnosis from their healthcare professional and compared the prevalence of obesity-related diseases between those with an obesity diagnosis and those who were undiagnosed.

“The findings on the substantial burden of diseases interrelated to obesity among individuals with vs. without a recorded obesity diagnosis, and over time in parallel with evolving obesity treatment options, may encourage [healthcare professionals] and healthcare systems to systematically diagnose and better manage obesity and these interrelated conditions,” the researchers wrote.

Researchers collected data from the Optum Clinformatics Data Mart in the U.S. and the Medical Data Vision database in Japan. Adults aged 18 years and older who met their country’s obesity cutoff of a BMI of 30 kg/m2 in the U.S. and a BMI of 25 kg/m2 in Japan from 2016 to 2024 were included in the study. Demographics, BMI and incidence of obesity-related diseases were obtained.

There were 3,584,120 people in the U.S. and 3,140,900 adults in Japan who had an elevated BMI. Of those, 70.1% in the U.S. and 2.3% in Japan received a diagnosis for obesity. The researchers noted there was a large difference in obesity diagnosis rates between the two countries.

“There are several potential reasons for the low diagnosis rates of obesity, including lack of recognition of obesity as a disease, social stigma and lack of infrastructure to manage people with obesity,” the researchers wrote.

Of adults with an elevated BMI, 95.8% in the U.S. and 67.4% in Japan had at least one obesity-related disorder. In the U.S., the most common obesity-related disorders were dyslipidemia in 80.4% of the study group, hypertension in 78.8%, type 2 diabetes in 43.5%, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in 32%, chronic kidney disease in 28.7% and heart failure in 19.2%. Of adults with an elevated BMI in Japan, 46.2% had hypertension, 30.8% had dyslipidemia, 26.3% had type 2 diabetes, 18.5% had HF, 8.8% had CKD and 3% had OSA.

In the U.S., a higher percentage of adults who received an obesity diagnosis had dyslipidemia (84.9% vs. 70%), hypertension (83.6% vs. 67.4%), osteoarthritis (60.5% vs. 39.5%), type 2 diabetes (49.3% vs. 29.9%), OSA (39.1% vs. 15.4%), CKD (32.9% vs. 18.8%) and HF (23.3% vs. 9.8%) compared with those who were not diagnosed with obesity. Among Japanese adults with an elevated BMI, a higher percentage of those diagnosed with obesity had dyslipidemia (43.2% vs. 30.6%), type 2 diabetes (42.2% vs. 25.9%), OSA (11.9% vs. 2.8%), CKD (14.3% vs. 8.6%), and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (14.5% vs. 3.9%) than those without an obesity diagnosis.

In an additional analysis, researchers compared disease burden for adults diagnosed with obesity in 2024 with those diagnosed with the disease in 2016 to 2020. Adults with a more recent diagnosis of obesity in the U.S. were more likely to have dyslipidemia (72.8% vs. 63.9%), osteoarthritis (41.9% vs. 32.2%), anxiety (32.2% vs. 19.6%) and CKD (20% vs. 13.5%) than those diagnosed in 2016 to 2020. Conversely, in Japan, disease burden was mostly similar or slightly less for adults diagnosed with obesity in 2024 vs. 2016 to 2020.

Researchers outlined several potential ways healthcare professionals may improve obesity diagnosis rates globally.

“Numerous leading institutions have recently sought to redefine obesity, aiming to promote measures with increased focus on adiposity (waist circumference, waist-to-height ratio, and percent body fat) and proposed combinations of these measures, to identify treatment targets that reduce the risk of interrelated diseases of obesity,” the researchers wrote. “U.S. guidelines recommend screening all adults for obesity. A missed obesity diagnosis is common in primary care, so approaches such as automated electronic medical record dashboard notifications for when a BMI threshold is recorded could improve rates of obesity diagnosis and increase the involvement of primary care providers in obesity care.”

Horn DB, et al. Obesity. 2026;doi:10.1002/oby.70264.

Disclosures: Horn reports consulting for Amgen, AstraZeneca, Boehringer Ingelheim, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Zealand and receiving institutional research funding from Eli Lilly, KVK Tech, Novo Nordisk and WW. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures. The study was funded by AstraZeneca.
