In short, the socioeconomic world underlying the new scenarios is somewhat more crowded and less wealthy per person than the one the SSPs originally imagined.

Another notable change is the shift in the SSP that underlies the highest future emissions scenario.

In the original SSPs, the “very high” SSP5-8.5 scenario was based on SSP5, while the new “high” scenario in CMIP7 is based on SSP3.

The GMD study explains that this is because IAM teams that developed the scenarios found that SSP3 and SSP5 variants produced similar emissions. They judged that the “fragmented” SSP3 world – which is characterised by large challenges to adaptation – to be more relevant for exploring high-end risks.

In another important change, the authors of the CMIP7 scenarios decided to eliminate “baseline” scenarios that assumed a world without any climate policy. These scenarios were previously used as a counterfactual against which to compare climate-changed worlds.

Instead, the range of future emissions scenarios starts with current policies and explores ways that they could be strengthened, weakened, or kept the same. The high scenario explores a plausible “rollback of current mitigation policies“.

The medium scenario, by contrast, extends climate policies officially implemented as of 2025, without assuming countries achieve their Paris Agreement pledges – known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs) – or net-zero targets that are not yet backed by legislation.

In their GMD paper, the authors of the CMIP7 scenarios emphasise that the medium scenario “should not be considered as a ‘most likely’ scenario”, but that it can provide a benchmark against which the effect of future policy strengthening or weakening can be measured. It is roughly analogous in its emissions levels to the old SSP2-4.5 scenario.

The new low scenario explores a world where climate policy is rapidly strengthened and warming by 2100 is limited to below 2C. This makes it analogous to the old SSP1-2.6 scenario.

The very-low scenario limits global warming to around 1.5C by 2100, similar to the old SSP1-1.9 scenario. However, it involves a greater degree of overshoot mid-century, reflecting the fact that global emissions did not begin to rapidly decline in 2020 as envisioned by SSP1-1.9. As the authors of the GMD ScenarioMIP paper point out: “At this point of time, some overshoot of the 1.5C seems unavoidable.”

In addition, there are a number of scenarios that start on one path before undertaking rapid mitigation. These high-to-low, medium-to-low and low-to-negative scenarios are intended to explore futures where mitigation is further delayed, followed by a rapid turn-around later in the century.

The scenario developers noted that there is no specific likelihood or probabilities assigned to any scenario, but rather only a judgement that all are within the realm of plausibility given where the world is today. They also said that “there might be potential futures outside the ScenarioMIP scenario range”.

In addition to the shift away from baseline scenarios, there are three other notable design changes made in CMIP7.

First, CMIP7 models will be driven by emissions of CO2 and other greenhouse gases, rather than set atmospheric concentrations.

In every previous generation of models, the ScenarioMIP experiments required that modelling groups simulate future climate using the same set of CO2 concentrations. For CMIP7, models with an interactive carbon cycle are asked to run in “emissions-driven” mode for CO2, calculating atmospheric concentrations themselves based on emissions.

This is a significant improvement. It means that the substantial uncertainty in carbon-cycle feedbacks will now show up directly in the range of projected warming, rather than being overlooked. (The change applies to CO2 only; methane, nitrous oxide and halocarbons remain prescribed as concentrations.)

Second, emissions match observations up to 2023. IAM modellers were asked to stay close to observed trends up to 2025 to avoid emissions diverging from reality before models were run. Scenario differences only open up after 2026, avoiding an earlier problem of scenarios diverging from reality years before the models were even run.

Finally, the period over which models are being run has been extended from 2100 to 2150. This is important as the world is already more than a quarter of the way through the 21st century.

The extended model runs out to 2150 will provide a more thorough exploration of the warming that people born in the coming decades may experience within their lifetimes.

In addition, all scenarios have extensions to 2500 where temperatures are eventually stabilised. These allow scientists to explore changes to long-term Earth-system processes, such as ice sheets and sea level, as well as whether warming is reversible.

Overall, the new scenarios provide a notably more narrow range of future CO2 emissions than the SSP scenarios used in CMIP6.

The figure below shows net global CO2 emissions (combining fossil-fuel and land-use emissions) for the seven new scenarios, alongside the five SSP scenarios used for climate model runs in CMIP6 (e.g. SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5).

At the bottom of the range, the new scenarios closely track their predecessors: the very-low scenario reaches net-zero CO2 around mid-century much like SSP1-1.9, while the low scenario lands close to SSP1-2.6.

The chart below shows total emissions for the same scenarios for the period 2024-2100.

The lowest emissions scenarios now have somewhat higher total emissions, reflecting the failure of the world to rapidly reduce emissions after 2020 that occurred in the lower SSP emissions scenarios, such as SSP1-1.9 and SSP1-2.6. The very-low scenario results in 310bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2) cumulative emissions between 2024 and 2100, compared to around 110GtCO2 in SSP1-1.9.

At the top end, the change is particularly dramatic. The high scenario in CMIP7 reaches 55GtCO2 per year in 2100. The previous high scenario, SSP5-8.5, by contrast, reached around 126GtCO2 per year in 2100.

In cumulative terms – which is what matters most for global warming – high reaches around 3,820GtCO2 over 2024-2100, half the roughly 7,600GtCO2 of SSP5-8.5 and about three-quarters of the 5,140GtCO2 of SSP3-7.0.

To put it another way: the top of the new scenario range sits between SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 in cumulative emissions terms, which is territory that CMIP6 treated as its middle ground.

To make the scale of this shift clear, Carbon Brief analysed the CO2 emissions trajectories in each of the prior generations of high-end emissions scenarios, using the same simple climate model – FaIR – to calculate future warming.

Below, four different generations of emissions scenarios are examined. The SRES scenarios were originally published in 2000 and used in the IPCC’s third (2001) and fourth (2007) assessment reports (and the corresponding CMIP3 model runs). The RCPs were developed in the early 2010s and used in the IPCC fifth assessment report (AR5; 2013) and CMIP5, while the SSPs were developed in the late 2010s and used in the IPCC AR6 report and CMIP6.

Over the past two decades, the highest emissions scenarios all resulted in comparable amounts of warming in 2100: SRES A1FI (the highest SRES scenario) reached 4.6C in 2100 (5-95% range; 3.5-6.1C), RCP8.5 reached 4.9C (3.7-6.5C) and SSP5-8.5 reached 4.6C (3.5-6.2C).

(RCP8.5 edges out its successor despite lower CO2 emissions because it assumed considerably more methane and nitrous oxide.)

CMIP7’s high scenario comes in remarkably lower, at 3.3C (2.6-4.4C).

The downward revision of future emissions in CMIP7 reflects two key changes since RCP8.5 was published back in 2011. First, the plausible baseline of a repeal of current policy has fallen. Cheap solar, wind and batteries, a global plateau in coal use and more than $2tr per year in clean-energy investment mean that a rollback in climate policy would not result in coal deployment levels assumed in the RCP8.5 scenario.

The GMD study states that CMIP6’s high-emission levels “have become implausible, based on trends in the costs of renewables, the emergence of climate policy and recent emission trends”.

(For more, see Carbon Brief’s recent factcheck of false claims around the retirement of the SSP5-8.5 emissions scenario. Also see Carbon Brief’s recent interview with Prof Detlef van Vuuren, a key architect of both the old SSPs and new scenarios.)

Second, part of the apparent decline reflects a correction of how scenarios are communicated – rather than real-world progress. The old high-end scenarios always represented an estimate of worst-case scenarios at the time, rather than likely outcomes.

Genuine progress in reducing emissions probably accounts for around 0.7C of the roughly 1.7C gap between SSP5-8.5 and today’s current-policy trajectory, with the remainder reflecting that the baseline was never particularly likely.

To compare warming outcomes across scenario generations on a like-for-like basis, Carbon Brief ran both the seven CMIP7 scenarios and the CMIP6 SSP emission scenarios through the same simple climate model.

(This is FaIR v2.2, using the 841-member ensemble calibrated and constrained to match the assessment of climate sensitivity in IPCC AR6, historical warming and ocean heat uptake).

These values may differ from the ultimate results that are found by CMIP7 climate models, but give a sneak peak of what those results may look like when they become available.

The seven scenarios produce warming in 2100, relative to pre-industrial (1850-1900), that ranges from 1.6C (with a 5-95% range of 1.1-2.5C) in the very-low scenario to 3.3C (2.6-4.4C) in high, with the current-policy medium scenario reaching 2.9C (2.2-3.9C). Warming also continues after 2100 in both the medium and high scenarios.

The figure below shows the range of 2100 warming (5th to 95th percentile) relative to the preindustrial period expected in each of the old SSP scenarios and the new CMIP7 ones, along with a central estimate (white dots).

The largest changes are, unsurprisingly, at the top. CMIP7’s high scenario (3.3C in 2100) produces less warming than SSP3-7.0 (3.7C in the same ensemble) and far less than SSP5-8.5 (4.7C).

The entire CMIP6 “high” tier (e.g. SSP5-8.5 and SSP3-7.0) now sits above anything in the new scenario set, at least up to 2100. Extended beyond 2100, however, high keeps climbing towards levels the previous extreme scenarios reached earlier.

At the low end, the picture is more similar. The very-low scenario (1.6C in 2100) lands close to SSP1-1.9 (1.5C) and low (1.8C) is essentially indistinguishable from SSP1-2.6 (1.8C) in 2100.

However, the new low scenario involves more rapid late-century emissions reductions and greater amounts of carbon removal than its SSP analogue, while the very-low scenario involves greater overshoot of 1.5C mid-century.

In addition to calculating 2100 and 2150 warming, Carbon Brief has calculated the likelihood of passing different global warming levels (2C, 2.5C, 3C, 4C and 5C) over time in the new CMIP7 scenarios.

The chart below uses the IPCC approach of calculating the crossing year based on a 20-year average, rather than when a single year exceeds the warming level.

Under the medium scenario, which reflects a world where current policies are maintained, passing 1.5C is essentially locked in.

Most models cross the threshold by the late 2020s or early 2030s. The 2C limit is crossed around 2050 on average and 3C by around 2110. The chance of exceeding 4C is around one-in-four by 2150, but, ultimately, rises to roughly 50% if emissions continue after that point.

Under the high scenario, 2C arrives in the 2040s, 3C in the 2080s and the chance of exceeding 4C by 2150 is around 60% (and around 95% by 2300). Even 5C is reached by 2150 in roughly 20% of climate model simulations.

The lower scenarios tell a different story. In the very-low scenario, the chance that peak warming (which the IPCC determines using a 20-year average of warming) ever exceeds 1.5C is around 90%. This reflects the fact that passing 1.5C is almost unavoidable at this point.

However, the chance of surpassing 2C sits at around 30% and the scenario has warming falling after mid-century as more CO2 is removed from the atmosphere than is added.

Every scenario that has global warming peaking and declining requires pulling CO2 back out of the atmosphere. Otherwise, warming from CO2 emissions will persist for millennia.

CO2 removal (CDR) remains one of the few levers available to reduce future temperatures – particularly given additional warming caused by cuts to aerosol pollution.

The chart below shows the total CDR deployment in each of the different scenarios by year, reflecting the sum of both land-based and engineered approaches (top), as well as the total CDR deployment between 2024 and 2150 (bottom).

Every scenario that deeply cuts global emissions in CMIP7 also involves a large amount of CDR.

The low-to-negative scenario pulls a cumulative 2,360GtCO2 out of the atmosphere by 2150, roughly 60 years of today’s emissions run in reverse.

The high-to-low scenario has around 1,480GtCO2 cumulative CDR, medium-low has 1,450GtCO2 and low has 1,360GtCO2.

Even the very-low scenario, which seeks to minimise CDR use, requires 655GtCO2 of removals between 2024 and 2150.

The degree to which scenarios rely on “engineered” removals – such as the use of biochar or direct air capture – or land-based removals – including afforestation and reforestation – ranges  across models.

In the low scenario, roughly one-third of the removals is from the land “sink”, while low-to-negative relies almost entirely on engineered methods, with direct air capture alone reaching around 16GtCO2 per year by 2100.

The chart below shows the deployment of engineered removals by year (top), as well as the total engineered CDR used between 2024 and 2150 (bottom). The lower plot also includes a breakdown between the portion of CDR that requires geologic storage (e.g. DAC and BECCS) and the portion that does not (e.g. enhanced weathering and biochar) and compares the total to a recent “prudent” total CO2 storage limit published in the scientific literature.

(For more on limits to carbon storage capacity, see Carbon Brief’s 2025 guest post.)

The amount of CDR going toward geological storage is most highest in the low-to-negative scenario, which injects around 1,750GtCO2 of BECCS and direct-air-capture CO2 underground by 2150.

The high-to-low and low scenarios each commit around 800GtCO2 to storage by 2150. This is within the range of available geologic storage, but would require that the storage industry handles more CO2 than the mass of oil currently moved by the fossil-fuel industry.

That said, there are other potential CDR approaches – such as enhanced rock weathering, surficial mineralisation and ocean alkalinity enhancement – that do not require injection of CO2 into geologic formations. In-situ mineralisation approaches that inject CO2 into alkaline rock formations such as basalt or peridotite could also open up more potential CO2 storage.

It is worth noting that the amount of CDR deployed in these scenarios would require planetary-scale engineering at the cost of trillions of dollars, while many of the engineered CDR approaches are still relatively early-stage technologies.

The goal of scenarios is to span a range of possible futures. While it may be tempting to treat current climate and energy policies – and the medium scenario – as a forecast, there is no reason to expect that they will not change in the future.

It is likely that policies will continue to be strengthened, as has been the case over the past two decades. However, they may also be weakened if national priorities or politics change, as has happened in the US during the two terms of the Trump administration.

In the new CMIP7 scenarios there is no “business-as-usual” scenario, but rather a narrower range of futures than was available in CMIP6, reflecting greater clarity among scientists on where the world is heading in terms of future energy use and emissions.

The fact that the worst-case scenarios of the past have become increasingly implausible is good news. However, this is tempered by the fact that the very-low emission scenarios have, in turn, become harder to achieve given that global emissions have yet to decline.

There is also real uncertainty in the climate-system response to emissions. This is due to uncertainty around how sensitive the climate is to a build-up of CO2 in the atmosphere, as well as how the carbon cycle will respond to emissions.

The CMIP7 medium scenario – which has a central estimate of 2.9C of warming by 2100 – still has around a 3% chance of reaching 4C by that date. If emissions continue, those odds increase to 25% by 2150. This remains far outside anything resembling a safe outcome for the climate system.

The scenarios are now being run using the new CMIP7 models, whose emissions-driven runs will fold carbon-cycle uncertainty directly into projections. These projections will subsequently be analysed in the reports of AR7.

Ultimately, it will be decisions made by governments, businesses and individuals that decide which of these seven futures become closest to reality.

Emissions scenarios shown in this article are the seven CMIP7 ScenarioMIP scenarios set out in van Vuuren et al. (2026), harmonised to observed 2023 emissions, with rule-based extensions to 2500 generated using the FLEX methodology, as set out in Kikstra et al. (2026). Emissions through 2100 match the ScenarioMIP database; extension trajectories are indicative and may differ from the final published extensions.

Temperature projections use FaIR v2.2 with the fair-calibrate v1.4.5 constrained ensemble (841 members set out in Smith et al. (2024), which matches the AR6 assessed climate sensitivity (ensemble ECS median 3C, 5-95% 2.0-5.1C), historical warming and ocean heat content.

Historical emissions (1750-2022) use the FaIR historical emissions dataset, with scenario emissions spliced in after 2023.

Solar and volcanic forcing are updated through 2025 from the Climate Indicator forcing timeseries; future volcanic forcing ramps to the 1850-2021 climatological background by 2035 (following the CMIP7 protocol) and solar forcing follows a SOLARIS-HEPPA-derived cycle projection to 2300.

All warming is expressed relative to 1850-1900.

SSP comparisons run the RCMIP-harmonised CMIP6 scenario emissions through the FaIR ensemble, which yields 2081-2100 warming 0.1-0.3C below the AR6-assessed values at the high end (e.g. SSP5-8.5: 4.2C vs 4.4C assessed), reflecting differences between the AR6 assessment and the FaIR configurations used here. Updating the volcanic dataset to use CMIP7 values (which revises the eruption-rich 1850-1900 baseline period) raises all reported anomalies by 0.03-0.05C.

For CDR, the scenario database reports the technology split (for example, BECCS, direct air capture, enhanced weathering, biochar, ocean-based, soil carbon management). Agriculture, forestry and other land-use  (AFOLU) removals are available only as a net flux, so are shown as the net sink where negative. Soil-carbon management is grouped with land-based rather than engineered removal, and the geological storage comparison uses BECCS plus direct air capture only.

The figure showing high-end scenarios for the past four CMIP generations runs SRES A1FI through the same ensemble using the A1G MiniCAM model from the SRES database v1.1, spliced onto historical emissions at 2000, and covering CO2 (fossil and land use), methane, nitrous oxide and sulphur; SRES-era ozone-precursor projections (nitrous oxide, carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds) lie outside the calibrated range of FaIR, so RCP8.5 values are used instead. RCP8.5 uses RCMIP v5.1 emissions, with 13 minor halogenated gases absent from the RCP database following SSP5-8.5.

It’s back to school for colleges across the United States, and if U.S. President Donald Trump has it his way, more and more students will be studying to transform the country into a critical minerals superpower.

The depleted state of the U.S. mining workforce has been a thorn in the side of the Trump administration’s ambitions, with more than half of the current mining workforce—or around 221,000 workers—estimated to retire by 2029, according to the Society for Mining, Metallurgy, and Exploration (SME), a professional association based in Colorado.

It’s back to school for colleges across the United States, and if U.S. President Donald Trump has it his way, more and more students will be studying to transform the country into a critical minerals superpower.

The depleted state of the U.S. mining workforce has been a thorn in the side of the Trump administration’s ambitions, with more than half of the current mining workforce—or around 221,000 workers—estimated to retire by 2029, according to the Society for Mining, Metallurgy, and Exploration (SME), a professional association based in Colorado.

Analysts have warned that the United States does not have the people to power a mining renaissance, as years of largely outsourcing the industry overseas have left the country with an aging workforce that isn’t equipped to contend with Chinese competitors.

“It’s like all of a sudden, if you told me that we’ve got to set up a cricket league that’s got to compete against India and Pakistan next year,” said David Abraham, a rare-earths expert and author of The Elements of Power. “It’s a huge challenge.”

In August, the Trump administration unveiled plans to pump some $180 million into U.S. mining schools, with the goal of turbocharging talent pipelines and doubling their number of graduates within the next two years. And at the forefront of that effort are mining engineers, who oversee the lifecycle of mines and can take on careers in areas ranging from mine design and safety to environmental specialties.

The United States is currently home to 14 mining schools, down from 25 in the 1980s. Those schools collectively graduate between 150 and 200 mining engineers a year, which doesn’t even meet the current demand for graduates, said Aaron Noble, the head of the mining and minerals engineering department at Virginia Tech.

That number also pales in comparison to the mining graduates that China boasts—a gap that Trump himself pointed to when announcing the administration’s newest investments last month.

“For years, mining schools and colleges that are essential to training the future leaders of this industry have been absolutely and sadly disappearing,” he said. “Accredited mining programs in the United States now graduate less than 170 mining engineers each year, while China graduates more than 3,000.”

In fact, just one Chinese university enrolls more mining engineering students than all of the U.S. mining programs combined, according to 2022 data from SME.

That discrepancy has stark ramifications for the expertise available in the United States. “It’s difficult to find the talent” outside of China, said Wade Senti, the president of Florida-based Advanced Magnet Lab, which manufactures permanent magnets.

At the university level, student interest in the sector has largely fallen over the decades. In recent times, undergraduate mining engineering enrollment and the number of degrees awarded in the field peaked a little more than a decade ago, around 2013 and 2014, according to data from SME. Since then, both numbers have broadly declined until 2023—the last year of publicly available data—although there has been a slight uptick in the number of degrees awarded.

“To be honest, mining is not sexy,” said Jaeheon Lee, a professor in the mining engineering department at the Colorado School of Mines. The challenge is “to make our program more attractive, not only to students, but also these days, [to] their parents.”

Mining may now be getting a makeover. While the sector has a fraught environmental and social reputation, with a long legacy of pollution and mine disasters, the Trump administration has made mineral security a top priority as commodity supply chains have been weaponized in trade wars. The geopolitical spotlight on so-called critical minerals—or a grouping of minerals deemed essential to economic and national security—may now have elevated them in the public eye.

“I think the whole conversation on critical minerals is a whole rebranding exercise,” Abraham, said.

Anecdotal evidence suggests that that surge in attention is translating to an increase in university enrollment. At the Colorado School of Mines, undergraduate enrollment in mining engineering has doubled in recent years, from around 100 students three years ago to 200 this year, said Bill Zisch, the head of the school’s mining engineering department.

“Frankly, one of the challenges that we’re having as we start the school year is finding out where we can find classrooms to put the increase in students,” he said. “We’re starting to see direct impacts from, I think, the recognition of its importance.”

Virginia Tech is also seeing an explosion in interest. Noble, the head of the school’s mining engineering department, told Foreign Policy that in the 2020 admissions cycle, only two students applied to the university indicating interest in mining engineering, which was “effectively nobody,” he said. In this last admission cycle, that number was 55.

Demand for graduating students is high. The university hosts its own mining-specific career fair, which can only accommodate 50 companies due to space limitations, Noble said. The companies are primarily U.S. firms and broadly cover the mining sector, ranging from crushed stone and aggregate producers to various equipment and service providers. Those 50 companies recruited from a graduating pool of roughly 30 students last year, and 20 students the year before that, he said.

“You’ve got 20 graduates, 50 companies there, most of the companies seeking full-time employment,” he said, adding that all his students graduate with multiple job offers. “You can imagine what that looks like from the student’s perspective and the employer’s perspective.”

As the Trump administration aims to double the number of mining graduates, one big challenge will be scaling up academic capacity and hiring, as well as investing in faculty. SME estimated that more than half of the mining workforce—or around 221,000 workers—will retire by 2029, and universities are grappling that reality at the same time that is Trump going all-in on mining education.

“Most of the faculty right now are approaching retirement age, some very specialized fields of study,” Noble said. “There’s only a handful of people in the U.S. with that type of expertise, and so we have a continual need to think about our capacity.”

All that training takes time. For some skill sets, it could take years for individuals to gain the necessary experience, including undergraduate schooling, advanced degrees, and potential industry experience, Senti said.

Given the amount of time that it takes to build up that domestic expertise, one option could be recruiting foreign talent to help plug its mineral vulnerabilities. But the administration’s crackdown on immigration has also made it more difficult for U.S. firms to hire and retain foreign talent, on top of complicated compliance rules for defense-related issues.

“If someone’s on H-1B, they may not be able to work on certain things,” Senti said. “Honestly, it limits your ability to hire potential talent that’s not a permanent U.S. citizen.”

Washington’s immigration measures appear to be clouding the academic sector, too. Ian Lange, a mineral economist at the Colorado School of Mines, said that the school’s mineral economics program—which is the only one in the country—was about half foreign students in 2022 and 2023. Those numbers are now down, he said.

“Certainly, it’s been more difficult for foreign talent to get to the United States in the last two years,” he said. That has “translated into employers sort of shying away from hiring foreign talent out of universities.”

The Trump administration, for its part, is moving ahead at full speed. But for all of Washington’s investments in mining education, it will take time for them to pay off, analysts said.

“It takes people a tremendous amount of time to get in, to understand,” Abraham said. “We’ll eventually get there, but we don’t have the people who can compete broadly at the moment.”

Maxine Davey contributed graphics assistance.

In November 1998, Gaza International Airport opened to much fanfare, a bagpipe and red carpet on hand to welcome the landing of the first jet. U.S. President Bill Clinton subsequently hailed this moment as a tangible outcome of the Oslo peace agreements. European countries had footed much of the airport’s $86 million bill.

Three years later, during the Second Intifada, Israeli forces bombed the airport’s control tower and later bulldozed the runway—while also destroying other EU-funded development projects. The fate of the Gaza airport came to symbolize the predicament Europe found itself in. When it comes to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Europe is seen as a “payer, not a player.”

In November 1998, Gaza International Airport opened to much fanfare, a bagpipe and red carpet on hand to welcome the landing of the first jet. U.S. President Bill Clinton subsequently hailed this moment as a tangible outcome of the Oslo peace agreements. European countries had footed much of the airport’s $86 million bill.

Three years later, during the Second Intifada, Israeli forces bombed the airport’s control tower and later bulldozed the runway—while also destroying other EU-funded development projects. The fate of the Gaza airport came to symbolize the predicament Europe found itself in. When it comes to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Europe is seen as a “payer, not a player.”

As Europe now faces a reckoning over its Israel policy and grows less willing to defer to Washington, the EU has a chance to become a player. Through “constructive conditionality”—backing Israel’s legitimate security needs while making further cooperation contingent on respect for international law and Palestinian rights—it can advance a more independent foreign policy and, by building a landing pad for eventual U.S. policy shifts, extend the weight of its choices beyond its borders.

For decades, European policy toward Israel has largely deferred to Washington. The 27 EU member states are deeply divided. Historically, a minority, led by Ireland, has strongly favored Palestinian independence, while a bigger group, led by Germany, has unwaveringly stood by Israel, with others shifting according to their government. These divisions have hampered Europe from taking any initiative beyond providing material assistance to U.S. peace efforts and to the parties directly. The EU was excluded from the Trump-orchestrated Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and four Arab states in 2020. It still contributed funds after the fact.

The EU started to change tack during the Biden administration. In these years, one of us served as the EU special representative for the Middle East peace process. The White House, laser-focused on creating official ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia, underestimated the international community’s wish to end the decades-long Israeli occupation. This meant Washington was following rather than leading when, on Sept. 18, 2023, the EU and Saudi Arabia, together with Egypt, Jordan, and the Arab League, launched their own peace initiative. It involved some 60 states, including a reluctant U.S., and focused on identifying political, economic, and security support that would facilitate a comprehensive regional peace.

But three weeks later the situation changed irrevocably, when Hamas launched an attack on Israel that killed roughly 1,200 people and took hundreds of hostages. Israel’s military response, backed by U.S. political and military support, has killed an estimated 73,000 Palestinians to date, reduced Gaza to rubble, and led to accusations of an Israeli-perpetrated genocide. It has also pushed both the U.S. and Europe to reconsider their long-standing Israel policies.

A majority of the U.S. public now holds unfavorable views of Israel, driven by growing public criticism of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and its seemingly endless military actions across the Middle East, including a semi-dormant war with Iran. In a survey published in April, Pew found that 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up 7 points in a single year and almost 20 points since 2022. The shift is particularly pronounced under Democrats, but the decline in support is bipartisan, albeit generationally skewed. A majority of Republicans under 50—57 percent—now view Israel unfavorably. Among younger Democrats, 84 percent hold unfavorable views.

While the popular shift within the U.S. has not yet materialized in concrete policy changes, it has shaped the political narrative in the United States. Foreign-policy debates within the Democratic Party have focused on diagnosing the failings of the Biden administration on Gaza and identifying an alternative path forward that reckons with this legacy. In several recent Democratic primaries, progressive candidates challenged mainstream Democrats over their support for Israel. Within the Republican Party, isolationists and anti-war Republicans have tested the party’s traditional pro-Israel platform. Vice President J.D. Vance, who is widely expected to run for president in 2028, has sought to reemphasize his more isolationist rhetoric on Israel in recent months while also leaning into some of the party’s more right-wing, conspiratorial views.

The emerging recalibration in the U.S. trails a realignment already visible across Europe. Citizens in Western Europe have long advocated for Palestinian rights and supported a two-state solution even as many governments refused even the lightest pressure on Israel in that direction. This changed following Israel’s scorched-earth campaign in Gaza. Massive demonstrations in many European cities have coincided with a more critical turn in capitals. In the Netherlands, both of our country of origin, Foreign Minister Caspar Veldkamp resigned over disagreements about tougher measures on Israel, throwing the government into further disarray.

Several European nations have taken steps to hold Israel responsible. At least seven countries enacted full or partial restrictions on military exports to Israel. Among these was Germany, Israel’s second-largest arms supplier after the U.S., which announced a partial and temporary arms embargo in August 2025. At the level of the EU, a change also appears underway, though unanimity requirements have limited the results. The EU’s most powerful tool is the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which provides Israel with preferential access to EU markets and programs, contingent on “respect for human rights and democratic principles.” Despite an official finding that Israel was in breach of the agreement, Germany and Italy blocked a proposal for its suspension.

European nonaction on the association agreement is routinely justified by referring to ongoing U.S.-led peace efforts. But as U.S. policy toward Israel is increasingly viewed as one-sided and ineffective, this argument has lost value. Europe’s growing reluctance to defer to Washington could further embolden European capitals to take action on their own. But without coordination between a more Palestinian-minded Europe and an increasingly Israel-skeptical U.S., there will be no peace to broker—and no Nobel Peace Prize to win.

Some Israelis worry that he might manufacture a security crisis ahead of the vote.

For Amman, Israeli annexation of the West Bank looms as an existential risk.

Instead of waiting for a new American policy, or for shifts following Israeli or Palestinian elections, European capitals should develop a more proactive foreign policy. This should focus on three tenets: 1) support for both legitimate Israeli security concerns and the security and well-being of the Palestinians and their regional neighbors; 2) practical support for—and commitment to—international law; and 3) a more transactional approach whereby cooperation with Israel hinges on adherence to the first two tenets.

First, even Israel’s harshest European critics must acknowledge that Israelis live in a volatile region, and that Europe carries a historic responsibility for the country’s safety. Europe must therefore be willing to support the protection of Israel against legitimate security threats. Yet this support must be paired with a demand for a durable Israeli strategy that meaningfully addresses the root causes of instability, rather than exacerbating them through violence and deprivation. It cannot come at the expense of Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem who deserve security, protection, and independence—the absence of which continues to be a major, and self-defeating, flaw in Israeli security policy.

Second, relations with Israel must be based on respect for international law. Protecting Israel against illegal aggression is unsustainable if one continues to turn a blind eye to Israel’s own illegal aggression. Europe should therefore also push back against Israeli military expansionism beyond its own borders, including illegal land seizures and the displacement of populations in Lebanon and Syria that continue to hamper mediation and regional stabilization efforts.

Third, any policy must have teeth. Under our proposed constructive conditionality approach, Israeli state-supported settler violence should not merely be condemned but checked by concrete actions. This means prohibiting trade with settlements and blocking the export of any materials that help build them. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s decision to ignore the EU’s (and America’s) long-stated red line on building new settlements in E1—Palestinian land around East Jerusalem—must be met with a response, as is now cautiously being discussed in Brussels.

The EU, which remains the biggest provider of external assistance to the Palestinians, should also seek compensation for the destruction of its humanitarian projects. After Israel’s razing of the Gaza airport, the EU reserved “the right to claim reparations in the appropriate forums.” By 2026, the damage to EU-funded infrastructure was reported to have reached at least 150 million euros. Yet, to date, no action has been taken against the destruction of EU-funded Palestinian schools, even as Israeli universities and other entities have received some 1.28 billion euros under an EU research program dear to the Israeli state.

The basis for a European constructive conditionality policy already exists. The Arab-EU initiative that was cut short by Oct. 7 reemerged in 2024 as the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution. It is now led by Saudi Arabia, France, Norway, and others. Based on a declaration supported by 142 states, the global alliance meets regularly to identify how it can advance an Arab-Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement focused on security, political, and economic integration, even when one or more of the parties is not yet ready to engage.

By investing in the global alliance and extending a hand to Washington, the EU can further strengthen the group’s reverse-engineering approach. The alliance starts from the desired end state—the establishment of a Palestinian state living side by side in peace and security with Israel—and works back toward the steps needed to achieve it. An initiative that was capable of uniting Germany, Ireland, China and Russia can surely find room for an America represented by President Donald Trump—and his successor.

A comprehensive European policy is unlikely to emerge piecemeal, given the continued differences among EU member states on smaller policy changes. Relevant changes come either in major crises such as over the stability of the euro, or during the budget negotiations forcing the 27 to agree on hundreds of billions of euros to be spent over seven years. A comprehensive EU approach can therefore take the shape of a grand bargain struck by the EU heads of state and government while they are engaged in high-stakes negotiations over the 2028-2034 expenses.

By then, with U.S. national elections approaching, any potential shift in American policy will also come into sharper focus. As Washington weighs a reset of its relationship with Israel, Europe would be well positioned to play a significant role. Ultimately, only constructive conditionality—pursued both by Israel’s most important ally, the United States, and its largest trading partner, the EU—stands a real chance of forging a more constructive relationship with Israel and building momentum for peace.

Sven Koopmans is the chair of negotiation and conflict resolution at the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies, former EU special representative for the Middle East peace process, former head of delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, former member of parliament in the Netherlands, former senior mediation advisor to the United Nations, and author of Negotiating Peace: A Guide to the Practice, Politics and Law of International Mediation (Oxford University Press).

Grace Wermenbol is a senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, a senior fellow at the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies, and an adjunct professor at Georgetown University. She previously served in a number of Middle East-focused national security and foreign-policy roles across the U.S. government, including at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Department of State. She is the author of A Tale of Two Narratives, a book on Israeli and Palestinian societies in the post-Oslo era (Cambridge University Press).

In July, the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, Ukraine intercepted only 29 of Russia’s 195 incoming ballistic missiles, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

As Russia intensifies its ballistic missile attacks, Ukraine is running dangerously low on the interceptors needed to defend against them. Neither of its major sources of support appears willing and able to fill the gap: European allies have already drawn heavily on their own air defense stocks, and the United States continues to deplete its own missile-defense interceptor inventories in its war against Iran. On Aug. 5, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that supplies of air defense missiles from allies this year have fallen to roughly one-third of their 2025 levels.

In July, the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, Ukraine intercepted only 29 of Russia’s 195 incoming ballistic missiles, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

As Russia intensifies its ballistic missile attacks, Ukraine is running dangerously low on the interceptors needed to defend against them. Neither of its major sources of support appears willing and able to fill the gap: European allies have already drawn heavily on their own air defense stocks, and the United States continues to deplete its own missile-defense interceptor inventories in its war against Iran. On Aug. 5, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that supplies of air defense missiles from allies this year have fallen to roughly one-third of their 2025 levels.

Ukraine has explored domestic options to replenish supplies, including seeking permission from Washington to manufacture Patriot interceptors and developing its own Freyja ballistic missile interceptor. But Washington has so far rejected the former, and bringing the latter into service would require substantial capital; engineering work; testing; and, crucially, time.

With Ukraine’s domestic capacity still years away from meeting its needs and U.S. and European supplies constrained, South Korea is one of the few countries capable of filling the gap. Zelensky has appealed to Seoul, saying: “We would very much like to receive support from South Korea in the form of what we lack—air defense systems.” But Seoul has so far declined.

That is a mistake. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, South Korea has emerged as a major arms supplier to Europe. Providing air defense systems to Ukraine would give Seoul an opportunity to prove that it is not merely an arms exporter to Europe but also a genuine security partner.

South Korea is particularly well suited to help, because it has developed sophisticated, multilayered missile-defense capabilities to counter North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats, and it has enough surplus to export to other countries. Its homegrown Cheongung-II system has already been battle-tested in the United Arab Emirates with a 96 percent success rate. Its systems are also competitively priced: A Cheongung-II interceptor costs about $1.1 million, roughly one-third the price of a Patriot interceptor. South Korea also produces about 95 percent of the system domestically, reducing its exposure to foreign supply-chain disruptions and export restrictions.

Perhaps most importantly, South Korea is also known for its ability to scale production rapidly and deliver systems on time. Although there are concerns that South Korea may lack the capacity to provide these systems to Ukraine quickly due to high demand, its defense industry has noted that existing production facilities are operating below capacity and that factories under construction in Poland and Romania could potentially be utilized to expand production.

Yet in response to Zelensky’s request, a South Korean Foreign Ministry official stated, “Our defense supplies … have been provided while complying with relevant domestic laws and policies.” Indeed, South Korea has maintained its long-standing policy of not directly supplying lethal weapons to countries at war, thus far providing Ukraine with humanitarian assistance and nonlethal military equipment and supplying ammunition indirectly through the United States.

This, however, is not a categorical legal prohibition, let alone a constitutional ban, as Zelensky has suggested. Some point to Article 5, which stipulates that “The Republic of Korea shall endeavor to maintain international peace and shall renounce all aggressive wars,” as a legal basis for opposing arms transfers to Ukraine. Yet one could argue that assisting a country that has been invaded in violation of international law—and thereby helping to uphold international peace and security—is more consistent with the spirit and purpose of the article.

More relevant is South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Act, which allows the government to restrict exports of defense material when necessary to maintain international peace and security, protect national security, or avoid diplomatic friction. The government retains discretion over whether to authorize such exports. The Foreign Trade Act restricts arms exports to “peaceful uses,” but it does not clearly define what constitutes a “peaceful use.”

Whether to provide Ukraine with air defense systems is thus, fundamentally, a political choice. If Seoul has the political will, it could approve such transfers on the compelling grounds that they are defensive weapons intended to protect a country subjected to illegal aggression.

Pyongyang’s military is sharpening itself on Ukrainian battlefields. What does that mean for U.S. defense coordination?

Russia’s ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine pose an urgent question for NATO leaders.

Building an independent defense industry does not mean going it alone.

Seoul’s hesitation is understandable. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has sought to maintain workable relations with Russia, which remains economically and strategically important to South Korea, rather than distance itself on values-based grounds, as his predecessor Yoon Suk-yeol did.

Before the war, annual bilateral trade amounted to roughly $27 billion. Russia has also traditionally been an important actor on Korean Peninsula issues because of its leverage over North Korea, although the extent of that influence has ebbed and flowed over time.

The relationship became particularly thorny when South Korea imposed economic sanctions against Russia after its invasion of Ukraine; more recently, Moscow has protested South Korea’s humanitarian aid to Ukraine and defense industry cooperation with NATO. Direct arms transfers to Ukraine would likely cross what Russia considers to be a red line—as a South Korean diplomat reportedly noted—and could make it significantly more difficult for Seoul to repair relations with Moscow after the war ends.

Moreover, South Korean policymakers worry that directly arming Ukraine could encourage Moscow to deepen military cooperation with North Korea, including transfers of sensitive technologies relating to nuclear-powered submarines, military satellites, or other systems. These technologies would enhance North Korea’s precision-strike capabilities, improve the survivability of its nuclear forces, and strengthen its deterrent against the United States, thereby undermining the credibility of the U.S. security guarantee. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has also suggested that Russia could provide North Korea with the latest nuclear weapons technology if South Korea were to lend Ukraine military support.

However, it is questionable whether South Korea’s efforts to manage its relationship with Russia would ultimately bear fruit. As Russia-North Korea ties have deepened into a treaty-based alliance, it is increasingly unlikely that Seoul will be able to restore its previous relationship with Moscow—or, even if it does, that Moscow would support South Korea’s broader geopolitical objectives. Moreover, Russia is reportedly already providing North Korea with some sensitive technologies, although the nature and extent of these transfers remain difficult to verify.

On top of that, whatever value Seoul sees in managing its relationship with Russia should be weighed against what it may lose by doing so—namely, the opportunity to consolidate its security partnership with Europe.

Cooperation between South Korea and Europe has expanded considerably in recent years, with Seoul participating in NATO summits and signing a security and defense partnership with the European Union. This relationship has become more important than ever, as both face growing security threats from neighboring powers amid waning confidence in U.S. security commitments.

South Korea’s defense industry has already become an important part of Europe’s effort to expand military capacity: From 2021 to 2025, South Korea was the second-largest supplier of major arms to European NATO countries, after the United States. That partnership has been driven most visibly by rapid deliveries of howitzers, tanks, multiple-launch rocket systems, and aircraft to Poland, alongside deals with Romania, Norway, Finland, and Estonia.

Yet the political environment in Europe is changing, and the “Buy European” sentiment is gaining momentum as governments seek to revitalize the continent’s defense-industrial base. The European Union’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program has allocated approximately $175 billion to support defense procurement and industrial expansion within Europe but requires at least 65 percent of the component value of funded projects to originate within the European Union. South Korea’s exclusion from SAFE could make its systems less attractive for EU-funded procurement.

South Korean policymakers and defense industry leaders increasingly recognize that Europe cannot be treated simply as a destination for Korean weapons. Sustainable cooperation must become more reciprocal cooperation and a broader security partnership.

Lee has articulated this ambition, saying that South Korea must “go beyond exporting advanced products” and become “a trusted partner in security cooperation.” In other words, deepening defense cooperation with Europe—whether in the defense-industrial sphere or more broadly—would require Seoul to establish itself symbolically as a trusted security partner, rather than just a business partner.

Ukraine presents the clearest opportunity to demonstrate precisely that. Ukraine is the front line of European security, and strengthening its ability to resist Russian aggression directly contributes to Europe’s deterrence and defense at a time when the continent faces its most serious security challenges since the end of the Cold War.

South Korea cannot aspire to become one of Europe’s trusted security partners while simultaneously insulating its relations with Moscow from the consequences of that choice. Providing Ukraine with air defense systems would show that South Korea is prepared to contribute to European security when the stakes are highest—not simply profit from European demand.

Lami Kim is the Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security, and defense at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The U.S. debate over how to navigate China’s role in developing and governing advanced artificial intelligence is stuck between two extremes. One camp calls for full-blown international treaties even though the two countries cannot yet agree on AI’s most serious risks, let alone how to manage them. The other is deeply skeptical of dialogue, believing progress will only be possible if the Chinese side is desperate.

A grand bargain may be too ambitious, yet focusing only on what can be agreed on today could lock both sides into a policy regime that becomes obsolete as technology evolves. Doing nothing is even worse because regardless of whether it was developed in San Francisco or Hangzhou, an AI model that makes it easier for terrorists to synthesize deadly pathogens or hack into the infrastructure that underpins financial markets threatens everyone. These risks are becoming all too real as AI systems demonstrate cyber- and biological capabilities that match or exceed those of human experts on increasingly complex tasks.

The U.S. debate over how to navigate China’s role in developing and governing advanced artificial intelligence is stuck between two extremes. One camp calls for full-blown international treaties even though the two countries cannot yet agree on AI’s most serious risks, let alone how to manage them. The other is deeply skeptical of dialogue, believing progress will only be possible if the Chinese side is desperate.

A grand bargain may be too ambitious, yet focusing only on what can be agreed on today could lock both sides into a policy regime that becomes obsolete as technology evolves. Doing nothing is even worse because regardless of whether it was developed in San Francisco or Hangzhou, an AI model that makes it easier for terrorists to synthesize deadly pathogens or hack into the infrastructure that underpins financial markets threatens everyone. These risks are becoming all too real as AI systems demonstrate cyber- and biological capabilities that match or exceed those of human experts on increasingly complex tasks.

The recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, in which AI agents collaborated to break out of their testing environment and gain access to the internal infrastructure of external organizations, made clear that AI already operates beyond human control in ways that can unwittingly impact third parties. It is only a matter of time before these threats cross borders, and Beijing will certainly want clarity from Washington should one of its companies become the next accidental victim of a U.S. model going rogue—and vice versa.

As Tsinghua University’s Xiao Qian recently wrote in Foreign Policy, “Sustained dialogue is a strategic necessity.” She is right. And there is a middle path forward. When U.S. and Chinese delegations gather this month to discuss AI risks, rather than pursuing a comprehensive agreement, they should start with a series of narrower measures focused on preventing extreme risks, managing crises, and investing in verification tools. Each small agreement helps build the understanding and trust needed for more ambitious deals, allowing the two countries to cooperate where they already agree without requiring consensus on everything else.

Of course, any bilateral agreement must recognize the powerful incentives for governments and companies on both sides to continue competing against each other. But even within this environment, each country can take steps that advance its own interests while building tools that make reciprocal commitments more credible down the line.

One of the biggest obstacles for negotiators is that neither country has developed tools that can confidently evaluate whether AI models are safe, nor safeguards capable of mitigating AI’s most extreme risks. These challenges affect both countries but are particularly acute for China, whose AI safety evaluations are improving but still less mature than the West’s. Given the transnational nature of AI risks, it is in both countries’ interests to have robust safety infrastructure, but governments have been hesitant to participate in technical exchanges, afraid of revealing information that could enhance a rival’s capabilities.

But it is possible to have carefully scoped, working-level technical exchanges that discuss best practices without exposing models’ inner workings, vulnerabilities, or advanced capabilities. In general, the two sides should compare broad approaches but withhold tactical details and refrain from granular, riskier discussions of the specific methods they use to elicit unsafe model behavior. They could, for instance, discuss how to scale evaluations to cover more models, behaviors, and potential threats, as well as how to use AI systems themselves to help identify and respond to threats. They could also discuss important, publicly available lessons on monitoring AI models to ensure they don’t escape their sandboxes—a topic that should be of mutual concern following the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

The two sides should also discuss safeguards using the same principles, comparing general approaches to detecting harmful activity, restricting dangerous use, and managing risks once models are deployed without discussing specific techniques for bypassing safeguards or proprietary details about how models are built.

U.S. experts might be able to offer insights from how they determined which actors should have access to Mythos, Anthropic’s most advanced model, explaining the broad criteria they used to evaluate safeguard effectiveness. They should also talk about the limitations to their current safeguards, explaining how they decided when dangerous, dual-use capabilities warranted tighter restrictions on model access. Similarly, U.S. third-party evaluators could use the public report from METR and Redwood Research on the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident to examine why safeguards were insufficient.

If these discussions go well, a next step could be to create technical working groups to establish voluntary best practices, soliciting input from companies and independent third-party organizations.

China would ultimately assess lessons from these exchanges on its own terms, but insights that align with its national security interests could shape decisions that reduce risks for everyone.

Even if the United States and China have a mutual understanding of AI risks and do everything they can to mitigate them, serious crises can still unfold.

Though China has the world’s most extensive AI regulations, it lacks clear rules for catastrophic risk management. The biggest U.S. AI companies are now subject to California’s SB 53 law, which requires them to disclose safety practices, report certain critical safety incidents, and protect whistleblowers. But these rules have not yet been federally adopted, limiting what the government can do when a serious incident occurs.

Practical cooperation should exist alongside competition.

A state-backed push is raising the question: Who pays?

Silicon Valley obsessions may have led Washington down a dead end.

Thus, the United States and China should discuss how to share key information and communicate effectively in a crisis. On the domestic front, each side should commit to setting up its own reporting systems to track cases where AI caused, or may cause, material harm—for example, if a model escapes a contained sandbox to attack telecommunications infrastructure or gain access to sensitive medical patient data. These incident-reporting systems can vary according to each country’s preferences, but they should collect broadly similar information and have similar categories and thresholds for severity.

In parallel, the countries should explore creating a bilateral information-sharing channel, which  would be voluntary at first, with the ability to change requirements later on. U.S. companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have already voluntarily shared information on certain safety incidents, but having a private channel can help both sides navigate cross-border incidents and proactively warn counterparts if a model is behaving in unintended ways that might be perceived as malicious.

Critically, though, crisis channels must fit how governments actually make decisions. Chinese interlocutors, for example, have explained in Track 2 conversations that they face strong disincentives from answering phone calls on “hotlines” because no individual answering the call has the authority to respond without consulting superiors. Using written communication could circumvent some of those challenges.

Even if the United States and China wanted to reach a bilateral AI agreement, they might not trust that the other side will follow through on its commitments. Tools that enable both countries to verify the other’s compliance can allow both sides to feel confident about the other’s safety practices. This mutual confidence, in turn, could enable further agreements and governance applications.

The first verification prototypes are just now being developed, and it may take years until they are sufficiently mature and trusted by both countries. That’s why the United States and China need to begin talking about the technology now, explicitly supporting technical research to develop verification tools for bilateral AI agreements.

China has been historically hesitant to participate in hardware-based verification regimes. These concerns could be alleviated if the two countries discussed at these early stages what types of verification technologies could be politically acceptable and who should build them to make them credible to both sides. And if specific proposals are brought to the table, the delegations could have a more concrete discussion on a given technology’s strengths and limitations.

The United States and China may never need some of these tools, and the agreements they could enable may ultimately not be desirable. But developing credible verification technologies takes both time and institutional capacity, and to be useful, they must be designed and built long before they are needed.

The upcoming dialogue should not be evaluated on whether the United States and China reach full agreement on all these issues. It will be a success if it lays the foundation for a serious second meeting and eventually a permanent high-level channel supported by both leaders. If talks break down early, the two sides might not get back to the negotiation table for months or even years.

These goals may seem modest, given the urgent need for international cooperation to combat extreme risks. But sequenced strategically, small diplomatic breakthroughs may lead to more ambitious measures, and each minor agreement will open possibilities for the next.

The United States and China may be competing to build the potentially defining technology of our time, but rivalry need not foreclose pragmatism. This September, both countries can take the first step in that direction.

Scott Singer is a fellow and co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. X: @Scott_R_Singer

As the West’s ideological and material hegemony continues to wane, a new multipolar world is taking shape. This change is structural—a product of the unstoppable diffusion of power. The transition from the industrial era to the digital age has meanwhile destabilized the liberal democracies that long oversaw global governance. A combination of automation and free trade has undermined the industrial-era social contract, hollowing out Western middle classes and the political centrism that sustained liberal internationalism. These dual tectonic shifts are stoking geopolitical rivalries and eroding international rules and institutions, putting out of reach the collective initiative needed to govern a globalized world.

U.S. President Donald Trump is a symptom more than a cause of this disarray and the anti-establishment anger it has provoked. He and other populists promise to tear down the old liberal order. But they lack the skills and inclination to build what comes next. The policy community needs to urgently prepare for the post-Trump era by generating a plan for governing an interdependent world that is in the process of falling apart.
