U.S. President Donald Trump is a symptom more than a cause of this disarray and the anti-establishment anger it has provoked. He and other populists promise to tear down the old liberal order. But they lack the skills and inclination to build what comes next. The policy community needs to urgently prepare for the post-Trump era by generating a plan for governing an interdependent world that is in the process of falling apart.

Building order in the world to come should begin with recognizing the renewed importance of regions; the diffusion of power logically necessitates the decentering and devolution of authority. Order will need to come from the bottom up, drawing on regional groupings that tap into the natural order-producing effects of geographic proximity, commercial ties, and common cultures. The regionalization of governance sets the stage for a polycentric international system: a multiorder world of considerable ideological and political diversity.

A key challenge will be to construct a global order that strikes the right balance between top-down and bottom-up governance.

Yet precisely because the emerging multipolar world is set to remain globalized and interdependent, the centrifugal force of regionalization must be offset by order that comes from the top down. Multiple regional orders will require collective supervision. A concert system—a network of high-level coordinating councils—offers the most realistic and feasible option for overseeing global governance. Like the 19th-century Concert of Europe, which preserved peace for decades after the Napoleonic Wars, flexible and informal steering groups can provide a vehicle for genuine and sustained strategic dialogue and for dampening and managing conflicts of interest.

A concert system would complement, not replace, the United Nations. The U.N. would be buttressed from above by this network of steering groups and from below by regional bodies. A key challenge will be to construct a global order that strikes the right balance between top-down and bottom-up governance. An international system that is at once centralized and regionalized offers the best—and perhaps only—hope of maintaining order in the world that lies ahead.

DOUG CHAYKA ILLUSTRATION FOR FOREIGN POLICY

Our world is hurtling toward a decentered international system. No single country or coalition of countries will dominate. Assuming they can restore their political health and continue as strategic partners, the United States and its democratic allies will remain a formidable coalition but no longer a preponderant one. China will emerge as a peer competitor, but even if its partnership with Russia endures, it will have neither the power nor the appeal to anchor a Sinocentric world order. A host of rising powers—Brazil, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, and Turkey among them—have made it clear that they will chart their own courses, leading to shifting alignments and uncertain coalitions.

The coming international system will be not only decentered but also politically and culturally diverse. Each center of power and governance will play by its own norms and reflect its own civilizational and cultural attributes. The diffusion of power and devolution of authority and responsibility to diverse regional groupings will naturally produce a world that is polycentric and multiorder.

This essay is adapted from Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come by Charles A. Kupchan (Yale University Press, 328 pp., $32.50, October 2026).

This organic process of regionalization is already underway. The United States remains a truly global power, but Trump is reasserting U.S. preeminence in the Western Hemisphere and encouraging allies to assume more responsibility for security in their own regions. China and Russia look set to anchor a regional grouping that stretches from Eastern Europe to the Pacific, while Beijing simultaneously works to establish its own sphere of influence in its immediate neighborhood. Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and other regional powers are also seeking greater autonomy and influence, in part by advancing projects of regional integration.

The case for polycentrism rests not only on the inevitability of power diffusion and the decentering of the international system but also on the order-producing effects of a bottom-up, regionalized approach to global governance. Geography and proximity still matter. The countries closest to a threat usually have the strongest interest in countering it. Although the United States—due to its unmatched military muscle—led this year’s air campaign against Iran, regional players such as Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have the strongest interest in containing Tehran’s revisionist ambitions. The parties with the sturdiest motivation to counter extremists in Africa are those directly threatened by the violence and its spillover. To encourage regional solutions to regional challenges is to tap the will of the parties most keen to address those challenges and aggregate regional effort.

The same goes for trade. Globalization has peaked, and the international economy is becoming fragmented. Almost one-third of U.S. trade is with Canada and Mexico, some two-thirds of European Union trade takes place within the bloc, and intra-regional trade makes up more than half of Asia’s international commerce. These trends are poised to deepen due to tariffs, friendshoring, the repatriation of supply chains, and other forms of economic decoupling. Regions are becoming increasingly important sites of commercial activity.

A polycentric approach to global governance would also capitalize on the ordering effects of regional power asymmetries. The largest countries in a region usually rely on their geopolitical and economic heft to play a leading role in designing and overseeing regional initiatives. At the same time, projects of regional integration produce institutions and practices that bind major powers to consensual rules and norms. Regional bodies both empower and check their largest countries, one of the reasons they enjoy buy-in among bigger and smaller countries alike.

Regions are becoming increasingly important sites of commercial activity.

EU membership may expose less powerful member states to the outsized sway of Germany and France, but these smaller countries also have a compelling interest in entering a compact that constrains and dilutes the influence of their big neighbors. The same goes for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), which both enables and restrains Saudi Arabia, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which does the same for Indonesia. The size of China’s economy gives it immense influence within the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, but this regional trade pact also binds Beijing to consensual rules.

By encouraging major powers to hold sway in their own neighborhoods, the regionalization of global governance would to some extent bring back and legitimize spheres of influence. Yet that outcome is inevitable in a world of diffusing power. Ideally, tomorrow’s spheres of influence would be less coercive than past ones. The global delegitimation of imperial rule makes it more likely that major powers would wield their influence largely through consensus rather than coercion.

Admittedly, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and Moscow’s defense of what it considers its sphere of influence has been anything but benign. Yet the Kremlin might well be less aggressive toward its neighbors if it believed that other major powers—the United States in particular—would refrain from extending their strategic reach into Russia’s rimlands. In similar fashion, if the United States and China can dial down their rivalry, Beijing might pursue its regional objectives through less coercive means.

The regionalization of global governance is also suited to a world in which regions have different priorities. Certain challenges, such as climate change, are global in reach and require a coordinated global response. Yet other issues on the international agenda have salience and import in some regions but not others. In Latin America, combating organized crime and drug trafficking is a much higher priority than in most other regions. In Africa, building state capacity and alleviating poverty animate efforts to advance regional governance. The Middle East’s priorities include managing sectarian cleavages, taming Iran, and resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In short, one size does not fit all. A polycentric order would be fit for purpose in a world of diverse regional priorities.

Finally, the regionalization of global governance would capitalize on the cooperative potential that comes with cultural ties. Across history, zones of stable peace have most frequently taken shape among nations that enjoy ethnic, racial, or religious commonalities. The sense of likeness that accompanies shared cultural practices and symbols encourages solidarity. A communal identity helped establish the social and political foundations of the EU, which has established a flag, common passport, and single currency. The African Union’s founding charter commits its members to build on the work of “generations of Pan-Africanists” to advance a “common identity” and “achieve greater unity and solidarity.” ASEAN has adopted a motto—“One Vision, One Identity, One Community”—as well as a flag, emblem, and anthem. In a decentered world of ideological diversity, a polycentric system of governance would tap into the ordering effects of shared regional cultures and identities.

Left: A police official peers out from between national flags during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Vientiane, Laos, on Oct. 9, 2024. TANG CHHIN SOTHY/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES   Right: German soldiers hoist a European flag in front of the Bundeswehr Memorial in Berlin on Nov. 10, 2025. TOBIAS SCHWARZ/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

The EU, the Commonwealth of Independent States, ASEAN, the Arab League, the AU, the Organization of American States—these are among the major regional institutions that will need to serve as key building blocks of global order in a polycentric world. Some regional bodies, such as the Arab League, will have to mature considerably if they are to play a more robust role in anchoring a regional order. New regional bodies will need to be created in South Asia and Northeast Asia, where capable institutions are lacking largely because of the geopolitical tensions that continue to arrest regional integration.

There is no neat, widely accepted understanding of where regions begin and end or of what regional family some countries belong to. Egypt is a member of the Arab League as well as the AU. Russia’s ongoing effort to subjugate its neighbor emerged from Ukraine’s desire to leave a relatively coercive Eurasian community for a more voluntary European one. Regional organizations develop as they see fit, and their membership evolves as nations perceive value in joining them—or sometimes leaving them.

But even if location does not determine alignment and regional affiliation, geography powerfully shapes national and regional interests. Europe, though part of a trans-Atlantic strategic bloc, has successfully pursued its own project of regional integration. As Chinese power continues to grow, U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific will need to navigate Beijing’s inevitable effort to build a more Sinocentric regional order in its neighborhood. Canada, alienated by Trump’s America First policies, is looking for a new home among middle powers. But like it or not, Canada will remain deeply integrated into North America both strategically and commercially.

Regional bodies are layered within a network of institutions that extends both below and above them. Below them are subregional groupings, which can be important sites of localized governance and consensus-building. The Economic Community of West African States is a subgroup of the AU, just as the Visegrád Four and the Three Seas Initiative are subgroups of the EU, and members of the GCC are also members of the Arab League.

Multilateralism is at a dead end, but powerful blocs are getting things done.
By Stefan Theil

Above regional institutions is a proliferating array of transregional bodies. Some, like NATO, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), explicitly seek to build ties across geographic regions. NATO traverses the North Atlantic, APEC spans the Pacific Rim, while the SCO groups China and Russia with states in Central, South, and West Asia. Other transregional bodies—such as the G-7, the G-20, and BRICS—base their membership not on geography but on economic size. The G-7 is a league of wealthy democracies, the G-20 includes wealthier democracies and autocracies alike, and BRICS is an expanding club of large countries that aims to counterbalance the West and advance the aspirations of the global south.

Regional groupings are set to be the primary vehicles for building international order from the bottom up. But a polycentric approach to global governance must also capitalize on the subregional and transregional linkages that are very much a part of a complicated architecture of international institutions. The challenge will be to use this messy structure of nested and overlapping bodies to build collective initiative.

Collective efforts will be easier to come by if alternative groupings end up being complementary and additive rather than competitive and adversarial. Russia and China may intend BRICS and the SCO to serve as counterweights to Western institutions, and to some extent they do serve that purpose. But the Western democracies should approach them pragmatically and welcome their delivery of public goods; BRICS, for example, provides loans and other financial support to emerging economies, while the SCO has advanced cooperation on countering trafficking of humans and weapons.

This lattice-like network of regional, subregional, and transregional institutions constitutes the substructure of a polycentric global order; it must be effectively tapped to maximize international cooperation. If the bottom-up elements of governance represent the skeleton of a globalized and multipolar world, such a system will still need a central nervous system. For that, we need to look to history.

And it cannot be revived by China, Europe, post-Trump America, or the global south.
By Jo Inge Bekkevold

An illustration depicts the Congress of Vienna, circa 1814, which gave birth to the Concert of Europe.WIKIMEDIA COMMONS

Even as a significant measure of order comes from the bottom up, the world needs a global architecture to provide governance from the top down, dampening great-power rivalry, addressing crises as they emerge, and coordinating collective action across the world’s regions. The U.N. and its supporting network of international institutions are meant to fulfill this function. But the U.N. system is manifestly inadequate: It is too big, too bureaucratic, and too often paralyzed by the veto power wielded by the permanent members of the Security Council. The gap between the demand for global governance and its supply grows by the day.

A concert system offers a pragmatic and workable means of establishing such centralized governance. The Concert of Europe is the prototype. Fashioned in 1815 at the end of the Napoleonic Wars, this steering group of five major powers preserved peace in a multipolar and ideologically diverse Europe for decades to come. Two liberalizing countries—Britain and France—worked comfortably alongside three absolute monarchies in Austria, Prussia, and Russia. The concert centralized governance through great-power congresses while also regionalizing leadership by granting each member special sway in its own neighborhood. It was informal and flexible, shunning charters and fixed rules and instead, according to a British memo from 1818, allowing consensus to “arise out of the circumstances of the time and of the case.”

Concert diplomacy has distinct advantages when it comes to providing top-down governance in the world to come. Concerts put at the table only the influential parties best suited to tackle the task at hand, facilitating consensus by limiting the number of voices in the room. Small-group formats may be exclusive and violate the norm of sovereign equality. But by deliberately sacrificing broad representation in favor of efficacy, they offer the best means of forging agreements in a decentered and ideologically diverse world.

As during the Concert of Europe, a contemporary version would deliberately span regime type, helping to overcome the bitter cleavages that have lately emerged between democracies and autocracies. Member states would consciously set aside differences over matters of domestic governance and political rights to ensure that these issues do not hinder international cooperation. A new concert system would also have the flexibility to put at the table nonstate actors such as NGOs and CEOs when they can effectively contribute to collective initiative and problem-solving.

The U.N. system is manifestly inadequate: It is too big, too bureaucratic, and too often paralyzed by the veto power wielded by the permanent members of the Security Council.

Concerts work not only because of their limited and select membership but also because they avoid institutionalization, legalization, and binding procedures. To be sure, international governance would ideally be formalized and legalized, buttressed by enforceable rules and commitments. But most states, especially the major powers whose interactions have the biggest impact on the inter-national system, are unwilling to compromise their sovereignty by submitting to the will of international bodies.

These obstacles to institutionalized cooperation will only become more acute in the years ahead. As the diffusion of power heats up geopolitical rivalries, formalized agreements will be harder to reach. Meanwhile, the political backlash against socioeconomic dislocation, globalization, and immigration is intensifying domestic opposition to, in Trump’s words, “international unions that tie us up and bring America down.” Amid a widespread surge in populist nationalism, institutionalized multilateralism will be increasingly elusive. Indeed, stalemate in the U.N. Security Council, the World Trade Organization, and other bodies is already the norm; the U.N. far more regularly serves as a forum for public grandstanding than for constructive diplomacy.

The shift to informal, small-group diplomacy is already underway—more by default than by design. Since well before the arrival of Trump’s pronounced unilateralism, the United States and other countries were already gravitating toward greater reliance on coalitions of the willing and informal pacts.

A contact group of Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Russia, and the United States led the successful effort to bring peace to the Balkans during the 1990s. The P5+1 grouping (the five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council plus Germany) negotiated the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran. More recently, Oman, Pakistan, and Qatar have been leading efforts to mediate between Iran and the United States, Trump’s Board of Peace has been seeking to pacify Gaza, and Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and the United States have teamed up to try to end Sudan’s civil war. Ad hoc groupings and coalitions of the willing have become the new normal.

An explicit move to regularize concert diplomacy would thus channel a shift that is already taking place, driven by both geopolitical and domestic realities. Rather than lamenting the decline of institutionalized multilateralism and struggling to restore it, the international community should normalize concert diplomacy and seek to make the most of its cooperative potential.

How the United States can rejuvenate the global institutions it created.
By Gordon Brown

A contemporary concert system would consist of a Global Concert supported by a network of subconcerts. It would put at the table the influential actors that need to be there—regardless of their regime type. It would include autocracies as well as democracies and developing as well as developed countries. It would be large enough to be globally representative but small enough to be effective. Major powers have been busy sorting themselves into rival groups—the G-7, BRICS, the SCO. They should now channel that cooperative impulse into a new grouping that cuts across geopolitical and ideological dividing lines and aims to surface and further common interests.

The Global Concert would serve as a great-power directorate, a steering group tasked with overseeing global governance.

The Global Concert would serve as a great-power directorate, a steering group tasked with overseeing global governance. Its initial members would be the familiar heavyweights: China, the EU, India, Japan, Russia, and the United States. Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America would be represented by emissaries from their main regional bodies—ASEAN, the Arab League, the AU, and the Organization of American States. Having Europe be represented by the EU rather than by Germany, its most powerful state, would legitimize the inclusion of emissaries from regional bodies. Having representatives from ASEAN, the Arab League, the AU, and the Organization of American States would encourage these bodies’ members to aggregate their voices and advance regional integration—while also sidestepping the controversy that might accompany invitations to only the largest country from each region. The members of the concert would have the flexibility, through consensus, to alter the body’s composition over time.

As in the Concert of Europe, ideological differences over domestic governance would be fenced off from matters requiring international cooperation, and concert diplomacy would take place alongside the devolution of authority to regional groupings. Unlike the Concert of Europe, whose congresses occurred sporadically and in various locations, the Global Concert would meet on a continuous, daily basis. Its headquarters should be located in a city that sits between West and East and North and South, such as Istanbul or Dubai. Fly-in, fly-out summits, whether of the G-7, the G-20, or BRICS, are woefully inadequate. By providing a vehicle for continuous face-to-face dialogue, the Global Concert could realistically mute and manage geopolitical and ideological differences and foster consensus.

In addition to serving as a high-level steering group, the Global Concert would also function as a council of councils. It would set up a network of subconcerts—bespoke contact groups—to tackle pressing issues that require sustained engagement and collective initiative. Subconcerts would be established to address geopolitical flashpoints such as Ukraine, Israel-Palestine, Iran, and Taiwan. Focused dialogues on the underlying disputes will not guarantee their resolution. But active and sustained diplomacy is better than no diplomacy, and at a minimum, it reduces the chances of mis-understandings, mishaps, or inadvertent escalation. Other subconcerts could focus on international commerce, climate change, technological advances, global health, and human development. These groups would put at the table not only powerful states but also relevant nonstate actors. The subconcert focused on the regulation of technology and artificial intelligence, for example, could include representatives from the major tech companies as well as experts from NGOs and universities. Additional subconcerts would be set up as needed to respond to emerging crises or other longer-term challenges.

The Global Concert, backstopped by the subconcerts, would primarily be a consultative body; it would tee up decisions that would often be finalized and implemented by the U.N. and other global and regional institutions. Concert members would be behind closed doors, meeting on a continuous basis, and disarmed of veto power, boosting the likelihood of forging a diplomatic consensus that existing bodies could build on. A concert system would provide a venue for a sustained conversation that does not now exist, bolstering the current international architecture and strengthening, not sidelining, the U.N. by facilitating agreement and thereby making the body more effective.

The concert system would thus serve as a global governance hub, providing the governing core needed to anchor a polycentric world. The overall logic of this approach is to marry the bottom-up governance that will accompany power diffusion and regionalization with the top-down oversight and coordination that would be provided by a concert system.

Ordering moments tend to follow major wars. The Peace of Westphalia emerged in 1648 after a century of war sparked by the Protestant Reformation. The Concert of Europe took shape in 1815 in the aftermath of the Napoleonic Wars. The establishment of the League of Nations in 1920 followed the close of World War I, and the U.N. was founded in 1945 just after the end of World War II. Wars are wake-up calls that encourage humankind to try to end the cycles of bloodshed that have come before.

The world now needs a new ordering moment—but before, not after, another great-power war. Unfortunately, neither in the United States nor anywhere else has a constructive dialogue begun about building an order fit for an era of globalized multipolarity. Instead, diplomacy and public dialogue are afflicted by growing rivalry among nations and political division within them.

The pragmatic vision of order laid out in this essay is neither elegant nor grand. Putting it into place would not entail the great fanfare that accompanied the launch of the League of Nations or the U.N. Nor is this vision of a reimagined global order a magic bullet. Even if regional bodies mature, they will at times fail to prevent conflicts and fall short of adequately delivering public goods. Concert diplomacy cannot solve all problems. The national interests of great powers will still come into conflict even if they all join the Global Concert. Climate change will remain a vexing challenge even after a steering group to tackle it is up and running.

But the current system of global governance is manifestly inadequate. A polycentric order anchored by a concert system is the best available option for managing the world to come. It offers a pragmatic approach to advancing the cause of global governance and peace in an era of globalized multipolarity. At this historical inflection point—as democracies stumble, geopolitical fracture mounts, global challenges intensify, and collective initiative grows more elusive—we need a workable and attainable plan for where we go from here. Let the debate begin.

Three years ago, on a clear day, you could stand at the Lebanese border with Israel in the village of Marwahin and see the Baha’i Gardens on Mount Carmel, looking down over the Israeli city of Haifa. The view suited the widespread talk at the time about an Iran-led “axis of resistance” based in Lebanon and Gaza and intent on liberating Palestine. Then Oct. 7 happened.

That was when the “axis of resistance” finally met another regional dynamic head-on: an expansionist Israel that was increasingly willing to strike first against its adversaries. What has transpired over the past three intense years of war—in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran—has been the collapse of Iran’s deterrent strategy. The axis was Iran’s first line of defense in its grand strategy against Israel and the United States. But the axis’s forward strongholds were no longer protecting its core; it was no longer possible to keep war away from Iran’s borders.

Three years ago, on a clear day, you could stand at the Lebanese border with Israel in the village of Marwahin and see the Baha’i Gardens on Mount Carmel, looking down over the Israeli city of Haifa. The view suited the widespread talk at the time about an Iran-led “axis of resistance” based in Lebanon and Gaza and intent on liberating Palestine. Then Oct. 7 happened.

That was when the “axis of resistance” finally met another regional dynamic head-on: an expansionist Israel that was increasingly willing to strike first against its adversaries. What has transpired over the past three intense years of war—in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran—has been the collapse of Iran’s deterrent strategy. The axis was Iran’s first line of defense in its grand strategy against Israel and the United States. But the axis’s forward strongholds were no longer protecting its core; it was no longer possible to keep war away from Iran’s borders.

Iran entered a new era, one that necessitated a rethinking of its grand strategy for confrontation and even survival. Iran’s previous strategy, based on containment and strategic patience, has not survived the current war. Tehran has instead been forced to rely on what had previously been its second and third lines of defense. The second line consisted of its missile and drone arsenal, and the third relied on its geographical superiority: vast expanses of land; mountainous terrain; and, most importantly, the Strait of Hormuz and its significance for global trade.

This last line had never previously been tested, and Iran remained wary that its use might fail. But the country has now been testing its ability to fight alone on the battlefield.

What has been particularly painful for Iran is that it has been forced to reverse the roles between itself and its allied groups and organizations. Instead of these factions preventing the war from reaching Iran, as the plan had been, Iran rushed to their defense when necessary.

Hezbollah was transformed in an instant from a spearhead in the conflict to an organization under pressure, cut off from supplies after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, and besieged by the Lebanese state, which is negotiating with Israel while the militant group strives to maintain its existence, with Iran doing what is necessary to protect it militarily and diplomatically.

This profound shift in its function was reflected, in turn, in the arrangement of power tools within the Iranian strategy. The Hezbollah that existed on the eve of the Oct. 7, 2023, events and Hamas’s attack on Israeli settlements surrounding Gaza is no longer the same. Its previously declared objectives are no longer valid, and the role that Hezbollah played on a regional level, from Iraq to Syria and Yemen and decades earlier in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is no longer viable. The war and the fall of Assad in Syria returned Hezbollah to its Lebanese sphere of influence, which in turn altered its function for the axis in general and for Tehran in particular.

This shift prompted Iran to explore its latent power, which had remained untested for years in the very confrontation that it had long been talking about. The war appeared simultaneously as a challenge and an opportunity for a nation that, for nearly half a century, had never missed an opportunity to declare its hostility toward the United States and Israel. The activation of the Strait of Hormuz has given the Iranians an unprecedented advantage in the conflict. But Iran has also been confronting two nuclear powers with one of the most advanced air forces in the world, a sophisticated early warning system, and a multilayered air defense system.

What has become clear is that U.S. President Donald Trump, confronted with Iran’s new strategy, prefers normalization to a protracted war with Tehran. What complicates this matter is the team that is now in charge in Iran.

This team is a product of the war’s unstated fourth objective. From the early days until now, the rhetoric has focused on eliminating the Iranian nuclear threat, destroying its missile infrastructure, and dismantling its regional network. On the sidelines, Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have stated their desire to overthrow the regime. Then, after Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s assassination, Trump repeatedly declared that the regime had fallen.

In practice, the regime has indeed changed, but in a direction contrary to what the United States and Israel wanted. The change has produced a more rigid and cohesive system than its predecessor, even if differences have emerged. These differences, however, do not yet appear to be at a level that could divide the country into two opposing camps.

As Trump’s economic warfare takes its toll, Tehran will be tempted to go on the offensive in search of greater leverage

This was evident in the recent change that affected the position of the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in early August. Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr—who succeeded Ali Larijani, who was killed during the war—disagreed with other leaders over how to deal with ships passing through the strait. He threatened to resign after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted them. He was then replaced by former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei, whose appointment coincided with subsequent appointments that filled most of the country’s vacant military leadership positions; Zolghadr himself became an advisor to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who still rules from behind the scenes.

The appointment of Rezaei carries a message in more than one direction. He had spent the spring and summer arguing that it was not possible to negotiate and fight at the same time. This is a position that Mojtaba Khamenei had conveyed to other Iranian officials in June, as told to me by an Iranian official who refused to reveal his name.

But Rezaei may also be closing the circle on Iran’s evolving strategy, which has seen shifts in its defense priorities. In late August, Rezaei went further than any senior Iranian official had in years. In a television interview, he questioned the entire logic of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, arguing that membership in it had not prevented the United States and Israel from bombing Iranian nuclear sites anyway, and he asked on air: “Why shouldn’t we also seek to acquire nuclear weapons?”

Rezaei elaborated extensively on the nuclear issue, more so than any previous secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. This occurred while the Iranian parliament was debating withdrawal from the Nonproliferation Treaty and while the new supreme leader had yet to confirm his adherence to his father’s fatwa prohibiting the use, production, stockpiling, and acquisition of nuclear weapons, but also had not declared anything to the contrary.

This leaves the issue open to all possibilities, especially since Iran had stated on numerous occasions before its recent wars against the United States and Israel, through various officials, that it would reconsider its nuclear doctrine if targeted.

The nuclear issue brings us back to Iran’s defense strategy. If we combine all the elements that we mentioned earlier and prioritize them, we find that Iran hasn’t changed its strategy but rather reshaped it. The network of allies still exists; although it has been weakened, it hasn’t been eliminated, and Tehran continues to benefit from its existence in various ways. Hezbollah is exhausted after two difficult wars with Israel, but it is preparing. Iran’s allied Iraqi factions are facing pressure at a time when U.S. influence is growing again in Iraqi politics, while its Syrian corridor disappeared with the fall of the Assad regime. The Houthis, however, are still able to exert pressure on Saudi Arabia, which has spent two years trying to avoid this war through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait without fully activating that front.

The missile and drone programs have become a higher priority, especially given Iran’s heavy reliance on them. It appears from the past few months that Iran is investing heavily in developing these missiles and drones to increase their effectiveness and the leverage that they can exert in any future confrontation.

As for Hormuz, the third layer, this is the card that Tehran has forcefully pushed to the forefront since the cease-fire, and it now uses it in various ways while trying to establish a legal reality for itself.

The question that remains unanswered is whether a fourth layer, this time nuclear, will join the three existing layers.

From Iran, we return to southern Lebanon, where the areas that a journalist like myself can see from the last point not occupied are shrinking. We can no longer stand in Marwahin to see Haifa, nor even in Naqoura, which is now itself within Israeli-occupied territory. I find myself standing in Haniyeh, observing from there Mansouri and some of the slopes that connect to the sea and lead to Naqoura.

This new equation imposed by Israel on Lebanon was the product of a larger battle across the entire region. It is the same battle that brought the Strait of Hormuz to the forefront in a completely opposite equation, an equation in which Iran seeks to establish a new reality in the region—one in which it sees no U.S. presence to challenge it.

With this new reality, Iran no longer needs to focus on seeing Haifa. That goal, and the Lebanese front built for it, has quietly become less important. Israel, however, still wants to keep an eye on Tehran, which is why Iran won’t give up its influence in southern Lebanon, no matter the pressure or how weak its hold becomes. At the very least, Iran keeps an early warning system there, staying close enough to Israel to spot any signs of a new war and rebuild its presence however it can.

Still, this is now a lower priority for Iran. The main focus is now on rebuilding its missile and drone program, which played a key role in the war and is being rapidly expanded. The old defense line in the south won’t return soon. But what replaces it starts inside Iran’s own borders.

Ali Hashem is a journalist and researcher covering wars, diplomacy, and political transformations across the Middle East. He is a correspondent with Al Jazeera and a research fellow at the Centre of Islamic and West Asian Studies, Royal Holloway, University of London. X: @alihashem

“Medicare for All” has once again become a rallying cry for progressives on the 2026 midterms campaign trail. Picking up on a theme that Sen. Bernie Sanders elevated in Democratic politics during his 2016 primary run, the idea that Medicare—a program that provides hospital and physician insurance to elderly Americans should be expanded to cover everyone has considerable popular appeal.

The best way to deal with the healthcare crisis, progressives argue, is to expand an existing program that has proven to be enormously popular: Rather than starting from scratch, why not just build on the program that already works so well?

“Medicare for All” has once again become a rallying cry for progressives on the 2026 midterms campaign trail. Picking up on a theme that Sen. Bernie Sanders elevated in Democratic politics during his 2016 primary run, the idea that Medicare—a program that provides hospital and physician insurance to elderly Americans should be expanded to cover everyone has considerable popular appeal.

The best way to deal with the healthcare crisis, progressives argue, is to expand an existing program that has proven to be enormously popular: Rather than starting from scratch, why not just build on the program that already works so well?

Medicare for All has received strong support across the progressive spectrum, from Sanders to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who wrote a book on the subject and has made the idea a centerpiece of his campaign. Meanwhile, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who has supported previous Medicare for All proposals, is now distancing himself from such legislation.

Yet what many Americans do not know is that Medicare for All actually has Republican roots. In 1970, when the Republican Party was very different than it is today and U.S. politics had not yet shifted so far to the right, New York Republican Sen. Jacob Javits advanced a proposal that gave birth to the idea.

When Congress created Medicare in 1965, many of its supporters saw it as a first step toward universal coverage for every American regardless of age. The original proposal to provide hospital insurance for older Americans through Social Security emerged out of liberal frustration with President Harry Truman’s failure to enact national healthcare insurance. Truman, the first president to propose such a policy, had faced intense opposition. The American Medical Association (AMA) conducted a fierce campaign against his proposal, warning that it would lead to “socialized medicine.” As Princeton sociologist Paul Starr showed in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Social Transformation of American Medicine, the doctors’ association tapped into the deeply rooted belief, dating back to the rise of modern medicine in the early 20th century, that the doctor-patient relationship was sacrosanct and should remain free of government interference. Physicians found crucial political support in the conservative coalition of southern Democrats and Midwestern Republicans.

During the 1950s, liberals shifted course. Instead of pursuing health insurance for all Americans,

liberal organizations and legislators adopted a narrower strategy, focusing on elderly Americans, who were widely viewed as particularly deserving of government assistance, especially after a lifetime of work. Liberal advocates also sought to place the program within the Social Security system, which by then had become enormously popular with both Democratic and Republican voters. Beginning in 1957, Democrats such as Rhode Island Rep. Aime Forand repeatedly introduced legislation to provide hospital insurance for those who were 65 or older. The effort won strong backing from organized labor. Yet the AMA continued to denounce it as socialized medicine and House Ways and Means Chairman Wilbur Mills of Arkansas refused to allow the bill to move through his committee. President John F. Kennedy, who made a major push for the legislation, grew increasingly frustrated by its inability to gain traction.

Eventually, there was a historic breakthrough. Following Arizona Sen. Barry Goldwater’s landslide defeat in the 1964 presidential election, which discredited right-wing conservatism and was accompanied by massive Democratic majorities in a Congress that leaned to the left, the political landscape shifted dramatically. Mills, who could read the writing on the wall, shifted from being the chief obstacle to national healthcare reform to the architect of legislation much grander than previous supporters had imagined. In 1965, Congress passed legislation creating Medicare Part A, which provided hospital insurance funded through payroll taxes; Medicare Part B, which offered voluntary physician insurance financed through general tax revenues and beneficiary premiums; and Medicaid, which provided health coverage for low-income Americans who fell outside of Medicare’s social safety net.

Javits played an important role throughout the Medicare debates. Born into a poor family in New York’s Lower East Side, Javits was part of a liberal Republican coalition that, before the conservative turn of 1980s, exerted significant influence within the party on issues like healthcare and civil rights. Javits saw himself as a legislator capable of building bipartisan and inter-regional bridges to break the deadlock that had stalled healthcare reform throughout the 20th century. Javits was particularly important in shaping a number of key features of the final legislation, including the decision to use private insurance to administer the program rather than concentrating authority wholly in a centralized government bureaucracy

The liberal proponents of Medicare (a term supposedly created by a newspaper editor who needed a name that would fit neatly into headlines), including Wilbur Cohen and Robert Ball, both veterans of the Social Security Administration, always envisioned that the program would be a first step toward broader national health insurance, just as Congress had gradually expanded Social Security after 1935 to include more people and benefits. The vision was not some kind of conspiratorial plan. As more Americans saw the benefits of Medicare and understood that federal intervention would not destroy the virtues of the private system—and instead serve as a complement—elected officials anticipated finding the political space to do more.

The closest the nation came to Medicare for All was with Javits’ proposed legislation in 1970. In April, he introduced the National Health Insurance and Health Services Improvement Act, which would have gradually expanded health insurance coverage to all Americans. “Medicare For All is Asked by Javits,” read the New York Times headline. He found support from several like-minded Republicans.

They did in 2006—but only when framed by Democrats in one specific way.

President Franklin Roosevelt enlisted entertainers to make the case for fighting Germany and Japan.

A new movie shows how the president conferred with State Department experts before each meeting.

Javits pushed the proposal at a moment when policymakers across the political spectrum had become increasingly concerned about the deep structural problems of the nation’s healthcare system, including the fact that tens of millions of Americans lacked any insurance and that medical costs were continuing to rise. For Javits and his allies in Washington, these challenges underscored the need for a more active federal role in guaranteeing access to good healthcare.

The plan languished, however, as it faced the traditional attacks from the AMA and conservatives as threatening socialized medicine. Javits also struggled to build a coalition as a result of competing proposals. While some liberal legislators, such as Sen. Ted Kennedy of Massachusetts, continued to champion the creation of a new national health insurance system modeled on those established in European social democracies, and conservatives promoted tax credits to subsidize private coverage, Javits believed a basis for the best solution was already on the books. In his view, Congress could achieve universal coverage by gradually expanding Medicare to additional group coupled with improvements in benefits. He proposed paying for the program through payroll taxes and general revenues, as Medicare was funded. Private insurance carriers would continue to serve as administrative intermediaries. His proposal included increased reliance on prepaid group practices (later called health maintenance organizations, or HMOs) and other reforms to improve efficiencies in the delivery of care. President Richard Nixon, who agreed that the nation’s healthcare system badly needed reform, proposed a limited update of the system in 1971 and then advanced a bolder proposal in 1974: the Comprehensive Health Insurance Plan, which relied on a mix of improved Medicare benefits, employer mandates, federal insurance for poor Americans, and incentives to expand HMOs.

In the end, nothing happened. The proposal that had the best odds of passing, Nixon’s plan, fell victim to the turbulent politics of the era. Watergate, the economic pressures of stagflation and the oil crisis, and Mills’ own scandal involving a stripper, combined to derail the legislation and extinguish what had become a strong bipartisan push for national health insurance.

In 1993 and 1994, President Bill Clinton moved the national debate further away from the Medicare for All vision when he advanced a healthcare plan that looked more like Nixon’s, built around employer mandates, regional healthcare alliances, new insurance regulations, and federal subsidies for those who fell outside the private system. (The administration rejected a proposal from Democrat Pete Stark to expand Medicare.) Clinton’s plan failed and opened the door to the Republican takeover of Congress in 1994—which pushed national politics, including on healthcare, further to the right. The public’s problems worsened, as Jonathan Cohn argued in his 2009 book Sick, leaving middle class Americans even more vulnerable to the consequences of illness.

When President Barack Obama successfully moved the Affordable Care Act through Congress in 2010, he largely built on the framework that Clinton had championed, though backing away from some of the bolder reorganization his Democratic predecessor wanted and abandoning serious cost-control measures with the hope of encouraging private stakeholders to buy into the proposal. In 2006, Massachusetts Republican Gov. Mitt Romney signed into law a healthcare program that revolved around using mandates to incentivize healthy people to buy insurance, a free-market framework Obama later incorporated into his bill. Obama also agreed to remove the public option, a government-run insurance plan that supporters viewed as the closest the nation had come to Medicare for All since Javits’ 1970 proposal.

Today, Medicare for All is associated with the left wing of the Democratic Party. The fact that so many Americans view the proposal in that light reflects how dramatically the political boundaries of the debate have shifted since 1980s. During the decades before Ronald Reagan’s presidency, proposals to expand government-sponsored health insurance were supported by a broad range of liberal Democrats and moderate Republicans. A plan that a Republican senator could proudly champion in 1970 would today be seen as radical.

The shift also reflects how much the Republican Party has changed since then. The liberal northeastern wing of the GOP, which once proudly boasted of New York governors Thomas Dewey and Nelson Rockefeller, has vanished. By the late 20th century, conservatives had supplanted the party’s liberal and moderate factions. Since the 2010s, Tea Party and MAGA Republicans have left no room for the kind of policymakers Javits represented.

As a result, efforts to reform the healthcare system have suffered. For all the progress achieved with the Affordable Care Act—including its prohibition on insurance companies discriminating against people with preexisting conditions, as well as expanding Medicaid—the practical considerations created by Tea Party Republicans required Obama to work within limited boundaries. The final legislation left many big problems unaddressed, including weakly regulated costs and ongoing gaps in coverage.

The origins of Medicare for All serve as a reminder that there was a time in U.S. history, not so long ago, when members of both parties saw merit in expanding the nation’s largest universal health insurance program to ensure that no American would have to confront illness and fear financial disaster. Javits’ vision rested on the belief that no American should have to worry that basic medical services would be out of reach.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. His most recent book is The Presidency of Joseph R. Biden Jr.: A First Historical Assessment. X: @julianzelizer

In the aftermath of the al Qaeda terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 on Sept. 11, 2001, the 9/11 Commission Report lamented a “failure of imagination” on the part of the U.S. government and intelligence community. After all, the primary weapons used in the simultaneous attacks were boxcutters, knives, and ultimately, passenger jets.

Terrorists hijacking planes was certainly conceivable. Between 1968 and 1972, there were more than 130 attempted hijackings in the United States, most bound for Havana. Abroad, there were spectacular hijackings across Europe and the Middle East, often conducted by Palestinian terror groups primarily motivated by nationalism. And while these hijackings did not result in terrorists flying planes into buildings, the idea that they could had been discussed at length for decades. In fact, legendary terrorism scholar Brian Michael Jenkins warned about exactly that in 1989 at an international conference on aviation security in Israel: “The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.”

Abroad, there were spectacular hijackings across Europe and the Middle East, often conducted by Palestinian terror groups primarily motivated by nationalism. And while these hijackings did not result in terrorists flying planes into buildings, the idea that they could had been discussed at length for decades. In fact, legendary terrorism scholar Brian Michael Jenkins warned about exactly that in 1989 at an international conference on aviation security in Israel: “The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.”

U.S. Representative Tim Roemer (left) and Carie Lemack hold copies of The 9/11 Commission Report during a news conference on Dec. 6, 2004. Lemack also holds a photo of her mother, Judy Larocque, who died in the terror attacks.Getty Images/Joe Raedle

Twenty-five years after 9/11, airports can no longer be considered soft targets for terrorists. However, terrorists and violent extremists have access to a range of technologies today that either didn’t exist or were in their infancy two and a half decades ago. The internet has been most consequential for terrorists, allowing them, through websites and social media platforms, to spread their message widely; to make contact with aggrieved individuals; and to radicalize and recruit. But advances in encrypted communications, 3D printing, unmanned aerial systems (drones), virtual currencies, and artificial intelligence (AI) also can serve as force multipliers for lone actors and terrorist organizations planning attacks. Over the last decade, barriers to entry for engaging with these technologies have been appreciably lowered, and access has been commercialized, meaning everyday citizens can now acquire and master tools once obtainable only by states.

In late 2026, a failure of imagination persists, though its form has evolved. While the counterterrorism community today is aware of emerging technologies in the hands of terrorists, it continues to struggle with creatively thinking through how these can be combined or applied to novel use cases. While it is beyond the scope of this essay to assess every possible tool terrorist groups could misuse, it makes sense to consider what adoption and use patterns can tell us about the potential misuse of current technologies. We tend to avoid publishing terror-attack scenarios—we’re not in the business of giving bad people good ideas. Our intent is instead to describe existing vulnerabilities so that policymakers, intelligence officials, and law enforcement agencies might pay attention and prepare accordingly, and never again suffer such a consequential failure of imagination as in the lead-up to 9/11.

Smoke from a forest fire near the southern Lebanese village of Shebaa, close to the northern border of Israel, after the Israeli army shot down a Hezbollah drone on July 4, 2024.Getty Images/Rabih Daher

Terrorist groups have already used drones successfully in combat and to commit attacks on the battlefield. Twenty years ago, in 2006, Hezbollah launched multiple drones into Israeli airspace, loaded with explosives. Although most of the drones were shot down, the combination of capability and intent was foreboding. Since then, a number of terrorist groups have weaponized drones, including Hamas, the Houthis, the Islamic State, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, Iraqi Shia militias, and violent non-state actors in Pakistan, Syria, and Venezuela.

Drones are now used not just in sporadic attacks, but in combined arms warfare and maneuvers by a range of violent non-state actors. However, though there have been several high-profile plots that have been disrupted, there has yet to be a spectacular terrorist attack in the West perpetrated by a group using drones. Upon closer inspection, some of these plots were nearing fruition and would likely have struck their intended targets if they had proceeded as planned. Individuals, acting independently (rather than as part of the rank-and-file of designated terrorist groups), have been experimenting with drones too. Instructional guides by Islamic State supporters have given detailed, incremental instructions to others on how to weaponize drones; these resources also make clear that drone weaponization is seen as more accessible following the advent of widely available generative AI tools. Conflicts where drones loom large—such as the Russia-Ukraine War—have also expanded the boundaries of what is possible.

Although only recently commercialized, generative AI has featured in several recent terrorist plots and attacks, including on U.S. soil. AI has also been used at the organizational level by terrorist groups, including for propaganda purposes (as the Islamic State Khorasan Province has demonstrated over the past several years) and operational purposes (as seen with Boko Haram). There have been myriad examples of AI being used by lone terrorists for operational purposes as well, including assisting extremists with instructions to build bombs; providing tips on practicing exquisite operational security; and red teaming (that is, simulating the actions of adversaries looking for weaknesses) by prompting AI chatbots to have back-and-forth conversations about how to refine tactics, techniques, and procedures. While the AI safety community predominantly focuses on existential risks, violent non-state actors’ exploitation deserves serious resources and interventions too—especially as open-weight AI models become more capable and can be used by terrorists and violent extremists with no leakage. In general, agentic and generative AI may let terrorists execute organizational and operational tasks more efficiently, providing additional uplift with minimal effort.

When we think about terrorists’ using emerging technologies, the reality is not “either/or”—it’s “and.” In other words, terrorists can use encrypted platforms to communicate and fund their operations with virtual currencies, and use 3D-printed components that will augment drones, and have AI assist with target selection and even pre-program the drone’s attack route. Back in 2018, conflict analyst Daveed Gartenstein-Ross openly mused about this possibility in an op-ed for Defense One, writing: “What of the next generation of terror drones? Will they use AI-enabled swarming to become more powerful and deadlier? Or think bigger: will terrorists use self-driving vehicles for their next car bombs and ramming attacks? How about assassinations?”

Orchestrating a terror attack using a drone targeting a dense urban environment in the West is not a difficult feat. Indeed, it is surprising we have not yet seen a successful attack along these lines. Whether an outdoor farmer’s market or a summer concert in a park, crashing an explosive-laden drone into a crowd of civilians would be a devastating attack that, in addition to killing and injuring people, would have immense psychological impact.

        |
        
    
    Brian Finucane

Most worrisome are the terrorist threats missing from the document.

Degrading command and control over proxy groups could make them more dangerous and unpredictable.

Congress must act to address new and old executive abuses.

The internet is the pervasive facilitator that allows these technologies to be adopted by terrorist groups, their supporters, and acolytes. Without ecosystems of social media platforms, websites, self-hosted servers, messaging applications, and forums in which individuals are presented with engaging media from terrorists and violent extremists—ranging from propaganda, doctrinal essays, lifestyle content, and instructional manuals on everything from drones to operations security to AI—many of these technologies would not be readily used.

Not only has the internet democratized access to information about technology, but it has also facilitated connections between terrorists and their supporters separated by vast distances. At the peak of the Islamic State’s caliphate, British hacker turned Islamic State member Junaid Hussain became the group’s “chief terror cybercoach,” remotely directing jihadist recruits in other countries on how to carry out violent attacks. Today, the Salafi jihadist terrorist threat landscape in the West is largely driven by individuals who have never set foot in a conflict theater. Nor have they received sustained guidance from terrorist rank-and-file in attack planning.

Virtual currencies are used as terrorist groups solicit donations in propaganda magazines distributed online; drone weaponization manuals can be accessed in supporter forums. Even the benign internet—from online hobbyist communities to the social platforms and AI models we all use—can be misused to engineer explosives. Terrorist use of the internet is the leitmotif in terrorists adopting technology. Without access to information online, terrorists would have little choice but to travel directly to training camps, as the al Qaeda militants who perpetrated the 9/11 attacks did, congregating under the protection of the Taliban in Afghanistan.

But in 2026, particularly after the foreign fighter phenomenon that saw tens of thousands of militants from dozens of countries travel to Iraq and Syria, there are far more counterterrorism measures in place to detect and disrupt terrorist travel. Perhaps most effectively, a technical infrastructure has integrated different data streams to significantly narrow the mobility of any terrorist: Fingerprinting and iris scans, forensic innovations able to identify latent prints on bomb fragments, machine-readable passports, and harmonized passenger name records have proven effective in denying travel to terrorists. Engineering marvels, specifically precision guidance, have made ultra-precise strikes possible. Perceptual hashing has made it harder for terrorists to propagate their propaganda online and has been cheap to implement.

Disrupting terrorists’ use of the internet is not about preventing it entirely—which is rather unrealistic—and more about raising the costs and effort of using it to finance, recruit, radicalize, spread propaganda, and plot attacks. This requires robust cooperation between the public and private sector, with governments, law enforcement, and tech platforms working hand in glove to identify threats and prevent terrorists from exploiting the internet.

Advances in artificial intelligence could prove promising for improving content moderation and removal. Machine learning has been used to identify potential terrorist propaganda for hashing. Text, speech, and vision classifiers filter millions of posts across languages, and ranking models can demote borderline content. AIs are also used to apply content policy directly. This infrastructure has been used across counterterrorism—for object detection in CCTV footage, to spot anomalies in financial flows, or to rapidly search freshly seized documents from terrorist groups.

Police checkpoints on and around Bourbon Street after a vehicle plowed into a crowd in New Orleans on January 1, 2025.Getty Images/Patt Little/Anadolu

Beware shiny object syndrome, though. While terrorists openly discuss how new technologies and modes of war can be used for their purposes, attacks and disrupted plots in the West in recent years reveal reliance on simple methods. As terrorism and political violence have atomized—and perhaps because they primarily feature lone actors—stabbings, vehicle ramming, and shootings have become the most commonly executed attacks. These are predominantly perpetrated by individuals who are largely radicalized through online pathways.

This does not mean that these simple methods cannot be optimized through tech-facilitated operational planning. The man who attacked New Orleans on New Year’s Day 2025 used smart glasses for reconnaissance months earlier but used vehicle ramming and a firearm during his attack; recent Islamic State-inspired individuals in Italy used a chatbot to gain information on where to strike someone optimally to paralyze them. Shiny object syndrome also plagues the counterterrorism apparatus at times: While technology has demonstrably been useful in counterterrorism, community interventions and deep human cultural knowledge have proven effective as well and should not be supplanted by technology when not appropriate.

A second plane approaches the World Trade Center before crashing into the second tower on Sept. 11, 2001.Getty Images/Seth McAllister

Twenty-five years after 9/11, the day that planes, the all-American invention of the Wright brothers, were turned into a weapon against Americans, a similar affliction befalls the West: Its innovations are continuously misused by terrorists against it. To prevent the next strategic surprise, serious consideration must be given to how technologies can be used in new creative ways by terrorists in order to optimize casualties, and—as is always a consideration for such actors—cause a violent spectacle.

And technology is a two-way street. While it provides some advantages to terrorists and violent extremists, technology can also be harnessed by actors combating them to recognize patterns in large volumes of data and to enhance structured analytic techniques that fuse myriad streams of intelligence. Moreover, it appears that terrorists’ use of chatbots for operational planning has already become a method of intelligence gathering and, ultimately, plot disruption by law enforcement.

Governments are not destined to suffer from a failure of imagination. But to ensure that the past is not prologue, it is crucial to avoid a creeping sense of complacency 25 years after the most devastating attack on U.S. soil.

Colin P. Clarke is the executive director of the Soufan Center. X: @ColinPClarke

Clara Broekaert is a security researcher focused on foreign interference, technology, and terrorism. X: @ClaraBroekaert

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia.

World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia.

World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

In a nationally televised address on Thursday, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to sanction companies drilling for oil near the Falkland Islands, a British-controlled territory that is also claimed by Argentina. Milei also announced new funding for a naval base in the country’s southernmost province, which would increase Buenos Aires’s military presence near the islands.

“Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security,” Milei said, using the Argentine term for the archipelago.

The sanctions threat is aimed at halting development on the Sea Lion project, a deep-sea oil field operated by the U.K.’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum. The companies intend to start drilling in the next few months and begin pumping oil in 2028. Rockhopper said in a statement that it doesn’t expect Milei’s announcement to have a “material effect” on those plans.

U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meanwhile, affirmed Britain’s “absolute and unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands on social media. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said, referring to a 2013 referendum in which the islands’ residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining in the United Kingdom.

Britain has ruled the islands almost continuously since 1833. In 1982, the Falklands War erupted when Argentina seized the islands. The British military retook the territory after 74 days, but the dispute over the islands’ sovereignty remains contentious. When Argentina and England met on the soccer pitch during the World Cup this summer, Argentina’s players celebrated their victory by holding a banner reading “Las Malvinas Son Argentinas” (“The Falklands Are Argentine”).

When he took office in 2023, Milei appeared to de-emphasize the Falklands to prioritize a closer relationship with the United States, which has long maintained neutrality on the issue. However, he has increasingly expressed the traditional Argentine position in recent months in what some analysts see as an effort to counter falling domestic ratings.

“Milei’s belated embrace of the Falklands demonstrates why Argentina’s claim to the islands will only grow more insistent going forward: Domestic politicians almost universally use the Falklands to prove their nationalist credentials,” Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in Foreign Policy in July.

Milei’s move to reignite the Falklands issue was also likely influenced by Britain’s fraying ties with the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump hinted earlier on Thursday that he may not support Britain in a conflict over the islands because of the country’s lack of support for the U.S. war against Iran. During his speech, Milei praised Trump and stressed the leaders’ close relationship.

“Claiming British territory is no longer the obstacle that it once was for Argentina’s ties with Europe and the United States, which means that Argentine leaders no longer have to choose between issues,” writes De Loera-Brust.

Escalating violence. At least 81 people were killed and thousands displaced in Yemen after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a ground assault on Thursday toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key chokepoint for international shipping at the southern end of the Red Sea.

The attack is part of a Houthi effort to sever the government-controlled city of Taiz from the coast, capture the port city of Mokha, and ultimately control all traffic through the strait. Since declaring a blockade on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in July, the Houthis have continued to attack Saudi ships and facilities, raising concerns that a full-blown war with Riyadh could reignite.

That would add an additional squeeze on global shipping and energy prices. U.S. diesel prices on Friday hit an all-time high at $5.85 a gallon. Experts say fuel prices are likely to stay high until shipping fully resumes in the Strait of Hormuz.

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance insisted on Thursday that the Trump administration is doing “a lot of things” to pressure Iran to stop shooting at commercial ships in the strait, and on Friday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against a minor Turkish investment bank and two subsidiaries that do business with Tehran. “While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

Yet repeated U.S. military strikes, an oil blockade, and crushing economic sanctions have so far failed to convince Iran’s leadership to back down.

Treacherous skies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that international airlines are beginning to heed his call to suspend flights to Russia. This follows his announcement earlier this week that Ukraine would be expanding drone attacks near Russian airports in an effort to disrupt Moscow’s economy.

Ninety-seven flights to Russia were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightRadar24, including services operated by Turkish, Emirati, Egyptian, Armenian, Kuwaiti, and Tajik airlines. Air Tanzania announced that flights to Moscow would be suspended until Monday.

“[W]e are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said in a Tuesday post on X.

Ukraine has intensified its air campaign against Russia in recent months, with a new peak of around 16,000 drones crossing into Russian airspace in August. According to Russia’s Defense Ministry, its forces downed 416 Ukrainian drones between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.

Fraught forum. The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), a six-day gathering of officials from 18 countries and territories, came to a close on Friday. The region has emerged as a primary strategic arena in the past decade amid a battle for influence between global powers such as China and the United States. The meetings, which were held in Palau this year—one of only 11 countries worldwide that recognize Taiwan—were marred by geopolitical tensions.

Addressing China’s ballistic missile test-launch in the South Pacific in July was at the top of the agenda. But although the forum members agreed on Thursday to register their collective “concern” about the launch, the statement was far from a harsh rebuke, and even then it wasn’t unanimous: Nauru, an island nation that severed its diplomatic ties with Taiwan in 2024, dissented.

Nevertheless, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters that he thought the assembly had “got to a very good place,” and that even though Nauru “dissociated itself” from the joint statement, “that shouldn’t be a reason for why we shouldn’t be able to express a PIF position or a consensus position.”

Last-minute withdrawals of top leaders from five member nations—Kiribati, Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, and the Solomon Islands—overshadowed proceedings from the get-go and prompted suggestions that Chinese influence, stemming from its displeasure over the host location, could be to blame. New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters refrained from directly accusing Beijing of interfering, but he said that the collective absence was “highly suspicious.”

Provisional results on Tuesday showed that voters had approved a referendum on a new constitution in Guinea-Bissau. The new charter would expand presidential authority. Which of the below is not one of the powers it would grant to the president?

A. Appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet
B. Create and abolish ministries
C. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget
D. Dissolve parliament in a political crisis

It may be that “good things come to those who wait,” especially when it comes to the famously long Guinness pour, which takes 119.5 seconds to complete. But thieves wasted no time pulling off a heist of two truckloads of the stout beer this week from a depot near Liverpool in the United Kingdom. British police are now trying to recover the 70,000 pints, worth $155,000. Here’s hoping the thieves don’t plan to drink it all themselves.

A. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget

Coup leaders across Africa have changed strategies to retain power, sometimes extending transitional government windows, delaying elections, or using elections to legitimize their continued grip on power, Salah Ben Hammou and Sydney Dobbins wrote in July 2025.
