The war on terror is over. It lasted from Sept. 11, 2001, to the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021. As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, it is useful for both historical and policy reasons to define the parameters of this conflict.

The war on terror had three primary qualities that define it as a historical period. The first was that policymakers viewed terrorism as a form of war and a high-level strategic threat. The second was that counterterrorism strategy sought not only to protect the U.S. homeland but to change the international system in order to attack the root causes of terrorism. The third was that the war on terror was essentially an attempt to deal with the rise of global jihadism.

The war on terror is over. It lasted from Sept. 11, 2001, to the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021. As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, it is useful for both historical and policy reasons to define the parameters of this conflict.

The war on terror had three primary qualities that define it as a historical period. The first was that policymakers viewed terrorism as a form of war and a high-level strategic threat. The second was that counterterrorism strategy sought not only to protect the U.S. homeland but to change the international system in order to attack the root causes of terrorism. The third was that the war on terror was essentially an attempt to deal with the rise of global jihadism.

These three traits have now faded or been eclipsed by other priorities. The era in which terrorism formed the lodestar for U.S. strategy has ended. Realizing this not only helps policymakers situate themselves in the world but offers them the chance to bury habits that plagued U.S. foreign policy during the war on terror itself. These habits included the tendency to concede too much to countries that assisted in fighting terrorism and turning other countries’ terrorist enemies into U.S. enemies.

U.S. troops of the 82nd Airborne Division stationed at at Forward Operating Base Orgun-e in Afghanistan stand at attention before a U.S. flag flying at half-staff for the one-year anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.Getty Images/Chris Hondros

On a basic level, the war on terror was a response to 9/11, which vaulted terrorism to the top of the strategic hierarchy. On a deeper level, however, it was a response to the vulnerabilities engendered by a globalizing world. The 9/11 attacks marked the culmination of modern international terrorism, an asymmetrical strategy in which small groups seek to take advantage of changes in media, transportation, and weaponry to gain leverage and attention.

It prompted a shift to a new bipartisan paradigm for viewing terrorism as war rather than crime. This had been a back-and-forth debate for decades, but 9/11 demonstrated that terrorism had the potential to disrupt modern society and destroy human life on a mass scale. It prompted a shift to an offensive military approach that sought not only to hunt terrorist groups around the world but also to remove or punish the regimes that supported them.

The war on terror’s next essential trait was that terrorism needed to be countered on a systemic level through political reform. U.S. President George W. Bush and his administration concluded that the stagnant, autocratic status quo in the Middle East was breeding radicalism and needed to be changed. This was the foundation of the Freedom Agenda, or the idea that democratizing and modernizing the Middle East would resolve terrorism’s root causes.

Finally, the war on terror stemmed—on a structural level—from the escalating efforts of radical Islamists to collapse the U.S.-backed order in the Middle East by driving the United States out. While this was not a “clash of civilizations,” the United States conducted military operations almost exclusively against radical Islamists. Terrorism was not the enemy; for U.S. policymakers, the enemy was radical Islamist groups and the regimes that sustained them.

These were the war on terror’s defining characteristics: the war paradigm, the linkage of reform and counterterrorism, and the struggle with global jihadism. Still, this was not a homogeneous conflict. The war on terror had three phases, which are defined by changes in objectives, domestic politics, and the perception of the threat’s severity, creating significant overlap between presidencies.

                It’s Time to Rein in Trump’s ‘Wars on Terror’            


    
    	Congress must act to address new and old executive abuses.    	        
            


        
        Argument    
        |
        
    
    Brian Finucane


    


             
                    
                
    
            
                    
        
        
        U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on May 11.
    
        
        U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on May 11.
    
    
        
    
                What Makes Trump’s New Counterterrorism Strategy So Alarming            


    
    	Most worrisome are the terrorist threats missing from the document.    	        
            


        
        Argument    
        |
        
    
    Colin P. Clarke, 
    Clara Broekaert

Congress must act to address new and old executive abuses.

Most worrisome are the terrorist threats missing from the document.

The first phase, which I call the radical phase, dates roughly from 2001 to 2006, when the George W. Bush administration launched an ambitious project that included regime change wars and intensive nation-building crusades. It asserted a unilateral right to strike nations that were ostensibly developing weapons of mass destruction and supporting terrorists, even if it could not prove an attack was imminent.

The administration also concluded that the world order and Middle Eastern politics must be transformed in order to address terrorism’s origins, which it believed emerged from the despair and anger bred by the Middle East’s deficits of democracy and modernity. This became a critical justification for the Iraq War as well as increased pressure on Arab allies to open their political systems.

This phase of the war on terror was radical in both its means and its ends, but it burned out quickly. Iraq’s collapse into civil war fueled the jihadist problem. In Afghanistan, the security and hope of building democracy faded as the Taliban reemerged in the mid-2000s. Finally, efforts to pressure Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to reform fizzled, and Hamas’s victory in the 2006 Gaza elections soured U.S. officials on democracy promotion.

The demise of the radical vision prompted a shift to the second phase: consolidation, which dates roughly from 2007 to 2018. Consolidation was defined by efforts to lower strategic expectations, put counterterrorism on a more sustainable basis, and gradually relegate it behind other priorities. This phase began under the George W. Bush administration with the moderation of rhetoric about democracy and the lowering of ambitions. The 2007 troop surge in Iraq, for instance, was aimed not at democratization but at rescuing the country from civil war. U.S. President Barack Obama continued consolidation, although his counterterrorism policies were more limited in scope and objectives. He had opposed the Iraq War, and he did not prioritize global hegemony or democratization.

However, terrorism was still a high priority for Obama, and he intensified nation-building efforts in Afghanistan as a means of counterterrorism. In late 2009, he sent an additional 30,000 troops to Afghanistan to wage a counterinsurgency war and expand the central government’s writ into the countryside. However, in keeping with his desire for a more balanced approach, Obama also imposed an 18-month timeline for drawing down the surge.

In the early 2010s, Obama devised a more sustainable counterterrorism approach that would still be effective but enable a shift to other concerns. In his light footprint strategy, he limited troop deployments while using special forces, drones, and intelligence resources to kill and capture terrorist leaders and disrupt their operational capacity. He defined this as moving away from “a boundless global war on terror” toward “targeted efforts to dismantle specific networks of violent extremists.”

U.S. President Barack Obama delivers an address to the American people on U.S. policy and the war in Afghanistan during his visit to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan on May 2, 2012.Getty Images/Kevin Lamarque-Pool/

However, Obama’s attempt to level out the war on terror was disrupted in 2014 by the Islamic State’s seizure of swathes of territory in Iraq and Syria. The Islamic State also formed or inspired cells that carried out attacks in Europe and the United States. Obama responded with a “by, with, and through” strategy that provided weapons, intelligence, training, special operations, and air support to forces combatting the Islamic State. Obama also had to reescalate in Afghanistan in response to a series of Taliban offensives in 2015 and 2016. While the number of U.S. troops devoted to counterterrorism declined significantly under Obama, his role in the war on terror was essentially consolidation of terrorism as a major priority of U.S. foreign policy.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s first two years in office continued consolidation while taking a further step back from political reform and nation-building. He blasted the Freedom Agenda and counterinsurgency wars as a waste of lives and resources. Instead, he promised a legally unrestrained counterterrorism campaign. As president, he increased the use of drones, loosened targeting restrictions, and embraced autocratic allies in the struggle against terrorism.

Nonetheless, Trump’s impulses were modulated by his tendency to let his more conventional advisors handle policy details. Much of the counterterrorism machine that Bush and Obama had created churned onward, especially in the continuing struggle against the Islamic State, wherein Trump essentially continued Obama’s strategy.

Trump, however, also planted the seeds for the third and final phase of the war on terror: extraction. Two key developments drove this shift. The first was the defeat of the Islamic State as a territorial entity in 2017-2018. This enabled Trump to declare victory and begin lowering the U.S. troop presence in Iraq and Syria.

The second was the stagnant situation in Afghanistan. Trump believed this was a pointless conflict, and he initiated talks with the Taliban that led to the 2020 Doha Agreement. Under this deal, the United States declared that it would withdraw all troops within 14 months if the Taliban agreed to a cease-fire, talks with the Afghan government, and a guarantee to not support terrorist groups like al Qaeda.

The agreement was a critical step in ending the war on terror because the United States was extracting itself, however cynically, from the original campaign of this conflict. U.S. President Joe Biden then continued Trump’s policy by beginning the removal of all troops from Afghanistan in April 2021. As the Afghan government disintegrated, he fatefully decided against reinserting U.S. forces, which enabled the Taliban to retake the country.

An U.S. Air Force aircraft takes off from the airport in Kabul following U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, seen on Aug. 30, 2021.Getty Images/Aamir Qureshi

August 2021 marked not only the end of the war in Afghanistan but also the end of the war on terror. Both Biden and Trump in his second term relegated terrorism to a lower place in the strategic hierarchy and avoided major ground deployments in support of counterterrorism. They shifted to a new set of priorities: great-power competition, nuclear proliferation, regional wars, industrial policy, and so on.

Terrorism is no longer a central paradigm for U.S. foreign policy as it was during the war on terror. The idea of defeating terrorism through reform, moreover, is dead in both parties. Despite their differences, Biden and Trump finished the extraction phase of the war on terror and effectively ended this conflict.

U.S. President Joe Biden walks through Arlington National Cemetery to honor fallen veterans of the Afghan conflict, seen in Arlington, Virginia, United States, on April 14, 2021.Getty Images/Brendan Smialowski

Saying that the war on terror is over does not mean that the United States is no longer conducting counterterrorism operations, as it remains engaged against al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan, and a variety of partner support and training missions. The term “war on terror” would have little value if it simply referred to any counterterrorism operation at any time. This statement also does not mean that the governmental structures and legal regimes created during this conflict have dissolved.

No historical period has clean endings, but the legacy of a conflict is not the same as the conflict itself. The Cold War has enduring effects that are still playing out, but as a global competition between communist and democratic-capitalist superpowers, it firmly ended between 1989 and 1991. The same is true for the war on terror, a conflict whose consequences will spin out for decades but has essentially ended.

This article is featured in the FP Weekend newsletter, a curation of our best book reviews, deep dives, and other reads that take a step back from the drumbeat of the news. Get the lineup directly every Saturday.

The war on terror created many habits among U.S. policymakers that are best left in the past. One was the willingness to give the benefit of the doubt to countries like Russia and Pakistan, which, while supporting the war on terror, were working cross-purposes to U.S. interests at the same time. Russia, for example, was a critical partner in fighting jihadism in Central Asia and in sustaining logistical networks for the war in Afghanistan. However, cooperation on terrorism not only created the false hope of a better relationship with Russia but also prompted policymakers to downplay increasing signs of Russian authoritarianism and revanchism in the late 2000s and 2010s.

Another problematic tendency was making other countries’ terrorist enemies into Washington’s enemies. For example, Bush dramatically expanded U.S. aid to Colombia after 9/11 to combat the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) insurgency, which the country’s leaders sold as part of the war on terror. This was a questionable use of resources to combat a group that did not threaten the U.S. homeland, and it fed the Colombian government’s brutal counterinsurgency war. In the present, the United States should not enter new wars or compromise its principles to combat other countries’ enemies, like Hamas or Hezbollah, that do not pose a significant threat to U.S. territory.

Finally, acknowledging that the war on terror is over should push U.S. policymakers to accept that terrorism is a fact of life in a globalized world but not an existential threat. The belief that the United States had to conduct regime change and nation-building campaigns to remain safe from terrorism led to a vast and wasteful overextension of U.S. power that made the initial problem worse. A mix of military, intelligence, and legal tools to combat terrorism can still be effective without letting this menace swallow U.S. grand strategy as it did for the first two decades of the 21st century.

Joseph Stieb is an assistant professor of history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the author of The Regime Change Consensus: Iraq in American Politics, 1990-2003.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/04/con.author: Luke Nicastro and Heather Penatzer
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/04/con.text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made waves in July by publicly calling for the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, should he come to town for the United Nations General Assembly later this month. “I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani told the New York Times, because “[h]e’s a war criminal.” It is a view apparently shared by many: According to a recent poll, 49 percent of Americans believe the United States should arrest Netanyahu, compared to only 27 percent who think it should not. (The rest are unsure.)

The mayor’s legal team has concluded that New York City lacks the necessary authority to make the arrest, and instead, Mamdani urged the federal government to join the International Criminal Court (ICC) and execute its warrant against Netanyahu.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made waves in July by publicly calling for the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, should he come to town for the United Nations General Assembly later this month. “I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani told the New York Times, because “[h]e’s a war criminal.” It is a view apparently shared by many: According to a recent poll, 49 percent of Americans believe the United States should arrest Netanyahu, compared to only 27 percent who think it should not. (The rest are unsure.)

The mayor’s legal team has concluded that New York City lacks the necessary authority to make the arrest, and instead, Mamdani urged the federal government to join the International Criminal Court (ICC) and execute its warrant against Netanyahu.

The Trump administration, unsurprisingly, has no intention of doing so. It has, rather, sought to paint the ICC—and, by extension, the operationalization of international law itself—as an existential threat to U.S. sovereignty. “As we speak,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned in a recent video message, “the ICC and its friends are waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles, but with statutes and compacts and the force of so-called international law.” Earlier this year, President Donald Trump was more blunt: “I don’t need international law,” he said following the U.S. seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

But conservatives haven’t always been so hostile to international law. Indeed, some of the most prominent right-wingers of yore saw in it the sole foundation upon which a desirable world order could rest.

One such figure was Sen. Robert Taft, the Ohio politician who so thoroughly embodied mid-century conservatism that he earned the sobriquet “Mr. Republican.” Despite his unimpeachable GOP credentials, Taft was a passionate advocate of international law, as well as the robust mechanisms necessary to give it teeth. He viewed law as the only force strong enough and solid enough to prevent a third world war. As he argued in a 1949 speech opposing the North Atlantic Treaty:

[T]here is only one real hope of peace in the world to come—an association of nations binding itself to abide by a law governing nations and administered by a court of legal justice. Such a judicial finding must not be subject to veto by any nation and there must be an international force to enforce the court’s decree.

Similarly, Elihu Root—who helmed the War and State Departments under President Theodore Roosevelt, and later served as a Republican senator—believed fervently in the importance of international law and its enforcement. “Next to the preservation of national character,” he proclaimed in 1915, as World War I was killing off nearly an entire generation of European men, “the most valuable possession of all peaceable nations, great and small, is the protection of those laws which constrain other nations to conduct based upon principles of justice and humanity.”

Even that old arch-conservative Metternich, widely considered among the progenitors of foreign policy realism, believed states could legitimately act only so long as they remained within the compass of the law of nations. Not “blood and iron,” but “Kraft im Recht” was his heraldic motto—“strength in law.”

A relief at the the U.S. Supreme Court depicts Hugo Grotius and French King Louis IX.Universal History Archive/via Getty Images

To answer that question, we must distinguish between what conservatives have traditionally understood to be the nature and purpose of international law, and what generations of bureaucrats, international organizations, and academics have made of it since.

International law is in some sense coeval with systems of states; traces can be detected as far back as the letters exchanged among the Bronze Age rulers of the Near East . But it was the 17th century jurist Hugo Grotius who gave us the first really coherent formulation. This was a vision of the jus gentium, basic rules binding all because of their derivation from natural law—that is, universal moral principles inherent in nature and discernible through reason. These rules require things like honoring treaties and respecting ambassadors, making war only for just causes and avoiding the deliberate harm of innocents, and allowing all nations freedom of the seas.

This understanding made slow but steady progress over the ensuing centuries. It was shaken by the French Revolution and the decades of war that ensued, reified again in the post-Napoleonic settlement, and regnant—at least among European nations—until August 1914, when the first total war of the industrial era sounded its death knell.

There were several reasons this older vision appealed to conservatives. It accommodated the belief that human affairs should be grounded in a transcendent moral order, and that conduct—whether at the individual or the collective level—must be measured against some sort of absolute standard. It purported to draw not just on natural law but customary usage, further enhancing its stature in the eyes of precedent-minded traditionalists.

It also reflected conservatives’ skepticism of man’s perfectibility (or even his capacity for significant improvement). In a fallen world, the natural selfishness and viciousness of our species poses a constant threat to collective welfare. Anarchy and civilizational breakdown are always possible; and just as maintaining a fragile order within nations requires the promulgation and enforcement of rules, so too does maintaining this order among them.

But after 1945, international law was developed and understood in a very different way. The old vision had apparently failed to prevent two cataclysmic world wars; perhaps something more revolutionary and intrusive was needed. A complex web of international organizations began to emerge, which aimed to coordinate the world’s growing interdependence both by expanding into previously unregulated domains (e.g., monetary policy and public health) and, most significantly, by reaching inside states, often in the name of human rights.

Perhaps the most notorious example of this was the “responsibility to protect.” This concept, which emerged from diplomat Francis Deng’s earlier notion of “sovereignty as responsibility” (which made sovereignty conditional rather than absolute), allowed the claims of non-state actors to be wielded to chip away at states’ sovereignty. It and similar developments threatened what had heretofore been a foundational or constitutional principle of international law: namely, that governments were its sole legitimate subjects.

Thus, this vision sought to transform international law from something that was constitutive of world order into a force that—by introducing a destabilizing, purposive function—actively threatened it. As the great IR theorist Hedley Bull noted five decades ago:

Carried to its logical extreme, the doctrine of human rights and duties under international law is subversive of the whole principle that mankind should be organized as a society of sovereign states. For, if the rights of each man can be asserted on the world stage over and against the claims of his state, and his duties proclaimed irrespective of his position as a servant or as a citizen of that state, then the position of the state as a body sovereign over its citizens, and entitled to command their obedience, has been subject to challenge… The way is left open for the subversion of the society of sovereign states on behalf of the alternative organizing principle of a cosmopolitan community.

There are, then, two types of international law. The first is law among states: horizontal and in some sense procedural, designed to support pluralism, facilitate trade, and contain the risks of conflict. The second is law over states: vertical, purposive, and homogenizing, susceptible to hijacking by elites who would revolutionize the present political organization of the world in the service of utopian dreams.

    	We may come to miss the hypocrisy.

                How U.S. Allies Can Resist Washington’s Bullying            


    
    	The attack on the ICC offers a chance for solidarity on shared values.    	        
            


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, 
    Christopher K. Lamont

We may come to miss the hypocrisy.

The attack on the ICC offers a chance for solidarity on shared values.

Conservatives have good reason to oppose the second interpretation. But the first, which has historically commanded considerable allegiance on the right, deserves another hearing.

Because without it, we are left with nothing but the law of the jungle.

Witness the so-called flexible realism promulgated by the Trump administration. It has, in practice, proved to be a cover for simple predation: the strong taking what they will, and the weak suffering what they must. The United States has used its immense power to threaten the seizure of Greenland from a treaty ally on a baseless pretext, spirit away the leader of Venezuela and claim as much of its oil as possible, and starve the Cuban people into submission to effect regime change. (And that’s just in the Western hemisphere.)

What we would condemn in an individual, much of the right has been willing to tolerate—even celebrate—in a nation. But obviously this view is untenable: Our ethical obligations are not somehow waived when we come together to act as a commonwealth. Nor do the basic rules that apply to societies of individuals cease altogether to govern societies of states.

At this point, some conservatives may object on realist grounds. Hasn’t recent history—particularly the excesses of the war on terror—shown conclusively that moralism should be kept as far away from foreign policy as possible?

We would reply that one can have morality without moralism. The critical distinction is the treatment of domestic affairs; we hold with Taft that international law must account for the fact that

Interference in domestic policies… [is] more likely to make war than to prevent it. The test is: is the subject one on which the people of the United States would be willing to have other nations interfere with our internal actions? If not, we should not attempt to impose such interference on others.

Once stripped of the emphasis on human rights and the imperative to remake societies, international law is in practice cautious and prudential. Indeed, it is no coincidence that the two most egregious disasters of recent U.S. foreign policy—the Iraq and Iran wars—could not have been launched by administrations that took international law seriously.

Conservatives have also historically distinguished between liberty—the authentic use of freedom, which depends upon self-discipline and the observation of a higher law—and license—the abuse of freedom, the indulgence of every base appetite and selfish impulse without compunction or constraint. What must be avoided is the invocation of realism as an excuse or justification for license on a global scale. Rather, the proper use of realism is as a guide, a way to steer the ship of state through the world as it is, toward those far shores of peace, prosperity, and virtue.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 13, 2025. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

To return to the issue with which we opened: What of the ICC and Benjamin Netanyahu? While it is possible to have international law without a world court, the existence of the latter is a major boon to the former. The ICC is far from an ideal adjudicator, as baked into its remit is precisely the emphasis upon human rights that distorted the original vision of international law. Yet it is better than nothing, and reform of an existing institution is easier than de novo creation.

As for Netanyahu, at least one of the charges on which both the ICC and Mamdani want him booked is squarely within the domain of international law. This is the accusation of war crimes, specifically the use of “starvation as a method of warfare” and “intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population.” These would be crimes whether or not the ICC existed, and the United States is obliged to treat them as such, even though it has not acceded to the Rome Statute that established the court. (Israel’s actions implicate the Geneva Convention and the strictures of the UN Charter, both of which Washington is party to, as well as the traditional understanding of the laws of war.)

Obviously, there is no prospect of a change of heart on this issue from the White House. But 2028 is on the horizon; and as we inch ever closer to a post-Trump future, those conservatives interested in buttressing world order, protecting U.S. interests, and promoting the common good should return to the wisdom of their forebears—and take another look at international law.

Domed cities—those classic symbols of science (and climate) fiction—make an appearance in both of the novels we’re reading this month, which transport readers to the United States after a second civil war and an eerie utopian community on a Greek island.

Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026)

Domed cities—those classic symbols of science (and climate) fiction—make an appearance in both of the novels we’re reading this month, which transport readers to the United States after a second civil war and an eerie utopian community on a Greek island.

Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026)

The United States is known as a country of relentless—and sometimes naive—optimism. So it’s striking that, in recent years, serious thinkers from across the political spectrum have taken to warning of the possibility of a second civil war, or some other form of U.S. societal collapse.

In a stunning new novel, Emily St. John Mandel imagines what might come after that potential rupture. Unfortunately for human civilization, Mandel—a veteran of dystopian fiction—has previously proved herself an unwitting forecaster of very real geopolitical crises. Her 2014 novel Station Eleven was set in the wake of a global pandemic. Readers flocked to it six years later, and an HBO adaptation was quick to follow.

Mandel—who, I should note, is Canadian—begins Exit Party in Los Angeles in 2031, when a curfew and foreign military occupation of the city are lifted after a U.S. civil war. “The United States had come undone following a coup d’état. Several states had seceded within a week of the coup, either alone or in alliances with neighbors,” she writes. The Republic of California is now its own country, one of “multiple small nations and city-states with ever-shifting borders and countless combatants, militants battling for control across the former nation.”

To mark the first curfew-free night, protagonist Ari Waker and her friends attend a party. Mandel describes the fete in painstaking detail. Only later in the story does it become clear to readers that this technical play-by-play has a function: The party—and the bizarre, inexplicable events that occur there—are the foundation for a sci-fi journey through two parallel trajectories for the former United States. Understanding what occurred at the party is essential to understanding all that follows.

Although the Republic of California is comparatively stable (“and therefore unaffordable,” Mandel writes—some things never change), most of the rest of the former United States is in shambles. Abandoned Staples office supply stores have become camps for internally displaced people, whose children attend makeshift schools housed at TGI Fridays; militias set up their headquarters in erstwhile shopping malls. (Washington, D.C., locals may be interested to learn that one of the most powerful armed groups is based in Silver Spring, Maryland.)

To make ends meet, Ari finds herself drawn into a criminal web dealing weapons to rival militias—a journey that eventually leads her to flee to Paris. But while European borders seem mostly intact, the continent has its own problems. “In those days France was dangerous because everywhere was dangerous,” Mandel writes. Countries seek to gird against the effects of climate change by building Simpsons-esque domes over wealthy areas, creating new classes of haves and have-nots.

It is in France that Ari, through links to that party in Los Angeles—and a dose of quantum physics—discovers an alternate path for the former United States. In the totalitarian United State, surveillance ensures prosperity. Futuristic bullet trains crisscross the country, and the entire population is immunized against cancer. But democracy is a thing of the past. Secret police not dissimilar to the East German Stasi make sure that “people who broke the rules disappeared.”

Each of Mandel’s make-believe futures for the United States is equally unsettling. As Ari and fellow party guests toggle between scenarios of havoc and order, clashing with and sometimes abetting authority, it becomes clear that both systems have drawbacks. “There was a world where my homeland had fractured into disarray, and another where my homeland had closed like a fist,” Ari observes.

What the two versions of the United States have in common, however, is that residents are tired—of tyranny, tumult, and struggling to get by. In believing that it’s “an exhausting moment to be alive,” they are no different from their real-life compatriots in 2026. As Ari narrates: “We were Americans, which is another way of saying that chaos felt like home.”—Allison Meakem

Ben Eastham (Astra House, 288 pp., $26, September 2026)

If there is anyone well positioned to write satisfying fiction about contemporary art, it’s Ben Eastham. The co-founder of the White Review and a regular critic for the Guardian, Eastham has made a name for himself by variously decoding the art world’s relationship to its bedfellows of power and capital, and dissecting—with compassion—works of art in ways that render them accessible, anew, or otherwise worthy of attention. So it is little surprise that Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World, is at once a humorous send-up of this rarefied but often-mocked industry and a moving meditation on morality, grief, and the miracles that art may yet offer.

The premise of Eastham’s novel slots neatly into the ultrarich-on-an-island genre popularized in recent years by films such as Glass Onion and The Menu, though it perhaps owes more to The Magus, John Fowles’ 1965 masterpiece about a young Englishman enthralled by an enigmatic Greek art collector. Like Nicholas Urfe, the disillusioned yet romantic protagonist of that novel, Eastham’s unnamed narrator is a writer who arrives on a remote island in the Aegean to find himself swept up in schemes beyond his grasp, soon unable to decipher reality from artifice.

This recently widowed narrator has left London for Greece to work on an immersive exhibition by a renowned artist that will inaugurate the so-called Floating World, an island community ensconced in a giant dome. A settlement was originally constructed on the island in the 1950s as a utopian community for mine workers and their families after the discovery of rare-earth deposits, only to be abandoned during an economic downturn two decades later. Now, a billionaire heir to an arms manufacturing corporation has set his sights on resurrecting the site as a climate haven. The project is described, by various characters, as a “tax haven,” the heir’s “ideal city-state,” a “doomsday bunker for billionaires,” and “a sustainable, holistic, homeostatic community for powerful people who want insurance against the end of the world.”

The narrator is aware that his work amounts to propaganda for an ethically dubious project but is eager for a distraction from his grief. And while he is often critical of the art world and its excesses, he is also attuned to art’s capacity to console and delight, especially amid the great crises of our time, from inequality to humanitarian suffering to ecological catastrophe. (Incidentally, the narrator’s emotional state appears to correlate to his charitability—or lack thereof—toward the individuals and artwork he encounters. “I could overhear an artist telling the minister for National Heritage that his work resisted categorization, even though I knew his work to be categorically shit,” he recounts at one particularly low point.)

Contemporary art may be the cultural expression of runaway capitalism and globalization, the narrator thinks, but hasn’t art always been entangled with economic realities, whether that took the form of Renaissance masters exalting Italian merchants or the abstract expressionists propping up the U.S. vision of free-market liberalism?

The art world, like much of society, may be fallen, but that hardly makes it irredeemable. At one point, the narrator reflects on a postcard of a painting based on an Albrecht Dürer engraving: “This cheap reproduction of a picture that is preserved in a palace built on state power and spiritual corruption, painted five hundred years ago by an unremembered copyist from a copperplate engraving, is itself a miracle. It moves me in a way that I cannot rationalize away by its formal qualities … It exceeds the infrastructures by which we strive to make sense of it.”—Chloe Hadavas

Booker Prize-winning Jamaican author Marlon James returns with The Disappearers, a 640-page queer epic centered on 1980s Kingston. In Doireann Ni Ghriofa’s genre-defying Said the Dead, the archives of a storied asylum in Cork, Ireland, are brought to life. Autofiction meets sci-fi in video-game designer and novelist Naomi Alderman’s The Strangers. In the 12 stories collected in The Queen of Bad Influences, Jim Shephard finds humanity across catastrophes from 16th century Madrid to the seas of World War I. Min Jin Lee, of Pachinko fame, chronicles the impact of the 1997 Asian financial crisis on one Korean family in American Hagwon.

With the fictional memoir Agrippa, historical fiction stalwart Robert Harris turns his eye toward the Emperor Augustus’ right-hand man. The long shadow of colonialism haunts a Brazilian family in Itamar Vieira Junior’s Saving the Fire, translated from the Portuguese by Johnny Lorenz. In Chloe Benjamin’s Under Story, a portal found at a scientific research base in Antarctica opens to a parallel universe. Vikas Swarup, the Indian diplomat whose debut novel inspired Slumdog Millionaire, offers up another high-stakes thriller, The Girl With Seven Lives. And Canadian playwright and novelist Jordan Tannahill’s The Living Realm doubles as a ghost story and a paean to queer Berlin.—CH

Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away.

The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world.

Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away.

The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world.

The Invite takes place over one night and is set almost entirely in one location—a desirable-but-not-ostentatious San Francisco apartment in a sonically porous building. The apartment is owned by a jaded music instructor who has abandoned his rock star dreams (we learn he inherited the pad from his parents) played by Seth Rogen, and his deeply unhappy wife played by Olivia Wilde (who is also the director of the film). There’s an early-teens daughter in the mix, but she’s luckily away for the night, so Wilde’s character has sprung a surprise dinner party on her husband. The neighbors, the ones they talk about constantly, are coming over.

The ongoing spousal chatter, which is partially a source of shared humor but mostly a wellspring of deeply held animus, comes from the upstairs couple’s regular and thunderous lovemaking sessions—a matrimonial hobby we’ll soon learn the downstairs couple have long since quit. The upstairs duo is played by Edward Norton, a kind but devilish firefighter, and Spanish actor Penélope Cruz, a ravishing, earthy therapist who exudes continental sophistication and excitement.

In short time, the downstairs couple reveal themselves to be a bickering, miserable mess, but they briefly put aside their sniping when the upstairs couple shares that they are swingers, and the sleep-depriving sounds come from group sex adventures with a revolving door of participants. As the evening continues, the titular invite comes—would Rogen and Wilde’s characters, neurotic sourpusses though they may be, care to join Norton and Cruz’s for an intimate interlude?

The movie is extremely funny, but also insightful and sad, thanks to a sharp screenplay by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones, as well as all four of the performances—especially Wilde, who skitters between debilitating insecurity, marital revulsion, and brazen lust, sometimes all within the same shot. She’s given life-or-death stakes to what could otherwise be a diverting filmed play, aided by rapid editing and a tension-rich original score by Devonté Hynes. The movie is a highwire act, and during the promotional cycle, she regularly cited the influence of Mike Nichols’ adaptation of Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, a key New Hollywood text.

A scene from the film Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf, directed by Mike Nichols and released in 1966. FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images

Wilde’s references to Nichols are certainly apt, but deviate from a more exact comparison: The Invite is a remake of a recent Spanish film, The People Upstairs (also called Sentimental), which writer-director Cesc Gay adapted from his own play.

The People Upstairs came out in 2020 and between then and Wilde’s film’s release, there were four (yes, four) other versions of this story produced—in Switzerland, Italy, South Korea, and France. (A Belgian/Dutch version is en route.) While international remakes are not uncommon, I feel confident in saying that what’s happened with Gay’s work is unprecedented both in its speed and numbers.

In the early days of “talking pictures,” one could sometimes find business-minded producers who would crank out alternates of a movie using the same sets and crew but (usually) different actors in different languages for foreign markets. Most of these iterations are now considered lost films, but several are notable.

The all-star revue Paramount on Parade from 1930 holds the record with 13 different variants, including ones in Hungarian and Serbian. When Alfred Hitchcock shot Murder! in 1930, he stayed in the director’s chair for the German version, released as Mary in 1931. (He was used to this sort of thing, having filmed both the silent and talking versions of Blackmail in 1929.)

Translations went the other way, too. An English version of Josef von Sternberg’s 1930 classic The Blue Angel starring Marlene Dietrich was considered lost for decades until a copy was found in a German archive and presented in 2009.

The most celebrated example is George Melford’s Spanish-language Dracula from 1931, which was shot at night (spooky!) after Bela Lugosi and director Tod Browning left Universal’s stages. That English-language Dracula gave us iconic lines like “I never drink … wine,” and was, of course, an instant classic, but if you have hours to kill, I recommend visiting film snob message boards to see how many cinephiles are eager to argue that the Spanish Dracula is greatly superior. (I say they are both good!)

But there’s a key difference between then and now. The profusion of versions of The People Upstairs does not represent a production entity looking to maximize profit. It is an organic recognition of a story with legs across different cultures.

From a practical standpoint, one can see why local film industries, still wobbly from COVID safety protocols in the early part of this decade, would want to sink their teeth into a one-location movie with just four performers. Quick and easy. But those mechanics aside, what does it say about the world that so many of us are understood to be interested in sex-deprived married couples thunderstruck by their lustful neighbors?

(From Left) The South Korean, Swiss, Spanish, Italian, and French posters from the respective international versions of The People Upstairs.By4M Studio/Ascot Elite/Filmax/Medusa Film/Nac Film

Of the six versions of this film that now exist, only the original Spanish and current Hollywood versions are easily found in North America. But leaping across borders is what we at Foreign Policy are all about. After many rounds of emails, Instagram DMs, and the deployment of some translation software, I am proud to say that I have seen each rendition.

I immersed myself in this tale of would-be spouse-swapping hoping to learn more about specific cultures. Whether or not my discoveries are truly foundational to a national character is open to discussion, but pages and pages of notes show that this exercise was, if nothing else, fascinating. For starters, I now know that German-speaking Swiss are more into slapstick than I was previously aware, if Die Nachbarn von Oben (The Neighbors From Upstairs) director Sabine Boss is a true representative.

Like Brahms interpreting Handel, some scenes of Cesc Gay’s original Spanish film only exist in the bones of each variation, but a few melodic lines remain constant. All six versions retain the reveal that the downstairs woman intentionally crosses her unshaded window while naked, knowing that the upstairs man is likely looking at her. Similarly, she urges her husband not to complain about the lovemaking upstairs because she is happy that the upstairs woman is having such aggressive orgasms—and Wilde is terrified that discussing it will ruin it for her. (This is played as a joke.) There’s also a big laugh across all six versions when the invitation comes, and the downstairs woman starts verbally going through her calendar, causing the downstairs man to complain that it isn’t normal to schedule an orgy.

In the Hollywood version, Cruz’s exoticism comes from her Iberian origins, and she even brings over a flan. No other version makes her a foreigner, and in the Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions, she makes an unspecified Indian dish that is spicy and (the upstairs man jokes) an aphrodisiac. In the French version, she makes “tapas,” and in the South Korean version, some kind of elaborate fried eggplant on a cake stand with a bow on it.

                A ‘Lord of the Flies’ for Our Time            


    
    	This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

    Jordan Hoffman

                Are Movies to Blame?            


    
    	A renowned film historian asks if moving pictures led us to something rotten.    	        
            


        
        Review    
        |
        
    
    Jordan Hoffman

Would even extraterrestrials inspire humanity to unite these days?

This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

A renowned film historian asks if moving pictures led us to something rotten.

Music comes up a lot. In the Hollywood film, the downstairs husband is a frustrated rock musician. In Spain and Switzerland, his repertoire is classical piano; in Italy, it is jazz. In South Korea, he’s not a musician at all, but a film director stuck in years of development on a television project he isn’t that enthusiastic about to begin with.

The South Korean film (also called The People Upstairs) is the version with some of the bigger changes. For starters, the downstairs neighbors do not have kids or a pet. (The French version includes not just a daughter, but a pivotal dog.) Moreover, the upstairs sex-positive neighbors are deliberately cast as older and more conservatively dressed. Indeed, the upstairs woman looks like a newscaster and the upstairs man initially comes across as a bit of a dork, wearing a cardigan with ducks on it.

Each version shows that the downstairs man has an office, but the South Korean spin strongly suggests that it functions as his nightly bedroom. There’s a gag in each film when the downstairs couple admits how long it has been since they last made love. Most versions, including the Rogen-Wilde version, say “about a year.” But the South Korean couple say four years. (The French version evades the question with, “I can’t even remember the last time.”)

Indeed, the two ends of the sexuality spectrum are represented by South Korea and France. In every version, when the upstairs neighbors talk about their group sex encounters, they say they usually limit them to four to six people, except one time when there was 10 for someone’s birthday. (This builds to a variation of a “well, birthdays are special” joke.) The French version keeps this gag but doubles the number: There were 20 participants one New Year’s Eve, apparently.

Penélope Cruz plays the upstairs neighbor Piña and Olivia Wilde plays Angela in The Invite in this undated photo. A24

There’s also a funny moment where the upstairs neighbors talk about sexual boundaries and proclivities, with some versions getting more lewd than others. (Quite frankly, the Hollywood version may be the dirtiest of them all.) In multiple versions, the upstairs man declares that his partner is fond of anal sex, and she plain-facedly confirms it. But the South Korean version includes dialogue about enjoying sex “Korean style.” (Here I must tell you, reader, that I have no clue what this means. Furthermore, asking Google “what is Korean-style sex” did nothing but poison my algorithm such that I can no longer use my laptop at the public library. We’re just going to have to accept that not everything translates.)

All six versions of the movie build to their conclusion by raising the stakes in different ways. Seth Rogen’s back gives out in the Hollywood version; in the Swiss film, there’s a piano on fire then drunken nakedness. The French version, however, has a wild twist: The off-screen daughter isn’t a preteen at a friend’s sleepover, but a 20-year-old who only comes back from school now and again. It is soon discovered that a particularly noisy night of lovemaking came from the upstairs man seducing her. (To his credit, he didn’t realize who she was.)

While this leads to expected anger from the downstairs man, the upstairs woman is also upset—because she wasn’t involved. “We’re supposed to be libertines together!” she cries. (The downstairs woman, the mother of the seduced, isn’t too bothered by the story at all, for what it’s worth.)

Across the six films, the story ends with the downstairs couple confronting the fact that their marriage has collapsed, and the next step—separation—is presented as a reasonable, maybe even happy, ending. The big question is whether or not they go through with it or stay in their rut. All versions are ambiguous. The Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions suggest rapprochement. (I’ve barely mentioned the Italian version, simply called Neighbors, because it’s pretty boring—though it does feature the nicest apartment.) The French and Hollywood versions lean more toward a breakup, but suggest that, in deciding to do so, the couple will grow in maturity and maybe even deepen their friendship.

The South Korean version is the true outlier—our younger couple downstairs seems to be quite happy, and maybe, just maybe, has gotten there thanks to their new hobby of swinging. If and when that version (called The People Upstairs, for future reference) ever becomes more widely available, you can watch it and judge for yourself.

1. Voters in Iceland on Sunday rejected a government proposal to reopen talks to do what?

Create an official standing army

Join the European Union

Absorb Greenland as a new province

Expand U.S. military access to the country

The move was prompted by concerns over Iceland’s lack of a military and its reliance on the U.S. security umbrella, Gloria Dickie wrote last week.

2. U.S. President Donald Trump posted an artificial intelligence-generated video on Sunday depicting U.S. military forces doing what?

Lifting weights as part of “Make America Healthy Again” promo content

Parachuting into Venezuela to protect oil fields

Dancing to the Village People’s “YMCA”

Attacking Iran’s Kharg Island

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran has almost certainly irreparably damaged his foreign-policy toolkit and led to the premature peak of his global influence, FP’s Ravi Agrawal writes in an exclusive prerelease from our latest magazine.

3. Why did China’s Pacific islands envoy on Monday threaten “consequences” for participating members of the Pacific Island Forum, which held a meeting this week?

They required that attendees wear Hawaiian shirts.

They criticized China’s actions in the South China Sea.

They allowed Taiwan’s foreign minister to attend.

They issued a joint declaration in support of AI regulation.

Australia and other members of the forum pushed back against China’s attempt to influence the meeting, FP’s James Palmer reports in China Brief.

4. Why did the United Nations’ food agency say on Tuesday that it is halving food assistance to Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank starting this month?

Due to severe funding shortages

In protest of Israeli settlers’ violence against Palestinians

Under pressure from the Israeli government

To increase food assistance to Gaza

Preventing the next large-scale conflagration in the West Bank—not Gaza— should be Trump’s priority, Azriel Bermant argued last month.

5. Provisional results on Tuesday showed that voters had approved a referendum on a new constitution in Guinea-Bissau. The new charter would expand presidential authority. Which of the below is not one of the powers it would grant to the president?

Appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet

Create and abolish ministries

Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget

Dissolve parliament in a political crisis

Coup leaders across Africa have changed strategies to retain power, sometimes extending transitional government windows, delaying elections, or using elections to legitimize their continued grip on power, Salah Ben Hammou and Sydney Dobbins wrote in July 2025.

6. Oil giant Chevron confirmed on Wednesday that it planned to expand its operations in which Latin American country?

Also this week, Trump announced an agreement with Venezuela’s interim government that will allow the United States to take a partial stake in Venezuela’s oil. The deal won’t lower gas prices anytime soon and is likely illegal, FP’s Keith Johnson reports.

7. Argentine President Javier Milei said on Thursday that he would assert the country’s claims on the Falkland Islands, currently a British overseas territory, by doing what?

Deploying Argentine military units

Sanctioning oil companies drilling there

Funding Spanish-language schools and cultural centers

Blockading the islands

Claims to the islands are a rare point of national consensus in Argentina, while younger British voters care less and less about them, Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in July.

8. Finland’s border guard said on Friday that it was investigating whether an object found on its southern shore had violated its territory. What was the object?

A low-Earth-orbit satellite

The discovery comes as Germany and Russia escalate a diplomatic standoff over what is believed to be an attempted Russian drone attack on German territory, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.

9. Soccer superstar Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday. Across 21 years as a member of the Argentina national team, Messi scored 125 goals, placing him second in all-time goals scored by men at the international level. Who is in first place?

Belgium’s Romelu Lukaku

Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo

Messi wrote his retirement letter shortly after the World Cup, but decided to make it official following the death of his father, Jorge, on Aug. 8, ESPN reports.

10. French President Emmanuel Macron joined King Charles III, Queen Camilla, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British Museum in London on Wednesday to view a nearly 1,000-year-old embroidery depicting what event?

The Norman conquest of England

Romans’ Battle of the River Medway in England

The Battle of Thermopylae

The coronation of Charlemagne

The Bayeux Tapestry’s loan to the British Museum marks its first time on English soil since its creation, Reuters reports.

When Israel recognized Somaliland in late December 2025, it caused an international kerfuffle. The Arab League called it “illegal” and a threat to regional stability. The African Union “reject[ed] any initiative or action aimed at recognizing Somaliland as an independent entity.” Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs described it as a “unilateral secessionist move that violates international law.” The Qataris, Egyptians, Turks, Algerians, Yemenis, Omanis, Sudanese, Iraqis, and others echoed these sentiments. The European Union also chimed in, declaring that it “reaffirms the importance of respecting the unity, the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Somalia.”

Territorial integrity is of course important. The crackup of other countries in the region—say Syria or Iraq—would be catastrophic to the security and stability of the Middle East. But staking opposition on Somalia’s territorial integrity was transparently disingenuous. Somaliland voluntarily agreed to be a part of Somalia after its independence in 1960, decided to secede in 1991 after a decade of war within the country, and has been basically independent ever since. The Saudis lived with two Yemens between 1967 and 1990; the Qataris and Turks supported Idlib, a breakaway province of Syria, until President Bashar al-Assad fell; and Turkey is the only country in the world that recognizes the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which Ankara sliced out of the northern third of the Republic of Cyprus—now a member of the EU. The opposition to Israel’s move is not rooted in principle, but rather in geopolitics, which underlines the importance of Somaliland, especially now.

When Israel recognized Somaliland in late December 2025, it caused an international kerfuffle. The Arab League called it “illegal” and a threat to regional stability. The African Union “reject[ed] any initiative or action aimed at recognizing Somaliland as an independent entity.” Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs described it as a “unilateral secessionist move that violates international law.” The Qataris, Egyptians, Turks, Algerians, Yemenis, Omanis, Sudanese, Iraqis, and others echoed these sentiments. The European Union also chimed in, declaring that it “reaffirms the importance of respecting the unity, the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Somalia.”

Territorial integrity is of course important. The crackup of other countries in the region—say Syria or Iraq—would be catastrophic to the security and stability of the Middle East. But staking opposition on Somalia’s territorial integrity was transparently disingenuous. Somaliland voluntarily agreed to be a part of Somalia after its independence in 1960, decided to secede in 1991 after a decade of war within the country, and has been basically independent ever since. The Saudis lived with two Yemens between 1967 and 1990; the Qataris and Turks supported Idlib, a breakaway province of Syria, until President Bashar al-Assad fell; and Turkey is the only country in the world that recognizes the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which Ankara sliced out of the northern third of the Republic of Cyprus—now a member of the EU. The opposition to Israel’s move is not rooted in principle, but rather in geopolitics, which underlines the importance of Somaliland, especially now.

Americans brought up on Mercator projection maps—which inflate the size of lands far from the equator—might not fully grasp the geographic and thus strategic, political, economic, and cultural connections between the Middle East and the Horn of Africa. Saudis, Emiratis, and Qataris are multibillion-dollar investors in Africa. Egypt has a vital strategic interest in East Africa given its dependence on the Nile River (which originates in Ethiopia, Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda) for the country’s survival. Turkey has among the largest contingent of embassies on the African continent and has focused on Somalia as a Turkish beachhead in the region with anywhere from 800 to 2,500 troops in the country. The Israelis currently enjoy strong relations with Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, and now Somaliland. The Horn of Africa has become part of the great game among Middle Eastern powers.

Somaliland has a pretty good story to tell. Like Somalia, it has benefited from Emirati and some Qatari as well as Turkish investment. But unlike many African states, Somaliland has eschewed a relationship with the Chinese government. Its diplomats and spokespeople emphasize that they want a partnership with the United States, including military bases and access to minerals, and they have vowed to join the Abraham Accords. Somaliland has functioning political institutions. In 2024, there was a peaceful transition of power to the political opposition when Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (aka Irro) won the presidential election.

Things are hardly perfect. There are accusations that the authorities constrain civil liberties and there is opposition to the government among some clans, especially in the east, where sentiment runs in favor of ties with Mogadishu rather than Hargeisa—Somaliland’s capital. This raises the possibility of violent inter-clan conflict in Somaliland. It is a legitimate concern. The good news is that Irro says he is committed to peaceful dialogue. Even taking into account this problem, Somaliland stands in contrast to Somalia itself, which has been a fount of terrorism, piracy, and extremism in the Horn of Africa for decades. The Turks, Qataris, and Saudis argue that part of what they are doing is helping the Somali government overcome that instability, but it is hard to see progress. In fact, recent reporting points to ties between Somalia’s al Qaeda affiliate, al-Shabab, and Yemen’s Houthis.

The United States has so far resisted recognizing Somaliland’s independence, but senior officers from U.S. Africa Command have visited Hargeisa. The visit makes sense given that Washington’s security interests are connected to Somaliland. Iran’s muscle flex in the Strait of Hormuz highlights the equally important Red Sea. Before the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, about 15 percent of global trade passed through the Red Sea, and it is now an important escape route for Saudi oil that otherwise would have transited Hormuz. In recent months, that shipping has been targeted by Iran’s allies, the Houthis, in yet another challenge to Washington’s commitment to freedom of navigation.

What country sits on the African shore of the Gulf of Aden? Somaliland. With the deep-water Berbera port that is undergoing modernization, plus a large adjacent airstrip, a desire to be on Team America, and strong ties with some of Washington’s other regional friends (Israel, Ethiopia, and the United Arab Emirates), Hargeisa seems like a fine candidate to be a new partner in the Horn of Africa. It would be hard to find a better staging area the United States could use to monitor the Houthis, and when necessary, apply pressure on them and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Some Somalilander commentators have argued that it would be shortsighted of the United States and Israel as well as risky for Somaliland if the totality of relations with Hargeisa involved military bases. They want a broader and less security-specific relationship. That sounds about right, though with Washington’s hands full almost everywhere and a State Department that is a mere shadow of itself, it is hard to imagine the United States has the ability to do much more than securitize a relationship with Somaliland.

U.S. recognition of Somaliland would risk the ire of other American friends, notably Turkey, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia. It may be worth the hard conversations and anger, though. Turkish, Egyptian, and Saudi leaders should not have a veto over U.S. policy, especially when high-stakes issues like confronting the IRGC and the Houthis as well as shoring up freedom of navigation are in play. They far outweigh Saudi Arabia’s pique with Israel and the UAE, Turkey’s regional ambitions, and Egypt’s spat with Ethiopia—for which one can imagine a diplomatic resolution.

The United States has good reason to recognize Somaliland. In the Middle East and Horn of Africa, where it is hard to find a good opportunity, upgrading relations with Hargeisa represents one. Somalilander officials want Washington as a partner, and importantly, they have something to offer. For the sake of both Somaliland and U.S. interests, it is time to give up the pretense of Somalia’s territorial integrity.

Steven A. Cook is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Eni Enrico Mattei senior fellow for Middle East and Africa studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. His latest book is The End of Ambition: America’s Past, Present, and Future in the Middle East. X: @stevenacook

“I sell. That’s as simple as that,” says José Mourinho, the legendary soccer coach, in an eponymous new documentary on Netflix. He could be talking about the American Express advertisement the interview highlights, or any of the plethora of brands he has lent his face to, from Coca Cola to Kalshi.

But what Mourinho means is that he is the ultimate draw. Mourinho sells like sex sells. The message is that the brands he endorses are all the richer for their association with him—as are the soccer teams, superstar players, and fans who have been fortunate enough to be graced by his aura.

“I sell. That’s as simple as that,” says José Mourinho, the legendary soccer coach, in an eponymous new documentary on Netflix. He could be talking about the American Express advertisement the interview highlights, or any of the plethora of brands he has lent his face to, from Coca Cola to Kalshi.

But what Mourinho means is that he is the ultimate draw. Mourinho sells like sex sells. The message is that the brands he endorses are all the richer for their association with him—as are the soccer teams, superstar players, and fans who have been fortunate enough to be graced by his aura.

That aura and persona is something Mourinho has spent his entire life crafting. And it is predicated on two fundamental obsessions: football (as soccer is called in most of the world) and winning. Mourinho has won every major trophy in European soccer across the sport’s biggest leagues, with its biggest teams, multiple times over.

“Football is to win. And … I won a lot,” he says matter-of-factly, one of several quintessential Mourinho quotes peppered throughout the three-part series. “You don’t do a documentary with a guy that wins nothing.”

While I am an obsessive football fan myself, that’s not the reason I wanted to write about the self-anointed “Special One” (more on that below) for Foreign Policy. Rather, it’s what his life, career, and relentless self-aggrandizement can tell us about geopolitics and the world we live in today.

As the documentary lays out, Mourinho expects and inspires unflinching loyalty and will ruthlessly cast aside anyone who fails to give it to him. He has a need for ultimate control, a litany of grievances against his perceived enemies, and a deep conviction that no one can be bigger than him. If you stand against him, either you leave, or he does. It’s Mourinho versus the world. You just have to decide which side you want to be on. Sound familiar?

Mourinho during a press conference at the Chelsea training ground on Feb. 25, 2005.Getty Images

“He didn’t even have to say anything to make you aware that you could get on the wrong side of him,” says England football legend Frank Lampard, who played for Mourinho in the mid-2000s and is one of several superstars interviewed in the documentary. “You’re either with him or against him.”

Mourinho, in other words, is football’s ultimate authoritarian. As a viral social media post once put it, he was “born to be a dictator” but “forced to be a football coach.” He serves as a potent symbol for the world we seem to be living in—one where might makes right, winning is everything, and empathy is scoffed at rather than emulated.

One can debate whether that is the right approach to leadership, but Mourinho’s ever-growing mythology and continued success—despite openly embracing the role of villain—is something most politicians would kill for.

How much of it is an act and how much of it is really Mourinho? In the documentary, he reveals just enough for viewers to wonder but not enough to answer the question.

“People think they know me, but they don’t know me. And I’m happy they don’t,” he says. “It’s a privilege for the ones that know me.”

A photo of a young Mourinho from the documentary.Netflix

Mourinho grew up in the 1960s and ’70s in Setúbal, Portugal, where his mother was a teacher and his father played and then coached football professionally at the local club. Mourinho followed that career path but says he was “not a very good player,” quitting in the late 1980s before embarking on a coaching career that took him across Portugal and Spain’s top leagues as a translator and assistant coach.

But the documentary focuses on a series of big breakout moments that began in 2002—months after he took charge of top-tier Portuguese club FC Porto—when he boldly pledged that he would win them the league title the following year. He did. He also won the UEFA Cup, at the time the continent’s second-most prestigious club honor. The next year, he went one better, topping the league once again but this time also winning the Champions League, Europe’s most prestigious club competition.

Days later, he moved to the English Premier League, widely considered the world’s most competitive, to take charge of London team Chelsea. That was where his aura would go truly global, powered by the British tabloids and media. Mourinho won back-to-back titles with Chelsea in his first two seasons, breaking the dominance of two of the greatest managers in English history—Manchester United’s Alex Ferguson and Arsenal’s Arsene Wenger. Backed with a hefty budget to sign players thanks to Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea, Mourinho and his team seemed unstoppable.

“The one thing that José did have at the time was complete strength and power at the club,” Lampard says.

Mourinho celebrates along with players during the trophy presentation after Chelsea won the League Cup final at Wembley Stadium in London on March 1, 2015. Glyn Kirk/AFP via Getty Images

But what happened next showed the limits of how much authority a coach could have. Mourinho repeatedly clashed with Abramovich over some of the Russian owner’s personnel decisions; Chelsea failed to get a three-peat; and Abramovich sacked Mourinho early into his fourth season in charge. While politics has sometimes shown otherwise, in football, when an authoritarian goes up against an oligarch, the oligarch often wins.

Mourinho simply went and continued winning elsewhere. He joined Italian giants Inter Milan, winning the Italian league in his first year and another Champions League in his second—defeating Chelsea on the way to the trophy.

                How Soccer Became ‘Un-American’            


    
    	The sport is a marker of a particular relationship to the wider world.

    Bronwen Everill
