                The Geopolitics of Soccer            


    
    	What does the World Cup tell us about the state of the world? Mehreen Khan, a former sports journalist and now the economics editor of The Times, joined FP Live to discuss.    	    


        
        FP Live

The sport is a marker of a particular relationship to the wider world.

What does the World Cup tell us about the state of the world? Mehreen Khan, a former sports journalist and now the economics editor of The Times, joined FP Live to discuss.

His recounting of that win over Chelsea in the documentary shows that in Mourinho’s worldview, no one matters but him. Not the 22 players on the pitch. Not the fans. Just him.

“I was playing against a guy that sacked me. I go home happy, and he goes upset,” he said of Abramovich. “I know how much he loves Chelsea. I know how much he loves to win. But I needed revenge. Because football belongs to people like me.”

There are two consistent themes about Mourinho’s career that he repeatedly comes back to throughout the documentary. One is his unbridled obsession with football at the cost of everything else; the other is his perception of football not as sport but as something far more serious. “It was not to play football. It was to resist in a war,” he said of the Inter Milan defeat of Chelsea.

Mourinho charges forward in celebration after Inter Milan wins a Champions League match against Barcelona in Spain on April 28, 2010. Filippo Monteforte/AFP via Getty Images

Mourinho refers to football as “war” or “battle” several times through the documentary, and the players interviewed—all of them superstars in their own right—make clear how much he instilled that mindset in them.

“He made me want to fight for him,” says former Chelsea captain John Terry, laying out what he described as Mourinho’s “magical spell” over the players. “I’ve never seen a group of individuals follow one person like we did him,” he adds. “I would leave that pitch in a coffin for him.”

It continued beyond Chelsea. “José was our leader,” says former Inter Milan defender Marco Materazzi (the recipient of that famous World Cup headbutt). “We were all willing to die on the field to get to the final.”

Swedish striker Zlatan Ibrahimovic, who won trophies with Mourinho at two different clubs and is known for his own narcissistic arrogance, says Mourinho “changed my game, he made me more of a killer. So when I entered the field, I was feeling untouchable. I could destroy anyone.”

But no one is as good at mythologizing Mourinho as Mourinho himself. “Strong guys, I make them stronger,” he says. “Shit people, they are in trouble.”

Mourinho celebrates after the Copa del Rey final between Real Madrid and Barcelona at Estadio Mestalla in Valencia, Spain, on April 20, 2011. Manuel Queimadelos Alonso/Getty Images

The documentary offers several windows into how Mourinho sees himself, but one of the most revealing is when he talks about being Portuguese. “I feel proud of what we were before—this little corner in the end of Europe, navigators discovering new places,” he says, referring rather romantically and casually to colonialism.

He then makes it clear that he sees himself as a modern-day conquistador of sorts. “I feel responsibility because I am one of the faces of our country. I’m not an ambassador, but I am,” he says. “I am a navigator, centuries later, fighting for life, fighting for career, with talent and courage.”

Mourinho’s conquests continued after he won the 2010 Champions League with Inter Milan.

Days later, he took the biggest job in world football, one that even casual watchers of the sport would know, by taking the helm at Real Madrid. “I went to Real Madrid to break the dominancy of Barcelona,” he says in the documentary, referring to the club’s archrivals.

There’s a mythological backstory there too. Mourinho was assistant coach at Barcelona in the 1990s, where one of his main roles was working as a Spanish translator for the English head coach Bobby Robson (a characterization he bristles at). But Barcelona appointed its former captain Pep Guardiola as manager in 2008, in what was seen by many as a snub to Mourinho. Guardiola would turn Barcelona into one of the most dominant teams in Europe, with one Lionel Messi as its star player.

Mourinho did break that dominance, winning the Spanish league title in his second season with a star of his own in Cristiano Ronaldo. But he was sacked again before completing his third season after clashing with several players, including club captain Iker Casillas and even Ronaldo himself.

Fights follow Mourinho wherever he goes—with the press, with rival managers, with his own players. “I don’t run away from controversy,” he says. “And I try to use it when I feel that it can be positive for my side.”

Mourinho sits on the bench as photographers mob him during the Champions League Group H match between FC Porto and Chelsea in Porto, Portugal, on Dec. 7, 2004.Christopher Lee/Getty Images

The pattern of euphoria followed by implosion has become another hallmark of his career, and following his early period of success, the highs have gotten shorter and less impressive. After Madrid, he returned to Chelsea, winning another league title before being dismissed acrimoniously midway through the following season when results fell apart. He continued in England with Manchester United (a stint I’m painfully familiar with, as a fan of the club) and Tottenham; moved back to Italy to manage Rome’s top team, AS Roma; had a brief Turkish sojourn with Fenerbahce; and then went back to Portugal to manage Lisbon-based Benfica. Many of those stints saw him win a handful more trophies but also ended with premature sackings.

In the documentary—as in his life—Mourinho’s self-aggrandizement is relentless. “I wanted to make history, and nothing was going to stop me,” he says. While talking about his win over Ferguson’s Manchester United en route to his famous Champions League triumph with Porto, he describes it as “the moment when I introduced myself to the world.”

There are several moments where he gets to the edge of humility or self-reflection, only to retreat back into his ego. “Was I naive? Arrogant?” he asks at one point, only to quickly follow up with: “I don’t think so.” In another monologue, he admits that he can be “really nasty” and “aggressive,” before adding: “It’s a place where, normally, I win.”

Mourinho even tries to downplay his most famous quote, uttered during his first press conference with Chelsea back in 2004, when English journalists questioned his ability to manage in a tougher league. “Please don’t call me arrogant,” he said at the time, “but I’m European champion and I think I’m a special one.”

“The Special One” became a nickname in the British tabloid headlines, one that has followed him throughout his career and one that it’s clear he revels in. But in the documentary, he takes pains to point out that he said a special one, not the special one. “The Special One is some special shit, some guys in England they found for me,” he tells the filmmakers while showing them the trophy room in his home in Setúbal, to which one of them promptly replies: “I love that you’re saying that while there’s a mural of yourself behind you.”

A few frames before, the camera reveals the words “Special One” engraved on the side of the Ferrari that Mourinho drives them to his house in.

Mourinho, head coach of Benfica, is shown a red card by a referee during a Champions League match between Benfica and Real Madrid in Lisbon on Feb. 17. Angel Martinez/Getty Images

The Mourinho Netflix release was sandwiched between two other premieres that put his narcissism and brazenness in even starker relief.

One was the latest season of Ted Lasso, which depicts Jason Sudeikis as a folksy (U.S.) football coach from Wichita, Kansas, who hops across the pond to take over an (English) football team, winning over the stuffy Brits with his quintessential midwestern charm. While it’s as wholesome a depiction of trans-Atlantic relations as you’re likely to get, it feels positively anachronistic in the current trans-Atlantic moment.

The other release, a week after Mourinho’s, was a behind-the-scenes documentary on his archnemesis Guardiola’s final seasons at Manchester City, with whom he has dominated English football for the past decade. That documentary shows Guardiola crying in front of his players, speaking openly and vulnerably about his divorce, blaming himself for the team’s mistakes, and, even in the middle of reprimanding Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland, telling him he loves him “like a father.”

Mourinho would never. At least not in public. “I’m not nice,” he says in one of the documentary’s more revealing exchanges. When the director asks him how it feels to say so openly, Mourinho promptly replies: “I feel with pride.”

In the documentary, Mourinho literally scoffs at Guardiola taking a sabbatical after leaving Barcelona. “Some guys, they need a sabbatical. … I hate that word. For me, sabbatical means weakness,” he says. “I don’t need a rest. I will have a rest when he decides to say: ‘Come up.’”

Mourinho gestures toward the crowd during a match between Juventus and Manchester United in Turin, Italy, on Nov. 7, 2018. Isabella Bonotto/AFP via Getty Images

Guardiola is now on another sabbatical after departing Manchester, and Mourinho is on to his next, rather surprising, job. In June, after a season with Benfica in which the team finished third in the Portuguese league despite being undefeated, Real Madrid suddenly announced that Mourinho would return to the club—13 years after his bitter departure.

He will now be managing some new big egos, including superstars Kylian Mbappé, Jude Bellingham, and Vinícius Júnior. If anyone can do it, it’s probably Mourinho. He’s claimed he is now “calmer” but has already sniped at a journalist who cited sources within the club who said he seems more relaxed.

If the documentary is any indication, Mourinho remains unapologetic as ever. “I don’t try to manipulate,” he says. “It’s not about the manipulator, it’s about the people that are open to be manipulated.”

And then comes the line that will make you truly thankful he chose to be a football coach and not a dictator.

“It’s just when you reach a certain level, you want to stay there forever, no?”

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: The United States announces a stake in Venezuela’s oil, four South American countries agree to cooperate on critical minerals, and Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi retires from international competition.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: The United States announces a stake in Venezuela’s oil, four South American countries agree to cooperate on critical minerals, and Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi retires from international competition.

Sign up to receive Latin America Brief in your inbox every Friday.

After the U.S. military intervention in Venezuela on Jan. 3, officials from both countries promised major oil sector investments. Several of those deals finally materialized this week.

On Wednesday, U.S. firm Chevron and Italian firm Eni announced new plans for oil production in Venezuela. Chevron aims to increase its production by more than 300,000 barrels per day, or around a quarter of the country’s current output, over the next five years.

But the deal that really turned heads was a recent one announced by the U.S. and interim Venezuelan administrations. The U.S. government will take a partial stake in production at 17 Venezuelan oilfields “at zero cost to the United States” and benefit by buying some of that oil at a discount, the White House said on Monday.

U.S. President Donald Trump said the agreement would last a century, while interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez said that its term would be 25 years.

The details were not immediately made public, but the deal drew criticism from across Venezuela’s political spectrum.

“It’s the same opacity that has characterized the country’s oil revenues so far in 2026,” opposition figure Henrique Capriles wrote on social media. Rafael Ramírez, who ran Venezuela’s state oil company under former President Hugo Chávez, called the deal “new colonialism.”

Critics seized on the fact that there had been no public bidding process for permission to drill in the 17 oil fields. Such a process would have allowed potential partners to compete for the best deal with the Venezuelan government.

Rodríguez said that under the U.S. deal, around $19 from each barrel of oil—based on an assumption of a $65 price for the full barrel—will flow “directly to our country.”

Venezuelan economist Francisco Rodríguez of the Center for Economic and Policy Research said the number is comparable to the government’s cut in neighboring Guyana and “not absurdly low.” But, he added, there is no way for Caracas to know if it is being dealt an unfair hand. “This is the first time since the Russian oil privatizations [of the 1990s] that I’ve heard about contracts of this magnitude being given out without a public bidding process,” he said.

Over the past week, news of the U.S.-Venezuela oil deal ricocheted around the region. An editorial in La Jornada, a left-leaning Mexican newspaper, called it “robbery.” Some policymakers in the region viewed the murky nature of the deal with concern.

“Venezuela’s sovereignty has been under threat since January 3,” said a senior Latin American diplomat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive topic. This agreement “was not made between equals.”

While a White House spokesperson said on Wednesday that oil from the new partnership could reach U.S. reserves by November, the deal’s full execution still appears distant. Some of the 17 blocks being opened to drilling will need to effectively start operations from zero, FP’s Keith Johnson reported this week. Others produced oil in the past but will need lots of new cash to function.

The private company partnering with the U.S. government, North American Blue Energy Partners, said it envisions investing $100 billion as part of the arrangement, but it still needs to raise that money. It only reported investing $1 billion in Venezuela in the past two years.

What’s more, the deal is at risk of being repealed by any future democratic Venezuelan government, analyst Jimena Zuniga said at a virtual Bloomberg event on Wednesday.

Some analysts and opposition figures have argued that the desire to keep the deal alive could make Washington less open to a democratic transition. While U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has repeatedly said that eventual democratization is part of the U.S. plan for Venezuela, Trump said on Wednesday that the country was not ready yet for elections.

Rodríguez, the Venezuelan economist, said that when thinking about potential democratization in Venezuela, the comparison to Russia was again apt. “In Russia during the 1990s, some people became immensely wealthy with the privatizations of state-owned enterprises. Those ended up being the same oligarchs that blocked democratic reforms,” he said.

“[I]f your wealth has been obtained through opaque dealings … you aren’t going to want a democratic system that will review those contracts,” Rodríguez said.

Sunday, Sept. 6: Jamaican officials visit the United Kingdom to lodge a complaint calling for reparations for slavery.

Monday, Sept. 7, to Thursday, Sept. 10: The International Court of Justice holds hearings in a Nicaragua-led case against Germany over its support for Israel’s war in Gaza.

Friday, Sept. 12 to Saturday, Sept. 13: Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attends the BRICS summit in India.

Critical minerals cooperation. Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, and Peru last week signed a pledge to step up their cooperation on critical minerals such as copper and lithium. Mining ministries from the countries said that they planned to coordinate training for their mining workforces, align regulatory standards for the minerals, and seek funding from multilateral financiers.

While the joint declaration did not contain specific deadlines, Peru’s mining minister characterized it as a step toward creating more processed mineral products in South America rather than simply selling the raw materials abroad. Chile plans to increase its exports of mining technologies to its neighbors, officials said.

The pact is the latest sign that regional cooperation on industrialization is not only the purview of the South American left. These four countries all have right-wing presidents.

A coming battery boom? One processed mineral product that the region generally imports is large-scale batteries to store the energy generated by solar panels and wind turbines. It will need more such batteries soon.

Last week, consultancy Wood Mackenzie upped its forecast for how much energy storage will be deployed in Latin America over the next decade. It expects that total installed capacity in 2035 will be 34 gigawatts, which is more than 13 times what was last year.

This change partly reflects the rollout of renewable energy. Unlike coal-fired power plants, solar and wind plants can’t produce energy at all hours, so battery storage is needed to hold the energy before injecting it into the grid when the wind isn’t blowing and at nighttime.

Furthermore, some old electricity grids in the region lack the capacity to handle the high amount of renewable energy being generated. That’s the case in Brazil, which has been blocking some solar energy generators from supplying the grid in recent years in order to prevent it from being overwhelmed. Without more batteries, Brazil cannot use all the renewable energy that it generates.

People pay their respects during the funeral procession of Uruguayan singer and songwriter Rubén Rada in Montevideo on Aug. 28. Eitam Abramovich/AFP via Getty Images

Afro-Uruguayan star. Iconic Uruguayan musician Rubén “El Negro” Rada passed away on Aug. 26 at the age of 83. He was honored by lying in state in the country’s legislature in Montevideo, where a line of Uruguayans waiting for their turn to pay respects snaked around several city blocks. Many of them were dancing, as Rada had requested fans to do when he died.

Rada’s 2000 hit “Who will sing?” echoed through Montevideo. It asks “who will sing and dream and play the melody of love” if all the world cares about is work.

Over decades, Rada shone not only as a star of the Afro-Uruguayan music genre candombe but also fused its sound with other music traditions, like jazz, funk, and rock. Born to a Brazilian mother and a Uruguayan father, he was also beloved across the River Plate in Argentina. Rada’s 1985 song “Candombe for Gardel” crosses candombe with Argentine tango.

What is the name of the Montevideo neighborhood home to Uruguay’s legislature, where Rada’s funeral was held?

It means “the watering place.” Historically, it was the site of wells that supplied the city with drinking water.

A mural depicts Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi in his hometown of Rosario, Argentina, on Aug. 8. Luis Robayo/AFP via Getty Images

Argentine soccer phenom Lionel Messi announced on Monday that he will no longer compete for the country’s national team. “The time has come,” Messi wrote in a letter he shared on social media. Messi competed in six World Cups for Argentina, with some critics writing that 2026 arguably saw Messi’s best World Cup performance at the age of 39.

Despite that, Argentina lost this year’s World Cup final to Spain. Around the same time, Messi’s father fell ill; he passed away on Aug. 8. Messi wrote in his announcement that his father’s death made him more convinced of his decision to retire from the national team.

Messi, who is widely considered to be the greatest soccer player of the 21st century, still plays for the club Inter Miami, where his contract extends to 2028. But in the eyes of Argentines, his international career is what mattered most. Starting Wednesday night, every soccer game across Argentina is being paused at the 10-minute mark for a stadium applause for Messi. (He wore the number 10 jersey.)

In his decades-long career, Messi was not just a star athlete. He mobilized the soft power of soccer itself in international relations. Saudi Arabia in 2022 appointed him as a tourism ambassador for the country; U.S. presidents from Barack Obama to Trump have sought meetings with him.

In the wake of Messi’s announcement, Argentines have argued that he stood for the best of their country on the world stage: perseverance, devotion, and a bit of inexplicable magic. “He was the symbol of the country we wanted to be and see,” wrote Osvaldo Pepe in Clarín, and he “gave happiness to a country that is used to suffering.”

Messi once had a more complicated relationship with Argentine fans. For years, some argued that he appeared to be trying harder when he played for his European club team, FC Barcelona, than when he wore the Argentina shirt. A statue of Messi in Buenos Aires was vandalized after a 2017 national team loss. But Argentina’s 2022 World Cup victory silenced those doubters.

“I swear I gave it my all, not only in the last few years when we were winning everything, but before, too,” Messi wrote in his retirement note. “I thank God for making me Argentine.”

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

ALREADY AN FP SUBSCRIBER? LOGIN

Sudan has been descending into hell for years. The United Nations Security Council now has a chance to do right by the people of Sudan and remember what it was created to do: stop wars, keep the peace, and protect lives. But it can do those things only if its members are willing to step up.

Sudan is experiencing the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. More than 33 million people are in need of basic assistance. An estimated 19.5 million people, disproportionately women and children, face acute hunger. Almost 9 million people have now been driven from their homes, another 4.5 million have fled the country, and at least 150,000 are dead. Yet somehow, this historic catastrophe has generated little more than horrified whispers from the West’s most vaunted institutions.

Sudan has been descending into hell for years. The United Nations Security Council now has a chance to do right by the people of Sudan and remember what it was created to do: stop wars, keep the peace, and protect lives. But it can do those things only if its members are willing to step up.

Sudan is experiencing the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. More than 33 million people are in need of basic assistance. An estimated 19.5 million people, disproportionately women and children, face acute hunger. Almost 9 million people have now been driven from their homes, another 4.5 million have fled the country, and at least 150,000 are dead. Yet somehow, this historic catastrophe has generated little more than horrified whispers from the West’s most vaunted institutions.

The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its allied militias have committed genocide, murdering men and boys on an ethnic basis and raping women and girls. The U.N. estimates that more than 12 million Sudanese women and girls—roughly half the country’s female population—are at risk of sexual violence. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have committed atrocities, too.

More than 130 humanitarian workers have been killed since the war began. Both sides loot and block food, aid, and other supplies. They also brandish access to lifesaving aid as a tool of suppression, with the lives of local recipients hanging in the balance. And now, with the advent of drone warfare, both sides are finding it easier and cheaper to inflict more lethal damage.

Last year, at least 2,670 people, a number that includes combatants and civilians, were killed in drone attacks. That represents a 600 percent increase in drone-related deaths over a single year. In just the first five months of this year, drones killed more than 1,000 people, making up roughly 80 percent of civilian deaths during that period. Markets, hospitals, schools, and aid routes have become fair game for thugs with remote controls. The barrier to entry for mass violence in Sudan has never been lower, yet the U.N. is policing the conflict with an arms embargo written more than two decades ago. Security Council Resolution 1591, which imposed an arms embargo on Darfur in 2005, is older than Apple’s iPhone—let alone the drones hovering above Sudan today.

The international community’s approach to Sudan has simply not kept up with the times.

First, there’s the battlefield. The war has spread into the Kordofan region and Blue Nile state. The Security Council’s embargo stops at Darfur, several hundred miles away from the new arenas of conflict.

Then there’s the international meddling, which has undoubtedly prolonged the fighting and heightened the heavy toll on civilians. More than a dozen countries with diverse motives are providing some form of military support to the warring parties. Mercenaries have been recruited from as far away as Colombia. Foreign networks of all stripes supply drones, weapons, parts, money, and their own renditions of expertise.

Munitions do not become duds and drones do not fall out of the sky if they cross imaginary embargo lines on maps, for example where Kordofan begins and Darfur ends. Neither do smugglers sit on their hands when they can move weapons from other parts of Sudan. They adapt—just as the RSF and SAF have.

But the U.N. has failed to adapt. For more than 20 years, the Security Council has kept the same geographic embargo in place while the battlefield, the weapons, and the players supplying them have shifted unrecognizably.

That’s why the G-7—including the United States—has called on the Security Council to expand the embargo across all of Sudan.

So let’s do it.


    
    
        Read More
        
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        Solidarity activists take part in a Hands Off Sudan march in London on Nov. 9, 2024.
    
    
        
    
                Washington Must Confront Abu Dhabi Over Sudan            


    
    	If Trump truly wants to be a peacemaker, he should banish the UAE from the negotiating table.    	    


        
        Argument    
        |
        
    
    Suha Musa


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        In a landscape almost entirely covered with light brown sand, a small cemetery in the foreground is filled with mounds of dirt marked with sticks or small stones. Beyond that, a woman in an ankle-length dress and a headscarf walks by, her shadow long behind her. Low-rise buildings in a similar sandy color are visible beyond a fence behind her.
    
    
        
    
                Horrors in Sudan Highlight Deterioration of Western Diplomatic Corps            


    
    	Decades of neglect have hollowed out expertise and experience.    	    


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    David Raikow


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        Mona Ibrahim, a displaced Sudanese mother, and her children sit on the ground in the famine-stricken Zamzam camp for Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) in northern Darfur, Sudan, on Jan. 21.
    
    
        
    
                Why Won’t the UAE End the War in Sudan?            


    
    	An independent inquiry has established the complicity of external actors.    	    


        
        Argument    
        |
        
    
    Mutasim Ali, 
    Yonah Diamond

If Trump truly wants to be a peacemaker, he should banish the UAE from the negotiating table.

Decades of neglect have hollowed out expertise and experience.

An independent inquiry has established the complicity of external actors.

The United States has presented a resolution to the Security Council that would expand the arms embargo nationwide, making clear that sanctions and member state implementation of those rules apply to all the networks keeping this war alive—on both sides, with no carve-outs. Yes, it will even apply to the arms traffickers, procurement agents, mercenary recruiters, state-backed patrons, established financiers, drone suppliers, and genocidal commanders who have for so long evaded justice.

Already, some on the Security Council are posturing to oppose or abstain from this resolution. They may try to portray this embargo as taking sides in Sudan’s civil war. Others may try to deny their own direct involvement in Sudan, suggesting instead that private traders and intermediaries are responsible for the flow of weapons into the country.

There is irony in both arguments. For one, the new blanket embargo would apply to the RSF, the SAF, and any actors that feed either side munitions. If anything, evangelizing the current embargo, evidently porous and incomplete as it is, betrays that those warning against “taking sides” already have.

Then there’s the cognitive dissonance in blaming rogue traders and freelance brokers as the real culprits while opposing a resolution designed to reach precisely those actors. If private financiers, smugglers, and unofficial procurement networks are really to blame, then help us identify them, sanction them, block their arms trafficking, and shut them down. A government that truly has nothing to hide should have no objection helping the U.N. monitor and close arms channels it claims are operating beyond its control.

Under President Donald Trump, the United States has already gone to work. We have sanctioned individuals and entities facilitating mercenary recruitment, foreign fighters, procurement, and other support to this war. Other countries should do the same at and beyond the U.N.

Think of this resolution as a rubric. Those tearing Sudan apart will be graded for their actions. But it will still be the member states that must enforce consequences.

The U.N. will monitor violations, identify the networks moving weapons, and document who flouts the embargo. And for member states, most of which place a premium on acting pursuant to clear U.N. authority, this resolution removes any ambiguity or excuse. With the Security Council’s mandate behind them, member states can—and should—stop shipments, freeze assets, tighten export controls, and move against the networks violating the embargo.

In the end, Sudan’s warring parties must still stand down. We, for our part, believe they should do so via a humanitarian truce that the United States has proposed alongside a U.N. mechanism to deliver aid and create space for a broader peace process.

As long as weapons are easier to come by than food in Sudan, cooler heads have little chance to prevail. And it appears that some on the Security Council are just fine with that. Any Security Council member considering abstaining or voting no should understand what it is voting for. It will mean business as usual in Sudan—and all the wanton violence that entails.

At best, vetoes and abstentions alike turn a blind eye to drones bombing hospitals and markets, aid blocked from starving families, and millions of innocents paying the price for others’ geopolitical voyeurism. At worst, those who would veto or abstain should welcome the question: Why are you aiding and abetting those on either side who are destroying Sudan, its people, and its future?

Neither the RSF nor the SAF has any legitimate claim to govern Sudan when this war ends. Both have committed atrocities against the Sudanese people, and both have forfeited any suggestion that they possess political legitimacy. Sudan’s future cannot belong to whichever armed faction is left standing. It must come from a credible, independent civilian dialogue that gives the Sudanese people themselves—not the men with the most guns or the deadliest drones—a say over their future.

The United States will not rubber-stamp another year of descension into hell. We and the world will note who stands with the Sudanese people and who stands against them.

Michael Waltz is the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. He previously served as a U.S. representative from Florida, national security advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, and in the U.S. Army as a combat-decorated Green Beret.

Massad Boulos is a senior advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump for Arab and African affairs. He advises the president on regional diplomacy and leads U.S. engagement on key political, security, and economic priorities, including efforts to end the war in Sudan.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The USS Abraham Lincoln finally ends a 286-day deployment, Ukrainian intelligence agencies fight in the streets of Kyiv, and U.S. companies warn of AI’s threat to global cybersecurity.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The USS Abraham Lincoln finally ends a 286-day deployment, Ukrainian intelligence agencies fight in the streets of Kyiv, and U.S. companies warn of AI’s threat to global cybersecurity.

The USS Abraham Lincoln has seen better days. The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier docked in Thailand on Wednesday after 286 grueling days at sea—the bulk of which were spent in the Middle East supporting the U.S. war against Iran—and it’s covered in rust.

The Lincoln is now receiving repairs as its crew members enjoy some much-deserved R&R. The condition of the Lincoln, while not unexpected after a prolonged deployment, is an unsettling metaphor for both the state of the Iran war and the U.S. military more broadly at the moment.

The Iran war has left the U.S. military overextended, pulling vital resources and personnel away from other regions and priorities. And much like the war itself, the carrier’s deployment lasted far longer than the Trump administration expected or planned.

The 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard reportedly faced a range of challenges, from food shortages to sewage issues. The indefinite timeline surrounding their deployment also apparently (and quite understandably) had a detrimental effect on the mental health of some personnel aboard, leading family members to raise grave concerns. Multiple crew members reportedly attempted to jump overboard.

Their hardships can’t be divorced from the fact that they’re serving under an administration that has struggled to define its goals in the Iran war from the start. As retired Gen. Joseph Votel, the former Central Command chief, told John in July, “The military has done exactly what has been asked of them, and they’ve done that to the best of their ability,” but it’s been challenging “to appreciate what the long-term strategic objectives” are in the war.

Directionless. The Iran war reignited this week after a lull in fighting (for the umpteenth time), and this cycle appears to be poised to continue so long as the Trump administration refuses to change course in a significant way (or cut its losses).

This means that the U.S. military will keep using up already dwindled stockpiles of key munitions, and tens of thousands of U.S. troops will continue to be deployed in the region.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is extending Middle East troop deployments into 2027, despite reported warnings from top military leaders that the prolongment of large-scale operations is unsustainable.

Pentagon problems. Meanwhile, there’s trouble on the home front as Hegseth’s controversial approach to leadership—and his efforts to consolidate power and ensure loyalty—continues to push key Pentagon figures out.

In one of the highest-profile departures under Hegseth’s tenure to date, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned on Monday. Driscoll met with Trump at the White House ahead of his resignation. A U.S. official briefed on the meeting, who requested anonymity to discuss internal conversations, told SitRep that Driscoll used that meeting to present his concerns to Trump about the Army’s future and direction under Hegseth’s leadership. Driscoll also told Trump that Hegseth’s firing of several top generals made it difficult to implement the changes within the Army that Driscoll wanted, the official added.

Driscoll’s wartime exit has led congressional Democrats and even some Republicans to call for Hegseth’s resignation. GOP Sen. Thom Tillis wrote in a post on X that he’s “never witnessed more inept management” of the military, describing Hegseth as “intimidated by competence” while urging Trump to “find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

Though many in Washington are convinced that Hegseth is no longer (or never was) the man for the job, Trump has apparently not given up on him just yet. But with Trump’s polling numbers in the gutter amid the unpopular Iran war, it could become increasingly difficult for the president to overlook the dysfunction and negative press engulfing the Pentagon under Hegseth.

Estonian Defense Minister (and former SitRep interviewee) Hanno Pevkur resigned on Wednesday amid a defense procurement scandal, in which the country paid more than $80 million for artillery shells meant for Ukraine that turned out to be faulty. The contract was given to an Indian-owned, Italian-registered defense firm that had never sold a single artillery shell. In an exit interview with Estonian broadcaster ERR, Pevkur said that “the minister does not negotiate contracts” but that he was resigning to “take political responsibility” for the scandal.

Multiple reports indicate that Hegseth’s preferred candidate to succeed Driscoll as Army secretary is current Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell.

Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov was in Washington this week, where he met with Alex Karp, the CEO of U.S. defense tech company Palantir. Karp is set to be the first lead investor in a defense tech company that Fedorov—whom Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky controversially fired earlier this year—is setting up, Fedorov said in a post on X. Fedorov also met with former U.S. cyber ambassador Nate Fick.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Kyiv shoot-out. Officers from Ukraine’s two leading intelligence agencies were involved in a shoot-out against each other on the streets of Kyiv this week, leaving at least three of them injured in what Zelensky described as an “absolutely shameful” event. Personnel from Ukraine’s civilian intelligence agency, known as the SBU, reportedly opened fire on their counterparts from the country’s military intelligence arm, known as the HUR. The SBU has accused senior Ukrainian military commander Stepan Kaplunov of working on behalf of Russia, and the shoot-out occurred while its officers were searching Kaplunov’s apartment.

Cyber warnings. Some of the United States’ leading companies this week issued fresh warnings about the threat to global cybersecurity from advances in artificial intelligence. An open letter calling for “collective action on cyber defense” was signed by more than 130 major companies, including leading AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic as well as Adobe, Capital One, Google, General Motors, Microsoft, PayPal, and Uber.

“In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter warned. “The companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk.” The letter comes after a series of high-profile hacks by AI models and a targeting of U.S. water systems by cyberattackers. It calls for companies, governments, and global organizations to urgently partner on cybersecurity.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hosts the 2026 G-20 financial meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, United States, on Sep. 1.Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images

Monday, Sept. 7: The 63rd session of the U.N. Human Rights Council begins.

The annual “Freedom Edge” joint military exercise—involving the United States, Japan, and South Korea—begins.

Tuesday, Sept. 8: Canada’s retaliatory tariffs against the United States go into effect.

Wednesday, Sept. 9: The International Space Summit begins in Paris.

“This piece of shit should never be allowed in the US.”

—U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego, referring to Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who posted a since-deleted AI-generated video on X depicting plump Palestinian prisoners being funneled into a prison camp on a conveyor belt and coming out emaciated and crying.

The U.S. Mint appears to have sold out of new $1 coins with Trump’s face on them just hours after releasing them on Wednesday. The mint’s website shows the coins, which feature Trump’s presidential portrait on one side and the presidential seal on the other, as “not currently in stock.” That’s despite each coin costing far more than the $1 they’re valued at—the mint is selling a roll of 25 coins for $61 and a bag of $100 coins for $154.50.

A Qatar-based firm is seeking staff for gold mining in Venezuela, becoming one of the few companies known to have taken up the Trump administration on its push to attract investment into the country’s troubled mining sector.

In a job listing posted two weeks ago, UCC Holding advertised for an executive director for its “Gold Division” in Caracas. “The role will oversee the full mining value chain, including exploration, greenfield project development, tailings recovery, sediment resource projects, mining operations, processing, and commercial activities,” according to postings on job boards and LinkedIn.

A Qatar-based firm is seeking staff for gold mining in Venezuela, becoming one of the few companies known to have taken up the Trump administration on its push to attract investment into the country’s troubled mining sector.

In a job listing posted two weeks ago, UCC Holding advertised for an executive director for its “Gold Division” in Caracas. “The role will oversee the full mining value chain, including exploration, greenfield project development, tailings recovery, sediment resource projects, mining operations, processing, and commercial activities,” according to postings on job boards and LinkedIn.

The company also posted four jobs in Venezuela related to airport construction, including one titled “Project Controls Manager – UCC Venezuela Airport Project.” One job post describes a “major Airport EPC Construction Project.” EPC stands for engineering, procurement, and construction, a method of construction in which the builder provides a ready-to-use final product.

UCC has not previously announced investments in gold or airport construction in Venezuela.

The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Foreign Policy, nor did Venezuela’s information ministry.

The job announcements follow a March visit by U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to Venezuela, where he was accompanied by U.S. mining sector officials representing more than two dozen companies. Burgum later told reporters that Venezuela’s government would provide security guarantees to companies interested in investing in its mining sector, which is plagued by criminal group involvement.

Such U.S. engagement has increased in the wake of the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on Jan. 3. Since then, acting President Delcy Rodríguez has ruled the country, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly playing a significant role as well.

Venezuela sits on ample gold reserves estimated at 2,343 metric tons, ranking it fifth in the world, according to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

However, few international companies so far have expressed an interest in gold mining in Venezuela, according to media reports. The Canada-listed mining company Gold Reserve, which had a mining venture in Venezuela that was seized in 2009, has said it will resume mining, and Swiss commodities firm Trafigura has said it will partner with Venezuela’s state gold mining company.

Christopher Ecclestone, a mining strategist at the financial advisory firm Hallgarten & Co., said he was not aware of any other foreign companies investing in Venezuelan gold operations.

Developing Venezuela’s gold resources will require companies to overcome significant physical, legal, and security challenges, according to the CSIS report.

There aren’t 65 billion barrels, they won’t be lowering gas prices, and they won’t refill the SPR.

As Delcy Rodríguez clings to power, dissidents wonder who to trust.

A look back at the U.S. intervention in Venezuela that the president wants to replicate.

The country’s gold reserves are largely underdeveloped, with 19 of the country’s 24 gold mines currently inactive. Mining is further complicated by the Venezuelan government’s tight grip on the sector following a decision in 2011 to nationalize the industry. Security is also an issue, with much of gold mining in Venezuela now controlled by criminal groups and state groups operating illicitly, according to CSIS.

“No respectable Western mining company is going to go into Venezuela in the current situation because it’s going to rebound on them badly at some point,” Ecclestone said. “A puppet regime awarding licenses to anyone is then ripe for having them rescinded the second that the puppet regime is no longer there.”

It’s unclear what expertise UCC may have in gold mining. The UCC website lists mining as a business interest, but the company is primarily known for energy projects and construction deals, including a $4 billion deal to invest in the Damascus airport. It is unclear where the company’s airport construction in Venezuela would occur, but it could potentially be aimed at the country’s main airport, which suffered severe damage in two earthquakes in June.

UCC’s chairman and president are Moutaz Al-Khayyat and Ramez Al-Khayyat, respectively. The two Syrian-born brothers have also invested in a luxury resort in Albania with Ivanka Trump, U.S. President Donald Trump’s daughter, and her husband, Jared Kushner, who also serves as a top diplomatic envoy for Trump. The planned resort has sparked mass protests in Albania, initially over the environmental impact of the development.

The Khayyat brothers separately courted U.S. congressional representatives in a bid to lift U.S. sanctions on Syria, according to the New York Times. These sanctions, primarily under the Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act, posed a barrier for various Khayyat investments in the country. The sanctions were eventually lifted last December with the repeal of the Caesar Act.

UCC has also invested in Venezuela’s energy industry through a stake in a venture with BP, becoming one of the few companies to answer the Trump administration’s call for energy investments.

FP’s Christina Lu contributed to this report.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Europe’s response to alleged Russian hybrid warfare, who is being blamed for the deadly Ceuta mass crossing, and Estonia’s multimillion-dollar defense spending scandal.

Tit-for-tat retaliations between Russia and Germany appear to be brewing into a larger diplomatic war as European nations join Berlin in punishing Moscow for an attempted drone attack on German soil.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Europe’s response to alleged Russian hybrid warfare, who is being blamed for the deadly Ceuta mass crossing, and Estonia’s multimillion-dollar defense spending scandal.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

From right, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO chief Mark Rutte give a press statement at European Union headquarters in Brussels on Sept. 2.OMAR HAVANA/GETTY IMAGES

Tit-for-tat retaliations between Russia and Germany appear to be brewing into a larger diplomatic war as European nations join Berlin in punishing Moscow for an attempted drone attack on German soil.

On Aug. 4, local authorities discovered an explosive-laden drone near Ukrainian cargo planes at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine. On Tuesday, Berlin formally blamed Moscow for the attempted operation, claiming that agents working “on behalf of Russian state entities” had controlled the drone.

As punishment for the alleged attack, Germany closed a Russian diplomatic mission in the city of Bonn, tightened restrictions on Russian travelers, and called on the European Union to impose greater sanctions on Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers and cargo ships. In response, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Berlin of planting evidence to make the Kremlin a scapegoat for Germany’s political problems.

But the crisis has not ended there. A day later, the heads of NATO and the EU issued strong warnings against Russia, vowing to respond to this “new normal” of Russian hybrid warfare against Europe.

Europe and NATO “won’t just maintain our pressure on Russia. We will increase it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X on Wednesday, adding to a previous message pledging the EU’s “full solidarity” with Germany. Meanwhile, NATO chief Mark Rutte called the alliance’s commitment to collective defense “ironclad” and promised to “continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat—including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig.”

Individual member nations have also taken up the call to diplomatic arms. During an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Ireland on Wednesday, top diplomats from Belgium, France, and the Netherlands announced that they had summoned their respective Russian ambassadors to protest the failed operation.

“We will not let an act of such gravity go unpunished,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said.

Since then, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Lithuania, Poland, and the United Kingdom have followed suit, summoning senior Russian diplomats stationed in their countries over what London called Moscow’s “egregious and reckless” attack.

At the same time, several EU countries—including Poland, Spain, and Sweden—have pushed for more than $224 billion in frozen Russian assets to be repurposed to help Ukraine. And Lithuania has reiterated that if Russia were to cause injuries or major damage on its territory like it targeted Leipzig, then it would “immediately” act in self-defense.

Moscow, however, maintains its innocence. On Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced plans to shutter German cultural centers across the country in response to Berlin’s closure of Russia’s Bonn facility. “They [Germany] deliberately took this step,” Lavrov said, according to Russian state news agency Tass. “They could not have failed to understand, which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia.”

Pointing fingers. There is no evidence to suggest that Morocco orchestrated a mass migrant crossing into the tiny Spanish exclave of Ceuta in late July, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told his parliament on Thursday.

“I can assure you that no institution—not the diplomatic service, nor ​the European Commission, nor any international body—has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that ⁠Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez said, denying allegations from a Spanish police report published last month that accused Morocco of deploying smaller-than-usual security teams to the area and failing to seriously try to disperse the crowds.

Sánchez also rejected claims that Madrid had mishandled the deadly crisis. “It’s absurd to think that the government knew and did nothing,” Sánchez said on Thursday. His address came less than 24 hours after tens of thousands of people backed by opposition parties held anti-government protests across the country, including in Ceuta, where at least 5,000 migrants remain stranded nearly five weeks after the mass crossing. More than 70,000 people initially fled from Morocco into Ceuta in late July.

Still, Sánchez is struggling to quell mounting domestic pressure over the incident, including calls for him to resign. On Thursday, he revealed that Madrid had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on Aug. 21 over “unacceptable statements” made by the country’s justice minister, who said that Rabat had a “historic right” to the Spanish territories of Ceuta and Melilla. However, it is unclear if that revelation will help Sánchez curry the public’s favor.

Defense spending scandal. Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur resigned on Wednesday over a controversial $81 million defense contract that was revealed in a National Audit Office report published on Friday.

In 2024, Estonia agreed to purchase artillery shells from Datasel SRL, an Italian-registered company owned by the India-based Neco Defense Munitions; under the deal, Tallinn would then supply Ukraine with this ammunition using money from the EU’s European Peace Facility. Estonia paid millions of dollars to Datasel in advance, but the shipments were delayed for months. Once the first batch finally arrived the following year, the ammunition was “not of sufficient quality,” according to Pevkur. It later became clear that Datasel had never previously sold a single artillery shell.

Pevkur took responsibility for the ministry’s failings in a Facebook post announcing his resignation on Wednesday, though he stressed that he was not personally involved in the Datasel contract. “A leader must have size and courage to take responsibility,” Pevkur wrote, “even though the minister does not count socks and cartridges and does not hold contract negotiations.”

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal convened an emergency cabinet meeting on Wednesday to discuss the report’s findings and Pevkur’s resignation. The country’s Prosecutor’s Office is also examining the report as part of an ongoing criminal investigation opened in 2025 into the Defense Ministry’s accounting.

Mega dinghies. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted French President Emmanuel Macron at Downing Street on Thursday, marking the first visit by an EU leader since Burnham took office. The two discussed “shared challenges,” including how best to support Ukraine in its war against Russia as well as ways to bolster EU cooperation with the United Kingdom. However, their primary topic of concern was migration.

In recent years, British authorities have recorded tens of thousands of people crossing the English Channel from France via small boats—nearly all of whom have claimed asylum. Although the number of migrants attempting the dangerous voyage dropped 43 percent thus far in 2026 compared to the previous year, the use of “mega dinghies” has introduced a new challenge for immigration enforcement officers. Just last month, a 15-meter-long vessel was spotted carrying a record 230 individuals.

“Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and we need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating dangerous crossings,” Burnham wrote on X on Thursday, calling the “small boats crisis” a “shared European challenge.” He announced that London and Paris had agreed to increase the total number of deployed French officers tackling the issue to nearly 1,050 people.

A Hungarian man may have played a little too much Grand Theft Auto. Hungarian authorities allege that on Saturday, an intoxicated 24-year-old decided to take a Cessna 172 parked at Kalocsa Airport out for a joyride. But when he flew a little too close to Paks Nuclear Power Plant, the country’s sole commercial nuclear facility, defense radars deployed two standby fighter jets to intercept the aircraft. The man touched down in a sunflower field minutes later—only to then try to steal a car to get away. Local authorities managed to detain the man before he made it on the road, though, and officials have since opened criminal proceedings against him.

There’s a fatal flaw to the Trump administration’s recently announced “economic D-Day” against Iran. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that the new U.S. sanctions and pressure campaign was designed to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime” in Iran. But Iran’s single greatest lifeline, China, went unnamed.

China has long been the largest buyer of Iranian oil, with some estimates claiming that about 90 percent of Iran’s oil is shipped there through a network of “shadow fleets.” China also offers access to the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) that facilitates bank transfers outside of the U.S. dollar system, and through which volumes have gone up from 680 billion renminbi (RMB) per day to 790 billion RMB since the Iran war was launched. Thus, if the United States actually wanted to seriously harm Iran economically, it would have to go after China.

There’s a fatal flaw to the Trump administration’s recently announced “economic D-Day” against Iran. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that the new U.S. sanctions and pressure campaign was designed to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime” in Iran. But Iran’s single greatest lifeline, China, went unnamed.

China has long been the largest buyer of Iranian oil, with some estimates claiming that about 90 percent of Iran’s oil is shipped there through a network of “shadow fleets.” China also offers access to the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) that facilitates bank transfers outside of the U.S. dollar system, and through which volumes have gone up from 680 billion renminbi (RMB) per day to 790 billion RMB since the Iran war was launched. Thus, if the United States actually wanted to seriously harm Iran economically, it would have to go after China.

And yet, Beijing is hardly quivering in its boots. When the secretary was asked repeatedly at a press conference if “Operation Economic Outcast” would target Beijing, he demurred, without mentioning China directly: “No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions.” And when pressed on why the Treasury Department is issuing a threat rather than just imposing the sanctions, Bessent simply said, “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”

Judging by the lackluster Chinese response, Beijing doesn’t seem too concerned by the new U.S. steps. China’s foreign ministry spokesperson condemned the announcement as “illegal” but went little further. One Chinese analyst writing on the China Internet Information Center, a State Council news outlet, described Bessent’s announcement as an “act of helplessness” that has more to do with addressing American frustration at home than with pressuring Iran. One private Chinese media outlet also pointed out how vague and slow-moving the new U.S. sanctions are.

Nevertheless, China has already said publicly that it would retaliate if the U.S. goes after its companies, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping knows it has the power to do so. So do at least some people in the Trump administration.

Beijing has recently armed itself with a legal framework for retaliation. In May, China invoked its new policy of “blocking rules” for the first time in response to U.S. sanctions against several of its biggest independent oil refineries. These rules effectively constitute a legal prohibition on any companies inside or outside China complying with the U.S. sanctions on Iran. So far, China has chosen not to enforce this rule, but it continues to signal to the United States that it is ready to do so if needed.

Most importantly, China knows it has an ace in the hole. Beyond its ability to take simple retaliatory measures, Beijing can also escalate its competition with Washington. Among its most powerful tools is a ban on the export of rare earths, which China knows that it can impose again. Freezing exports of rare earths to the U.S. last year brought some sectors of U.S. manufacturing to a standstill, particularly in the defense sector, and forced a rapid climbdown by Trump on Chinese tariffs.

The U.S. has made grand statements about developing alternative supply chains here but has struggled to reduce its overall reliance on China. It is competing with decades of Chinese investments in those refining capabilities, but it also quite willingly offshored many of these refining processes because they are so polluting.

Furthermore, China is clearly willing to call Washington’s bluff. The U.S. has already sanctioned one of China’s largest independent refineries, as well as 40 shipping firms, and this latest package targets 60 smaller intermediaries. But the U.S. hasn’t yet gone after the more significant Chinese banks that support these refineries or tried to dismantle the intricate system whereby China funnels funds to Iran. In Beijing’s view, nothing in the recent U.S. announcement signals a serious desire to escalate the sanctions regime.

That suits China perfectly. Xi needs economic stability to continue reforming China’s economy, which has been struggling since the impact of COVID and the collapse of the property bubble, away from a reliance on exports and toward greater domestic demand. That requires a stable relationship with the U.S. Accordingly, Beijing is also seeking to keep the planned September summit in the U.S. between Trump and Xi on track.

China would only interpret meaningful U.S. sanctions as a pretext for opening new lines of attack in their trade war. No matter how Washington frames it, Beijing sees Iran as a distraction from its fraught bilateral relations with the U.S.—and, ultimately, neither China nor the U.S. appears willing to reignite the trade war or escalate tensions.

It’s going to take more than showing up.

This dynamic may ultimately benefit Iran. If the U.S. is unwilling or unable to bring to bear serious, concerted economic pressure on Iran’s chief economic lifeline, it will have to hope that its continued blockade of Iranian ports and military pressure is enough—despite decades of Iranian resilience to this kind of pressure. The U.S. seems to recognize that squeezing Iran depends on squeezing China. But so long as the Trump administration would rather avoid another trade war and another rare earths embargo, that squeeze will remain at best a half-hearted one.

Henry Tugendhat is a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and research associate at the China-Africa Research Initiative at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies.

Grant Rumley is the Meisel senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, where he directs the Glazer Foundation Program on Great Power Competition and the Middle East.

In August, Turkey’s parliament passed a law that will allow thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to lay down their weapons and thousands more political prisoners and exiles to return to normal life. Over the coming months, hundreds of PKK members are expected to travel to Turkey to take advantage of the new law and reintegrate into a country that they left behind to take up arms against. This was unimaginable only a few years ago, when Turkey and the PKK were locked in a conflict that stretched across Turkey, Iraq, and Syria. Now, for the first time in 30 years of on-and-off negotiations between the PKK and the Turkish state, a legal basis for the end of armed conflict exists.

For decades, a peaceful resolution to the Kurdish conflict was long seen as vital for Turkey’s full democratization. Yet last month’s development was met with widespread criticism from some of the most outspoken supporters of Turkish democracy. Their concern, which has been voiced widely in Turkey, is that the agreement is a cynical ploy by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to win Kurdish support for perpetuating his authoritarian rule. Moreover, many question whether the government will actually follow through and provide real political concessions to the country’s Kurds.

Over the coming months, hundreds of PKK members are expected to travel to Turkey to take advantage of the new law and reintegrate into a country that they left behind to take up arms against. This was unimaginable only a few years ago, when Turkey and the PKK were locked in a conflict that stretched across Turkey, Iraq, and Syria. Now, for the first time in 30 years of on-and-off negotiations between the PKK and the Turkish state, a legal basis for the end of armed conflict exists.

For decades, a peaceful resolution to the Kurdish conflict was long seen as vital for Turkey’s full democratization. Yet last month’s development was met with widespread criticism from some of the most outspoken supporters of Turkish democracy. Their concern, which has been voiced widely in Turkey, is that the agreement is a cynical ploy by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to win Kurdish support for perpetuating his authoritarian rule. Moreover, many question whether the government will actually follow through and provide real political concessions to the country’s Kurds.

When it comes to Erdogan, suspicion is always prudent, and the concerns raised about the peace process are hardly unreasonable. It is true that Erdogan faces constitutional constraints on securing a third term that require him to navigate significant parliamentary hurdles. It is also true that he will seek to extract domestic political benefit from this process, as he does from most political developments.

Yet this is not the full story. The government’s willingness to make peace with the PKK is also driven by important national security concerns. Understanding the agreement on foreign-policy terms is crucial to appreciating why it will likely succeed—and ultimately prove beneficial for Turkey.

The primary drivers of this peace process have always lain beyond Turkey’s borders, in a cascading series of events that began with Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and led through the destruction of Hezbollah, fall of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, and the current war with Iran.

The fall of the Assad regime “is a direct result of the blows we have inflicted on Iran and Hezbollah,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed at the time. He was not wrong, and in Turkey, Devlet Bahceli, the leader of the ultranationalist Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) and Erdogan’s coalition partner, agreed with him: “The fire that began in Gaza spread to Lebanon, extended its shadow over Syria, reached Iraq, and ultimately produced a shock wave that penetrated the heart of Iran.”

In October of 2024, shortly before the rebel assault that brought down Assad, Erdogan spoke at the opening of the Turkish parliament. In his speech, he warned that “Israel’s next target will be Turkey” and called for the “strengthening of the home front.” The very same day, Bahceli shook hands with pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party representatives in parliament—something that he had previously refrained from doing with members of a party that he had called to be banned on multiple occasions. This action alone immediately ignited talks of a new peace process between Turkey and the Kurds.

Amid these geopolitical dynamics, Erdogan’s domestic political concerns played a more complicated role in the process. While he no doubt ultimately hopes to secure Kurdish support for a new term in office, any concessions to the PKK or the Kurdish movement also risk an intense nationalist backlash. Erdogan has consistently appeared uncertain about how the process would be received by Turkish nationalists and whether the Kurdish support he may be banking on will be sufficient to carry him over the line in the next election.

Indeed, it was precisely the same fears that led to the collapse of the last significant peace process between the two sides more than 10 years ago. In this context, Bahceli himself has often taken the lead in publicly promoting the process, working to overcome the delays by pushing for several measures that the government had been slow to implement.

Initially, as Turkey’s regional anxieties overrode Erdogan’s political hesitations, the peace process got off to a hectic start. Numan Kurtulmus, the speaker of the Turkish parliament and a senior figure in Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, framed the urgency of the new peace process through a familiar conspiratorial trope in Turkish nationalist and Islamist traditions: the belief that external powers seek to weaken and ultimately partition Turkey. Warning that “in the so-called ‘Greater Israel’ project, Turkey is seen as the primary force to be absorbed,” he argued that this reality requires Ankara to “fortify its home front.”

Since the outset of the process, fortifying the home front against “global imperialist conspiracies and Zionist ambitions” has emerged as a central organizing concept across the Turkish government’s public messaging. While the Palestinian cause is an ideological issue for Erdogan, the widening instability in the region—and its implications for Kurdish aspirations—is a unifying concern for the entire Turkish political and security establishment.

Aliza Marcus’s “Resurgence and Revolution” sheds light on the past and future of the Kurdish cause.

With Operation Midnight Hammer in 2025, a major fear for Turkey had become reality. Iran—the country with the second-largest Kurdish population after Turkey—was now in the crosshairs, and, after Iraq in 2003 and Syria in 2011, the Kurds once again appeared to be poised to take center stage. In both Syria and Iran, the most capable forces on the ground are PKK-affiliated groups—the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and the Free Life Party of Kurdistan (PJAK), respectively. In an attempt to get ahead of the curve, the Turkish government turned to negotiating with the person whom both organizations see as their leader: Abdullah Ocalan.

Ankara’s main concern was that regional upheaval, especially in Syria and Iran, could strengthen Kurdish autonomy or political leverage in ways that eventually reverberate inside Turkey. A second concern is the prospect of Israel deepening ties with Kurdish actors—again, especially in Syria and Iran.

From Ankara’s perspective, closer Israeli-Kurdish relations would not only empower Kurdish movements in ways that complicate Turkey’s own domestic challenges but would also alter the regional balance of power by enhancing Israel’s reach and capabilities in the emerging Turkey-Israel regional rivalry. While it was widely reported last year that Syrian Kurdish officials had met with Israeli counterparts, such contacts remained far removed from the kind of sustained and institutional engagement that Ankara fears. Ankara regularly hosts Hamas, but we remain far from seeing the PKK in Tel Aviv.

In effect, the presence and operational capabilities of the SDF and PJAK have given Ocalan more leverage in his negotiations with the Turkish government than the PKK ever possessed within Turkey alone. It is no coincidence, then, that the earliest and most visible outcomes of the negotiations have so far materialized in these two arenas. Ocalan reportedly intervened in Syria to help peacefully resolve the fighting between the SDF and the new government in Damascus at the beginning of this year, leading to the SDF’s integration into the new Syrian state.

The Turkey-PKK peace process’s impact on Iran has yet to fully manifest itself, but Turkish columnist Abdulkadir Selvi—widely seen as a conduit for government messaging—recently argued that it prevented the United States from deploying PKK-affiliated groups into Iran during Operation Epic Fury, forcing Washington to instead engage with less-capable Kurdish organizations.

The chain of regional events set in motion on Oct. 7, 2023, coupled with a need to transcend Turkey’s historic vulnerabilities, have both energized and unified Turkey’s ruling elites around a new Kurdish policy. Even the main opposition party has backed the peace process, despite its leading presidential contender, Ekrem Imamoglu, being imprisoned in what is widely viewed as a politically motivated trial.

This exceptionally rare political consensus reflects a deeper, if paradoxical, reality: No other country has grasped the significance of Kurdish agency in the Middle East quite like Turkey has.

In a recent statement, Bahceli characterized the peace process as “not merely a matter of security, but one of strengthening brotherhood, national unity, and solidarity.”

In a country where a significant portion of the population has been willing to take up arms in pursuit of ethnic rights, there is a lot to do for true unity to be achieved. It will ultimately require legal and constitutional reforms that allow Kurds to govern their towns and their local economies without the risk of arbitrary intervention by the government. What’s more, it is unrealistic to expect Kurds to feel secure in their rights unless Turkey’s authoritarian downtrend is reversed and members of other political parties are no longer being systematically jailed.

That said, the PKK’s immediate expectations are more limited and pragmatic than a wholesale democratization of Turkey. At the outset of negotiations, Ocalan made it clear that he had no cultural or ethnic preconditions for ending the armed struggle. At this stage, the process rests on the PKK’s confidence that it can transition from an armed movement into a legitimate political and civil actor without being dismantled or excluded from public life.

The most immediate test for Ankara will be Ocalan’s status. The PKK expects improvements to his working conditions in prison and, crucially, greater access to the outside world so that he can communicate freely with the movement and play an effective role in managing its transition away from armed struggle.

None of this necessarily requires Erdogan to stop repressing political opponents or suddenly embrace liberal democracy, and Ocalan’s willingness to bring the process this far without such commitments suggests that he does not regard broader democratization as a prerequisite for taking the first steps.

But for the process to advance beyond disarmament, the PKK will need evidence that laying down its weapons creates political space rather than simply eliminating the only leverage that it has possessed for half a century. In that sense, the immediate question is less about whether Erdogan is prepared to democratize Turkey than whether he is prepared to accommodate the PKK’s transformation into a legitimate, exclusively civilian actor.

Peace does not guarantee democracy, but it is a prerequisite for it. Pro-democracy critics of the current process should recognize that even while the fate of Turkish democracy will remain dangerously uncertain whatever happens with the Kurds, ending the state’s military conflict with the PKK is an important achievement in its own right. The PKK has now laid down its arms. If Turkey permanently ends its military operations against all Kurdish organizations, including those in Syria, Iraq, and Iran, then the process will have succeeded on geopolitical terms. This will measurably improve the lives of all people in the region and set the stage for the fight for democracy to continue on more favorable terrain.

At a moment when the Middle East appears to be poised for prolonged turbulence, stabilizing the Kurdish question at home may prove to be Turkey’s most consequential strategic investment in its own future.

Giran Ozcan is the fellow for Kurdish affairs at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America.
