Israeli elections are less than two months away, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s prospects are not looking good. Opinion polls show support for his Likud party stagnating or even declining, while the main opposition party is steadily rising. The scare tactics that Netanyahu employed so successfully in the past against his rivals aren’t gaining traction this time. Meanwhile, a clutch of new right-wing parties threatens to divide his bloc and steal votes from Likud.

So, what can Netanyahu do to rescue himself from the very real risk of  being voted out of power?

Israeli elections are less than two months away, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s prospects are not looking good. Opinion polls show support for his Likud party stagnating or even declining, while the main opposition party is steadily rising. The scare tactics that Netanyahu employed so successfully in the past against his rivals aren’t gaining traction this time. Meanwhile, a clutch of new right-wing parties threatens to divide his bloc and steal votes from Likud.

So, what can Netanyahu do to rescue himself from the very real risk of  being voted out of power?

Political analysts and commentators have warned that Netanyahu might disrupt the election by encouraging (if not orchestrating) violence, deploying the police against the opposition, delegitimizing the Central Elections Committee that oversees the vote and, if all else fails, raising Trump-style “stolen election” claims after the polls close. While none of these threats has materialized so far, the campaign gets underway in earnest only on Sept. 7, when the parties submit their final election slates.

However, there is one campaign tactic that Netanyahu may have already set into motion, namely, to create one or more security crises. The aim would be to polish his now-tarnished “Mr. Security” reputation and give more moderate voters who have fled the Likud second thoughts about putting the country into the untested hands of Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu wouldn’t necessarily have to start a full-fledged war. Instead, he could instigate a military confrontation and allow it to escalate—to a point where he could plausibly argue that there was no choice but to go to war.

A preview of this may have occurred Aug. 18, when Israeli fighter jets bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in Syria. Netanyahu and his defense minister, Israel Katz, said the attack was meant to warn Turkey against deepening its military presence in Syria. A Turkish military delegation had indeed visited the base, reportedly  to deploy drones and air defenses there. Israel has legitimate concerns about Turkish aspirations in Syria and elsewhere in the Middle East, but many observers—including Tom Barrack, U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy to Turkey and Syria—expressed doubts about the security claim. “One theory is they were just baiting Turkey, and it’s a very aggressive, but maybe well-received, pre-election concept,” Barrack speculated.

On other fronts, Netanyahu’s ability to stir up trouble is constrained by Trump. Iran, which remains the Israeli public’s biggest source of anxiety, has effectively been put off limits by the U.S. president, who has made it clear that he doesn’t want war to flare up again, at least until after the United States’ midterm elections in November. In Gaza and Lebanon, where Trump has imposed cease-fires, Netanyahu also has limited room to maneuver.

Aggressive behavior on the Syrian-Turkish front poses risks, as well. Washington is backing Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s efforts to stabilize the country and align it with the West, and views Turkey’s military assistance as a helpful component. The United States, which has presided over security talks between Syria and Israel, doesn’t want Israel to undermine Sharaa. Striking Syria and precipitating a crisis or worse with Turkey, therefore, might be too risky in terms of Netanyahu’s already strained relations with Trump.

Still, in recent weeks, the Israeli prime minister has been increasingly calling out Turkey as a threat, as if he is preparing the public for a confrontation. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has responded with inflammatory rhetoric of his own toward Israel. Given Trump’s short attention span and historic tolerance for Israeli cease-fire infractions in Gaza and Lebanon, Netanyahu may get the green light he needs.

The real danger, however, is the West Bank. The violence by extremist settlers that began not long after the 2023 Hamas attacks has grown in recent weeks and become more brazen. Extremists are not only assaulting Palestinians and their property, but the foreign media, pro-Palestinian activists, and even Israeli soldiers if (as rarely happens) they try to intervene. The Israeli army’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has warned that the situation has gotten out of control and is deploying more troops there.

Netanyahu and his cabinet have turned a deaf ear. Worried that they may soon be out of power, the government’s religious far right sees the violence and settlement expansion as a last chance to create facts on the ground—including land grabs and the displacement of Palestinians from their homes. In their best-case scenario, the attacks will precipitate the mini apocalypse that they have been hoping for, whereby Palestinians finally fight back, allowing the army and the settlers to respond with a full-fledged assault that leads to the mass expulsion of the Palestinian population.

Netanyahu doesn’t share the far right’s messianic fantasies, but his refusal to publicly criticize the violence, much less crack down on it, reflects a cynical willingness to exploit the crisis for his own benefit. Faced with a wave of Palestinian counterattacks and memories of Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023, the average Israeli won’t be asking who started it all but who’s best-suited to deal with the problem. Netanyahu is betting that the public will see him as the safer pair of hands.

The Middle East’s newest rivals in the Levant region are Washington’s two key allies there.

A White House endorsement could improve the Israeli leader’s chances of winning.

The Trump administration has been far less critical of Israeli provocations in the West Bank than in other theaters. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has called out the violence, but Trump himself hasn’t (publicly, at least) said anything. Thus, the risk of getting into a public confrontation with the U.S. president seems low, certainly compared to the other options.

If the situation escalates in the West Bank, or if a security crisis elsewhere leads to a resumption of war, then Netanyahu might try to use the emergency to delay elections altogether. It’s an unlikely scenario, but Israeli election law entitles the Knesset to act, albeit only with a supermajority that Netanyahu would struggle to obtain. Nevertheless, his harshest critics don’t dismiss such a maneuver out of hand. Like Trump, Netanyahu has tested democratic norms and would almost certainly have the backing of his coalition partners.

It might seem counterintuitive that after nearly three years of nonstop war, Israeli voters would reward the man who wants to entangle the country in more confrontations. But public opinion is complicated. There is a certain amount of war fatigue, but it is more than counterbalanced by the sense that the wars have not left Israel safer. A July poll by the Institute for National Security Studies found that more Israelis thought Israel’s security situation was bad or very bad (37 percent) than believed it was good or very good (26 percent). Oddly enough, among respondents who support the Netanyahu government, 49 percent thought it was bad or very bad. A large part of the Israeli public regards the wars as unfinished business.

Yet it is far from obvious that Netanyahu would benefit from stoking the flames of war. Polls show that most Israelis believe Netanyahu is making his military decisions based at least in part on electoral calculations. He and his cabinet generally enjoy less public trust than the army and the rest of the defense establishment, even among  coalition voters. Yet, Netanyahu has a history of employing devious tactics to stay in power that other politicians would hesitate to use, and this election is shaping up to be no different. For Netanyahu, losing really isn’t an option. It would almost certainly end his political career, destroy his legacy by opening the way for a full and impartial government investigation into the Hamas attacks, and make it harder to further delay his criminal trial or reach a plea deal to end it on favorable terms. With that in mind, Netanyahu may just go for broke.

David E. Rosenberg is the economics editor and a columnist for the English edition of Haaretz and the author of Israel’s Technology Economy.

For most of his presidency and especially since Russia launched its full-scale war, Ukrainian voters have rallied around Volodymyr Zelensky as a pillar of national resilience and unity. That’s for good reason: He has been an effective wartime leader and helped mobilize the democratic world on Ukraine’s behalf.

But now, after more than seven years in office, four and a half years of war with Russia, and a series of scandals involving his leadership team and close friends, Zelensky appears to have lost the nation’s political support. Indeed, polling published in early August points to a major mood swing among Ukrainians, suggesting that many of them have lost faith in Zelensky and would vote him out of office at the earliest opportunity.

For most of his presidency and especially since Russia launched its full-scale war, Ukrainian voters have rallied around Volodymyr Zelensky as a pillar of national resilience and unity. That’s for good reason: He has been an effective wartime leader and helped mobilize the democratic world on Ukraine’s behalf.

But now, after more than seven years in office, four and a half years of war with Russia, and a series of scandals involving his leadership team and close friends, Zelensky appears to have lost the nation’s political support. Indeed, polling published in early August points to a major mood swing among Ukrainians, suggesting that many of them have lost faith in Zelensky and would vote him out of office at the earliest opportunity.

This swing in sentiment is likely to gain further momentum amid a new scandal involving the president’s key staff. Regrettably, Zelensky has spoken little of the alleged misdeeds of those in his inner circle. He highlights that he is not the subject of any investigations by anti-corruption agencies—a deceptive claim, since the Ukrainian Constitution bars such institutions from investigating or bringing criminal charges against a sitting president.

This lack of moral compass is all the more shocking given the extravagant promises that Zelensky made during his electoral campaign in 2019, when he guaranteed prosecutions and convictions of corrupt officials within months of taking office. Yet more than a dozen members of his party’s legislature, numerous government ministers, and members of his presidential office have been implicated or charged with corruption and illegal enrichment.

Recent polling from Ukrainian political research company SOCIS shows that Ukrainians now regard corruption as a greater problem than the war itself, in part because they link Ukraine’s fate on the battlefield to corruption at the highest levels of the state. Fully 90 percent of Ukrainians believe that corruption stands at a high or extremely high level. Most significantly and most emblematic of the shift, nearly 57 percent of Ukrainians blame Zelensky for the prevalence of corruption, nearly double the number in a similar poll by SOCIS in April 2025. The SOCIS polling also projects that three different rivals would beat him in a second-round election, each by a landslide margin of around 2-to-1.

Zelensky’s loss of support is largely a self-inflicted wound, the product of a philosophy of governance based on rule through a small group of functionaries prized for their personal loyalty. For years, Zelensky has touted and defended this highly centralized system of governance, in which nearly all decision-making emanates from the presidential office. In December 2023, he famously declared that he relies on a team of five to six key managers to run the country’s affairs. Such centralization, while in violation of the constitution, was long accepted by the public as necessary amid the wartime emergency.

In the past year, however, numerous scandals inside the heart of Zelensky’s office have shaken public confidence, and his system of rule through close confidants and managers is a shambles. Four of Zelensky’s top managers are implicated in allegations of illicit activities.

Andriy Smyrnov, a former deputy head of the presidential office, was indicted and brought before the High Anti-Corruption Court on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering. In January, Rostyslav Shurma, a former deputy head for economic issues in the presidential office, was served with a notice of suspicion of involvement in a multimillion-dollar scheme involving state “green tariffs” earned by his brother’s solar power facilities; he now lives in Germany and has not returned to Ukraine.

Oleh Tatarov—a deputy head of the presidential office and perhaps Zelensky’s most influential current aide—likely benefited from the transfer of a bribery case against him from the independent National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) to the prosecutor general’s office, which is firmly in the hands of Zelensky loyalists.

And of course, there is the notorious case of Andriy Yermak, Zelensky’s former chief of staff, who was charged by NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) in May with money laundering. He is accused of being part of a group laundering illicit cash and using some of it to build luxury housing. He is currently free on bail.

On Aug. 19, Iryna Mudra was dismissed as deputy head of the presidential office amid an investigation by NABU’s “Operation Forrest Gump” into an alleged $3.3 million money-laundering operation conducted through a state-owned bank to meet the bail requirements of a former government minister.

Mykhailo Fedorov hopes anti-corruption rhetoric can carry him to power.

Their husbands died defending the country—and now their families are struggling for compensation.

From refugees to abducted children, Russia has wreaked havoc on young Ukrainians.

Mudra’s activities have deeper implications, as they appear to go further up the chain of command. The prosecution has presented evidence of phone conversations in which she says that she worked at the instruction of her “chief” to facilitate the illicit effort to raise bail. Many Ukrainian journalists believe that the chief she refers to is likely the head of the presidential office, Kyrylo Budanov, who is widely believed to have launched the effort to raise the bail funds at Zelensky’s behest.

In addition, a major corruption scandal involves Timur Mindich, a key business partner in Zelensky’s film and TV production company and a business partner of Serhiy Shefir, whom Zelensky entrusted with handling some of his assets after he became president. Recorded conversations and indictments by Ukraine’s anti-corruption agency suggest that Mindich was part of a criminal group that allegedly included a former justice and energy minister, a former deputy prime minister, and Zelensky’s chief of staff. That group is said to have engaged in extortion, benefited from government favoritism, and profited from state institution revenues. The wiretaps also suggest that Rustem Umerov, the man the president just named to run Ukraine’s foreign intelligence, may have worked to advance Mindich’s private business interests.

As the Mindich scandal was emerging, Zelensky’s administration appears to have used the country’s prosecutor general and the Ukrainian Security Service to open more than a dozen investigations of NABU agents and arrest several on charges of treason and trading with the enemy. Some of these charges came against Viktor Husarov, a detective, and Ruslan Mahamedrasulov, a top anti-corruption official, both of whom were investigating Zelensky’s circle of friends, appointees, and aides. These attacks, seen by some as designed to discredit anti-corruption agencies, were coupled with legislative initiatives launched by Zelensky’s office and party to end NABU’s and SAPO’s independence.

After a week of mass protests and pressure from Western donors, Zelensky relented. Eventually, charges of treason were dropped against Husarov, and Mahamedrasulov was released from arrest. His case is believed by most anti-corruption activists to be without foundation.

Zelensky’s descent into public disfavor has also been influenced by his erratic personnel policies. The first significant blow to Zelensky’s popularity came in February 2024 with the dismissal of Gen. Valery Zaluzhny, the popular and successful commander in chief of Ukraine’s armed forces. This was followed by the firing of Dmytro Kuleba, his effective foreign minister, and most recently, in mid-July, the dismissal—after six months on the job—of Defense Minister Mykhaylo Fedorov, who had helped spur Ukraine’s digitalization and shift to artificial intelligence- and drone-centered combat. Each of the dismissed officials enjoyed high levels of public trust and popularity in Ukraine.

The frequent firings of key officials have also eroded support for Zelensky. Under his presidency, there have been eight ministers of defense and seven economic ministers. Prime ministers have fared a bit better; there have been five in all, of which three were quiet and subservient to Zelensky and his top managers.

In the past, Zelensky recovered after dips in support—for example, after Zaluzhny’s dismissal and after the tense public White House showdown at the hands of U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance. But since last summer, public unhappiness with the charges of corruption in the Zelensky inner circle and the recent firing of Fedorov has solidified the public’s turn away from Zelensky.

To be sure, Ukrainian voters understand that conducting an election would be difficult amid a hot war, with its endless Russian attacks on cities and civilian targets. There are strong reasons why the Ukrainian Constitution delays all elections during time of war. But almost two-thirds of Ukrainians surveyed in the SOCIS poll now say that elections should come quickly in the event of a negotiated cease-fire or peace.

And while Zelensky maintains a strong core of loyalists, representing more than 20 percent of voters, few voters backing other candidates say they would support Zelensky if their candidate did not make it into a second round of voting. Thus, it isn’t surprising that the SOCIS polling indicates that in a second round, Zelensky would currently lose to Zaluzhny with 34 percent to the former commander in chief’s 66 percent, Fedorov with 36 percent to 64 percent, and Budanov with 38 percent to 62 percent.

Until a future election takes place, what are the implications of Zelensky’s diminishing popularity now?

While the SOCIS polling shows that 55 percent of Ukrainians believe Zelensky is governing ineffectively, the public shows strong unity and understands that it must continue to support Zelensky as the nation’s wartime commander in chief, even as they reject his domestic policies and style of rule.

Moreover, not everything in Ukraine’s war effort is dependent on Zelensky and the state. Ukrainians’ resilience and innovative capacity have been major factors in the turnaround on the battlefield. Civil society answered the initial call to mobilize and added vigor to the country’s resistance. And it was a small group of mainly women activists from nongovernmental organizations who initially trained thousands of combatants in drone operations, thereby creating a market for military drones that was initially supported through crowdfunding and only later by the state.

At the same time, Zelensky’s high levels of public disapproval carry risks. Disaffection with his leadership can affect morale on the battlefield. Moreover, Ukraine already faces serious problems with draft evasion. Growing public cynicism about the country’s rulers could exacerbate this problem. Just as importantly, attacks on civilian targets are on the rise. This winter will challenge Ukrainian morale when, given the scarcity of anti-missile interceptors, Russia is expected to seriously degrade Ukraine’s electricity and heating. Long blackouts and mounting destruction of civilian infrastructure will require civic courage and a leadership team that can—as in the past—inspire the people to hold on. It is unclear how much longer Zelensky can play that role and how effectively.

There are two ways of resolving this problem. The first—a wartime election—has little support among Ukrainians, remains logistically complex, and is currently illegal. The second is to reboot the system of governance by reducing presidential involvement in running the domestic government agenda, creating a government of national unity, and opening the door to a pool of effective and untainted officials from rival parties and the vast pool of effective officials whom Zelensky has dismissed because he saw them as potential competitors.

Unfortunately, nothing suggests that Zelensky can take such a step. He has always had absolute confidence in his decision-making and surrounded himself with a team of loyalists who rarely challenge his judgments. The time for centralized rule through a small group of cronies has long passed, and Western leaders and his own people should press him at every opportunity to take steps to ensure national unity and effective governance. With his own political future in tatters, it is time for him to try something new. A Ukraine at war requires no less.

Adrian Karatnycky is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, the founder of Myrmidon Group, and the author of Battleground Ukraine: From Independence to the War with Russia.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/iran/why-.author: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj

ESFANDYAR BATMANGHELIDJ is Founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation and an Adjunct Professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

The Sources of Tehran’s Economic Resilience

Esfandyar Batmanghelidj

For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.”

The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line.

Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela.

Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar.

But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself.

Iranian officials have acknowledged the country’s economic difficulties. “No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament and a key power broker, on August 21. (Bessent cited this quote as evidence that U.S. economic warfare was having its intended effect.) During a television interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian expressed frustration that some of his fellow political leaders continue to deny that sanctions are harming the country. “Some say sanctions have no effect at all; I really don’t know what to say to those people,” he remarked.

The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian reflect genuine concern about Iran’s economic trajectory. The speaker and the president are understandably worried about deteriorating public opinion, given the inherent connections between general economic welfare and political legitimacy. But U.S. officials should be wary of overinterpreting these statements. Contrary to what it might seem, neither leader is suggesting that the country’s economy is on the brink of collapse.

American assessments of the Iranian economy and the success of economic coercion fail to account for the ways in which sanctions have transformed Iran’s political economy, altering the distribution of economic resources in ways that reinforce its existing power structure. The Iranian leaders who are most vocal about the suffering of ordinary people are not worried about the country’s imminent economic collapse; they are dissenting against a political consensus that has long enabled Iranian elites to deliberately push the pressure of sanctions onto ordinary people. Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended.

Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments of the Iranian economy miss important dynamics. Typically, the effects of sanctions are described in terms of macroeconomic indicators, including rates of growth, inflation, and currency depreciation. But these measures mainly capture price levels: the value of goods and services. They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy. To take a functional view, one must look at the dynamics at the firm and household level; they reveal why deteriorating figures in the headlines have not led to Iran’s capitulation.

The fundamental dilemma for policymakers in any comprehensively sanctioned country is how to respond to balance-of-payments vulnerabilities, such as when a country runs out of the foreign currency it needs to pay for imports. There are, broadly speaking, two approaches. Policymakers can use expansionary monetary policy to fuel investment, restoring the trade surplus through a combination of higher exports and increased domestic production. Alternatively, policymakers can use monetary tightening and austerity measures to suppress import demand, restoring the trade surplus at similar export levels.

When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, Russian policymakers took the first approach. They increased fiscal stimulus, driving a rapid expansion in industrial activity and manufacturing employment that created a distinct war economy. This spending was necessary to increase military production, but it also had the effect of dramatically tightening the labor market, raising real wages for ordinary Russians. That, in turn, blunted the initial effects of sanctions-related inflation. This approach eventually reached its limits, and inflation is starting to bite, but the economic strategy allowed Russia to persist in its war aims despite U.S. sanctions pressure.

Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course of action. When major financial and energy sanctions imposed by the Obama administration first pushed Iran into a recession in 2012, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called for Iran to adopt a “resistance economy,” focusing on domestic capacities to counteract the sanctions pressure. But Iranian economic policymakers never managed to implement a new industrial policy or set up a new welfare system. Instead, they tolerated inflation, effectively pushing the pain of the sanctions away from the government and onto households and firms. They ran austerity budgets and refused to rationalize production or consumption through direct administration, such as by instituting quotas or price controls. The worsening economic crisis led to weakness in the labor market, allowing employers to engage in wage repression and leading to further pressure on household incomes.

At first, this may seem like a policy failure. But in reality, Iranian authorities appear perfectly content to see economic activity slow. Doing so, they believe, will give them staying power in their confrontation with the United States.

Microeconomic data reveal the effects of U.S. pressure on economic activity at the firm and household level. A review of Purchasing Managers’ Index data compiled by Iran’s Chamber of Commerce makes clear how the country’s economic crisis has intensified. Between 2019 and 2023, Iran’s overall economy was in contraction for two-thirds of the period thanks to Trump’s initial maximum pressure sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and disruptions related to the “Women, Life, Freedom” protests. But throughout this period, Iranian non-oil industries experienced modest growth. At the start of 2023, Iran even began to exit its long recession as the overall economy and the industrial sector grew in tandem. By March 2024, living standards were beginning to rise again, buoyed by a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes.

This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes on Iran. Since then, the economic uncertainty associated with recurring military conflict has triggered a prolonged decline in industrial activity, pushing Iran into an even deeper recession. Industrial firms have reported deteriorating conditions for eight consecutive months. But that does not mean these firms are insolvent. Over the last two decades, Iranian companies have developed a practice of maintaining large inventories. This practice allows firms to mitigate the effects of sanctions on supply chains and helps shore balance sheets in a high-inflation environment in which cash loses its value but goods do not. According to filings made by companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, the average “days inventory outstanding” level among Iranian industries is around three months. In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days.

These large inventories have been a source of significant economic resilience during the war. Iranian supply chains came under strain as ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled. A shift toward overland trade could not compensate for the loss of container traffic through Iran’s southern ports. But with an ample inventory of raw materials, semifinished goods, and finished products, Iranian producers could keep customers supplied—or at least customers with the means to pay.

Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins, passing higher input costs onto consumers. And as the war continued, these higher prices led to demand destruction. Iranian households, embattled by years of persistent inflation, began to consume less. When they did buy, they increasingly relied on consumer credit, including new buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans. Even in special categories such as food, Iranian retailers reported diminished sales volume.

The sharp drop in household consumption is clear evidence that economic welfare in Iran is declining. It is why Iranian officials have been forced to acknowledge the pain felt by ordinary people. But even so, the government has thus far failed to intervene to control rising prices. Not only have officials failed to introduce price controls—a move that successfully blunted the economic pain associated with the Iran-Iraq War 40 years ago—they have also discussed the elimination of cash transfers and energy subsidies for large portions of the population. In this respect, demand destruction has acted as a form of rationing, providing a structured way for Iranian political and economic elites to push the costs of the war and sanctions onto ordinary people. Although the government continues to face significant fiscal pressure, it has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent, Iran is still a long way from the kind of hyperinflation—typified by monthly inflation of over 50 percent—that will make the government’s strategy untenable.

Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers for the real economy. In financial terms, the Iranian economy is in a worse position than at the outset of the war, but in functional terms, inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025, and supply and demand may find a new balance at a lower level of overall economic activity. Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade remains its persistent need for imports, which totaled $17 billion in the first five months of this Iranian calendar year beginning in March. That means imports will likely total around $40 billion by the end of the year, down significantly from $58 billion in the previous year and $72 billion in the year before that. The fall in import demand, driven by inflation and currency devaluation, is evidence of a deeper economic crisis. But in the near term, it will help Iranian policymakers forestall a wider economic collapse, possibly for several years.

When Bessent evoked the imagery of an “economic D-Day” in his August press conference, he failed to consider who is standing on the other side of his planned invasion. Although it may not seem like it, the success of Iranian authorities in transferring the costs of both sanctions and the war onto ordinary people represents a form of wartime mobilization. Ordinary Iranians may not wish to be mobilized in this way, but they do not have a choice.

In a recent social media post, Trump asked, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” But even if ordinary Iranians were to take to the streets again to protest the financial repression they are enduring, they would once again face the brutal violence of the Islamic Republic. With multiple repressive tools at their disposal, many Iranian leaders believe that the country’s population can be made to tolerate more pain, especially if it is necessary to defeat the United States militarily. To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms. But as breathing slows in parts of Iran’s economy, ample oxygen will remain for the country’s elite.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.author: Daniel Byman
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.text:
DANIEL BYMAN is a Professor in the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown University and Director of the Warfare, Irregular Threats, and Terrorism Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

How America Contained—but Didn’t End—the Terrorist Threat

Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth.

The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it.

But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience.

Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power.

* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost.

In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate.

The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend.

Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes.

Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world.

Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead.

Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise.

After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives.

Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq.

The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations.

Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world.

No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks.

Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens.

The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing.

It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims.

Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups.

Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders.

The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries.

By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment.

Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021.

Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars.

The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers.

This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance. Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak and security assistance fails to move the needle significantly—or if, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, Washington cuts its aid entirely—jihadi groups will remain active.

The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish. For now, U.S. and allied counterterrorism campaigns and jihadis’ poor track record are keeping these groups relatively contained. But it will take continued, constant effort—intelligence cooperation with allies, drone strikes on jihadi operatives, and military training for local partners—to ensure that they cannot start rebuilding in weak states. All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States. If Washington can maintain vigilance without overextending itself, it can keep jihadism a manageable danger rather than letting it once again become a defining threat.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/ho.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/ho.author: Holmes Liao, Dennis Blair
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/ho.text:
HOLMES LIAO is Senior Adviser at the Taiwan Space Agency and a former Honorary Chair at the War College of Taiwan’s National Defense University.

DENNIS BLAIR was Commander in Chief of U.S. Pacific Command from 1999 to 2002 and Director of National Intelligence from 2009 to 2010.

A Nimbler Navy Can Deny China

Holmes Liao and Dennis Blair

Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships.

Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet.

The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually.

Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault.

Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues.

Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war.

In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations.

Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes.

Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz.

As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force.

Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks.

A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion.

These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion.

A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective.

The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices.

But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them.

After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.author: Anna Nelson, Cary Fowler
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.text:
ANNA NELSON is Executive Director of the Food Security Leadership Council. A career civil servant at the Departments of State and Defense under three administrations, she served as Deputy Special Envoy for Global Food Security from 2024 to 2025.

CARY FOWLER is President of the Food Security Leadership Council. He served as U.S. Special Envoy for Global Food Security from 2022 to 2025, and he is a 2024 World Food Prize laureate.

What Washington Can Do to Stop Starvation

Anna Nelson and Cary Fowler

In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern.

Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included.

In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge.

It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states.
