* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated.

Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public.

The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations.

Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters.

Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself.

Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior.

Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks.

Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones.

The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges.

The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them.

The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners.

But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one.

Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards.

At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership.

That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests.

Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it.

America Can Win If It Stays the Course

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/china/how.author: Adam Y. Liu

The Trouble With Overestimating Beijing’s Soft Power

Andrei Soldatov and Irina Borogan

As Russia’s war in Ukraine becomes increasingly costly with no end in sight, the Kremlin has kept tightening its grip over Russian society. Along with expanding repression, including of some officials and civil servants, and the silencing of negative reporting about the war and the economy, this suffocation has included, in recent months, frequent Internet shutdowns and draconian new restrictions on social media. For Russians themselves, these measures are a stark contrast to the moderate freedoms they were allowed before 2022, when the war began.

Less apparent, though, is the dramatic shift in domestic security doctrine that undergirds these efforts.

https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.text:
The 26-year-old who has since joined Paris Saint-Germain is one of six Spanish World Cup winners on the list, alongside 2024 laureate Rodri and last year's runner-up Lamine Yamal.

In the women's section, three-time winner Aitana Bonmati did not make the shortlist after breaking her leg midway through the season, but her former Barcelona team-mate Alexia Putellas, the winner in 2021 and 2022 and now a London City Lionesses player, is there.

Torres also won La Liga with Barcelona in May but is now teaming up with last year's Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele at PSG.

France international Dembele is one of nine PSG team-mates on the list to have won the Champions League in each of the last two years.

With Torres having joined the club, that makes it 10 current PSG players in total on the list.

Among them, Fabian Ruiz is the only player to have won the Champions League and World Cup in 2026.

Flying Georgian winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was one of the stars of PSG's successful Champions League defence, alongside Portuguese midfield pair Vitinha and Joao Neves, and all three are nominated.

Eight-time Ballon d'Or winner Lionel Messi received his 17th nomination, but his eternal rival Cristiano Ronaldo did not make the cut this time.

Messi helped inspire an ill-disciplined Argentina to the World Cup final, where they took almost 120 minutes to muster their first shot against Spain in a one-sided final.

England captain Harry Kane, who won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich, is included as is his French team-mate and wing wizard Michael Olise.

Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham earned his nomination with an impressive World Cup for England, scoring seven goals -- matching Erling Haaland's tally and beaten only by Messi (eight) and Kylian Mbappe, on 10.

Mbappe is there, after becoming the first player to win the World Cup golden boot a second time, while also scorching to the top of the tournament's all-time record scorer list.

Yamal is also nominated in for the Young Talent award, which he has won the last two years.

Vozinha, the 40-year-old who was one of the heroes of Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has made the goalkeeper list.

Barcelona will also have a handful of contenders for the women's award.

Putellas is one of seven players who won the women's Champions League with the club in May to be on the list, including Poland's Ewa Pajor, who scored a brace in the 4-0 final victory over Lyon.

Three of the men's nominees play outside Europe. Messi is a MLS franchise Inter Miami and Sadio Mane and Julian Quinones play in Saudi Arabia.

The women's award spreads its net a little wider. Zambian Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride in South Africa, Mexican Scarlett Camberos who plays in her native country and Malawian Temwa Chawinga amd American Rose Lavelle, who play in the NWSL, on the list.

The winners will be announced in a ceremony at the London Palladium Theatre on October 26.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Middle East live: Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions on settlements
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israeli opposition leaders on Tuesday called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unfit to serve after a bombshell report that the United Arab Emirates had warned him before the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

Haaretz newspaper, in a report excerpted from a forthcoming book by its reporters, said UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack and told him that Hamas was planning a major operation.

Netanyahu's office denied the report by the left-leaning newspaper, saying in a statement late Tuesday: "No warning was given to the Prime Minister from the United Arab Emirates before October 7th."

Britain's chief rabbi, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described the plans for sanctions as "a dark day for British Jews" and accused the UK government of "gesture politics".

"These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to ​target," Mirvis wrote on X.

French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that Israeli settlements in the occupeid West Bank undermined prospects for a two-state solution.

"Systematic settlement expansion in the West Bank, including the Government of Israel's latest decision to progress the E1 settlement, as well as the dramatic increase in settler violence, pose a direct and urgent threat to that vision for peace," the leaders said in a joint statement.

The main produce from West Bank settlements is agricultural, including dates, citrus fruits, herbs and wine, and makes up only a tiny fraction of Israel's ​total exports.

Given the small volume of exports from the settlements, the trade bans are largely symbolic, and will not dent larger bilateral trade flows, but are part of wider efforts to reinforce support for the ​two-state solution.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the sanctions could be destabilizing for the West Bank, adding that Washington would not follow Britain, France and Canada in blocking imports from Israeli settlements.

Former British Prime Minister Jeremy Corbyn said the sanctions on illegal settlements did not go far enough. He demanded Britain end arms sales, military cooperation, and what he called "all forms of support that sustain Israel’s system of apartheid, occupation and genocide".

The ban will take in imports of all goods from the settlements and bar companies from providing services for the settlements, including financing, construction, infrastructure, real estate and advertising, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

“I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," Miliband said.

The economic impact is likely to be limited, since the settlements produce only a small amount of largely agricultural exports. But the move is a symbolic expression of displeasure with Israel by some of its closest allies, and it offers a new sign of the Israeli government's growing isolation as a result of the Gaza war.

The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway have either banned goods from settlements or are in the process of doing so, Miliband said on Tuesday, while Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden have pledged to “support further action”.

British foreign minister Ed Miliband accused the Israeli government on Tuesday of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank. Miliband told parliament the UK government would introduce "an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories", in a move coordinated with other countries. Jordana Miller, ABC correspondent in Jerusalem, told FRANCE 24 that the ban was evidence of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's failure to rein in the far-right elements of his government that has facilitated the growth of settlements.

The Israeli foreign ministry issued a list of 12 British nationals who will be refused entry if they seek to visit. They include Jeremy Corbyn, the former Labour Party leader and outspoken Palestinian advocate, as well as Zarah Sultana, who joined Corbyn in breaking away from Labour to form the left-wing Your Party.

Also on the ban list is Diane Abbott, a Labour MP who came under fire for remarks downplaying the extent of antisemitism and was admitted back into the party under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

"Successive Canadian governments have held the position that a two-state solution is the way forward for long-term peace that also addresses Israel's legitimate security concerns. Illegal settlements in the West Bank significantly undermine these objectives," Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand wrote on X.

France, also introducing a ban on West Bank products, cited the "frenzied expansion" of settlements there and a "flare up of violence" as the reasons for it taking action.

Britain, ‌France and Canada were joined by the foreign ministers of 10 other countries, including Denmark, Norway, Poland, Spain and Sweden, in a statement reaffirming support for a negotiated two-state settlement.

"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," they said.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Britain ⁠would no longer be able to allowed to participate in the U.S.-led ​coordination mission for Gaza in Israel, ‌that British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank would be ‌terminated, and that some elected UK officials and other ​nationals would be banned from entering Israel.

"The British move is morally distorted, and constitutes blatant ​interference in the affairs of ​a sovereign state and ​its electoral process," he said, labelling what he described ​as accusations made by Foreign Minister Ed Miliband earlier as "outrageous lies".

Israel said on Tuesday it ​was closing ‌Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem in response to plans by the UK, France ⁠and Canada to block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

British foreign minister Ed Miliband accused the Israeli government on Tuesday of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank.

Miliband told parliament the UK government would introduce "an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories", in a move coordinated with other countries.

Welcome to our live coverage of events in the Middle East.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

France will launch a process to ban products from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël ​Barrot said on Tuesday, amid rising settler violence that has further undermined prospects for a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

"France is going to put an end to its commerce with Israeli settlements in Palestine, along with 11 other ​countries which have ‌also undertaken similar engagements," Barrot wrote on X.

"Why are we doing this? Because ⁠the West Bank is close to exploding – there is frenzied expansion of the settlements, a flare up of violence against Palestinians by extremist settlers, and acts ‌of terror which have been attacked by Israeli authorities themselves," added Barrot.

The move comes as ⁠frustration has grown among some European Union states, which have sought for the bloc to take a decision, but failed to gain a qualified majority with the notable opposition from Germany.

​France announced a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied ‌West Bank in coordination with the UK and Canada on Tuesday.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the UK parliament that the "British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists". He said there had been “houses bulldozed, roads and public infrastructure destroyed, families displaced from their homes”.

Miliband said that he feels “a deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community”.

Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden have pledged to “support further action”.

The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway have either banned goods from settlements or are in the process of doing so.

"Given the situation on the ground we can't wait, so we are taking this national decision," a French diplomatic source told reporters in a briefing ahead of the announcement. The modalities of the ban ‌have yet to be finalised and it was not immediately clear when it would be implemented.

More than 100 former French and UK diplomats urge action against Israeli settlement policies

"This announcement is part of the joint initiative between the ​President of the Republic and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, which was discussed in particular during their meeting in London and to which several of our partners in the European Union and beyond have signed ​up," the source said, adding as many as a dozen countries would follow suit.

The source said it ​was not a boycott of Israel.

Britain's decision was met by some ​angry reaction in Israel, with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich calling for the UK ambassador to be expelled.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said that the ban would be “a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history", while Foreign Minister Gideon Saar warned that “if Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain”.

France's ties with Israel have been strained for several months and took a ​turn for the worse last September after France led efforts at the United Nations to recognise a Palestinian state.

The source said the acceleration of settlements was undermining the prospect of a viable Palestinian state and the decision by the Israeli government to publish tenders for the E1 project was deemed a red line not only for Europe ⁠but also for the vast majority of the international community.

"We have also seen an intensification of violence committed by settlers, which is unacceptable ⁠and, moreover, poses ​an increasingly serious risk of destabilising the West Bank and the region. We regret that no sufficient measures have been taken to put an end to this situation," the source said.

Under Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction in the West Bank — seized by Israel in the 1967 Mideast war — has surged. The international community overwhelmingly considers such construction to be illegal and an obstacle to peace.

Netanyahu’s government views the West Bank as the biblical and historical homeland of the Jewish people and is opposed to the creation of a Palestinian state.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/u.title: Five killed as Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv after pause for US envoys' visit
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Russia is using ballistic missiles as Ukraine continues to experience a shortage of interceptors. (Reuters)

Russia has resumed strikes on Kyiv, after a brief pause in strikes on Ukraine's capital to allow US envoys to visit.

Five people were killed and close to 30 were injured in the latest strikes.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin held a phone call where they discussed allegations Russia was launching sabotage attacks in Europe.

Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks on the Ukrainian capital after a brief halt for the visit of US peace negotiators, and killing five people.

Russia's main targets in its attacks on Monday night and Tuesday morning were Kyiv and the Odesa region of southern Ukraine.

The overnight attack caused fires in several districts across the Ukrainian capital, damaging at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.

Two people were killed in a strike on a warehouse, bringing the total death toll in the city to five, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Close to 30 people have been injured, authorities said. Officials from Russia reported three people killed and 13 wounded in areas it controls.

Explosions reverberated across the city as Russia kept menacing it with jet-powered drones into Tuesday afternoon.

"Kyiv was exploding and burning," Katarina Mathernova, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, said in a social media post.

Explosions were heard in Kyiv for nearly five hours, according to Ukraine's Minister of Internal Affairs of Ukraine Ivan Vyhivskyi.

More than 50 sites were damaged during the overnight attack, including residential buildings, dormitories, schools, shops, gas stations and a flour production plant, he said.

In a separate strike, a Russian drone partially destroyed a Ukrainian TV channel building in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called it "a horrific attack" and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of undermining US peace efforts.

"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Mr Sybiha said on X, referring to Mr Putin.

Kyiv has been battered in recent months by near-nightly drone and missile attacks. (Reuters: Yan Dobronosov)

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight launched a massive strike on Ukrainian military industry facilities.

It provided a detailed list of its targets, including places storing Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles, as well as transport, logistics and distribution centres for military cargo in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, the ministry said.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv for separate talks with Mr Putin and Mr Zelenskyy over the weekend.

It signalled the Trump administration's renewed push to end Russia's four-and-a-half year war in Ukraine.

The meetings appeared to produce no substantial breakthrough but the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of three-way negotiations also including the United States.

Both Moscow and Kyiv halted strikes on their capitals for three days to ensure the security of the US peace negotiators after which both then resumed their deadly air war.

In a call held between the two leaders on Tuesday, Mr Putin assured US President Donald Trump Russia did not harbour aggressive intentions towards Europe, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating sabotage attacks on its soil.

Yuri Ushakov, Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser, said the hour-long conversation between Mr Putin and Mr Trump was "constructive and quite frank".

Vladimir Putin shows no signs of backing down from his demands for concessions from Ukraine. (Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova)

There was no immediate White House comment on the call.

Mr Ushakov told reporters that "in view of the speculation about Russia's alleged hostile intentions toward European countries, it was underlined that we don't have any aggressive plans regarding Europe."

Mr Ushakov also said Mr Putin told Mr Trump about the combat situation in Ukraine and Russia's plans to make battlefield gains and achieve its military goals.

He said that Moscow has a positive view of the results of the weekend visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner.

"An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation's goals and tasks was given," Mr Ushakov said.

Meanwhile, Mr Zelenskyy said he is counting on meeting with Mr Trump around September 20, about the same time that the UN General Assembly is being held in New York.

He indicated he will press Mr Trump to provide more Patriot air defence systems that Kyiv needs to counter Russia's ballistic missiles.

Ukraine needs 300 Patriot missiles from its partners' stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors and $US2 billion ($2.7 billion) for more drones, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the meeting of countries providing help.

Also on Tuesday, the European Commission approved a loan of 3.2 billion euros ($5.1 billion) for Kyiv to purchase components for Patriot air defence systems, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on its Telegram channel.

Mr Zelenskyy thanked US officials for their efforts to unblock negotiations with Russia, which have been stuck since early this year with little progress.

"As for the peace package that Kushner spoke about and the new ideas, I'll tell you frankly, there were indeed a couple of very good, worthwhile ideas," Mr Zelenskyy said in audio messages answering reporters' questions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.title: New documents reveal what NYC knew about air toxicity after 9/11
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
September 11 Attacks

New York's World Trade Center was destroyed in the attacks on September 11, 2001. (Reuters: /US Navy Photo by Photographer's Mate 2nd Class Jim Watson)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has released thousands of documents detailing what was known about toxic smoke from the September 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center (WTC).

This Friday will mark 25 years since Al Qaeda terrorists flew hijacked planes into the Twin Towers, the Pentagon and into a field in Pennsylvania.

Mr Mamdani says the documents show NYC administrations did not release all they knew about the toxic effects of smoke from the WTC collapse.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has released more than 170,000 pages of documents showing that the city did not disclose all it knew about air toxicity after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

The release comes ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that killed 2,977 people, in the United States, mostly from the collapse of the Twin Towers in New York.

More than 9,400 have died from illnesses linked to their exposure to the area in the years since, according to a federal medical monitoring program.

"These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability," the mayor told a news conference.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani held a large event with advocates and politicians to announce the release. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

Mr Mamdani said the thousands of documents contain information on health concerns, air quality and the city's response to the attacks.

The release is part of an agreement with 9/11 Health Watch, a victims' advocacy group that had taken legal action to compel the city to make the documents public.

"For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as City officials continued messaging to the public that the air was 'safe and acceptable'," the group's director Benjamin Chevat said in a statement.

When asked about the names of officials who had withheld information from the public, Mr Mamdani said, "this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted."

Rudy Guliani was mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks.

In recent days, politicians including Mr Guliani and some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mr Mamdani, NYC's first Muslim mayor, to skip this year's memorial. Other families have defended the mayor who says he will attend despite the criticism.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/y.title: Dozens injured as Yemen's Houthis launch strikes on Saudi oil facilities
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

The Houthis claim they targeted trucks coming from Saudi territory on the Saudi-Yemen border on Monday. (Houthi Media Centre via Reuters)

At least 73 people, including children, have been injured in strikes on four Saudi Arabian cities.

Multiple oil facilities in the region have also been targeted.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could disrupt Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen's Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, setting fire to oil facilities and injuring more than 70 people.

The Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas including the capital Sanaa, said they have launched an operation deep into Saudi territory, deploying drones and missiles to strike a Saudi air-base in the southern city of Khamis Mushait.

They also claim to have targeted spots belonging to Saudi Arabia's state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border and Jazan, a major Red Sea port city that houses a large refinery and power plant.

The move appears to be a major expansion of the war in the Midlde East which is now in its sixth month.

The Houthi rebels, described as one of Iran's "merchants of chaos", have threatened to widen the conflict in the Middle East by declaring a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. Here's what could happen next.

The reports of such large numbers of injured people suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt in the attacks.

NASA satellite images showed a thick cloud of black smoke over the Jazan refinery and a column of white smoke rising from an oil distribution centre in Abha.

A satellite image shows smoke rising from the Saudi Aramco distribution centre. (NASA Worldview via Reuters)

Confirmed images of the aftermath of the attacks in Saudi cities were not immediately available, and witnesses could not be reached in a country where media is tightly controlled.

The Houthis released pictures showing thick smoke and explosions of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia that they had hit in separate strikes at the border on Monday.

Houthi-controlled media reported later on Tuesday that Saudi war-planes had carried out four air-strikes in Yemen's Jubah district east of Sanaa.

Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching air strikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.

But Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said they "will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confronts its hostile approach".

Saudi military spokesman Colonel Turki al-Malki says Saudi Arabia "will take all necessary operational measures to deter" the Houthis. (AP: Amr Nabil)

Tuesday's attacks hit Saudi oil facilities connected to an alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb, a strategic waterway off the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The International Organization for Migration said more than 18,500 people had fled their homes because of fighting along Yemen's west coast over the past three days.

Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war's global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

These latest attacks, along with Iran and the US exchanging fire over the weekend, has sent global oil prices surging back towards the prices seen at the peak of the war.

The Iran war is showing signs it could drag on into next year as Iran seemingly looks to prolong Donald Trump's political pain for as long as possible.

Brent crude oil reached $US99.46 ($138) on Tuesday, the highest since mid-July, although the price eased a bit later in the day.

Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz, while cutting off Iran's exports with a blockade.

Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a "maritime exclusion zone" that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.title: Israel closes UK consulate in East Jerusalem as three G7 countries ban settlement imports
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.author: Riley Stuart and Matthew Doran
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announces ban on imports from Israeli settlements. (Supplied: House of Commons)

A dozen countries including the UK, Canada and France, on Tuesday announced plans to introduce or support import bans on goods from Israeli settlements.

The move sparked an immediate backlash from Israel, which says it will close Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem which serves occupied Palestine.

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong told parliament this week Australia would not pursue a similar ban "at this time".

Britain, France and Canada will ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, in a move that prompted a swift retaliation and could spark a broader geo-political storm.

While several smaller nations have already adopted similar policies, Tuesday's announcement from the three G7 powers is much more significant.

The United Kingdom's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband revealed the plan in a speech in parliament on Tuesday, and two hours later, his Israeli counterpart Gideon Sa'ar announced that in response, his country would close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, among several other measures.

That facility had served as Britain's representative office for occupied Palestine. The UK's embassy in Tel Aviv remains unaffected.

An estimated 700,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which are considered illegal under international law, although Israel disputes this.

Ma'ale Adumim, near Jerusalem, is among the most established Israeli settlements in the West Bank. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The announcement was widely telegraphed and drew condemnation from right-wing politicians in Israel, the country's president Isaac Herzog and US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee even before it was made official.

Israeli's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the British ambassador to be expelled.

Meanwhile, Mr Sa'ar said on top of closing the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, the country's representatives would be removed from a support centre in Gaza and a training program in the West Bank. He also said 12 UK politicians who were "antisemitic" would be denied entry to Israel.

Israel's government and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have been criticised by much of the international community for accelerating the construction of settlements in the West Bank and not doing enough to stop violent attacks by Israelis on Palestinians there, while multiple wars have raged in the Middle East over the past three years.

The announcement by France, Britain and Canada on Tuesday also included commitments from nine other European nations that they intended to introduce or support similar bans in the future.

In his speech, Mr Miliband said "settler terrorists" were carrying out "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the West Bank, and accused Israel's government of turning a "blind eye" to this.

Israel's government and PM have previously condemned settler violence, although some ministers have also openly campaigned for it.

France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced his country's ban on imports from Israeli settlements in a post on social media.

"Why are we doing this? Because the West Bank is close to exploding — there is frenzied expansion of the settlements, a flare up of violence against Palestinians by extremist settlers, and acts of terror which have been attacked by Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote on X.

The import restrictions are not expected to have a significant impact on the economies of France, Britain, Canada or Israel, and experts have warned it will be difficult to enforce.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar did not take long to announce retaliatory measures on the UK. (Reuters: Agustin Marcarian )

Dr Julie Norman, an associate fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at London-based think tank Chatham House, said the announcement was still significant.

"I think this is really important for middle powers to think about, that maybe directly their own ban or prohibition may not have a huge financial weight, but collectively with others, it will," she said.

Dr Norman said the ban could be extended in the future to include, specifically, IT companies, which would could hurt Israel's economy more.

Australia was not part of Tuesday's announcement, and in parliament earlier in the day, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the government was "not at this time pursuing a blanket-style import ban" on goods from Israeli settlements.

However, she said Australia would look at "targeted measures" to "deter illegal settlements and settler violence".

Several countries, including the UK and Australia have in the past 12 months announced they would or have recognised a Palestinian state.

Israel's decision to press ahead with plans to build a settlement on a particularly controversial parcel of land near Jerusalem, called E1, has been denounced as a diplomatic red line by several Western governments, and was referenced specifically by the nations introducing bans as one of the reasons behind their decisions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/p.title: Legendary horseman Paddy Payne Sr dies aged 90
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Death and Dying

Paddy Payne Sr was the head of one of the most famous surnames in Australian racing. (ABC: Bridget Brennan)

Legendary horseman and patriarch of the famous Australian racing family, Paddy Payne Sr, has died aged 90.

He was father of Michelle Payne, the first woman to win the Melbourne Cup, and husband to late Mary Payne, whom he had 10 children with.

Daughter Michelle took to social media to pay a tribute to her father, saying "RIP Dad. You finally get to go and see Mum again".

Paddy Payne (left) with daughter Michelle (centre) and son Stevie (right). (ABC Ballarat: Dominic Cansdale)

Racing Victoria issued a statement acknowledging the passing of the "legendary Ballarat horseman".

"Paddy was the patriarch of the Payne family as they established themselves as one of the most famous surnames in Australian racing," the statement continued.

Racing Victoria Chief Executive Aaron Morrison said "Paddy was the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing and provided us with so many great memories".

Eight of Payne's 10 children became professional jockeys.

Daughter Michelle enjoyed multiple Group One triumphs, including her trailblazing 2015 Melbourne Cup win.

Paddy Payne said unlike many punters he thought Prince Of Penzance had a good chance of winning Australian racing's biggest prize.

Son Patrick also achieved great success in Group One racing, both as a jockey and a trainer.

Paddy Payne was immortalised in a film about Michelle's Melbourne Cup victory titled Ride Like a Girl, where he was played by the late Sam Neill.

Payne's wife Mary died in a car accident in 1986, leaving him to raise their children when Michelle was just six months old.

Later in life, two of his daughters died — Brigid in 2007 and Bernadette in 2025 — both were jockeys.

In an interview with the ABC in 2015, Payne said: "We've had some good success and some bad luck as well."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.title: Three attacks in Tehran could 'amount to war crimes', report finds
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.author: Matthew Doran
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Amnesty said the strikes that damaged residential areas could amount to war crimes. (AFP)

Three attacks the US and Israel carried out on Tehran in March may amount to war crimes, Amnesty International has said in a new report.

The human rights organisation said that while the targets of the strikes may have been justified under international law, the damage to surrounding civilian areas was "entirely predictable".

Amnesty International is calling for the US and Israel to allow independent investigations into the attacks.

Amnesty International is demanding formal investigations into three American and Israeli attacks on densely packed suburbs in Tehran that killed at least 41 civilians, arguing the devastating impact and choice of weapons may amount to war crimes.

The advocacy group examined the March incidents, analysing photos and videos of the attacks available on social media as well as eyewitness accounts and official reports in Iranian state media to question the legitimacy of the strikes.

It found that the targets of the strikes, namely police stations and paramilitary compounds, may have been justified under international law.

But Amnesty said the damage to the surrounding areas, specifically civilian apartment blocks and businesses in congested neighbourhoods, should have been cause to rethink the attacks because of "entirely predictable consequences for civilians".

"Military combatants have to take feasible precautions to avoid civilian casualties," Andrew Witheford, a spokesperson for Amnesty International Australia, told the ABC.

"If it's possible, they need to give warning, and the strike itself and the action taken need to be proportionate to the military objectives that are being sought.

Amnesty, which describes the US and Israel's war with Iran as unlawful, said the two countries must allow independent investigations of their conduct relating to the three attacks, as well as the widely criticised strike on the Minab school on the very first day of the war which killed 150 people, including 120 children.

When asked whether those countries would launch independent investigations, Mr Witheford said: "It saddens me to say that it's not looking good so far."

Early video from the scene of a strike on an Iranian school.

One of the attacks investigated by Amnesty was on Niloufar Square in central Tehran on the evening of March 1, the second day of the war.

A police station appeared to be the target, but significant damage was reported to nearby apartment buildings and shops in the area.

Iranian officials said at least 20 civilians were killed in the strikes.

Amnesty said it had spoken to a local journalist, whom the organisation named "Kiana", who said that the scene was "horrific" and that between 15 and 20 apartment buildings had been damaged in the blasts.

Residential buildings were reduced to rubble near Niloufar Square. (AFP)

She told the organisation that a father and son working in a bakery were believed to be among the dead.

The second strike was on the Resalat neighbourhood in eastern Tehran, where Iranian officials said at least 16 people were killed, including 12 members of the same family, on the afternoon of March 9.

The strike there appeared to target a building belonging to the Basij, the Iranian regime's notorious paramilitary branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Amnesty's investigation revealed another three buildings were badly damaged, but the organisation could only verify one as being a residential block.

One source it spoke to insisted the residents of the building, known as Number 12, were all civilians, and said he had seen horrific injuries and bodies blown to pieces.

Three Iranians share their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month.

At the time, the Israeli military had announced it was hitting Basij targets across the Iranian capital.

The third attack scrutinised by Amnesty occurred on March 13 in Javadieh, southern Tehran, where at least five people were killed.

The group described it as a "low-income neighbourhood characterised by aging infrastructure and small, closely packed homes and other civilian structures".

Again, a police station appeared to be the target. But Iranian state media reported a number of other buildings were either destroyed or seriously damaged, including an apartment block and nearby businesses.

Amnesty said it had reviewed a photograph published by state media and believed it showed components of an American guided missile system used by the US and Israeli militaries.

The United States and Israel are yet to respond to Amnesty's report but have previously defended their military actions as lawful.

Both countries have said they do not target civilians.

Amnesty said the control the Iranian regime has over the country's police force may have made the police stations lawful military targets — despite police generally being considered civilian in many circumstances.

It also said the Basij, being paramilitary, may also have qualified "as a military objective under international humanitarian law".

But it argued its analysis of the three strikes raised "serious concerns" about breaches of international law, "particularly the principles of distinction and precautions in attack."

The women of Iran's war. (Karishma Vyas)

In Niloufar, Amnesty argued the presence of civilians was predictable.

"Even if the police station could qualify as a military objective … the timing and location, the presence of civilians in surrounding residential buildings, restaurants and public spaces required the attacking forces to take all feasible precautions to avoid or minimise incidental death of or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," it said.

"The extensive blast damage affecting numerous apartment blocks, a school, and commercial premises, coupled with reports of significant civilian casualties, suggests the use of explosive weapons with wide area effects.

A new 300-page report alleges Israel has and continues to undertake acts of genocide against Palestinian people in Gaza.

In Javadieh, Amnesty said the concerns around harm to civilians should have been considered.

"The reported blast radius, extending up to 50 metres, and the scale of damage to homes and commercial properties indicate that the effects of the attack were not limited to the intended target," it said.

In Resalat, the organisation said it was likely a building other than the Basij compound was hit in a separate strike.

"Investigations should clarify whether any residential buildings that were struck were intentionally targeted, or whether they were struck recklessly despite indications that they were civilian objects," Amnesty said.

"If so, those attacks may amount to war crimes."

Hundreds of civilians have been killed since the Iran war began on February 28, with estimates ranging from 1,700 to more than 3,400.

Mr Witheford said Iran had also contributed to civilian deaths during the war, both through attacking other countries and executing its own people.

"The laws of war apply to the Iranian military as well, and they have dropped the ball in this case as well," he said.

Mr Witheford said Amnesty approached both the Israeli and United States militaries for input on its report and did not receive a response.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/w.title: Football league says Swans scandal comments 'clearly insensitive'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Whyalla Football League described the comments as "unacceptable" and "insensitive".  (Supplied)

At a recent awards night for the Whyalla Football League, the master of ceremonies made light-hearted reference to the scandal currently engulfing the Sydney Swans.

The MC suggested that a local club "manufacture a good old-fashioned scandal just to get that team going", suggesting the same had worked for the Swans.

The league described the comments as "insensitive" and "unacceptable", but said that, "in his defence", the man was attempting "to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve".

A country football league has distanced itself from "insensitive" and "unacceptable" comments made at a recent awards event at which the master of ceremonies joked about the Sydney Swans scandal.

But the league also said that, "in his defence", the man was attempting "to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve".

In video posted online, the MC at the Whyalla Football League's event made light-hearted reference to the Swans scandal, citing it in the context of local club South Whyalla's upcoming match.

The man, Jock Sleep, suggested the local club draw inspiration from Sydney's win over Brisbane in Saturday's AFL qualifying final, linking that performance to the scandal engulfing the Swans.

"My advice to the Souths' coach … [is] maybe we can manufacture a good old-fashioned scandal just to get that team going," the MC said.

"It worked for the Sydney Swans. I'm just talking a scandal — not a real big one."

Last week, Victoria Police detectives spoke with four Sydney Swans players as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the club.

A still from the video shared online. (Facebook)

The man's remarks at the Whyalla awards night were strongly condemned by Australian Femicide Watch's Sherele Moody, who shared video on her social media pages and described the comments as "terrible".

"The crowd at the awards night laughed along with him. There was no attempt to shut down the conversation by the organisers," she wrote.

In a statement, Whyalla Football League president Keith Sichler said Mr Sleep was a "well-known local identity" and local football historian.

"His comments and joke were clearly insensitive and not indicative of current attitudes. In his defence, it was merely an attempt to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve with the intent of improving their performance. Nothing more," Mr Sichler said.

"Nonetheless, references of this nature are unacceptable and inconsistent with the inclusive and respectful environment we expect across our League.

"The WFL has spoken with him, and he understands the impact of his remarks and has expressed regret for any harm caused."

The ABC has reached out directly to Mr Sleep for comment.

Last week, the Swans said five players would remain stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August, regardless of how an ongoing police investigation unfolded.

Victoria Police has interviewed four Sydney men as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations during a post-AFL match party at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.title: Thieves steal two paintings from Renoir Museum worth 9 million euros
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Police officers patrol in front of the entrance of the Musee Renoir after paintings valued at 9 million euros were stolen from the museum.   (AFP: Valery Hache)

Thieves have stolen four paintings from the Renoir Museum in France, worth 9 million euros ($14.5 million).

The group broke into the museum in the early hours of the morning, stealing four artworks, dropping two as they fled.

The museum remains closed while the thieves are being "actively sought", according to the local mayor.

Thieves have stolen two paintings from the Renoir Museum in France via a hole made in a garden fence.

The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, said a group of "well-equipped" and "well-informed" thieves broke into the museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, early Tuesday, local time.

They sliced through a fence and entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Mr Masson said.

Coco Lisant (1905) by Renoir, one of the paintings reportedly stolen. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

The museum had 12 works by Renoir in total, four were stolen, but two canvases were dropped during the police chase and found in the museum garden.

Local French newspaper Nice-Matin reported the paintings as Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895), Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), Coco Lisant (1905) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The mayor confirmed Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune fille au puits were the two artworks still missing.

Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (left) and Portrait of Madame Pichon (right) by Renoir. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

Mr Masson's office estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros ($14.5 million).

"Spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran," Mr Masson said.

Mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer Bryan Masson makes a statement outside the Musee Renoir after four paintings were stolen.   (AFP: Valery Hache)

"The museum alarm went off at 5:48am. At 5:53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene.

"Since this morning, both the municipal and national police have been deployed to the site.

The museum was closed Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.

The mayor said it took five minutes for authorities to respond. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The Renoir Museum was opened in 1960 in the painter's last home before his death in 1919.

Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes, and nudes painted by the artist.

The theft comes less than a year after jewels valued at around 88 million euros ($141 million) were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris.

The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items still have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.

Here are the details on the items stolen in the Louvre heist that unfolded in broad daylight in Paris.

In August, three century-old paintings, including a Renoir, stolen by an organised gang from an Italian museum during a three-minute heist were recovered.

The artworks included Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's Still Life with Cherries, and Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Days after their recovery, another four paintings were stolen from another Italian museum.

Artworks by 15th century painter Antonello da Messina were taken from the Museo Regionale di Messina — the pieces some of the only surviving work by the Renaissance painter to have remained in his native city.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/f.title: Gun law reform in Tasmania on knife's edge with independent holding casting vote
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/f.author: Josh Duggan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The proposed reforms were a response to calls to tighten gun laws in the wake of last year's Bondi terror attack. (ABC News)

Debate on whether to include gun ownership limits in the Tasmanian government's firearms legislation is on a knife's edge, with the House of Assembly appearing to be split on Tuesday with 17 votes to 17.

MPs have outlined their positions on Labor's amendment to the bill, which would allow individuals to own up to five guns, except for farmers and sport shooters who could have 10.

Debate will continue on Thursday,  with independent George Razay to hold the deciding vote.

Independent MP George Razay has emerged as holding the deciding vote on whether ownership firearm limits will be included in the Tasmanian government's firearms reform legislation.

Debate on the highly contentious legislation, tabled by Police Minister Felix Ellis, began Tuesday with the lower house members outlining their positions on the bill, and several amendments being flagged.

While the bill does not include an ownership cap, Labor will move amendments to include an ownership cap of five guns for individuals.

The proposed legislation was tabled by Police Minister Felix Ellis. (Facebook: Felix Ellis)

Under the opposition's plan, primary producers and sporting shooters would be eligible to own up to 10 guns, while exemptions would also be available from the police commissioner.

While debate on the amendments is not expected to take place until Thursday, numbers in the House of Assembly on the issue of caps appear to be locked at 17–17.

The Greens are expected to support the caps, as are independents Kristie Johnston, Helen Burnet and Peter George.

But the caps are not supported by the Liberal government; Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Carlo Di Falco; or independents David O'Byrne and Craig Garland.

About 20 amendments have been flagged for Thursday's debate by the opposition and cross-bench. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

It leaves independent Bass MP George Razay as the deciding vote, however, he did not reveal his position in his second reading speech.

Dr Razay told the house that he understood the issue would be up for consideration during the committee phase of the debate, where amendments are discussed.

The bill, a response to the Bondi terror attacks of 2025, is expected to pass the lower house in some form.

Among other reforms, the bill introduces mandatory minimum jail terms for firearms offences and for setting up Tasmanian requirements for a National Firearms Register.

Mr Ellis told the house that the tabled bill represented the "most comprehensive legislative reform" to the Firearms Act since it was introduced in 1996.

Labor's Police spokesperson Jen Butler told parliament on Tuesday that MPs had "a responsibility" to question its strength.

Ms Butler said there was evidence that owners with a high number of guns were targeted by thieves. Relatively few guns were also recovered after being stolen, she said.

The state government has said caps would unfairly target law-abiding firearms owners, and there was no evidence the caps would improve public safety.

Some firearms will be put into a more restrictive licence category under the proposed reforms. (ABC News)

The opposition has claimed this equates to support for "unlimited guns" — something Premier Jeremy Rockliff hit back at during the debate.

"Tasmania does not have unlimited gun ownership today, and this bill does not create it tomorrow," he said, pointing to significant regulations on gun ownership.

Independent MP David O'Byrne said compelling evidence that gun caps would improve community safety was needed, and that it would mean the same number of people owned guns, even if they each had fewer.

Police Commissioner Donna Adams is supportive of ownership caps. Earlier this year, she wrote to Mr Ellis, saying "public safety must take precedence over the privilege of firearms ownership".

More than 11,000 Tasmanians have signed a parliamentary petition opposing ownership caps.

The government's bill reclassifies straight pull rifles and shotguns to the more restrictive category C licence, available to approved collectors and primary producers.

Tasmania's government says its proposed gun reform legislation strikes the right balance and will result in a significant uplift in community safety — but critics say the laws are a "betrayal" and won't make Tasmania safer.

However, those arrangements would be grandfathered, meaning that current owners of those guns could retain ownership without an upgraded licence.

Instead, transition arrangements would be included, so people could keep the guns while they applied for a category C licence.

"There may be sound reasons for this transition, but parliament should ask whether the sound reason for reclassification is fully achieved if the firearms already in circulation remain unaffected," Greens Police spokesperson Tabatha Badger said.

The government's bill also makes Australian citizenship a requirement for holding a firearms licence — with exceptions for New Zealanders or those with a genuine work-related reason.

While Labor has said it wanted to amend the bill to remove grandfathering provisions, that proposal is expected to fail.

The Greens indicated that it may put non-citizens "at risk of unreasonable outcomes".

The 87-page bill makes other changes to firearms laws in Tasmania, including the introduction of mandatory minimum jail terms for those who commit serious firearms offences, along with increases to penalties.

The bill would also allow the set up of the National Firearms Register, a buyback scheme, and looks to increase intelligence-sharing capabilities between law enforcement agencies.

There are also new rules for antique firearms, which Mr Ellis said would simplify the process for possessing, displaying and storing antique firearms.

Owners would need to provide contact details, information about the type of firearm, and where and how it is stored, while display requirements have been updated.

All fields are required unless marked optional.

Enter a suburb or postcode in Australia and select from the list

About 20 amendments have been flagged for Thursday's debate by the opposition and cross-bench.

These include attempting to reduce the licence renewal period from five years to two, to remove the mandatory jail terms, and expand the 'fit and proper persons' test.

Ms Johnston will seek an amendment to allow police to consider a person's history of family violence or coercive control behaviour, even if no offence or protection order has been recorded.

She recounted the story of one constituent, which she said still haunted her.

"No shot was fired, but she could see what was intended with that act."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.title: 'People are furious': RBA deputy governor says more needs to be done on inflation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.author: Marina Freri and Paul Johnson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Reserve Bank Of Australia

Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, Andrew Hauser, says what people "want us to do is our job and bring inflation down".

The RBA deputy governor has identified inflation as the "one big problem" still facing Australia's economy.

Andrew Hauser says the RBA stands ready to raise interest rates further if the central bank believes it is needed.

The RBA board meets at the end of September when the next rates decision is made.

The Reserve Bank's Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser knows Australians are "furious" about inflation and while he is determined to bring it down, he says the RBA is not at the point where it has to take more drastic action.

In a wide-ranging interview, Mr Hauser told 7.30 that inflation is the major problem for Australia's central bank, as he acknowledged Australians are struggling with the continued high cost of living and rising interest rates.

He indicated those rates could rise higher in the coming months.

While Mr Hauser defended the Australian economy as "doing quite well" on issues of unemployment and real household incomes, he signalled out the continuing scourge of inflation as the nation's biggest problem.

Headline inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in the year to July, despite the continued efforts of the RBA and government to bring it down.

The four major banks are all forecasting the RBA will lift interest rates by the end of the year. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Hauser acknowledged the anger and frustration in the community.

"People are furious about inflation," he said, calling it the RBA's "one big problem".

"I understand why. It's unfair. It hits people on low incomes, it damages price signals, it makes the job of companies difficult.

"What [people] want us to do is our job and bring inflation down.

"Everywhere I go, I hear cost, cost, cost, inflation, inflation, inflation, and that's our responsibility. We have to put that right.

"When people go to the supermarket every week, they look at the price of the goods they're buying, they compare them to where they were a few years ago and they say, 'Hell, what's going on here?'.

"That is a very lasting and pervasive issue that is a function of the pick-up in inflation after COVID and will take years for us to fully resolve."

As to why Australia is still struggling with inflation, Mr Hauser says it is a three-headed monster.

"One is the Middle East and the ongoing crisis there, one is a really unexpected global boom driven by AI, and one is the weakness of the supply potential of the Australian economy."

One solution to fixing inflation could be hiking interest rates dramatically, but Mr Hauser said the RBA was unlikely to do that just yet.

"We could decide, 'You know what? We no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective. We're going to bring inflation down come hell or high water.'"

Mr Hauser said Australia was not at that point just yet but gave a strong indication that the central bank is contemplating hiking interest rates this month as the economy continues to grow — albeit slowly — and the labour market remains tight.

He denied a rate hike was "inevitable" but said the bank was very focused on bringing inflation down.

"Inflation is too high and that's why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year," Mr Hauser said.

Australia's four major banks are all forecasting the central bank will lift interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6 per cent by the end of the year.

Mr Hauser's comments came hours after his RBA colleague, assistant governor Sarah Hunter, said the central bank "may well have to raise interest rates" if it senses inflation is stronger than its forecasts."

The RBA board will meet at the end of September to decide whether to move or hold the cash rate — currently sitting at 4.35 per cent.

New inflation figures, however, will only become public a day after that crucial decision — on September 30.

Mr Hauser says he expects house prices to fall "a little bit more". (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Asked about the current downturn in the housing market, Mr Hauser said the bank was watching it closely as the price adjustment will have an impact on consumption growth.

He expected prices to fall "a little bit more" but said current conditions in the housing market are not a key factor in the bank's forecasts.

"While house prices play a role in the economy, they're not really as big as some of the things we talked about earlier in the conversation, global growth trends, productivity, the risk environment globally, in the Middle East and so on and so forth," he said.

Compared to nations including the UK, Canada and the US, Australia has been slow to bring inflation down.

The RBA projects inflation will return to its target by early 2028.

Last year, the central bank began cutting interest rates before being forced to change course this year just before the war in Iran started.

Mr Hauser said that at the time it looked like a "sweet spot" but that the RBA had consistently updated its position when needed.

Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"When the facts change, we change our position," he said.

Mr Hauser rejected the notion that the RBA was not prepared to answer a question on the role of government spending in the economy.

“We are an equal opportunity monetary policymaker. A dollar of demand, whether it comes from the government or it comes from the private sector or it comes from overseas, has roughly the same effect on the outlook for inflation as a dollar for demand from anywhere else," he said.

“We take government policy as given. It's part of our judgement about the outlook for inflation, but it doesn't have a special status."

Mr Hauser said a recent trip to the US made him more concerned about the global economic outlook as he defended the RBA's longer-term move on inflation.

"We are doing it over a longer period than some other central banks have done. And we're doing it in order to try to protect the jobs gains that happened during COVID," he said.

"We will raise interest rates further than otherwise we would need to do so. We're not at that point yet, but some of these upside risks to inflation are certainly on our mind, and I come back from the US a bit more worried about them than I did when I went."

The Deputy Governor's recent trip to the US saw him look firsthand at a productivity bonanza and an investment boom in artificial intelligence.

Mr Hauser says only time will tell if investments in data centres will pay off. (ABC News: Daniel Irving)

While he said he could see the adoption of the technology, he warned the jury was still out on whether AI companies would all make a fortune — and said the million-dollar question on AI was how to value a future income stream deriving from it.

"Much of it may be a failure," he said.

"Much of it may turn out to be a wrongful allocation of technology to tasks that won't actually solve its purpose, but there is an enormous vibrancy to that process."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/p.author: Keira Proust
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Transport Accidents and Incidents

A child has died and six others have been taken to hospital after the crash at Parwan. (ABC News)

A child has died in a single-vehicle rollover west of Melbourne, while six others have been taken to hospital with injuries.

One of those children had critical injuries and was flown to the Royal Children's Hospital.

Police are investigating the crash.

A school-aged child has died and six others have been taken to hospital with injuries after a single-vehicle rollover on a regional road in Parwan, west of Melbourne, this afternoon.

One child was flown to the Royal Children's Hospital in a critical condition.

Emergency services received reports of a crash near the Nerowie and Parwan-Exford road intersections, south-west of Melton, just before 4pm.

Victorian Police said one child died at the scene while six others were injured.

"Despite CPR being performed, one school-aged child died at the scene," a spokesperson said.

"A second child was airlifted with critical injuries. Five more children were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

"One woman was taken to hospital for observation."

Ambulance Victoria said several children had been taken to the Royal Children's Hospital, including the one who was flown by helicopter.

A Western Health spokesperson said three children were being treated at Sunshine Hospital and all were in a stable condition.

An adult was taken to the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Ambulance Victoria said many of its specialist crews responded to the incident.

A child has been flown to hospital with critical injuries after a fatal car crash west of Melbourne. (ABC News)

"Two specialist Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter crews, two Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance paramedic crews and seven Advanced Life Support paramedic crews assessed eight people at the scene," an ambulance spokesperson said.

An investigation into the crash is ongoing.
