https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/c.title: Smokers should face tougher penalties over illicit tobacco, police chief suggests
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

South Australian Police Commissioner Grant Stevens has said the absence of enforcement for the purchase of illegal tobacco is "a question that needs to be considered". (ABC News)

SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens has said consumer-side penalties for the purchase of illicit tobacco "is a question that needs to be considered".

It is illegal in SA to sell or import unauthorised tobacco products, but not to buy them, the commissioner said.

The comments coincide with the seizure of more than one million illegal cigarettes and vapes in interstate raids, as well as national debate about ways to curb the illegal trade.

South Australia's police commissioner has again raised the possibility of tougher illicit tobacco laws that would crack down on those who purchase — rather than just those who sell or traffic — the black market product.

Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide this morning, Grant Stevens said the matter of penalising people caught buying illegal cigarettes was one that "needs to be considered".

"There is an opportunity for people to avoid significant costs by purchasing illicit tobacco, and I think that there are questions that need to be asked about how we can kill off the market," the commissioner said.

"Why are there no sanctions for people who are, essentially, creating the market for organised crime?

"It's illegal to sell it [illegal tobacco], it's illegal to import it — it's not illegal to buy it and use it."

The Liberals and One Nation have a simple solution to end Australia's tobacco black market. But Labor says there's no easy fix.

Tobacco laws are enforced jointly by federal, state and territory authorities.

The commissioner, who issued a similar call two years ago, said while the problem was "not anywhere near as bad" as what it had become in the eastern states, it had nevertheless led to significant criminal activity in SA.

"We certainly have a problem with illicit tobacco distributors being the target of criminal offending, including arsons; we've had some drive-by shootings, we've had assaults," he said.

"This is because there is this illicit market that has crept into South Australia.

"We have a dedicated taskforce that are investigating the criminal offending associated with the illicit tobacco market, and this illicit market that is being exploited by organised crime exists because the market has been able to flourish."

His comments coincide with the seizure of more than one million illegal cigarettes and vapes in a series of raids throughout Western Australia and the Northern Territory, as well as national debate about ways to curb the illegal trade.

The federal opposition last week announced that a future Coalition government would take steps including slashing the tobacco excise by 80 per cent and legalising and taxing vapes and nicotine pouches.

Last month, One Nation unveiled a plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent.

But Labor has argued there is no evidence a dramatic cut would end the illicit trade and said slashing the excise would "kill people".

"If we drop the excise, in the way that is being suggested by the Coalition, that's a guarantee we will see smoking and vaping rates in this country increase. That will lead to deaths," Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said earlier this month.

The SA government has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/n.title: Hundreds face homelessness within weeks amid government funding stand-off
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/n.author: Roxanne Fitzgerald and Jacqueline Breen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Roxanne Fitzgerald

Christine Martin, with her grandson Azai, says she's unsure whether the house she has been promised will be ready before YiSSA closes.  (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

Hundreds of residents living at Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility are facing eviction within weeks and say they fear they will end up homeless.

The Commonwealth has offered to split the cost of buying the facility with the Northern Territory government, but negotiations appear to have reached a stalemate.

Resident's living at the YiSSA centre say they are angry and worried, while Aboriginal service providers are calling on the NT government to negotiate with the Commonwealth.

Darwin's largest homeless shelter is on track to close within weeks despite an offer from the Commonwealth to split the cost of buying the facility to keep it open.

The imminent closure of the YiSSA centre has left more than 230 residents living there fearing the prospect of homelessness as early as next month.

They include 85 children, people undergoing renal dialysis and facing serious health problems, and families escaping domestic violence.

The facility's closure would also mean more than 300 people currently on a waitlist to live there would be left with nowhere to live.

Two months ago, the Northern Territory government announced YiSSA would close in October after its offer of $3 million for the buildings was rejected by the owner Ausco Modular, which is seeking $6.5 million.

Robyn Cahill first announced the closure of YiiSSA in July.  (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

In August, Federal Senator Malarndirri McCarthy wrote to NT Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill offering to split the cost of purchasing YiSSA between the NT and federal governments to keep it open.

"I am prepared to consider a Commonwealth contribution of up to $3.5 million," she wrote.

However, negotiations appeared to reach a stalemate last week, with Ms Cahill criticising the terms of the federal government's proposal, and arguing the facility was ageing and not fit-for-purpose beyond another two to three years.

Hundreds of residents fear they could be left homeless after the Northern Territory government announced it will shut a Darwin short-stay accommodation centre in less than 90 days.

The conditions of the Commonwealth offer include funding Yilli Rreung Housing Aboriginal Corporation to continue running YiSSA for at least another five years and for the NT government to decommission the site when it eventually closes.

Yesterday, Senator McCarthy criticised the NT government on social media over its refusal to negotiate, saying YiSSA residents "deserve answers".

She also questioned why the Territory government had not yet announced a transition plan or explained how it would meet the need for short-stay accommodation once YiSSA closed.

The ABC has contacted the NT government about whether it is continuing to negotiate a deal, but has not received a response.

The Territory government has repeatedly promised to find accommodation for all those living in the facility, but today many residents said they were fearing the worst and voiced concerns about being kept in the dark about where they would be going.

Rose Laynba says residents are worried about where they will end up.  (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"We are worried. We are sad. We are thinking, 'What's our next movement? Where will we go?'" long-term YiSSA resident Rose Laynba said.

She said she was angered by the governments "arguing over money".

"Instead of arguing, just throw it in and pay for it, stop making excuses," she said.

"First Nation people here are struggling and they're arguing who's going to pay, who's going to buy it — it's just plain stupid.

"We are becoming refugees, refugees in our own backyard."

Ausco has confirmed it is seeking $6.5 million for the infrastructure.  (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

For fellow resident Christine Martin, YiSSA has been a lifeline, after she spent more than six months staying in hotels, unable to find a home in Darwin.

While she has been told she is on a list for a house, she said the lack of information had left her feeling uncertain.

"Maybe this place will close before I even get a place.

"There's a lot of people here that have nowhere to go … and they're going to have to be on the streets, because if they can't return [to their community] there's no other place."

She said with just a few weeks left until closure, people were increasingly feeling desperate.

"Most of the people I talk to, they're like, 'Where are you going?'" she said.

"We all don't know what's going on."

Grandmother Francis Gaykamangu said she was one of the lucky residents who had been offered a priority house to live in, but she said she was sad to be leaving her home.

Francis Gaykamangu and her granddaughter Shana are among the lucky residents who have somewhere to go.  (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

A group of NT Aboriginal service providers, including the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency and Danila Dilba Health Service, are calling on the Territory government to prevent YiSSA from closing and to negotiate with the Commonwealth.

Hundreds of residents living at Darwin's largest homeless shelter have been told they need to be out by October.

The NT already has the highest rate of homelessness in the country — more than 12 times the national average — but the organisations say the closure of YiSSA would risk even more people sleeping rough in parks, shopping precincts and on beaches.

Danila Dilba Health Service chief executive Rob McPhee said the closure would also put a strain on emergency departments and other frontline support agencies.

"If YiSSA closes, our teams will spend far more time trying to locate clients across multiple locations, making it harder to provide consistent care and increasing the likelihood that people will end up presenting to emergency departments," he said.

"This will place even greater pressure on hospitals and emergency services that are already operating under significant strain."

The service providers also said allowing YiSSA to close would contradict the NT government's own homelessness strategy, which aims to prevent homelessness and deliver culturally safe services.

The NT government has previously said YiSSA will close on October 11.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.title: Inquest to begin into Russell Island house fire that killed father and five boys
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.author: Talissa Siganto
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Wayne Godinet Junior and his five sons died in the Russell Island house fire in 2023. (ABC News: George Roberts)

Claims of domestic violence, non-compliant smoke alarms and point of origin will all form part of an inquest into the deaths of five children and their father in a house fire in south-east Queensland.

Wayne Godinet Jr,  and his sons Zackary, Harrison, Kyza, Koah, and Nickolas died of smoke inhalation after a home on Russell Island burned down in August, 2023.

Sixteen witnesses including fire experts, police, and the boys' mother Samantha Stephenson, who survived the fire, are expected to be called to testify at a 10-day hearing.

An inquest is set to probe whether domestic violence had anything to do with a house fire that killed a man and his five sons in south-east Queensland, after triple-zero callers claimed the boys' parents fought often and that they believed "one day they would kill these kids".

In August 2023, 34-year-old Wayne Godinet Jr, 11-year-old Zackary, 10-year-old Harrison, four-year-old twins Kyza and Koah and three-year-old Nickolas died of smoke inhalation inside their Russell Island home after it caught alight in the early morning.

The children's mother Samantha Stephenson and her sister managed to escape the blaze unharmed.

All six deaths will be the subject of a coronial inquiry which has been set down for November in Brisbane.

The charred remains of the home on Russell Island. (ABC News: George Roberts)

On Tuesday, counsel assisting the coroner Corinne Leach told a preliminary hearing Ms Stephenson lived at the home with the boys and her sister at the time, and Mr Godinet Jr would stay with them occasionally.

"As he worked on the mainland during the week and he and Samantha's relationship was on and off," she said.

Five boys and their father were killed in the blaze, the state's worst house fire tragedy since 2011.

The court heard Ms Stephenson had told investigators her and Mr Godinet Jr had both been underneath the house in a makeshift entertainment area the night before the fire broke out.

Ms Stephenson told investigators she recalled the pair smoked cigarettes and fell asleep cuddling on the couch, before she woke up some hours later and saw black smoke everywhere.

She recalled watching Mr Godinet Jr run up an internal staircase, which was partially on fire, and then seeing flames near a generator and a work bench downstairs where she was.

Ms Stephenson said she then ran outside and saw the external stairs were also on fire, and then heard her sister and Mr Godinet Jr screaming from inside the upper level.

She also told investigators she later saw her sister on the verandah and she told her to jump, which she did, and she expected Mr Godinet Jr and the children to follow, but they did not emerge.

The court heard 20 calls were made to the Queensland Fire Department (QFD), with some people reporting they had heard frequent fighting and screaming coming from the home in the past.

One person reported hearing arguing from about 5am that morning before the fire started, while another claimed "there was domestic violence in there all the time".

Another caller told operators, "we knew that one day they would kill these kids, but nobody has done anything" and "the house is f***ing horrid I've called the police a number of times."

Ms Leach told the court these people would be called to give evidence.

"Whether the domestic and family violence reported contributed to the fire that caused the deaths is an issue that will be explored at inquest," she said.

A preliminary hearing heard Ms Stephenson lived at the home with the boys and her sister, and Mr Godinet Junior would stay with them occasionally. (Supplied)

The court heard a fire investigation report was completed by QFD which found it was probable the blaze had developed in the ground floor area.

However, the court heard the exact point of origin was unable to be determined and human initiated ignition could not be categorically ruled out.

Whether the source of the fire was an electrical issue was also unable to be eliminated due to the extensive damage to the property. This will be another issue for the coroner.

The court heard the house, which was a raised Queenslander, had been relocated to Russell Island in 2012, and was renovated the following year.

Underneath the home was not built in, and the court heard it had been converted by Ms Stephenson and Mr Godinet Jr recently as a place to watch television.

The court heard the pair used blankets to cordon it off, and to power the area they used a five-point power board, which was plugged into an extension cord leading from a room upstairs.

Ms Leach told the court the power points in the house were described as "bad, hanging out, and with exposed wires".

"The power point from which the extension lead was plugged was known to short out and did not sit properly in the wall," she said.

A 61-year-old woman was fined for failing to have compliant smoke alarms installed. (ABC News)

The lack of compliant smoke alarms installed in the home will also form part of the inquest.

In the months after the blaze, the homeowner pleaded guilty to breaching the Fire Services Act and was fined but no conviction was recorded.

The emergency response will also be considered at the inquest, including whether Russell Island has sufficient resources to deal with house fires.

Sixteen witnesses including fire experts, police, and Ms Stephenson are expected to be called to testify at a 10-day hearing.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/n.author: Nick Campton
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Thu, 3 Sept, 9:50 am, Final score, Bulldogs 20, Broncos 34

Fri, 4 Sept, 8:00 am, Final score, Titans 20, Dolphins 24

Fri, 4 Sept, 10:00 am, Final score, Rabbitohs 50, Roosters 20

Sat, 5 Sept, 5:00 am, Final score, Warriors 31, Sea Eagles 30

Sat, 5 Sept, 7:30 am, Final score, Cowboys 30, Raiders 50

Sat, 5 Sept, 9:35 am, Final score, Sharks 20, Storm 24

Sun, 6 Sept, 4:00 am, Final score, Dragons 24, Eels 22

Sun, 6 Sept, 6:05 am, Final score, Panthers 38, Wests Tigers 10

Fri, 11 Sept, 9:50 am, Game not started, Rabbitohs versus Knights

Sat, 12 Sept, 6:05 am, Game not started, Warriors versus Dolphins

Sun, 13 Sept, 6:05 am, Game not started, Panthers versus Roosters

Francis Manuleleua is one of a number of young Knights who will play their first NRL final on Friday night.  (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"Nah, let's go for it G," Manuleleua said when offered the chance to forgo a handshake, just in case.

"It's gotta be strong."

The 22-year-old's right arm bent in a way that right arms are not supposed to bend in the Knights loss to the Warriors a fortnight back.

Manuleleua suffered a dislocated elbow against New Zealand two weeks ago.  (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

It looked gruesome — Manuleleua was straight on the green whistle and phrases like "bony deformity" were used in analysis of the video.

But with Newcastle already without key men Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti due to injury and suspension ahead of Friday's sudden-death semifinal against South Sydney and after being cleared of a fracture, Manuleleua will push to play.

He was named on Tuesday for what would be his NRL finals debut and is one of an unheralded mix of youngsters and journeymen in the Knights forwards who will be tasked with taking down the Rabbitohs.

In terms of star power it's a no-contest. Every player in the South Sydney starting pack has played either Test or Origin football except for Tallis Duncan, who might not have to wait long to join them.

Australia are facing a shortage of backrowers for this year's Rugby League World Cup but South Sydney tyro Tallis Duncan could prove to be the answer.

Manuleleua has a mere 11 NRL matches to his credit and fellow second rower Jermaine McEwen is wrapping up his first full season as an every week player.

The baby of the side is starting prop Cody Hopwood, still just 20, although at 196cm and 105kgs that's a damn big baby.

He's great mates with eight-gamer Lachlan Crouch, who received his first Knights cap from Paul Harragon himself upon his NRL debut earlier this year.

Both the rookies played their juniors in Maitland, as did the more seasoned Thomas Cant and Pasami Saulo who both fit the image of the honest toiler.

Cant has played almost 40 NRL matches since his debut in 2023 and is yet to score a try but that pales compared to Saulo — he's about to finish his ninth season in the league without a single four-pointer to show for it.

Injuries have ripped through the Knights pack in recent weeks.  (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Newcastle will lean heavily on the experience of 300-gamer Tyson Frizell and the underrated Matt Croker at lock as they match it with a South Sydney pack that is both fully loaded and battle-hardened.

Cameron Murray, Junior Tatola, David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi all have 150 NRL games or more to their credit and all but Fifita have been through multiple finals campaigns.

Even Duncan, by far their least experienced starting forward, has made more first grade appearances than Manuleleua, Crouch, Hopwood and McEwen combined.

Given he's marking up on the reborn Fifita, Manuleleua might be facing the biggest task of all and certainly the hardest test of an NRL career that began just a few months ago. He can't wait for it.

"He's a big, powerful boy and there's a job to do. But I'm keen for the challenge," said Manuleleua.

"They've got a lot of strengths on their edge with Fifita, Latrell Mitchell and Jack Wighton and a great ball-player in Cody Walker, so it's a good challenge for us edges.

"But that's the kind of footy we want to play anyway. We want to go after that challenge, go after them and see what happens."

Despite making his NRL debut in Round 3, a steady start is leading to a big finish for Manuleleua.

It wasn't until Round 20 that he became a regular starter following Lucas going down with an ankle injury.

But with six line breaks, two tries, five try assists and 23 tackle busts in the six games since, Manuleleua has proven to be one of the finds of the season.

He's a big, explosive man who can do big, explosive things and has it in him to be a wrecking machine but he's also fresh enough that so much of this is still new.

The match against the Warriors, for example, was the first time the Papatoetoe junior got to play back in New Zealand and over 25 family members and countless friends packed out the stands to see him.

Manuleleua scored a try on his return to New Zealand last week.  (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

"It's pretty surreal. I still can't believe it. I didn't think I'd be playing finals footy this early in my career," said Manuleleua.

"It was gun, that game against the Warriors. They (my family) were loud as hell, Warriors had 25,000 fans but I could still hear my family and it was the first time I played an NRL game in front of them at home.

"It was bittersweet because we couldn't win the game but they were just happy I scored a try."

Manuleleua's clash with Fifita might be the most difficult job but it's not the biggest — that belongs to Hopwood, who will start at prop.

He did the same in the club's most recent clash with South Sydney in Round 19, when Hopwood and Crouch got in the mix with the Rabbitohs amid a torrid physical battle.

The two Maitland boys are popular members of the Knights squad given they have a special brand of front-row charm, as Manuleleua explains.

"They're intentionally funny. They'll do something weird but it'll be funny," said Manuleleua.

"When it comes to the game they look like monsters but they're kind at heart, they're good people."

Hopwood doesn't have time to think about what Manuleleua is talking about given he's about to play the biggest game of his life.

Hopwood will start in the front row for an NRL final at just 20 years of age. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

"I have no idea what that means. I don't think I want to know either," said Hopwood.

"Whenever you're out and about people are wishing you luck for Friday night, the town's flying and we're all excited.

"I'm really confident, I'm in a good spot mentally and physically. Attack it front on, that's probably the best way to go. Just go hard and try to go for longer."

Hopwood was a highly rated junior, representing New South Wales Under 19s twice, but despite making his NRL debut in the final round of last season he never thought he'd play as much first grade in 2026 as he has.

"Not at all, but I've had some really good people around me that have helped with the transition," said Hopwood.

"I thought I might only play two or three games this year, so it's all come pretty quick.

"I'm feeling really supported and I don't want to let anyone down, I want to repay that faith."

Hopwood did not expect to play more than one or two NRL games this year.  (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar )

Hopwood's done a fine job with it so far, starting seven of his 14 games this season, and seems the type who never learned to take a backward step.

Whether that will be enough against players like Koloamatangi and Murray remains to be seen but Hopwood isn't thinking about the odds stacked against him or his side.

Like any good Novocastrian, he has dreamed of making a difference for the Knights his whole life and was there as a 17-year old in the crowd for their last finals win three years ago.

Dom Young roaring down the sideline for a length-of-the-field try is a memory that will never leave him and now all he wants is to give Knights fans another moment that lasts forever.

"I remember thinking how much I'd love to be a part of something like that and I get to live it on Friday night," said Hopwood.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/c.title: Gigantic mechanical 'esky lid' is Brisbane's newest defence against flooding
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/c.author: Kenji Sato
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Albert Street esky lid will automatically lower in the event of high flooding. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Engineers have unveiled an 80-tonne flood barrier at Albert Street Station.

The Cross River Rail Authority has dubbed the contraption "The Esky Lid".

Cross River Rail is due to open in 2029, after repeated blowouts.

Engineers have completed an 80-tonne mechanical contraption named "The Esky Lid" designed to protect Brisbane's new underground tunnels from flooding.

The Esky Lid was unveiled today at Albert Street Station, which will be part of Brisbane's Cross River Rail underground train network.

Albert Station's Esky Lid being raised. (Supplied: Cross River Rail Authority)

The 22-metre by 10-metre barrier will be able to descend from the ceiling over the station's main entrance, sealing it shut from floodwaters.

Sliding panels allow the barrier's modules to click into place, blending in with the station ceiling when not in use.

During intense flooding, shutters will also close off the entrance to the northern side of Albert Street Station.

Albert Street Station will be the most important line of defence, since it will be the deepest point of the 10-kilometre Cross River Rail network.

The station itself is in a low-lying, flood-prone area of Brisbane's CBD.

The lid will keep the station flood-proof up to about 10.3 metres above street level, which is rated as a 1-in-10,000-year probability.

Cross River Rail Delivery Authority program director Jeremy Kruger said they called it The Esky Lid because it could close like the lid of an esky.

Jeremy Kruger says it is unlikely that the company Esky will try to sue them over the name.  (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Mr Kruger said passengers would be evacuated before the esky lid came down in the event of an extreme flood.

However, Mr Kruger said there was a good chance that people alive today would never see this "ingenious" feat of engineering in action.

"This will be a nice, open amenity 99.999 per cent of the time," Mr Kruger said.

"For that 0.001 per cent flood, it can come down, seal, deploy, and protect the station."

Mr Kruger said construction work would finish in early 2027, with safety tests to follow afterwards.

However, he said passenger services were not due to begin until 2029.

Cross River Rail was originally due to open in 2024 at a budget of $5.4 billion, but the project has suffered repeated blowouts over the years.

Mr Kruger said the project was now expected to cost around $19 billion, almost four times the original estimate.

It will be Queensland's single largest and most expensive infrastructure project in history.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.title: Australia records worst-ever maths and reading scores in global test
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.author: Conor Duffy and Miwa Blumer
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australian students' PISA scores in maths, reading and science have continued a 20-year-decline. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Australia's reading and maths results in a major international high school test have continued a 20-year decline.

Australian 15-year-olds have sat the Programme for International Student Assessment exams every three years since 2000.

Australia's test scores have been in decline for two decades, but other OECD countries are declining faster.

Australian high school students' scores in maths and reading have hit their lowest point on record, according to a major international test.

While the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) exams showed a slight improvement in science results since the last test in 2022, Australia's long-term learning decline continued overall.

The 2025 test results released today showed Australia continued to perform above the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average, with Australian students ranking 10th in science and reading and 16th in mathematics among the 91 countries and economies that sat the test.

"What the data shows us is that we see long-term declines in reading and in mathematics. We were able to stabilise our scores in science," said Jonas Bertling from the Australian Council for Educational Research (ACER), which administers the test.

According to the OECD, 20 points on a test score is roughly equivalent to one year of learning for the average student.

Those declines mean science students today are almost one year of learning behind students who sat the exam in 2006.

In reading, students last year were roughly two years behind where they were in 2000. In mathematics, they were a little over two years behind the 2003 results.

"What PISA shows is that we see a decline in especially reading and mathematics where we haven't caught up with the levels from 10 or 20 years ago, when PISA started," Mr Bertling said.

Jonas Bertling says Australia is still performing well overall in the PISA testing. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)

Blaise Joseph from the Centre for Independent Studies think tank said the long-term picture was "troubling".

"We also have fewer high performers and more low performers across all three subjects," Mr Joseph said.

Australian students reported improved discipline in classrooms compared to earlier findings, but remained among the lowest countries in the world on that measure, ranking 69th out of 80.

The disciplinary climate is measured by surveying science students, and 21 per cent reported they could not work well in most or all lessons compared to the OECD average of 19 per cent.

Forty-one per cent of Australian students reported there was noise and disorder in their classrooms compared to the OECD average of 31 per cent, echoing a report released last week that found one-third of lesson time was being lost to misbehaviour.

"Disruption remains a challenge in our Australian classrooms," Mr Burtling said.

"I think it's important that we see disruption in the larger context of the Australian system and see what resources are needed in the classroom to improve on this."

Mr Joseph blamed the high rates of misbehaviour for Australia's lack of learning growth.

"Students cannot learn effectively when classrooms are regularly disrupted," he said.

Fifteen-year-olds in Australia have sat the PISA exams every three years since 2000. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Australian students also skipped school at almost twice the OECD average, with 44 per cent of students reporting skipping a day of school in the two weeks before testing compared to the OECD average of 24 per cent.

Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said the results showed the importance of reforms the government introduced to classroom teaching practice and increased public school funding.

He said the United Kingdom introduced similar reforms 20 years ago, and in this year's PISA testing it rose three places in reading, four places in maths and seven places in science.

"This shows why the reforms we are rolling out are so important. The UK results are impressive. It's also hard-earned. It's something almost 20 years in the making," Mr Clare said.

"In Australian schools that have been doing this for a while we can see the same thing that has happened in the UK. But we have to keep going and roll it out everywhere."

Mr Clare said too much screen time might be a problem in Australian schools.

"This doesn't mean there is no place for tech in schools. Students need to learn digital skills. That includes how to use, and how not to use AI," Mr Clare said.

One big positive from the latest results was Australia's performance in the "learning in the digital world" category, designed to measure a student's ability to learn in technology-rich environments.

Australian students achieved a mean score of 532 points compared to the OECD average of 500 points, with 75 per cent of Australian students reaching the national proficient standard.

James Casey, a year 10 student at Gymea Technology High School, a public school in Sydney's outer south, took the test last year.

James Casey took the new "learning in the digital world" test last year. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"This was more simply a test of just pure logic and reason and ability to think," James said.

School principal Katherine Edwards said the learning in the digital world results would help equip students for the jobs of the future.

Katherine Edwards says STEM skills are becoming increasingly important to have. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

She said the school had a strong focus on science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM).

"It's an area that our students, as they're moving into the workforce, need more and more, and the jobs that they're moving into are relying on those STEM skills," Ms Edwards said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.title: Court bolter tackled by police wanted to kiss partner goodbye
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.author: Mackenzie Heard
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Edwards asked the judge if he could kiss his partner and child goodbye and was refused a second time. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

A north-west Tasmanian man who fled police custody in a Burnie court has been sentenced for various offences, including escape and assaulting police officers.

The Burnie Magistrates Court was shown footage of the moment Stephen Keith Edwards, 29, ran from a courtroom after he was remanded in custody and chased by police.

Edwards was sentenced to 14 months' imprisonment, backdated to November 7, 2025.

A man who escaped police custody wanted to kiss his partner goodbye, a court in Burnie has heard.

Stephen Keith Edwards, 29, appeared in the Burnie Magistrates Court via video link on Tuesday for sentencing after pleading guilty to one count of escape, two counts of assaulting police and several other charges.

Edwards also pleaded guilty and was sentenced for several unrelated offences, including stealing, burglary, common assault, resisting police, breaching bail conditions, and possessing drug paraphernalia.

Magistrate Jackie Hartnett said body cam footage played to the court was evidence of a "significant struggle", and that Edwards did not stop resisting police.

Ms Hartnett said instances of escape were always taken seriously, and that she viewed the assault of police officers as "particularly serious".

Defence lawyer Lizzie Arnold told the court Edwards wanted to say goodbye to his partner and "panicked".

Following the sentencing hearing on Monday, Edwards was remanded in custody and again asked the court if he could say goodbye to his partner, who was outside the courtroom at the time, and give her and their baby a hug.

His request was again denied, and Edwards led himself to the dock and was taken into custody.

The court heard Edwards was taken into police custody on December 6, and taken to the Burnie courthouse for an after-hours session.

After he was remanded in custody, the court heard Edwards wanted to kiss his partner goodbye but was denied, which Magistrate Hartnett described as "entirely appropriate".

Edwards then pushed open the door to the dock, ran past two police officers in the courtroom, and ran towards the exit.

CCTV footage played in court showed Edwards exit the courtroom and run through the courthouse foyer towards the front entrance as the police officers chased after him.

Prosecutor Sam Reid said Edwards damaged a sliding glass door at the courthouse entrance as he was attempting to leave the building and was caught by police.

In body cam footage played to the court, police officers and court security guards could be seen struggling with Edwards, who thrashed around for several minutes as police attempted to restrain and handcuff him.

The prosecution told the court Edwards struck both police officers in the face during the altercation, and a court security guard was pushed.

Ms Arnold told the court the escape was "short-lived" and that Edwards was "embarrassed by his actions".

A second body cam video from outside the courthouse showed Edwards continuing to resist police as they attempted to put him in a police van.

Throughout the footage played to the court, police could be heard yelling at Edwards and telling him to stop resisting.

"Stephen, what are you doing? You're going in either way, mate, just give up," one of the officers said.

After a prolonged struggle, police administered pepper spray and eventually shut the van door with Edwards inside.

In addition to the escape incident on December 6, 2025, Magistrate Hartnett also sentenced Edwards for a range of offences including stealing, burglary, common assault, resisting police, breaching bail conditions, and possessing drug paraphernalia.

Edwards was sentenced to 14 months' imprisonment, backdated to November 7, 2025, accounting for time already served.

After Magistrate Hartnett handed down the sentence, Edwards's partner yelled "I love you" from the courtroom, and Edwards replied over video link, saying: "I love you darl, so sorry."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.title: Popovic knocked back four-year Socceroos contract extension
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.author: David Mark
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tony Popovic says he turned down a contract extension that would have taken his reign to 2030. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract extension to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

Popovic signed a six-month contract in June to coach the Socceroos until the end of the 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.

The Socceroos play Brazil over two matches in Townsville and Brisbane later this month.

Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

Popovic instead signed a six-month extension during the World Cup to take the team through to the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia, which begins in January.

"It was my choice to go until the Asian Cup. Although I was offered a four-year deal, I decided to go to the Asian Cup," Popovic told journalists on Tuesday.

"And I think that is something that I think is good.

"It gives the FA the opportunity if they want to go in a different decision they can, and I'm very comfortable with the decision that's been made."

Football's major governing bodies continue to fight over the failed plan by FIFA president Gianni Infantino to sell off the rights for the World Cup, with the global governing body accusing European body UEFA of a "smear campaign" against the president.

Popovic led the Socceroos to the round of 32 knockout stage of the World Cup in the United States, where the team lost to Egypt in a penalty shoot-out heartbreaker.

His side won its opening match against Türkiye, lost to the United States and drew with Paraguay before the fateful match against Egypt ended the Socceroos' dream run.

He led the youngest side at the World Cup of all 48 nations with an average of 25 years and 155 days.

Some of the Socceroos stars of the tournament have since signed transfer contracts worth up to $33 million, including Lucas Herrington (Hull City), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting Lisbon), Alessandro Circati (Benfica), Patrick Beach (Troyes) and Paul Okon-Engstler (Köln).

When asked directly whether he wanted to continue coaching the Socceroos, Popovic declined to give a direct answer, instead elaborating on his focus on fostering young talent.

"I love coaching the Socceroos," he said.

"When we qualified there was obviously 12 months before the World Cup.

"I ended up signing [his six-month contract] the last week before the first [World Cup] match, and we started this evolution of the team for 12 months without knowing whether I'd be there or not.

"I've never shied away from the expectation of results.

"But I've always had an eye on the future, and I think that was reflected in the squad we chose, the players we played and how much the team changed in 12 months."

The Socceroos exited the World Cup in the cruellest possible manner, on penalties to Egypt. But the roots of the defeat could be found in the 120 minutes of play, which clearly showed where Australia must improve.

He said he was happy to make those decisions without the security of a long-term contract.

"I had no concerns about whether I signed or not and if I hadn't signed I would have been happy with what I had done and what I have left behind," he said.

"The same will be after the Asian Cup.

"I know the legacy that I will leave behind.

"And if it's someone else that takes it forward, that's fine; if it's me, great, if we agree to do this together," he said.

Popovic's decision to not take up the four-year contract offer gives him the option of pursuing a club contract now that he's been able to shop his talents through the World Cup window.

In his first press conference since returning from the World Cup, Popovic reflected on the decisions he made at the tournament and said there was little he would change.

He drew criticism from commentators for the goalkeeper substitution minutes before the penalty shoot-out against Egypt, which the Socceroos ultimately lost 4-2 when Harry Souttar and Lucas Herrington missed penalties.

Popovic introduced captain Matt Ryan, who hadn't played a minute in the World Cup, for Patrick Beach, who had been outstanding, conceding just three goals in four matches.

He said he would make the same decision again.

"There are many reasons why Matty came in," he said.

"Matty has experience; Matty saved two penalties for us in the qualifiers; Matty saved penalties for [his Spanish club team] Levante.

"Patrick Beach has not saved one penalty in any shoot-out, pretty much.

"In that moment it was very clear to me that Matty should come in.

"And like I said the next day I would have done the same thing."

The Socceroos play their first Asian Cup match against Singapore on January 9, where Popovic said he would continue his youth policy.

There will be a lot of young players probably at the Asian Cup, and that will be done without losing any expectation that I believe that we should be challenging for the Asian Cup," he said.

"Once you're there, you want to win it.

"I think that should happen for Australia."

The team has two friendlies later this month against the might of five-time world champions Brazil in Townsville and Brisbane.

Popovic said the team would have a chance to play another round of matches during the November friendly window, most likely in the Middle East.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.title: Australian found safe in Nepal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.author: Meghna Bali and Patrick Martin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Emergency teams are still working to find people following the floods in Nepal and Tibet. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi)

An eighth Australian has been found after the Nepal-Tibet flood.

The ABC understands that the person was not in the disaster zone.

Thirty-five other Australians remain unaccounted-for following the disaster.

Another Australian who had been unaccounted-for following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet has been found safe.

The ABC understands that the person was not in the disaster zone.

The person is the eighth Australian to be found since the floods, with 35 others still unaccounted-for.

Of those, 34 were on the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage, while one was not part of the tour.

For many Australian families, a relatively small area of mountainous terrain near the Nepal-Tibet border has become critical in the search for survivors, or at least answers.

Most Australians still unaccounted-for went missing near the Gyirong border crossing, north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, or in nearby areas inaccessible following the disaster.

Many were on spiritual pilgrimages to Mount Kailash, a mountain in south-western Tibet that Hindus consider sacred.

In Nepal, rescue teams are continuing to focus on hydropower tunnel projects where some 900 people are missing.

Nepal's army said on Tuesday that 121 people could be trapped inside the tunnel network, with the remainder working elsewhere on the sites.

A Chinese national was rescued by soldiers from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project last week. (AP: Nepal Army)

Nepal's disaster authority chief Dharma Raj Upreti told Reuters they were still focusing on finding survivors.

"Our bigger focus is on the Chilime hydroelectric project, where we believe people are trapped, because there was a canteen, residency and arrangements for food," he said.

He said teams were also focused on tunnels of the Upper Trishuli 3A and 3B projects, which were linked by an interconnected tunnel, where oxygen had been supplied by pipes and further equipment had been sent to build a passage to trapped workers.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said rescue operations would not stop.

"We know our responsibility and its sensitivity. We are translating the humanitarian spirit of the Nepali people into practice through the search and rescue operation," he said in a social media post late on Monday.

At least 1,399 people have been killed and more than 5,400 are still missing in Nepal and Tibet.

Chinese state media reported on Tuesday that none of the bodies recovered in Tibet were foreign nationals.

A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing, Chinese officials said, as they worked to identify the victims.

At least 43 people were killed in Tibet, with another 519 people still missing.

China's foreign ministry announced on Tuesday that a fourth batch of emergency aid had been sent to Nepal to help with rescue efforts.

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/s.title: Billions of dollars and billboards failed in Solomon Islands. What changed?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/s.author: Nick Sas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Foreign Affairs

One of the many Australian government billboards in Solomon Islands' capital, Honiara. (ABC News: Chrisnrita Aumanu-Leong)

In Solomon Islands' capital Honiara, the roadside billboards are a little different.

The nation's number one rice brand Solrice is everywhere, advertising its latest deals. And Telekom, the biggest mobile phone provider, takes almost every second spot, talking about its "outrageous" data plans.

But, curiously, another entity dominates the local billboard scene: the Australian government.

About a dozen big white Australian government billboards are scattered in prime positions off the capital's main road, promoting in English and Solomon Islands pijin all the wonderful things Australia has done for the country.

Bin sapotim yufala longtaem (We've been supporting you for a long time), one of the billboards shouts. Nambawan patna long sekiuriti (Your number one security partner), proclaims another.

A billboard promotes the "Australia-Solomon Islands partnership".   (ABC News: Chrisnrita Aumanu-Leong)

Looking like they've been created in Microsoft Paint by the office intern, they're rather uninspiring; you can just imagine Todd Sampson on The Gruen Transfer rolling his eyes at the sight of them.

The billboards started popping up en masse a few years back in the aftermath of 2019's "The Switch", when Solomon Islands kicked Taiwan out of the country and embraced China, later signing a controversial security pact with Beijing.

Despite spending billions in aid over the past decade on a range of transformative projects, Australia found, with a combative leader at the helm in the form of firebrand Manasseh Sogavare, gaining any traction in the country was hard graft. The billboards are a case in point.

But it turns out Australia didn't need bland roadside advertising to push its narrative in Solomon Islands. Canberra just needed a change in leader.

In his three months as Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale has performed a full directional diplomatic twist for Solomon Islands, the type an Olympic gymnast would be proud of.

From years of panic in Canberra that China could even build a military base in the country, the ABC yesterday revealed that Australia had reached in-principle agreement with Solomon Islands on a sweeping new treaty, with Canberra committing almost a billion dollars to the Pacific nation.

Australia and Solomon Islands have reached an in-principle agreement over a new treaty.

It came just days after Wale fended off a surprise no-confidence motion, forcing him to abruptly leave the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau to save his job (and in all likelihood the treaty itself).

New Zealand's foreign affairs minister Winston Peters even suggested he was "highly suspicious" about whether foreign interference (insert China) had played a part in it all.

Solomon Islands PM and outgoing Pacific Islands Forum chair Matthew Wale makes shock departure from the PIF leaders meeting to deal with looming leadership challenge back home.

But leaving all the James Bond spy stuff for a second, a billion dollars is a lot of money, particularly as political parties such as One Nation pledge to reduce foreign aid and spending in the region.

So, it begs the question, is the Albanese government's multi-billion push in the Pacific worth it?

"Well if you look at the overall defence budget of around $60 billion annually, this [the treaty] is a massive return on investment," Pacific Islands program director at the Lowy Institute, Oliver Nobetau, said.

What Australia will get in return in the treaty has not yet been revealed, but Nobetau said the "likely" scenario would be language that cemented Australia as being the security partner of choice to eventually "shut out" countries such as China.

Solomon Islands still has a security pact with China, which Nobetau said would not be "suddenly cut off".

"Australia will need to demonstrate over time that it can be that security partner pragmatically," he said. "And over time it would want to push a shift towards it, rather than shutting the door on China."

The treaty with Solomon Islands comes on the back of a wave of activity in the region, with the Australian government spending billions to shore up support to become the region's number one security partner, in what it describes as its "permanent contest" with China.

This week, perhaps for the first time in a long time, some sections of the Pacific are signalling a slight adjustment to their relationship with China.

Treaties or agreements with Papua New Guinea (PukPuk Treaty), Fiji (Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance) and Vanuatu (the Nakamal Agreement) have been inked.

Then there's the Falepili Union with Tuvalu (signed in 2023) the Nauru-Australia Treaty (2024), and Canberra is also in discussions with Tonga on the Kaume ' a Ofi agreement.

Looking at a map, it's now pretty much a web of treaties across the Pacific. It's a map no doubt Beijing will be looking at with contempt.

But with its relentless push in the Pacific, its undeniable security focus and constant narrative around China, another question must be posed: Is this being well received by Pacific Islanders?

"I think Australia has got better at listening," Nobetau said.

"You can't bulldoze these agreements through and you have to listen to exactly what it is that Pacific Island countries want."

Back in Solomon Islands, the devil will be in the detail when the full treaty is made public.

But in what one commentator said showed Australia was willing to do "whatever it takes" to get the treaty over the line, we know Australia is committing $68 million for what it called MPs' "development priorities".

These "development priorities" are loosely defined, but appear to resemble the controversial constituency development funds — money given to MPs to essentially use at their discretion.

With so much scrutiny brought on China when it made a similar move, the microscope should rightly be put on this money to make sure it is used appropriately.

That pool of money is no doubt being offered to win favour from potentially sceptical local MPs and their voters, who still question Australia's motives in the country.

A billboard promotes the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.  (ABC News: Nick Sas)

And on that, if there is one topic that will undoubtedly help Australia in its quest to win favour, it is visas.

The leaked texts accessed by the ABC reveal a large sum of money for unspecified "visa improvements", a long-held bugbear of the Pacific community.

I was in Solomon Islands last month and a old friend brought this up.

He told me the Albanese government talks about the "Pacific family" as they force Pacific Islanders through a long-winded and expensive process just to come and visit Australia.

"That's what you do to family?" he said "That's like making your uncle or auntie fill in a form, pay $200 and wait 30 days before being allowed in the house for Christmas lunch."

Either way, with the treaty looking like it will be signed in the coming weeks, one thing's for sure: those billboards in Honiara will need an upgrade soon.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/f.author: Emily Smith

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Paul Bartlett, formerly of Tasmanian Labradoodles, posing with puppies in an image from his business's social media page. (Facebook: Tasmanian Labradoodles)

Elizabeth Anne Bartlett and Paul Alan Bartlett have each been charged with 12 offences that date back to June 2024.

The couple were the owners of Tasmanian Labradoodles.

The matter was adjourned, with the pair next due to appear in December.

A Tasmanian couple has been charged with cruelty to animals and a string of other offences related to their care of hundreds of dogs in northern Tasmania.

Labradoodle breeders Elizabeth Anne Bartlett and Paul Alan Bartlett were listed for a plea hearing in the Launceston Magistrates Court today, but the matter was adjourned until December 8.

The pair were the owners of Tasmanian Labradoodles.

They will each face 12 charges, including three counts each of cruelty to animals.

Court documents show the complaints against the pair were made by Biosecurity Tasmania's Justin Helmich, "on or about" June 25, 2024.

The documents show each is accused of breaching the Animal Welfare Act 1993, for allegedly failing to provide enough nutritional food when caring for approximately 246 dogs, which was reasonably likely to result in "unreasonable and unjustifiable pain or suffering" to the animals.

It said the offence occurred at 13121 Midland Highway, Cleveland.

The pair were also each accused of having 46 dogs with emaciated or poor body condition scores.

Other charges relate to the dogs' condition, with some reported to have severely matted coats.

Other allegations against the pair include failing to provide or seek appropriate medical treatment for a sick or injured dog, failing to ensure sleeping areas were clean, protected from the weather and large enough, and failing to ensure the dogs get enough exercise.

Six of the charges are made under the Animal Welfare Act 1993, while the other six are under the Animal Welfare (Dogs) Regulations 2016.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/q.title: Qld premier takes aim at 'overseas elites' amid questions over Olympic course
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/q.author: Claudia Williams and Aaron Kelly
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Olympic Games Venues

International rowers have raised concerns about the prospect of rowing on the Fitzroy River.  (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Queensland's premier has hit out at "overseas elites" after international rowing leaders questioned Rockhampton's suitability to host events for the Olympic Games.

The Fitzroy River has been selected by the state government for rowing and canoe sprint races for Brisbane's 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The location, which has been subject to debate since last year, requires final sign-off from the sport's governing body.

At last week's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam, representatives from New Zealand, Canada, Germany and the UK raised concerns over its sustainability and location.

On Tuesday, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said he was confident it would be a "world-class" venue and would be held in the beef capital.

"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said.

David Crisafulli says the criticism comes from athletes and supporters "who believe that a regional area is not befitting of them". (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."

The questions followed a virtual presentation by Brisbane 2032 chief executive Cindy Hook and chief sports officer Kit McConnell.

With a map showing the distance between Brisbane and Rockhampton on his laptop, German Rowing Federation president Moritz Petri said he had been contacted by athletes who had heard "rumours about Rockhampton" and had questioned its sustainability.

German Rowing Federation president Moritz Petri said there's a "big question mark" over the use of the Fitzroy River for Olympic rowing. (Supplied)

"They were saying if we are not being in the core of the Olympic city, and not being part of the Olympic village, why we are then not using the former Sydney 2000 regatta course which should still be there?

"Isn't it more sustainable from an environmental perspective?"

British Rowing chief executive Tom Salisbury said concerns had also been voiced to him about "fairness and delivery" at the course.

Rowing Canada president Tracey Black questioned whether building a new facility would be considered if the assessment was not as "favourable" as hoped.

There has been scrutiny over the river's natural bends, the course having a current, being prone to flooding and being home to crocodiles.

As the governing body, World Rowing will have the final sign-off on the venue.

President Jean-Christophe Rolland said its in-depth technical assessment of the course was ongoing and World Rowing would ensure athletes had the "conditions they deserve to compete and perform".

Ms Hook told the congress the organisers would come up with "contingency plans as we would for any venue".

"I also just caution everybody, there are a lot of people talking about this, not always with full facts, especially when it comes to throwing out other potential locations," she said.

Rockhampton MP Donna Kirkland quashed any suggestion rowing and canoe sprint events would be held outside the region.

"I can emphatically say that rowing and canoeing for the Olympic and Paralympic Games will be held right here in Rockhampton," she said.

"Our community have absolutely no concerns around the validity of this as a perfect site, a perfect place to host the Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing."

The Fitzroy River requires final sign-off from the sport’s governing body. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

The latest criticism of the Fitzroy River comes as Rockhampton prepares to host one of Rowing Queensland's pinnacle state regattas on the sport's annual calendar.

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will bring more than 800 school-aged rowers from across Queensland to Rockhampton for three days of racing on the Fitzroy River from September 19 to 21.

It will be the first state-level rowing event held at the venue in five years, placing a renewed spotlight on the Fitzroy River's suitability for major competition.

A major state rowing championship is set to put Rockhampton's proposed Olympic venue under the spotlight, but local representatives have been warned against discussing the Games in media interviews.

Rowing Queensland last month imposed strict media restrictions on participants preparing for the state championships, with Olympics questions "off-limits" in any interviews.

Ms Kirkland said if it was good enough for local schoolchildren to compete on it was good enough for Olympians.

"We're going to have the state rowing competition for our schools right here," she said.

"All the lanes are in, they're ready to go, they'll be rowing, and if it's good enough for them to row on the Fitzroy River, then it's good enough for the Europeans, for the Americans, for the Canadians, for those coming from Japan and China, all around the world."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/b.author: Matt Brann
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Beef Cattle Farming

Benmara Station has been snapped up by UK-based livestock producer Shaun Davis. (Supplied: CBRE)

Benmara Station in the Northern Territory has sold for $26 million.

The property has been bought by a UK livestock producer.

Previous owner WealthCheck had planned to run a large carbon project on Benmara, but it never happened.

Benmara Station in the Barkly region of the Northern Territory has sold for $26 million, which is $14 million less than its last sale price in 2023.

The 450,000 hectare station has been bought by UK-based livestock producer Shaun Davis, trading under the newly formed Benmara Land Holdings.

Located about 100 kilometres west of the Queensland border, the station had been "largely destocked" over the past 18 months.

According to documents from the NT Land Titles Office, the property settled on September 2, ending a very complicated period of ownership.

Benmara Station on the Barkly Tablelands was bought in 2023 for $40 million. (ABC Rural: Daniel Fitzgerald)

Benmara was last purchased in 2023 for $40 million bare (no cattle) by Sam Mitchell, the founder of Sydney-based investment company WealthCheck.

It was one in a series of significant NT property purchases by WealthCheck, including Conways Station in Arnhem Land for $14.5 million, and also Maryfield and Limbunya Stations for more than $100 million.

WealthCheck and its US investment partner Hartree had plans to run a large carbon project on Benmara.

The station had a carbon project registered with the Clean Energy Regulator (CER) based on the controversial Human Induced Regeneration (HIR) methodology, where the landholder makes changes to allow vegetation on the property to regrow and store more carbon.

According to the CER website, the Benmara carbon project never generated any carbon credits and the project was revoked in December 2025.

The HIR methodology has since been shelved by the federal government, with no new projects to be registered under the method.

Questions raised about the integrity of multi-billion-dollar carbon credit schemes. (ABC 7.30: Ashlynne McGhee)

In 2024, WealthCheck went into liquidation and Benmara was listed for sale in 2025, "priced to sell at $35 million or nearest offer".

ABC Rural contacted CBRE Agribusiness, but agents were not able to comment on the sale to Mr Davis.

On its website, CBRE said Benmara was offered with an estimated carrying capacity of 17,500 adult equivalents, although the property had been "largely destocked over the past 18 months".

"The property offers ample potential for further development," it said.

Meanwhile Maryfield and Limbunya Stations, previously owned by WealthCheck, have been relisted for sale this week.

Benmara is a 450,000 hectare station and was bought in 2026 with an estimated carrying capacity of 17,500 adult equivalents. (Supplied: CBRE)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/w.title: Packed courtroom for Neo-Nazi group's appeal against ban
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/w.author: Jade Toomey
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-08/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

White Australia's leader Thomas Sewell and supporters gathered outside the High Court. (ABC News: Jade Toomey)

White supremacist organisation White Australia has made opening arguments in its appeal against new federal hate speech laws under which it was banned.

The group argues the laws lack guardrails, while the Commonwealth says the group is seeking protection for its violent rhetoric, by claiming to be a political party.

The matter is being heard in the High Court on September 8 and 9, with judgment not expected for several weeks or months.

There was barely a seat spare in the gallery of the High Court of Australia's largest courtroom this morning, when one of the country's highest-profile neo-Nazi groups began making its case against new federal hate speech laws.

Members of White Australia and legal teams, 12 members strong, had quickly filled Courtroom One, spilling observers into the upstairs mezzanine and other spare courtrooms where, prepared for the overflow, a video feed of the proceedings was playing.

Even though it determines the country's most important legal decisions, it is unusual for the High Court to be so popular.

But the constitutional case it is hearing will have significant legal and political consequences.

Security was increased on the first day of the hearings (ABC News: Jade Toomey)

Laws introduced by the federal government in January, in the wake of the Bondi Beach attack, are being challenged by White Australia and its leader, convicted criminal Thomas Sewell, as constitutionally invalid.

The group, also known as the National Socialist Network, had been attempting to form a political party to run in federal elections when it was effectively outlawed in May by the federal government, which used the new laws to declare the party a prohibited hate group.

White Australia and Sewell argue the laws burden the implied freedom of political communication, breach the separation of powers, and were not validly made within the Commonwealth's range of powers.

But even before the hearings got underway, the High Court forecourt was busy.

Several legal experts believe there is a significant prospect that Neo-Nazi group White Australia may have its ban overturned by the High Court.

Sewell was pacing quietly near a water fountain, where a group of men dressed in suits — many bearing reflective sunglasses in bright colours — were waiting for the court doors to open.

Other supporters arrived with a dedicated camera operator to film content in front of the High Court's tall glass facade.

A visible police presence accompanied them — while there are often a couple of officers on patrol when the High Court sits, it is unusual to see so many.

And of course there were cameras, as press gallery journalists ventured down from Capital Hill to cover the case.

The group, represented by barristers Peter King and Shahed Sharify argued the total ban was like using a "sledgehammer on a nut."

Even if the group's beliefs were "unpopular or controversial", they did not justify political overreach, Mr King said, adding that its members may be "awful but lawful."

The case is set down for two days. (ABC News: Gregory Nelson)

Their submissions relied on the historical legal precedent set by the federal government's failed attempt to ban the Australian Communist Party in the 1950s.

The plaintiffs also criticised the hate speech laws for lacking "tailoring" — guardrails that it argued should curtail the government's wide-ranging power to ban a group.

The laws, White Australia said, offer banned groups no reviews, no hearings, no written submissions, no sliding scale of punishment, no carve-outs for fair comment, no retrospective time limit, and no ability to subpoena the minister for their reasons behind their decision to prohibit.

The Commonwealth, led by barrister Brendan Lim, said the laws served a legitimate purpose of protecting the Australian community from organisations that engaged in seriously harmful conduct and posed a threat to Commonwealth security.

It argued White Australia's claim to be a "political party" was a cynical attempt to attract legal protection for prohibited speech.

"[The group] is a neo-Nazi organisation that has engaged in violent conduct and violent rhetoric calculated to inspire violent conduct," the Commonwealth submitted.

The High Court will also hear from interveners, including the Free Speech Union and state attorneys-general, before White Australia is afforded a chance to respond.

The hearings will continue into Wednesday.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japanese helicopters to join Indonesia’s wildfires battle this weekend
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
JAKARTA – Japan will deploy three CH-47 Chinook transport helicopters and their 180 crew members to Indonesia this weekend to help contain wildfires, Indonesian defense officials said Tuesday.

Indonesia has intensified efforts to tackle wildfires that have been raging for months, focusing on six hardest-hit provinces on the islands of Sumatra and Borneo, where 76,933 hectares (190,106 acres) of land have been burned.

The Japanese helicopters will arrive on Wednesday and will be based in Pontianak in West Kalimantan, the worst-affected province, where they will conduct flight tests prior to operations from Sept. 12 to 19, said Tri Budi Utomo, an Indonesian Defense Ministry official.

The spread of the wildfires in the disaster-prone archipelago has been exacerbated by the onset of dry weather from June, with Indonesia deploying more than 50 aircraft for water bombing and seeding activities and expecting September to be its biggest battle.

The fires have caused widespread haze and spikes in air pollution levels in affected areas, prompting concern in neighboring Singapore and Malaysia.

The Chinooks are en route to Indonesia aboard the JS Kunisaki, a vessel previously deployed for disaster relief and humanitarian exercises, along with 150 of its personnel. The operation will be adaptive and dynamic based on the movement of fire hotspots, Tri told a press conference.

The conditions of forest and land fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra were still dynamic and the Indonesian military has deployed thousands of personnel to contain fire via land and air, Tri said.

The main challenge in containing fires was finding water sources, said Muhammad Nas, a spokesperson of the military, adding it had started drilling water sources in several areas.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Japan will deploy three Chinooks and 180 crew members to Indonesia this weekend. Indonesia has intensified efforts to tackle wildfires that have been raging for months. The spread of the wildfires in the disaster-prone archipelago has been exacerbated by the onset of dry weather.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Kenichi Horie, 88, to sail solo across Pacific Ocean — again
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
NISHINOMIYA, HYOGO PREF. – Ocean adventurer Kenichi Horie, 88, said Tuesday he will try to sail solo and nonstop across the Pacific Ocean by yacht next spring.

If successful, he will break the world record for the oldest person to complete such a feat, a record he himself set at age 83.

Horie, a resident of Ashiya, Hyogo Prefecture, plans to depart from San Francisco in March and sail to Japan, with the voyage expected to take about two months.

“The magma of my desire to sail has erupted,” Horie said at a news conference in Nishinomiya, Hyogo, on Tuesday, his 88th birthday.

“I do not want this voyage to be my last,” he added, expressing his intention to take on further challenges.

In March 2022, Horie, then 83, departed from San Francisco beneath the Golden Gate Bridge and reached his destination in the Kii Channel off Cape Hinomisaki in Wakayama Prefecture in June. Guinness World Records recognized the voyage as the oldest solo Pacific crossing.

In 1962, when Horie was 23, he departed Nishinomiya aboard a small yacht, the Mermaid, and became the first person in the world to sail solo and nonstop across the Pacific Ocean.

He later chronicled the experience in a book, titled “Kodoku: Sailing Alone Across the Pacific,” which became a bestseller.

He plans to depart from San Francisco in March and sail to Japan, with the voyage expected to take about two months. Horie set the world record for the oldest person to complete such a feat at age 83.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: AI-discovered lung drug reverses aging markers in study
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Amber Tong
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
An experimental lung disease drug developed using artificial intelligence showed promise in reversing biological signs of aging, pointing to broader potential use of the treatment, according to its developer.

In a midstage study, Insilico Medicine’s drug rentosertib helped reduce biological age as measured by six different aging clocks examining chemical changes in the body, according to an analysis published in Nature Biotechnology on Monday. Those who were given a placebo saw little change in their biological age on those same clocks, the Hong Kong-listed company said.

“If your biological age is lower, you are likely to die later,” the AI drug discovery startup’s CEO, Alex Zhavoronkov, said in an interview. He cautioned that the results are still early and the long-term health effects of the drug on larger groups of people are unknown. The analysis included 42 patients with a chronic lung disease.

Aging clocks are tools that estimate someone’s biological age, as opposed to chronological age, reflecting how well their cells and tissues are functioning. The six aging clocks used in the study — developed by teams at Insilico, Harvard University, China’s Peking University and others — each use different metrics and methods.

While longevity enthusiasts have long embraced the repurposing of existing medications to delay aging, efforts to develop novel anti-aging drugs have often ended in failure. But with the advent of GLP-1 treatments whose benefits now appear to extend far beyond weight loss and diabetes, major pharmaceutical players are increasingly showing interest in the field.

Companies including Insilico have chosen to focus on dual-use therapies that can tackle age-related ailments while helping people live longer along the way. The latest study is part of a phase 2 trial that also measured rentosertib’s efficacy in treating idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Rentosertib is currently in a late-stage clinical trial in China for the incurable lung disease.

Insilico plans to run similar analyses for at least half of the drugs in its pipeline.

AI promises to compress drug research timelines, increase chances of success and propose ideas humans may not otherwise have. Insilico first identified the target behind rentosertib as one implicated in aging with an AI tool that trawls through large amounts of data to rank potential targets. It then designed and refined the drug using another that screens molecules virtually and suggests ways to optimize them.

For its analysis, Insilico collected blood from patients at various time points during the trial and partnered with external researchers to analyze changes in proteins. Four weeks after the initial dose, patients taking rentosertib saw their average biological age dropped by as much as six years, although the benefit narrowed later in the trial.

The study offers a template for future anti-aging drug development, Zhavoronkov said. While it’s currently impossible to win regulatory approval specifically for aging, he suggested the results would open the door for doctors to prescribe or test rentosertib for aging — or age-related diseases — once the drug is approved for other uses.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Insilico Medicine’s drug rentosertib helped reduce biological age as measured by six different aging clocks. The study included 42 patients with a chronic lung disease. Those who were given a placebo saw little change in their biological age on those same clocks.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan issues highest level heavy rain warning as flood risk rises
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Japan issued its highest-level emergency warning for heavy rain and flooding in some parts of Aichi and Gifu prefectures on Tuesday evening.

The Level 5 warning was issued for the Shonai River, which flows through both of the prefectures.

“It is necessary to ensure your safety by moving to higher ground that is less prone to flooding,” Takuya Hosomi, the Japan Meteorological Agency’s chief forecaster, said during a news conference.

The special warning affects 14 cities and towns. In Aichi Prefecture, these include the capital Nagoya, and the cities of Seto, Kasugai, Komaki, Ichinomiya, Inazawa, Kiyosu, Kitanagoya, Ama, as well as the towns of Toyoyama, Oji, and Kanie. In Gifu Prefecture, the warning was issued for the cities of Tajimi and Toki.

A level 5 warning urges residents to assess their surroundings and move to the safest possible location, such as a nearby tall building or the second floor or higher of their own homes.

The JMA said torrential rainfall in the hour through 4:53 p.m. hit a record 104.5 millimeters in Nagoya.

In parts of Chikusa, Moriyama and Meito wards, people were warned not to linger in underground areas, as drainage systems are unable to keep up with the incessant rain, and there is a risk of water flowing into underpasses, underground shopping arcades and underground parking garages.

Images posted to social media showed cars driving through roads with the waterline rising up to their doors in the city.

NHK also reported that underpasses and other areas in the city’s Minato Ward had flooded, forcing people to abandon their vehicles.

Authorities told the public broadcaster that all occupants of the vehicles were able to escape on their own, and that no one was trapped.

The Level 5 warning was issued for the Shonai River, which flows through both of the prefecture. The special warning affects 14 cities and towns in Aichi Prefecture.

Japan is tightening measures against private jet pilots who fail to follow instructions from air traffic control, with three strikes resulting in a ban from Tokyo’s Haneda Airport.

The move comes as the government tries to attract business jets and other private jets to airports nationwide. But as the number of private jet flights increase, so too have pilots who fail to comply with traffic controls, which could lead to large-scale accidents.

Last year, there were five instances of foreign-owned private jets not following instructions from air traffic control, according to the transport ministry.
