https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Key ministers, LDP leaders expected to keep positions amid personnel changes
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Eric Johnston
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi appears to be opting for continuity and stability ahead of the autumn session of parliament, as key members of her Cabinet and the Liberal Democratic Party’s leadership are expected to remain when personnel changes are announced next week.

Takaichi secured a mandate Tuesday morning during a party officials meeting to carry out party executive appointments as early as Sept. 16. Those will be followed by a Cabinet reshuffle, but major changes may not be coming, especially in the party leadership where it appears policy chief Takayuki Kobayashi could remain.

LDP Vice President Taro Aso, the party’s powerful behind-the-scenes kingmaker who turns 86 on Sept. 20 and whose support was crucial for Takaichi winning the LDP presidency last year, is likely to remain in his position. LDP Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki — Aso’s brother-in-law — and Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, a close ally of Takaichi, are also expected to stay on.

Kobayashi appears likely to stay put or, possibly, receive a Cabinet post. As policy chief, he played a key role in getting controversial legislation — including that to revise the Imperial House Law, one establishing a secondary capital concept and another that punished acts of vandalizing the national flag — passed in parliament.

Kobayashi maintaining his current position means he would take the lead on the party’s parliamentary legislation this autumn, particularly on a bill to reduce the food consumption tax from 8% to 1% that has many LDP members concerned about how the Takaichi administration plans to cover the lost tax revenue.

Remaining policy chief or having a Cabinet position could also make it more difficult for Kobayashi to challenge Takaichi in next year’s presidential election. He ran against her in last year’s contest and is considered a potential rival next year.

The prime minister may keep Shinjiro Koizumi as defense minister for similar reasons as with Kobayashi — to have an experienced hand at the post and to keep Koizumi, a potential rival who lost the presidency to Takaichi in a runoff last year, at bay.

Other key LDP members who could be part of a reshuffle include Minister of Internal Affairs Yoshimasa Hayashi and Koichi Hagiuda, a powerful senior LDP executive. Hayashi also ran against Takaichi last year and may do so again.

Hagiuda was caught up in a slush fund scandal and received a one-year suspension from the party in 2024. Though on good terms with Takaichi, there is some concern within the LDP that appointing him to a Cabinet position could create public backlash that hurts the party.

We picked a helluva time to go RVing in Canada. My wife and I crossed the border in Maine as recent trade talks in Washington were collapsing, and we awoke to news of a major escalation in tariffs and even talk of war. It made for some awkward moments in the days that followed.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Tokyo’s Taito Ward, long popular with tourists, looks to ban minpaku in certain areas
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Spencer Landers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Tokyo’s Taito Ward, home to popular tourist spots such as Asakusa and Ueno, is moving to ban minpaku in certain parts of the ward beginning next year, as local governments across Japan begin restricting the short-term private-residence lodging system.

An ordinance was submitted to the ward assembly Tuesday that proposes effectively ending the program for new minpaku in residential areas and locations where traditional hotels and inns are restricted. It will do so by limiting the number of days that such minpaku can operate to zero.

The ward cited increasing reports of bad behavior such as improper trash disposal and loud noises as being behind the new ordinance.

Both the number of minpaku in Taito and the number of complaints stemming from them have risen dramatically in recent years. The number of new minpaku applications tripled in 2025 compared with the year prior, hitting nearly 1,400, while the number of complaints accordingly increased fourfold to 257 cases.

In addition to the proposed policy on new minpaku, Taito Ward will begin enforcing fresh restrictions on all minpaku later this year. While the ward currently allows them to operate on any given day up to the nationwide legal limit of 180 days a year, beginning in October they will only be able to accommodate guests on weekends and holidays.

The minpaku program allows approved operators to provide lodging in their private residences. Since starting in June 2018 as a way to meet higher tourist demand and fill houses vacated by Japan’s diminishing population, the system’s popularity has rapidly grown, especially in recent years.

Taito’s potential ban comes as other municipalities around the country are introducing restrictions. Since July, when the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism notified local governments that they had the authority to limit minpaku operations, Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward as well as the city of Kyoto have moved to implement bans, both referencing an increasing number of local complaints.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Taito Ward will begin enforcing new restrictions on minpaku in certain parts of the ward beginning next year. The number of new minpakaku applications tripled in 2025 compared with the year prior. The new policy will limit the number of days such minpkus can operate to zero.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan not confident that U.S. relations will improve after Trump, survey finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Elizabeth Beattie
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Japan views the United States as a necessary partner, but has low confidence it will become “a better ally” after U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term ends, according to a new study.

Just 26% of Japanese surveyed said that the U.S. will improve as an ally post-Trump, compared with 45% of Australians and 46% of Americans, according to the study by the University of Sydney’s United States Studies Center.

The researchers polled more than 1,000 people from countries that make up “the Quad” security grouping — Japan, the U.S., Australia and India.

“Japanese respondents are much less confident,” the study noted, referring to their views of Tokyo’s security ally once the U.S. president leaves office.

Trump’s transactional approach to U.S. alliances and his freewheeling use of tariffs or the threat of them has tested diplomatic ties.

Around 53% of Japanese surveyed said Trump’s second term has been a negative for Japan, with just 8% viewing it positively for the country.

Despite this, the countries surveyed still characterize their relations with the U.S. overall as very important, with 36% of Japanese respondents feeling that the alliance with the U.S. is more necessary than ever. The same sentiment was voiced by 44% of Indians and 49% of Australians.

But while the U.S. relationship is viewed as vital, in Japan, confidence in the country as a protective force has been dented.

While in 2023, 77% of Japanese surveyed felt confident that the United States would come to their country’s aid if they were attacked by China, that figure sank to 60% in this year’s survey.

Tokyo’s ties with Beijing have deteriorated since November, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi publicly commented about Japan intervening militarily in the event of an attack on Taiwan by China. Despite this, there was a slight decline in the belief among Japanese that an armed conflict with China will occur within the next 10 years.

A majority in Japan, 66%, view China as a danger while 28% see it as an economic partner, with a similar picture among Americans (55% danger, 43% economic partner), and Indians (59% danger, 43% economic partner). Australia, however, stands in stark contrast, with 64% viewing China more as an economic partner, while 47% consider it a threat.

Americans were also more critical of their government’s “handling” of China, being the largest Quad member to characterize it as “too aggressive,” with 20% responding in this way. Only 4% of Australians and 7% of Japanese felt the same way about their respective governments’ approaches.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japanese carmakers brace for profit hit after yen strengthens
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Nicholas Takahashi
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Toyota Motor and other Japanese carmakers risk taking a hit to their bottom lines after the yen strengthened to its highest level in more than six months.

The currency traded just above ¥153 against the dollar on Tuesday, its strongest level since February. That’s squeezing many of Japan’s export-focused automakers, which have partly based their earnings forecasts on weaker yen assumptions.

At ¥160 yen to the dollar, Toyota has the most bearish projection. The world’s biggest automaker said in August its annual operating income falls by about ¥50 billion ($326 million) each time the yen appreciates by ¥1.

The swings are a source of uncertainty for Japanese automakers, highlighting the economic cost of a volatile currency. A stronger yen erodes the value of overseas earnings when they’re brought back to Japan, hurting companies that generate much of their sales in the U.S. and Europe.

The yen is currently outperforming the assumptions of all Japanese carmakers except Nissan Motor, which projects it at ¥150 against the dollar for the fiscal year through March 2027. Toyota and Suzuki Motor revised their projections upward in August from May.

Japan’s automakers have long embraced conservative currency assumptions, helping them to meet or exceed forecasts when posting results. Many of them produce cars and even parts closer to final sales markets, creating a natural hedge because production expenses can be paid in the same currency.

Toyota is better equipped to tolerate the risks that come with adopting a weaker-yen assumption. Its earnings are among the most global in the industry and are spread across financial services and other businesses, giving it additional operational flexibility to offset adverse swings.

While the weak yen has threatened to drive up inflation and import prices in Japan, it had offered the island nation’s largest exporters a much-needed respite from U.S. tariffs, soaring oil prices and supply chain snags.

In late June, the yen was trading at its lowest since 1986, prompting the U.S. and Japan to make their first joint intervention in 15 years.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: The yen is currently outperforming the assumptions of all Japanese carmakers except Nissan Motor. The swings are a source of uncertainty for Japanese automakers, highlighting the economic cost of a volatile currency.

It started at the end of 2023, when a company called Evergreen Hill Enterprise spent $669 million on a specialized paper business in the United States. A year later, Evergreen paid €360 million ($418 million) for an Austrian manufacturer of cigarette papers.

In all, some nine entities based in Singapore and London tied to the billionaire Hartono family have invested at least $1.4 billion abroad, according to filings and interviews with people close to the group.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Trump and Xi should align on artificial Intelligence
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
GENEVA – When Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump meet in Washington this month, AI will be near the top of the agenda. If they view the issue through the lens of technological rivalry and mutual suspicion, reaching any kind of understanding will be nearly impossible. But there is a way to reframe their thinking about the technology that puts them on the same side — and marks the first step toward confronting the existential challenge AI may well pose.

The current agenda for the U.S.-China summit appears centered on keeping powerful AI models safe and out of the hands of terrorists and criminals. But crowding this goal are the two sides’ competitive grievances, from semiconductor restrictions (on the Chinese side) to open-source models and unauthorized distillation (on the U.S. side).

All of these issues rest on a single, unexamined premise: that AI is a tool which is, and will remain, under control. This premise limits the conversation to questions such as, “How does my side gain a competitive edge in AI?” and “Who gets to access, let alone control, the technology?” Questions outside this premise — in particular, “What happens when the tool becomes something more?” — cannot be asked.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: If Japan is behind the bond market’s ruckus, then good
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Jonathan Levin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
A new explanation for the global ruckus in sovereign bonds is becoming popular: Maybe markets and economies are simply returning to normal. After all, weren’t the preceding years marked by an extraordinarily abnormal constellation of economic circumstances, policy responses and borrowing costs?

What’s missing is an acknowledgement that one normalization — the one afoot in Japan — matters much more than the others, because of how extraordinarily far that country’s $4.3 trillion economy had ventured from the status quo. Now that the pendulum is swinging back, the spillovers are showing up everywhere, but the outcome may not look anything like what the doomers describe.

After a quarter century battling deflation and almost a decade of negative interest rates, the Bank of Japan has been raising policy rates (and may do so again this month) and reducing its purchases of sovereign bonds it had conducted to stimulate the economy (which it’s on schedule to do again in the final quarter of the year). As a result, Japan’s 10-year note yields have climbed to the highest in around 30 years. But they’re not unusual given the circumstances; they’re what you would expect in an economy with moderate inflation and positive (though still uninspiring) real economic growth.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: GPIF still considering need for asset allocation review, minister says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Nao Sano
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Health minister Kenichiro Ueno, who oversees the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), said the fund is still considering whether a review of its asset allocation is needed.

The fund “decided in March that there wasn’t a need for it, but my understanding is that it’s continuing to consider the matter in an appropriate way,” Ueno said at a regular news conference in Tokyo on Tuesday. He also said that the investment environment hasn’t diverged too much from the GPIF’s assumptions for its portfolio.

The GPIF’s allocation decisions are closely watched by traders around the world due to its mammoth size, overseeing about ¥318 trillion ($2.1 trillion) in assets at the end of June. That means that on paper a 1 percentage-point change in allocations can translate to more than ¥3 trillion in fund flows.

The pension fund now tries to hold 25% each of four asset classes in its investment portfolio — domestic bonds, overseas debt, Japanese shares and foreign equities. But analysts have said that after surges in Japanese bond yields in past months, there’s scope for GPIF to expand its allocation target for domestic bonds.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama have also called on Japanese pension funds to park more funds in the home market.

GPIF’s management committee convened on Aug. 21, its first publicly announced meeting during the holiday month in seven years. The gathering spurred speculation that the fund may change its allocation.

NEW YORK – Naomi Osaka’s fourth-round U.S. Open defeat on Monday extended her wait for another Grand Slam title, but she put the setback into perspective, saying motherhood and life beyond tennis had changed how she viewed success.

The Japanese player won the last of her four major titles at the Australian Open in 2021, before stepping away from the sport and giving birth to daughter Shai three years ago.

Despite encouraging results since returning to the tour, including a U.S. Open semifinal and Wimbledon quarterfinal, Osaka said so much had happened in her life that the drought felt both long and short.

“I had a kid, you know? There’s a lot that happened in that time,” Osaka said after her 6-1, 6-4 defeat to Elena Rybakina.

“If I reflect on my career and the things I’ve been able to do, there’s nothing that I regret or there’s nothing that I’m sad about.

“If I win another Grand Slam, it’s not going to change my life. That’s crazy that I can say that, because I remember the first slam that I won, it was a huge whirlwind. I think it wouldn’t feel as long.”

Osaka won her first Grand Slam title at the U.S. Open in 2018, repeating the feat in 2020. She claimed another major at Melbourne Park in 2019.

The 28-year-old, who had to manage an Achilles injury in her loss to Rybakina on Monday, said she was continuing to learn from her defeats.

“Today, if I was to say I’m sad, I was just sad that I couldn’t push off on my foot. I’m sad that I couldn’t do what I had set out to do,” she added.

“If I think about my life, my daughter is healthy, everyone in my family is great. I had an opportunity to play this slam. I got as far as I could. So it’s only up from here.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Emmet Sheehan struck out 10 in his return from the minor leagues and the Los Angeles Dodgers turned Shohei Ohtani’s return to the lineup into a 6-3 victory over the visiting Cincinnati Reds on Monday.

Sheehan (5-8), who lost his roster spot when left-hander Tarik Skubal joined the rotation last month, threw 5⅔ innings of one-run ball. He gave up three hits and one walk while tying his career high for strikeouts.

Teoscar Hernandez hit a three-run homer as Los Angeles (87-57) extended its winning streak to five games.

Ohtani went 0-for-3 with a walk and two strikeouts after sitting out the previous four games because of left knee, right biceps and neck discomfort. He is 2-for-26 (.077) with no RBIs in his past seven games.

Elly De La Cruz and Eugenio Suarez homered while Chase Burns threw three scoreless innings for the Reds (69-75). Cincinnati lost the series opener to the two-time defending World Series champions after winning three consecutive series against playoff contenders.

Burns allowed no hits, walked one and had five strikeouts in an abbreviated outing. The Reds are limiting the 23-year-old All-Star’s usage down the stretch.

De La Cruz gave Cincinnati a 1-0 lead on Sheehan’s fourth pitch when he sent a fastball over the wall in center field with one out in the first inning. It was his 24th homer of the season.

The Dodgers had two runners aboard with two outs in the fifth when Miguel Rojas hit a high chopper to third that Ke’Bryan Hayes fielded before making a wild throw. Hernandez and Alex Call scored on the play.

Los Angeles’ Freddie Freeman and Max Muncy walked in the sixth inning against Brandon Williamson (3-4), and Hernandez followed his 13th long ball for a 5-1 lead. Hernandez, who finished 2-for-3, is now 13-for-29 (.448) with 11 RBIs over his past eight games.

Suarez inched Cincinnati closer with a home run to center in the seventh, his 22nd.

The Reds had runners on second and third with one out in the eighth inning against left-hander Jack Dreyer but scored just once, on a groundout by pinch hitter Dane Myers to pull within 5-3. A pinch-hit sacrifice fly from Will Smith in the eighth gave the Dodgers their final run.

Los Angeles right-hander Evan Phillips pitched a perfect ninth inning for his first save of the season.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Spain’s renewables experience shows battery storage needed for decarbonization
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
Spain’s big bet on renewables got started early, if slowly.

By the mid-1990s, the industry was still so low-tech that when a turbine blade broke at what was then Spain’s largest wind farm, Jose Manuel Entrecanales would bring in a windsurfer friend to repair it with the same equipment he used to fix surfboards.

It was an extremely rudimentary and artisanal business,” said Entrecanales, now chairman and CEO at Acciona, one of Spain’s largest developers of renewable projects. “The business was barely profitable, but for us, renewables were a business opportunity and a backdoor to access the electricity sector.”

Today, renewables account for about 60% of electricity on the Spanish grid, compared with about 50% across the European Union and one-third globally. That bold bet has lowered Spain’s power bills — which are now cheaper than they were before the latest Middle East conflict or the invasion of Ukraine — and put the country on track to meet its 2030 renewable targets. Spain is both ahead of the clean-power curve and the fastest-growing major economy in Europe, proof that deploying green energy at massive scale isn’t at odds with growth.

But as the renewables sector matures and a brutal European summer of wildfires and deadly heat waves underscores the energy transition’s urgency, the Spanish model is reaching its limits.

Solar and wind installations can only take the country so far down the path to decarbonization, according to experts, companies and government officials. Massive investment in large batteries and the power grid is also badly needed, and investors and foreign governments are paying close attention to the challenge Spain faces.

Renewable-energy generation this summer is the highest on record, according to provisional data from power-grid operator Red Electrica.

Surging investment in solar over the past 15 years has created a glut of electricity so large that Spain’s energy prices have increasingly fallen well below zero during peak times. Solar parks have plummeted in value, leaving investors looking for an exit and pushing some developers out of business.

At the same time, the inherent instability of renewable energy has led to sharp swings in power frequency, contributing to the massive blackout that briefly plunged the Iberian Peninsula into darkness in April last year.

Battery storage, and lots of it, can help fix oversupply by absorbing excess solar power during the day and feeding the grid at night. Batteries can also stabilize the grid by releasing stored electricity when power drops, such as when the weather changes. Unlike the nuclear and gas power plants that currently serve the purpose, batteries need no time to ramp up and can be turned on instantaneously.

But on this next step of the energy transition, Spain is lagging behind.

The country had about 400 megawatts of installed battery storage capacity in 2025, according to BloombergNEF. That’s less than 2% of the 22.5 gigawatts the country is targeting by 2030. While BNEF expects installed capacity to more than triple in 2026 and see continued growth in the years that follow, delayed regulation and the lack of a capacity market to help ensure energy-supply security have so far discouraged investors.

The government has sped up permitting processes and is subsidizing storage installations, said Joan Groizard, the country’s secretary of state for energy.

“Some changes you don’t see coming until suddenly they’re on top of you — I think that’s the case with storage in Spain,” Groizard said. “We’re right at the beginning of an exponential curve that will have a significant path over the next few months.”

But whether or not red tape is removed, there are still technological limitations, said Patricio Alvarez, a senior analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. Large batteries that can store power for two to four hours a day can compete with gas on costs, but longer-term storage is still expensive.

“You can’t fix this problem just with money,” Alvarez said. “It needs the technology to get there too.”

The Iberian Peninsula is an energy island, with few power-grid links to France and the rest of Europe. That has protected Spain and smaller neighbor Portugal from the recent energy price spikes that have hit much of the region.

The natural environment has also set the stage for Spain’s renewable ambitions, with plentiful wind and sun, large swaths of empty land on which to build energy projects and a vast network of reservoirs to provide hydropower. Over the past 10 years, the overall economics of clean energy have vastly improved and Spain’s capacity has more than doubled.

“Our electricity mix is more decarbonized than ever and it’s also more competitive on costs,” Groizard said. “We have gone from having one of Europe’s five highest power bills to one of the lowest, both for homes and industries.”

But while cheap energy is a near-term boon for consumers, low prices are weighing on energy-sector investors.

Prices go into negative territory when the grid is oversupplied, forcing power plants to curtail production. The phenomenon isn’t unique to Spain, but the country has had 681 hours of negative power prices this year through Sept. 4, exceeding the number recorded in the whole of 2025.

Larger solar producers generally have long-term contracts that ensure fixed prices, but smaller companies are vulnerable to spot-market volatility. At least four Spanish projects or companies have been offered for sale in recent months, people familiar with the matter said in June.

Very low prices mean it’s hard to sign long-term power contracts that give investors confidence to keep developing projects, said Alvarez. “The signals get distorted,” he said. “Investors are spooked.”

Last year’s blackout, the largest in Europe’s recent history, also raised questions of whether the deployment of renewables had gone too far, too fast. More than 50 million people were left without electricity for nearly half a day, taking electronic payment systems offline and closing businesses temporarily.

While the causes are still being investigated, several preliminary findings indicate that the Spanish grid wasn’t equipped to handle the sudden swings in power frequency coming from solar farms in the country’s south that day.

Grid investment is capped at 0.3% of Spain’s gross domestic product, the lowest spending-to-renewables ratio among EU countries and the U.K., according to BNEF. The grid also has little capacity left, meaning new renewable power, battery storage and data center projects are struggling to connect.

These constraints could slow investment and ultimately drive companies elsewhere, said Marta Sanchez, a partner at EY Spain who leads the firm’s energy-sector work.

The government has announced it will invest €13.6 billion ($15.8 billion) in the country’s grid through the end of this decade. The plan will increase the network’s high-voltage capacity 14-fold, allowing industrial projects worth around €7 billion that are currently halted to go forward, according to government calculations.

“The lack of grid capacity prevents demand from growing — if demand doesn’t grow, it limits the deployment of additional renewable energy,” Sanchez said. “To continue Spain’s successful rollout of renewable energy, demand needs to keep growing. And to grow demand, we need the grid.”

Large-scale battery storage can help to smooth out supply, retaining and releasing energy as required. But Spain has long struggled with installing big batteries.

Until recently, developers who wanted to add a battery to an existing solar or wind farm — a straightforward practice in other parts of the world — needed to go through the permitting process from the start. Slow guidance from the EU on capacity markets has delayed the establishment of a system where large storage can compete with gas and nuclear.

In recent years, the government has given close to €2 billion under different programs that include assistance for storage systems and has made permitting easier, according to energy state secretary Groizard.

“We are seeing a lot of interest in the sector,” he said. “We have thousands, literally thousands of megawatts of storage in different phases of approval.”

Battery businesses that try to take advantage of peaks and troughs in power prices can be profitable as long as the swings in spot markets are sharp, said Entrecanales.

While remuneration models are needed to encourage batteries, the more storage in the system, the more stable prices are and the less attractive that model becomes.

“If everyone installs them, highs and lows are gone,” Entrecanales said. “It’s one of the big risks in batteries — they have an element of cannibalism.”

And battery technology is still not mature, according to Alvarez. The economics are forecast to continue to improve with time and scale, but in most markets, very long-term storage is not yet cheaper than fossil-fuel alternatives.

“The risk is that batteries don’t become cheap enough to meet those lower power prices in Spain,” Alvarez said.

Still, firms like Grenergy Renovables SA see opportunity. Founded in 2007, the Madrid-based clean-energy producer initially built some solar projects in Spain before shifting to focus on foreign markets. The company once again sees potential at home.

“Spain has a historic opportunity to become an energy island with much more competitive energy than the rest of the continent — but that requires agile permitting,” Grenergy CEO David Ruiz de Andres said. “Batteries at a massive scale will shift the paradigm.”

While Spain is a leader in the rollout of solar and wind, only about 25% of its economy is electrified. The rest — from cars, to boilers in homes, factories and furnaces — still runs on fossil fuels.

The EU’s economy is currently roughly 23% electrified, with a target of 32% electrification by 2030. Turkey, which is hosting this year’s COP31 climate summit, wants countries to agree to a global target of 35% by 2035.

Increased electrification is the next leap in fulfilling the country’s net-zero promise and attempting to slow the pace of global warming.

There are positive signs that electricity demand is growing, such as the shift towards decarbonization by Moeve, Spain’s oldest private oil company. While the firm still draws most of its profits from fossil fuels, it has sold 70% of its oil-producing assets and introduced an €8 billion clean-technology investment plan that Moeve CEO Maarten Wetselaar calls “a cornerstone of our transformation strategy.”

But the risk remains that Spain fails to make the most of its renewables head start, as its economy and infrastructure get battered by the impacts of global warming. This summer, wildfires burned on the outskirts of the Spanish capital, Madrid, while heat has contributed to an estimated 5,000 deaths in the country.

“Electricity demand needs to be high enough to keep driving both generation investment and also grid investment,” Alvarez said.

If electricity demand doesn’t rise fast enough, “countries with a high renewable penetration rate, like Spain, start to see flaws in the investment signals needed to keep deploying batteries and to keep deploying grid investment.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Former head of Keizai Doyukai denounces Japan’s notion of being ‘presumed guilty’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Takeshi Niinami, former chair of the Japan Association of Corporate Executives, or Keizai Doyukai, has criticized Japan’s social trend of labeling people suspected of wrongdoing as guilty before the facts are known.

In September last year, the 67-year-old resigned as Keizai Doyukai chief and as chair of beverage giant Suntory Holdings after facing allegations he had imported illegal supplements into Japan. Prosecutors decided not to indict him in May this year.

In a recent interview, Niinami reiterated that the allegations were unfounded.

Based on his experiences of the public backlash over reports of his case, he voiced concerns that a climate of presuming people to be guilty in Japan may thwart efforts to invite overseas talent to work in Japan.

“A society where people are presumed guilty, even without knowing the facts, won’t succeed globally,” he said.

Still, Niinami said the entire investigation process involving the Fukuoka Prefectural Police department and other parties was “careful and detailed,” with those asking questions in the investigation being “polite.”

“I wasn’t under mental stress,” he said.

On his current plans, Niinami said he will start teaching students at Stanford University in the United States about crisis leadership this month as a visiting scholar.

He denied that he might return as an executive of a business group, saying he is better suited to filling a role assisting next-generation presidents, such as a chair or an outside director.

Touching on the growth strategy of the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which focuses on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum technologies, Niinami said that an institution should be established to oversee the plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle, with the private sector taking the initiative in such efforts.

China slapped anti-dumping measures on Japanese shipments of a chemical used in the production of semiconductors on Tuesday, a fairly targeted move that nonetheless escalates a diplomatic dispute with Tokyo over Taiwan.

The Chinese Commerce Ministry has unveiled preliminary measures on imports from Japan of dichlorosilane, a chemical required to process silicon wafers into chips. Companies importing the substance must now provide cash deposits of up to 99.2%.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Two arrested for allegedly referring man to criminal group for work
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Hiroshima police rearrested a construction company president and a former executive on Monday for allegedly referring a rejected job applicant to an anonymous criminal group, which had then sought to send him overseas to join a fraud scheme.

Riho Maehara, 32, president of a construction company, and former company executive Yuka Matsumoto, 30, both from the city’s Asaminami Ward, were rearrested on suspicion of attempting to abduct someone for transport overseas and violating Japan’s employment security act by referring a person to harmful work, Hiroshima Prefectural Police said.

Both have denied the allegations.

Police suspect the two acted as recruiters for a tokuryū, a fluid and anonymous criminal network whose members often communicate through encrypted apps and frequently change personnel.

The pair allegedly approached a 35-year-old man in Hiroshima Prefecture after rejecting him for a job at their construction company, telling him they could introduce him to “telemarketing work overseas where he could make good money.” They then allegedly referred him to the criminal group and attempted to have him sent to Southeast Asia between late March and mid-April, police said.

Maehara and Matsumoto were previously arrested on Aug. 17 on suspicion of abducting another person and sending them to Taiwan using a similar method.

Police believe the criminal group interviewed people whom Maehara and Matsumoto referred over video calls, instructing them to use highly secure messaging apps before then recruiting them as callers in specialized fraud schemes.

Investigators are examining the pair’s alleged roles and the broader structure of the group.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: New York leaders ‘lied’ about toxic air after 9/11, Mayor Zohran Mamdani says
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
The city is releasing thousands of files showing what officials knew about air quality around Ground Zero and what they kept from the public

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Tuesday the release of tens of thousands of documents showing the city did not disclose all it knew about air toxicity after September 11.

The release comes ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks in 2001 that killed 2,977 people, in the US, mostly in the collapse of the Twin Towers in New York.

More than 9,400 have died from illnesses linked to their exposure to the area in the years since, according to a federal medical monitoring programme.

“These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability,” the mayor told a news conference following the online release of 170,000 pages of documents on health concerns, air quality and the city’s response to the attacks.

The release is part of an agreement with 9/11 Health Watch, a victims’ advocacy group that had taken legal action to compel the city to make the documents public.

“For 25 years, four different mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the city actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Centre collapse, even as city officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” the group’s director Benjamin Chevat said in a statement.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/middle-e.title: US targets Iran’s airlines with sweeping new sanctions
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/middle-e.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/middle-e.text:
The US Treasury is aiming to ground Mahan Air and other firms in a sharp escalation of Trump’s economic pressure campaign

The US on Tuesday issued 36 ⁠fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector and other companies as part of a broad push to escalate economic pressure on Tehran as the war in the Middle East entered a seventh month.

The US Treasury Department said the action was aimed at grounding Iran’s Mahan Air, already sanctioned by the US and the European Union, and all other Iranian airlines.

The sanctions also ‌took aim at covert front companies, foreign intermediaries and deceptive transshipment routes that Washington says Iran relies on to obtain US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology.

The Treasury also issued an alert asking financial institutions to report any procurement networks supporting Iran’s aviation industry, while designating firms based in Turkey and the United Arab Emirates that it said helped Tehran procure US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology.

Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorisations that allowed overflights and permitted non-US airlines to fly US-origin or US-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran.

Tuesday’s actions marked a sharp escalation ⁠of the Trump administration’s renewed push to squeeze Iran’s economy and pressure Tehran to loosen its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz.

A US naval blockade ‌and tougher sanctions are curbing oil exports, restricting access to foreign currency and exposing growing strains in the economy.

The Treasury said any foreign firm or individual aiding Iranian airlines through aircraft transfers, cargo services or general sales agent support would face ‌serious consequences.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week had warned that the Trump administration was eyeing airlines as possible sanctions targets ⁠along with digital assets and the ⁠maritime industry.

“Under Operation Economic Outcast, we promised severe consequences for those providing financial lifelines to the Iranian regime,” Bessent said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Let this be a warning to anyone doing ‌business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”

The US Treasury has repeatedly targeted global networks supporting Mahan ‌Air. In ‌July, Treasury designated six entities and individuals in China, India, Russia and Iran, including several firms that act as sales agents for the US- ‌and EU-sanctioned airline.

Washington first sanctioned Mahan in 2011 over support it provided to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In 2020, Washington imposed sanctions on a China-based company ⁠it accused of acting on behalf of Mahan Air.

On Tuesday, Treasury designated 27 Iranian airlines, as well as several firms based in Turkey and ⁠the United Arab Emirates, for helping Mahan Air secure at least three Boeing B-777 aircraft this summer that had been retired elsewhere.

It also hit UAE-based Egyptian citizen Ibrahim Ali Mohamed Mohamed Mahran, the chief executive of ECT Aviation Support, as well as the British unit ‌of the firm.

OFAC also imposed sanctions ‌on two firms based in Turkey and Malaysia that it said had serviced Mahan Air’s international flights and coordinated cargo shipments.

As a result of the sanctions, all property and interests of the designated firms and individuals that are in the US will be blocked and must be reported to OFAC. Violations of sanctions can result in criminal and civil penalties.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/poli.title: Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, dies aged 89
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/poli.author: SCMP Reporter
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/poli.text:
Tung, who resigned as city leader in 2005 on health grounds, had not been seen in public since July 2021

Tung Chee-hwa, who served as Hong Kong’s first chief executive and oversaw the 1997 return of the city to Chinese rule, has died.

The former vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), died on Tuesday at the age of 89, according to a statement from his office issued in the early hours on Wednesday.

“Mr Tung Chee-hwa was a man of unwavering integrity who devoted himself wholeheartedly to the nation, his noble character and spirit will stay forever in our hearts,” the statement read.

The office said Tung was surrounded by his loved ones when he died.

He was last seen in public in July 2021 when he attended the premiere of a film to mark the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China.

It was believed that Tung was hand-picked by Beijing to be the special administrative region’s first leader, especially after his famous handshake with then-president Jiang Zemin at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996.

He was appointed chief executive in December that year after he won votes from 320 of the 400 members of the Selection Committee, beating his rivals, including the late Sir Yang Ti-liang, a former chief justice, and businessman Peter Woo Kwong-ching.

Tung’s tenure as chief executive, with public support and Beijing’s blessing, had a good start. The honeymoon was cut short by the Asian financial crisis, which weighed on the local economy and sent home prices diving.

Tung’s first-year pledge to build 85,000 homes annually, a target that had been dropped fast, is still remembered by many residents as the main vector behind tanking home prices in Hong Kong post-1997.

Tung secured a second term in 2002, but the severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) outbreak in 2003, along with his administration’s efforts to enact a national security law as required by Article 23 of the Basic Law, the city’s mini-constitution, dealt a heavy blow to his political standing.

The government was forced to shelve the national security bill after half a million people took to the streets amid fears that their freedoms and rights would be restricted. The July 1 march remained an annual fixture until 2019.

Tung resigned in 2005, for what were said to be health reasons, and was succeeded by his chief secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen. The former was later appointed by Beijing as a vice-chairman of the CPPCC.

Lau Siu-kai, currently a consultant at think tank the Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies, was tapped by Tung to head the government’s Central Policy Unit in 2002 and stayed in the position beyond Tung’s tenure until 2012.

The veteran political scientist said the former leader’s image as a modest gentleman and benevolent elder eased the anxiety of Hongkongers when Beijing took over from London in 1997.

Lau lauded Tung’s introduction of politically appointed officials and his vision of supporting strategic sectors, but lamented that the fruition of some policy goals was dragged down by short-sighted political elites at the time.

One of Tung’s signature projects, Cyberport, received criticism in the early 2000s for the direct land grant arrangements, but its office complex has also been a key incubator for local tech start-ups in the past two decades.

Tung also brought Asia’s second Disneyland resort to Hong Kong.

“His views on the governance and development of Hong Kong were quite ahead of his time. If more people in Hong Kong had a mindset of preparedness like Tung, Hong Kong would fare much better today,” Lau said.

Tung was born in Shanghai on July 7, 1937, at the start of the war between China and Japan.

Having moved to Hong Kong with his family in the 1940s, he took over the helm of his family’s shipping business Orient Overseas Container Line in 1982.

He left the corporate role in 1996 before running for the city’s top job.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: ‘Time waits for no man’: Chinese man’s 33-year, US$1.5 million world trip inspires many
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Fran Lu
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Chen draws a parallel between running a business and exploring the world – both require perseverance through challenges

A Chinese man has recently achieved his ambitious goal of travelling to 233 countries and regions around the world, sharing the life wisdom that “time waits for no man.”

Chen Jinwei, 53, returned to his hometown in Zhuji, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, after a remarkable 33-year global tour that ended when he returned from Peru after visiting various corners of the world.

Reports indicate that only about 70 individuals in China have previously travelled to 233 countries, territories, and regions.

As the owner of a machinery company, Chen invested a total of 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) into his journeys.

His international adventures began in 1993 with a trip to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.

At that time, the internet was still not widespread, and Chen felt a strong desire to learn “what the other side of the world looks like” – not through books or hearsay, but through his own firsthand experiences.

Chen integrated his world tour with his responsibilities of managing his business and family, often alternating between spending one month at home and one month on the road.

He strategically chose to start with challenging destinations, including the polar regions.

His quest to reach Antarctica required two separate journeys. In November 2015, he made his first attempt aboard the French expedition cruise ship Le Boréal, but he had to abandon the trip when the vessel lost power, emitting black smoke on the third day.

In January 2016, he set out again for the South Pole, successfully reaching his destination.

Chen identified Tokelau, a small island territory of New Zealand, as his greatest challenge.

In 2019, despite meticulous preparations and navigating complex procedures, he arrived in New Zealand only to be forced to cancel his Tokelau trip due to a public health emergency.

This year, he attempted the journey again and finally set foot on the atolls of Tokelau, expressing that he was “incredibly excited.”

Throughout his travels, Chen encountered many unconventional and challenging experiences, including contracting malaria in Africa and enduring an earthquake in Greece.

He said these challenges empowered him to become more adaptable: “When faced with a problem, first stay calm, then think about solutions.”

He emphasised that his journeys were about more than simply “checking off tourist attractions.” At each stop, he aimed to stay as long as possible and immerse himself in the local culture.

He collected currencies from 198 countries and donated them to the Xu Xiake Memorial Hall.

Xu Xiake (1587–1641), a renowned geographer and explorer from the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), can essentially be regarded as China’s earliest travel blogger.

Chen remarked that travelling and running a business share fundamental similarities.

“Regardless of the ups and downs, joys and sorrows, just persevere in whatever you do.”

For those eager to explore the world but often lamenting their lack of time or money, he offered straightforward advice: “Don’t wait. Time waits for no man.”

Now, Chen aims to spend more quality time with his children and parents. He also plans to interview 100 leading figures in the outdoor and tourism industry, documenting their life stories.

An online observer commented: “To achieve such a goal as Chen’s requires both time and money, which are luxuries for most ordinary people.”

Cambodia says it has flushed out a scam industry estimated to have stolen tens of billions of US dollars last year alone, but a string of arrests in recent days suggests the gangs behind it may have simply changed address.

The recent release of classic arcade games on the White House website, which allow players to deport migrants and build a border wall, has stoked more fear and anger among Filipino-Americans, as observers call out the “xenophobic” tactics in US President Donald Trump’s widening immigration crackdown.

For a few seconds during Blackpink member Jennie’s headline set at Tokyo’s Summer Sonic festival last month, it looked like something had come undone.

Calling the US Pacific strategy a “game of bluff”, Clark urges Wellington to defend its independent foreign policy tradition.

Bangladesh’s potential entry into a defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan could give Dhaka fresh leverage in its dealings with India, but observers warn the move risks fracturing its long-standing strategic neutrality and alarming a hawkish New Delhi.

Japan’s Mogami-class warship is turning out to be a hot item among global navies. Australia is buying 11, New Zealand is considering putting in an order – and now, even the United States is showing interest.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-uk-express-dism.title: EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-uk-express-dism.text:
The EU is deliberating an official response to the glorification of war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires over the display.

Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior.

Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony.

The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.

Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia.

EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event.

"The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X.

"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added.

A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth."

Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral.

"As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement.

"The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added.

The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region."

In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic.

"They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event.

Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level"

Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state.

The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad.

https://www.dw.com/en/50-years-after-his.title: 50 years after his death, Mao still shapes China
https://www.dw.com/en/50-years-after-his.text:
Mao Zedong was perhaps the most influential, and certainly one of the most controversial, figures in 20th-century China. Even five decades after his death, the legacy of his era continues to influence China today.

On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.

He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.

Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.

When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.

Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.

From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.

Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.

Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."

The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.

Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.

Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.

Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.

Zhang holds a similar view.

Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.

And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.

"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW.

The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.

Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.

"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."

Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."

In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.

The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.

Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.

The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.

Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.

Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.

Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.

First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.

Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.

Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.

"At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."

China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.

Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.

The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.

The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility.

Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.

In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.

The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.

Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.

https://www.dw.com/en/ratko-mladic-s-fun.title: Ratko Mladic’s funeral casts shadow over Bosnia and Herzegovina vote
https://www.dw.com/en/ratko-mladic-s-fun.text:
Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade, attended by Serbian and Bosnian Serb leaders, has deepened regional tensions and could affect the upcoming election in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Belgrade has made a point of insisting that it did not organize a state funeral for former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and crimes against humanity in 2017.

But when the body of a war criminal is flown home accompanied by the country's justice minister, when ceremonies unfold with military honors in state-controlled venues in the presence of senior political leaders and when clear condemnation of glorification of the deceased is absent, the message is unambiguous.

The impact of this message is being felt beyond Serbia's borders.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina — the state created by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which comprises two entities linked by a weak central government — reactions were as deeply divided as the country itself.

Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity covering about 49% of the country's territory, sent its officials to the funeral.

Public discourse there was dominated by narratives of "defending the people" and "the injustice of international courts."

"Without Ratko Mladic, there would be no Republika Srpska," was the refrain among thousands of mourners at the funeral in Belgrade.

Sarajevo, the seat of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sees this approach as a continued policy of relativizing war crimes and a threat to stability.

In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entity where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, the response was very different and the tone sharp.

Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic described Serbia's official response as a conscious choice by Belgrade, not something imposed on it.

He announced measures to cool diplomatic ties with Serbia, withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in Belgrade, leaving only the ambassador, explaining that he lacks the authority to close the embassy but can reduce its presence to a minimum. The move effectively froze day-to-day diplomatic communication on the ground.

"We will pull out everyone we can; consular services will be relocated to Zagreb and Podgorica," he said.

Denis Becirovic, chair of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called the funeral with military honors an "anti-civilizational act" and warned of far-reaching consequences for the entire region.

For representatives of Mladic's victims, any public glorification of the former general is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

Mladic's death and funeral are not just about the past.

At a time when both Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are facing general elections — Bosnia on October 4 and Serbia likely just a few weeks later — emotions become a resource.

In both countries, parts of the electorate still see Mladic as a symbol of resistance, which means that every gesture in support of him scores political points with these voters.

As the general election in Bosnia and Herzegovina approaches, sharp condemnations from Sarajevo are seen as evidence that the central government is "defending the state" and "the dignity of victims." This, too, is being turned into political capital.

In Republika Srpska, the presence of officials at the funeral and the narrative of "injustice" strengthen the position of those building their identity in opposition to international rulings.

Yet there are no "winners." The more political points anyone scores on this issue, the worse relations become and the further accession to the EU recedes into the distance — for both countries.

Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka, is clear about who is responsible for these political narratives: "The main culprits are the political elites, because in 30 years we have not moved forward. There has been no critical confrontation with the dark side of history," she says. "This is a darkening of civilizational consciousness."

Topic went on to say that Mladic's funeral "is a welcome gift to the protagonists of ethno-nationalist policies" and noted that these people still hold power in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Such an institutional stance towards crimes provokes a reaction on the other side, and then everyone exploits the situation, trapping us in a vicious circle where each tries to extract political profit," Topic says.

After Mladic's funeral, the Office of the High Representative (OHR) in Bosnia, which was created after the war to oversee the implementation of the US-brokered Dayton Peace Agreement, stressed that Bosnia's future cannot be built on glorifying those responsible for the worst crimes of the past.

"Glorifying convicted war criminals, as well as denying genocide and other war crimes, creates divisions, inflicts additional pain on victims and their families, and undermines the reconciliation process," said the OHR.

Bosnia remains a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 31 years since the war ended.

The fact that the ideology that helped spark that war still lives on, means that Mladic's funeral did not close a chapter in the region's history, it tore open a new one, measuring the Balkans' willingness to step out of the shadow of the 1990s.

While politicians seek to score political points, citizens pay the price of frozen relations.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

https://www.dw.com/en/bsw-and-afd-a-poli.title: BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
https://www.dw.com/en/bsw-and-afd-a-poli.text:
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could help the Alternative for Germany (AfD) into power in Saxony-Anhalt. But the BSW is riddled with infighting

Following the election in Saxony-Anhalt, there is no clear governing coalition because the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with its 44% share of the vote has fallen just short of securing an absolute majority. That means the formation of a new government in one of Germany's 16 federal states is more difficult than ever. This is also partly due to the success that the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which was founded only in 2024, has managed to achieve. Wagenknecht, a trained economist, was a longtime member of the socialist Left Party, formerly a communist who over time has distanced herself further from her political roots. Her party does not conform to traditional labels. Many people can no longer relate much to labels like "left" or "right," she says.

From the very beginning, Wagenknecht also showed no reluctance to engage with the AfD. Her long-held credo has been that the party includes people who are treated unfairly if labeled as Nazis.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Now, Sahra Wagenknecht and her followers are working towards seeking common ground with the AfD and can even imagine helping the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund into the role of state premier by abstaining from the vote. Wagenknecht mentioned this scenario before the September 6 election.

A few days before the vote, Sahra Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."

However, there is also a significant degree of agreement on issues other than German immigration policy: both parties call for an end to German arms deliveries to Ukraine, which has been attacked by Russia in violation of international law. Or they claim that freedom of speech no longer exists in Germany.

Whether the BSW will actually team up with the AfD remains completely open. AfD lead candidate Siegmund emphasized even before the election that he intended to govern only with an absolute majority of his own.

When the BSW was founded in January 2024, it had a spectacular start: Formed as a splinter party from the socialist Left Party, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) was swiftly elected to the European Parliament and in the same year received double-digit results in three state parliament elections. In the eastern German states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party entered straight into government coalitions. That would also have been possible in Saxony, but coalition negotiations with the CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) failed.

The BSW favors a tough approach to refugees. It opposes any form of military support, whether for Ukraine or for Israel.

The party's leader, Sahra Wagenknecht, is an economist who grew up in communist East Germany. She has had no reservations about contact with the AfD from the beginning. As early as 2023, she stated that some people within the party were being labeled Nazis unfairly.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt has ruled out a classic coalition. Following elections in Brandenburg and Thuringia in 2024, the branches in those states went against the stated will of their founder and joined governments alongside established parties. The permanent conflict between the federal leadership of the party and its state branches led to the breakdown of the coalition with the Social Democrats in Brandenburg, starting in 2025.

In Thuringia, led by a coalition of the CDU, SPD and BSW, most of the BSW lawmakers declared that they were leaving the party two days before the election in Saxony-Anhalt. However, they wanted to remain a part of the CDU-led state government.

"We have not been elected to tolerate flirts with right-wing radicals," is how Finance Minister Katja Wolf explained this decision, referring to the rapprochement with the AfD initiated by Wagenknecht.

The BSW's success in Saxony-Anhalt and accompanying key role in the formation of the government has given the party, at least for the moment, a largely unexpected significance. During the Bundestag federal election of 2025 the BSW narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament and, also due to its many internal conflicts, it seemed to have little credibility among the population.

Furthermore, its figurehead Sahra Wagenknecht has stepped back from the leadership of her party and is no longer running for its chairmanship. She continues to exert her influence in the background, though, and is a drawcard at BSW rallies, especially during election campaigns.

Following their successful entry into Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which according to pre-election polls was by no means guaranteed, Wagenknecht responded confidently.

"The BSW's comeback has begun," she told German news agency dpa.

How sustainable this upswing is will be revealed on September 20, when parliamentary elections will be held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.

This article was translated from German.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-court-rules-aga.title: EU court rules against Belgian far-right party in IKEA case
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-court-rules-aga.text:
A European court has backed Ikea's challenge against a Belgian far-right party, saying the use of Ikea-style visuals could harm the company's reputation.

A top European Union court ruled in favor of Ikea on Tuesday in a challenge brought by the company against Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang.

The popular Swedish brand may prevent the Belgian  party from using its signature illustrations. Vlaams Belang launched the "Ikea Plan" in 2022, a proposal to reform the country's migration and asylum laws.

The plan included images similar to Ikea's furniture assembly instructions. Ikea filed a legal complaint in 2023, accusing the far-right party of unlawfully using its branding.

"A proprietor of a trademark with a reputation may prevent that mark from being used by a political party where the latter has not demonstrated that its freedom of expression takes precedence over the rights and interests of that proprietor," the ECJ court said in a statement.

Vlaams Belang argued that the campaign was protected under freedom of expression. However, the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice found this argument insufficient, ruling that the use of Ikea's branding could harm the company's name and reputation.

The Luxembourg judges urged the Belgian court to issue a ruling on the matter in light of the decision by the European Court of Justice.

In a statement, Vlaams Belang said it had taken note of the judgement, adding that it "will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings."

Meanwhile, IKEA representatives welcomed the judgement.

"Inter IKEA strongly believes in and has great respect for freedom of expression. At the same time, the company cannot accept the use of IKEA’s trademarks in a way that harms their reputation or distinctiveness", Inter IKEA, a Netherlands-based holding company that handles the Swedish firm's intellectual property, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

Besides its anti-immigration stances, Vlaams Belang also advocates for the independence of Flanders — the northern, Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.

While it made considerable gains in 2024 elections, other parties refuse to cooperate with it.
