https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-electio.title: Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-electio.text:
False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.

On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.

In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.

DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.

Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."

The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.

There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.

The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.

Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.

Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.

"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.

The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.

Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".

One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.

"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.

Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections

Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.

Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".

The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.

Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.

The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."

The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-set-to-fee.title: Germany set to feel the impact of Saxony-Anhalt's AfD win
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-set-to-fee.text:
The state election could have major consequences for Germany's government. Pollsters cite dissatisfaction with Merz as one reason for the CDU's poor showing.

Only 1.6 million eligible voters were called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, September 6. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

For weeks it was clear that the vote had become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

The in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party  won the election, doubling its percentage compared to the last election five years ago, while the ruling CDU lost half of its support. If the AfD now manages to form a government, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.

Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW before the election. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

Koschmieder also predicted that a strong showing by the AfD would intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist. The CDU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Most analysts believe that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party.

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-kosovo-uni.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-kosovo-uni.text:
Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease and its vectors.

It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.

Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."

"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.

Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.

"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.

He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.

Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.

Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.

Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.

"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."

This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-plans-anti.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-plans-anti.text:
Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, according to Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.

On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.

German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.

Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."

The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.

The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.

Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.

The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.

On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by ​and ​large, the ​start of ‌a real war."

He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats.

"All ‌these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in ‌Europe once again — they are ‌being ​put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti.

He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.

The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.

The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.

The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.

These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.

Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.

The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-begins-hun.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-begins-hun.text:
Hungary's new prime minister promised he would recover billions stolen or diverted by the previous administration. A new "super authority" is about to begin that work. Its success or failure will have a big impact.

Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.

Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.

Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.

Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.

The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.

Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.

Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.

It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.

At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.

Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This time, things are meant to be different.

The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.

The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.

But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.

Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.

Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.

Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.

Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.

Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.

Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.

The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.

"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.

In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.

Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/croatia-toxic-wast.title: Croatia: Toxic waste protest draws tens of thousands
https://www.dw.com/en/croatia-toxic-wast.text:
The Zagreb demonstrators demanded that the government come up with a plan to clear illegal toxic waste in 20 days. Prime Minister Plenkovic has promised to tackle the issue.

A protest in Zagreb against Croatia's government drew tens of thousands of people who blamed the government for its lack of action over the illegal storage of toxic waste.

A landfill near the town of Gospic, located some 200 kilometers (124.2 miles) to Zagreb's southwest, is being used to hold toxic waste from several countries, including Germanyand Italy, according to reports.

The demonstration saw signs such as "ecocide equals slow genocide" and "halt waste import," with many of the people in attendance also holding Croatian flags.

The protesters called for all illegal landfills to be cleared due to them polluting groundwater, as well as a new waste management plan across the country within the next 20 days. They also demanded that the government put a temporary ban on waste imports in place.

An investigation in relation to illegal waste dumps has been ongoing since the arrests of 13 people in February 2025, with Europol cooperating with Croatian authorities in the investigation. Four companies are also under investigation.

According to Europol, most of the 35,000 tons of waste had come from Italy, but also from Slovenia and Germany, and consisted of plastic refuse and toxic hospital waste, bringing about a profit of some €4 million ($4.6 million) for the suspects, who had also likely forged documents falsely declaring plastic waste as suitable for recycling.

Local environmental activists dispute the number of waste tons and say 37,000 tons had been illegally dumped in Gospic alone.

Prosecutors also published a report in August that confirmed the Gospic soil contamination, also saying it had spread beyond the site itself.

This presents a "significant risk for the environmentand people's health," the report said, despite the drinking water in Gospic remaining so far unaffected, health authorities said.

Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic promised the toxic waste site in Gospic would be covered by mid-October before the waste gets removed from it.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-from-emigr.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-from-emigr.text:
Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven. "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-thous.title: Germany news: Thousands march at Saxony-Anhalt rallies
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-thous.text:
Ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday, a democracy festival by civil society groups has been held in Magdeburg. The far-right AfD organized its final campaign rally in the state capital.

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

It was the roundup of news and analysis from Germany on Saturday, September 5.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

A space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya.

"We’re in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X.

The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory.

The Spectrum rocket was launched on its first test flight last spring but crashed into the sea 30 seconds after takeoff.

The latest polls show the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is strongly favored to win Sunday's election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

In this interview, Tom Nuttall of The Economist examines voter frustration over migration, taxes and support for Ukraine — and whether Germany's long-standing political "firewall" against the AfD has unintentionally strengthened the party by keeping it out of power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out against the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) on the eve of state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking not in Saxony-Anhalt but in the neighboring state of Lower Saxony, Merz said "we must engage more effectively with this party."

"We must address the issues at hand," he said. "We must also address our choice of words."

Merz also referenced recent comments by AfD's state leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Reichardt, who said the modern German state had become "a lazy, anti-social bum reeking of dope."

The chancellor said such comments show "what these people think of our country."

"We will not let these people talk our country down," he added.

Merz said that "Germany can look back on a success story spanning almost 80 years, albeit with many problems and many challenges."

"But we are still one of the most prosperous countries in the world," he said. "We are still one of the safest countries in the world. And we are still a stable, well-established democracy."

Merz remains unpopular nationally. In a Trendbarometer survey published by broadcaster RTL earlier this week, just 14% of respondents said they were satisfied with the chancellor's work.

He has kept a relatively low profile in Saxony-Anhalt during the state election campaign. In recent days, he made two visits to the towns of Quedlinburg and Leuna where he held closed-door meetings with candidates from his party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Thousands of people joined a "march for democracy" on Saturday in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

Organized by a coalition called "Saxony-Anhalt: Open to the World," the march was called to uphold values of democracy, diversity and inclusivity ahead of a state election in which the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is comfortably leading opinion polls.

Germany's federal intelligence service has labeled the AfD state branch in Saxony-Anhalt as a right-wing extremist organization.

At the demo on Saturday, attendees carried signs that read "more love, less hate," "a better life without Nazis," and "the potato is also of foreign origin," among other slogans.

Police estimated that some 6,000 people participated in the march from Magdeburg's central station to Cathedral Square, where another 3,000 people joined them.

Among them were contingents from trade unions, church groups and other civic organizations.

"As initiatives, clubs, associations, and individuals, we are taking a stand and advocating for respectful coexistence in our state," the organizers stated in their call to action.

According to police, eight gatherings had been registered to take place in Magdeburg on Saturday. Others included a human chain for democracy and a democracy-themed cycling tour.

In an interview with German daily the Tagesspiegel, right-wing extremism expert Heike Kleffner praised the organizers' "paradoxical confidence" in being able to mobilize democratic masses despite being under attack.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned that Germany's democracy and rule of law need protection from those "who scorn and trample all over them."

Steinmeier was speaking ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to receive by far the most votes.

While not singling out any party, he appeared to take aim at AfD's policies and rhetoric, which critics describe as extremist and anti-migrant and supporters label a patriotic defense of national borders and security.

"Ethnic-based thinking and nationalist isolationism are simply not the answer to the challenges of the 21st century," Steinmeier told a community festival in Bonn.

Steinmeier, who steps down from office in March after ten years, described liberal democracy as an "achievement" and "a blessing for us all."

He said those who wish to protect and preserve democracy represent the majority and that anger and outrage offer no way forward.

"You cannot build a future on hatred and incitement," Steinmeier warned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police in Germany continue to hunt for a 48-year-old man suspected of causing deliberate damage to the country's electricity grid.

The most serious incident was on Tuesday evening at a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne.

Launch devices were used to fire cables across overhead lines, causing a short circuit that forced five units of the nearby Niederaussem coal plant to temporarily disconnect from the network.

Earlier the same day, a similar attack was carried out near the Jänschwalde plant in eastern Brandenburg. More than a dozen launch devices were found.

On Thursday, a passer-by found similar unused devices at a substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf.

Police say the objects matched the launch gear used in the other incidents.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's DPA news agency reported on Friday that a man from a town near Dortmund claimed responsibility for the incidents in two letters.

His motive is reportedly to draw attention to the use of fossil fuels in electricity production, which he called a "crime."

This week, officers found explosives in the 48-year-old's home, while a special operations unit stormed a truck in a wood, some 100 kilometers (62 miles) away. The suspect was not found.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the acts as "climate extremism."

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has added German national Bernhard Fritsch to its Most Wanted Fraudsters list.

Fritsch was convicted by a jury in Los Angeles last year of fleecing investors of about $26.8 million (€23.1 million) with a fake celebrity-influencer app.

Instead of building the product, prosecutors say the 65-year-old spent millions on cars, a yacht and a Malibu villa.

Fritsch was sentenced to 15 years in prison in absentia after fleeing to Mexico.

Despite being detained by immigration officials in Mexico, he then fled to Germany and is believed to be in the Munich area.

The FBI is prepared to pay up to $150,000 for any information about his whereabouts.

After a summer drought caused severe low water levels on the Rhine River, four of Germany's states have called on Berlin to increase funding to modernize inland waterways.

Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia said the federal government must invest at least €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) per year to boost maintenance.

Germany's waterways, including the Rhine, play a key role in moving raw materials across the country, carrying more than 5% of all freight transported,

They said politicians often focus on investing in roads and railways, while canals and rivers often get neglected.

Over the summer, the Rhine became almost impassable at one key location and many ships plying the Rhine had to operate with much-reduced cargoes.

Economists at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated the drought would cause an economic loss of up to €2 billion.

North Rhine-Westphalia's Transport Minister Viktor Haase called for new fleets of inland vessels that can reliably operate even in extreme low-water conditions.

Thousands of people are expected at rallies in eastern Germany's state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of elections for a new regional parliament.

Police said 12 events have been registered in the state capital, Magdeburg, with others in Halle.

Most of the demonstrations are against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which is widely expected to receive the most support in Sunday's vote.

Trade unions and civil society groups are organizing the largest rallies. Their events include a so-called democracy festival.

The AfD will also hold its final campaign event in Magdeburg.

The latest polls put the AfD at over 40% support, putting it on course to be the largest party in the state parliament by a wide margin.

However, without an outright majority, the chance of the AfD forming a government will get messy as mainstream parties have ruled out a coalition with the far right.

No smaller party expected to enter parliament has offered to formally support an AfD-led government.

The AfD could take office on its own only if it wins a majority of seats.

Guten Morgen from Germany, where more than a dozen rallies are planned ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

For the first time since World War II, a far-right party — the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — could win the most votes and could theoretically take power in the eastern German state.

After cargo shipping was disrupted due to severe low water levels on the Rhine River this summer, four German states have asked the federal government for additional support.

Also, the FBI has added a German businessman from Bavaria to its most-wanted list.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-would-an-afd-.title: What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
https://www.dw.com/en/what-would-an-afd-.text:
Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does it have planned?

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, has taken a massive lead in the Saxony-Anhalt election, although it was not clear if it will be able to form government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.

The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."

In its draft government program, the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.

The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.

Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.

And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.

The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.

However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.

To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.

Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.

"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."

The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.

For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.

The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.

On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.

Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."

Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.

A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.

It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy."

To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.

https://www.dw.com/en/outrage-as-maltese.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
https://www.dw.com/en/outrage-as-maltese.text:
Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity to murder journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Almost nine years after the attack, the question of who ordered her death remains unanswered.

"Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.

His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.

But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.

Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.

Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.

In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.

But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.

The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.

No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.

On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.

The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.

The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/outrage-as-maltese.summary: Yorgen Fenech found not guilty of complicity to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. FeneCh was acquitted of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist.

https://www.dw.com/en/in-saxony-anhalt-e.title: In Saxony-Anhalt election, small parties will be kingmakers
https://www.dw.com/en/in-saxony-anhalt-e.text:
The far-right AfD has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament this state election, enabling them to govern alone. It all depends on whether other parties make the cut.

It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On Sunday, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.

There hasn't been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony-Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.

Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months, the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.

Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties that can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.

All other parties have cause for concern: they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.

This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).

The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.

The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.

The environmentalist Greens may also not return to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.

And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European Parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.

The BSW never really recovered from this setback, and it went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.

Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote — paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.

Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood that the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.

On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.

If the CDU sticks to this resolution, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.

Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.

The Left Party is prepared to support State Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.

"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.

Pantisano pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.

Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/in-saxony-anhalt-e.summary: Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament. The AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote. The right-wing party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-leaning.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-civil-so.title: Germany's civil society alliance takes on the far right
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-civil-so.text:
Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage.

For Felix Pankonin, locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes, a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property. Pankonin's bicycles have been vandalized, and he has received threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.

Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political adviser at DaMOst, the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, said right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.

"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6 p.m. no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand," she said.

Kuperan's work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the AfD, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.

Miriam Zeller, a city councilor in Stendal, a city of 37,000 in northern Saxony-Anhalt, is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the election. Zeller told DW that the hostility against her was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.

"It can't get any worse than this," said Zeller.

However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.

For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.

The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists — people like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over 5 million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader has called for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," said Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association(LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann told DW.

The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlin has deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, said Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl said.

Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.

For his part, Lehmann is determined. "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he said.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-civil-so.summary: The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists. The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be a German democracy alliance.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-vulnerable-is-.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
https://www.dw.com/en/how-vulnerable-is-.text:
The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.

On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.

On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.

In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.

While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.

What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.

Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.

Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.

One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"

One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.

The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.

"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.

The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.

Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.

Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.

He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."

At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.

A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.

Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police.

As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."

Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves.

"Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said.

What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.
