https://www.dw.com/en/majority-of-german.title: Majority of Germans see Russia as a threat
https://www.dw.com/en/majority-of-german.text:
More than half of German citizens believe that Germany's security is threatened by Russia, according to the latest survey by public broadcaster ARD.

In the past few weeks, Germany has seen a drone attack on Leipzig Airport and an arson attack near defense contractors in Bavaria, while explosive devices and pyrotechnics were found at two substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia.

As the country enters a September featuring three vital state elections, attacks on critical infrastructure appear to be on the rise, and defense contractors are apparently in the crosshairs.

After some initial hesitation, the German government has now publicly blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack, but could the Kremlin also be behind the other attacks?

"We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in September 2025 already.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of Bavaria's conservatives, the Christian Social Union (CSU), has also warned that Germany has now become a "daily target of hybrid warfare," referring to measures that are not military, but are nonetheless meant to destabilize a country and unsettle the population — including cyberattacks, espionage, propaganda, disinformation and acts of sabotage.

The developments seem to have alarmed the German people. Some 56% of the eligible voters polled now see Germany's security as threatened by Russia, according to the latest Deutschlandtrend, for which the polling firm infratest-dimap conducted a representative survey of 1,319 German voters for public broadcaster ARD between August 31 and September 2.

But not all Germans feel this way. Nearly half of citizens in eastern Germany, for instance, feel only slightly threatened, or not at all, by Russia. The same goes for supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), some of whose prominent figures have expressed support for Russia. The survey found that two-thirds of AfD supporters consider the threat from Russia to be low.

The same divisions in the German population emerge on the question of arms exports to Ukraine. Just over half of Germans consider the country's military support for Ukraine appropriate, or think it should even be expanded, but for just over four in ten Germans, that support goes too far. Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine predominates in eastern Germany and among AfD supporters.

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, and the AfD continues to be way ahead in the polls and could even win an absolute majority — usually unheard of in German elections.

The party also continues to enjoy strong support at the national level. The new poll suggests that if a general election were held this coming Sunday, the AfD would receive 27% of the vote, one point less than in August, which would make it the largest party in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.

The CDU/CSU, meanwhile, remains in second place at 21%, well below the 28.5% it managed in the Bundestag election in February 2025. The Greens would receive 15%, while the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the socialist Left Party have seen slight improvements compared to August, reaching 13% and 12%, respectively (+1 each). All other parties would fail to clear the 5% threshold.

The latest poll also suggests that the current governing coalition of the CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats would no longer have a majority if an election were held now.

Only 15% of those surveyed are satisfied with the government's performance, and even among supporters of the governing parties themselves, a majority is disappointed with the incumbent coalition's performance. Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz fares even worse: Only 13% approve of his work.

This is consistent with how citizens assess the CDU/CSU's competence.

Also notable is that significantly fewer voters believe the CDU/CSU is capable of finding solutions in key policy areas. While just over a year ago, 31% still considered those parties competent to ensure peace in Europe, that figure has now dropped to just 23%.

A similar loss of confidence in the CDU/CSU is apparent elsewhere: On asylum and refugee policy, on pension reform, and on climate and environmental policy.

On the topic of the economy, the CDU/CSU still enjoys the highest level of public confidence at 24%, but here too, the figure has dropped significantly from 31% in February 2026.

In eastern Germany, the AfD is now the party in which citizens place the most confidence across all policy areas surveyed, with the exception of climate and environmental policy.

As many as 79% of respondents in the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey say the economy is doing poorly or very poorly. Here, too, however, there are significant differences depending on party affiliation.

As many as 41% of SPD supporters view the economic situation as good or very good, and 37% of Green Party supporters say the same. In contrast, only 3% of AfD supporters share this view — they are much more pessimistic, with 96% saying the economy is poor or very poor.

https://www.dw.com/en/the-hidden-environ.title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers
https://www.dw.com/en/the-hidden-environ.text:
As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.

Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land.

Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily.

AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University.

From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment.

Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating.

In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that.

And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency.

All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels.

One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year.

The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone.

And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal.

Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable.

However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries.

Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation.

A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume.

In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023.

There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%.

Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas.

Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away.

Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy.

Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%.

Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts.

First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities.

On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants.

One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year.

Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems.

In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus.

The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-how-the-fun.title: Serbia: How the funeral of Ratko Mladic is dividing a nation
https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-how-the-fun.text:
As the Serbian government leaves the decision about Ratko Mladic's funeral arrangements to his family, international pressure on the country is mounting. How do Serbs feel about the matter?

The body of the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has arrived back in Serbia.

Wrapped in the Serbian flag, Mladic's coffin was carried by members of the Serbian Armed Forces from the plane to a vehicle that transported his remains to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy.

Several groups of citizens gathered along the route from the airport to the hospital. Standing on overpasses, they greeted the motorcade carrying Mladic's body, holding banners that read "Thank you, General" and "Heroes never die."

Pro-government tabloids provided minute-by-minute coverage, referring to Mladic as a "Serbian general" and claiming that he had been "killed in The Hague."

Ratko Mladic was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague for the genocide in Srebrenica, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, the years-long siege of Sarajevo during the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and other war crimes, including the establishment of detention camps for non-Serb civilians and prisoners of war.

Belgrade media report that Mladic will be buried in Belgrade on Monday. Justice Minister Nenad Vujic had previously announced that the funeral would be held with the highest state honors.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, however, says the decision will be left to the family.

Security agencies estimate that tens of thousands of people could attend the funeral.

"We will be there to provide all kinds of logistical and transport support and to maintain public order and security," said the president, adding, "It is very difficult to ensure and guarantee the safety of everyone."

For Jasmina Lazovic, executive director of the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Center, which has spent decades working on transitional justice and dealing with the past, none of this comes as a surprise.

She points to the long-standing glorification of Ratko Mladic in Serbia and his legacy.

"There is no small town in Serbia without at least one mural glorifying Ratko Mladic. The narrative that he was unjustly convicted has existed for years," she tells DW. "Now a narrative has emerged that he was killed, despite the fact that he died at the age of 85 after suffering several strokes."

Lazovic says that these narratives suit the state leadership's portrayal of Serbia as a country that fought exclusively defensive wars and do not leave enough room for a discussion of the consequences of those wars and the victims they left behind — neither in the media nor in the education system and institutions.

"And there are hundreds of thousands of victims across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Above all, these were crimes committed against civilians, crimes that left the countries of the region — particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina — with a completely transformed ethnic structure," she said.

Lazovic says that the list of victims also includes those who survived rape and torture, as well as those who were forcibly displaced. "The list is long, and our knowledge is limited," she adds.

The announcement that Mladic could be buried with the highest state honors drew swift responses from the international community.

"Glorification of war criminals is contrary to European values. There is no place for it either in EU member states or in candidate countries. I hope the government in Belgrade is aware of that," said European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.

Aleksandar Vucic responded by accusing the West and the Hague Tribunal of blaming only Serbs for war crimes and failing to deliver justice for Serbian victims. But for now, he has officially left the decision on whether the deceased general will receive state honors to Mladic's family.

Jasmina Lazovic believes Vucic will once again take a pragmatic approach and that the final decision will depend on an assessment of what brings the authorities greater political benefit and what could cause greater damage.

She also points out that the issue is not only political, but legal.

"What is being overlooked here is the fact that Ratko Mladic was indeed a general, but he was sentenced to life in prison. Under the Law on the Serbian Armed Forces, anyone sentenced to more than one year in prison for a criminal offense loses their rank and, therefore, all the privileges that come with that rank," she says.

"If Ratko Mladic were buried with the highest state honors in accordance with the rank he held during the armed conflicts, that would be a direct violation of the law of this country."

On the question as to how they view Ratko Mladic, Serbian citizens interviewed by DW in several cities across the multi-ethnic autonomous province of Vojvodina expressed sharply differing views, ranging from those who are convinced that Mladic was unjustly convicted to those who accept the genocide designation without reservation.

"What was he supposed to do, let them kill all the Serbs? Thank you [Mladic], for everything," one man from Ruma told DW.

"For me, the matter was settled when the genocide verdict was handed down," said a student from Novi Sad.

But most people simply wave the question away. "I have enough of my own problems," said Svetlana from Zrenjanin.

Goran, from Novi Sad, believes that it is simply another political issue. "They've been making fools of us for years. Nothing is different now," he told DW.

Lazovic believes that most Serbs are apathetic about the matter.

For her, this is a greater problem than just the pro-government media portraying Serbia as wanting to say goodbye to Mladic as a general. She argues that confronting Mladic's legacy and the past is essential if Serbian society is to move forward.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-how-the-fun.summary: Ratko Mladic's body has arrived back in Serbia after being flown to the hospital. The Serbian government has left the decision on whether to give the deceased general state honors. Serbians are apathetic about the matter, says one Serbian woman.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-is-saxony-.title: Germany: Is Saxony-Anhalt's economy really struggling?
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-is-saxony-.text:
Germany's far-right AfD party has long claimed that the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt has been left behind. Is that really the case? A closer look at the data offers some interesting insights.

Germany is watching the upcoming state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with keen interest. Much of the attention is focused on the performance of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose state branch in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "right-wing extremist."

According to opinion polls, the AfD could emerge as the clear election winner.

In the last state election in 2021, the AfD won around 20% of the vote and has since been the largest opposition party. The state is governed by a coalition of the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP), with the CDU's Sven Schulze serving as state premier.

The AfD is campaigning on the claim that Saxony-Anhalt has been left behind — both socially and economically.

The unemployment rate in Saxony-Anhalt is higher than the national average, while median earnings for full-time employees are lower than across Germany as a whole.

Of Saxony-Anhalt's roughly 2.1 million residents, just under 800,000 are in jobs subject to social security contributions. The chemical industry has traditionally been one of the state's major employers and among the most productive sectors of the economy, particularly in the so-called chemical triangle around the cities of Leuna, Merseburg and Bitterfeld-Wolfen.

Machinery and plant engineering companies, including suppliers to the struggling automotive industry, also play an important role in the manufacturing sector.

The retail, transport and hospitality sector accounts for around one-fifth of jobs, including many positions in tourism. The Harz Mountains, the Luther cities of Wittenberg and Eisleben, and Quedlinburg, with its UNESCO World Heritage status, are key destinations.

The perception that the eastern German states have still not caught up with the former West German states appears to resonate with voters. The AfD has built broad support around this message, particularly among younger voters.

It is often claimed that pensions are lower in eastern Germany than in the west, but this is no longer the case. It is true, however, that the proportion of pensioners in Saxony-Anhalt is slightly higher than the national average. Many pensioners in the east also rely solely on their state pension, whereas many in the west receive company pensions or income from private retirement savings in addition to their state pension.

Partly because of its higher proportion of pensioners, Saxony-Anhalt has one of the lowest levels of economic output per capita in Germany, at just three-quarters of the national average. The state's economy has also generally grown more slowly than the national economy in recent years.

The AfD has also made immigration a central campaign issue in Saxony-Anhalt, warning of "too much immigration" and "foreign influence" — and appears to be gaining support with this message. This is even though, compared with other German states, relatively few non-Germans live there.

Although Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany's economically weaker states, its population has grown in recent years, according to migration figures.

Since 2016, more non-Germans have moved to Saxony-Anhalt than have left. The net migration balance for German citizens has also been positive for the past six years.

At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for around 9% of Saxony-Anhalt's population — roughly half the share in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state.

The claim that "foreigners are living off taxpayers" is also misleading. Compared with other German states, Saxony-Anhalt has a relatively low proportion of foreign nationals among potential recipients of welfare benefits such as basic income support.

However far the political and economic reality may diverge from the bleak picture painted by extremist parties, particularly the AfD, one trend appears evident: support for radical parties is becoming increasingly entrenched.

The two formerly dominant parties, the CDUand SPD, are bearing the brunt of this shift and steadily losing ground. The CDU is increasingly struggling to maintain its status as a broad-based mainstream party, while the SPD is edging closer to the 5% threshold, raising the prospect that it could eventually struggle to win seats in some state parliaments.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-north-korea-s-.title: Why North Korea's women's football team is so good
https://www.dw.com/en/why-north-korea-s-.text:
North Korea's young footballers enter the U-20 World Cup in Poland as defending champions — the 2024 title was their third. Why is the isolated state so good at the game?

A year ago, North Korea's women successfully defended their U-17 World Cup title after defeating the Netherlands 3-0 in Morocco. It was the fourth time that the country has won the competition.

Now the country's U-20 team enter the World Cup in Poland as defending champions, having won their third World Cup in 2024. North Korea's women have clearly cemented their status as the dominant force in women's youth football.

But what is it that makes a state that, according to the United Nations, "does not have any parallel in the contemporary world," so good at youth football?

"International sport is one of the few ways to demonstrate their sovereignty, existence and identity to the international community, so this type of big success, from their point of view, is an important occasion where they can wave their national flag in front of the international audience," Dr Jung Woo Lee, a senior lecturer in Sport and Leisure Policy at the University of Edinburgh, told DW.

"At the same time, domestically, North Korea often uses sport as their propaganda tool to glorify their leaders and also how great their country is."

Football is popular in the country, but recognizing that the gap to the top in senior football is much harder to close than in youth football, North Korea's leaders turned to women's youth football, where the gap is more manageable. It's also why success at this level hasn't benefited the senior team over the years. This strategy is not about pathways. It's about winning.

"The gap between established and developing clubs is also high because in many European countries, there is a professional league, and they get more support from a number of different stakeholders," Lee said.

"In youth football, I think European sport organizations highlight more on having fun when playing football. Whereas in North Korea, even if you are 13 or 14 years old, they join very highly disciplined, highly systematic and highly professionalized training regimes, so in early ages they can excel."

In Morocco, North Korea's U-17 team only conceded three goals in the entire tournament, and scored three or more on four occasions. This was a continuation of their form the year before, while the U-20 women in 2024 not only beat Argentina 6-2 but also secured three straight 1-0 victories from the quarterfinals onwards to win the tournament.

With the help of the Pyongyang International Football School where young girls are selected, developed and educated following a highly disciplined and scientific approach, North Korea has seen an opportunity and taken it.

In the eyes of North Korea, this is also a victory for the state itself.

"You need to remember that North Korea still maintains a very strong socialist and communist regime," Lee explained. "Particularly under Kim Jong Un, they try to compare capitalist and communist regimes and show the communist regime as superior to the capitalist. Also, when I look at some of the news reports about the North Korean performance in North Korean media, they highlighted that because they are (under) the communist regime, they do whatever they can, even if they're physically exhausted.

"Then they directly compare those mentalities with capitalist countries. In capitalism, when athletes are physically exhausted and injured, there is no way to perform. They need to be changed by their coach. But in socialist systems their will is more important than (a) professional opinion from the coach or any medical staff. So North Korea frames that as a superior system."

That psychological element has seemingly given the team an edge, but beyond a strong sense of patriotism and years of disciplined work lies the motivation of a life-changing reward.

"Although we often see North Korea as quite underdeveloped and very much agricultural and people experiencing hardship, those living in Pyongyang are quite different. They are kind of special," Lee explained.

As an incentive, he said, the regime can give players living outside the capital residence certificates, which are required to enter Pyongyang. At the same time, many players have been given apartments.

This motivation is not to be underestimated. Life in rural North Korea is tough, with shortages in food and health care reportedly common. Living in the big city is quite different.

"This is a way to change their life. It's kind of winning a lottery in a way," Lee explained.

For star players such as Yu Jong-hyang, topscorer at the 2025 U-17 World Cup, or Choe Il-son, a key player in both U-17 and U-20 World Cup victories in 2024, the instinctive reaction is to wonder which WSL (English top division) or NWSL(US top division) team will be trying to sign her, but that would be to forget the context in which she both lives and plays.

"I don't think it's impossible, but not so easy," Lee said of the idea of either stars playing abroad.

"First of all, (there are) the economic sanctions now imposed on North Korea," he added. "And also, whenever North Korean players joined a European league — there were a few occasions in basketball where any salary was not sent to the individual account of the players or the agent, but it goes to North Korea's government account, so I think that's another complexity involved."

While much about this team, like the country, remains a mystery, there is no denying that success at the youth level has always been the plan.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

This article was originally published on September 9, 2024. It was updated on November 9, 2025 to reflect North Korea's U-17 World Cup title win. It was also updated on September 4, 2026 ahead of the kickoff of the U-20 World Cup in Poland.

https://www.dw.com/en/2026-beethoven-fes.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
https://www.dw.com/en/2026-beethoven-fes.text:
The motto of this year's classical music festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.

Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle on Friday evening.

The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert.

For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explained, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics.

"We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure," Seliger added. This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, Andras Schiff, to perform at the festival this year.

The new hall isn't only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too.

Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed Festival Salon where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall.

The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music.

"For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," said festival director Steven Walter, who himself has lived in various places around the world. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections."

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos.

The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven, not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A Life," but said he is far from finished discovering the composer.

"Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today."

Artists at this year's Beethovenfest will introduce music from their homelands. Among them is Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war.

Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year.

As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace").

Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course.

Seventeen-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze, regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents, was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work.

Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music.

American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age.

"We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," said spokesperson Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music."

Beethovenfest runs from Sept. 3 through Oct. 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-volkswagen-s-h.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden
https://www.dw.com/en/how-volkswagen-s-h.text:
The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV onslaught?

Volkswagen has built one of the largest workforces in the global auto industry.

At nearly 630,000 people — 680,000 if you count joint ventures in China — VW employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, 140% more than Stellantis and nearly 240% more than Ford.

That headcount was once a sign of Germany's industrial might and VW's huge profits. Now, it's become a massive burden, one that's forcing the company to make painful job cuts to survive against agile Chinese competitors.

After already trimming thousands of positions last year as profits came under pressure, Volkswagen is now preparing to slash 50,000 additional jobs worldwide, including tens of thousands in Germany. The proposal got the backing of the VW Supervisory Board on Thursday, September 2.

VW also wants to close four German factories, a plan that the supervisory board on Thursday stopped short of agreeing to implement right away.

These cuts include VW luxury brands like Porsche and Audi. Other German automakers and suppliers are facing similar pressures. Mercedes-Benz is planning to cut several thousand jobs, and suppliers like Bosch have announced large cost savings.

Much of VW's headcount issue stems from long-standing strategic decisions.

Meghan Ostertag, an analyst for economic policy at the US-based Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, says VW's much larger workforce was needed because the firm chose to control more stages of production than its peers.

"The company makes many of its components and software internally, increasing the demand for labor and, of course, labor costs," Ostertag told DW, adding that factory expenses in Germany can be "up to twice those of the competition."

Other experts point to an aggressive acquisition strategy over the years, which brought brands including Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti into the VW fold — not to mention several truck makers.

"That strategy worked to some extent, but the complexities of integrating all those brands, supply chains and different designs make VW very complicated to operate," Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at the London-based Ultima Media, told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Although Volkswagen survived the 2015 Dieselgate emissions scandal without suffering lasting financial damage, the company incurred massive costs and soon faced a new set of problems.

The company was slow to transition its production to electric vehicles (EVs) — just as Chinese EV makers gained serious traction and a technological edge. That delay contributed to slower sales in China, which accounted for a third of total VW sales, as well as softening demand in Europe and other key markets.

VW also repeated a mistake made by the US auto industry decades earlier. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Big Three — Ford, GM, and Chrysler (now part of Stellantis) — were bloated and slow to adapt when Japanese and European competitors began eating into their market share.

By the time US carmakers shifted toward leaner production methods, a decade had passed, and they had fallen significantly behind, noted Ostertag.

Toyota, which produces a similar number of vehicles as VW, operates with nearly half as many workers by relying more on suppliers, higher automation and a simpler management structure.

In a research note, auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt pointed to another factor: the "stranglehold" that trade unions and a key shareholder have over VW. This, he said, had helped cause "years of neglect in readjusting workforce numbers."

The northern German state of Lower Saxony — home to Volkswagen's global headquarters in Wolfsburg — holds 20% of the company's voting rights, can veto major decisions, and has previously pressured executives not to close plants or lay off staff, notably during the Dieselgate and COVID supply chain crises. It's ramping up the pressure this time, too.

Over the decades, Germany's powerful unions, meanwhile, have repeatedly held out for high wage increases and generous benefits, which have made VW staff among the best-paid autoworkers in the world.

Analysts warn that the company may have to cut more than the annual €4 billion the firm hopes to save to secure its future.

The current proposals to cut 50,000 additional jobs, they say, will bring savings and help improve short-term profitability. But VW's underlying cost base and slow decision-making culture mean deeper, more radical reforms may well be needed.

VW should "invest more heavily in automation," Ostertag told DW, adding that it would allow the carmaker to "better compete with leaner firms," such as China's BYD, one of the fastest-growing EV brands in Europe.

Analysts say VW has lagged peers in plant automation levels but has stepped up investments in robotics and digital upgrades for its EV production. The company is also planning its first sub-€20,000 EV next year.

With China responsible for around 30% of VW's global vehicle output, Harrison predicts more production shifts to Asia and the potential to share VW's European plants with Chinese EV producers, a move previously seen as "unthinkable."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On the policy front, the German government is providing subsidies and loans for domestic EV battery plants to help reduce reliance on Chinese imports.

The European Union, meanwhile, is advancing the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA is meant to boost the bloc's competitiveness and shield strategic industries from unfair competition from China.

The EU has already imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese-made EVs. But they are far below the 100% levies that the US charges, which have largely shut Chinese competitors out of the US auto market.

Historian Niall Ferguson from Harvard University warned that Europe has been slow to respond to China's strategy of giving huge subsidies to EV makers that help undercut European rivals.

"Unless there's radical change, I predict: Europeans will be driving Chinese cars on a massive scale very soon," Ferguson told Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper earlier this year.

During the same interview, economist Moritz Schularick, President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, suggested using market access as leverage — only allowing Chinese brands to sell in Europe if they produce locally.

Schularick responded provocatively when questioned on VW's long-term future, predicting that Germany's auto giant would "likely be bought by a Chinese car maker like BYD."

Edited by: Ashutosh Pandey

https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-ber-airport.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-ber-airport.text:
Police have given the all-clear at Terminal 1 at Berlin's BER Airport following an earlier security scare and evacuation. The airport said some flights had been delayed but they were trying to avoid any cancelations.

Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare.

"The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman.

Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage.

"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency.

Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point.

Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days.

Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening.

"Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman.

She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport.

"Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays.

"Regular operations will resume on Friday."

The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.

Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said.

Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website.

An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

https://www.dw.com/en/norway-seizes-russ.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
https://www.dw.com/en/norway-seizes-russ.text:
Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.

Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.

Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.

Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.

Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead.

"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.

Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.

"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.

Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.

The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.

He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.

It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions.

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.

Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

https://www.dw.com/en/is-germany-s-econo.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
https://www.dw.com/en/is-germany-s-econo.text:
Despite a slew of negative headlines, the German economy has posted its best figures in years. There are reasons for optimism, but structural issues remain.

The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums.

The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters.

Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026.

Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August.

"It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery."

"The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," said Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research.

However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said.

The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up.

Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds.

This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards.

Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war.

Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year.

Brzeski told DW that many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefited from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil.

"There was a bit of a rechanneling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he said.

The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identified this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks."

It said that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains.

"Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added.

Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026.

"It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," said Fuest.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness.

It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," said Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy."

Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain.

The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined.

"Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" said Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist.

"Chinese competition is still there," he said. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse.

Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands.

In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums.

For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable.

"It could hardly have gotten much worse," said Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder ["economic miracle"] 3.0, we have to keep that in mind."

He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve.

"They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he said. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival."

For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He said three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows.

"It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-polic.title: Germany news: Police say arson attack targeted defense firm
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-polic.text:
Two people were arrested in connection with a small fire at a construction site near a defense tech company in Munich. Investigators are looking at a possible "political motive."

This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of news and analysis from Germany on Thursday, September 3.

We're closing the blog today. Thank you for reading, we'll be back tomorrow again!

German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not been honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

"If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency.

"The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region."

Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.

But CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Federal police say they evacuated Terminal 1 of Berlin's main airport on Thursday evening.

This was the result of a luggage security scare. A woman told officials she had a dangerous substance in her luggage, a claim that could not be immediately discounted. As a result, police cleared the building to investigate.

You can read the full, still developing story here.

Brandenburg police say they are investigating a lead on the apparent sabotage attempt targeting the electricity network near the Jänschwalde power plant in eastern Germany.

"A claim of responsibility in connection with the attack in Turnow-Preilack has come to our attention," police wrote on social media on Thursday evening.

"The authenticity of the text is currently being checked."

The apparent attack targeted high-voltage power lines near the coal-fired power plant with projectiles that state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said were similar to fireworks. It was discovered on Tuesday.

Authorities instigated investigations into a potential terrorist crime, given the seemingly intentional targeting of key state infrastructure.

Earlier on Thursday, police had said operations investigating the attempted sabotage continued and that traffic disruptions in the local area would persist, particularly on the L50 road.

News also broke this week of an potential sabotage attempt targeting a power station in Bergheim near Cologne.

Earlier this year, the far-left "Vulkangruppe" claimed responsibility for an attack on Berlin's power infrastructure that led to widespread power outages during particularly cold midwinter week.

The mass production of over 5,000 medium and long-range combat drones for Ukraine has started near Munich, according to the defense company Auterion.

The first drones were assembled under an order for the German government, Auterion and its Ukrainian joint-venture partner Airlogix said. Auterion is providing AI-powered software for the drones while Airlogix is providing the hardware.

The order is due for completion by mid 2027.

Industry sources estimate the order is worth some €300 million ($348 million).

The Ukrainian partnership was established in February this year.

The drones are part of Berlin's support for Ukraine in its fight against Russia.

Auterion is headquartered in the US state of Virginia but it maintains a major software development hub in Munich.

Ahead of Sunday's election in Germany's eastern Saxony-Anhalt state, a German journalist union has recorded an increase in attacks on journalists covering campaign events of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

The German Journalists' Association (DJV) said reporters faced dozens of instances of verbal abuse and obstruction of their work. Physical assault was reported in five cases.

The DJV called for consistent prosecution of those responsible for the attacks. It also said police must do more to ensure that journalists can report without being hindered.

The association expects a robust operational strategy to protect press freedom, DJV chair Mika Beuster said in a press release.

Polling shows the AfD with a commanding lead in Saxony-Anhalt, with the party aiming to secure enough votes to have a ruling majority in the state.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said Thursday that "arson attacks" early Thursday morning were targeting "defense and security companies in Munich" and likely had a "political background."

Two Bulgarian citizens were arrested after incendiary devices were thrown at a construction site, located in the immediate vicinity of the office buildings of defense contractors.

Police, who were called to the scene by a witness shortly after midnight, extinguished one small fire that didn't cause any damage, and defused a second incendiary device with a bomb disposal unit.

The incident comes as tensions are high in Germany following two suspected acts of sabotage targeting power infrastructure this week. It also comes as the German government on Tuesday officially blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4.

Bavaria's interior minister connected Thursday's arson incident with a broader trend.

"Overall, this incident shows that — as has already been the case in other parts of Germany in recent days — we now face an increased risk of attacks," said Herrmann.

"What we are seeing are attempted or actual attacks, such as the one at the Leipzig airport, the power substations in recent days, and now, specifically, attacks targeting companies active in the defense and security sectors."

The Bavarian Central Office for Combating Extremism and Terrorism (ZET), which is part of the Munich State Attorney General's Office, has taken over the investigation of the arson incident.

The public prosecutor's office stated that the investigation is focusing on whether this was a targeted attack on one of the companies housed in the nearby buildings.

"We must take these risks very seriously and be prepared for the possibility that something like this could happen any day, anywhere else in Germany," Herrmann said,

Bavaria's Minister of Economic Affairs, Hubert Aiwanger, called for better protective measures.

"We must face the reality that cowardly attacks on German companies and infrastructure are on the rise," he said. "Unfortunately, this is not the first time a technology company with ties to the security and defense industries has been targeted."

https://www.dw.com/en/macron-visits-baye.title: Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Andy Burnham
https://www.dw.com/en/macron-visits-baye.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron is on a shorter-term visit to the UK than the renowned on-loan 11th century tapestry. He viewed the ancient artwork with the UK monarch and relatively new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

French President Emmanuel Macron began a two-day trip to the UK by visiting another famous new arrival from France, the Bayeux Tapestry, with King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel joined King Charles and Queen Camilla to walk the length of the 70-meter tapestry in the British Museum.

Charles hailed the "unprecedented loan" as a "precious symbol of trust" between the UK and France, while Macron said the two countries were "as close as the threads" in the artwork.

The tapestry, which depicts the momentous events of 1066 culminating in William the Conqueror of Normandy claiming the English throne, is on temporary loan from its usual home in France. It's the first time it's touched British soil since its creation in the 11th century.

The embroidery is on loan for a 10-month exhibiton opening to the public next week, on September 10. The exchange was first announced during Macron's state visit last year.

Though it's thought to have been made in the British Isles, it had been on French soil ever since the 11th century. It's usually on show in Bayeux in Normandy in northern France, hence the name. The effectively priceless artefact was transited across the Channel in secret in July.

Prime Minister Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, called the tapestry's return "a landmark moment" in the history of the two countries.

He also hailed ties with Macron's French government more generally in the House of Commons on Wednesday, alluding to reduced illegal migration crossings of the English Channel — a bid to counter one of Reform UK's favorite summer talking points.

"The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation — the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low," Burnham said.

It's Macron's first UK visit since Burnham took office and their first in-person meeting as leaders.

The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millenium, and turned out to be the last one for a millenium.

The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.

https://www.dw.com/en/austria-women-ice-.title: Austria women ice hockey team fight for future generations
https://www.dw.com/en/austria-women-ice-.text:
Austria are getting ready for their first Women's Ice Hockey World Championship. But preparations have been overshadowed by a dispute about conditions, pay and getting men's cast-off kit. A solution now looks in sight.

When the Austrian women's national ice hockey team took to the ice in the Women's European Cup of Nations in Slovakia in August, they did so without 11 of their top players.

Captain Anna Meixner and the rest of her team were frustrated that the Austrian Ice Hockey Association (ÖEHV) still hadn't responded to a list of grievances outlined in a letter to the organization last March. Meixner stressed that the players only went public with their complaints as something of a last resort.

Among the nine complaints on their list of demands were the standard of accommodation, having to change in unheated dressing rooms in the winter and not being paid per diems during training camps and international tournaments. They also said they had to make do with hand-me-down equipment from the men's team.

"We really tried to respect the federation [ÖEHV] and we really tried to solve it from within, without outside noise," Meixner told DW in a Zoom interview on Wednesday.

"So we had been fighting for four or five months without going out to the newspapers. But when we realized that nothing had changed, we had to take the next step."

"The final straw, if you want to call it that, was a camp last February. It was the no-heater-in-the-locker-room situation," said the 32-year-old forward, who, after two seasons in North America's PWHL (Professional Women's Hockey League) with the Ottawa Charge and Vancouver Goldeneyes is returning to her previous team, Swedish outfit Brynas, for the 2026-27 season.

"Here were people that had been sitting on a train for 14 hours, who didn't get food when they arrived. We had to go on the ice straight away. So, I think that was when it really became clear to us that enough is enough."

Meixner also stressed that their aim was primarily to improve things for the women's national team in the longer term.

"We have this older generation right now and we're not going to play for the national team forever. We really felt it's time to give the next generation everything that we didn't have over the last 10 to 15 years. We brought it up with the team and everybody was on board right away," she said.

To ratchet up the pressure on the ÖEHV, the players also threatened to boycott the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship in Denmark in November ― a significant moment, as this is the first time Austria have qualified for the top IIHF (International Ice Hockey Federation) tournament.

"Going to the newspapers," as Meixner put it, seems to have worked.

In a press release following last month's tournament in Slovakia, in which Austria came second out of the four teams, the ÖEHV said it had taken the opportunity to hold "constructive conversations" with the players.

Now, Meixner appears cautiously optimistic.

"We have gotten some answers from the federation and we are just in the process of going over everything. But now, we're happy about the direction things seem to be moving in," said Meixner, who added that the players and federation were finally speaking on an equal footing.

"It feels like they [the ÖEHV] actually want to change something. If it stays that way, I'm sure we can figure something out and make it work. Because obviously the last thing we want to do is to miss the world championship."

Indeed, in a letter to the team sent on August 31, the ÖEHV responded to each of their nine demands outlining specific steps that had either already been implemented or were in the works.

These include a pledge to implement "clear regulations regarding per diems/remuneration and the timely payment of bonuses and travel expenses," to provide "adequate accommodation and reliable, needs-based catering" for training camps, "adequate cabin and gym facilities" as well as "sufficient time for travel and recovery."

The ÖEHV also noted that it would seek a "teamwear solution" as part of a new contract with the association's equipment provider.

While this all seems promising, Meixner still finds it frustrating that in 2026, she and her teammates have had to battle so hard for what she termed "bare minimums."

At the same time though, she said that if the players and the ÖEHV do actually manage to put aside their dispute, it will be bigger than everything she has achieved on the ice ― including winning the tournament in China last year that put Austria through to a first Women's Ice Hockey Championship.

"I'm unbelievably proud of us for staying hard at it for many months. There are so many girls from other nations reaching out saying, 'You know what? It's great that you're doing that and we should do the same,'" she said.

"We've heard the men's team stepping up, cheering for us. I think this is bigger than hockey. Hopefully this will be a big step for Austrian women's sports and Austrian women in general."

Unless an unforeseen hitch arises over the next few weeks, Austria will open their first-ever World Championship campaign against Czechia in Esbjerg, Denmark on November 6.

Mathias Brück contributed to this report.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-summons-russian.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-summons-russian.text:
The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a similar step.

The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.

"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest," Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.

Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks."

"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.

The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences."

He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict."

Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.

Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."
