https://www.dw.com/en/women-s-football-a.title: Women's football: Anyomi, London City and the German exodus
https://www.dw.com/en/women-s-football-a.text:
Nicole Anyomi has joined Alexia Putellas and other star names in signing for the ambitious English club London City Lionesses. The Germany winger told DW England is a better place to develop her game than back home.

The London City Lionesses have existed for less than a decade, have played in England's top flight for just one season and can't play in the Champions League. Yet, having broken the women's transfer record last year, the Lionesses have signed some of the game's biggest stars for the coming season as their ambition becomes ever more apparent.

As well as two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and her Spanish teammate Mapi Leon, England's Euro 2022 winning goalkeeper Mary Earps and French star Kadidiatou Diani, Germany winger Nicole Anyomi is among the new arrivals.

Anyomi left Eintracht Frankfurt, where she'd scored 50 goals in 101 Bundesliga games over five years, for what she considers a greater challenge in England.

"The next step was to go to the league to compete every single weekend and this is what I see here in this league," she told DW.

"I have some friends who already played in the WSL  (Women's Super League) and they told me about the league so I think this will be the perfect step for me."

Anyomi is one of several players to leave Germany's Women's Bundesliga for England this summer. Among them are Anyomi's international teammates Vivien Endemann (Wolfsburg to Liverpool), Selina Cerci (Hoffenheim to Arsenal), Carlotta Wamser (Bayer Leverkusen to Manchester City) and England's Georgia Stanway (Bayern Munich to Arsenal).

Anyomi pointed to the increasing gap in infrastructure, finances and coaching as the primary reasons for the exodus.

"In Germany you have two, three teams who are competing at the top but here in England there are five, six, seven, eight teams.

"Also, the facilities and the staff members. We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

With England's national team having won the last two Euros, a competition once dominated by Germany, and no German side having won the Champions League since 2015, there is a concern that Germany rested on its laurels for too long.

In an effort to address this issue, last December, the Frauen-Bundesliga FBL e.V. (Women's Bundesliga Association) was formed. Similar to the DFL, which operates the men's Bundesliga, the FBL is designed to improve the league's marketing and increase revenue. It is to take over operation of the league next July 1.

"They have to bring something, not new, but something different into the league so maybe the players would stay," Anyomi said.

"I think it's an investment thing, but I think now they are building something new, to do different things.  I'm going to see this season of course and watch the Bundesliga. I hope they are going to invest more, do more for the league so players also from abroad can come to Germany."

Her new club are the foremost example of the changing face of women's football. London City did not exist until 2019 when, effectively, they took over the license of another team, Milwall. Their progress has recently been accelerated by Michelle Kang.

The Korean-American businesswoman is a serial investor in women's football and added London City to an ownership portfolio that includes serial Champions League winners OL Lyonnes and US side Washington Spirit in December 2023. Kang's deep pockets and ambition mean London City are on track to compete at the top end of the WSL within the next few years.

But her ownership of OL Lyonnes prohibits London City from playing in the Champions League. UEFA, who organize the tournament, have enshrined laws that mean clubs that are in multi-ownership structures cannot both be in the same competition in the same season. Last season, in the men's game, this led to English side Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League to the Europa Conference league.

"Why would we want to preserve the sporting integrity of men's football, but not of women's football? It's out of the question," said UEFA's head of women's football and former Germany international, Nadine Kessler earlier this year.

"In any sport you want to preserve sporting integrity, that's the most important thing."

Anyomi, who must recover from a hamstring injury before she can make her debut, said she trusts the club, who have so far "done everything they promised" to find a solution.

But the lack of continental football means fewer chances to make her mark alongside the other new arrivals. Given that the World Cup in Brazil is at the end of the coming season, the move could be seen by some as a risk.

"I did think about that because I know I have to play at the club level, otherwise I won't be selected," she said. "I wanted to go abroad two years ago and I didn't in the end, so I decided to go this summer. I had the feeling this is the right step."

Whether it's to London City, or to the WSL more broadly, she's not the only Bundesliga player to feel that way.

Any escalation in the Baltic region will lead to a significant response, Moscow said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines flying across Russia, saying that Ukraine's drone operations would make the airspace unsafe.

"Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said in a statement on Tuesday evening. He said that Ukraine was not threatening civilian aviation or individual aircraft.

"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.

Just last week, Zelenskyy threatened the deployment of up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin branded Zelenskyy's comments "a declaration of state terrorism."

"They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists," Putin said in a televised news conference.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022 and has repeatedly managed to strike targets deep inside Russia with drones as part of its defense efforts.

Russia's military struck two cargo ships carrying military goods, the country's Defense Ministry said.

The vessels were hit in the port of Pivdennyi, ​near ​the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, ​and ‌in the Black ​Sea.

A Russian strike caused damage to a thermal power plant in the region of Odesa, southern Ukraine, state energy company Naftogaz said.

Elsewhere, Ukraine's military intelligence said that a strike by the Ukrainian army hit Russia's Novatek oil complex in the region of Leningrad.

Kyiv and Moscow have been exchanging blows in the past 24 hours, with energy infrastructure being targeted as part of the mutual  strikes.

Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.

"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. And they need to know this - it will be devastating for them," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at her weekly briefing.

It's not exactly clear what she was referring to, but earlier in the day a fire broke out at Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a drone attack according to the regional governor.

Separately, NATO scrambled military aircraft due to a possible air threat in Latvia's airspace near the town of Ludza, close to the Russian border.

Russia does not believe a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, a key grain shipping route, would bring a peaceful resolution to the war closer, Interfax quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko as saying Tuesday.

Both sides have stepped up attacks in the Black Sea in recent months, driving global grain prices higher.

In mid-August, Ukraine reportedly conveyed an offer to Russia through a third party proposing that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.

Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his country had prepared a plan to ensure the safe passage of grain through the Black Sea and was working on an agreement similar to the 2022 grain deal that would facilitate safe exports.

On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.

"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.

"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.

Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.

"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.

Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.

Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.

Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.

The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.

Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."

"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."

Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.

The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.

At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:

In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."

Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.

The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.

He did not immediately provide additional details.

Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."

At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.

European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.

Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.

There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.

The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.

The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.

The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.

Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.

EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.

The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.

Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-says-russi.text:
Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August. The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible."

The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin .

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He said the attack fit the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.

Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport.

German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday.

"We do not view Leipzig as an isolated incident, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions," he continued. "We assume that Germany will be the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia."

Dobrindt insisted that Germany is "not at war" but that it is "a daily target of hybrid warfare."

Therefore, he said, Germany would respond to the hybrid attack in Leipzig in a "proportionate and measured, yet resolute manner."

Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany's response would be coordinated closely with European Union and NATO partners.

"We are tightening entry controls for Russian nationals" and Berlin would propose the listing of more Russian individuals for European Union sanctions, Wadephul said, as the Russian ambassador to Berlin was summoned.

In addition to a strengthening of internal security, he also announced additional measures including the closure of the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn from September 18 and the rescinding of a contract enabling the operation of the "Russian House," a Russian cultural center in Berlin.

"Our message to the Russian leadership is clear," Germany's top diplomat said. "We are sticking to our security course. The attack on Leipzig shows that this is necessary. We will not allow our social cohesion to be divided by Russian attacks. We remain ready to react along with our partners when the protection of our population demands it."

Finally, he said that Germany would continue to support Ukraine in its "defensive battle against Russian aggression."

"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he added.

"The German government has taken strong measures and the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

"We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression," she continued. "We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security. Russia is seeking to sow distrust and fear among our societies. But it will fail. And we will stand by Ukraine for as long as it takes."

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,

https://www.dw.com/en/can-communities-be.title: Can communities be protected from melting glaciers?
https://www.dw.com/en/can-communities-be.text:
Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.

The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.

The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact."

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream."

The heat settles over the Swiss Alps like a magnifying glass. On the Rhone Glacier, the last of the winter snow is disappearing unusually early. The so-called "Glacier Loss Day" marks the beginning of a critical phase: From that point on, it is no longer the snow reserves that are melting, but glacial ice that is decades or even centuries old. For researchers, this is an alarming sign.

Matthias Huss is measuring ice melt on the Rhone Glacier. This year, Swiss glaciers will reach "Glacier Loss Day" as early as June 29. Only in the record-breaking year of 2022 did this turning point occur even earlier. "This is a truly alarming situation," warns glaciologist Huss. The glaciers still have three hot summer months ahead of them — and every day costs them precious ice.

Tourists observe the shrinking ice cave of the Rhône Glacier. Two heat waves, little snow in winter, and Saharan dust are all accelerating the melting at a massive rate. On the Rhône Glacier alone, one meter of ice disappears within a few days. Glaciologist Huss describes the condition as "very poor." The glaciers are losing more mass than they can replenish in winter.

The consequences are visible to the naked eye. Harry Block, a German tourist, has been visiting the Rhone Glacier for about 50 years. At the sight of the shrinking ice fields, he struggles to hold back his tears. "I could cry. You can see climate change right here." In place of the once-mighty ice walls, only bare rocks and scree remain.

Visitors take photos of the shrinking glacier tongue of the Rhone Glacier. The glaciers still feed large rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhone with their meltwater. This can only continue as long as there is enough ice. In just 24 years, Swiss glaciers have lost about 38% of their volume. And over the past 50 years, about 1,200 smaller glaciers have disappeared completely.

From a bird's-eye view, the extent of the melting at the Rhone Glacier becomes apparent. Researchers expect enormous ice losses by 2026. Matthias Huss warns: "If global warming continues, only small remnants of ice will remain by the year 2100." Conservationists are calling for stronger protection of the glaciers. It is still possible to halt the melting.

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.

"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze.

Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."

"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze.

"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.

But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze.

"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."

For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.

Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.

However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal."

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.

A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

Following the devastating flash flood in the border region between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet, the number of people missing has risen rapidly. According to authorities, more than 1,300 people are currently unaccounted for, including several hundred foreigners. Many deaths are expected.

A massive flood wave surged through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal at tremendous speed. The floodwaters first struck the northern district of Rasuwa. They then spread over more than 160 kilometers as far as Chitwan, near the Indian border. According to initial findings, the disaster was triggered by a glacier calving.

More than 5,000 rescue workers are on the scene. In Nepal alone, according to police and tourism authorities, more than 800 people are missing, including nearly 600 foreigners from more than two dozen countries. In Tibet, according to Chinese state television, more than 550 additional people have been reported missing. Nearly one-third are from other countries.

Helicopters delivered tents, food, and other relief supplies from India to the areas hardest hit. The United Nations also sent personnel and relief supplies. The United States has pledged $500,000 and the deployment of a disaster relief adviser.

In hospitals and relief centers, family members are desperately searching for missing friends and relatives. In some communities, up to three-quarters of the population is considered missing. Among the victims of the disaster are also numerous tourists and travelers, as the affected region is considered the gateway to Langtang National Park, one of Nepal's most important trekking areas.

Nepal is one of Asia's poorest countries, with particularly fragile infrastructure in its remote Himalayan regions. Severe weather often damages roads, bridges and transport links. Rasuwa District is a key corridor to Tibet and an important gateway for pilgrims traveling to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, which sees particularly high traffic at the end of August.

The extent of the damage is immense, and the survivors are in shock. "There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat," Sagar Pandey, the chief executive of a Himalayan tourism operator, told the Reuters news agency after flying over the zone in a helicopter.

"I've never seen a flood like this," reported an eyewitness. For everyone who was traveling on Wednesday in the Rasuwa border region between Nepal and Tibet, the disaster turned into a nightmare scenario. Many relatives have little hope that those missing will be rescued alive from the mud-covered rubble.

https://www.dw.com/en/mladic-s-death-bos.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
https://www.dw.com/en/mladic-s-death-bos.text:
The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton peace agreement ended the war, not the divisions that produced it.

The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.

Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.

When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.

For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.

In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.

Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."

Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called Mladic's death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."

In Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska, Mayor Drasko Stanivukovic expressed his condolences to Mladic's family and confirmed that Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle."

In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.

Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.

President Aleksandar Vucic accused the tribunal in The Hague of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.

Former Interior Minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative linking World War I to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."

In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.

Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice. "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.

Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.

The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia." It urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.

But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?

The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton peace agreement itself.

The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.

One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

That division was not an administrative technicality; it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Mladic.

The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.

Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.

It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."

In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.

In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.

Bosnia-Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.

Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.

This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.

The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, has subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.

The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Accords, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades. But in doing so it only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.

The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war, and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

https://www.dw.com/en/norway-s-new-king-.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
https://www.dw.com/en/norway-s-new-king-.text:
The new king swore to uphold the constitution in parliament in Oslo, the first major institutional step of his reign. Haakon VIII's wife Queen Mette-Marit had to skip the event in the aftermath of her lung transplant.

New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week.

This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9.

Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo.

House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath.

"I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said.

Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending.

She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June.

In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday.

"As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said.

Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century.

When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite.

Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-irks-germany-eu.title: US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
https://www.dw.com/en/us-irks-germany-eu.text:
Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.

G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks.

The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada.

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

"We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session.

The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close.

"Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said.

He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position.

The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media.

Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented.

"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia."

As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access to the meeting.

The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials.

Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter.

"I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded."

Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end.

Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran.

Iran has withstood decades of extensive US and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in.

"I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada.

This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US.

Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation.

"Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade."

https://www.dw.com/en/can-new-apple-ceo-.title: Can new Apple CEO John Ternus fix the tech giant's AI woes?
https://www.dw.com/en/can-new-apple-ceo-.text:
John Ternus is just the third Apple CEO in 30 years. His primary challenge is to correct the company's faltering AI strategy to preserve its position as a big tech leader.

On September 1, a new era begins at Apple as John Ternus becomes just the third man to hold the CEO role at the tech giant since 1997.

Ternus was announced as Tim Cook's successor back in April, bringing Cook's 15 years at the helm of one of the world's biggest companies to an end. Since then, Ternus, a leading hardware engineer at the company, has been working closely alongside Cook in preparation for the big job.

Just as Cook had when he took over from the iconic Steve Jobs, Ternus has big shoes to fill. Apple's share price has increased by more than 2,000% since Cook took over in 2011 and the company has sold more than 3.1 billion iPhones in that time.

Ternus faces a range of challenges at Apple, but his ability to keep the company at the top will hinge on how he reshapes its AI strategy.

Apple has struggled to successfully embrace the technology so far, with critics saying it has fallen far behind its rivals.

Ternus will make his public debut as CEO at Apple's autumn product launch event on September 9. Dubbed "Surprise and Shine," Ternus is expected to announce the company's first foldable iPhone as well as a new version of an AI-powered Siri, Apple's virtual assistant.

Francisco Jeronimo, VP for Data and Analytics at tech research group IDC, said Apple's forthcoming announcements were planned during Cook's time in charge and that it will be 2027 before the direction Ternus wants to take the company in becomes apparent.

"Of course, September 9 will be quite an important milestone for the company around foldables and around innovation," he told DW.

"But I don't think we have seen anything that could indicate that Apple is behaving in a different way or is showing a different kind of strategy because Tim Cook is not in the job anymore — yet."

What observers will be looking out for from Ternus on September 9 is the extent to which he focuses his remarks on AI.

While it was already undeniable when he was announced in April that the artificial intelligence boom would be pivotal to his time at the helm, it has become even clearer in the five months since the unveiling that the AI revolution is here to stay.

"It's becoming clear that AI is not a fad, is not something that will go away in the next two or three years," said Jeronimo. "It's something that will dictate the future of most tech companies and indeed all companies."

He reckons AI could be "the most consequential technology" for Apple because it could either help it maintain its lofty position or create a set of daunting challenges.

The biggest challenge he sees is that Apple doesn't "control" AI infrastructure the way it could previously in terms of designing and controlling both the hardware and software for its key products.

"Maybe that will be what John Ternus will be doing differently from Tim Cook, because at the moment, even if Apple built their own AI technology, the reality is that they still depend on someone else," he added.

Apple's reliance on other companies in the AI realm has led it into unfamiliar territory. It struck a deal with OpenAI in 2024 to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, but that has led to a bitter dispute between the companies. Apple sued OpenAI earlier this year, alleging that the AI company stole its trade secrets.

Earlier this year, it announced a deal with Google, whereby the search giant's Gemini models would be used for Apple's own AI models and its new AI-powered version of Siri.

"The risk for Apple is to become less relevant in a world where companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are leading in terms of technology, in terms of awareness, in terms of services and potentially in terms of hardware," said Jeronimo.

For decades, Apple's success has been built on its physical products, from the iPad to the iPhone.

"If devices from OpenAI become available, that could be very, very risky for Apple. They could completely disrupt the experience and the way we interact with technology. And if Apple is not on the front of that innovation, that is a big risk," he said.

Ternus' background as an engineer who worked on Apple's core products, as well as innovations such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, means he will be expected to lead the way on new AI-driven products for the company.

He also played a central role championing Apple's shift to designing its own chips instead of relying on external suppliers like Intel — precisely the kind of independence Apple would like to achieve when it comes to AI.

Jeronimo thinks Apple still has big advantages, given its massive volume of users as well as the company culture of having dominated innovation in tech for decades. He thinks if Apple can get to grips with AI under Ternus, it could lead to huge success. "What we will see in the next years will dictate whether Apple is on the right track or if they are really struggling," he said.

For Ternus, the first task will be to simply fit smoothly and convincingly into a role that both Jobs and Cook undeniably made their own. "Steve Jobs was the guru of innovation and disruption and Tim Cook was the guru of execution," said Jeronimo.

"I think John Ternus can be a combination of both."

https://www.dw.com/en/at-venice-film-fes.title: At Venice Film Festival, politics take center stage
https://www.dw.com/en/at-venice-film-fes.text:
With works about Gaza, Ukraine and Elon Musk, political cinema is in the spotlight at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.

The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, with politics and political cinema set to dominate the red carpet.

The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire.

Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will also get films about Israel and Gaza, Russia's war on Ukraine, the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man.

Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever.

This year's competition includes "Naza," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Russian President Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc.

Andrei Kutsila's "Letters From the Silenced Country" a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice.

As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece."

And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's deportation surge in Minneapolis last January.

This is a new look for Venice.

Under artistic director Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference.

Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin, and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them.

But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate, primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt.

At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers "have to stay out of politics." Later, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government at the awards ceremony for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job.

Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema.

Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death.

Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering of Palestinians.

But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day.

Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry, Culture Ministry and its embassy in Italy have issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections.

Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine.

In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war.

Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film.

Khrzhanovsky took to social media on August 20 with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote on Facebook. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil."

Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars.

Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri").

Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire.

George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement.

Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German.

Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara.

And for those who want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier
https://www.dw.com/en/at-venice-film-fes.summary: The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2. The festival is known for its political films and political films. The competition includes "Naza," a documentary from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

https://www.dw.com/en/canada-s-carney-ho.title: Canada's Carney holds firm against Trump tariffs
https://www.dw.com/en/canada-s-carney-ho.text:
Canada is facing new US import penalties after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China. Other countries are watching as the Trump trade clash turns into a fight over economic sovereignty.

Canada has been quietly praised for refusing to fold under pressure from US President Donald Trump in the long-running fight over trade tariffs.

The latest talks between the North American neighbors collapsed on August 21. Until the 11th hour, both sides were talking as if a deal was within reach.

The United States then put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa pledged to match those duties on US imports.

Until the talks folded, Canada's approach was to cut a deal that would reduce the tariffs and keep cross-border supply chains functioning, particularly in the automotive and steel sectors.

US negotiators were, however, accused of changing the terms at the last minute, which the Canadian side said would have forced them to match US tariffs on China.

According to Ottawa, Washington wanted a say on future trade deals with other nations and to prevent Chinese goods being routed through Canada to evade US duties.

Dan Ciuriak, a senior fellow at the Waterloo, Canada-based Center for International Governance Innovation, described Trump's tariff-matching plan as "fortress North America," which he said was now a sovereignty issue for Ottawa.

"Canada is a trading nation," Ciuriak told DW. "If we align perfectly with the Americans — primarily about China — we then end up sacrificing our trade policy."

There is a recent precedent. When the US imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles last year, Canada followed suit. Beijing retaliated with 100% tariffs against one of Canada's biggest exports — canola.

Canada's $4.9 billion exports of canola oil, meal and seed to China were cut in half last year, according to data from the Canada China Business Council.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The smaller country is the one that bears the brunt in this kind of game. So that's one very good reason for Canada to have an independent trade policy," said Ciuriak.

As the US-Canada talks collapsed, Ottawa also complained that Washington had sought relief from rules on French-language movies and shows. Canada said this amounted to interference in its language and culture.

Despite the uncertainty and higher cost to business from walking away, the Canadian prime minister's approach to negotiations with the US has broad public support.

A survey conducted by the Angus Reid Institute found that three-in-four Canadians backed the more hard-line move, despite concerns over the impact on the domestic economy.

Ciuriak noted how Trump's barbs of turning Canada into the 51st US state and threats to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America have emboldened ordinary Canadians to boycott US travel and products.

"Travel by Canadians to the United States has plummeted," he said. "There has been a popular consumer backlash against buying American products."

New government data show Canadians made nearly 500,000 fewer trips to the US in the first three months of 2026 and spent about $800 million less on those visits.

A survey last month by the Angus Reid Institute found that 40% of Canadian grocery shoppers were checking product origins, and that most of those shoppers avoided US goods when they could.

Although the two economies are tightly bound together, the new US duties apply to only about 5% of the $382 billion in goods that Canada exports to its southern neighbor.

The Royal Bank of Canada has warned that a no-deal would impact 0.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) and jobs, while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimated it could cost as many as 90,000 jobs.

Other governments are also watching to see how standing up to Trump plays out.

During their own negotiations, the European Union, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and dozens of smaller partners all agreed to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy.

Only China has so far met Trump's tariff threat head-on, matching tariffs with tariffs and negotiating as a fellow superpower, rather than taking the first deal on offer.

Speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney said middle powers must act together, warning that if they were "not at the table," they would be "on the menu."

But for now, Carney is holding the line largely on his own. New Canadian tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods — including steel, aluminum, dairy, electronics and farm equipment — take effect on September 8. They are likely to be met with US retaliation.

While matching US tariffs dollar-for-dollar sounds aggressive, Ciuriak thinks they need not "punish" the Canadian economy.

"Canada's tariffs ... apply to products Canada both buys from and sells to the US. As American tariffs cut off Canadian sales south of the border, the Canadian measures create space at home for that production."

From January, Trump has threatened to raise duties on Canadian autos, trucks, parts and steel unless production moves to the US.

He also refused to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) for another 16 years. Instead, the North American free-trade pact, which still covers most cross-border goods, will be reviewed year by year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With no new talks planned with the US, Canadian lawmakers are talking up trade opportunities in other markets and weighing other retaliatory measures, including backing away from an order for US fighter jets.

Canada had planned to buy 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, with 16 already on order. The rest are now on hold.

"When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," British Columbia Premier David Eby said last week.

https://www.dw.com/en/inside-the-sea-cuc.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
https://www.dw.com/en/inside-the-sea-cuc.text:
A quiet multimillion‑dollar black market is exploding across the Indian Ocean, driven by one unlikely animal: the sea cucumber.

When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade.

Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering.

Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory — local biologist Sangamesh Uday said they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks."

The 1,500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases.

It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification, which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps.

To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Historical records show they were traded between Indonesian fishers and Chinese merchants even 800 years ago.

They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine. And though there is some scientific evidence that the omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac.

Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally, with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally.

The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios by using sea cucumbers and other sea creatures to keep the money flowing.

These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders.

They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species.

Teale Phelps Bondaroff, a leading expert on sea cucumber crime, said awareness is critical in dealing with the issue.

"While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he told DW.

The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations.

Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant.

As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50 kilometers (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south.

It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy and police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch.

Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. Several have come back for the second or third time — risking being incarcerated again after completing full sentences.

Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable.

Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable.

"The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud."

Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished, or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers.

But Bondaroff thinks that tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue.

"This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he said. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime."

This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker
https://www.dw.com/en/inside-the-sea-cuc.summary: The problem requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue, says Bondaroff. The problem is a financial crime that enables sea cucumber crime, he says.

https://www.dw.com/en/ailing-djokovic-de.title: Ailing Djokovic 'despised' every moment of US Open defeat
https://www.dw.com/en/ailing-djokovic-de.text:
Novak Djokovic has exited in the first round of a Grand Slam for the first time in over two decades. Could time — or an unknown health condition — be catching up with the Serbian tennis legend?

Former world No.1 Novak Djokovic's US Open has ended with this earliest Grand Slam exit in two decades as he fell to Mariano Navone 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 on Sunday.

The defeat scuppered the Serbian tennis legend's latest bid for a 25th Grand Slam title, and ended a streak of 78 Grand Slam first-round victories, which began at the 2006 French Open.

Considering the obvious discomfort the 39-year-old Djokovic began feeling early in the match, it was truly impressive that he managed to take Navone, 25, the distance.

After battling through more than four and a half hours in the Arthur Ashe Stadium, Djokovic gracefully congratulated his opponent.

"I don't want to take too much out of his win. Congrats to him. He's a nice guy, a fighter," Djokovic said of the 25-year-old Argentine, currently 48th in the men's rankings.

"It's unbelievable," Navone said after triumphing in his first meeting with his childhood idol.

"It was a tough match, a battle. Playing against Novak the first time in the biggest stage we have in the world of tennis right now… I mean, it's crazy."

Throughout most of the match, Djokovic looked physically spent, repeatedly throwing up into a courtside bucket and regularly doubling over in pain.

Unsurprisingly, Djokovic said he had "despised" every moment of the ordeal at Flushing Meadows in New York.

"I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me," he said.

"It's something that I've been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year — you know, vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there.

"Then my whole body, you know, starts to collapse, basically, cramping and pain. Yeah, the back just gave up in the end, and the shoulder, and I couldn't close it out"

At Djokovic's last tournament, in Cincinnati two weeks ago where he threw up into a towel, he first revealed that he had been struggling with a "health issue" that affects him in hot, humid conditions for "many years."

Despite the unspecified medical condition, Djokovic reached the final of the Australian Open in January and the semifinals of Wimbledon in June. However, he said following his exit in New York that he's now simply not physically capable of going deep into tournaments.

This mystery ailment, coupled with his age, will have many asking whether Djokovic, who remarkably still sits at No. 5 in the men's rankings, could be approaching the end of his career.

Perhaps more alarming than the ailment itself is the fact that he simply doesn't know how to correct the problem. Still, he appears determined to battle on — at least for now.

"Can the issue be fixed? I don't know," he said.

"I'm trying, man. I'm trying. Let's see."
https://www.dw.com/en/ailing-djokovic-de.summary: Novak Djokovic has exited in the first round of a Grand Slam for the first time in over two decades. The Serbian tennis legend has been struggling with a "health issue" for years. Djokovi's defeat scuppered his bid for a 25th Grand Slam title.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-wants-drones-to.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides, but it could backfire
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-wants-drones-to.text:
The EU wants to lift a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air, allowing drones to be used for greater precision. But experts warn the plan could lead to even more pesticides being used in agriculture.

In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed.

The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030.

Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light.

"I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain."

"At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection.

Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved.

When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it.

To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment.

The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release.

European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years.

Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence.

The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important.

Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said.

Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved.

But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author.

Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically.

The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security.

What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change."

This article was originally published in German.
