Identifying state sponsors of gray-zone acts is extremely difficult—by design. But if a targeted country manages to identify the state sponsor of an attack against it, should it make its identity known? Earlier this month, Germany announced that Russia was behind the incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in which a suspicious drone was identified, thankfully before it could do damage. Berlin’s announcement was a brave decision, because attribution, particularly involving bellicose nations such as Russia, brings the risk of escalation. But with gray-zone acts proliferating in number and variety, this is a decision targeted country should be ready to make.

On Sept. 1, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul walked up to a podium in Berlin in front of a crowd of journalists.

Identifying state sponsors of gray-zone acts is extremely difficult—by design. But if a targeted country manages to identify the state sponsor of an attack against it, should it make its identity known? Earlier this month, Germany announced that Russia was behind the incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in which a suspicious drone was identified, thankfully before it could do damage. Berlin’s announcement was a brave decision, because attribution, particularly involving bellicose nations such as Russia, brings the risk of escalation. But with gray-zone acts proliferating in number and variety, this is a decision targeted country should be ready to make.

On Sept. 1, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul walked up to a podium in Berlin in front of a crowd of journalists.

“For some time,” Dobrindt said, “our security agencies have been monitoring a high level of threat posed by hybrid activities in Germany and across Europe. These actions target critical infrastructure, defense companies, and support efforts for Ukraine. Intelligence gathered by our own services and partner agencies points clearly to Russian involvement in these hybrid operations—whether planned, executed, or thwarted.”

Dobrindt continued: “Regarding the attempted attack at Leipzig airport on Aug. 4, we have the following information: The means employed—including the drone configuration, various components, and the explosive and ignition technology—are consistent with those known to us from other hybrid operations conducted by Russia and from its war against Ukraine. The technology found at the scene and the integration of the individual elements demonstrate a professional level of sophistication, revealing significant technical expertise and substantial organizational effort in both the planning and execution of the act. The actual carrying out of the attempted attack is attributable to low-level operatives.”

The interior minister provided more evidence, but the news had been delivered: Russia was the instigator of the attack. “The Russian consulate-general in Bonn will be closed,” Wadephul declared, adding that the rental agreement for the Russian House in Berlin—a cultural center suspected of also serving as a hub for Russian intelligence activities—would be terminated.

Ten, even five years ago, Germany and most other countries were extremely cautious in attributing gray-zone attacks to Russia or any other country. To be sure, in some cases, hostile states’ involvement was obvious: During the artificial refugee crisis that erupted on the borders of Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland in the summer of 2021, for example, Belarus didn’t even try to hide its involvement; Minsk had provided Belarusian visas for the mostly Middle Eastern nationals, then transported them to the border.

But in many cases where hostile-state participation was more difficult to trace, as in case of the devastating NotPetya malware, or with the assassination attempt on former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal, governments did make attributions—after having identified Russian involvement.

Part of the issue is that establishing state involvement beyond reasonable doubt—the bar that democratic countries set themselves—is difficult and sometimes impossible. There’s a reason why countries such as Russia often use proxies or hire gig workers to do their dirty work. But more importantly, publicly laying blame for an attack can put countries at risk. The attacker is likely to flatly deny involvement, as Russia has with every gray-zone act attributed to it by Western governments.

Worse, even as countries deny involvement, they can still retaliate for being blamed. This is, in fact, what happened after Dobrindt and Wadephul made their announcement.

“Leipzig, at the airport. They found a drone there and said it was Russian. No one ever clarified the matter. Strictly speaking, that marks the beginning of a real war,” Sergey Lavrov told Russian state television. Somehow, the Russian foreign minister managed to blend evasion and denial then add a threat, all in a single statement.

Germany’s response to the Leipzig incident—the closure of the consulate-general and the Russian House—is hardly provocative. If even such a moderate response prompts menacing theatrics from the Kremlin, what’s a targeted country to do?

Political appeasement won’t buy off hostile powers.

Saying nothing is certainly not an option, not anymore. With gray-zone acts, especially Russian ones, becoming more common and more brazen, the public has become aware of their existence and destructive power. If governments decided that public attributions were too dangerous and said nothing, then their citizens would call them cowardly and suspect nefarious intrigues.

What’s more, Lavrov can only accuse Germany of having started “a real war” a few times. If he and others complain about supposed new wars each time that a country identifies the Kremlin as the instigator of dangerous acts, they will start looking like the schoolyard bully that only has one response in his arsenal.

No—now that gray-zone acts have become part of daily life, those instigating them must be called out. And the calling out should be directed not only at the hostile state behind the deed but also directed at the public at home. By keeping the nation informed about the activities taking place in society’s midst, governments can help citizens understand the seriousness of the situation (without unduly frightening them).

Public reaction, perhaps predictably, has been mixed, between those who worry that the German government is escalating and those who insist that it should not back down. In one call-in show on the WDR public radio station, a listener voiced suspicion: “Do we really believe that the Russians would attack us using two little pistols and what I would call three toy drones? They have totally different options. Our governments and other governments want this to escalate.”

Another listener, though, wanted an even more forceful reaction: “What would happen if we didn’t react to these kinds of attacks?”

Even without taking radical steps, Germany and other targeted countries could respond more assertively by focusing on transparency. In the Philippines, the authorities have taken to documenting every act of Chinese harassment of Philippine vessels in the South China Sea and sharing the content with the world.

To be sure, documenting random acts of Russian sabotage would be harder than filming constant harassment by Chinese vessels. But whatever can be documented ought to be publicly shared. The public would, among other things, see the sorry figures who, for a small financial reward, set fire to buildings, sabotage railways, and try to wreak havoc with drones. That way, citizens would understand that while gray-zone aggression is dangerous and devious, it is also profoundly pusillanimous.

Elisabeth Braw is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, and the author of Goodbye Globalization. Bluesky: @elisabethbraw.bsky.social

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/08/yem.author: Alexandra Sharp

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure, Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs against the United States, and a British ban on all Israeli goods made in the West Bank.

Houthi rebels in Yemen launched a slew of missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, marking one of the largest Houthi assaults on the kingdom since fighting erupted in July. The strikes mark another major escalation between Riyadh and the Iranian proxy group, and they raise fears that renewed fighting could transform into all-out war.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure, Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs against the United States, and a British ban on all Israeli goods made in the West Bank.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Houthi rebels in Yemen launched a slew of missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, marking one of the largest Houthi assaults on the kingdom since fighting erupted in July. The strikes mark another major escalation between Riyadh and the Iranian proxy group, and they raise fears that renewed fighting could transform into all-out war.

Early Tuesday, the Houthi rebel group accused Saudi Arabia of targeting a Yemeni prison in Jawf province, killing at least 17 people and wounding around seven others. “Every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response,” Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, warned on Tuesday.

Hours later, Saudi military officials said that the Houthis had targeted four Saudi cities, injuring more than 70 people, including women and children. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the strikes also damaged critical civilian and military infrastructure, including oil facilities connected to Bab el-Mandeb strait, a logistics hub on the Red Sea coast, and King Khalid Air Base, located near Khamis Mushait.

These strikes signal a “dangerous escalation,” and the Saudi-led coalition will take “all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat,” Maliki said on Tuesday.

In September 2014, Houthi forces seized control of Yemen’s capital, sparking a devastating civil war. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to try to restore power to Yemen’s internationally recognized government. Although a 2022 truce largely eased fighting between the two forces, the Iran war’s destabilization of the region has risked upending that delicate detente, particularly after the Saudi-led military coalition attacked Sanaa International Airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Houthis flying back from Tehran from landing.

Since then, the Houthis have tried to advance on government-held positions, while Yemeni authorities have said that they aim to recapture all Houthi-held territory. According to the World Health Organization, renewed conflict killed at least 194 people and injured more than 880 others between Aug. 23 and Sept. 5. That includes at least 81 people killed during a Houthi ground assault near Bab el-Mandeb, which was part of a wider rebel effort to control traffic through the critical waterway; Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Global energy prices reeled on Tuesday in the wake of the Houthis’ missile and drone attack. Brent crude briefly surpassed $99 per barrel for the first time since late July, and West Texas Intermediate hit its highest level since early June.

“Dollar for dollar.” Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on around $20 billion worth of U.S. goods went into effect on Tuesday. The duties, which impact goods from textiles to cheese to furniture, mimic recent tariffs that the White House has imposed on Ottawa, and they signal the latest bout of escalatory measures in the two economies’ expanding trade war.

Last month, trade negotiations between U.S. and Canadian officials collapsed after Ottawa accused Washington of trying to destroy key Canadian industries. Both U.S. President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a slew of tariffs in response, with Ottawa pledging to go “dollar for dollar” with the White House’s duties. Accompanied by a war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, relations between the North American neighbors have reached one of their lowest points in years.

Canada’s latest tariffs—and its larger pivot away from the United States as its No. 1 trading partner—“will come at a cost,” Carney said in a video message on Tuesday. However, “it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still,” he added.

Just hours before Tuesday’s duties took effect, Trump took aim at Canadian plane manufacturer Bombardier on Truth Social, suggesting that the company will no longer be allowed to sell its products in the United States. “BUY AMERICAN. FLY ON AMERICAN AIRLINERS. ENJOY AMERICAN LIQUOR AND BEVERAGES. SAIL ON LAKE AMERICA,” Trump wrote. Last month, he signed an executive order requiring Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” in the U.S. federal government’s geographic names information system.

Punishing Israel. The United Kingdom announced its intention on Tuesday to impose sweeping trade restrictions on Israel, including a ban on all goods produced in the occupied West Bank. “Today marks the beginning of a new approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament, calling Israeli settlements in the West Bank “unlawful” and accusing extremist settlers of perpetrating “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians.” He added, “To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: You will face the full force of U.K. sanctions.”

Miliband’s announcement cements London’s support for an International Court of Justice ruling in July 2024 that found Israel’s presence in the West Bank to be in violation of international law, including prohibitions on racial segregation and apartheid. It also lends support to similar trade bans by Canada and France, which have denounced Israel’s occupation of the West Bank.

Although Western criticism of Israel’s West Bank occupation has grown in recent years, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has continued to shrug off foreign condemnation, and several of his cabinet members have repeatedly pushed for the construction of more settlements.

On Tuesday, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced that Israel will close the British consulate in Jerusalem, expel British representatives monitoring the Gaza cease-fire, end U.K. training of Palestinian Authority security forces in the West Bank, and bar 12 elected British officials from entering Israel, among other retaliatory measures.

An AfD victory. Thousands of people held a pro-democracy rally in Berlin on Tuesday to denounce the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party’s recent state election win. Carrying signs condemning some of the AfD’s trademark policies—including its anti-immigrant and pro-Russian stances—the backlash foreshadows what experts suspect will be two more tumultuous regional elections later this month.

On Sunday, the AfD won a landslide victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. With around 44 percent of the vote, this was a nativist party’s best-ever state election showing since the Nazi regime. Germany’s mainstream parties have long vowed to never work with the AfD, and the far-right party is classified as an extremist group in some regions of the country, including in Saxony-Anhalt.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has already ruled out any collaboration with the AfD, doubling down on the country’s so-called firewall against the far-right group. However, the hard-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance has signaled its intention to form a governing alliance with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt.

First, the Louvre. Then, Paris’s Museum of Natural History. On Tuesday, another French collection joined the list of museums targeted by art heists in recent months. Investigators said a group of “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves sliced through a fence to enter the Renoir Museum in the French Riviera’s Cagnes-sur-Mer, stealing four valuable paintings. Local police arrived around five minutes after the alarm was triggered, forcing the suspects to abandon two of the masterpieces in the museum’s garden. However, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well are still missing, and the culprits remain at large.

https://www.france24.com/en/trump-posts-.title: Trump posts AI map showing US 'takeover' of North America, Iceland and Caribbean
https://www.france24.com/en/trump-posts-.author: Vedika BAHL
https://www.france24.com/en/trump-posts-.text:
The map, posted on Truth Social without a caption or explanation, redrew continental North America in the US flag’s stars and stripes. Canada and Mexico appear annexed within US territory, alongside Greenland and Iceland, while Cuba, Jamaica and several French Caribbean territories, including Martinique and Guadeloupe, are also depicted as part of the United States.

The map labels the enlarged territory simply as the “United States of America”, while the Gulf of Mexico is shown as the “Gulf of America," given Trump's recent executive order to rename it.

It is unclear whether the post was intended as a joke, an attempt to provoke foreign governments or simply to generate attention, but it comes against a backdrop of increasingly provocative territorial rhetoric from the US president.

Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st US state, angering officials in Ottawa amid an escalating trade dispute. He has also expressed interest in acquiring Greenland from Denmark and has spoken of the United States “taking back” the Panama Canal.

The latest map goes further, however, appearing to bring countries and territories including Mexico, Iceland and French Caribbean islands into Trump’s imagined US borders.

The response from some of the countries depicted was swift. Iceland said it had summoned the US ambassador for a meeting, describing the post as “entirely inappropriate”.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum was equally unequivocal, saying Mexico would neither be a colony nor a protectorate of another country. “We are a free, independent and sovereign nation,” she posted on X.

Denmark, meanwhile, reiterated its opposition to any US takeover of Greenland, with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen telling reporters that both Greenland’s government and its people had repeatedly made clear that they did not want to become American.

Trump's latest map-making has also generated widespread ridicule online, alongside renewed speculation about Trump’s fitness for office.

California state Senator Scott Wiener called the behaviour "unbelievably dangerous" and accused Trump of having a "serious brain disease, whether dementia or something else", while other social media users mocked the president for posting what they described as imaginary maps after spending years criticising Joe Biden over his age.

These reactions were amplified as Trump, over the weekend shared an avalanche of posts at breakneck speed. According to an AFP count, Trump posted 60 times on Sunday alone, followed by another 37 posts in roughly 10 hours on Monday. Many featured AI-generated or AI-manipulated imagery.

The series of posts including one claiming that even the Moon belonged to the US, as well as a string of images renaming the state of New Mexico to "New America", prompting an angry reaction from the state's governor.

Users also declared Trump's online behaviour would be concerning if it came from an elderly relative, and Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree argued that Republicans should be asking whether Trump is fit to remain in office.

Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.title: Trump tells Putin he wants swift end to Ukraine war, Kremlin says
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone on Tuesday that he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, which would allow US-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said, adding that ​Putin had supported the ‌US president's view.

The call, which the Kremlin said lasted an hour, followed a weekend visit to Moscow ⁠and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are trying to revive stalled talks designed to find a way to end the fighting. Their weekend diplomacy did not appear ‌to result in any immediate public breakthrough although they did raise the possibility that three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine ⁠and the United States could be resumed.

The Kremlin, which has said it does not rule that out, made no mention of the possibility in its readout of the Putin-Trump call. Instead, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the two ​leaders had rated the US envoys' weekend diplomacy "with a plus sign" and that Putin had told Trump ‌what he believed the United States could do to help end the conflict and given him an assessment of what the situation on the battlefield was.

Trump, Ushakov said, had made it clear he wanted the war quickly finished. "Donald Trump clearly emphasised the desirability of bringing the conflict to an ‌end as soon as possible, which would immediately open up prospects – impressive and far-reaching ones at that – for the full restoration of relations between the US and Russia," said Ushakov.

READ MORE
US envoys bring ‘more effective’ Ukraine peace proposals to Kyiv, official says

"In his view, ​this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries. Donald Trump is keen to see a breakthrough achieved during his presidency. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin supported this approach."

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the ​war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, and both sides have escalated their attacks on each other in recent months. ​

A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before the trip by Trump's envoys, said Putin remained ​intent on taking full control of the remainder of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, something Kyiv has vowed to continue fiercely opposing with every weapon at its disposal.

Ushakov – who said Putin and Trump ​had also agreed on the need to continue prisoner exchanges – said he was not able to get into more detail about what had been discussed, but described the conversation as constructive and said the two leaders had agreed they would stay in touch and speak to each other by phone again if the need arose.

He said Putin had told Trump that Russia had no hostile intentions when it came to Europe ⁠despite repeated claims to the contrary by various European politicians.

"In light of speculation regarding Russia’s alleged hostile intentions towards European states, it was emphasised that we have absolutely ⁠no aggressive plans whatsoever ​towards Europe," said Ushakov.

"The myths being spread about the Russian threat merely serve as a pretext for Europeans to ramp up their support for Ukraine and their own military spending," he added.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202609.title: Messi, Mbappé and Kane headline Ballon d'Or shortlist, Vozinha named for Yashin award
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202609.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202609.text:
Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland ⁠and Lionel ​Messi have all made the 30-man shortlist for the 2026 Men's Ballon ​d'Or, while Cape Verde's World Cup hero Vozinha has been nominated for the Yashin award, organisers France Football announced on Tuesday.

Real Madrid's Mbappé did not win a trophy with his club this season but he scored 10 goals for France at the World Cup to become the tournament's all-time leading scorer.

READ MORE
'This might be the year': Mbappé embraces Ballon d'Or talk after World Cup exploits

Kane had a stunning season ​with Bayern ‌Munich and England, scoring 73 goals for club ⁠and country in 65 matches and helped secure a treble of Bundesliga, German Cup, and German ‌Super Cup as well as leading his nation to the ⁠World Cup semi-finals.

Haaland netted 58 goals in 64 games for Manchester City and Norway, while eight-times Ballon d'Or winner Messi ​had 75 goal contributions in 49 matches for Inter ‌Miami and Argentina, who he helped to reached the World Cup final.

Also among those on the shortlist are Jude Bellingham, Ousmane Dembélé and ‌Lamine Yamal but not five-times winner Cristiano Ronaldo despite the Portugal forward lifting the Saudi Pro ​League title with Al-Nassr.

The women's shortlist includes Poland's Barcelona quadruple-winner Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, who featured for Barca and Spain but has now ​joined London City Lionesses, and Manchester City's prolific Jamaica striker Khadija 'Bunny' ​Shaw.

Cape Verde's Vozinha was nominated for the Yashin ​Trophy awarded to the best goalkeeper, with his standout World Cup performances putting him on the ​10-man shortlist after he helped his country advance from the tournament's group stage.

He will compete against Spain's World Cup-winner Unai Simon and Argentina's Emi Martinez plus fellow African nominees Yassine Bounou and Edouard Mendy.

The 70th edition ⁠of the Ballon d'Or will be staged in London for the first time at a ⁠ceremony on ​October 26 as a tribute to Stanley Matthews, who won the first Ballon d'Or.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.title: Live: Invite-only grant scheme 'pork-barrelling by design': Haines
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.author: Courtney Gould
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Government and Politics

Independent MP Helen Haines has taken aim at an invitation-only grants scheme, calling it "pork-barrelling by design".

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Australian high school students' scores in maths and reading have hit their lowest point on record, according to a major international test.

While the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) exams showed a slight improvement in science results since the last test in 2022, Australia's long-term learning decline continued overall.

Education Minister Jason Clare has raised concern about the link between access to technology and lower scores.

"The PISA results are telling us that the children that are online more are getting lower results. The more you're online, the more your results decline," he tells ABC News Breakfast.

"The evidence is telling us that we probably need a good digital detox in our schools. It doesn't mean there's not place for technology."

Clare says it's not impossible to shift the dial, pointing to the UK and the "big changes" it made to the education system more than a decade ago.

The minister thinks Australia also needs to do the same but it's going to cost money to do so.

Don't worry, you're not alone, politicians get sucked into doomscrolling too.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says there are nights where she looks at the time and wonders: "What have I been doing? Why am I still on here?"

"Everyone knows that feeling of being sucked in…[the algorithm is] designed to do that," she said.

"It feeds harmful material because it manipulates our feeds, based on our emotions, our interactions, our data."

Following the government's announcement yesterday that it wants users to get control over whether or not an algorithm decides their feed, the Greens want action against the addictive nature of social media too.

She reckons some sort of "friction" to stop the auto-play of videos would help.

Australia's spend on age and service pensions is expected to drop from 2.3 per cent to 1.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2066, according to new analysis.

The government's intergenerational report (IGR), which will be released in full later this month, projects economic opportunities and obstacles over the next 40 years.

The analysis shows the share of older Australians, aged 67 or above, receiving a pension or income support will decline from 66 per cent to 52 per cent over the same period.

Speaking to the Super Members Council later today, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will state the reduced pressure on the budget is due to having superannuation "at the core" of the best retirement system.

"In comparison, that number is nearly 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand, and 6 per cent in the US," Chalmers will say.

The IGR has revised its 2023 outlook, which predicted the portion of GDP spent on pensions would fall to 2 per cent.

Chalmers will argue super needs to be preserved against "existential" threats, including One Nation, who earlier this week suggested dipping into superannuation early for those struggling with cost of living.

Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.

Independent MP Helen Haines has taken aim at an invitation-only grants scheme, calling it "pork-barrelling by design".

An investigation by the Centre for Public Integrity, reported by the ABC, found three-quarters of the funds from the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program went to electorates held by Labor at the 2025 federal election.

Haines says she found out about the grants program a year ago when a local golf club asked how they could get an invitation to apply for a grant.

"I subsequently asked the minister for infrastructure [Catherine King] about this in question time last November and she very clearly stated that this was a program that was designed to deliver election commitments," she tells ABC's News Breakfast.

"In other words, this was pork-barrelling by design, which makes it quite different actually to sports rorts, which was pork-barreling by deception. So we've got two methods here but the same outcome."

Haines is calling for the Commonwealth grant guidelines to be rewritten to include enforceable standards.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to Marrickville Golf Club, which he has not declared on his register of interests.

The golf club was promised $6 million at the federal election, which was awarded through a fund that heavily favoured Labor seats.

Records of the prime minister's register of interests dating back to his entry to parliament in 1996 do not mention a membership to the club, either paid or honorary.

"We have him on the books as an honorary member, but I think that dates from a long time ago, that hasn't been reaffirmed," a spokesperson for the Marrickville Golf Club told the ABC.

"I don't know when he was put on the books as an honorary member, that may have been 15 years ago or more."

The Prime Minister's Office did not respond to questions about Mr Albanese's membership.

Read more of this exclusive report by Jake Evans at the link below.

Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

The government released its long awaited first draft of its Digital Duty of Care legislation yesterday, confirming the bill would grant users a choice between an algorithm social media feed or to just see the accounts someone follows.

A little birdie has told me Anthony Albanese will be out and about on the media rounds this morning to spruik the plan on breakfast television.

Also expect there to be more questions about friend of the blog Jake Evans's report on Labor's use of an invite-only infrastructure grant.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Sabalenka stays alive at US Open by telling herself 'the match is over'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Aryna Sabalenka was down a break before coming back to win the deciding set. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Aryna Sabalenka has come back from a break in the third set to beat Linda Noskova in the US Open quarterfinals.

Sabalenka said she thought "the match is over" while trailing 2-4 in the decider, before coming back to win it in a tiebreak.

She will face the winner of an all-American clash between third seed Jessica Pegula and 26th seed Emma Navarro.

World number one Aryna Sabalenka has survived her toughest test of the tournament to beat Wimbledon champion Linda ​Noskova 7-6(7/1), 3-6, 7-6(10/7) and reach the US Open semifinals for a sixth consecutive year.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka had not dropped a set before facing the Czech sixth seed, who fired ​18 aces and saved ‌seven of nine break points but faltered when leading by a break at 2-4 in the final set.

Sabalenka, chasing a third straight title at Flushing Meadows, next plays the winner of ‌an all-American clash between Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro.

"What a battle. What ⁠an incredible player she is. I'm speechless right now because ‌I was pushing myself to ​the limit this match," ‌said Sabalenka, who has now won 21 of her past 22 matches at the year-end grand slam.

"In the third set I honestly thought, 'That's it, the match is over.' Probably that's what helped me to kind of feel loose and just go after my shots. Super happy to get this win."

By reaching the final four for a sixth straight time, Sabalenka matched the 2011-2016 run of Serena Williams, during which she won three of her six US Open crowns.

The Belarusian broke in the second game, whipping a forehand into the corner that Noskova did not even attempt to chase down, but the Czech broke back with a pair of powerful groundstrokes from the baseline in ​the ‌ninth.

Sabalenka, who reached a record 21 consecutive tiebreak wins at the slams earlier this year, was completely in her element in the opening-set breaker, ⁠where she sprinted through the first ‌six points.

But her firepower deserted ‌her in the second set and she struggled to contain Noskova's serve before handing the ‌Czech a 4-2 lead with a double fault.

After levelling the contest at one set all, Noskova set about pressing home her ‌advantage.

Sabalenka ​screamed in frustration when ⁠a pair of double faults midway through the third set helped her opponent secure another break.

Noskova seemed to be heading for an upset win before Sabalenka recovered her poise to level the contest in the ⁠eighth game.

And the Belarusian was right at home again in the decisive tiebreak, clinching it with an ace ‌before giving ‌credit to the fans for helping to propel her to ​the win.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Prince George and his parents arrive at Eton College for his first day.

Prince George has started at Eton College three decades after his father donned the same school uniform.

Cameras captured the future king's arrival at Eton College, a 600-year-old school with annual student fees of about $121,000.

Prince George's younger cousins, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are also due to start new schools in the UK this month, but it is not clear which schools they will attend.

Prince George has started his first day at Eton College, following in the footsteps of his father Prince William by attending the 600-year-old school.

Prince William and his wife Catherine, the Princess of Wales, were with King Charles's grandson when he arrived at his new school, with footage showing them smiling and looking relaxed as they were greeted by Eton's head teacher, Simon Henderson.

Rain was falling as the royal family arrived.  (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

The future king's uncle, Prince Harry, also attended Eton, which is close ​to the monarch's Windsor Castle, west of London, and where William and Catherine and their other two children Charlotte and Louis also have a home.

Fees for the all-boys boarding school, which was founded by King Henry VI in 1440, ​are about £65,000 ($121,000) a year.

The royal family meet head teacher Simon Henderson and provost Nicholas Coleridge. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Prince George, the second in line to the throne, was previously at the private Lambrook School, also near ​Windsor, with his sister and younger brother.

Prince George's younger cousins, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, the children of Prince Harry and Megan, are also due to start new schools in the UK this month, but it is not clear which schools they will attend.

Prince George is the second in line to the throne.  (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Prince William was the first member of the ​royal family to attend Eton. Charles went to Gordonstoun, the same private school ‌on ⁠the north coast of Scotland that his father, Prince Philip, attended.

It was all smiles for Prince George's first day.  (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Eton has ​long been the alma mater for many of ​the ⁠country's political leaders. Twenty British prime ministers, including Boris Johnson and David Cameron, went to the school, as did actors Hugh Laurie, Damian ⁠Lewis ​and Tom Hiddleston.

It retains many traditions. Pupils wear tail coats, waistcoats and gowns, and teachers are referred to as "beaks".

Eton College has educated many of Britain's political leaders. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Prince George's first day also happened to coincide with the fourth anniversary of the death of his great-grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.title: Rural towns finding the right medicine to end doctor drought
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.author: Liam O'Connell and Ellie Willcox
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Clermont had been relying on temporary doctors before the Royal Flying Doctor Service began servicing the town. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Nearly one-third of medical graduates are now studying to become GPs, easing concerns of widespread general practice shortages.

Peak training bodies say the focus needs to stay on training more doctors outside capital cities.

The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners is pushing for local, state and federal governments to help small communities establish sustainable healthcare models.

In his early days as a solo general practitioner in rural Queensland, Ewen McPhee remembers them as both exhilarating and exhausting.

"I have evidence I worked for three days without getting any sleep at all," he said.

Despite the long nights and mounting pressure, Dr McPhee ended up staying for decades in the central Queensland town of Emerald.

He said the turning point came with the arrival of the community-owned "super-clinic" in 2012.

Ewen McPhee says the workload of GPs has increased over the decades.  (Supplied: Ewen McPhee)

"The growth in the number of clinicians required is very much related to the complexity of general practice," he said.

"It's no longer coughs, colds and runny noses; it's chronic disease management."

Dr McPhee said the community model had a specific focus on the education of young career doctors.

"We're also allowing Central Highlands residents and nurses to have opportunities to train," he said.

Ewen McPhee says a community-owned model makes it easier to bring trainee doctors in.  (Supplied: Ewen McPhee)

The peak body for GPs said there had been further federal investment in regional health care, but it was still up to local doctors to make use of it.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) rural chair Michael Clements said a local practice's success came down to how well the three levels of government managed practice rents, hospital staff-sharing and Medicare exemptions.

"Generally, when a state government provides a health service, it's supposed to achieve that funding through national health reform agreements; they're not supposed to be tapping into Medicare," Dr Clements said.

"In rural and remote communities, there are exceptions."

Michael Clements says general practice has become more attractive for graduates.  (Supplied: RACGP)

Dr Clements has seen the changes himself.

His practice in Cloncurry in north-west Queensland was previously run by a single doctor stretched between hospital and general care.

When rebuilding the practice, Dr Clements said he secured agreements with Queensland Health and other health bodies to ensure trainees would be allowed to work in the remote town.

Cloncurry's new general practice has focused on balancing hospital and primary care responsibilities. (Supplied: Clements Medical)

"The doctors are all salaried via Queensland Health with all of those entitlements yet still able to work from a community, privately owned general practice."

Dr Clements said the money made from those GP appointments from Medicare then went back to Queensland Health.

He said the Cloncurry council also helped guarantee accommodation and access to health care for staff, which gave the practice its best chance to succeed.

Cloncurry is home to more than 3,000 residents. (Supplied: Cloncurry Shire Council)

The latest figures from the RACGP and its counterpart the Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine (ACRRM) show nearly 33 per cent of medical graduates were training to become either GPs or rural generalists.

That was music to the ears of John Burnett from community group Clermont4Doctors, who had advocated for more sustainable health care in his central Queensland hometown for close to a decade.

He said as far back as 1886, it was the Clermont community and not health authorities who made the town enticing for doctors, offering the modern equivalent of $150,000.

John Burnett says better healthcare in Clermont is vital to attracting young families and keeping older residents. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

More recently, the town was left without a permanent GP in January, leaving not just Clermont but the broader agricultural region and drive-in-drive-out mine workers in limbo.

Mr Burnett said people were driving 200 kilometres for treatment, only to be told the doctor was busy.

"They go, 'Actually, I won't come back tomorrow, I'll just treat myself with a bit of aspirin and maybe a bit of sheep dip,'" he said.

The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) has stepped into the breach, opening a Primary Health Care Clinic in the town of 3,000 which will run until next year.

RFDS chief operating officer for clinical services Dom Tait said the organisation was "excited" to run a clinic from within the Clermont Hospital.

"We know how important it is to have continuity of care from your GP," he said.

The RFDS will provide GP services in Clermont until early next year. (Supplied: RFDS)

"Our GPs will be fly-in and fly-out, but really importantly is those GPs are the same GPs on a rotation every four weeks.

"So, the community will get to know the GPs from the RFDS because it'll be the same GPs."

Dr Clements said the number of medical graduates taking on general practice was exciting, and he was optimistic more local practices could rebuild their training pipeline.

"It's actually competitive to get into GP training now," Dr Clements said.

"If you're a rural community and you've got the right recipe of a good, functioning practice with a good reputation for training, you can have a solution."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/n.author: Josh Becker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Narelle Zanker is Australia's Rural Woman of the Year. (Supplied)

South Australian dairy farmer Narelle Zanker has been crowned Australia's AgriFutures Rural Woman of the Year at Canberra's Parliament House.

She is a former teacher with a passion for farming.

The AgriFutures Rural Women's Award National Runner-Up was Northern Territory pilot and innovator Kelly Shotton.

When South Australian dairy farmer Narelle Zanker sees the recognition in a child's face when they realise that milk comes from cows and not a bottle in the fridge, she's reminded of the difference she's making.

Growing up on the family dairy farm on the banks of the Murray River near Mannum, just over an hour's drive east of Adelaide, Ms Zanker always wanted to be a teacher.

But four years into her new career, she experienced a "light bulb moment" when she realised she could merge her love for teaching with her love for farming. And so, with the support of her husband and family, Dairy Adventures was born in 2024.

"[Dairy Adventures] is a fun, educational, interactive experience for families and school groups to come onto the farm and bottle-feed the calves, milk the cows, tour the farm and learn about where their food comes from, from paddock to plate," Ms Zanker said.

Australia's Rural Woman of the Year will be announced in Canberra on Tuesday, September 8.

The only agritourism venture of its kind in South Australia, Ms Zanker said Dairy Adventures addressed a massive gap between farmer and consumer.

"People don't know where their food comes from, they don't know where milk comes from, they think it comes from the fridge in their house or from the shops," she said.

Now the former teacher has been recognised as Australia's AgriFutures Rural Woman of the Year at Canberra's Parliament House last night and will receive a $20,000 grant to develop Dairy Adventures further and take it nationwide through virtual classrooms.

"Having a love for education and farming is what makes it work," she said.

The AgriFutures Rural Women's Award National Runner-Up was Northern Territory pilot and innovator Kelly Shotton, founder of Stationly, a digital platform that helps remote stations monitor tanks, bores and other water infrastructure across vast properties.

The Rural Women's Award, originally established by ABC Rural in 1994 and now in its 26th year as an AgriFutures initiative, recognises women who are shaping the future of rural and regional Australia through innovation, enterprise and leadership.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/n.title: Inside the new police powers to target Sydney's criminal underworld
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/n.author: Anton Rose
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Organised Crime

New legislative changes are coming for a powerful NSW Police tool: Serious Crime Prevention Orders. (ABC News: Dylan Goolagong)

NSW Police are set to get extraordinary powers to tackle underworld violence, but whether the move will be effective remains to be seen.

Prompted by two mistaken identity gangland murders within 48 hours last week, the beefed-up serious crime prevention orders (SCPO) will be a valuable tool for crime fighters.

The deaths of Marco Tapia and Joshua Macdonald tragically marked the sixth and seventh murders of innocent people attributed to underworld hostilities in the space of a year.

Joshua Macdonald (left) and Marco Tapia were both killed in separate shootings in Sydney last week. (Supplied)

Though rarely used, the orders are broad powers restricting the activities of those who police suspect are involved in organised crime conflict.

Currently, police have to bring an application before the Supreme Court before one is made.

An SCPO can restrain who a gangster talks to, where they live, what bank accounts they use and force them to hand over passwords to email and social media accounts.

They restrict what they are allowed to wear, what phones they can use and what car they can drive.

The extraordinary nature of the orders is that those on the receiving end do not have to be charged with committing a crime to effectively be on conditions akin to house arrest.

Ghassan Amoun, Bassam Hamzy's brother, was jailed when he breached an SCPO. (Supplied)

Those who breach the orders can face jail, as Hamzy crime family member Ghassan Amoun found out in 2021, months before he was shot dead.

He was given a 12-month jail term for breaching his SCPO and was gunned down in South Wentworthville just days after being released from serving his sentence.

The catch has always been that NSW Police have to wait for Supreme Court approval for an SCPO, which could take weeks if not months.

And time is vital when underworld violence spirals out of control.

In 2022, one Sydney-based head of a bikie gang subject to an SCPO was only handed it six months after the acts of violence that sparked the order's necessity.

Fugitive Rafat Alameddine, previously subjected to an SCPO, now remains overseas. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Premier Chris Minns's announcement on Monday of an "interim" SCPO that does not require a court's approval essentially bypasses this hurdle for police.

While the legislative changes make the battle to stem the bloodshed easier for the state's crime fighters, NSW Police face another roadblock.

Unlike previous eras of tit-for-tat violence, police suspect most of the criminals orchestrating the recent attacks are not in NSW.

Their utility in stopping overseas-based crime figures organising kidnappings, assaults and murders this time around will be the first challenge for police.

Detectives believe the heads of the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel" and the Alameddine crime family remain scattered across Asia, eastern Europe and Lebanon.

A wanted Sydney underworld figure may have unwittingly helped police after posting social media messages mocking his underworld adversaries from overseas.

The Coconut Cartel consists of Pacific Islander Australians from the city's western suburbs and takes its name from a historical slur against Pasifika people.

The two groups, police believe, are at the centre of a surge in attacks, kidnappings and assassinations that culminated in last week's tragedies.

With key figures remaining offshore, those likely to be on the receiving end of SCPOs this time around are possibly their Sydney-based underlings and the fledgling teenage crime-for-hire groups they contract.

Those involved in the current conflicts plaguing Sydney's streets will be familiar with the acronym SCPO.

The orders were credited in police circles with stemming a wave of gangland violence between the Hamzy and Alameddine crime families in 2020.

Alleged crime figures Rafat Alameddine, Masood Zakaria, Ibrahem Hamze and others in the rival clans were subject to them for 12 months as police worked to calm tensions.

Similarly, that conflict also saw two innocent people killed in the crossfire: Toufik Hamze and Mustapha Naaman.

Police believe Mustapha Naaman was mistaken for a member of the Hamze family when he was shot dead in January 2021. (Supplied)

The orders granted police some of the broadest powers in NSW legislation, though the main complaint from crime bosses at the time was that it made them "sitting ducks" for their adversaries.

One of the state's top police officers has promised feuding gangs bringing terror to Sydney's streets will not exist "by the time we finish" as police stare down a new era of disorganised crime.

When the conflict spread to the Comanchero bikie gang and the Ahmad family in 2022, the upper hand police had on underworld violence found its limits.

The oppressive nature of the SCPO saw the gang's sergeant-at-arms Tarek Zahed and national president Allan Meehan move to Victoria and Queensland respectively to escape the scrutiny.

This is where the orders met their match.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.title: Women in Darwin forced to travel hundreds of kilometres for pregnancy scans
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.author: Roxanne Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Roxanne Fitzgerald

Sarah Williams says she wanted to get a nuchal scan during pregnancy to make sure her baby was OK.  (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Women across Darwin say they are struggling to book a range of time-sensitive pregnancy scans.

One woman, Sarah Williams, says she was told she could drive hundreds of kilometres to Katherine to get a nuchal scan, which is currently only offered at one private service in Darwin.

The Northern Territory government says it is providing the required scans in the public system, but advocacy group Our Birth, Our Voice says the government needs to increase access.

When Sarah Williams fell pregnant last year after losing a baby, she found herself holding her breath as the 12-week mark — when tragedy had struck before — crept closer.

She expected to be able to book a nuchal scan — a time-sensitive first-trimester pregnancy ultrasound that screens for abnormalities and checks that a baby is developing as expected.

But securing an appointment proved so difficult, she joined a growing number of expectant mothers across Darwin being forced to wait, drive hundreds of kilometres or travel interstate for the scan, or going without.

Sarah Williams says difficulties with accessing maternity care have made her rethink having another baby. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

While the Australian Medical Association's Northern Territory branch (AMA NT) said the nuchal scan is one "all women should be offered in pregnancy", the NT government said nationally, the scan is generally only provided through private health services.

Only one private provider offers the scan in Darwin, meaning appointments are difficult to secure.

Ms Williams said she was told she could try to access the scan in Katherine — 300 kilometres away from Darwin — or get a non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT) at a cost of about $500, which the NT government says is its "preferred medical test".

While she was desperate for reassurance her baby was OK, she said she was caught in an impossible situation.

She couldn't afford the NIPT, was unable to take time off work, had a toddler depending on her and no partner to help carry the load.

Ms Williams chose to go on the cancellation list, and was lucky to get a last-minute call for an appointment in Darwin.

"It was two or three weeks past the normal range for the scan," she said.

"I just dropped everything and went in."

Sophia Emberson-Bain says the government needs to expand access to pregnancy scans. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Darwin-based advocacy group Our Birth, Our Voice said it was time for the government to expand access through the public system for all pregnancy scans.

A survey by Our Birth, Our Voice, which spoke to more than 200 women since July, found many faced difficulties accessing early dating scans, the 11-13 week nuchal scan and the 18-22 week morphology scan.

Just 31 per cent of women said they could access the morphology scan through the public system, while almost 50 per cent said they had difficulty getting it within the recommended time.

Fewer than half of all respondents were able to access a nuchal scan within the recommended timeframe.

Three women said they had flown interstate for the scan and 24 women said they were unable to access it at all.

A survey has found many Darwin women face difficulties with accessing a variety of pregnancy scans.    (Pexels: MART PRODUCTION)

Another said: "We found out about a heart concern at 26 weeks because the public scan kept getting pushed back. If we'd known earlier, we would have had more options and more time to prepare."

"It’s extremely hard to get scans for the first 20 weeks of pregnancy … If something is wrong it helps make informed decisions early," one woman told the survey.

Another respondent said she had skipped meals to cover the cost of a scan privately.

NT councillor for the National Association of Specialist Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, Alia Vemuri, worked as an obstetrician at the Darwin Private Hospital until 2025, when the facility closed its maternity services.

A growing number of women in the NT are travelling interstate to give birth — or leaving the territory altogether — following the sudden closure of the only private hospital maternity ward. Now, the NT's last private obstetrician is closing her practice.

She said the closure translated to "reduced access for private obstetric patients in obtaining dating, point of care and growth scans".

Brydie Purbrick, a councillor with the AMA NT, and an obstetrician and gynaecologist, said another issue was the NT did not have enough sonographers or ultrasound machines to keep up with demand.

Brydie Purbrick says a shortage of sonographers and ultrasound machines means the public system is struggling to keep up with demand. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"And we're not attracting them here, we're not paying a competitive rate compared to the big cities, and so we're having trouble retaining good-quality ultrasound staff to provide the service."

Dr Purbrick said the public hospital had eight ultrasound machines that were used across all health sectors, and four of them were "out-of-date".

NT Health Minister Steve Edgington said the government was "doing enough" to ensure staff levels were adequate and women had access to the scans they needed.

"From a public perspective, we're delivering every scan that we need to deliver in the public system," he said.

Steve Edgington has disputed there is an issue with access to pregnancy scans. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

NT Health Chief Medical Officer Jeremy Chin said women who were concerned about accessing a scan within the recommended timeframe "should speak with their GP, midwife or antenatal care team".

Dr Chin said there were no vacancies at NT Health for pregnancy sonographers.

He also said there were trainees commencing every six months through an in-house training program supported by the department.

He added that eight ultrasound machines would be replaced in 2026-27.

For Ms Williams, who has often thought about bringing another child into the world, the difficulties with accessing basic antenatal care have made her rethink her plans.

"That would be a big factor in the decision as to whether I would have another baby or not," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.title: Small businesses fighting to stay open amid 'insidious cost creep'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.author: Liz Rymill and Becc Bird
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Small Businesses

Francene Martin says she did not have one customer during a Sunday trading day. (Supplied: Francene Martin)

Small business owners in rural and regional communities say they are under constant pressure from the rising costs of doing business.

One in eight cafes has closed in Australia in 2026, with payment defaults also rising nationally for the third consecutive month according to CreditorWatch.

From October 1, businesses will no longer be able to add a surcharge on card payments, with some small businesses electing to go "cash only" or be forced to increase charges for some items.

In the town of Keith, a natural halfway point between Melbourne and Adelaide along the Dukes Highway, Sunday afternoon draws to an end.

The main street of the agricultural town, home to a population of about 1,400 people, is quiet, as residents and travellers finish the day.

Clothing shop owner Francene Martin turns the sign on her store Retail Therapy to "Closed".

Today, she has not made a single sale.

Francene Martin says she feels "constant pressure" from mega competitors like Amazon, Temu and Shein. (Supplied: Francene Martin)

Across the country, countless small businesses from clothing retailers to cafes are counting the rising cost of doing business.

"I was quite despondent," Ms Martin said.

Across the border, in a rust-red brick heritage schoolhouse building in Ballarat, one of Victoria's largest regional centres, Prey cafe operations and social media manager Frazer Wyley posted online about the issue.

Frazer Wyley took to social media to share recent experiences behind the scenes at Prey cafe in Ballarat. (Supplied: Frazer Wyley)

"When I made the post, I was originally thinking about all our beautiful friends in hospitality and retail who are closing their doors or thinking about closing. I think it's been a conversation that a lot of people don't have in the open," he said.

Mr Wyley said insidious cost creep, soon to be exacerbated by changes to EFTPOS charges, was a struggle that went on behind the scenes for small businesses like Prey, run by father-son duo Eddie and Remi van den Akker.

While the Reserve Bank of Australia has estimated its reforms will save businesses $910 million each year in reduced transaction fees, some business advocates and industry experts have warned that ending credit and debit card surcharging risks shifting the burden of payment system costs onto many small businesses.

Mr Wyley echoed that concern, pointing to the slim margins small businesses already occupied.

Prey Ballarat's social media post attracted thousands of comments and shares after it highlighted the challenges for small businesses. (Supplied: Prey Ballarat/Frazer Wyley)

"Right now, thousands of operators are sitting up after close, staring at the week's takings and asking the same question, 'How do I make this work?'"

Mr Wyley highlighted the slim margin in the cafe scene's most treasured offering, a cup of coffee.

"Inside that cup of coffee are so many expenses; the cup, the lid, the water, the wages, the super, EFTPOS fees, the ingredients, when you break it down … the margins are so slim," he said in his social media post.

He said cafe owners put up prices as a "last resort", and he urged customers to band together with small businesses in their local towns.

"If you have some favourite businesses, or you see a new one opening, put them on a roster. If you can visit in store, that really goes a long way to helping keep doors open," he said.

"We need to share the love around and keep these communities strong together."

Prey Cafe in Ballarat has been open for just under 100 days and is building a regular client base. (Supplied: Prey Ballarat/Frazer Wyley)

According to CreditorWatch's Business Risk Index for August, one in eight Australian cafes and restaurants have closed in the past year.

Payment defaults are also rising nationally for the third consecutive month.

CreditorWatch chief economist Ivan Coulhoon said this year was one of mounting "shocks" for small businesses, particularly via changes in e-commerce, rising inflation and higher interest rates.

Mr Coulhoon said the cost-of-living crisis for consumers was affecting small businesses in a "cost-of-doing-business crisis".

"The cost of things is much higher than it was five years ago so even if inflation slows it doesn't mean prices are going down and these costs have reversed, it just means they're going up at a slower rate," he said.

Francene Martin is calling on people to support local businesses. (Supplied: Francene Martin)

Back in Keith, Ms Martin said she was determined to meet the challenges to keep her store open.

She said she felt "constant pressure" from mega commerce like Amazon, Temu and Shein offering huge discounts.

"Obviously, I can't compete with those businesses, but I have things they don't have. I've built up a rapport with my customers, I know their names, their stories, their size and style. It's a partnership."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.title: Polling officials say they were ignored after offering to work at SA election
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.author: Thomas Kelsall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The 2026 South Australian state election was plagued with administrative issues. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

Some former polling officials have told the ABC the South Australian Electoral Commission (ECSA) did not respond after they indicated a willingness to work at the March state election.

They were surprised to hear of staffing issues at booths, with some saying they had been willing to work “anywhere”.

ECSA's handling of the election is subject to an independent review, which is expected to be handed down in the next two months.

The South Australian Electoral Commission (ECSA) did not follow up with polling officials who had indicated they wanted to work at the 2026 state election, according to multiple former officials who say they were surprised to hear booths were understaffed.

The ABC revealed on Monday that ECSA was trying to find people to manage polling booths only hours before state election day, with frantic internal messages showing staff in tears on election eve because polling booths were so disorganised.

Since publication of that story, more than half a dozen people have contacted the ABC to share their experience with ECSA.

This includes several who said they had previous election experience and were willing to work "anywhere" at the state election but did not receive any follow up from ECSA.

The South Australian Electoral Commission was trying to find staff to manage polling booths only hours before election day, with internal messages revealing the extreme pressure officials were under.

Among those was retired Australian Defence Force member Crispin Boxhall, who said he had worked at three previous elections, including as a polling booth manager in the Adelaide Hills at the 2025 federal election.

Mr Boxhall said he applied online to work at the state election after being approached by ECSA, and his application was accepted three months ahead of the March poll.

"Because the confirmation email said, 'thanks very much for applying, we'll be in touch with you nearer the time to discuss specifics', I left it like that and allowed a month or two to go past," he said.

Mr Boxhall said he contacted ECSA a month before the election to "remind them I was here and looking forward to being appointed to a position".

"They hadn't even come back and said, 'hang on a minute we're having problems here', or 'you're not needed' … it just went silent.

"About two weeks out I contacted them again and said 'look, unless I hear from you, I'll take it I'm not needed'."

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with Thomas Kelsall at thomaskelsall@proton.me

Mr Boxhall said he did not have any communication from ECSA leading up to the election or after it.

"I just thought that they must be so flat out they must already have enough staff that they're not contacting people they don't need," he said.

"It wasn't till I read your article that I realised actually it's quite likely that there's something bigger afoot here.

"It just seems that maybe they didn't have enough people, and to not contact people who not only have applied but are actually following up looking to help out I thought was bit strange."

The March 21 state election saw various issues before, during, and after polling day. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

Semi-retired consultant Andrew West said he worked 10-days for the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) counting and aggregating votes for the Indigenous Voice to Parliament referendum in 2023.

He said he had ticked a box when signing up for the AEC indicating he would be happy to work at an SA election.

"I wasn't necessarily wanting to manage a booth, but I would have happily ticked off people's names, I would have happily travelled anywhere," he said.

Mr West said upon reading the ABC's story on Monday, he was "even more amazed that someone didn't ring me at the time of the election".

"I just don't understand why they didn't ring."

Long waits at several polling booths, like this one at Goodwood, were reported on election day. (ABC News: Evelyn Leckie)

ECSA's handling of the election is already subject to an independent review led by former Australian Electoral Commissioner Tom Rogers.

He is examining an array of issues including technical glitches, long queues, missing ballots, payment delays and Aboriginal voters being mistakenly turned away trying to vote in the First Nations Voice election.

Mr Rogers's report is expected to be handed down in the next two months, Premier Peter Malinauskas said on Tuesday.

Former Australian electoral commissioner Tom Rogers is leading an independent review into ECSA's performance in the 2026 state election. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"There were clearly logistical issues going on behind the scenes at the most recent state election that were avoidable," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Thankfully, there's no suggestion of any compromise to the integrity of the conduct of the election or otherwise, but there were logistical issues that had an impact on staff."

Former SA electoral commissioner Mick Sherry stepped down in June after overseeing the issue-plagued poll.

"The commissioner has resigned, I'm grateful for that," Mr Malinauskas said on Tuesday.

The ABC has contacted Mr Sherry for comment.

Acting South Australian electoral commissioner Leah McLay says she is looking forward to any recommendations from the review. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Acting electoral commissioner Leah McLay, who joined ECSA in January, said she was "concerned about issues relating to recruitment and training for positions at the 2026 state election, which have been raised by application and employees".

"We won't be pre-empting Mr Rogers' independent findings by commenting publicly about the issues he is investigating," she said in a statement.

"We look forward to receiving any recommendations from the external review to make improvements for future elections."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.title: Second child dies after crash west of Melbourne
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

An 11-year-old boy was flown to hospital after the crash but died overnight. (ABC News)

A second child has died following a single-vehicle crash at Parwan, west of Melbourne, on Tuesday afternoon.

Victoria Police said an 11-year-old boy died overnight after being flown to hospital with critical injuries.

A seven-year-old girl died at the scene after a 4WD carrying seven children rolled just before 4pm.

A second child has died in hospital following a single-vehicle crash west of Melbourne on Tuesday afternoon.

A seven-year-old girl died at the scene after a 4WD with seven children inside rolled near Parwan just before 4pm.

An 11-year-old boy was flown to hospital with critical injuries but died overnight.

The single-vehicle crash happened at Parwan, west of Melbourne on Tuesday afternoon. (ABC News)

Five other children were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries and the driver, a 34-year-old woman, was taken to hospital for observation.

Detectives are continuing to investigate the circumstance behind the crash, which happened near the intersection of Nerowie and Parwan-Exford roads.

Victoria Police said seven children were inside the vehicle when it rolled on Tuesday afternoon. (ABC News)

Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile from the Major Collision Investigation Unit said the woman had picked the children up from school.

"From my understanding, the scene was quite hectic, people everywhere, witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance," he said.

"Obviously, with seven children, they were distressed and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.

"This is just a really sad set of circumstances, very sad. We just ask the public to drive to the conditions and be mindful of their surrounds."

Police have asked anyone who witnessed the crash or has dash cam footage to come forward.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.title: Foreign 'AI slopaganda' network targets Australian politicians
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.author: Ange Lavoipierre
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A screenshot of a Facebook post showing Pauline Hanson, David Pocock and Larissa Waters from an AI propaganda page. (Facebook)

New research has uncovered a foreign network of hundreds of Facebook pages churning out AI deepfakes of Australian politicians.

Roughly one in 10 pages have been monetised, allowing the owner to profit directly from a commercially motivated "foreign influence campaign".

The researchers say it shows how "AI slopaganda" networks are targeting political systems globally on a "massive industrial scale".

Dozens of Australian politicians have been deepfaked by a "foreign influence" network operating on Facebook, and researchers say there are many more just like it.

Research organisation Reset Tech has tracked more than 200 Facebook pages impersonating Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, and many other political figures over the past eight months.

A report from the group has revealed the seemingly co-ordinated campaign and linked it back to an influencer business in Sri Lanka.

It found roughly 10 per cent of the network's pages have been monetised by Facebook, as part of the platform's in-house scheme to pay content creators, allowing a page's owner to profit directly.

"This isn't foreign interference as we traditionally think of it," Rys Farthing, chief research officer for Reset Tech, said.

A screenshot from one of the pages showing AI-generated images of Anthony Albanese and Peter Dutton. (Facebook)

Researchers found most targets were impersonated in short clips on Facebook Reels, where they were falsely shown saying something inflammatory.

The content often centred on anti-migrant, anti-Muslim, or nationalistic themes, and baited users into participating in polls.

Another common pattern was the use of sexualised images and videos of female politicians.

"Sometimes it is directly related to news events, but basically … it's just throwing spaghetti at the wall," Dr Farthing said.

"They work out which [posts] get them the clicks, which ones bring the money in, and then they create more like that again."

Senator Fatima Payman, who left Labor to sit on the crossbench, was among those targeted by a page called Australia Info Live.

Senator Payman, a Muslim, was falsely shown in an AI-generated clip to say: "Please don't deport me back to Afghanistan. It's not safe for me there. Vote no to support me."

The post has hundreds of likes and comments, and no apparent label to indicate it was false or AI-generated.

The AI-generated post of Fatima Payman was widely liked and commented on. (Facebook)

Crossbencher Allegra Spender has also been targeted. (Facebook)

Fellow independent senator David Pocock was targeted by a page called Australia Life & News, in a clip where he was falsely shown to say he had "joined forces" with One Nation.

Senator Pocock told the ABC he was not aware of the specific clip, although his team had been sent "a bunch of deepfakes of me over the last few months".

"I'm concerned deepfakes really undermine our democratic system," he said.

"As humans, when we see someone say something, we generally believe that it's them saying it".

As the first case under new anti-deepfake legislation goes before the courts, authorities and experts say the rise in the creation of the non-consensual sexually explicit material is concerning.

With names such as I Love Australia, Life in Australia, or Beautiful Australia, the pages are often designed for mass appeal.

Reset Tech said a common tactic was to lure audiences in with AI-generated images of animals, attractive women, or posts praising Australia's beauty.

Later, the page takes a political turn, although many pages are political from the outset.

"There's nothing domestic about this," Dr Farthing said.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, who has been deepfaked by the same network, said it was more important than ever for people to check their sources.

"Last election for the first time I saw photos of myself online with people I had never met," he said.

"In more recent times, I have seen videos … and interviews of some of my colleagues saying things they have never said."

Rys Farthing says propaganda networks are targeting political systems across the world. (Supplied)

Reset Tech found the same Sri Lanka-based network was also targeting France, Italy, the UK, the US, Canada and Mexico, among other locations, using the same playbook.

In total, it was believed to operate 1,864 coordinated Facebook pages globally, with mostly identical branding, and a combined follower base of 5.9 million users.

"We really wanted to highlight that this wasn't just a unique issue with one bad actor or a couple of bad actors misusing a platform system," Dr Farthing said.

Rather, she said, the research showed "AI slopaganda" networks were targeting political systems on a "massive industrial scale".

Reset Tech found relatively few instances where political AI slop on Facebook had been appropriately dealt with, in accordance with the platform's own policies.

Only one in three posts received AI labelling, and one in 33 posts was deleted, the report stated.

"We have a handful of researchers, and we were able to find this and detect all of these networks with ease," Dr Farthing said.

"If we can do it, I don't quite understand how these companies that have billion-dollar revenues can't do it."

Reset Tech said the network targeting Australia was in breach of several Facebook policies designed to target "inauthentic behaviour networks", as well as hate speech and AI deepfakes.

Regulators are removing record numbers of fake celebrity-endorsed investment scams, using AI images of famous faces.

Dr Farthing said ultimately, platforms were incentivising the creation of AI slop and failing to contain it.

"[The platforms] have made all of the decisions that enable their monetisation system to work, right?"

"And this is the result."

Senator Pocock said it was increasingly clear tackling the issue was not in the interests of social media companies.

The ABC has contacted Meta, Facebook's parent company, for a response to Reset's Tech report.
