https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.title: Woman allegedly attacked in Brisbane emergency department
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.author: Emma Pollard
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police said a 73-year-old woman was allegedly punched in the face "a number of times" in an unprovoked attack in the emergency department of the Princess Alexandra Hospital. (ABC News)

A 73-year-old woman was seriously injured last month after she was allegedly attacked by a man in the emergency department of the Princess Alexandra Hospital.

Australasian College for Emergency Medicine president Peter Allely says violence is a "hugely significant" and "hugely under-reported" occurrence in emergency departments nationwide.

The incident has prompted calls for action, including improved reporting of violent incidents and expanding hospital security.

A 73-year-old woman suffered serious injuries when she was allegedly bashed by another patient in a random attack inside the emergency department of a major public hospital in Brisbane.

It comes as medical groups continue to warn about escalating violence in overburdened emergency units across the country.

Queensland Police Service (QPS) said the woman was allegedly punched in the face "a number of times in an unprovoked attack" by a 43-year-old man shortly before 11:30pm on August 23.

The alleged assault happened at the Princess Alexandra Hospital in Woolloongabba.

"The woman sustained serious facial injuries during the incident," a QPS spokesperson said in a statement.

"Medical staff disrupted the incident, and the man was arrested shortly afterwards by responding police."

The 73-year-old woman was left with serious injuries after allegedly being punched in the face multiple times.  (ABC News)

Police said the man had been charged with one count of grievous bodily harm, was remanded in custody and is due to reappear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court later this month.

A spokesperson said the hospital was aware of "an alleged assault involving a patient and another unrelated patient" and support was provided to the person impacted as well as "the staff who witnessed the incident".

"The safety of our staff, patients and visitors is our number one priority, and we have zero tolerance for violence and aggressive behaviour in our hospital," the spokesperson said in a statement.

They said Metro South Health — which runs the Princess Alexandra Hospital — had taken "significant action" to address occupational violence and employed security officers who were "available 24/7 across the hospital".

"We have invested more than $37 million to increase the number of security officers, and implement additional CCTV, body-worn cameras, duress alarms, peer support programs, hospital ambassadors and de-escalation training for staff."

The woman has since been discharged from hospital.

The alleged assault took place in the PA Hospital's emergency department last month. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

ABC News asked Metro South Health for annual figures on the number of assaults on hospital patients and staff, but none were provided.

Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM) president Peter Allely said violence was a "hugely significant" and "hugely under-reported" occurrence in emergency departments nationwide.

"It shouldn't be accepted or normalised," Dr Allely said.

Peter Allely says violence and aggression from patients is "hugely common" in emergency departments. (Supplied: ACEM)

The Perth specialist said the "number one overwhelming driver" for an increase in violence and aggression was "the degree of overcrowding that our healthcare system faces".

He said violence was "not excusable" but it was exacerbated by the conditions in emergency units.

"This is in an environment where the lights are on 24 hours a day. There are minimal shower and toilet facilities and people may not have the ability to walk around the way that they normally would in normal aspects of life," Dr Allely said.

Have you experienced violence in a hospital?

Contact health reporter Emma Pollard at pollard.emma@abc.net.au

Last year ACEM published the report Breaking Point — An Urgent Call to Action on Emergency Department Safety.

It included national survey results that found nine out of 10 respondents reported an incident, or multiple incidences, of violence by a patient or accompanying person in their ED within the past week.

Recommendations included fostering a culture of, and systems for, reporting violent incidents and bolstering well-trained, directly employed, hospital security officers for emergency departments.

Long waits in overcrowded emergency departments are leaving patients frustrated and exacerbating violence towards staff, according to the peak body for emergency medicine.

Figures released in July by the Australian Institute for Health and Welfare show assaults were the second leading cause of injury hospitalisations, after falls, among healthcare workers in 2024–25, with the rate almost doubling since 2015–16.

Dr Allely said ACEM had not "seen a whole lot of tangible change" from governments on the challenge.

"We want a razor-sharp focus on overcrowding. That's going to have the biggest impact," he said.

The call for action was echoed by the Queensland Nurses and Midwives' Union (QNMU).

Secretary Sarah Beaman said the problem of violence and aggression in hospitals was "at crisis point".

"The impact on staff is that they're coming in with a level of fear, they just want to get in and provide care and when you're worried about whether you're going to get assaulted, that is problematic," Ms Beaman said.

Sarah Beaman says creating safe workplaces is a legal obligation. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

She said 82 per cent of respondents in this year's survey of more than 8,000 QNMU members said they had experienced occupational violence within the last 12 months.

The union called for more state government investment in a de-escalation security program called the Ambassador Model and a better reporting system.

Ms Beaman said workplace safety was essential for retaining healthcare professionals.

"The more people that leave the professions means that safe, free, high-quality care cannot be provided," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/e.title: 'Lowering the bar': New Tasmanian targets may mean longer surgery waits
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/e.author: Clancy Balen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A new performance target will allow for up to 30 per cent of elective surgery patients to miss the clinical time frame in which they should be treated. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Thirty per cent of elective surgery patients in Tasmania won't need to be treated within their clinically recommended time frame, under a new Health Department performance target.

The Australian Medical Association has criticised the revised target, which it says "is lowering the bar".

The department says the change reflects increased demand, service capacity and "ongoing issues with bed availability due to a lack of aged care and NDIS placements for Tasmanians".

A revised Tasmanian Health Department performance target will allow for up to almost one in three elective surgery patients to wait longer than they should for surgery.

There are about 9,500 people on the department's elective surgery waitlist.

Under its annual service plan — which sets out key performance indicators (KPI) for the year — the department has set the KPI for the percentage of patients waiting longer than clinically recommended for elective surgery as "not more than 30 per cent".

Put another way, the department has set a target of getting at least 70 per cent of elective-surgery patients treated within their clinically recommended time frame.

For the Australian Medical Association (AMA) Tasmania, it's a bar that has been set too low.

"No system is perfect," AMA Tasmania president Dr Meg Creely said.

Dr Creely said the way the KPIs were measured across subsequent years further complicated the picture.

Meg Creely says the revised elective surgery target will create a "two-tier health system" between those who can afford private healthcare and those who can't. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

In last year's plan, the health department's target for the amount of patients waiting longer than clinically recommended times for elective surgery was measured as a number, rather than a percentage.

That number was no more than 270 patients who should wait longer than clinically recommended for elective surgery.

"When you work it out as a percentage, it's gone from about 1.2 per cent to 30 per cent," Dr Creely said.

The lack of continuity between annual service plans made it difficult for health practitioners and members of the public to understand what was going on within the health service, Dr Creely said.

"It's really hard when there's different numbers that are used, where it's hidden in budget papers, hidden in annual services plans."

A Tasmanian Health Department spokesperson said the revised target reflected the increased demand for elective surgeries.

It is "a realistic and evidence-based assessment of current demand, service capacity and the health system operating environment caused by ongoing issues with bed availability due to a lack of aged care and NDIS placements for Tasmanians," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson did not answer a question from the ABC about whether the AMA's claim that the previous target has increased from 1.2 per cent to 30 per cent was accurate.

The latest data from July shows at 59 per cent of elective surgeries were delivered on time, meaning fewer than six in 10 patients across the state received surgery within the clinically recommended time frame.

And performance has deteriorated over the past year.

In July last year, the number of elective surgeries performed within the clinically recommended time frame was 64 per cent.

In Tasmania, elective surgeries are broken down into three categories.

Category 1 is deemed "urgent", with patients needing to be treated within 30 days.

In that most urgent category, 65 per cent were admitted within the recommended time frame in July, meaning more than one in three category 1 patients waited longer than the clinically recommended time.

Under its new plan, the health department said it wanted 95 per cent of category 1 surgeries performed within the clinically recommended time frames.

Category 2 is "semi-urgent", and is designated for patients to be treated with 90 days, while category 3 is for "non-urgent" elective surgeries which should be treated within 365 days.

Under the new 2026-27 plan, the health service aims to complete more than 21,500 elective surgeries, a slight decrease of about 400 from last year.

According to the state budget, health funding will increase by 8 per cent over four years, due to extra federal funding.

However, the Tasmanian government has also tasked the health department to find $702 million in efficiency cuts over four years.

The painful wait for public surgery in Tasmania

Dr Creely said the elective surgery backlog risked entrenching a two-tier system between those who can and can't afford private health care.

Within the new health department plan is another target: clearing its elective surgery backlog.

It lists a target of "zero" for the number of patients waiting for elective surgery prior to 30 June 2024.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Who is taking the biggest cut of the apple profits?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Warwick Long and Justine Longmore
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The average price for apples is higher than it was 18 months ago. (ABC News: Bec Whetham)

The cost of apples in the supermarket has gone up as supply shortages hit.

Apple growers have welcomed better returns but say the major supermarkets have made a bigger profit.

Apple and Pear Australia Limited wants the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission to better police the relationship between major supermarkets and farmers.

The price of apples has shot up in the past year because of supply shortages, but new figures show the major supermarkets took a big chunk of the profit.

The data collated by Apple and Pear Australia Limited (APAL) reveals the price paid for apples in the shops grew at a significantly higher rate than the price that was paid to the grower.

After a tough period of drought, particularly in Victoria's Goulburn Valley, orchard consolidation and growers leaving the industry, the shortage of apples started to emerge a year ago, leading to the price uptick.

The price of apples went from an average of $4.50 per kilogram 18 months ago, peaking at an average of about $6.20 earlier this year.

It is now averaging about $5.20 a kilo.

Apples are currently averaging about $5.20 a kilo. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

The APAL figures show the profit margin for major stores, including Woolworths, Coles and Aldi, got as high as 65 per cent in early 2026, up from the average of about 25 per cent.

"We saw an extremely large increase, a significant increase in the difference between the price of purchasing and the price of selling to the consumers," APAL general manager Jeremy Griffith said.

While the wholesale data did not detail the exact prices paid by the supermarkets to the growers, Mr Griffith said it was a good representation.

"It's a good proxy for what the market is doing," he said.

"The return for growers over the past six or seven years has been too low … so from the grower point of view, getting a better return, it's good, but we would be concerned if the supermarkets are taking an excess margin on top of that.

Jeremy Griffith says he would be concerned if supermarkets are taking an excess margin. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

The major supermarkets have defended their pricing decisions.

"Retail prices for fresh apples are strongly influenced by seasonal availability, market conditions, and supplier wholesale input costs," a Woolworths spokesperson said.

"We are proud to support Australian apple growers and bring high-quality, locally grown fruit to millions of customers.

"We work collaboratively with our suppliers to meet the needs of our customers every week of the year."

Coles also said the price of fresh produce reflected "a range of factors".

"[Those factors include] the price agreed with our suppliers, seasonal availability, weather events, quality specifications and the costs involved in getting fresh produce to customers," a spokesperson said.

"Coles is committed to providing customers with great value and high-quality fresh produce, and we are proud to provide 100 per cent Australian-grown apples."

Aldi was contacted for comment but did not respond to the ABC's questions.

APAL wants the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to better police the relationship between major supermarkets and the farmers that supply their produce.

APAL wants the ACCC to police the relationship between supermarkets and farmers. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

"If there's no significant change, it could undermine the long-term viability of the sector," Mr Griffith said.

"Every Monday night the growers are expected to put in the volume of apples or pears that they want to sell, the price that they want to sell them at."

The ACCC told the ABC that wholesale and retail prices are influenced by a range of market and supply chain factors.

"Supermarkets must at all times deal with suppliers in good faith, including when negotiating prices," a spokesperson said.

"Failure to act in good faith will make the large grocery business liable to civil penalties."

The ACCC did not say whether it would investigate the concerns of inflated prices for apples.

Mitchell McNab runs his family's orchard in Ardmona. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Despite what was happening with the supermarket prices, orchardists in Victoria's Goulburn Valley said the increases were helping their bottom line.

"Hopefully we can maintain that pricing going forward and continue to have that bit of positivity over the next couple of years," Fruit Growers Victoria chair Mitch McNabb said.

Fruit Growers Victoria industry development officer Michael Crisera agreed.

Michael Crisera says there is a bit more confidence in the apple industry. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"I think there's a bit of a buzz around, and I think obviously everyone's a bit happy when they've got more income, and they're a bit more profitable," Mr Crisera said.

"There's definitely a lot more confidence in the industry."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.title: Man wanted over axe attack arrested in Victoria's east
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Peter O'Ryan was arrested near Tyers on Tuesday night. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Police have arrested a Victorian man who had been on the run since Saturday after allegedly attacking family members with an axe.

Police allege Peter O'Ryan, 48, assaulted his brother, Paul O'Ryan, father, Keith O'Ryan, and mother, Janine O'Ryan, with the weapon before fleeing their home in Tyers on foot.

Mr O'Ryan was arrested on Tuesday night after officers were called to reports of a person acting suspiciously near the Tyers-Walhalla Road just before 9pm.

He will be interviewed in relation to the attack over the weekend.

His family remain in the Alfred Hospital where his father is in a critical but stable condition, while his brother and mother are in serious but stable conditions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/v.title: Victims of serious youth crimes to be told when offenders leave prison
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/v.author: Olivia Jenkins
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Significant youth justice system changes are due to take effect at the end of the month. (ABC News)

Victims of Victoria's most serious youth crimes will soon be able to apply to be notified when offenders are due to leave prison, bringing the state in line with the rest of Australia.

The change has been welcomed by social service groups and victims' families, who fear they are ignored in the justice system.

The change is among several youth justice reforms due to take effect at the end of the month.

Grieving and traumatised victims will soon be warned when youth criminals convicted of murders, home invasions and carjackings are set to be released from prison.

Unlike for adult offenders, there is no formal system in Victoria that alerts people directly impacted by youth crime if the offenders are released or there is an upcoming parole hearing.

Victoria is the only state or territory that does not allow youth crime victims to register to receive that information.

Police can choose to share it with some victims at their discretion, while the Youth Parole Board responds to victims' requests on a case-by-case basis.

But youth crime victims and their families will soon be able to apply to a register, which is currently exclusively for information about adult offenders, under significant changes that come into effect from September 30.

The eligible youth crimes include murder, rape, home invasions, carjackings, serious sexual crimes and assault.

However, the reform will not be applied retrospectively, meaning those affected by recent high-profile crimes are ineligible for the notifications.

While they cannot register themselves, the opt-in system has been welcomed by the family members of those killed in some of Victoria's most high-profile youth crimes.

Natalie Gordon, whose brother Ash Gordon was stabbed to death with a hunting knife by a 16-year-old boy in a home invasion in 2024, told the ABC she had always wanted the chance to be kept informed about his killer's movements.

Natalie Gordon is the sister of Ash Gordon, a doctor who was murdered by a 16-year-old in 2024. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"I don't know why it's not already an option," she said.

"Victims and victims' families aren't acknowledged, and that's probably the most heartbreaking and disappointing part of the system."

The offender, the son of a Victoria Police investigator, is serving a 17-year sentence for murdering Mr Gordon, with a non-parole period of 12 years.

Natalie Gordon says she is shocked Victoria does not already have systems in place to keep the families of victims informed. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

The ABC can reveal the teen is appealing his conviction and sentence.

Despite now being an adult, he still cannot be named because he was underage when he murdered Mr Gordon.

The youth justice changes will also require the Youth Parole Board to make families' concerns central to parole decisions.

Until now, only some families and victims could make submissions to the board about why they believed their attackers should be kept behind bars or released.

The changes place greater weight on the concerns of victims' families during parole decisions. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Ms Gordon said she often thought about the day her brother's killer would be released, and that she knew exactly what she would say when he was up for parole.

"I can't wait to tell him that your excuses for bad behaviour are pathetic," she said.

Minister for Victims Support Ros Spence said the new register helped put community safety first by giving victims access to information they needed.

"Victims and survivors should never feel like an afterthought in our justice system," she said.

"Their voices matter, and we're making sure they are heard."

Jesuit Social Services chief executive Julie Edwards said the register was only one part of helping victims heal while holding young offenders responsible for their actions.

She said it was important victims were also offered a chance to face their young attackers directly under a restorative justice framework — where victims and offenders agree to meet with each other.

"We support anything that will help a victim heal, but we don't think just putting your name on a register and finding out what date someone's getting out, or what date their parole hearing is, is sufficient," Ms Edwards said.

"We would really like to enhance that opportunity for the victim and use it as an opportunity to hold the young person to account, to take responsibility, to make amends and develop a plan to make sure they don't end up hurting anyone else."

Julie Edwards says support for victims should go beyond simply informing them of certain dates. (Supplied)

The new alert system will arrive as youths convicted of some of Victoria's most violent crimes approach the end of their sentences.

They include two young men who were 16 and 17 when they were involved in the fatal 2022 group stabbing of 25-year-old Khalid Mahat, and were sentenced to between two and three years in youth detention in 2024.

A 17-year-old boy who fatally punched Jason Langhans with a screwdriver hidden in his fist after gatecrashing a birthday party in 2021 also became eligible for parole in the middle of 2025.

However, as the register will not apply to existing convictions, victims' families in those crimes will not be eligible for notification.

The register is one of a host of changes coming into effect under the new legislation at the end of the month.

Among other changes are how police respond to youth offenders when placing them under arrest.

Internal force communications seen by the ABC show officers have been told to take the least invasive approach, instead of making an arrest, where possible.

Police will have a new framework for arresting young people. (ABC News)

Under the new framework, police can decide to take no action against a young person, issue them with a youth warning or caution or ultimately commence criminal proceedings.

They must also consider the seriousness of the offence, consider whether the youth has reoffended, and record their reasoning for the actions they take when determining whether to arrest a teenager.

A Victoria Police spokeswoman said the changes were designed to break cycles of offending in the long term and connect young people with appropriate support, but officers would not hesitate to put repeat offenders before the courts.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Anthony Albanese held undeclared honorary membership to golf club awarded $6 million
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Jake Evans
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Anthony Albanese has a long association with the Marrickville Golf Club. (Instagram: lewis_cavoodle)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to Marrickville Golf Club, which he has not declared on his register of interests.

The golf club was promised $6 million at the federal election, which was awarded through a fund that heavily favoured Labor seats.

The Coalition says the federal government must explain what process was used to construct the list of projects nominated for funding.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to the Marrickville Golf Club in his seat, which was promised $6 million at the 2025 election through an invite-only scheme, and which Mr Albanese has not declared.

Mr Albanese has previously spoken of his long association with the club, but records of his register of interests dating back to his entry to parliament in 1996 do not mention a membership to the club, either paid or honorary.

"We have him on the books as an honorary member, but I think that dates from a long time ago, that hasn't been reaffirmed," a spokesperson for the Marrickville Golf Club told the ABC.

"I don't know when he was put on the books as an honorary member, that may have been 15 years ago or more."

The Prime Minister's Office did not respond to questions about Mr Albanese's membership.

The register of interests requires MPs to declare membership of any organisation where a conflict of interest could foreseeably arise.

While it is generally expected that membership of a local community, sporting or charitable organisation would not pose or be seen to pose a potential conflict of interest, the prime minister has declared other honorary memberships over his time in parliament.

That includes an honorary membership to the Royal Sydney Golf Course, given in 2025, and an honorary membership of the Western Suburbs Lawn Tennis Association over multiple terms of parliament, as well as membership of the Marrickville Lawn Tennis Club.

The Marrickville Golf Club was one of 220 projects promised funding through an invitation-only grant program established to pay election commitments made by Labor.

A Centre for Public Integrity investigation found the $560 million program heavily favoured safe Labor seats, and marginal contests the party hoped to win.

Its chair, former justice Anthony Whealy, told the ABC on Tuesday that the government had a "heavy onus" to justify how projects were chosen for funding.

The federal government notes more than $1.7 billion in competitive grant funding was made available through other programs, and that its Major and Local Community Infrastructure (MLCI) program followed the grant rules and guidelines strengthened by Labor in 2024.

Marrickville Golf Club's management told the ABC that they had first approached Mr Albanese's electorate office after the club was brought back into the seat of Grayndler following a redistribution in October 2024.

The club says it did not speak with Mr Albanese directly, but rather with his office.

"That was an open-ended conversation, they were saying, well, PM would like — there is money available," a spokesperson said.

"They did say, look, what ideas do you have? What other needs may you have? Again an open-ended conversation. We came back with a presentation setting out our ideas, some of which we had on the boil already."

The club was awarded $6.05 million to fully renovate the clubhouse, including new outdoor dining, a fix to its sewage and stormwater systems, an accessibility ramp and landscaping.

The Centre for Public Integrity warns that the federal government appears to have pork-barrelled a $560 million "invitation-only" fund, directing the vast majority to safe Labor seats and marginal seats it wanted to win.

That promise was announced by the prime minister in April last year while on the campaign trail.

It was the only golf club invited for funding under the MLCI program.

The MLCI fund was established after the election to manage Labor's election commitments, including undertaking a value-for-money assessment.

The federal government has not explained who identified projects for a grant invitation, or what process was used to determine projects for funding.

Shadow Infrastructure Minister Bridget McKenzie questioned what role Labor MPs or candidates played.

"I'd hate to see a situation where you would have to stock the beer of your local member in order to get a grant in this country," Senator McKenzie said.

Mr Albanese has previously intervened to assist the Marrickville Golf Club.

In 2019, Mr Albanese and his Labor colleague and neighbouring MP Linda Burney joined a campaign against a local Greens proposal to cut the golf course in half to open up more space in the dense inner-west Sydney suburb.

Anthony Albanese joined a campaign to "save Marrickville Golf Club from developers" after a proposal to halve the 18-hole course to nine holes. (Instagram: Darcy Byrne)

A Daily Telegraph news article at the time noted Mr Albanese held a "non-golfing honorary membership" to the club, though his register of interests at that time does not include a membership declaration.

The proposal to shrink the 18-hole course to nine holes was defeated.

At a speech to the club's members arguing against the proposed course reduction, Mr Albanese spoke of his personal association to the club.

"I declare an interest, I live in Beecham Street … and I have been coming here for decades and using this club," Mr Albanese said.

Mr Albanese regularly walked his dog, Toto, at the course when he lived nearby. The clubhouse stocks Willie the Boatman's "Albo" beer, which is stocked in many places across his electorate and which the prime miinster has no financial interest in.

Willie the Boatman produced a beer in honour of Grayndler MP Anthony Albanese which is sold across his electorate. (Instagram: Marrickville Golf Club)

While the prime minister is not an avid golfer, he has received golf lessons there.

Mr Albanese also participated in Labor candidate launches at the Marrickville Golf Club.

In 2015, he joined the launch of state Labor candidate and now-member for Summer Hill Jo Haylen, which was hosted at the golf club.

And in 2012, Mr Albanese tweeted that he was at the Marrickville Golf Club for a "local Labor launch".

The ministerial code of conduct separately requires ministers to declare and register "personal interests", including but not limited to pecuniary interests, where it could give rise to a conflict with their public duties.

Marrickville Golf Club is one of the more affordable courses in the country. A full membership costs $1,100 annually.

In 2020, Labor challenged then-sports minister Bridget McKenzie over a $36,000 grant she had awarded to a gun club after it was revealed the senator held an undisclosed honorary membership with that club.

The senator told the ABC she ultimately resigned over a perceived conflict of interest in awarding that grant, since she was the responsible minister who signed off on it.

Bridget McKenzie challenged the government on the process it had used to award $560 million in grants. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The MLCI program sits under the Infrastructure Department, with Catherine King the approving minister except in her own seat, where grants are approved by another cabinet minister.

However, Senator McKenzie says the sports grants program was an open, competitive process with a departmental assessment process.

She said given the MLCI was invitation-only, and Ms King received a list of projects from the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, the government needed to explain its process.

"It's up for the ministers to explain who was the ultimate decision-maker, and how the project list was constructed," Senator McKenzie said.

The Greens have called on Mr Albanese to front the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters to explain how projects were chosen for funding.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.title: Will your feed be boring without the algorithm? Instagram gives us a hint
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.author: Erin Handley
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Internet Culture

Instagram users can already chose a feed featuring only their followers, but the model has been criticised. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Your social media feeds could soon look a little different.

The government is proposing new laws that allow it to require social media companies to send a notification to users, giving them the option of opting in or out of the algorithm on their feed.

But there are concerns social media companies could offer a substandard product, or engage in "protest design" by making non-algorithmic feeds less functional or more boring, to drive users back into the arms of the algorithm.

Several social media apps already have ways for you to exercise more control over what you see in your feeds, but these are often buried in the system settings, or have other limitations.

On Instagram, for example, you can limit your feed to just who you're following, although the app takes you back to the default every time you close and click back in.

Still, this could give us a hint of what an algorithm-free feed might look like.

Instagram users can switch their feeds to "following", but not everyone is happy with the offering.

An algorithm is sometimes described as a recipe or step-by-step instructions for how to manage data.

But the term "the algorithm" has become shorthand for recommender systems fuelled by AI and machine learning which curate content in a hyper-personalised way based on user engagement.

The aim is to keep you on the platform for as long as possible, so tech companies can monetise that engagement, selling ads between bits of content.

That means users get served content that they linger over, which includes both things they want to see, but also content they engage with out of outrage or morbid curiosity.

"It's the stuff that we're most likely to react to, but not necessarily in a good way," said Tama Leaver, a professor of internet studies at Curtin University.

Armed with a burner phone and a fake name, I set out to learn how Instagram’s algorithm really works. This is what happened next.

Critics of the algorithm say it pushes increasingly extremist content, leading users down rabbit holes and creating echo chambers that can warp a user's view of reality.

One minute you're looking at puppy videos and fitness routines, the next you're being fed rabid conspiracy theories.

"The platforms want a layer of curated content in front of you that is addictive, that is created to make you spend more time on the platform," said Belinda Barnet, a media and communications expert at Swinburne University.

"TikTok's incredibly successful at that. Their algorithm is amazing. Teenagers can spend six hours on it if you don't interrupt them."

One option is the reverse chronological feed — that is, showing you posts from accounts you follow in the order they were posted.

Proponents of this temporal model say it hails back to the "good old days" of the internet for early social media adopters, seeing posts from your family, friends and accounts you follow.

The government says the proposed laws will give social media users more of a choice. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Daniel Angus, director of the Digital Media Research Centre at Queensland University of Technology, said that puts the burden back on the user to be the curator.

"You are perhaps getting bombarded by those who are frequent posters," he said.

One benefit is that it could stop the infinite scrolling — if you get the feeling that you're all caught up, you can leave the app.

"The mindlessness turns into endlessness and soon enough we're in this spiral," said Rashina Hoda, a professor of software engineering at the Faculty of IT at Monash University.

"By giving this opt-out feature for that algorithm, you're bringing intentionality back into how we interact with social media."

She said the current opt-out option for recommender algorithms might not always be accessible or easily implemented.

Professor Leaver said that since it's been so long since social media users have had a chronological feed as a default, it might feel pretty weird at first.

"I'm quite sure that there will be a whole lot of protest design," Professor Leaver said, explaining tech companies may react by poorly designing features that are compliant but not user-friendly.

"If this is forced on platforms, they will probably make things a bit worse and then blame the government and say that they're perfectly happy to roll it back if the legislation went away.

"So it may not in the short term lead to a better experience, but I do think Australia's politicians at least seem more willing to stare down big tech and see who blinks first."

Consent advocate Chanel Contos wants Australians to be able to opt out of algorithm-driven content.

Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, told the Press Club last week the European Union's Digital Services Act pushed for mandatory "opt out" features, but it left room for social media platforms to "comply maliciously".

"Technically you can view a following-only feed in chronological order, but you can't access any other of the app's features and it resets back to an algorithm every time you close and re-open the app, punishing those who opt out of being force fed a diet of ads and polarised content," she said.

Professor Angus of QUT said another approach could be to move away from the algorithm vs non-algorithm binary.

Instead, he advocated for a hybrid approach that would give users more agency in how they curated their feeds.

He pointed to alternate social media spaces such as BlueSky and Mastodon, where people created lists to be able to discover like-minded creators.

Labor wants to make social media platforms proactively reduce foreseeable harms while giving users control over whether algorithms shape their feeds.

"That's a really interesting space where you put the creativity back into the community and you allow them to kind of self-govern and come up with the ways that they want to experience that space," he said.

"You end up with a hybrid approach where it's not like there's one algorithm driving everyone's experience and everyone is locked into that choice.

"The agency is with the user and they're coming up with the tools they need to try and swim within that river."

There are already steps you can take to control what you see on your feeds, but these steps are "typically buried a few levels deep inside of one's settings", David J Malan, a computer scientist at Harvard University, told ABC Radio National.

On Instagram, users can click on "not interested" to guide the algorithm about what they want to see. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

On Instagram, you can click on the logo to get a drop down, giving you the option of "following", which gives you a stream of posts from accounts you follow in reverse chronological order. But this will reset when you close and re-open the app.

In settings, you can also "snooze suggested posts" for 30 days, "reset" suggested, tweak "your algorithm" by clicking on what you want to see more and less of. You can also choose to see less political and sensitive content.

You can also flag content you don't like on several platforms by clicking "not interested", or unfollowing pages you don't wish to see.

TikTok and YouTube also have options for users to reset or delete history, telling the app to forget what it's learned about you and start fresh.

So will your social media feed be more boring under the proposed changes? It's possible.

But it's also part of the point to make platforms less addictive. Ultimately, we'll have to wait and see how companies react and what social media users choose.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.title: Can Australia produce another outback film classic?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.author: Sinéad Mangan, Christopher Testa, and Em Jensen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jason King fell in love with filmmaking after moving to the regional NSW town of Broken Hill. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

Forty years after Crocodile Dundee hit the big screen, it still stands as the number one box office success in Australia.

There have been plenty of great Australian stories produced in the outback since then, but none has quite matched the reach of the fish-out-of-water story of an Aussie bushie on the streets of New York.

The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and Crocodile Dundee showcased the Australian landscape. (Supplied: National Film & Sound Archive; IMDB, Paramount)

But it's regional Australia that has been key to so much of the country's cinematic success.

Films like The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, Wolf Creek, Red Dog, Mad Max, Babe, and Baz Luhrmann's Australia showcased the outback to the world.

James Ivor, an emerging filmmaker from Far North Queensland, says the next box office hit for Australia could be created in the regions.

James Ivor says Far North Queensland has become a popular backdrop for film and TV. (Supplied: Brendan Mounter)

"The only thing stopping the next Mad Max happening in Australia is the will to push boundaries and invest in filmmakers who have these ideas and there's many around me," he says.

"And everyone wants the next big hit. To get a hit is like lightning in a bottle.

"You ask, 'Is it possible?' I say, 'Yeah, of course it's possible.'"

Mr Ivor started his career as an extra on the set of The Pacific. Since then, he's turned actor, screenwriter and director, with his latest project, Storm Bird, screening in cinemas around Australia.

Director Shaun Wilson works on filming the TV show Rosehaven, which was filmed in Tasmania. (Supplied: Shaun Wilson)

Tasmanian TV director Shaun Wilson says despite advancements in film technology and CGI, nothing quite beats real Australian locations on screen.

"This is where location can do magical things," he says.

"I think it just speaks to the fact that something that's really great about cinema and TV is that there's a reason they can't get away with making all these films and TV shows in big sheds in Los Angeles.

"Where Australian stories have done really well is when we've done something that is really, truly of place."

Broken Hill and Silverton in far-west New South Wales have a rich history of producing cinematic masterpieces.

The iconic, stark, flat red earth stretching as far as the eye can see was the perfect backdrop for cult classics like Wake in Fright, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and Mission Impossible.

The Palace Hotel in Broken Hill was used to film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

Jason King moved to the town more than 20 years ago and became a filmmaker after learning of the town's movie history.

"It wasn't until I arrived in Broken Hill that I got a full appreciation for the full scale and the scope of the film history here and its contribution to Australian cinema," he says.

Jason King moved to Broken Hill to start a business but then fell in love with the landscape and the town's film history. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"The things that attract filmmakers out here definitely appeal to me.

"That countryside, the location as a character, even in town it has an energy and visual identity as well all of its own. I fell in love with the landscape.

Aside from the occasional advert or short film, productions are rarely being made in the region anymore.

Actor Ash Ricardo says the high cost of outback movie production is starting to be prohibitive to filmmakers. (Supplied: Daniel Asher Smith)

Local actor Ash Ricardo says the cost of filming in the outback town is prohibitive for small production companies.

"The big American, your Mad Maxes, Hollywood movies, can probably afford to pay a premium on accommodation, but a very small Australian production that doesn't have the budget just couldn't afford the cost of the accommodation," she says.

"It just became totally not doable sadly."

Over in Far North Queensland, Karen Jones scouts for film locations for production companies.

Karen Jones works as a scout for film companies and is pictured on location of reality TV show Survivor. (Supplied: Karen Jones)

"The reasons for them coming or not has got nothing to do with the location, often," she says.

"There're a million reasons why they need to be somewhere else; it's a fickle business.

"What we do is we bring a different point of view.

"We allow people to see their own region, their houses, their streets, their playgrounds, where they go every day in a different way.

A recent survey by Screen Australia found that most Australians take pride in local content and said they want to see more of it.

Plus, more than half of those surveyed said that they spent only one-third of their time watching Australian content.

The release of Crocodile Dundee in 1986 was credited with doubling visitors from the United States to Australia within three years of hitting the screen.

A follow-up Dundee-inspired ad campaign by Tourism Australia in 2018, featuring Chris Hemsworth, is credited with generating billions in extra tourism dollars.

The flat, red earth around Broken Hill has lent itself to iconic films, like Mad Max. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

State governments are keen to capture extra tourism dollars, with both Queensland and Western Australia ploughing millions into setting up film studios to attract international productions to their shores.

The $300 million Perth Film Studio will open its doors for the first time to the public on Friday to allow taxpayers to see what goes on behind the curtain.

It's been two and a half years since Screen Queensland opened a smaller state-of-the-art studio in Cairns in Far North Queensland.

Chief executive officer Jacqui Feeney says 12 productions have come out of the Cairns studio and the region's crew base has tripled to 250.

"I think one of the things that we're most pleased about is how we've been able to not just attract work to Far North Queensland but really build and invest in stories that showcase Far North Queensland as itself like Black Snow did, where the show was actually set in Cairns and shot in Cairns," she says.

Actor James Ivor stars in Storm Bird, that was filmed in Far North Queensland. (Supplied)

But ongoing funding for the studio will come from Screen Queensland's annual operational budget, which has been slashed by the state government by at least $13 million per year for the next two years.

Shaun Wilson believes competition between states to attract international productions to film locally is healthy for industry.

"I think the more we have to hassle our governments to put their money where their mouth is and get the benefit of these productions, the better in a sense," he says.

Shaun Wilson, centre, with Rosehaven stars Celia Pacquola and Luke McGregor, that was filmed in Tasmania. (Supplied: Shaun Wilson)

Magpie Pictures producer Lois Randall says there is so much more to regional storytelling than the familiar backdrop of red dirt.

"I also have heard recently international commissioners and also Australian commissioners expressed concern that there's too much red dirt on Australian screens at the moment and that we need to diversify," she said.

"I think that gives us a fantastic opportunity to show, to find fresh and unique and so far unseen, worlds that we can explore and unseen points of view that we can explore.

"And Australia, regional Australia, has just so much richness."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.title: Schumacher comparisons made as Antonelli continues historic F1 season
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kimi Antonelli became the first Italian in 60 years to win the F1 Italian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: Sutton Images/Sam Bagnall)

F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli has been compared to legend Michael Schumacher after his stunning win from 19th at the Italian Grand Prix.

New Zealand's Liam Lawson will spend a third consecutive weekend racing for Red Bull while French driver Isack Hadjar recovers from a wrist injury.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.

There were plenty of tributes to the great Michael Schumacher in Monza last weekend.

Ferrari ran special liveries to honour the seven-time world champion.

Drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton wore one-off racing suits with Schumacher's logo.

Meanwhile, former Ferrari driver Sebastian Vettel drove around the famous Monza circuit in Schumacher's 2002 world championship-winning car.

But perhaps the best tribute to Schumacher last Sunday was the performance by Mercedes gun Kimi Antonelli.

In a season of magical moments for the Formula 1 championship leader, Sunday's Italian Grand Prix victory was the stand-out performance.

At the start of the race, Antonelli lined up 19th on the grid due to a grid penalty and looked certain to have what was a 59-point lead in the championship reduced.

By the end of the race, he was standing on the top step of the podium, hoisting the winner's trophy as the first Italian to win the race in 60 years, and extending his gap to teammate George Russell in the drivers' championship to 66 points.

It was a monumental win, and one that has the 20-year-old in pole position to become the youngest F1 champion in history.

Kimi Antonelli was paraded by his fellow Italians after winning his home grand prix at Monza. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Andrea Diodato)

But what made Antonelli's win so impressive was the manner in which he did it.

He made 26 overtakes during the race, first taking the lead on lap 18 of 53, then chasing again when he took a pit stop with 24 laps remaining.

He passed rivals with precision, race craft and sheer pace, and it drew comparisons to Schumacher from a man who once went wheel-to-wheel with the legend.

Juan Pablo Montoya, winner of seven F1 grands prix which all came during Schumacher's dominant years with Ferrari, says Antonelli is so quick that rivals are not bothering to battle him on track.

Juan Pablo Montoya (left) battled Michael Schumacher (right) for many years in F1. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

Speaking on F1 TV's post-race program after Antonelli's win in Monza, Montoya specifically pointed out the difference between how Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who finished third, battled hard against Russell for the lead of the race but put up less of a fight with Antonelli.

"Something that was incredible was how easy he was passing people," Montoya said.

"It's a little bit [like] when I raced with Michael Schumacher. When Michael was coming through, people would get out of the way for Michael.

"And people are doing that [now]. They know Antonelli is going to get you, they're not even bother about fighting with him.

"He [Verstappen] ran Russell forever. When Kimi came it was completely different … and it was the right thing to do."

There are nine or 10 grand prix weekends left this season, depending on whether F1 will be able to race in the Middle East at the end of the year.

Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship is a whopping 66 points, almost double the lead Oscar Piastri had over Lando Norris (37 points) with nine race weekends left in 2025.

Piastri would suffer a form slump at the end of 2025, finishing 13 points behind Norris, and 11 points behind Verstappen who was a staggering 104 points adrift of the Australian with nine weekends remaining.

New Zealand driver Liam Lawson will race for Red Bull for a third consecutive weekend while Frenchman Isack Hadjar continues to recover from a fractured wrist.

Lawson, who was promoted to Red Bull from Racing Bull for the first two weekends of 2025 before being demoted back, will be Max Verstappen's teammate in Madrid for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix.

Hadjar has missed the previous two races in the Netherlands and Italy after suffering a wrist injury during F1's mid-year break.

Lawson finished seventh in the Netherlands, and 14th in Italy after starting from the pit lane.

"After racing for the team in Zandvoort and Monza, Liam will continue to drive alongside Max at this week's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid," a statement from Red Bull read.

"The decision has been taken as Isack's recovery continues to progress positively. While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team."

Yuki Tsunoda, who replaced Lawson in 2025, will again fill the Kiwi's seat at Racing Bulls.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Superannuation

Christine was left with more than $12 million in debt as a result of financial abuse.  (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Five years after her former partner left her with tax and other debts worth more than $12 million, Christine, whose name has been changed to protect her safety, is still trying to clear her name.

The physical abuse started when she entered the relationship.

But in 2021, after she had left the marriage, creditors threatened to seize Christine's home as they pursued her for $186,000 in alleged debts.

"I didn't know what I was served the bankruptcy notice for."

Christine soon realised that the debts were largely because her former partner had made her a company director of a business that she did not have any part in running. He also took out hefty loans under Christine's name without her knowledge.

If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero.

By the time Christine unravelled the extent of her financial abuse, the separated mother of two realised she owed millions to banks, credit agencies and the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).

She is still trying to clear the debts.

"I couldn't believe it [that] someone can do something like that. Knowing it's your husband," she said, breaking down in tears.

"We had a family. Did you [he] think about the kids? What was going to happen to us?

"You know you've done nothing wrong, and you've been prosecuted for something you didn't do."

Christine had no idea debts were being racked up in her name by her ex-partner.  (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is unveiling a suite of changes aimed at closing the opportunities for financial abuse.

Perpetrators of domestic violence would be punished rather than rewarded for their actions when committing abuse against their former partners by racking up tax and other debts in their name.

Daniel Mulino says he wants to stop financial abuse through the tax and super systems.  (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Financial and economic abuse is estimated to cost the economy almost $11 billion a year and affects more than 2.4 million Australians, according to research conducted by Deloitte, commissioned by CBA and published by Treasury.

If you have more information about this story please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com

Mr Mulino has been considering 61 recommendations made by a parliamentary inquiry into financial abuse.

Many perpetrators of financial abuse commit fraud by impersonating their partners, making them company directors in secret and putting business and tax debts in their name.

He said to prevent financial abuse from happening, he wanted to put a greater onus on all financial services providers, including banks, other credit lenders, insurance companies and superannuation funds.

The inquiry recommended various consumer codes of practice be amended to include specific reference to financial abuse under "vulnerable customers", and for lenders to develop systems to proactively contact customers who may be experiencing financial abuse.

"That can manifest itself through stronger codes of practice for different areas, but it can also just be companies making sure that they design products more safely," Mr Mulino said.

"For example, bank accounts or insurance products have safety mechanisms where one … party to the product, can't do things to the disadvantage of the other party, particularly where the bank or the insurer or the superannuation company has reason to suspect that there might be abuse being undertaken."

Financial abuse estimated to cost the economy nearly $11 billion a year. (Kirsten Aiken)

Mr Mulino said perpetrators needed to face tougher penalties if they coerced someone into being a company director to rack up tax debts in their name.

The federal government is consulting on major reforms to reduce financial abuse, including making it harder for directors to be appointed without clear consent.

Mr Mulino said he was considering changes that would stop perpetrators from being able to access a spouse's death benefits in cases where the spouse suffered financial abuse or committed suicide because of the abuse.

The inquiry into financial abuse suggested that the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993 be amended so that a beneficiary who had perpetrated domestic or family abuse against the superannuation account holder "can be declared an invalid".

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) would also be given powers to stop illegal withdrawals of super from self-managed super funds (SMSFs).

Perpetrators often set up a joint SMSF, clear money out of the fund illegally, and then leave the victim facing hefty penalties and risk of imprisonment after the money is gone.

Because perpetrators know the government is tightening controls around abuse committed through company directorship structures, abuse through self-managed super funds remains a "blind spot".

That is according to Jasmine Opdam, who works with the Redfern Legal Centre's Financial Abuse Service, a free legal service which assists victim survivors of financial abuse.

Perpetrators of domestic violence and financial abuse continue to be able to access the superannuation benefits and life insurance proceeds of their victims.

The illegal access could happen with SMSFs because the money is often held in a bank account which is easy to withdraw from, unlike APRA-regulated funds, where a person cannot access their superannuation as easily.

Ms Opdam said while there was no national data on the prevalence of financial abuse specifically within the self-managed super system, "we do know from ATO data from a few years ago that up to $250 million a year is being illegally accessed early from self-managed superannuation funds".

Jasmine Opdam worries SMSFs are a regulatory blind spot.  (ABC News: Keith Blackburn)

Mr Mulino said he wanted to give powers to the ATO to stop perpetrators of abuse accessing a victim's super in cases of suspected abuse.

Unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to consumers to convince them to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

In August, Mr Mulino unveiled a suite of changes at the National Press Club which included giving the ATO to power to stop rollovers in cases of suspected fraud.

"We'll then undertake detailed consultation on what those rollover powers look like specifically."

Consumer advocates want the government to compel super funds to proactively contact their customers when they are transferring their entire balance into an SMSF.

"This is very similar to how a bank might call a customer if there is a suspicious transaction," said Lily Jiang, director of advocacy at Super Consumers Australia.

Lily Jiang wants super funds to be more proactive. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Ms Jiang also wanted to see professionals such as financial advisers, accountants, and lawyers who often helped perpetrators set up an SMSF and facilitate illegal withdrawals held to account.

"Require them to set some professional standards to make sure that we don't have professionals either knowingly or unknowingly facilitating financial abuse through SMSFs," she said.

While the government's proposed changes to company directorships will go some way to helping victims, they do not account for debts created through other structures such as fraudulent tax returns, GST fraud and SMSFs, according to financial counsellor Julie Dal Pra.

The Tax Office is owed tens of billions of dollars worth of income tax debts it once dismissed as being "uneconomical to pursue". It's a shock for many taxpayers to now have the debts resurrected.

Ms Dal Pra, who works at non-profit community group Each, said she wanted the law to be changed to waive tax debts entirely in cases of financial abuse.

"Right now, we can't resolve financial abuse through the tax system," she said.

Julie Dal Pra says tax debts should be waived in cases of financial abuse. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Ann Kayis-Kumar, the founding director of UNSW's tax and business advisory clinic, also said she wanted the government to waive ATO debts in cases of financial abuse, and said that should include abuse through self-managed super funds.

She said that in the United States, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) had legal provisions that recognised victims of domestic violence as being deserving of special protection.

"It's devastating. Not only do they realise that all of their superannuation has been taken away without their knowledge … but also then have the system effectively weaponised against them and risking fines of $16,000 to $82,000 and even imprisonment on top of it," she said.

Ann Kayis Kumar says tax debts for victims are waived in the US.  (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mr Mulino said he was considering how penalties for tax debts could be waived.

Financial and economic abuse is estimated to cost the economy almost $11 billion a year. (Nassim Khadem)

All the financial counsellors ABC News spoke to also called for greater funding for specialist support services, which Mr Mulino said he was considering.

As Christine fights to clear the debts in the name, she hopes that federal authorities dealing with victims of abuse take a different approach — not just in recognising and waiving debts, but in terms of how they treat victim survivors.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Student visa refusals hit 10-year high, shattering dreams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Natasya Salim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Angelica Felincia says her student visa application was refused in a day. (Supplied: Angelica Felincia)

Read the story in bahasa Indonesia

Angelica Felincia has dreamed of studying in Australia since her first year of high school.

"I wanted to experience life outside of Indonesia and see different cultures," she said.

"Australia has many beautiful places, and I feel that I connect with the culture there."

Ms Felincia, who said she enjoyed being around children, found that early childhood education was a "well-regarded and popular field in Australia".

She said her desire to study in Australia had made her give up a place at an Indonesian university.

However, her visa application, which included a 27-page statement on why she wanted to study in Australia, was rejected within a day.

The case officer questioned why she could not pursue her studies in her home country.

"The letter said that my Genuine Student statement did not provide a strong enough reason for studying in Australia."

Department of Home Affairs (DOHA) data shows refusal of student visa applications has hit a decade high, with the rate climbing from 7.9 per cent in June 2016 to 24.2 per cent in June this year.

More than 51 per cent of all student visa applications from Nepal were rejected in 2025-2026, while India saw more than 40 per cent knocked back.

China recorded a rejection rate of 5.8 per cent for the same period.

Nepali applicant Asif Rahim lodged his application in March to study an accounting master's degree in Melbourne but was rejected in April.

He said he witnessed "a massive rejection" among his Nepali friends who also applied at the same time.

Mr Rahim said the department was not satisfied with his study proposal.

"I'm very disappointed with the rejection because I've invested 15 to 16 months preparing everything," he said.

The refusals were recorded as international students became the centre of discussions around migration cuts in Australia.

Last week, the government shut down a Vocational Education and Training course amid concerns students were using it to maintain their visas rather than for genuine study.

Applications for student visas are assessed based on the government's Genuine Student criteria. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

To obtain a student visa, the DOHA website states applicants have to provide a "Genuine Student (GS) requirement", which details a "student's intention to genuinely study in Australia".

Source: Department of Home Affairs

But several migration agents questioned how case officers assessed the applications under the GS criteria.

Umar Ashraf, a migration agent at Magpie Consultants, said he understood that the government would refuse a visa when there was a time gap in studies, misalignment of career pathway, or an intention to stay longer than necessary in Australia with the student visa.

But he was confused by many of the offshore application refusals he had seen.

"About 60 to 70 per cent of those refusals, I feel, the department is just throwing it back," he said.

Phu Vu Minh, a migration agent at VisaEnvoy, said the department gave "unreasonable" reasons in their refusal letters, which she said were often "vague".

"It's like copy-paste from one to the other," she said.

"It doesn't … show that the case officer has carefully assessed all the evidence submitted together with the application."

The ABC has reviewed some refusal letters from the department, finding almost identical paragraphs, minor wording changes, and paraphrased sentences used to outline why the assessment points in the applicant's documents were not accepted.

Phu Vu Minh says visa applications are often subjective to the case officer reviewing them. (Supplied: Phu Vu Minh)

Ms Minh said despite applicants submitting up to 15 pages to address the required points, the GS assessment was "highly subjective to the case officer".

"You may get approval from one case officer, but with the same case [or application] you may get refused by another case officer," she said.

Work Visa Lawyers' Chris Johnston said he had seen a fivefold increase in the number of appeals launched by onshore applicants against refusals in recent months.

He said the "very common patterns" in refusal letters for offshore applicants, who could not appeal, were "concerning".

"When someone pays the money and gets everything ready … the evidence should be considered on its merits," he said, adding applicants had to pay up to $2,500 to apply.

"That's not fair if they [the government] are just refusing because they don't want people to come to Australia."

Immigration lawyer Chris Johnston says the government should assess visa applications on merit. (Supplied: Chris Johnston)

DOHA said a range of measures had been implemented to "strengthen the integrity and quality of the international education sector and student visa program".

A spokesperson said the action had resulted in "greater scrutiny of applications and higher refusal rates for applications that do not meet visa requirements".

"Student visa applications are assessed on their individual merits against the requirements of Australia's migration legislation," the spokesperson said.

Ly Tran, an education professor at Deakin University, said there was "a legitimate need to address poor-quality providers, course-hopping, and the misuse of student visas in Australia".

Experts say visa refusals towards genuine international students could deter others from studying in Australia. (AAP: Paul Miller)

But she said she "would be cautious about a broad "crackdown' approach".

"There is also a risk that repeated restrictive measures create the impression internationally that Australia is becoming much less welcoming to international students."

She said international students had become "an easy target", with their cohort being one of the largest components of temporary migration.

"My bigger concern is that international students are increasingly being treated as political objects rather than primarily as students and members of our education community," she said.

The federal government is preventing new enrolments in a graduate diploma it fears is being used by non-genuine international students to switch courses and prolong their stay in Australia.

Luke Sheehy, CEO of Universities Australia, said current student visa processing was having a "detrimental effect" on universities.

"[It's] devastating, particularly for our regional universities and some of our universities in the growth corridor areas of our country," he said.

"It takes years … to engage with the student, go to their country, talk to them … so they can come to Australia and study at our world-class institutions."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.title: Whistleblowers allege fraud in $7.2b battery subsidy plan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.author: Michael Atkin and Lucy Kent
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Energy Industry

Allegations of fraud and misconduct were contained in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Allegations of fraud and misconduct have been revealed in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.

The untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information request.

Shadow Minister for Energy Dan Tehan is calling for an independent Senate inquiry into the revelations.

There are fresh claims a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded program to encourage households to install solar batteries is being rorted by unscrupulous operators.

They are accused of mocking up installs, forging signatures, using unlicensed tradies for cash jobs and leaving customers with unsafe or broken systems.

The allegations of fraud and misconduct were contained in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Albanese government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program.

These untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, which did not detail any regulatory action that may be underway.

The federal scheme offers up to 30 per cent of the cost of solar battery systems. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The Cheaper Home Batteries Program offers a generous subsidy for households — up to 30 per cent of the cost of solar battery systems.

Australians have rushed to sign up, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025.

The program is estimated to cost more than $7.2 billion over four years — about $5 billion more than originally announced.

Solar and consumer advocates have labelled the accusations "absolutely shocking".

The federal opposition will push for a Senate inquiry to probe the allegations while advocates want an urgent increase to safeguards, including more inspections and better consumer protections.

Do you know more about this story? Email michaelatkin@protonmail.com or contact him via the Signal secure messaging app +61 447 279 901.

The FOI documents included 95 tip-offs detailed over hundreds of pages and sent between March and June to the Clean Energy Regulator (CER).

The tips were primarily about the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.

The names of installers, retailers and individuals have been removed, and no responses from accused parties were included.

Finn Peacock, founder of the comparison website Solar Quotes, is a supporter of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.

Finn Peacock says the generous rebate had encouraged some customers to choose larger battery systems than needed until a recent change. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

However, he said the original design of the program, which saw companies paid through tradeable certificates known as STCs, created strong incentives for larger battery installations and attracted what he dubbed "battery cowboys".

In a bid to clamp down on over-selling, changes to the scheme were announced in December last year to reduce the subsidies from May 1.

"There was a massive temptation to get as many of those jobs installed as possible before the deadline," he said.

The CER has strict requirements for installers when putting in solar batteries.

However, whistleblowers alleged some operators manipulated the photo requirements, including pictures being time-stamped with the location, to claim rebates for incomplete jobs.

One tipster claimed a Queensland solar installer was fraudulently putting in claims for battery installations that were "staged" and the behaviour appeared to be "systematic".

The FOI documents included pictures of a poorly-finished job. (Supplied)

Extra batteries were positioned temporarily, "then removed after [STC] claims have been submitted", with the customers unaware.

In one case, equipment was "staged in front of a roller door without visible cable connections", they wrote.

A similar tip came from another installer.

The Clean Energy Regular requires installers to submit photos, time-stamped with the location. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

It was allegedly done by "unpacking the battery boxes … stacking the batteries and just taking enough photos to show on their STC Trading Application".

"This is illegal and whoever is behind this must be held accountable," they wrote.

In one extreme case, a customer alleged an installer turned up at night to remove their fully paid-for batteries two months after the installation.

The man and his wife felt threatened and called the police.

Mr Peacock said he was shocked by the allegations of "outright theft" from staged jobs.

Stephanie Tonkin, the CEO of the Consumer Action Law Centre, said if the claims of rorting were proven it would undermine the "policy goals and the trust in that system".

Dan Tehan is calling for an inquiry. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said the federal opposition would seek support across the parliament for a Senate inquiry.

"Given the seriousness of the revelations as a result of the unearthing of these FOI documents, we need an independent inquiry," Mr Tehan said.

Installers must be accredited by Solar Accreditation Australia to install batteries under the federal scheme.

But industry tip-offs alleged some operators used unlicensed workers, falsified paperwork and claimed rebates before installations were complete.

One whistleblower said they were offered cash to sign off on jobs completed by unlicensed foreign workers and raised concerns about manipulated site photos, while another similar claim involved "systematic" non-compliance at a company.

The documents included claims installers made jobs appear completed to claim a higher rebate. (Supplied)

Mr Peacock said unscrupulous operators could cut worker costs by using unlicensed crews instead of paying qualified solar electricians, but they risked getting caught.

It also came with serious risks including battery fires, injuries, or poor system performance.

The CER has inspected more than 3,600 batteries out of the more than half a million already installed and shared results with state and territory regulators and Solar Accreditation Australia.

Multiple consumers feared installers had claimed the government rebate even though their system was not working.

Others said they were thousands of dollars worse off after companies failed to put in the system before the rebate deadline.

The CER declined an interview.

In a statement, a spokesperson said it had "an active compliance program", and confirmed allegations were currently under investigation.

Installers must be accredited to install batteries under the federal scheme. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The regulator has the power to suspend companies from the scheme or take civil or criminal action.

"Where matters relate to sales practices, contracts, refunds or consumer guarantees, responsibility sits primarily with state and territory consumer protection agencies and the ACCC."

In 2025–26 it received 315 formal referrals about the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme, which included installer conduct under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program with 17 referred for formal investigation and 106 referred to external agencies.

Solar Power Nation is spruiked by a number of current and former sports stars, but the major retailer is facing investigations in multiple states as consumer complaints rise into the hundreds.

Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen was unavailable for an interview.

In a statement, a spokesperson said: "The government has zero tolerance for poor behaviour from installers.

"The Cheaper Home Batteries program utilises the tried-and-tested Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) framework, which includes built-in product, installer and electrical safety requirements, including compliance with state and territory electrical safety and consumer regulation, which has operated since 2011, under consecutive governments."

Mr Bowen also said a new National Technical Regulator would soon be created to ensure household solar and batteries met requirements, including that they were properly installed and commissioned.

The peak renewables body, the Smart Energy Council, said anyone flouting electrical licensing and battery accreditation laws "should be named, shamed and punished".

However, it said the regulator's statistics showed few were doing so.

"Of the 530,000 batteries installed in Australia in just over a year — more than the entirety of the United States — just 17 are being formally investigated for legal compliance by the Clean Energy Regulator."
