https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.title: Boyfriend of Simone Strobel breaks silence after 20 years
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.author: Richard Baker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tobias Moran has always denied killing his girlfriend, Simone Strobel. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

A Perth man police long suspected of killing his backpacker girlfriend Simone Strobel has protested his innocence and accused investigators of "tunnel vision" in his first media interview since her death in 2005.

For almost 20 years, New South Wales Police regarded Tobias Moran as the main suspect in the murder of his 25-year-old German girlfriend.

Tobias Moran (then known as Tobias Suckfuell) and Simone Strobel, whose killer has never been brought to justice. (Supplied)

Following a 2024 inquest that disagreed with key aspects of the police theory, Mr Moran, previously known as Tobias Suckfuell, has spoken to the ABC's Unravel: Lies In Lismore podcast to claim he was not involved.

"I made mistakes and I'm here to sort of own them, but I'm not a murderer,'' he said.

"I did not kill Simone."

Tobias Moran says he was untruthful to police because he did not believe they were taking the investigation seriously at first. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Ms Strobel disappeared from a caravan park in Lismore late at night after the pair had an argument in February, 2005.

Her naked body, which had been covered by palm fronds, was found less than 100 metres away from the couple's campsite six days later.

Mr Moran, who was 24 at the time, became an early suspect after he lied to police about arguing with Ms Strobel the night she disappeared, and about how much they had to drink.

Simone Strobel went missing after an argument with Tobias Moran. (Supplied\)

He also lied about not smoking marijuana and encouraged two other German travellers, Mr Moran's sister and a friend, to tell the same lies.

In 2022, Mr Moran was charged with murder and intending to pervert the course of justice.

The lies he told were a central part of the case against Mr Moran, but the charges were dropped the following year.

Simone Strobel was missing for six days before her body was found. (Supplied)

A NSW Local Court later found he was charged without reasonable grounds.

Mr Moran told Unravel he lied because he believed police were not taking her disappearance seriously.

He claimed police were reassuring him that Ms Strobel was probably OK and had likely hitchhiked to another town.

"I was not lying for any other reason than to get these guys to take Simone serious," he said.

"I knew … that she was not on a bender in Nimbin or having a great time in Byron Bay."

NSW Police did not respond to specific questions about Mr Moran's criticisms about the early investigation.

Police accused Tobias Moran of killing Simone Strobel in their campervan and moving her body, possibly with assistance. (Supplied)

Last year, NSW State Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan rejected a finding from an earlier inquest that said there was a "very high suspicion" Mr Moran was involved.

The more recent inquest finding cast doubt over key aspects of the police theory as to how Mr Moran allegedly killed Simone.

Police had long alleged Mr Moran killed Ms Strobel by suffocating her in their campervan and then moving her over a road with the help of one or both of his fellow German travellers.

Neither of those people have ever been charged and both have denied any involvement.

Tobias Moran and Simone Strobel were travelling with two other Germans when Simone died. (Supplied)

The coroner found both of the fellow travellers were "unlikely" to have been involved and that Mr Moran was "unlikely" to have acted alone.

Judge O'Sullivan stopped short of finding it was "very unlikely" that Mr Moran was involved and recommended the case be transferred from Lismore detectives to the Unsolved Homicide Unit.

She also recommended a review of forensic exhibits, including DNA profiles.

Tobias Moran, seen here with his wife Sam Moran, says the police owe him and his family an apology. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

In his interview with Unravel, Mr Moran claimed he had been unfairly targeted by police due to what he called "tunnel vision".

"This entire case has been based on a theory, on a hypothesis, and crucial evidence has not been considered," Mr Moran said, adding that he believed the killer was still at large in Lismore.

"It's time for someone from the New South Wales Police to step forward and go, 'Sorry, we are really sorry' … they should apologise to my wife and my kids for locking me up."

NSW Police declined to answer detailed questions from the ABC, instead issuing this statement:

"The matter is currently being assessed by the Unsolved Homicide Unit and a forensic review is being conducted in line with the coroner's recommendations," it said.

"No further information is available at this time."

Ms Strobel's parents, Gabi and Gustav, still regard Mr Moran's lies as suspicious and believe he is yet to tell them the full truth of what happened to their daughter on the night she died.

"We have always been confounded by the multiple and conflicting versions Tobias gave to the Australian and German police about important events surrounding her death," they said in 2023 after the charges against Mr Moran were dropped.

The mystery of what happened to Simone Strobel remains unsolved. (Supplied)

The Strobels told the ABC that they were disappointed with the result of the more recent inquest.

Lies in Lismore, the latest season of the ABC's true crime podcast Unravel, is out now. Find Unravel on ABC listen or wherever you get your podcasts.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/l.title: Colin from Accounts star leads new thriller set in bushranger country
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/l.author: Hannah Story
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Fresh off the series finale of Colin from Accounts, its star Patrick Brammall leads new Apple TV thriller Last Seen. (Supplied: Apple TV)

Patrick Brammall wasn't sure he was the right fit for the new thriller TV show Last Seen.

"When I was cast, I was like, fantastic, amazing, what a role'," Brammall tells ABC Radio National's The Screen Show. "But 5 per cent of me was going, 'I think they made a mistake'."

It's not an unusual feeling for the actor, who is perhaps best known for his roles in Offspring and ABC TV supernatural drama Glitch, and as the co-creator and star, with his wife Harriet Dyer, of the internationally lauded comedy Colin from Accounts.

"It's important that doubt is there because you're required to put it all on the line every time you embody a character — especially so for me with this role, which is really vulnerable," he says.

Brammall (right), with co-stars Brendan Cowell and Chloe Jean Lourdes at a screening of Last Seen in Sydney in September. (Supplied: Apple TV)

In Last Seen, Brammall plays Ian, an alcoholic emergency dispatcher and former police officer trapped by grief at the disappearance of his daughter, Maggie, 11 years ago.

When the remains of a girl are discovered near where he lives on the Victorian coast, Ian seems to finally be about to find closure.

Instead, the discovery pits Ian in opposition to the reclusive fundamentalist Henry (Brendan Cowell), who has a 14-year-old daughter of his own.

It's a return for Brammall to a more dramatic mode after a year that has seen him play Anne Hathaway's love interest in the Devil Wears Prada sequel and wrap up the final season of Colin from Accounts.

Brammall and Dyer were even writing the season, its third, while he was filming Last Seen in regional Victoria in early 2025.

"It was a great relief to inhabit that world as opposed to this world," he says.

"[But] I don't approach comedy any differently than I approach drama. It's not like, here's a different style.

"The tone is all embedded in the writing. If it's written well, it unlocks those things in you."

The darkness of Last Seen — with its story of grief in the wake of child abduction, paired with high-intensity car chases and shoot-outs — might have made for a difficult experience on set.

Brammall describes Last Seen as "psychologically real and character-driven". (Supplied: Apple TV)

But Brammall describes the shoot as joyful.

"We had the space and the grace to have these emotional and highly charged moments, but to let off steam there was a lot of laughter on set," he says.

Brendan Cowell, whose character Henry is devoted to protecting his feeble wife (English actor Maxine Peake) and sheltered daughter Sarah (newcomer Chloe Jean Lourdes), describes the atmosphere on set as reliant on mutual respect.

Last Seen is Lourdes's first screen role. She says the cast and crew began to feel like family. (Supplied: Apple TV)

"I tend to have more fun on the darker [shows] because you need the humour and you need each other," he says. "We formed this kind of feral gang in a lot of ways."

Working with dark material is a "strange occupational hazard", he says.

"We have to live on the edge of our own emotions and experiences to access them. Our pain and our history and our experiences are our instruments.

"Every now and again, you dig into some father stuff or you find some rage that's kind of distressing, and you've just got to walk that off or let it pass."

Still, for Cowell, the grittiness of Henry isn't too far from other recent roles, which include the ruthless whale hunter Captain Scoresby in two Avatar movies and the titular down-and-out ex-rugby player in Plum, the TV series he adapted from his own novel.

Cowell describes both Henry and Ian as "unequivocal" about getting what they want. (Supplied: Apple TV)

"I was reading [the script for Last Seen] and I thought, 'I never get offered that role of the cop or the guy in the suit, the guy that has a proper job'," he says.

"But when I started reading Henry, I was like, 'No, I'm happy here'.

"I like trying to allow audiences some access into how these kinds of characters operate and I try to make them likeable and understood."

The series reunited Brammall and Cowell with Australian screenwriter Kris Mrksa, who adapted the series from American author Ryan David Jahn's book The Dispatcher.

The Screen Show brings you reviews and in-depth conversations with leading film and TV directors, actors and screenwriters.

Mrksa was a writer on Glitch, and he and Cowell were both writers on the TV adaptation of Christos Tsiolkas's much-loved family epic The Slap.

Cowell credits the writer with coming up with the idea of transplanting the story from the American Midwest to regional Australia.

That makes it the first Apple TV show to be both made and entirely shot in Australia.

"I think it was [Mrksa] who said, 'Why not Australia?'" Cowell says. "We keep the scale, but it's in bushranger territory, with Aussie talent."

Thus, the show leans into Australian humour and "menace", he adds, but not so much as to isolate international viewers.

"For overseas projects, I've been asked to do my Australian accent, but 'well-read Australian, so we can understand what the hell you're saying'," Cowell says.

"I feel like we lent into [the Australianness] because it offers so much in a thriller."

Brammall understands Cowell's experience all too well, after three seasons of Colin from Accounts. He and Dyer resisted suggestions to change Australian slang — like saying "arvo" instead of afternoon — and just let the show "be what it is".

The final season of Colin from Accounts opens with Gordon (Brammall) and Ashley (Dyer) dating other people. (Supplied: Binge/John Platt)

"I grew up exposed to American and British stuff and there's a lot of references I didn't get, but it didn't stop my enjoyment of those shows," he says.

That theory is reflected in the growing international appetite for Australian-led stories, seen in the success of My Brilliant Career — which reached number two on Netflix's English-language TV chart last month — and homegrown comedies like Fisk and Colin from Accounts.

Brammall reckons Australian productions consistently hit the "quality of storytelling" needed to find a global audience but "it takes some help to expose it to the rest of the world".

"We don't all have to do a remake for the American market. We don't have to put subtitles on so much. We'll watch something from Ireland or Korea.

"But you do need to have the support."

Last Seen is streaming on Apple TV.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.title: US accuses Chinese AI firms of ‘malicious’ copying of AI technology
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.text:
The allegations of IP theft through distillation come ahead of a meeting between leaders Xi and Trump in the US this month

⁠The US government on Tuesday accused Chinese artificial intelligence companies of maliciously copying technology from American AI firms, potentially complicating relations ahead of a planned meeting between leaders of the world’s two biggest economies later this month.

The Chinese companies ‌copied US AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation, according to a statement from US law enforcement and intelligence officials.

Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.

US officials accused ⁠six Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of tapping variants of American-made AI models ‌to train their AI products more quickly. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

The companies did so “likely with Chinese government awareness”, according to the statement from US officials, who added ‌that the Chinese companies targeted AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and ⁠SpaceX.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: White House pulls ‘Build the Wall’ game after warning from Tetris
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
Arcade games on the White House website had drawn condemnation for racist themes and questions about potential copyright violations

The White House on Tuesday pulled a Tetris-style game called Build the Wall from its new online arcade, four days after a warning by the classic game maker that it takes copyright infringement seriously.

The block-stacking game, subtitled Zombie Border Siege, told players to “protect the border from the coming horde”.

It was no longer available on the website on Tuesday. The White House did not immediately respond to a request asking why it was removed.

The Tetris Company said on Friday that it played no part in the game’s creation.

“The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of Build the Wall and did not authorise or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game,” it said, adding that it was “currently reviewing the matter” when asked whether it was weighing legal action.

“At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” the company wrote on social media.

“P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously,” the post continued.

The arcade, launched on Thursday on the White House website, drew condemnation for racist themes and questions about potential copyright violations.

The games and the promotional clips the White House posted on social media borrowed imagery resembling that of Sega, Microsoft-owned Xbox and the Flappy Bird Foundation.

In one clip, the letters of the Sega logo morph into Maga, the acronym for US President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again slogan.

Other games remained playable, including Flappy Bill, in which a bald eagle dodges columns against a backdrop resembling Washington, and Rio Run, a Snake-style game themed on deportations.

“This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the president’s many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said Thursday in a statement.

Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has moved aggressively to conduct deportations.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-economy-fre.title: German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
https://www.dw.com/en/german-economy-fre.text:
The AfD won the election in the eastern German state by a wide margin. While politicians and election analysts are still debating the reasons for the far-right party's popularity, economists are sounding the alarm.

The results came in as predicted: The AfD, which is considered far-right extremist in parts, won the election in Saxony-Anhalt and could now put forward the state’s minister-president and take over the state government.

What hardly anyone expected, however, was this: The governing CDU is now barely half as strong as it was, while the other parties have been left far behind. Calling it a landslide victory for the AfD is no exaggeration. And many commentators go so far as to call it a turning point in Germany’s postwar history.

"A state government led by the AfD would certainly be seen by many as a turning point and would further fuel the debate over how best to deal with the party," Commerzbank economist Ralph Solveen told Reuters.

At the same time, he advises waiting to see what happens, saying that things are rarely as bad as they seem.

"Many of these decisions are unlikely to affect the economy until the medium to long term," he said. "Decisions on most taxes, the structure of the labor market and social security systems are made at the federal level. That is why the AfD, in many of its pledges, only promises to advocate for something in the Bundesrat, which is unlikely to succeed given the foreseeable isolation of an AfD-led government."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many business community concerns had already been raised before the election. It also became clear that there are differing views within the AfD, which could lead to unpredictable policies.

For example, DW reported two months ago that Hannes Loth, a member of the AfD and the mayor in Raguhn-Jessnitz, Saxony-Anhalt, sought to have six new wind turbines installed. This pledge puts him at odds with the official stance of his own party.

Whether this is a sign of internal party pluralism or simply local political pragmatism will become clear during the coming legislative term, especially if the AfD ends up in the state government. It is not, however, serving to reassure business leaders.

One issue the AfD campaigned on was a promise to limit the number of foreigners. But will the party actually be able to implement its goal? On this point, Michael Berlemann, director of the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), remains skeptical.

"A large part of the measures it has promised cannot be implemented at the state level because the federal government is responsible for them," he said. "Another part would be illegal and would be overturned by the courts after some delay: The AfD cannot restrict the immigration of foreign skilled workers in Saxony-Anhalt."

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski pointed to the national shortage of skilled workers: "Forced deportations in Saxony-Anhalt would probably be limited. However, the symbolic effect cannot be underestimated. As with Trump, such headlines would act as a deterrent for foreign skilled workers."

Wido Geis-Thöne, an economist at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, sees it the same way.

He told DW that the AfD would "do everything in its power to pursue its migration policy goals." However, it could only "do things that actually fall under the responsibility of the state rather than the federal government."

Geis-Thöne said the state itself would be the main victim of such a policy: "With an anti-immigration state government, Saxony-Anhalt will become significantly less attractive a destination for foreign skilled workers, regardless of whether anything actually changes for them from a legal perspective."

For HWWI Director Berlemann, the indirect impacts of the AfD's plans are particularly problematic. The measures announced would mean "that many skilled workers who are particularly needed in health care and nursing, hospitality and tourism, the food industry and agriculture and in construction and logistics will avoid the state in the future."

This would exacerbate the shortage of skilled workers and widen the state's economic gap.

Saxony-Anhalt must remain a state where people from around the world want to live and work and where companies want to invest and new technologies can emerge, Bitkom President Ralf Wintergerst warned.

He told the Catholic News Agency KNA: "The digital economy thrives on openness, diversity and international cooperation. Companies invest where they find good conditions and where skilled workers from Germany and abroad are welcomed."

Regarding foreign investment, ING Chief Economist Carsten Brzeski told Reuters: "Sure, there could be a symbolic effect on foreign investors. But let's not forget: Saxony-Anhalt is not the entire German economy."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DIW President Marcel Fratzscher painted a bleak picture of the economic future after the Saxony-Anhalt election.

"Regardless of the makeup of the next state government, a controversial or weak government and the polarization during the election campaign are likely to accelerate the departure of people and companies from Saxony-Anhalt, thereby significantly worsening conditions in the state," he said.

He told Reuters that the election result was "above all a vote of no confidence in the federal government." The consequence, he added, must be "that the federal government changes course and implements far-reaching structural reforms involving subsidies, bureaucracy, taxes, the social security system and Europe."

Tanja Gönner, managing director of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), took a similar perspective. Following the state election, she called on the federal government to be single-minded in pursuing a reform agenda.

"The response to this state election result must not be political paralysis at the federal level," she said.

The federal government must now consistently implement and expand reforms to boost investment, innovation and growth, she told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland, adding that "the positions of radical parties are not suitable for this."

The political center must now show that it is capable of taking action, BDI's managing director said, adding that what is needed is a policy focused on competitiveness and growth at both the state and federal levels. A single state election result must not distract from that goal, she concluded.

This article was originally published in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/fifty-years-after-.title: Fifty years after Mao’s death, China has transformed. DW looks at why his political legacy still matters.
https://www.dw.com/en/fifty-years-after-.text:
Mao Zedong was perhaps the most influential, and certainly one of the most controversial, figures in 20th-century China. Even five decades after his death, the legacy of his era continues to influence China today.

On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.

He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.

Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.

When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.

Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.

From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.

Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.

Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."

The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.

Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.

Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.

Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.

Zhang holds a similar view.

Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.

And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.

"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW.

The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.

Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.

"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."

Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."

In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.

The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.

Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.

The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.

Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.

Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.

Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.

First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.

Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.

Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.

"At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."

China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.

Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.

The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.

The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility.

Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.

In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.

The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.

Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yd.title: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yd.text:
Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.

Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.

Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.

The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.

They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.

Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.

For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.

Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.

Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.

And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.

As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.

That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable.

Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.

Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.

Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment.

But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.

Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.

But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.

For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress.

The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".

In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".

Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.

The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.

Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.

In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.

But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.

Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.

So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yd.summary: Britain and 11 other countries ban trade with Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank. Israel's reaction to the move shows how important this moment is, writes David Frum. Israel is deeply troubled by the action by the UK and 11 others, which includes France, Spain and Canada.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99d.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol, motorbikes and other goods
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99d.text:
The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motorbikes, as its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.

In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said that Canada is "discriminating" against the US and outlined the import ban, which will begin 29 September.

Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".

Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.

The BBC has contacted Carney's office for comment.

The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The sides have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other.

Generally more than two-thirds of Canada's total exports go to its neighbour.

On the other hand, Canada is the second-largest trading partner of the US, after Mexico, although its exports are far more diversified.

Business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall.

Last month, the White House imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down.

Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as some sporting and fishing equipment businesses.

Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday.

Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting US goods while not doing the same to the same products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday.

Some products, like whey and non-alcoholic beer, have been banned from import entirely, while tariffs have been further hiked for others, including cheeses and motorboats.

On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moves manufacturing there.

Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging levies have upset many of the States' traditional allies.

Some Canadians have led a massive boycott of US products like alcohol, which have vanished from some store shelves after Trump launched his global tariff campaign last year.

Trade expert Deborah Elms, from the Hinrich Foundation, told the BBC the import ban could have a "strong" impact on any Canadian business with US buyers, though early estimates show a "modest impact" affecting around $1bn worth goods.

Canada will likely "hold course for now" and adjust their business support measures to account for the US' latest moves, Elms said.

"The bigger question is what it will take for the two sides to sit back down together. The language in these proclamations, as an example, isn't helpful in getting to the negotiating table," she added.

Those facing higher import taxes include:

Carney said on Tuesday as Canada's counter-tariffs came into effect: "There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still."

Tension between the US and Canada has also moved beyond tariffs.

In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some in the US.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyr.title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyr.text:
The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".

But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.

Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.

The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.

On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center.

"After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.

Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".

A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.

Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.

The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.

Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.

But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial.

"My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said.

"Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.

Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.

Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about.

"I want to concentrate on the memories," he said.  "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."

Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died.

"They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."

Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.

He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".

But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".

He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.

Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case.

"Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.

She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.

John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.

The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."

During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.

Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice.

"If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."

Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.

The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.

Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.

Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.

Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions.

"My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are.  I just want them convicted," he said.

Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal.

"It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.

Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there.

"My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."

With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event".

"I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."

When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.

Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in".

"If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.

As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo.

"It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyr.summary: The trial of alleged mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is yet to begin. Relatives of victims say torture of defendants have blocked their right to justice. The trial will start at Guantanamo in early 2025.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.text:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse

Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.

The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.

Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP) says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.

When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."

The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.

About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.

After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.

The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.

When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.

The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.

But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.

Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material

"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.

The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.

According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.

TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.

According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.

In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.

"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.

TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.

For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."

For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.

When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000".

TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed.

This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down.

Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings.

TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers.

The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM.

Meta has said it prohibits promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images.

One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them".

"We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added.

The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].

Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.

Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.

After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".

But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.

These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.

TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.summary: Ad agency Meta says it prohibits promotion of nudify apps. Ad partners in China channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn45.title: Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader dies aged 89
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn45.text:
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89.

The former shipping scion took over the reins from the last British Governor Chris Patten in July 1997 when the UK handed Hong Kong back to China, ending more than 150 years of British control.

Tung's rocky tenure was marked by the Asian Financial Crisis, two major epidemics, and historic protests which attracted criticism of his administration. He eventually resigned in 2005.

Tung died on Tuesday night surrounded by loved ones, local media reported. His office described him as a man "devoted to his country and its people".

"His noble character and integrity will live on forever in our hearts," it said in a statement.

Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from Liverpool University in the UK before moving to the US, where he worked at General Electric for almost a decade.

In 1969, he moved to Hong Kong and worked in his father's shipping conglomerate, the Orient Overseas, eventually taking over the reins in 1979.

His political career began in 1992 when he was appointed a member of Patten's executive council.

Despite having little political experience, Tung was believed to be handpicked by Beijing to lead Hong Kong after the handover. He was seen as a loyalist, especially after China's state-run banks helped rescue his family business during a global slump in the mid-1980s.

During a reception at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996, China's then-president Jiang Zemin walked across a packed room to shake Tung's hands – a widely photographed gesture that at the time famously signalled Beijing's backing of Tung for the top job.

The Asian Financial Crisis hit shortly after Tung took over, which sent home prices diving. His administration was also beset by a series of public health challenges, including a bird flu outbreak from 1997 to 2002 and the 2003 outbreak of Sars, also known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome.

But Tung's biggest political challenge took place in July 2003 during his second term, when half a million Hongkongers took to the streets to protest against a proposed national security law they feared would threaten their civic rights.

His administration abandoned the proposed legislation following the massive outcry, which also contributed to Tung stepping down in March 2005.

At the time his declining health, but some say he was pressured by Beijing to step down.

Beijing ultimately imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which authorities have argued is necessary to maintain stability. Critics however have called it "the end of Hong Kong" and say it has created a climate of fear in the city.

Tung's last public outing was in July 2021, at an event marking the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. He underwent heart surgery months later, according to reports.

He is survived by his wife and three children.
