https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Australia breaks from international pack on Israeli sanctions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Laura Tingle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Economic Sanctions

Australia has broken from the pack in not adopting the trade sanctions against West Bank businesses. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

It's almost 12 months since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese joined 10 other countries in recognising the state of Palestine at the United Nations General Assembly.

The move was dismissed by some critics as too late, or only symbolic, at the time.

And at that time, the prospects of a Palestinian state ever emerging were already pretty grim, with Gaza largely reduced to rubble and Israel in the process of expanding settlements in the West Bank at a record pace.

In the intervening year, with the world's attention distracted by the conflict with Iran, and by Israel's invasion of a vast swathe of Lebanon, the Israeli cabinet has defied growing criticism from the international community by only escalating its efforts to make a Palestinian state a physical impossibility.

The overnight move by the international community, spearheaded by the United Kingdom but including Canada, France and other European nations, is a significant escalation of attempts to stop Israel from doing that.

The move is not just significant because it escalates penalising actions into trade sanctions.

It is important because of what goes with that, as well as the changing context of Israel's actions.

In the past, Israel has justified many of its moves to clear Palestinians from their homes — in Gaza, in Jerusalem or the West Bank — on specific security grounds: that houses and the people who lived in them were responsible for, or represented, a security threat.

Even many Israelis who are not fans of the settlement movement will say that, while they don't like them, their presence makes them feel more secure.

But settlers themselves tend to justify their takeover of Palestinian land in the West Bank on the grounds of an assertion of sovereignty, based in the Bible, rather than any immediate security threats emanating from any particular village.

Those past security concerns, and UK Labour's fraught history of allegations of antisemitism, have been part of the reason why Westminster has hesitated to adopt findings against Israel in the international criminal system.

Britain, France and Canada are banning imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in a move that has prompted swift retaliation and could spark a broader geopolitical storm.

As British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday, "For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel."

On Tuesday, local time, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the House of Commons that the British government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank — perpetrated by settler terrorists".

"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians," he added.

"Now for a long time, the British government has rightly said settlements are illegal.

"But we have remained silent on the question of the legality of the occupation as a whole, which in 2024 the International Court of Justice concluded was unlawful.

"Today I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful."

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announces ban on imports from Israeli settlements

The significance of this is that the UK — along with countries like Australia — previously legally separated the status of the settlements from the status of the military occupation of the West Bank as a whole.

The occupation was viewed as a temporary, unresolved political dispute — even though it has been in place since 1967 — to be settled via bilateral negotiations.

Miliband also foreshadowed the likelihood of the International Court of Justice making a finding of genocide against Israel, and that the UK would accept such a finding, and the possibility of further actions at the UN General Assembly in New York later this month.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his pledge at the time of the UN move last September, saying his government was "going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state".

"This place belongs to us," he said.

Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the 80th United Nations General Assembly in New York City last September. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

In March this year, Israel announced another 34 settlements in the West Bank, as well as allocating billions of shekels to fast-track infrastructure, roads, and security connectivity for these sites.

In August, it provocatively pushed ahead with a development that Miliband described to the House of Commons on Tuesday as "crossing a long-standing red line": the issuing of tenders for more than 1,200 homes in a 12-square-kilometre tract of land immediately east of Jerusalem known as E1.

The proposed housing development would start to cut the West Bank — Palestinian territory — in half, and also cut it off from Jerusalem, destroying the prospect of a viable Palestinian state.

While settlements — and the increasing violence shown by settlers towards Palestinian landowners (tolerated or even sometimes perpetrated by the Israeli military) — are the most visible signs of Israeli actions in the West Bank, it is also in a state of virtual war on the West Bank economy.

While settlers physically attack Palestinians, they also uproot their trees and divert the water supplies of villages, which make them viable.

But on a larger scale, Israel has increasingly made economic life impossible.

World leaders have fought this Israeli "doomsday" settlement plan in the West Bank for decades. But some fear the war in Gaza could change everything.

Israel has withheld tariffs and revenue it collects on behalf of the Palestinian Authority — which is supposed to fund its provision of day-to-day services. It leaves the Palestinian banking system in a perpetual state of uncertainty by refusing to guarantee it will offer exchange services with the Israeli banking system.

It puts strict limits on how much paper money — even though it is Israeli shekels — can be exchanged between the Palestinian and Israeli economies.

The settlements themselves are often economically unviable. They are not just the odd caravan on a hill but often mini cities.

Though the Israeli government does consider informal settlements, known as outposts, illegal, they often later authorise them as formal settlements.

The Israeli government doesn't just tolerate the violence; it provides massive subsidies to encourage people to move to the settlements, including reduced income tax rates, security gear for unauthorised or "young" outposts as well as funds to purchase vehicles, drones, security cameras, generators, electric gates, and perimeter fences.

That's what makes the various economic trade sanctions announced overnight by the UK, France, Canada and 12 European countries both so significant and also so potentially difficult to implement.

They are also one of the reasons Australia has, on this occasion, broken from the pack of other nations in not adopting the trade sanctions against West Bank businesses.

The argument goes that it will be almost impossible for international companies to distinguish between Palestinian businesses in the West Bank and settler businesses, or between sanctions that only hurt settlers and those that might also hurt the Palestinian economy.

The Albanese government knows it remains exposed by its position, which one Labor source described as "rhetorically less impressive", but there are signs it may act further in the coming weeks and months.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the Senate on Tuesday that the "Netanyahu government's actions in the West Bank, the rapid expansion of settlements, the proposed E1 settlement development and flagrant settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution".

Australia is "not, at this time, pursuing a blanket style import ban", she said, because "we have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis".

Penny Wong tells the Senate that Israel's actions are "extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution".

The real effectiveness of any blanket bans is likely to be in the realm of finance, rather than sanctions on, say, date farms in the West Bank.

A particular issue for the UK in recent months has been investor "expos" inviting people in Britain to come along and find out how they could invest in the West Bank, in illegally occupied land.

The UK signalled action "against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion", Mr Miliband said.

It will also ban the advertising in the UK of illegal settlements.

Just what specific actions France and Canada will take in support of the UK position are unclear, although they have said they will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.

The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway have already either banned goods or are in the process of doing so, while Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden also pledged to take further action overnight.

To date, the US has been notably quiet about the UK actions, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio not condemning the UK action but saying the US would "obviously" not be going along with it either.

"Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don't have any comment on it right now," Rubio told reporters in Miami.

The US does not want to see "anything destabilising going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region", he added.

"We were made aware that they were going to make this decision," he said.

"We heard their arguments as to why. But we share the goal of stability. We don't want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region."

The ABC recently spoke to a West Bank villager who was under siege by settlers.

But there already has been more than an "uptick" in conflict on the West Bank, and little sign that the US-led peace initiative for Gaza is making any progress.

Some analysts have expressed concern that the Israeli government would be quite happy to see a full-scale uprising on the West Bank ahead of next month's Israeli elections.

And that raises another aspect of this story: that international actions against Israel often galvanise public opinion in favour of the government.

The UK-led actions this week come just as Netanyahu's standing with voters came under huge new pressures this week with revelations that he had been warned by the United Arab Emirates of the likelihood of a major Hamas attack in the days leading up to October 7, 2023, but failed to pass this intelligence on.

The man who has emerged as the greatest challenge to Netanyahu at next month's elections is Gadi Eisenkot.

While he supports maintaining established settlement blocs in the West Bank and opposes Palestinian statehood, he has also opposed unilateral annexation, criticised provocative outposts, settler violence and controversial construction plans like the E1 development, in part because of the diplomatic toll such moves impose on Israel's international standing.

In the Israeli landscape of 2026, that is quite a different position from that of the current government. But it's unclear whether it would be enough of a change to satisfy an increasingly frustrated international community.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt

Topic:
Mining Environmental Issues

Uncovered iron ore train carriages travel approximately 200 kilometres to the Geraldton port.  (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

A state government investigation into dust complaints in Geraldton has found magnetite from "industrial activities" as a contributor to dust polluting homes and businesses.

The Department of Water and Environmental Regulation says it will meet with the Mid West Ports Authority and Chinese-owned Karara Mining in a bid to change some operating licence conditions to reduce dust impact on the coastal community.

The Department of Water and Environmental Regulation is still investigating other dust complaints.

Western Australia's environmental regulator says it will look to change the operating licences of a Chinese-owned mining company and the Mid West Ports Authority after months of investigation into dust pollution around Geraldton.

Investigators from the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) began examining the nature and source of dust earlier this year, after a surge in complaints of red, black and pink dust from residents and businesses around the city, with complaints localised around its port.

Uncovered trains filled with black iron ore enter the Geraldton Port daily. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Iron ore is the port's main export, with Chinese‑owned Karara Mining, which ships magnetite concentrate, and WA‑based Fenix Resources, which exports hematite, the two key players.

In a statement released today, DWER said its investigation of the "black dust" complaints found magnetite dust emitted from "certain industrial activities" was a contributor to overall dust pollution around the city.

"As a result of this investigation, the department is engaging with Karara Mining Limited and the Mid West Ports Authority in relation to potential licence amendments to deliver improved dust management outcomes," a DWER spokesperson said.

DWER did not disclose the changes it would ask the port and miner to make.

Karara Mine is a large iron ore project in Western Australia's Mid West region, majority-owned and operated by China's Ansteel Group. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

There have been consistent calls from Geraldton residents and community leaders for wagons pulled by Karara's trains, which carry its iron ore from mine to port, to be fully covered.

In a region known for its strong southerly winds, the path from mine to port loops to the south of schools, hospitals and houses.

Residents have previously told the ABC that black dust picked up by the winds was coating their homes and businesses, and costing thousands of dollars to clean.

A Karara train loaded with iron ore being delivered to Mid West Ports. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

DWER said its investigation into the separate complaints around pink and red dust were ongoing, but nearing completion.

"While substantial information has been assessed, further technical analysis is needed before conclusions can be reached regarding other dust sources or potential regulatory action," DWER said.

"Such investigations can take time to ensure evidence is thoroughly assessed, findings are supported by evidence and processes are fair and defensible."

Iron ore is the main export from the Geraldton Port. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Both Karara Mining and Mid West Ports have been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.title: Auditor-general finds nearly half of Victoria's road in very poor condition
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.author: Danielle Pope
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A pothole on the Murray Valley Highway at Ebden, Victoria.  (Supplied)

Almost half of Victoria's state-managed roads are in very poor condition, the auditor-general has found.

It says more than $3 billion a year is needed to maintain the state's roads.

Roads Minister Paul Hamer has accepted that Victoria's roads are not good enough and has promised to deal with it.

A new report from Victoria's auditor-general has found almost half of Victoria's road network in poor condition and is crumbling faster than the government can repair it.

The report, tabled in parliament this morning, examined more than 23,000 kilometres of state roads and found that about 48 per cent of the network was in poor or very poor condition in 2024 compared to 39 per cent in 2021.

Newly-appointed Roads Minister Paul Hamer said the government accepted that the roads were not good enough, promising the government would fix the way it deals with roads if re-elected.

Paul Hamer says the government is working to make road repairs a priority.  (ABC News)

Late last month the government announced an extra $352 million of funding to double the number of potholes fixed this year.

"That includes bringing road maintenance back in-house," he said.

"It meets higher standards, it means more accountability, it means more transparency, and it means more local delivery and local expertise."

This figure is in addition to the $1.04 billion allocated to road asset management in this year's budget, bringing the total funding to $1.39 billion.

The report found that the government's current funding commitment falls short of completing the maintenance required to fix the state's roads properly.

According to the auditor-general the funding shortfall led to a focus "more on reactive and safety-critical repairs rather than preventative works".

The Department of Transport and Planning's 2026–27 road maintenance business case, which informs the state budget process, estimated it would cost more than $3 billion per year to maintain road pavement condition at existing levels, while replacing aging assets.

Mr Hamer would not be drawn on whether he would ask Premier Ben Carroll to boost funding.

"We've had record investment over the last few years in each of those financial years, but we need to do more. We are not shying away from that," he said.

More than half of the state roads in the Loddon Mallee region were in very poor condition.  (Supplied: Victorian Auditor-General's Office)

State roads account for about 15 per cent of the Victorian road network by length, but carry most of Victoria's traffic.

Around 82 per cent of state roads are in regional Victoria.

The report found increasing road use and traffic is adding to the pressure on the network, with growth expected to continue.

The Loddon Mallee region recorded the highest proportion of roads as being in poor or very poor condition, with 69.1 per cent of the region's state roads receiving the rating.

The report found the Loddon Mallee region had the highest proportion of state roads in a poor or very poor condition. (Supplied: Victorian Auditor-General's Office)

Victorian opposition roads spokesperson and Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said the findings were damning.

"This is an indictment on the Labor government's inability to look after our roads, to maintain them properly," he said.

Danny O'Brien says the government is not doing enough for the road network. (ABC News )

Mr O'Brien said the Coalition's promise to reinstate the $288 million Country Roads and Bridges Program if it wins government in November would help address the issue.

The Coalition has also promised $5 billion to fix the state's potholes.

It also plans to spend $288 million over four years by providing funds to rural and regional councils to spend on road repairs.

"I believe if we actually do the preventative maintenance, we get on top of it after a couple of years, that will require less money in the longer run," Mr O'Brien said.

The report also highlighted that Victoria has a large and growing road maintenance backlog where the network is deteriorating faster than the pace of repairs.

Based on defect job records, which includes potholes or hazards such as structural failure, the gap between the number of defects identified and the number of defects rectified more than doubled between January 2025 and June 2026.

RACV head of public policy James Williams said the report confirmed what the agency was hearing from motorists.

James Williams says there should be greater transparency around how funding for road repairs is spent. (Supplied: RACV)

"It's no surprise for RACV that the state of the roads in Victoria is not good and probably not a surprise for most Victorian motorists," he said.

So we've seen our road network crumbling and that's after many years of a lack of investment in road resurfacing and that has a direct impact on both safety and productivity."

RACV says it has received a significant increase in reports of damage caused by potholes, with 112,000 tyre punctures recorded last year.

"This causes not only an inconvenience issue, but a safety and productivity issue as well," Mr Williams said.

Mr Williams said a key takeaway from the report was that decision-making around repairs was being conducted by four major contractors who were outsourced to by the government, and not the government or the department.

He said there needed to be greater transparency around how government funding for repairs was spent.

"RACV is very concerned that the decision maker is not the government, it's not the department and therefore there is a lack of transparency there," he said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Pegula sets up Sabalenka rematch for third successive U.S. Open semi
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Janina Nuno Rios
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
NEW YORK – Jessica Pegula reached the U.S. Open semifinals for a third successive year, coming from a set down to beat Emma Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3 in an all-American clash on Tuesday.

The 32-year-old will face two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka in a rematch of the 2024 final after securing her fifth straight win over her compatriot, including a victory at last month’s Cincinnati Open.

The clash, dubbed by American media as the “Battle of the Billionaires” because of their backgrounds, began more than an hour later than scheduled after Frances Tiafoe’s marathon victory over Alex Michelsen in another all-American contest.

The wait did little to help either player find their rhythm, with the match instead marked by errors and few sustained bursts of momentum.

The 26th seed had the edge in a scrappy opening set as both players struggled to settle. They traded early breaks and each hit five double faults, with an extra break allowing Navarro to move one set ahead.

The miscues continued in the second, but Pegula found a slight improvement that allowed her to level the match, finishing a long exchange with a fine forehand winner to make it one set apiece.

Pegula carried that momentum into the decider, where an extra break put her in control before she closed out the victory.

“It was really tough, really physical, I wasn’t serving my best, I was fighting a lot of demons out there,” Pegula said on court.

“I do a great job on having a short term memory, I know every time I come out no matter what I have to tell the negative me to shut up and just play tennis and compete.”

The victory was also Pegula’s 50th of the season, making her the first player on the women’s tour to reach that mark in 2026.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: CRA heads toward disbandment after failed merger with CDP and Komeito
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Kenji Yoshida
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA) is moving toward a disbandment, with lawmakers who were previously members of the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDP) set to form a new party while those from Komeito return to their original party.

CRA leader Junya Ogawa and other executives agreed Tuesday to a plan under which almost all CRA lawmakers will depart. But the party will temporarily retain a single member to settle its finances and wind down its local branches before disbanding altogether.

The party is expected to formally approve the plan Wednesday, following a meeting of its lawmakers and a separate one of its extraordinary executive scheduled in the afternoon.

The CRA would still seek to maintain cooperation with the new party and Komeito in the Lower House by establishing a parliamentary caucus to preserve their combined strength as the chamber’s largest opposition bloc.

“Despite the various difficulties we have faced over the past six months, the pledges, friendship and trust shared by all 49 of us will remain unchanged,” Ogawa said early last week after a plan to merge the CRA with the CDP and Komeito — both of which still maintain a presence in the Upper House — fell through.

Of the CRA’s 49 Lower House members, 21 are formerly with the CDP while 28 are ex-Komeito members. Most of the former CDP members are expected to form a new party, while the ex-Komeito contingent will rejoin Komeito as early as this month.

CRA executives likely chose to keep the party temporarily intact, as an immediate and complete dissolution could result in cumbersome bureaucracy that might delay the formation of a new party, possibly until after the autumn session of parliament.

This decision might also have to do with the allocation of state subsidies. With the CRA’s continued existence, it will receive undistributed state subsidies amounting to about ¥1.17 billion ($7.6 million).

Most of the funds will be used to repay loans the CRA incurred and to continue supporting candidates who were defeated in February’s Lower House election, people familiar with the matter told local media.

An immediate and complete dissolution of the CRA means the undistributed funds will go to neither the CRA nor the new party formed by its departing lawmakers.

The CRA must also decide what to do with the approximately ¥117 million it raised through crowdfunding. Ogawa told reporters Friday that returning donations to donors was one option under consideration.

The CRA was formed in January by Lower House members of the CDP and Komeito to contest the February general election as a unified centrist force against the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. Upper House members of the CDP and Komeito as well as their local chapters were expected to join the CRA via a full merger process.

But those plans faltered after the CRA suffered a crushing defeat that saw its Lower House presence reduced by more than two-thirds, with the party stuck with single-digit approval ratings and unable to gain wider traction in the months following the election.

The CDP decided late last month not to proceed with the full merger amid opposition from its lawmakers and local chapters. Komeito followed suit by formally abandoning the plan last week.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Germany is in a very dark place — and time’s running out
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Chris Bryant
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
The far-right Alternative for Germany’s dramatic election win in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday is a watershed in the country’s postwar history. In a nation known in the modern era for stability, Germans in this small federal region have embraced populist, nationalist ideas in large numbers.

Whether this electoral censure marks the low point for Germany or the start of a descent into something far worse is now up to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition. It needs to deliver economic growth and a renewed sense of optimism and trust in democracy. I’m not confident that Merz is up to the task.

After gaining 44% of the vote, the AfD doesn’t quite have the seats in Saxony-Anhalt needed to form a state government by itself. While various permutations are possible, in theory it could still end up ruling there, either by securing defections from other parties or with the tacit support of the BSW, a leftist but culturally conservative and Russia-friendly group. Governing would give it authority over domestic security and education.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: To end global hunger, invest in rural communities
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
URBANA, ILLINOIS – The United Nations recently released its State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report, which, perhaps surprisingly, delivered some encouraging news. While roughly 645 million people experienced hunger in 2025, that was nearly 14 million fewer than in the previous year. For the first time in a decade, the number of hungry people in Africa also declined.

But despite these positive developments, significant regional disparities persist. Most notably, the report finds that food insecurity remains more prevalent in rural communities and disproportionately affects women. The key question facing governments and development organizations, then, is how to improve food security in those communities and accelerate progress toward eliminating hunger.

Four priorities stand out. First, enhancing food security in rural communities requires boosting agricultural productivity on existing farmland in ways that are sustainable and minimize environmental impacts. As growing populations place increasing demands on agricultural systems, simply expanding farmland risks accelerating deforestation and environmental degradation. Producing more on existing farmland is thus essential to meet rising demand without further damaging natural ecosystems.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Putin’s shadow war against Europe is getting more intense
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Hal Brands
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Grueling wars are now the global norm. For years, a brutal conflict has consumed Ukraine. For months, a grinding faceoff has convulsed the Persian Gulf. Now Russia is escalating a different kind of fight: a shadow war of violent, quasi-covert coercion against Europe. The continent, once a paragon of post-Cold War peace, faces a dangerous struggle, just as ambiguous signals from Washington make Moscow harder to deter.

In May, a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Romania, part of a broader uptick in drone incursions into NATO airspace. In July, a Russian missile detonated on Polish soil. German officials just recently blamed Russia for an explosive drone discovered last month at an airport in Leipzig. Attacks on German power plants have not been definitively attributed to Moscow, but suspicions run rampant because the pattern of Russian behavior is clear.

Russia has been waging shadow warfare against Europe for more than a decade. In 2014, Kremlin intelligence agents set off massive explosions at arms depots in the Czech Republic. This campaign intensified after Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine turned into an ugly slog, as the U.S. and Europe compounded Moscow’s miseries by helping Kyiv inflict a ghastly toll on Russian forces.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Tiny technology deepens the geopolitical divide
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Brad Glosserman
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
The driver of global division is, or will soon be, technology.

Adoption of particular technologies — reflected to some degree in brands, but more importantly standards — will determine with which side a country aligns itself. Six years ago, experts warned of a digital iron curtain descending; my metaphor is barbells — two spheres of economic activity, the connections between them increasingly slim.

We got a glimpse of that future when the United States demanded that its allies and trusted partners refuse to put Huawei’s 5G equipment in their national telecommunications stack. U.S. administrations warned that the company was an extension of the Chinese Communist Party, either a willing accomplice or unable to resist the commands of the Beijing government. One way or another, the company would tap or steal the information traversing its networks or sabotage the organizations using them.

https://www.scmp.com/business/companies/.title: China needs monkeys: lab animal shortage could hinder biotech growth
https://www.scmp.com/business/companies/.author: Themis Qi
https://www.scmp.com/business/companies/.text:
As fundraising and out-licensing deals in China grow, so does demand for monkeys and other primates for testing

China’s biotechnology market has “significantly” driven up the demand for primate experimental models as the market recovers, tightening the supply of laboratory monkeys, according to a leading biotech firm.

Primate experiments typically use monkeys and other non-human species to test the safety and efficacy of a drug under development before clinical trials on humans.

Over US$110 billion worth of Chinese-developed drug candidates were traded in 81 out-licensing deals in the first half of the year, equivalent to 80 per cent of the full-year value in 2025, data from China’s National Medical Products Administration showed.

Joinn added that the price increase resulted from the tightened supply of non-human primates for experimental use in China, as their breeding rate has remained relatively stable.

Shanghai Medicilon, another global contract research organisation, also told investors in July that the overall supply of lab monkeys had contracted amid the biotech industry’s recent recovery.

The shortfall of lab monkeys in China was projected to range between 15,000 and 20,000 from 2026 to 2028, according to a note by Zheshang Securities in March.

In the first half of the year, Joinn reported a net profit of 747.5 million yuan, an 11-fold growth year on year, primarily citing the paper gains of “biological assets”.

Joinn said it owned over 20,000 non-human primates used for breeding and non-clinical research as of December 2025. In its interim results report, the firm said its inventory grew steadily from January to June, though did not divulge specific figures.

In 2022, Joinn spent 1.8 billion yuan to acquire two companies in China’s southwest with a combined inventory of nearly 20,000 non-human primates.

WuXi AppTec, another Chinese biotech giant, acquired a Suzhou-based company for about 804 million yuan, with one of its acquired entities holding about 20,000 macaques.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.title: Trump slams Australia’s social media crackdown as ‘extortion’
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.author: SCMP’s Asia desk
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.text:
The White House warns Australia over its proposed algorithm opt-out bill, as Anthony Albanese defends national sovereignty

US President Donald Trump has condemned Australia’s recent moves to clamp down on social media – predominantly run by American tech companies – as “a form of extortion”, hinting at more threats to come.

“President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector,” White House economics spokesman Kush Desai said on Tuesday night, as reported by news.com.au.

“The administration remains committed to raising these issues with our trading partners.”

Under the new “My Feed, My Way” initiative announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday, Australians would have the option to opt out of powerful social media algorithms. Draft legislation introducing a mandatory “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to parliament this week.

“We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC on Monday.

“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” added Wells, who led Australia’s world-first social media ban for children under 16. “Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards.”

On Wednesday, Wells told News24 Australia that US officials had not contacted her office over the proposed law, and ‌rejected the suggestion that her government’s social media reforms amounted to “extortion”.

If passed, the law requires firms including Meta Platforms, Google and TikTok to protect younger users from damaging material – such as content promoting harmful behaviour or causing serious mental distress – while offering users over 16 control over their social media curation.

“We’ll require social media platforms provide user empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 genuine and enduring choice about what they see in their feeds,” Albanese said, according to news.com.au.

“We have an opportunity to shape technology for the better rather than let it shape us. That is what our reforms are all about.”

Under the proposal, social media platforms will be required to send notifications giving users a choice over their default feed, according to US public broadcaster NPR. Users can opt to have personalised content recommended by an algorithm or a chronological feed showing only posts from people they follow.

Digital services, including online games, apps and AI chatbots, will also be required to ensure children are shielded from design features promoting harmful behaviours such as addiction.

Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to A$100 million (US$65 million), according to Wells.

However, a media analyst has questioned whether users will take advantage of the option.

“The government has handed Australians a switch. Whether anyone flips it is another matter,” Lisa Harrison, a lecturer in communication and media at Flinders University, told Agence France-Presse, citing a 2025 survey across six countries where only one in five people said they would switch off personalised recommendations.

“The algorithm is good at its job, and the minority who do opt out will find a feed of friends and creators feels quieter than the one they left,” Harrison said.

The move is the latest in Canberra’s broader campaign against big tech firms. Last month, Australia passed the News Bargaining Incentive to compel major digital platforms to fund local journalism – a measure the White House similarly called extortion.

The National Foreign Trade Council, a US business association, raised concerns last week after the Australian Tax Office reclassified cloud computing and streaming revenue as royalties, subjecting them to higher tax rates.

“Australia has become more and more aggressive on the tax front, and a less and less hospitable environment for investment across the board,” Anne Gordon, the council’s vice-president for international tax policy, told The Sydney Morning Herald.

Trump and Albanese are set to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York later this month.

Asked if he expected pushback from the US president, Albanese said: “We’re a sovereign nation; we decide our policies based upon the Australian national interest. But my relationship with the US president is indeed very good, and I look forward to seeing President Trump in New York in a couple of weeks’ time.”

Douglas Head has been formally designated a Conservation Area by the Manx government.

Douglas City Council said it "welcomed" the move, recognising the headland's "significant historical, architectural and cultural importance".

It follows years of campaigning by local historians and two public consultations, the most recent of which found 92% support for the move.

While the designation does not prevent all development on the headland, it does restrict the kind of changes owners to property within the boundary can make without first obtaining planning permission.

This includes for things like replacing windows or altering roofs.

Applications consider whether any alterations would preserve or enhance the area's character.

The Isle of Man's Area Plan says applications within the boundary "will generally not be supported."

Douglas Head already has eight registered buildings, more than almost anywhere else on the island outside of central Douglas.

They include the Great Union Camera Obscura (1892), Douglas Lighthouse, the Harbour Swing Bridge Tower and its original 1895 machinery, and Harold Tower.

Read more stories from the Isle of Man on the BBC, watch BBC North West Tonight on BBC iPlayer and follow BBC Isle of Man on Facebook and X.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k.title: 'Adrenaline got us through New Forest wildfire'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k.text:
"It was almost apocalyptic," recalls retained firefighter Matt O'Hare, as he describes the scene that greeted him at the devastating wildfire in the New Forest.

Fire spread from a blazing van on the A31 on 9 August, destroying ancient oak and beech trees, rare heathland and wildlife across an area of more than 100 hectares.

O'Hare, 27, was sent with crewmates from Fordingbridge Fire Station.

"As we went through the New Forest, we could see the huge smoke plume and we thought, 'This is big'," he said.

"It was really weird. You had all the cars that had been stopped on the A31 parked up either side, people in the road.

"Just trying to get through to the incident was our first challenge."

As the wind rapidly swept the flames across the forest, O'Hare and his colleagues went towards the fire.

"At that time, we were going, 'How on earth are we going to stop this?' But we were told where to go by senior officers and you just sort of deal with the area that you are in as best as you can," he said.

A major incident was declared, and fire crews from neighbouring counties and beyond helped tackle the fire.

About 130 firefighters were on the scene of the fire at the peak of the incident, working in heatwave conditions.

It would be two weeks before the last crews were able to leave the scene.

Like many retained firefighters, O'Hare has another job that he needed to keep up alongside his firefighting duties.

"I was doing 10-to-12-hour shifts on the A31, then coming home early in the morning and working from 08:00 to 18:00 at my manufacturing job.

"But everyone does it because they love it."

Watch manager at Fordingbridge Fire Station Shaun Lincoln, 59, said it was the largest fire he had been to in 21 years as a firefighter.

"It was off the scale, very, very tiring. I think adrenaline keeps you going and community spirit," he said.

"We live in the New Forest, it's quite personal to us, we wanted to get there and do our bit."

Thank you cards are displayed on the front door of Fordingbridge Fire Station.

Lincoln said all the crew had been touched by the gratitude shown by local people, who clapped as they returned from fighting the fire.

"There were hampers, cakes and hydration drinks. It was really, really nice, a little bit of fuel for the guys coming back from a long shift," he said.

"I am really, really proud. Everyone worked their socks off, day in, day out. The guys just didn't stop from day one to the end."

You can follow BBC Hampshire & Isle of Wight on Facebook, X (Twitter), or Instagram.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k.summary: Fire spread from a blazing van on the A31 on 9 August, destroying ancient oak and beech trees. Firefighters from neighbouring counties and beyond helped tackle the fire. About 130 firefighters were on the scene at the peak of the fire at the time.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w4.title: Nature GCSE backers want more 'greenlightenment'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w4.text:
Naturalist Steve Backshall and Lost Gardens of Heligan co-founder Sir Tim Smit have called for more "greenlightenment" to put nature education at the heart of school curriculums.

It comes as the government has been consulting on a new natural history GCSE, which Sir Tim said was a "seismic moment for British education", adding "a deep understanding of the natural world is fundamental to humanity's future".

Backshall, who hosted the Wild Heligan experience to excite young people about wildlife, said: "I see every day how nature revitalises, restores and fills people with joy."

A survey by Heligan of 1,004 parent and child groups across England found 55% of children had never climbed a tree.

Backshall said: "We can get so much from the wild world, but now more than ever the wild world needs us.

"Young people who are engaged with nature will be happier, healthier and more likely to take on our planet's problems."

Sir Tim said: "It is our responsibility to equip the next generation with the tools to protect nature so it doesn't become history."

He added children had not lost their interest in nature but had lost opportunities to experience it.

The survey found "ordinary contact with nature" was unfamiliar to many children and 61% of children had never collected a conker or camped in a tent.

The research also found 34% of children they asked said they would definitely choose the proposed natural history GCSE if their school offered it, with another 41% saying they probably would.

The government said, if brought in, the GCSE would "ensure that children are equipped with the highly sought after skills for the workforce of a changing world" and could help reduce the number of number of young people not in education, employment or training.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyk.title: Cowboy builder tore my home apart and disappeared off the face of the earth with £14k
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyk.text:
A rogue builder tore Sheri Ingram's home apart and "disappeared off the face of the earth" with £14,000.

In February, Lee Slocombe, from Swansea, was jailed for six years after defrauding nine victims of £400,000 - with this his latest conviction in a decade of offending.

The UK government announced in August plans to give people greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a database of trusted traders.

Ingram, from Cardiff, welcomed it, but questioned where the incentive would be for tradespeople to sign up to the voluntary scheme.

Another couple who were "scarred for life" by a rogue trader who left them £30,000 out of pocket said it would give more confidence to homeowners.

"He (Slocombe) was recommended to us by a serving police officer who my ex knew," Ingram said.

"So why on earth would we have not trusted him?"

Slocombe's offending covered a period of 11 years, and he even targeted nine people to carry out work on their homes when on bail using a false name.

It began in 2015 after Ingram and her now ex-partner bought a house in Aberbeeg, Blaenau Gwent, which they planned to renovate and move into.

The then 21-year-old appointed Slocombe to build an extension and make the ground floor of the home open plan.

She admitted they were not experts in building work, and while it looked like lots was going on, Slocombe kept finding problems and asking for more cash to solve them.

For the first six weeks, he was "very responsive", Ingram said he then "disappeared off the face of the earth" with £14,000.

Her ex-partner eventually managed to get hold of him, but he insinuated all the money was gone.

Slocombe suggested he was expecting a payout from an injury that he suffered on another building job, and would get the cash back and continue with the work.

But that never happened.

The home was later restored by Channel 5 programme Cowboy Builders - aimed at helping families who have been exploited by them.

In February, Slocombe, then 33, of Delhi Street, Swansea, was jailed for six years after carrying out dangerous building work at properties in Cardiff, Bridgend and Swansea.

The £400,000 fraud cost his nine victims more than £547,000 in total when adding costs for rectifying his dangerous work, according to Cardiff council.

He had pleaded guilty to participating in a fraudulent business between March 2021 and May 2023, with one charge against him and one against his company, LSP Developments.

Slocombe was on Crown Court bail when these offences were committed.

It was the third time he had been given a prison sentence for offending that dated back to 2015.

That year, he was jailed for 43 months for three offences of fraud, and in 2023 he received a sentence of five years and five months after defrauding seven families of £150,000.

Cardiff Crown Court heard in February that Slocombe had called himself Lee Lewis to avoid his previous convictions being discovered, and on two occasions took a fake and unqualified gas engineer to properties, leaving them in a "potentially lethal state".

He was also made subject to a Criminal Behaviour Order, banning him from carrying out building, maintenance or gardening work in the UK for life, and disqualified from being a company director until 2031.

Ingram said the plans were a "good step in the right direction" as "the power imbalance is just so big" between people looking to renovate their homes and builders.

"There needs to be better protections in place, there has to be," she added.

"I would expect the government to take accountability if the project did go wrong if I used the database.

"I don't think traders would sign up and the reality is they don't need to."

The UK government plans to create greater protections for people renovating their homes against "cowboy builders", through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards.

Traders signing up to the scheme will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

He added they gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and hoped to put "the cowboys out of business".

The UK government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months had experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority, suggesting customers lost more than £10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

Barry and Shelley Sawkins, from Flintshire, lost more than £30,000 to rogue builder Christian Williams, who left their new extension unfinished, with water pouring into their home.

Williams, 54, is currently serving a two-year prison sentence after admitting theft and three counts of fraud by false representation involving four families.

In a Proceeds of Crime Act hearing in June, Mold Crown Court heard Williams, trading as Chris Williams Construction, benefitted to the tune of £163,051.70 from his offending, but his assets meant he could only pay back £1.

The extension remains unfinished three years after work began in 2023, and Shelley said this makes it hard for the couple to love their home.

"We're in a place now where we are stuck," she added.

"It has scarred us for life really."

They hope to eventually move to St Athan, Vale of Glamorgan, to be closer to their daughter once the work is complete.

"I really do respect him [Andy Burnham]. I like his approach. He speaks from the ground up," Shelley said.

"I think the government plans would help give people more confidence."

The Federation of Master Builders also raised concerns over the voluntary nature of the scheme.

Chief executive Brian Berry said: "The prime minister's push to crack down on rogue builders is a great move for the industry.

"However, it is a real concern that this is just another voluntary programme without regulation behind it."

Minister for the future of work Kate Dearden was questioned on BBC Breakfast about the scheme and said: "We want to act quickly and get support to people as soon as possible.

"Of course if it was compulsory, that would take a little bit more time for us to develop and to work to.

"However, we are going to be watching this really closely in terms of the uptake and the impact that it has in the sector."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyk.summary: UK government plans to give people greater protections against "cowboy builders" Lee Slocombe, from Swansea, jailed for six years for defrauding nine victims of £400,000. Federation of Master Builders also raised concerns over voluntary scheme.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: 'We were target of sinister heating oil theft and want to warn others'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
The head of a rural community charity has warned of the growing risk of home heating oil theft after her own organisation fell victim to thieves.

Kate Clifford, director of the Rural Community Network (RCN), arrived at the charity's offices one morning to find the heat was not working.

"We initially thought there must be a leak, but then we could see damage to the tank and knew something was seriously wrong," she said.

The charity had only recently filled its tank with more than 1,000 litres of oil which police later confirmed had been stolen.

Clifford said: "The tank at our offices isn't easily accessible, and somebody must have known we had recently filled up, so the worrying thing was it felt very premediated, and that felt quite sinister.

"We are a charity, so we have to be very careful with our funds, so to lose this was a huge expense to us and then we had to spend money on extra security measures."

The theft at the charity's Cookstown offices happened in 2024, but the charity is speaking out as new figures show there have been 600 reports of oil and fuel thefts in Northern Ireland since 2021.

Home heating oil is a key energy source for heating and hot water in the majority of households across Northern Ireland.

The Consumer Council for Northern Ireland said its tends to get more reports of oil thefts during an energy crisis when the price of oil is often pushed up because of geopolitics and global events.

Police figures show that oil thefts in Northern Ireland peaked around Russia's invasion of Ukraine and have been fluctuating ever since.

So far this year, there has been a small increase in oil and fuels thefts in the first six months of 2026, which saw oil prices impacted by the US-Israel war with Iran.

From January to June, there were 45 oil thefts in Northern Ireland compared to 59 during the whole of last year.

In March, BBC News NI spoke to a family from Limavady who had to move out of their home after heating oil thieves struck and turned the property into a "massive biohazard".

"In March 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, 500 litres peaked to around £663 and 900 litres peaked to around £1,182," said Raymond Gormley, head of energy policy at the Consumer Council.

"This time period corresponded with the highest number of oil thefts, with the police figures showing 37 in a single month.

"This year geopolitics in the middle east are once again affecting things and we've had contacts from families impacted by thefts, so it's definitely something people need to be aware of."

Gormley said there are a number of steps that people can take to improve security around their heating oil.

"Install a lock or alarm on your oil tank and fit hardened flexible casings to any visible fuel hoses so that they are harder to cut.

"Another thing people can do is keep your garden or drive gates closed and securely locked as well as installing security lighting which can warn you or alert a neighbour of an intruder."

In May, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) published a social media post warning the public of the dangers of oil thefts in Mid-Ulster following a number of incidents in the Moneymore area.

In July, the Consumer Council reported that the average cost of 500 litres of home heating oil jumped from £346.59 to £445.37 in the space of three weeks – an increase of £98.78 (29%).

The organisation said the price rise was in response to the recent escalation in fighting between the US and Iran.

At the beginning of September the average cost of 500 litres of oil in Northern Ireland had risen to £491.00.

Almost two-thirds of homes (62.5%) in Northern Ireland use oil for heating, the highest proportion among UK nations.

In rural parts of the country, the dependency on home heating oil rises to about 80%.

Clifford believes home heating oil theft highlights a wider inequality facing rural Northern Ireland.

"While urban households often have access to gas networks and a choice of energy suppliers many rural households depend on a single fuel source stored outside their homes," she said.

"This creates a unique vulnerability to crime that disproportionately affects rural residents, particularly older people, low-income households, and farms."

"Rural communities are often at their strongest when neighbours look out for one another, so if you notice suspicious activity, unfamiliar vehicles repeatedly visiting an area, or anyone behaving unusually around fuel tanks, report it to the PSNI."

A spokesperson for the PSNI said fuel tanks can often be seen as "easy pickings" for thieves.

"By taking precautions you can protect your oil – lock and disguise your tank, fit a 'level Gauge' with audible alarm and consider installing security lighting and CCTV."

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.title: U.S. military says it destroyed 5 Iranian oil tankers after attacks on Navy warship
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.text:
A motorboat travels past commercial vessels anchored amid haze in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war.

Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. Jordan's military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom's military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer.

The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.

The U.S. forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, "if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet." Iran later said it planned to announce a new "exclusion zone" near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.

"Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.

Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact to the global economy.

"There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem," he said on social media. "Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control."

U.S. Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. "The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it said in a statement.

It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandoned ship before the attacks.

Iranian state television also reported the U.S. strikes, saying U.S. forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.

An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the U.S. military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.

A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country's economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.

Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.

Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.

“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”

“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.

Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.

Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.

“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”

Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.

A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.

The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.

“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.

The trial is expected to run until the end of September.

Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.summary: Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad. The men were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft. The trial is expected to run until the end of September.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.title: Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text:
A continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline, report suggests

Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline.

The report, based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but disillusioned public.

It found that 68% of respondents spoke about Europe in terms of a “general deterioration or loss of normality”, compared with just 12% who said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal”.

Many recognised the major challenges facing Europe, including war (43%), economic pressures (33%) and the need for greater international autonomy (29%). But 74% said Europe was not dealing well with them, and 56% believed its future was “in danger”.

The problem is not lack of ambition: an overwhelming 73% of respondents harbour a strong European vision of unity and political integration (35%), peace and security (28%) or prosperity (19%), while only 13% hope for “less Europe” or EU dissolution.

For many, said the study’s author, Pawel Zerka, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, the problem was “not that they’ve stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it’s achievable”.

The result, Zerka added, was an “imagination gap. People can picture the kind of Europe they want, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be. These are matters of policy, not just communication.”

A week before the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is due to deliver her annual “state of the union” address in Brussels, Zerka said the evidence suggested the bloc needed “fewer grand promises” and more “proof of trajectory”.

The study cites dozens of conversations with Europeans. “I’m regularly relieved I live in Europe. It’s not perfect and some things are going in the wrong direction, but no region in the world is safer, freer and more democratic,” one German said.

However, while he identified the climate crisis and far-right parties as the continent’s greatest challenges, he said they were not being tackled effectively. “Elections focus too much on the here and now, and not enough on the future,” he said.

The respondent said he would like Europe in 20 years’ time to be “free, democratic, sustainable, less indebted, politically further to the left [and] peaceful”. Asked whether he thought that was likely to happen, he said: “No.”

The study classed Europe’s voters in four categories. The Positives (19%) are staunch pro-Europeans who view current crises as a catalyst for a stronger, more integrated union. The Negatives (39%) believe Europe’s best days are behind it.

Almost half of people in France, Germany and Italy – and almost all who voted for radical-right parties such as Germany’s AfD, France’s RN, the Dutch PVV and Reform UK – were Negatives, with 83% speaking of Europe in terms of loss and decline.

The Disconnected (12%) are generally apathetic voters for whom EU integration is distant background noise, and the Uncertain (31%) share pro-European values but doubt the continent’s ability to act decisively, keep citizens safe or uphold its values.

Almost a third (32%) of respondents across all countries surveyed mentioned “Europe’s slowness” in their responses. As one young Polish citizen, born in the 2000s, put it bluntly: “The EU fundamentally discusses a lot, but does nothing.”

The bloc’s failure to stand its ground when confronted by powerful actors was also a recurring theme, mentioned by almost a third (30%) of all respondents, with the EU’s recent tariff concessions to Donald Trump a particularly humiliating symbol.

Zerka said the Uncertain group was key to the future trajectory of Europe. “Leaders tend to preach to the Positives or bow down to the Negatives,” he said, but it “is among the ‘uncertain’ where belief in Europe’s future remains up for grabs.”

Unlike hardened Eurosceptics, Uncertain voters retain a strong emotional attachment to the European project, the report argues, but are alienated by institutional inertia, bureaucratic slowness and perceived geopolitical weakness.

Winning back those doubters would require politicians to demonstrate that collective European action can solve tangible domestic crises, from energy security and defence to climate change and the cost of living crisis, Zerka said.

Just 12% said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal’

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Burnham urged to tackle inequality with policies including wealth tax
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Key thinkers suggest other radical measures in Compass report such as free personal social care and abolishing Lords

Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers.

In the lead-up to the first budget of the chancellor, John Healey, this autumn, the Compass thinktank has collated 70 policy options from 15 leftwing thinkers that they argue would deliver on the prime minister’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.
