Not signed in before? Create an account

Introducing the report, Ending Business as Usual, Michael Jacobs, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, and Neal Lawson, director of Compass and a close friend of Burnham, praise what they call the prime minister’s “invaluable aura of authenticity”.

However, they warn that while he has ambitious plans “there is no guarantee that he will be given any longer to deliver results than his immediate predecessor”. The authors argue that it is “simply not the case that a British government can no longer govern from the left of centre”.

Among the policy proposals, which the organisation states is “a menu of policy options, not a manifesto”, are a £50,000 cap on political donations, the abolition of the House of Lords and an immediate cost of living package.

The plans also include a raft of far-reaching tax policies, including the introduction of a wealth tax on net assets of more than £10m, which would raise about £24bn a year, according to Caitlin Boswell from Tax Justice UK.

Other mooted policy ideas include equalising capital gains tax with income tax, which would raise a further £11.3bn a year – enough “to fund the building of 90,000 new social homes”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued such a move would risk lowering total tax revenue and investment, and lead wealthy individuals to move their money or leave the country.

The essay also calls for what it describes as the “regressive, outdated and unfair” council tax as well as stamp duty to be replaced with a proportional property tax, noting such a move would result in 23% of households – concentrated in London and the south-east – paying more.

“If the new Labour government is serious about rebuilding public confidence and delivering material improvements to people’s lives, it must be prepared to address one of the structural causes of inequality: a tax system that favours wealth over work,” writes Boswell.

Suggested social policy changes in England include introducing free personal social care, paid for by a surcharge on income tax rates for people aged over 40, and a contribution from housing wealth. Sebastian Rees, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argues that personal care needs, such as washing, dressing and eating should be covered by the state with accommodation or ordinary living costs, remaining the responsibility of the individual and their family, a model currently in place in Scotland.

Stating that a 1% surcharge on income tax for the over-40s would raise between £8bn and £9bn, it also argues that care costs could be secured against a property and recovered after sale or death. This would “would allow housing wealth to contribute to the cost of reform without requiring people to sell their home when they first need care,” says Rees. Elsewhere, the report calls for universal free childcare, which it argues would “boost the economy, support children’s development, help families and promote gender equality”.

Chris Hayes, from Common Wealth, calls for government-owned companies to be put in charge of running energy networks, as well as the setting up of regional energy boards, while the director of politics at Green Alliance, Holly Brazier Tope, argues for a climate resilience standard for critical infrastructure.

Michael Jacobs, professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, said Burnham and his chancellor must resist pressure to conform to the “moderation and orthodoxy” that he argues ended the tenures of Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves.

“There are a wealth of alternatives,” he says. “As Burnham knows, the public is disillusioned with politics and angry with their politicians. He does not have long to prove to voters that, when he says he wants to end business as usual, he means it.”
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Compass thinktank collated 70 policy options from 15 leftwing thinkers. They argue they would deliver on PM's promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism. They include a £50,000 cap on political donations, abolition of the House of Lords and immediate cost of living package.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation

N
ot all that long ago, Europe was a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.

Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They were written in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewish émigré whose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.

Now momentum is with the nationalists again. Victory for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in the region of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is not the biggest electoral prize won by a far-right party in Europe in recent years, but it is one of the most shocking because it is Germany. No country had more to learn from history if it wanted to immunise its democracy against extremism. None pursued a more systematic programme of inoculation. The word for it is Vergangenheitsbewältigung – hard to say and tricky to translate, meaning roughly coming to terms with a shameful past.

There is no excuse of ignorance about the AfD’s rise. It is a knowing repudiation of atonement. The party flirts with Nazi imagery and embraces racist definitions of nationhood, seeking to deport Germans whose credentials it sees as biologically improper. It is extreme enough to induce squeamishness in Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (RN). She has spent years carefully cultivating respectability and is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. She doesn’t want to jeopardise her mainstream credentials by affinity with it.

That is less of an impediment across the Atlantic. Elon Musk is an AfD fan, deploying his control of X to boost the party’s campaign messages. Last year, the US vice-president, JD Vance, met Alice Weidel, AfD co-leader, during a visit to Munich. There was no space in his diary for Olaf Scholz, then the German chancellor. Clearly, the AfD meets the criteria for endorsement set out in Donald Trump’s national security strategy, which pledges support for “patriotic resistance” movements committed to halting the “civilisational erasure” of Europe by immigration.

In Britain, Nigel Farage could once have assumed entitlement to that status as an early and enthusiastic cheerleader for Trump. But in the competition for Maga accolades, Reform UK has lost ground to parties and people even further to the right – Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain; ultra-nationalist agitator Tommy Robinson; pretty much anyone who can muster a mob of blackshirts or a passing troll who catches Musk’s eye posting racist conspiracy theories online.

It would be absurd if it wasn’t so effective. “We never fall into the same abyss twice,” writes Éric Vuillard, the French novelist. “But we fall in the same way, in a mixture of ridicule and dread.”

The reach and pungency of the US right, drenched in white supremacism, interferes with Farage’s old strategy of banking far-right support and feinting moderation to make gains in the mainstream. Chasing credibility with fanatical racists in an international digital arena makes it hard to reassure a domestic analogue audience that he should be allowed near Downing Street.

The tension shows in Farage’s attitude to the AfD. He spoke at a rally for it in 2017. Now he describes it as a “mixed bag” of a party, whose cultural stances are “utterly respectable and decent” but whose enthusiasm for dictators is “very difficult”.

Farage has called AfD support for Vladimir Putin “hard to understand”. It can’t be that far beyond comprehension for a man who, in 2014, described the Russian president as the world leader he most admired, albeit “as an operator, not a human being”.

If Farage needs further insight into what might motivate a Kremlin fellow traveller, he could reach out to Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, who is serving a prison sentence for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speeches in the European parliament when he was a Brexit party MEP.

Proximity to the Moscow line is a fairly reliable measure of fanaticism and venality on the spectrum from far-right to even further-right politics in Europe and the US. The same applies on the left, where a credulous appetite for Russian propaganda endures decades after the demise of Soviet ideology.

Thankfully, there is not much of a market in British politics for openly pandering to Putin. That is one reason why Trump is also unpopular, although opinion polls suggest he is viewed more favourably by Reform supporters than the wider public. Farage has stopped boasting of his White House connections, perhaps because they have dried up, or maybe because sycophantic flapping around a foreign tyrant, even an American one, doesn’t project strength in a wannabe prime minister.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It is striking how little the Reform leader has to say about the rest of the world and Britain’s place in it. The topic was hardly mentioned at the party’s annual conference last week.

There was a theatrical appearance by Jordan Bardella, the young Le Pen protege and likely prime minister if she wins the presidency. He signed a legally meaningless “deal” with Farage on stopping small-boat traffic across the Channel and was immediately criticised back home for selling out to the UK. The likelihood of a French far-right government taking in more migrants as a policy favour to the UK is close to zero. Having xenophobic nationalists setting the agenda in Paris and London wouldn’t make relations easier, no matter what ideological amity they now claim.

As the architect of Brexit, Farage is one of the most consequential politicians of his generation, but he can’t plausibly claim it as an achievement, even when addressing an auditorium of loyal fans. They know it has failed as well as everyone else.

Farage probably misses the simplicity of his old crusade against Brussels. He might envy nationalist counterparts on the continent, who get to rail against liberal Europeanism while enjoying the economic and strategic privileges afforded by EU membership. They don’t have to explain why it’s so cold on the outside. They play the Eurosceptic game, mobilising the same resentments, targeting the same scapegoats, but modifying the demands in recognition that Farage’s victory was pyrrhic. It doesn’t pay to actually leave. The ambition is to capture the European project, not destroy it, although it amounts to the same thing if the transformation happens through connivance with Maga ideology and Kremlin money.

This doesn’t have to be Europe’s destiny. Nationalists do not form a monolithic bloc. The essence of their creed militates against cross-border partnership. Their egos generate more rivalries than alliances. Their selfishness sabotages deals. Countervailing forces can be mustered. There is no law of history that says a height of liberal optimism must be followed by an equivalent fall into chaos. The “binding power of tolerance and conciliation” was not defeated in the 20th century and it won’t be suffocated in this one either. We see the abyss. We can pass without plunging to the bottom.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: ‘It’s like a death sentence’ says British widow facing deportation from Sweden
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Lisa O’Carroll in Värmland
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Joyce Thomas, 78, describes her ‘nightmare’ hours before the deadline for her removal from country

A 78-year-old British widow facing deportation over from Sweden over Brexit has said she feels she is facing a “death sentence” just hours before she was due to be removed from the country.

“I just want this nightmare to go away before I die,” says Joyce Thomas. “It is dragging me down. I am really not the same person I was. This has taken years. I just feel sick,” she adds as she packs her bags.

Thomas, a retired nurse, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years, was given four weeks to leave the country in August, separating her from her son, grandchildren, large network of friends, her church and her husband’s grave.

Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit.

Her subsequent application to stay in the country in 2023 missed the official deadline but she said her husband who looked after all the household administration, had previously been told there was nothing the couple needed to do after Brexit.

She was first told to leave the country in November and after an appeal received the news in August that the administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that she could not stay.

The migration agency says that simply not knowing she had to apply to stay by the cutoff date at the end of 2021 was not a “reasonable ground” for staying in the country.

So Thomas had little choice on Monday: she got up at 6am to thoroughly clean her flat, cook for supporters that night, and pack her bags for the UK.

Then, late on Monday evening, she was advised that she could stay pending a late application by a lawyer for a review of the removal order.

However, her plight remains the same with the threat of a deportation merely in abeyance.

“I am very stressed,” she says kneeling over two suitcases beside Tia, a collie lent to her for company in the past few weeks by a friend.

“I just want this nightmare to go before I die. I need a peaceful life at my time of life. This is what I want. I just want to get up and be normal,” says Thomas.

Thomas is one of hundreds, potentially thousands of Britons who have either been told to leave voluntarily or removed forcibly through deportation since Brexit.

Last week the migration agency confirmed it had already deported 458 including one 34-year-old who had been in the country since he was 10. Another British businessman was taken into detention last week in Stockholm to be deported.

“I just wish one of those people [in the authorities] had parents in my situation. I think they would think twice because it is the worst think they can do to a human being,” says Thomas.

She appealed to the European Commission and the Swedish government to intervene not just for her but for all the British citizens who have simply made “a mistake” because they did not know Sweden required a formal application to remain after Brexit.

“Please, please can you hear us. We have done nothing wrong. We are not criminals,” she says. “People here are suffering mentally, physically.

“It is cruel. It is inhumane. They must read the papers to know that I am really low. I just feel sick.”

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

No British minister has said anything about Britons being deported from Sweden since the controversy erupted, apart from the former business secretary Peter Kyle who appealed to the Swedish government on behalf of Thomas’s son, who lives in the constituency next to his.

Her local MP, Håkan Svenneling, raised her case in the Swedish parliament, claiming the controversy is damaging relations between the EU and the UK, while the opposition Centre party has vowed to offer a repreive to Britons with new laws if it gets into power after Sunday’s general election.

She says she has been a brilliant “actor” and gives people the impression she is coping but that is far from the truth.

“This waiting month by month, year by year is like a death sentence. That is how I feel because I am not getting a clear answer [about my future] and I am in limbo all the time.

“At the start of this I was ready to take my life because I was so depressed. I am coping now with a lot of help from good people but it is still hard. Inside I am not coping at all.”

Sweden is among 13 countries, along with the UK, that opted for a “constitutive” system requiring citizens to formally apply to remain in the country. Others, like Spain, opted for a less onerous “declaratory” system requiring registration in the country, something many Britons would already have done at their town hall.

But campaigners at Brits in Sweden say countless British citizens were either given no information or incorrect information about what to do after Brexit by the authorities.

“All I did was make a mistake, a mistake,” says Thomas. “Even with a parking fine they give you notice if you have not paid the fine; why didn’t they tell us we had to apply, and send us a reminder? We got nothing, never mind a reminder.”

The migration agency has said it had no mandate to contact British citizens on the population register to tell them what to do.

Under the withdrawal agreement late applications for permits to remain resident after Brexit were permitted as long as there were “reasonable grounds”.

On Friday the Swedish migration agency told the Guardian it had “no indication” that Sweden had in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. “The Swedish migration agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions,” it said.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Joyce Thomas, 78, was told to leave Sweden in August and was told she could not stay. She has been told she must leave voluntarily or removed forcibly through deportation. Swedish migration agency says it has no mandate to contact British citizens.

Apple might recycle the name from Microsoft’s dual-screen device for its first folding iPhone.

Apple might recycle the name from Microsoft’s dual-screen device for its first folding iPhone.

With only a few hours left until the first iPhone launch event since John Ternus took over as the CEO of Apple, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman says the name of the company’s long-rumored folding phone is the iPhone Duo. The midnight report suggests it will have a price starting at $2,000 for a model with 256GB of storage, shipping starting as soon as October in two colors: white and dark blue.

So far, the rumored foldable has been mostly referred to as the iPhone Ultra, while the Duo name would raise a title that Google used for one of its many ill-fated attempts at messaging and chat, and that Microsoft already applied to its own foldable devices, with the Surface Duo and Surface Duo 2.

Meanwhile, its starting price could make it more expensive than the cheapest versions of Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 which start at $1,899, but lower than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s $2,099.99 price.

As the rumors have said, it’s expected to be able to run side-by-side iPhone apps, handle iPad-like multitasking, and support using the Apple Pencil as a stylus. We should know the official details soon, check back here at 1PM ET / 10AM PT for all of the updates as they’re revealed.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/fx-curre.title: G10’s ‘surprise’ currency star could stumble as peers hike interest rates
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/fx-curre.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/fx-curre.text:
The British pound has gained against many of its peers in the year to date, though strength from earlier has begun to fade.

Traders thought the Bank of England may be pushed to hike interest rates in response to an inflationary shock from the Iran war, but the central bank is now seen as more dovish than those in the euro area and the U.S.

Sterling faces a further test from the October budget which will be closely watched for its impact on the U.K.’s growth trajectory, debt levels and borrowing costs.

The British pound has largely shrugged off another change of government and geopolitical shocks to outperform many of its peers this year, but the currency’s recent weakness could be set to deepen.

Sterling has gained around 1.6% against the euro
 year-to-date, adding 2.8% against the Swiss franc
, 4.9% against the Swedish krona
 and 1% against the Canadian dollar
.

It is near-flat against the U.S. dollar
 over the same period and down 1.3% against the Japanese yen
.

The resignation of Prime Minister Keir Starmer on July 20 left Britain facing its seventh leader in 10 years, with markets watching closely whether a new administration would hold to the “fiscal rules” repeatedly emphasized by former Finance Minister Rachel Reeves.

U.K. borrowing costs have risen under Starmer’s quickly appointed successor Andy Burnham, also of the center-left Labour Party, but that has occurred in lockstep with a global government bond sell-off.

Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at financial services firm Ebury, said that a “clean and orderly transition of power” had “removed a potential banana skin and eased the perceived political risk premium attached to the pound.”

In a Friday note, Ryan said sterling had been “the surprise outperformer” among the G10 group of wealthy nations over the past three months, tying this to an unexpectedly resilient U.K. economy.

Gross domestic product grew by 0.4% in the second quarter, following 0.6% expansion in the first quarter — one of the strongest performances among advanced economies. Sunny weather and excitement around the FIFA World Cup boosted consumer spending, while business activity remained surprisingly resilient despite the volatile geopolitical backdrop.

The pound also drew support at the start of the Iran conflict in April on outsized market expectations for a monetary policy response to inflation fears from the Bank of England, Jane Foley, senior FX strategist at Rabobank, told CNBC.

The U.K. is highly vulnerable to higher oil and gas costs, both of which have spiked this year, helping push headline inflation near 3%.

Despite the resurgence of price pressures, the Bank of England has held its key interest rate at 3.75% throughout this year.

Current market pricing suggests low odds of a rate hike at its September meeting. In contrast, there are high expectations for a hike by the European Central Bank on Wednesday and, increasingly, the Federal Reserve later this month.

Central bank rate hikes typically boost their home currency.

Dovish messaging by the BOE on Sept. 17 would “further expose the pound” just before markets get anxious for the first annual budget announcement of Burnham’s administration on Oct. 28, Foley of Rabobank noted.

New U.K. Finance Minister John Healey said in a Monday speech that he would remain committed to fiscal discipline, while targeting a more even distribution of economic growth around the country — in contrast to the concentration of growth in powerhouse London.

JP Morgan U.K. economist Allan Monks said his remarks suggested a cautious approach to tax and spending changes given the backdrop of higher borrowing costs. The budget is likely to retain a focus on devolution, greater public control of public services and more private sector partnerships, but contain little to change the macro outlook, Monks said in a note Monday.

Ebury’s Matthew Ryan said the budget contained a high level of political risk, and was likely to contain “a combination of higher ancillary tax rates and an increase in debt issuance in order to fund Burnham’s spending ambitions.”

These could include changes to taxes on property purchases and local council duties, an introduction of a “mansion tax” and tighter pension and personal investment account relief, he said, adding that markets would be jumpy over anything that looked likely to dampen growth and squeeze the private sector, while simultaneously requiring more borrowing.

The British pound has largely shrugged off another change of government and geopolitical shocks to outperform many of its peers this year

The highlights this week: China is making ground on Taiwan in the region, Prabowo swings by Russia again, and Thailand sends mixed messages about AI.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: China is making ground on Taiwan in the region, Prabowo swings by Russia again, and Thailand sends mixed messages about AI.

A Shift in Stance on Taiwan

China is making ground on Taiwan in Southeast Asia.

The issue swam into view last month. First, the Indonesian navy performed a joint exercise with the Chinese navy off the east coast of Taiwan—which it then hastily downplayed.

A few days later, on Aug. 16, Al Jazeera aired an interview with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, in which he made comments suggesting sympathy with China taking military action against Taiwan.

“I always take Malaysia as an example. If one province decides to break away, do we use force? I think I will protect the sanctity and unity of the nation,” Anwar said when asked if he would condemn China using force against Taiwan.

Anwar subsequently walked back these comments, emphasizing that a peaceful approach was best.

However, while his comments were unusually strong, they reflect a slow drift from Malaysia toward Beijing’s line on the matter.

Just compare Malaysia and China’s joint statements past and present. One in 2014 affirmed that “Taiwan is an inseparable part of China” but also pointedly mentioned support for “peaceful reunification.” But in 2024 and again in 2025, there was no specific mention of peace.

Other countries have also dropped mentions of peace. Joint statements with Cambodia included it last in 2019 but not since 2022.

Thailand has also subtly shifted its position. In 2023, statements simply recognized “Taiwan as an inalienable part of China.” In 2025, new language appeared declaring that Thailand would not “support any call for the independence of Taiwan,” and in 2026, it “firmly supported peaceful reunification.”

The Philippines, while keeping to the “one China” policy, has usually taken a stiffer line on potential force against Taiwan. This reflects its closeness to the United States and its own strong stance against China in the South China Sea. However, this year has seen President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. soften somewhat.

Taiwan has attempted to bolster its position. In 2016, it launched the New Southbound policy, aimed at deepening diplomatic ties with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and India.

The ideological resonance of democracy can also cultivate sympathies in the region. From 2020 to 2021, citizens of Thailand, Myanmar, Taiwan, and Hong Kong expressed solidarity with one another in the face of authoritarian pressure from China and domestic governments.

Taiwan also sometimes pushes back. In July, Cambodia was removed from Taiwan’s visa-privilege programs, which all other ASEAN members are part of, because of its repeated “inappropriate statements denigrating Taiwan’s sovereignty.”

Still, overall, the various diplomatic moves toward China’s position in the region show Taiwan has lost ground.

Do these shifts in wording, stray comments, and ill-judged exercises add up to anything substantive though?

Some might argue no. Whatever Anwar says, all Southeast Asian nations are acutely aware that an invasion of Taiwan would be, at best, an economic catastrophe for the region. At worst, it could suck in the United States, turning the area into a charnel house—and that’s before we even consider nuclear risk.

Furthermore, most Southeast Asian countries continue to maintain strong relations with Taiwan, covering trade, investment, and migration of Southeast Asian workers. So long as these beneficial ties persist, Southeast Asian countries are unlikely to take actions such as blocking flights carrying Taiwan’s president or denying Taiwanese citizens entry to their countries, as some African countries have done.

However, it is undeniable that China clearly sees such shifts as valuable and puts a lot of effort into achieving them. As analyst Aniello Iannone rightly pointed out, China will be quoting Anwar’s statements and citing Indonesia’s actions as precedents.

The shift underscores that with China rising and the United States erratic, a number of countries in Southeast Asia are recalibrating their approach along the edges.

Russia again. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto visited Russia last week, his fourth visit to Russia since he assumed office in October 2024 and his second this year after dropping by in April.

It seems this is one of his favorite countries to visit—only France and the United Arab Emirates have also received four visits, and only one country, Malaysia, has had five. Russia maybe gets another half-point as Prabowo also met President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Beijing in September 2025.

So, what does Prabowo have to show for this concerted shuttle diplomacy?

In December 2025, Indonesia inked a free trade deal with the Eurasian Economic Union—a grouping consisting of Russia, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan.

But this time around, not much new was announced. Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Russia, on Sept. 3, Prabowo declared, “For Eurasian businesses, Indonesia is a natural entry point to ASEAN.” Concrete results, though, were thin on the ground—still, Prabowo talked up potential cooperation on energy for both oil and gas and nuclear.

On Moscow’s side, a warm relationship with Jakarta, even if results are for now a little thin, is good to have. Since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine torched relations with Europe, Russia has worked hard to strengthen diplomatic ties in other parts of the world, including Southeast Asia.

Yes to AI, no to data centers. On Friday, Thailand announced that it was pausing 166 data center projects, more than 45 of which were already under construction.

The government has stressed that this is a temporary measure while it sorts out regulations for issues such as data centers’ use of water and power and where they can be built. This fits into a regionwide trend where citizens of countries across Southeast Asia have, as in the United States, grown skeptical of the benefits of having data centers in their backyards.

However, the stance is slightly at odds with the Thai government’s enthusiastic embrace of artificial intelligence in other areas. On Aug. 31, it launched the TH-AI Passport, which offers free access to a suite of AI tools for up to 5 million Thais. Uptake seems to have been limited, though, with only 1.5 million people signed up and around 110,000 active users. The suite of tools aren’t anything special, either.

One area Thailand has done well with in AI is investments and exports. In the first half of 2026, Thailand attracted 886 billion baht (about $27 billion) related to AI and data centers. Electronics exports have also boomed.

Arrests, bail, and heart attacks. It was a week of dramatic arrests in the Philippines. First came Friday’s arrest order of Vice President Sara Duterte on charges of having threatened to have the president and his wife assassinated, something she is also currently being impeached for.

She posted bail on Saturday, which she said was necessary for her personal safety.

“I have no trust in the police. I have no trust in the courts. I do not feel safe at all,” Duterte told media as she left court. She added that “if I die tonight,” the police ‌would “wash their hands and call it an accident.” She also accused Marcos of harassment.

Then on Monday, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin of Marcos, was charged with plunder over his role in the sprawling flood corruption scandal that has consumed Philippine politics. He is personally accused of the misappropriation of 7.4 billion pesos (about $118 million).

Reportedly, when he learned of this, Romualdez suffered a “cardiovascular event” and was taken to a private hospital in Manila. On Monday, he was arrested in his hospital bed.

Meanwhile, the jobless rate in the Philippines has hit a four-year high.

A satellite view of the Anak Krakatoa volcano in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait on July 15.GALLO IMAGES/ORBITAL HORIZON/COPERNICUS SENTINEL DATA 2026 VIA GETTY IMAGES

The recent eruption of the Anak Krakatoa volcano and five other volcanoes came as Indonesia also battled enormous wildfires and the fallout of a recent earthquake.

Meanwhile, Ulta Levenia, a so-called expert on terrorism and geopolitics attached to the Office of the President, suggested the simultaneous explosions were suspicious and could be caused by (what else) foreign interference. She postulated the nefarious root could be the U.S. HAARP project, which studies the ionosphere, and linked this to Prabowo having just met with Putin.

Thanks for sharing, Ulta…

FP’s Most Read This Week

A Vietnamese tradition of ceremonially entombing whale corpses washed onto the shore is giving conservationists new insights into the country’s historical biodiversity, Anne Pinto-Rodrigues writes in Nikkei Asia.

Lethwei, or the art of nine limbs, is Myanmar’s traditional martial art. As civil war rages, it continues to thrive, Agence France-Presse reports.

Indonesia’s richest family has quietly moved over $1 billion overseas as it worries about politics at home, by Chanyaporn Chanjaroen, Harry Suhartono, and Pui Gwen Yeung in Bloomberg.

In Focus: Anti-Indian Racism Worries Singapore

On Sunday, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke out against racial prejudice in Singapore and in particular anti-Indian sentiment.

Singapore is ethnically diverse, though with a Chinese majority, and the People’s Action Party (PAP), which has ruled the city-state since independence, has long worried about the potential for communal tensions.

Two incidents pushed these concerns to the fore.

First, floods in Nepal left nine Singaporean citizens missing. Racist online comments suggested that the missing were likely ethnically South Asian so were not real Singaporeans or could be ignored.

Second, news that Air India was seeking money from investors prompted racist speculation about the ethnically Indian CEO of Temasek, Singapore’s state investment fund. Temasek is a majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines, which owns a stake in Air India.

In June, the government also raised concerns about the promotion of racist comments on social media suggesting ethnic Indians were displacing Chinese in Singapore. It said these comments likely originated on a China-based social media platform.

Responding to the latest incidents, K. Shanmugam, Singapore’s home minister and coordinating minister for national security, said on Sept. 5 that lately, “there have been more racist comments, particularly when it comes to Indians in Singapore.”

He called such comments “shameful, nasty, and totally unacceptable.” He further added that while he was not sure if the recent anonymous online comments came from Singaporeans, the people behind them should be “unmasked and dealt with.”

In his Facebook post on Sunday, Wong also condemned “racist” and “anti-Indian” comments: “Singapore has held together because we have consistently rejected attempts to divide us along racial or religious lines.”

The PAP has historically done a creditable job managing inter-ethnic relations. However, issues remain; ethnically Indian and Chinese friends of mine in Singapore note quieter prejudices persist, especially on issues such as interracial relationships and at work.

Still, the overall trend has been toward acceptance. In 2025, nearly 20 percent of marriages in Singapore were inter-ethnic, up from 7.6 percent in 1990.

The liberal international order, flawed and unequal as it was, is gone. Personally, I’ve grown tired of wringing my hands at what is no more. I’m focused on what might come next—and how we can shape it to be peaceful and fair.

“It’s time to throw some spaghetti against the wall,” one former diplomat suggested to me recently. Consider this issue to be exactly that: an assortment of new, perhaps even radical, ideas. Some of them won’t be quite al dente, but all good dishes are born of trial and error. And the current moment, ahead of the U.S. midterms, is exactly the time to experiment.

The liberal international order, flawed and unequal as it was, is gone. Personally, I’ve grown tired of wringing my hands at what is no more. I’m focused on what might come next—and how we can shape it to be peaceful and fair.

“It’s time to throw some spaghetti against the wall,” one former diplomat suggested to me recently. Consider this issue to be exactly that: an assortment of new, perhaps even radical, ideas. Some of them won’t be quite al dente, but all good dishes are born of trial and error. And the current moment, ahead of the U.S. midterms, is exactly the time to experiment.

The question we wanted to grapple with is how countries and companies can survive in a world without rules. And as they do that, what kind of order should come next?

Hal Brands takes a stab at a survival guide for the here and now. Don’t be nostalgic, get ready to pay higher risk premiums, and start investing in your own defense and manufacturing, he advises. That might get countries through the next few years, but what then?

Charles A. Kupchan has a plan. The world’s only real hope of maintaining order, he argues, is a system that has both a bottom-up and a top-down component. The former is necessary because that is the direction in which the world is already headed—a diffusion of power and a bigger role for regional groupings. The latter, however, is where we’ll have to get creative, especially since the United Nations won’t magically start working again. Kupchan proposes a flexible and informal steering group resembling the 19th-century Concert of Europe, sitting above the U.N. and directing a symphony of tiered groups. I found the idea compelling and thought-provoking, and I hope you engage with it. Now there’s just the small matter of getting Beijing and Washington on board.

We had to explore how the flow of money fits into our rewiring of power, of course. Countries in the global south have struggled of late with the trend toward nationalism and protectionism and without the tailwinds of unfettered free trade and globalization. Michael Beckley makes the case that there’s a useful synergy right in front of our eyes. The developed world is cash-rich and labor-poor, while the developing world is cash-poor and labor-rich; each side needs the other for its future growth, so why not embrace their respective opportunities for arbitrage? Beckley explains how to get there.

Mariana Mazzucato injects a dose of fairness. The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were created as global organizations but in reality concentrate power in a handful of countries. Mazzucato argues that a world without rules is the crisis we needed to rewrite some of those rules with the common good at the center.

The final essay in our cover package is by me, and it’s a deliberate provocation. U.S. President Donald Trump started his second term with a bang, as we all know. He has been incredibly disruptive for global order. But Trump has peaked, I argue. His coercive powers are now in decline, in large part because of his own policies. The key example is this year’s Iran war and how it has drained the U.S. military of munitions. Countries and companies are already realizing this and adapting how they navigate Trump—and how they will approach discussions about a future world order.

Weighty stuff, I know. But change is afoot in the United States, if you look at the polls for the midterm elections. And after those elections, the political conversation will inevitably move to the race for the White House. My hope is that amid that race, serious thought is given to Washington’s role in the world. This issue is our humble attempt to play a part.

Lots more in the issue, as always. If you’re in the Northern Hemisphere, I hope you’ve had a lovely summer. And if you make it to New York for the U.N. General Assembly meetings in September, I hope to run into you somewhere!

Ravi Agrawal

https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-0.author: Kallee Buchanan and Kate Forrester
https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-0.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Agricultural Chemicals

David Pocock has launched a senate inquiry into the APVMA's decision to continue the use of paraquat in Australia. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Senator David Pocock has launched a senate inquiry into the continued use of the controversial chemical paraquat.

It follows chemical regulator APVMA's decision in June to continue to allow the use of the popular herbicide after a decades-long review.

Public submissions are open until October 22, 2026.

The chemical regulator's decision to allow the continued use of controversial weed killer paraquat will be scrutinised by a Senate committee inquiry.

Independent senator David Pocock successfully referred the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) decision to the Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport References Committee, with support from the Greens and the Coalition.

"We've seen the APVMA having a rolling review of paraquat for nearly 30 years," Senator Pocock said.

"In the meantime, 70 countries have banned paraquat because of the health risks.

In June, the APVMA concluded a 30-year review of the herbicide, restricting its use and application rates, but stopped short of a complete ban.

The decision was criticised by experts and advocates, who accused the regulator of ignoring evidence of the links to increased rates of Parkinson's disease.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority concludes its nearly 30-year review of the controversial but popular herbicide.

"I have had so many experts in this space raise concerns about the way that the APVMA looked at evidence, the weighting that they gave to different studies, and that's really concerning," Senator Pocock said.

"The APVMA concluded that the available evidence did not convincingly demonstrate a direct causal link.

"That seems counter to what the scientific consensus is."

At the time of its decision, the APVMA said it received 171 submissions from scientists, doctors, the agricultural industry and other interested parties, which included concerns about human health, farming viability and environmental impact.

The APVMA has been contacted for comment.

Earlier this year, the APVMA imposed new limits and conditions on the ways farmers can use the controversial herbicide paraquat. (Supplied: Jake Hamilton)

Senator Pocock said the inquiry would consider the broader issues of transparency and integrity, which could have ramifications for other chemicals and the regulatory framework.

"This is an opportunity for the Senate to actually look at all of this, weigh it up and ensure that we're protecting our farmers if there is a material risk to them," he said.

"I've heard from farmers who have parents who've developed Parkinson's … and from really good farmers who are using low-till, no-till agriculture and relying on paraquat.

"This is something that needs to take all of that into account and ensure that we're making decisions that put farmers' health front and centre."

But WA Farmers grain council president Mark Fowler said he had not heard from Senator Pocock, and the inquiry risked undermining the APVMA's independence.

Mark Fowler says "risk has to be taken into account" when using paraquat. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

"[The Senate] can't provide a decision on paraquat, but they can certainly set the framework and parameters in a different way, which is very much about popular politics rather than scientific and regulatory processes."

Mr Fowler said comparisons with countries that have already banned the chemical failed to consider differences in how it was used and regulated in Australia.

"In a lot of other countries they apply a hazard approach, where if something is dangerous without regard to the dose or the exposure or the risk, it can sometimes still be banned.

"Lots of those other countries also have popular politics involved in their process in a far greater way than Australia."

Sugarcane farmers will no longer be able to use paraquat on their crop under the reviewed regulations from the APVMA. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Mr Fowler said he was shocked to learn the Coalition had supported the inquiry.

"This does not reflect that at all.

"Politicising one of our cornerstone chemicals for the system we depend on in Australia is not in grain growers' or farmers' interests."

Parkinson's Australia chief executive Olivia Nassaris welcomed the inquiry, and said she would continue campaigning for a ban on paraquat.

Olivia Nassaris says Parkinson's Australia is calling for a total ban on paraquat. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"Why else have about 70 countries so far, including the UK, the European Union, China — and just in July, India — all banned the use of the chemical?"

According to a study published by the British Medical Journal in 2025, the number of people living with Parkinson's globally was expected to more than double by 2050, affecting about 25 million people.

Ms Nassaris said this put pressure on the health system and economy.

"We have to do something to stop it," she said.

The inquiry is expected to deliver its report early in 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: Health concerns grow as volcanic ash spreads across Indonesia after eruption
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Tri Ardhya
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Volcanic Eruptions

Volcanic ash fall has fallen in several parts of Indonesia, particularly in southern Sumatra and western Java. (Reuters: Sammy)

Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has sent volcanic ash across parts of Java and Sumatra islands, disrupting thousands of flights, hundreds of thousands of travellers and impacting local communities.

Indonesia's Geological Agency said a 25-hour continuous eruption ended on Sunday, but smaller intermittent eruptions had continued and the likelihood of further eruptions "remains high".

A three-kilometre exclusion zone around the volcano remains in place.

The volcanic ash caused temporary flight disruptions through Jakarta. (Reuters: Yuddy Cahya Budiman)

Jakarta's main Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and four other airports reopened on Tuesday after winds cleared ash from surrounding areas.

More than 340,000 travellers, including Australians, and nearly 3,000 flights were affected by cancellations and delays, according to InJourney Airports that manages commercial airports across Indonesia.

Ash has disrupted communities living nearby, such as in Lampung province, about 75 kilometres north-east of the volcano.

Elizabeth Amelia, who lives in the city of Bandar Lampung, said she was concerned about the health of her two-year-old child and her 63-year-old mother.

"I'm worried it could affect their breathing. If it's inhaled too much, it could cause a respiratory infection," Mrs Amelia said.

Elizabeth Amelia lives with her husband, daughter and mother in a coastal area of Lampung. (Supplied)

She said her daughter and mother had not gone outside since the ash fall began, while she and her husband were wearing masks to go to work.

She said she noticed what first looked like "rain" on Saturday night, before realising it was volcanic ash.

Elizabeth Amelia says cars were covered in ash when she returned from church on Saturday. (Supplied)

She said the ash fall felt worse than in 2018 because it had lasted for several days.

In 2018, volcanic activity at Mount Anak Krakatau triggered an undersea landslide and tsunami in the Sunda Strait.

Lightning and a large plume of smoke from Indonesia's erupting Mount Anak Krakatau. (Instagram: @asdin88)

The disaster killed at least 430 people, injured 1,485 and displaced about 20,000.

Living less than 1 kilometre from the coast also made her anxious about the risk of a tsunami.

"I am scared. If I were to stay in a hotel, for how long? We don't know how long this situation will last," she said.

She said the uncertainty had made her consider permanently moving inland.

The Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) has advised residents in ash-affected areas to reduce outdoor activity and use masks and protective glasses.

It also warned volcanic ash could "irritate the eyes and respiratory system, particularly among vulnerable groups such as children, older people and those with respiratory conditions".

Volcanic ash is visible on the roof of Rosyidah Khairiyyah's home in Bogor. (Supplied)

In Bogor, more than 100 kilometres from Mount Anak Krakatau, Rosyidah Khairiyyah lives with two of her children while her husband teaches at a boarding school in neighbouring Banten province, where their eldest child studies.

Mrs Khairiyyah said her husband and eldest child usually returned home only once every two months.

Rosyidah Khairiyyah says cleaning the ash has added to her daily workload. (Supplied)

She was concerned that a sudden emergency could split the family.

"I might not be able to reach the children or the emergency bag, or I could leave my phone behind and not be able to contact my husband or children," she said.

Rosyidah Khairiyyah says she has to shake out or rewash clothes left outside to dry because of the ash. (Supplied)

She said their emergency plan was for her husband to stay with their eldest child, while she would take the two children at home to a safer area.

But she said she was not aware of government plans about where residents should go if they needed to leave.

As ash continued to fall, Mrs Khairiyyah said she was mopping her terrace about five times a day and placing wet towels along gaps under the doors to stop ash from entering the house.

One of her children studied from home this week, but returned to school on Wednesday.

Her children also developed what she described as a "weird cough".

A drone view shows Mount Anak Krakatau volcano spewing hot ash during an eruption, in South Lampung, Lampung province, Indonesia, September 5, 2026. (Retuers:  Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation (PVMBG))

Ade Ervin, the chairman of Balawista Indonesia, a national water-tourism safety and rescue organisation, said he was at the organisation's base in Carita, on Java's west coast, when the volcano mount began erupting.

Ade Ervin says his team continues to monitor visitors and distribute masks while tourism areas remain open. (Supplied)

He said there had been "remarkable progress" in conditions since Tuesday morning, although light ash was still falling in some areas.

He said about 120 of his team members were deployed across coastal areas in western Java and southern Lampung.

He said tourists treating the eruption as a "spectacle" was a problem, with some visitors gathering to watch instead of moving away from potentially dangerous areas.

"This lack of awareness becomes a psychological challenge in situations like this, because it makes the job harder for responders and volunteers," he said.

An eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau in December, 2018. (Reuters: Antara Foto, Bisnis Indonesia, Nurul Hidayat)

Despite the disruption, Indonesia's Geological Agency said communities along the Banten and Lampung coastlines could continue normal activities while following official advice.

Teuku Faisal Fathani, the head of the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), urged the public to remain calm and avoid panic.

He said BMKG and other government agencies were continuing to monitor volcanic ash movement and potential hazards.

However he urged people in areas exposed to volcanic ash to remain vigilant.

"Let's take care of vulnerable groups around us … BMKG continues to update weather, aviation, and geophysical data regularly, so that the public can carry out their activities with peace of mind by referring to official information," Mr Faisal said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.author: Tessa Flemming
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Royal commentators have speculated Prince William's happy days at Eton spurred Prince George's enrolment.  (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

There are very few schools that can guarantee its graduating cohort will be future prime ministers, royals or esteemed stars.

Britain's Eton College may just be the exception.

The exclusive boy's school — just a stone's throw away from Windsor Castle — boasts itself a venerable list of alumni.

More than one in three British PMs including Boris Johnson and David Cameron attended the college, as did author George Orwell, actor Hugh Laurie and adventurer Bear Grylls.

But perhaps the most noted figures to walk the hallowed halls are its generations of British royals.

That includes Prince William and Prince Harry.

And now William's eldest, Prince George, who started his first day at the school this week.

But behind its 586-year history also lies unbending tradition, royal upset and controversy.

Prince George will become the latest royal to enrol at Eton.  (X: KensingtonRoyal)

The school was founded in 1440 by Henry VI to provide free education and a gateway to Cambridge for 70 poor boys.

Its noble origins didn't last long.

The charity mission was soon scrapped by Edward IV who annulled the school's grants and transferred a large number of its assets and treasures to St George's Chapel, Windsor.

Today, Eton is one of the UK's most expensive schools — with tuition costing about of 65,000 British pounds ($121,000) a year.

That is if you can pass its enrolment interviews, tests and references.

Admission tests where, as recently as 2011 prospective students were asked to imagine they were prime minister and write a speech arguing that employing the army against violent protesters, and killing many of them, was "both necessary and moral".

The pupils of Eton, ever the bastion of tradition, wear the uniform of a black tail coat over a black waistcoat and pinstriped trousers. (Reuters: Steve Parsons/pool)

Still, it remains one of the most coveted educations boys can acquire.

Some reports say the school sees around 1,300 registrations a year for approximately 250 spots.

And Boris Johnson — at age 16 — was quoted extolling its virtues to parents because "you will imbue your son with the most important thing, a sense of his own importance".

Prince William and Harry are perhaps the two Eton alumni who were born already knowing their Commonwealth importance.

While more than half a dozen royals have attended the college, very few were as hounded as the brothers, who graduated in 2000 and 2003 respectively.

At 18, Prince William posed at Eton, showing off his cooking skills, polo practice and studying.  (Getty Images: Ken Goff)

On his 18th birthday, William spoke about leaving Eton.

"I'll miss my friends and Dr Gailey (housemaster) who has been a tremendous support to me," he said.

As for why he was doing a photo shoot at the college on his birthday?

"I knew there would be a lot of media interest in my 18th and I didn't want a whole host of media involved," he answered.

"Neither did I want any distractions as I was revising for my A-levels."

While Prince William faced his first day at Eton with Princess Diana at his side, Prince Harry entered the school freshly grieving.  (Getty Images: Stefan Rousseau/ PA Images)

His brother's experience wasn't quite the same.

In his memoir Spare, Harry wrote William wanted him to pretend they didn't know each other at school.

The Duke of Sussex also called the school a "profound shock", though soon clung onto the school's strong rugby traditions.

"Sport held me together," he told Time in June.

"I was one of those kids at school who did not enjoy classroom work.

Further controversy also engulfed Harry's Eton years in 2006, when he was embroiled in cheating allegations.

Dismissed teacher Sarah Forsyth said she had ghostwritten the prince's A-level art project — though Harry was later cleared of the allegations by the exam board.

Prince Harry with his teammates, the Oppidans, after competing in the traditonal Eton wall game.  (Getty Images: Pool Photograph/Corbis/Corbis)

And as Prince George begins his Eton journey, the school faces a fresh challenge: escaping further scandal.

For an institution cloaked in tradition, it has also repeatedly been the perpetuator of institutional cover-up.

Dating as far back as the 1920s, MI5 investigated allegations US actress Tallulah Bankhead seduced its students while headmaster Cyril Alington fought to keep the scandal from headlines.

"He wants to do everything possible to keep Eton out of the scandal," an investigator noted.

In recent years moves to progress the school have been met with both outrage and encouragement.  (Reuters: Eddie Keogh )

Several teachers have also been convicted of child sexual abuse.

As recently as 2020, former teacher Matthew Mowbray was jailed after abusing boys in the dorms, with the pretext of discussing schoolwork.

The same year, teacher Will Knowland was dismissed for teaching students male aggression was a biological fact and that "saying smash the patriarchy … amounts to saying smash human nature and biological reality".

A letter asking for his reinstatement later gathered thousands of signatures.

In 2022, girls visiting from a nearby state school were also reportedly subjected to misogynistic language and racial slurs.

Eton's traditions, even including the joyful Fourth of June Day celebrations, face increasing scepticism.  (Reuters: Eddie Keogh)

Increasingly, Eton faces a world sceptical of its archaic elitism.

Oxford and Cambridge admitted more Etonians each year than the country's entire pool of boys poor enough to get free school meals, The Economist cited in 2009.

It has also been accused of rorting the EU's farm subsidies, scoring £2,652 ($4,979) in funding.

Even Australian venture capitalist Mark Carnegie noted Eton's above-average influence in Sonia Purnell's 2012 book about Boris Johnson

"It became clear to me how powerful Eton is as a manufacturer of cultural capital," he remarked about Mr Johnson's education.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan looks to clamp down on spread of invasive beetle species
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The government has outlined a draft strategy for combating the red-necked longhorn beetle, designated as an invasive alien species that damages fruits and roadside trees, sources said Wednesday.

Setting a goal of stopping the insect from proliferating and reducing the affected areas by 2030, the outline calls on the government to provide technical and financial support to local governments to substantially strengthen countermeasures.

The strategy is expected to be finalized by a relevant central government task force.

The red-necked longhorn beetle, native to East Asia, is about 30 millimeters long.

In Japan, the beetle was found for the first time in 2012 in Aichi Prefecture. It is believed to have entered Japan via cargoes on ships bound for the country. The insect has a high fertility rate, with a female adult laying more than 1,000 eggs in summer.

The outline shows concerns about the impact on tourism, such as the beetle killing cherry blossom trees, on top of damage to fruits such as plums and peaches.

Measures cited by the outline to curb the expansion of the beetle’s habitats include cutting down damaged trees, killing larvae and spraying pest control chemicals. Prefectural governments were mainly asked to take these measures.

The national government will develop control methods, dispatch experts to affected areas and extend sufficient financial aid. The state will also consider expanding support for measures to prevent the beetle’s habitats from expanding, as well as initial control measures.

In collaboration with universities and other research institutions, the government aims to develop trees that are less susceptible to damage and more effective chemicals against the instects.

The outline advises 22 prefectures that have sustained damage from the beetle to draw up regional pest control plans promptly. These plans will include pest control targets, with municipalities taking charge of assessing damage, giving necessary advice and guidance to farmers, and raising awareness among local residents.

Unaffected prefectures are also asked to take action, such as compiling preemptive measures and steps that would allow them to swiftly detect signs of damage.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: The red-necked longhorn beetle is an invasive alien species that damages fruits and roadside trees. The beetle was found for the first time in Japan in 2012. The government has outlined a plan to curb the expansion of the beetle’s habitats.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan adds drones to arsenal against bears
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Amid a surge in bear-related incidents across Japan, local governments and companies are increasingly turning to drones as part of efforts to prevent attacks and minimize damage.

Beyond their use in aerial searches for bears, drones are proving effective as a preventive tool to help keep the animals away from human settlements, including urban areas.

At the same time, however, Japan faces a shortage of personnel capable of operating drones safely.

In early June, a bear entered residential and commercial areas in the city of Utsunomiya in Tochigi Prefecture. Around 20 sightings over four days prompted the city to close all municipal elementary and junior high schools.

In response, the city government deployed a drone equipped with a thermal-imaging camera capable of detecting heat sources. From above, the drone searched bushes, the shadows of buildings and other hard-to-see areas at Utsunomiya University, where the bear had been spotted.

It was the first time for Utsunomiya to use a drone in a bear search. Although the animal was not found, a city official said the operation had been worthwhile. “We were able to thoroughly search areas that are difficult to see with the naked eye,” the official said.

In June, the city government of Nagai in Yamagata Prefecture, also began using drones to patrol areas along school commuting routes. Equipped with loudspeakers, the drones emit warning sounds intended to deter bears and drive them away before children leave home for school.

The initiative is also designed to reduce risks for people involved in patrols. One aim is to “avoid endangering the lives of those conducting patrols, including members of local hunting clubs,” an official in the city’s agriculture and forestry section said.

According to preliminary figures released by the Environment Ministry, bear sightings nationwide, excluding Hokkaido, reached 50,801 in fiscal 2025 through March this year. Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost prefecture, does not release comparable data.

The total was 4.6 times higher than three years earlier, while the number of human casualties reached a record 216. In April and May, sightings were 90% higher compared with the same period of last year.

Manufacturers of small uncrewed aerial vehicles, including drones, are viewing the growing concern over bears as a business opportunity. Tokyo-based Terra Drone has developed a bear-deterrent drone that can be operated from up to 1 kilometer away and can spray a liquid containing pungent compounds derived from chili peppers. The company is marketing the model mainly to local governments.

KDDI SmartDrone, also based in Tokyo, has installed a dedicated permanent drone port on the rooftop of the town hall in Shintotsukawa, Hokkaido. The system enables a drone to be launched within five minutes of a request and dispatched to the site in question.

Government deregulation has helped accelerate the use of drones in response to bear sightings in urban areas.

Last December, the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism partially revised the civil aeronautics law to allow the immediate use of drones in densely populated residential areas during emergencies, such as when there is an urgent need to prevent attacks by wildlife, without prior ministry approval.

This exception was applied in the case of Utsunomiya. According to the city government, flight approval procedures previously took nearly a full day to complete. Following the revision, however, drones can now be deployed more flexibly.

The main challenge is a shortage of drone operators. A national pilot qualification is required to operate drones beyond visual line of sight, including in mountainous or forested areas, or at night.

According to the transport ministry, there were about 45,000 holders of uncrewed aircraft pilot qualifications in Japan as of the end of June this year.

Although the number of qualified pilots is rising, opportunities to fly drones outdoors remain limited due to regulations under the civil aeronautics law and other rules. As a result, many licensed operators lack the practical experience needed to refine their skills.

KDDI SmartDrone is discussing plans to launch drone training courses for hunting associations. “It’s important not only to introduce new technology but also to develop local human resources,” a company official said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Japan faces shortage of personnel capable of operating drones safely. In early June, a bear entered residential and commercial areas in Utsunomiya in Tochigi Prefecture. In June, the city government of Nagai in Yamagata Prefecture also began using drones to patrol areas along school commuting routes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvz.title: US strikes Iranian oil tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvz.text:
US forces struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday, sinking one, in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship, US Central Command (Centcom) said.

Four Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) were targeted, as well as another near Kharg Island, a major oil terminal off Iran's coast, Centcom added.

Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.

Oil prices rose in Asia trading. Benchmark Brent crude was up by 1.5% at $99.35 (£73.35) a barrel, while US-traded oil was 1.3% higher at $94.23.

Jordan said it had shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said.

After warning of further retaliatory strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 "non-compliant vessels" trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.

The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks.

In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".

One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel.

Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil.

Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland.

Pressure on oil prices has been exacerbated by wider regional instability.

Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities.

The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.

When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was "pretty straightforward".

"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia.

The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz.

US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations".

The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing.

With additional reporting from Peter Hoskins.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvz.summary: US strikes on five Iranian oil tankers, sinking one, in response to Tehran's missile attacks. Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they have attacked two US vessels, eight oil tanker and 10 "non-compliant vessels" Iran says it attacked two U.S. vessels and eight oil tanks in Strait of Hormuz.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68.title: Beavers 'could boost wildlife and tackle drought'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68.text:
Supporters of a plan to reintroduce beavers to a county say they could help landscapes become more resilient to drought and climate change.

Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust and Forestry England are surveying different parts of the county to assess their suitability for a new reintroduction programme.

"Beavers are a keystone species" said Emily Bowen of the Beaver Trust. "They are ecosystem engineers, which means that they can have a massive impact on the landscape around them."

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which would have to approve the measure, said it could make a "huge difference to nature recovery".

"By changing the land to suit their needs, they can change it in such a way that boosts biodiversity and increases resilience in terms of climate change," Bowen added.

As semi-aquatic mammals, beavers are known for building dams that create ponds and wetlands.

Even small streams can feed a substantial wetland habitat that will then support an abundant array of biodiversity.

Beavers are a native species, but have not been a regular sight in the west of England for around 400 years, after hunting for food and medical ingredients forced their numbers to dramatically decline.

A Defra spokesperson said: "Reintroducing beavers has the potential to make a huge difference to nature recovery, and we are proud to champion this work.

"We will continue to support our partners and ensure that the return of beavers benefits both wildlife and communities."

Beavers have already been living at Greathough Brook in the Forest of Dean since 2018 and regular surveys have revealed a dramatic increase in biodiversity.

"I've seen stoats, I've seen weasels, I've even seen pine martens," said Kate Wollen, from Forestry England.

"The beavers have created this amazing habitat that has brought in all the insects that are at the bottom of the food chain and then it brings in all the other animals that then feed on them, it's just a whole wonderful network of habitats."

A new re-introduction programme in the Severn Vale area would require a government licence.

Studies are being carried out to find suitable locations and a consultation is underway with landowners and users who might be affected by the change in the landscape.

"We have to make sure that we are working really closely with people who live, work and manage the areas that we're thinking about putting beavers," said Mega Adamou, of Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust.

"We'll be seeing more complex wetland habitats being created," she added.

"We'll be seeing a little bit more resilience to drought in those areas where the beavers might end up living."

"It's been really interesting to see how the general public have taken to beavers and getting people thinking about seeing them back in our countryside."

There have been three licensed releases of beavers in England to date, with about 100 animals expected to be released this year.

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.title: TSA brings back gate access for some people without plane tickets 25 years after 9/11
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.text:
FILE - Travelers walk through a TSA security checkpoint at Reagan National Airport in Washington, March 24, 2026.

LAS VEGAS — Airport security checkpoints have been the end of the line since soon after the 9/11 attacks for most friends and relatives who want to see off departing passengers. That is changing at some U.S. airports.

The Transportation Security Administration is allowing eligible TSA PreCheck members without tickets to pass through security and enter gate areas, reviving a tradition that largely disappeared after the attacks 25 years ago this week.

"As an exclusive benefit for our most trusted travelers, this new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel," TSA said on its website.

The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck" is free, but interested members must apply online one to three days before their planned visits and receive approval before going to the airport. If approved, they can enter security using a TSA PreCheck lane with an acceptable form of identification. The passes are valid for one calendar day, but reentries are allowed on that day.

TSA says members of other trusted-traveler programs who have a Known Traveler Number also can apply for access to the gates.

The program is initially available at 13 airports, including Los Angeles International Airport, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City International Airport, according to TSA. The agency says it plans to expand the program to more airports in the coming months.

Before the Sept. 11 attacks, individuals without tickets generally could accompany ticketed passengers to their gates. The attacks prompted sweeping changes to airport security, including restrictions on access to secure areas of airports.
