https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/t.title: Lynagh makes timely return after Wallabies fly half Gordon breaks leg
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tom Lynagh returns to action this weekend in the Super Rugby AUS. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Tom Lynagh will make his return to the rugby field this weekend after a horror run of injuries have kept him sidelined.

Lynagh was the Wallabies starting fly half for all three Tests against the British and Irish Lions in 2025, but managed just 18 minutes with the Queensland Reds this year.

The four-week Super Rugby AUS competition begins this weekend with Reds vs Force, and Brumbies vs Waratahs.

Tom Lynagh's timely return at number 10 for the Queensland Reds and Zac Lomax's move to the centres for the Western Force will have Wallabies ramifications in a pre-season Ballymore hit-out.

Super Rugby AUS starts on Saturday in Brisbane and there will be immense interest in how both fare ahead of next year's World Cup on home soil.

Lynagh, the starting fly half in all three British and Irish Lions Tests last year, managed just 18 minutes for the Reds because of a series of injuries last season.

A penalty try close to full-time sees the Wallabies and Pumas finish in a 28-28 draw in Mendoza, giving the visitors a history-making series win on Argentine soil.

All going to script, he will get at least 40 minutes against the Force at Ballymore in new Reds coach Vern Cotter's first game in charge since his historic move from Auckland's Blues to replace Les Kiss.

Lynagh's return comes as Reds teammate and fly half Carter Gordon enters two months of rehabilitation after fracturing his fibula in last weekend's Test draw against Argentina in Mendoza.

Gordon had established himself as the Wallabies' first-choice fly half, leaving Kiss with some big calls ahead of a clash with South Africa and a two-Test Bledisloe Cup in the next six weeks.

"I'm really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role," Cotter said of the son of former Wallabies great Michael.

"He's got a great head on his shoulders, he sees the game well, he's calm and decisive.

"With the niggles he has had, we will probably be a bit careful with him, so it probably won't be 80 minutes, but certainly a good 40 minutes to start with.

"He's a great player in organised play but brilliant at unstructured (play).

"It's a good opportunity for Tom to get out there and boss the team around … pull a few strings and get some combinations."

Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, released by the Reds to join the Force this season, will oppose Lynagh and consider himself in the thick of Wallabies discussions after being part of their training camp earlier this year.

Kurtley Beale has been named on the bench for the Force, but new signing James O'Connor, another sure to be in Kiss's considerations, will not play.

Lomax, an Australian and NSW State of Origin rugby league winger, revealed this week he would be deployed in the number 13 jersey against the Reds.

A dominant showing there would add intrigue to Kiss's midfield selection headache after fellow code-hopper Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii's struggles to nail down the jersey in 24 Tests.

Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell, replaced in the number 15 by Tom Wright after one Test in July despite a good showing against Ireland, will also get a chance to show something when he comes off the bench for the Reds.

Fellow Wallabies Matt Faessler, Zane Nonggorr and Josh Flook have been named, while Australian under-20s captain Tom Robinson will wear the number 6, and exciting fullback Will McCulloch will start.

NSW Waratahs lock Miles Amatosero, red-carded in his second Test appearance in Osaka, will mount his comeback against the ACT Brumbies on Sunday in Bungendore, east of Canberra.

Teddy Wilson and Max Burey, after earning an early release from the Force, will partner in the halves, while Sid Harvey will start at fullback.

Triston Reilly will wear the Brumbies' number 15 against his former club a week after piloting the First Nations and Pasifika XV to victory in Tonga, while Wallabies wing aspirant Corey Toole will add pace on the flank.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/v.title: Melbourne mosque community mourns children killed in crash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Victoria Police said seven children were inside the vehicle when it rolled. (ABC News)

The two children who died in a single-vehicle rollover west of Melbourne yesterday have been identified as Ossama El Hawli, 11, and Sarah El Hawli, seven.

Sarah died at the scene, while Ossama was flown to hospital with critical injuries and later died.

Five other children ranging from toddler to teenager are in a stable condition at the Royal Children's Hospital.

A community is mourning the deaths of 11-year-old Ossama El Hawli and seven-year-old Sarah El Hawli in a single-vehicle crash west of Melbourne yesterday.

The Australian Islamic Centre said the two children, who are relatives, were "beloved young members of our community".

"Their loss has deeply affected our entire AIC community," the statement said.

"Our hearts are with their parents, family and loved ones as they face an unimaginable loss."

Al Iman College in Melton South told the ABC it was focused on supporting the children's families at this time.

A funeral notice for the pair states their burials will be held tomorrow.

"The El Hawli family with heavy hearts and profound sadness announced the passing of their beloved Ossama El Hawli and Sarah El Hawli," the notice said.

Emergency services were called to Nerowie and Parwan-Exford roads just before 4:30pm yesterday, where a 4WD had rolled over.

Police said the eight-seater vehicle, driven by a mother who had just picked up children from school, inexplicably rolled.

The single-vehicle crash happened at Parwan, west of Melbourne. (ABC News)

A fleet of ambulance crews attended the scene, including two Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter crews, two Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance (MICA) paramedic crews and seven Advanced Life Support (ALS) paramedic crews.

Paramedics worked to treat Sarah El Hawli, but she died at the scene.

Ossama El Hawli was flown to the Royal Children's Hospital with critical injuries, but died in hospital overnight.

Five other children, including a toddler, three primary-aged children and a teenager, were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Ossama El Hawli was airlifted to hospital with critical injuries and later died. (ABC News)

The Royal Children's Hospital said today all five children were in a stable condition.

A 34-year-old woman was taken to the Royal Melbourne Hospital for observation.

Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating the circumstances behind the fatal crash.

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has CCTV or dashcam footage, or information, is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or submit an online report.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japanese 15-year-olds rank top in core subjects among OECD countries for the first time
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Japan ranked first among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in reading, mathematics and science in a global assessment of 15-year-olds, according to results released by the organization Tuesday.

The country ranked top for the three core subjects among the OECD’s 38 members for the first time since the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) began in 2000.

PISA measures how well 15-year-olds nearing the end of compulsory education can apply knowledge and skills to real-world problems, rather than simply testing what they have memorized in school.

The 2025 assessment was conducted by computer from June through August and involved about 760,000 students from 91 countries and economies. About 6,500 first-year high school students from 183 schools in Japan participated in a sample designed to be nationally representative.

Among all participating countries and economies, including non-OECD members, Japan ranked fourth in reading and fifth in both mathematics and science. Singapore ranked first overall in reading, while the Chinese grouping of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang led mathematics and science. Macau and Taiwan were also among the highest-performing participants.

Japan scored an average 538 points in science, down nine points from the previous assessment in 2022, and 525 in mathematics, down 11 points. Reading fell 13 points to 503, however, which the OECD deemed a significant decline from the country’s score of 516 in 2022.

The 2025 PISA also included a separate assessment known as “Learning in the Digital World,” which measures students’ abilities to solve problems using digital technologies such as programming tools. Japan scored 557 points, ranking first among OECD members and fourth among all participating countries and economies.

The results come as average academic performance has weakened across many OECD countries over the longer term, helping Japan rise in the rankings even as its own scores remained broadly stable.

A comparison by gender showed that boys accounted for a larger share of high-performing students than girls in both science and mathematics. Boys were also more likely to give positive responses to survey questions about the enjoyment of, and interest in, learning science.

Performance was also linked to students’ socioeconomic backgrounds, with those whose parents had higher levels of education or whose households had greater financial resources being more likely to achieve higher scores.

However, in Japan, this explained 7.6% of the variation in students’ science scores, compared with an OECD average of 11.6%. The organization said this demonstrates that socioeconomic background has a relatively smaller effect on variation in science performance in Japan.

However, the results highlighted areas of concern despite the country’s high overall ranking. The proportion of students in the lowest proficiency group increased from the previous assessment in all three subjects.

A questionnaire conducted alongside the assessment pointed to other potential weaknesses in students’ approaches to learning.

About 62.6% of Japanese students said they were curious about a wide range of things, compared with an OECD average of 73.5%. Japanese students were also less likely than the OECD average to say that they plan how to approach their studies or that they change their methods when they realize an approach is not working.

Japan ranked last among the OECD’s 38 members in the frequency with which students used generative artificial intelligence in class.

Just 7% of Japanese students said they used generative AI for learning support in class every day or almost every day, compared with an OECD average of 19.1%. Some 43.8% said they never or almost never used it.

Students who used AI moderately for schoolwork tended to record higher science scores both in Japan and across the OECD, according to the survey, although the organization said that it is important to address the technology’s negative effects while maximizing its benefits by ensuring that all children develop information literacy and the ability to effectively use information in a balanced and reliable manner.

The government is considering addressing these issues in its next national curriculum guidelines, which are expected to take effect in elementary schools from fiscal 2030. The plans include helping students with cross-disciplinary learning as well as teaching them more explicit strategies for how to study while encouraging them to reflect on what they’ve been taught.

Japan plans to substantially expand digital and information education under its next curriculum guidelines, including more systematic teaching about generative AI.

The government plans to create a financial framework to provide loans to businesses that turn vacant houses into affordable homes for young families and low- and middle-income households.

The move comes as the number of akiya, or empty dwellings in the nation, continues to rise.

The Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Ministry  — which included the plan in its budget request for fiscal 2027 beginning next April — said a lack of funding opportunities for developers was a major roadblock for them renovating vacant homes.

The plan calls for the government-affiliated Japan Housing Finance Agency (JHF) to work with local governments and developers to help finance the renovation of vacant houses that are in relatively good condition.

The funding plan is part of the ministry’s long-term goal to turn the increasing number of akiya in the nation into affordable housing for young people and child-rearing families, particularly in urban areas, and to help prevent existing houses from deteriorating or being abandoned.

The ministry hopes to limit the number of dilapidated and damaged vacant houses with no plans to be used to around 1 million by 2035, although this would still be an increase from the 900,000 recorded in 2023, the latest year with available figures.

Funding to support the program will come out of a ¥2.1 billion ($13.7 million) budget request that is earmarked for the JHF in the next fiscal year.

In 2023, there were 3.86 million abandoned or vacant dwellings that were not for rent, sale, or in use as a secondary home, which made up 5.9% of the total of existing houses in the country. That number is about 370,000 higher than in 2018 and up by over 1 million compared with 2008.

The trend is expected to continue in the future, as Japan’s population shrinks and buildings age. According to the Japan Research Institute, there will be nearly 6 million empty dwellings not on the market or in use by 2043, which would represent over 8% of all housing in Japan.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Could Japan see more avalanches like one that hit Nepal?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Tomoko Otake
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
While scientists are working to pin down the exact mechanism behind last month’s deadly mudslide in Nepal, they say that climate change had a role in the ice-rock avalanche that resulted in massive flooding.

Though the scale and mechanisms may vary, Japan is not immune to the risk of catastrophic mudslides hitting mountainous communities, experts say. The country has already seen warming intensify extreme heat and flooding in recent years.

In Nepal, where over 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 are still missing, scientists say climate change and natural geology likely combined to spur the disaster. The affected mountain range is made up mostly of sedimentary rocks, which are prone to weathering and erosion, said Farooq Azam, a cryosphere specialist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

“Glaciers are receding and exposing rock surfaces underneath, which absorb heat,” he told a news briefing last week. “When glaciers are receding, there is always some loose … debris left behind. So it seems like a combination of both climate treatment as well as the geologic process.”

Azam added that there are chances that “because of the extreme warming over the recent decades, permafrost layers below the surface are also warming up and are degrading.”

Seita Emori, a climatologist at the University of Tokyo, said mountain slopes around the world are generally becoming more unstable due to the warming-induced melting of glaciers and permafrost, though the direct cause of the Nepal disaster remains unknown.

In Japan, however, the size of mountain glaciers is very small compared with the Himalayan region, so the scale of mudslides caused by changes in the cryosphere will be much smaller, he said.

For Japan, heavy rain — rather than glaciers — is a bigger risk for slope collapses, as torrential rain and floods are becoming more frequent, he said, citing the 2014 Hiroshima mudslides. That disaster, which caused 166 slope failures, killed 77 people.

Katsuhisa Kawashima, professor of glaciology at Niigata University, likewise said the size and process of glacier formation in Japan are different from those abroad. But, he added, Japan has seen its share of disasters caused by the melting of perennial snow patches.

Following the 2004 collapse of a snow patch on Mount Arasawa in Niigata Prefecture that killed three amateur photographers, Kawashima analyzed disasters caused by snowfield collapses across the country, based on newspaper reports from 1965 through 2004. There were 45 incidents, all the way from Hokkaido to Gunma to Toyama. Victims have been mostly mountain hikers, tourists and vegetable pickers.

As rainfall in Japan has intensified in recent years, the chance of mountain snow disasters happening could rise in the future, Kawashima said.

“Heavy rainfall degrades permanent snow and glaciers,” he said. “When rain falls and enters the bottom of the glacier, it can make ice easier to glide. It can make the glacier movement active and prone to collapsing.”

On the other hand, since the volume of permanent snow is small in Japan, rises in temperatures may lead it to melt and disappear, he added.

“In that case, the risk (of avalanches in Japan) would go down. So it’s difficult to say the risk will universally rise with warming.”

Another key question in Nepal’s flood disaster is whether an early warning system could have reduced the damage.

Azam said that this event was a “sudden-onset hazard that could not be captured by conventional warning systems,” noting that, even with such a system, it would have been difficult to identify the breakpoints, because they can be below the bedrock or glaciers and cannot be analyzed by satellites.

Japan is also confronting issues over the accuracy of rain-related disaster forecasts. In 2022, the Japan Meteorological Agency began issuing warnings up to half a day in advance of a linear rainband, which forms when successive, well-developed thunderstorms organize into a line and linger in the same area for several hours. Such linear rainbands often lead to landslides, as well as river overflow and road flooding.

In May, the agency added a system to warn three hours before a rainband forms. This year, the rate of accurately predicting linear rainbands three hours in advance stood at 30% as of Aug. 30, meaning that rainbands formed 16 times out of the 53 times predicted, below the agency’s expectation of getting it right 50% of the time.

Still, Japan’s warning systems help people better prepare for disasters, especially for typhoons, for which alerts are issued well in advance, Emori said.

At the same time, given the call by the Nepalese government for the world’s biggest carbon emitters to pay for the damage caused by the flood, Japan should stay committed to not just adapting to, but also mitigating climate change, including through its net-zero goals, Emori said.

“I think we have to use this disaster as a wake-up call for the international community to realize more strongly that, if we don’t stop climate change, we could see devastating events like this happening in many places around the world,” he said.

https://www.scmp.com/business/china-busi.author: Julie Zhang
https://www.scmp.com/business/china-busi.text:
Study finds 50 companies had fully, partially or planned to scale AI, tech which could slash drug discovery costs by US$26 billion globally

“It’s only through that translation that companies can turn AI-driven speed into profit, and patients into real beneficiaries,” Yung added.

Some 72 per cent of respondents said their companies were either “scaling” or had “fully scaled” AI across research and development, and no company reported having no plans to adopt the technology, the survey found.

Yet that enthusiasm comes with a caveat. Only 24 per cent of respondents expect AI to deliver a significant improvement in drug success probability, while 56 per cent expect only a moderate uplift, “not a wholesale revolution,” according to the survey.

Another 34 per cent said human biology, clinical judgment and execution will remain as bottlenecks, regardless of how much AI is deployed.

The findings suggested “executives are genuinely optimistic [with AI], but they are not naive about the complexities of biology”, the survey noted.

Executives saw the biggest near-term payoff in early-stage discovery rather than in the clinic. Target identification and validation was cited by 70 per cent of respondents as an area where AI was expected to improve success rates, followed by lead optimisation and hit identification and screening.

Most respondents expected double-digit budget increases for AI-related R&D spending over the next 12 months.

Shortening discovery timelines was the leading commercial reason companies sought outside AI partners, with 84 per cent surveyed engaging with external AI companies, the survey found.

Business consulting and market research firm Frost & Sullivan estimated AI could save the industry US$26 billion globally at the drug discovery stage and a further US$28 billion in clinical research – about half of current spending in those phases.

Unlike many US companies in the sector that remain loss-making, several Chinese leaders, such as Shanghai-listed DNA-encoded-library maker HitGen and Hong Kong-listed AI drug researcher Xtalpi were already profitable, according to Citi.

They “should see earnings accelerate as robust demand translates into stronger utilisation and operating leverage”, Yung said.

However, valuations paint a different picture.

Leading Chinese AI drug discovery companies trade at a median price-to-sales ratio of 19 times projected 2026 sales, a steep discount to the 93 times commanded by their US peers, according to Citi. Price-to-sales ratio refers to a measure of how much investors are paying for each dollar of a company’s revenue.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: Chinese grandparents let court jail granddaughter for stealing US$3,000 to teach her a lesson
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Fran Lu
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Traditional Chinese values emphasise family as a collective, where parents typically share wealth with children, regardless of age

An elderly Chinese couple reported their granddaughter to the police after she took 20,000 yuan (US$3,000) and a gold bracelet from their home without permission, igniting intense discussions online.

The woman, identified by her surname Chen and hailing from northwest China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, received a six-month jail sentence for theft, along with a fine of 2,000 yuan, according to the Legal Daily on September 1.

Chen had taken the money and jewellery from her grandparents while her grandfather was napping at home.

Subsequently, she sold the gold bracelet for over 27,000 yuan and squandered the entire amount.

Even during her trial, she maintained that she should be acquitted of all charges, stating: “It is my grandparents’ money that I took. They will forgive me and won’t hold me accountable. This is our family matter.”

However, the elderly couple opted not to grant her forgiveness.

They said that they had indulged their granddaughter, whom they described as lazy and always wanting to “reap without sowing.”

Previously, she had taken other valuables from their home, each time of greater worth.

Consequently, they decided to utilise legal measures as a means to educate her.

The sentence Chen received sparked passionate discussions on Chinese social media.

“She must have repeatedly stolen their money and ultimately disappointed them,” commented one observer.

“The grandparents acted appropriately. This isn’t solely about the money; it’s an opportunity for her to completely reform,” remarked another.

Some believed the elderly couple had overreacted.

“They could have resolved the issue privately, but instead, they chose to push her into a corner and jeopardise her future,” remarked an online commenter.

Traditional Chinese values regard the family as a collective, where parents often share their wealth with children, regardless of their age.

For instance, Chinese parents typically cover their children’s educational expenses even as they pursue advanced degrees.

It is also common for young couples buying property to tap into the so-called “six wallets,” referring to pooling their savings alongside those of their parents and in-laws.

In recent years, another term, “full-time children,” has emerged to describe this traditional Chinese familial dynamic, wherein more young adults live with their parents and function as household carers in exchange for monetary support.

For parents with substantial pensions who can financially support their children, this “salary” is perceived by some as a new form of pocket money generously provided to alleviate their children’s financial burdens.

Echoing the Chinese ethos of shared wealth, another commenter backed the grandparents’ decision: “You can ask me for money, but you cannot steal from me.”

According to Chinese Criminal Law, individuals who steal considerable amounts of public or private property, or who commit repeated theft, face imprisonment of up to three years.

While stealing from family members or close relatives is generally not classified as a crime if forgiveness is obtained, offenders may still receive leniency if pursued for criminal liability.

https://www.dw.com/en/putin-rejects-mobi.title: Putin rejects mobilization rumors, many Russians unconvinced
https://www.dw.com/en/putin-rejects-mobi.text:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has dismissed rumors about military mobilization. But many Russians, including many DW users, say they are preparing for the possibility.

Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors "complete nonsense" and described them as an "information attack" against Russia.

Two days later, on September 3, at the Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said that "there is no scenario today that would require mobilization."

DW's Russian service asked readers in Russia, on condition of anonymity, whether they see signs of an impending mobilization. The most common response from DW readers concerned receiving summonses from military enlistments offices.

"My nephew received a summons for data verification," wrote a reader from the industrial city of Naberezhnye Chelny.

"I received a summons ordering me to appear for data verification. I'm self-employed. What should I do?"  wrote a user named Maxim.

"One of my friends, a school teacher, received a summons through the government services portal [Gosuslugi] on July 9 to update his records," said another reader, Sergei.

People fear that they may be called up for military service or lose the ability to leave the country freely. As a result, some of those who have received draft notices are seeking to travel abroad as quickly as possible, while restrictions on leaving the country have not yet taken effect.

"One acquaintance of mine left Russia two months ago after receiving a summons for data verification from the military enlistment office," one reader wrote.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Not everyone, however, sees emigration as a realistic option in the event of mobilization.

"As for leaving, that's a fantasy. Where would you go, and more importantly, with what money?" one DW reader wrote.

In June, reports emerged from Russia's Penza region that men were forcibly taken to military enlistment offices and pressured into signing military contracts. According to local reports, the practice became widespread enough that residents organized protests in support of relatives and neighbors. Journalists reporting on the issue say such raids are continuing.

"People are being detained, particularly near the entrances to their apartment buildings," Lena Lemyasova, a journalist with news outlet Important Stories [Vazhnye Istorii], told DW. "Often men who have been drinking. Unknown individuals approach them, or vehicles pull up — often cars provided by local authorities. The men are simply seized and taken away, then their families and neighbors hear nothing more. Later, information sometimes emerges that they were transported to military units. They are often held there before being sent to the front."

Important Stories specializes in investigative journalism. Its publisher, Roman Anin, spent ten years as investigations editor at well-known independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta.

Does receiving a military summons mean a person will be sent to war? According to lawyer Artem Klyga, a summons issued "for data verification" does not in itself mean that someone will be drafted, mobilized or deployed. Data verification notices are one of several legally established reasons for calling someone to a military enlistment office.

"These summonses only show that military enlistment offices have significantly improved their military registration procedures. If mobilization begins, such records would help authorities quickly summon the people they need," Klyga explained to DW.

Russians have also increasingly reported receiving mobilization orders issued in advance. In peacetime, such orders do not oblige individuals to take any action. However, if mobilization is declared, recipients are required to report to their designated military enlistment office.

"They were issued before the war and during the war [against Ukraine] as well. But what changed in the first half of 2026 is that, judging by all indications, they began to be distributed in the hundreds of thousands," Russian lawyer Timofei Vaskin told DW. "We do not know the exact figures because the information is classified. But judging from social media reports and the number of inquiries we and our colleagues received, the increase was dramatic, by dozens of times."

At the same time, the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described reports of a new mobilization wave as "fake stories." Yet critics note that Peskov also denied reports of a possible mobilization beginning in May 2022.

Just eight days before the announcement of partial mobilization, he said: "At the moment, this is not being discussed."

As of August 8, DW found several vacancies on the Russian job platform HeadHunter seeking specialists in "mobilization preparedness." 40 such vacancies are available in Moscow and the surrounding region and 13  in St Petersburg.

For example, some companies are looking for specialists responsible for ensuring that the organization has a mobilization plan in place and knows how it would operate if the state were to place the economy on a wartime footing. Their duties also include preparing the company for emergencies and civil defense measures, as well as helping to transition the organization to a special operating regime in the event of wartime conditions.

The positions were advertised by both private companies and state institutions.

Summonses, military training exercises, the expansion of military registration systems and active recruitment efforts help explain why official denials have failed to put the rumors to rest.

"The way to look at this is that bureaucrats have been tasked with preparing the system for any decision Putin might make. And if that decision is mobilization, they are expected to be ready," Artem Klyga said.

In late July, the independent outlet Agentstvo counted 197 vacancies around Russia containing the term "mobilization preparedness" and more than 2,600 vacancies related to "military registration" on the same recruitment platform.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

https://www.dw.com/en/dallas-republican-.title: Dallas Republican convention: How Trump looms over midterms
https://www.dw.com/en/dallas-republican-.text:
Donald Trump is not on the ballot in the midterm elections — but the first Republican midterm convention is putting him center stage. It's a strategy that could prove risky for the party.

In the midterm elections on Nov. 3, US President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot. Nevertheless, his party is putting him at the center of a major convention two months before the election. On Wednesday and Thursday, Republicans are gathering at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, which can hold around 20,000 spectators, for the "Republican Midterm Convention."

In the United States, this sort of large party conventions are normally only held before presidential elections. Democrats experimented with similar gatherings in the 1970s and early 1980s, but for Republicans, the format is a first. In Texas, they want to mobilize Trump supporters for Republican candidates.

Republicans are heading into the campaign with an unpopular president. According to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, Donald Trump had an approval rating of just 33%. On top of that, Democrats are currently much more energized. Nearly half of their supporters say they are especially enthusiastic about the midterm elections, compared with just 31% of Republicans.

Even so, the convention is entirely centered around Trump. The president will appear on both nights, putting him even more prominently in the spotlight than the Republican candidates who will actually be on the ballot for the Senate and House of Representatives in November. But for some of those candidates in particular, being seen as close with Trump poses a risk. A survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and lawmakers by Politico found considerable reluctance toward the convention.

Numerous candidates in competitive districts appear to shy away from being too closely associated with the president. The fact that some candidates are even avoiding their own party's convention altogether highlights the Trump dilemma. On the one hand, he could mobilize the MAGA base. On the other, his presence could also alienate moderate voters and even boost the opposition.

Despite the president's weak poll numbers, the convention's choreography initially focuses on a positive record of his time in office so far. Topics such as the economy, border security, trade and public safety are intended to show what Trump has already accomplished from the Republicans' perspective.

With segments such as "Two Visions for America" and "The Opposition Contrast," the convention is designed as an attack on the Democrats. Republicans portray them as a party dominated by the political left and a Democratic congressional majority as a threat to Trump's policies so far. In fact, it could block his agenda over the next two years and give Congress significantly more power to oversee and investigate the administration.

Trump's economic record is a particularly hard sell. The convention program focuses on what Trump has already done: his tax cuts, lower drug prices and efforts to promote domestic production.

Whether he can offer anything substantially new in Dallas remains unclear. Political scientist Sascha Lohmann of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) considers that unlikely. In such campaign settings, Trump's speeches are usually poorly structured and rarely outline specific policy measures, he says.

"What we see there is almost a kind of 'stream of consciousness,'" Lohmann continues. Trump tends to reveal over an extended period "whatever may happen to be going through his mind at the time."

The problem for Trump is that his telling of an economic success story does not match the perceptions of many Americans. In a recent FT/Focaldata poll, nearly two-thirds say the US economy is heading in the wrong direction. A total of 57% even say their personal financial situation has worsened since Trump took office again.

Perhaps the most striking element of the planned program is that the Iran war hardly figures in it. Among the 109 announced program items and speakers, there is a segment marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks alongside economic topics, but there is no attention paid to the ongoing war with Iran.

The convention organizers seem keen to keep the politically thorny issue out of the limelight as much as possible. Trump himself, however, has so far taken a different approach and continues to portray the war as a success. Lohmann expects him to maintain that line in Dallas as well.

He says that Trump's argument is "that Iran has been weakened to a greater extent than any president before him has ever managed, that its nuclear program has been wiped out and that the Iranians are now virtually begging for an end to the conflict."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Officially, Dallas is about the midterms, but straight after the midterm elections, talk will move on to the next presidential election. Trump's Vice President JD Vance has been given a prominent role at the convention, while his potentially most important party rival, Marco Rubio, is not on the speaker list so far.

Trump will almost certainly not crown Vance as his successor in Dallas, but his vice president will have an opportunity to present himself to the MAGA audience as a potential heir to the movement.

"It seems likely that the vice president will be a central focus in Dallas," Lohmann says, "not least because Vance has so far had to bear very little political responsibility for the war with Iran."

This article was originally published in German.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp93.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp93.text:
The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.

"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.

Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.

The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.

The official name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.

"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.

Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.

But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.

A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.

In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.

Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.

And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.

Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.

During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.

After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."

The new season of South Park will premiere on 16 September.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3v4.title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3v4.text:
There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East.

The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state. And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct.

This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to.

It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution – a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel.

The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act – and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News.

There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach.

"We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time."

The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America.

UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened.

And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated.

As for the domestic political context, plenty in the Labour movement and the wider British left have long clamoured for this to happen.

Around 140 Labour MPs went public with this demand at the beginning of the summer, and Burnham was explicit in his criticism of his predecessor's approach to the Middle East, writing in July: "Labour's initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry about that."

In recent years Labour has haemorrhaged support in many communities with a significant Muslim population, and so for a new Labour prime minister seeking to lure as many on the left – and beyond – under Labour's umbrella, this diplomatic intervention makes sense.

But the reaction of the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in the Jewish Chronicle, is a reminder of another challenge for Burnham, both political and societal.

"Once again, British Jews find themselves warning their own government that its relentless demonisation of the world's only Jewish state risks fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home," Badenoch said.

Later, the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was "truly a dark day for Britain's Jews".

Last October, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was the local figurehead during the grim reality of an attack at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in the city.

Miliband has sought to address concerns about what Badenoch calls "demonisation" by making his view clear that "holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, pure and simple".

But Labour figures are keenly aware that at points in the last decade, under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour Party's relationship with many British Jews was dire, a situation Starmer sought to rectify as a priority in the early years of his leadership.

In other words, the party's recent relations with many British Jews has been fragile for some time - and many in the community already felt vulnerable after last year's attack in Manchester, and the later arson attacks on Jewish community ambulances in north-west London in the spring.

Burnham has to manage that anxiety while making the case for the changing stance the government is announcing, in the weeks before he meets many of his international counterparts for the first time.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Sarah Basford Canales
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
The former National Socialist Network is challenging ban in high court, arguing law breaches implied freedom of political communication

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The White Australia party is a “modern manifestation” of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi movement and would motivate hate crimes against sections of the country, the high court has heard.

The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.

It is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.

It also argues the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.

The commonwealth’s lawyer, Brendan Lim, told the court on Wednesday the group sought to create a political party after anti-hate laws passed in the wake of the Bondi terror attack threatened to disband it.

The hate group listing means that supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitutes a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

Lim said the group sought “protection” under the guise of creating a political party but remained the same group with the same goals.

The barrister cited a series of examples, including inflammatory rhetoric to encourage communal violence, an alleged physically violent attack by some of its members on Camp Sovereignty in 2025, and past criminal convictions of its leader, Thomas Sewell.

Justice Robert Beech-Jones asked whether the commonwealth believed the group were the “modern manifestation” of Hitler’s Nazi movement. Lim responded: “Yes.”

“There are few legitimate reasons, outside of history books and museum, that warrant the use of Nazi symbols,” Lim said.

Citing a briefing from Asio and public speeches by its director general, Mike Burgess, Lim said the prohibited hate group listing was necessary because the group were security conscious and its operations savvy enough to work within the limits of the law.

“The existence of the group itself is the source of harm,” Lim said.

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Lim said stochastic terrorism – the use of media and public discourse to demonise sections of the community – could lead lone wolves or fringe members to commit racially motivated hate crimes.

Lim said the anti-hate laws go “no further than necessary” to remove that harm.

Lawyers for the party argued on Tuesday a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.

Barrister Shahed Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to outlaw any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.

Sharify said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.

Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/s.author: Amanda Meade
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/s.text:
Downing Centre court hears that the alleged victim was usually outgoing but his demeanour changed at a meeting with Jones at his apartment

Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial

A politician who worked with an alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court the man looked uncharacteristically “sunken and diminished” when meeting with the broadcaster at his Circular Quay apartment.

The former MP, who Guardian Australia has chosen not to name because it may lead to the identification of the alleged victim, known as complainant C, said the man was usually outgoing and engaged but his demeanour changed once he sat down at a table with his former boss.

The court heard C, who was Jones’s driver as a young man, was “anxious and uncomfortable” when the three men sat at a rectangular table for a meeting in Jones’s waterfront property.

C had gone on to work for a politician after leaving Jones, and he accompanied his boss to a meeting with Jones about a board role.

The witness said C did not speak and did not make eye contact which was highly unusual for someone who usually had a lot to contribute.

In his evidence-in-chief last month C said the meeting at the Toaster left him anxious and uncomfortable. He was challenged by the defence because he had sent Jones a text at the time saying how much he enjoyed seeing him.

Earlier on Thursday, the court heard from multiple friends and colleagues who testified that C told them that as a young man he was indecently assaulted by the broadcaster.

The second alleged victim to give evidence at the trial, C has said that over the years he had mentioned to people in his life that he had been touched inappropriately by Jones.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching against six complainants.

In a day of rapid fire evidence, the Downing Centre court heard from six people who said that C would sporadically confide in them how his then-boss would touch him inappropriately.

A former colleague who worked with C in a government role said one day he was driving with C along the Hume Highway when he made an allegation about his time working as a driver for Jones.

“We were talking about 2GB and he was reminiscing about driving Mr Jones around and he communicated that [Jones] had reached into his crotch and squeezed it,” the witness said.

Asked by the prosecution how he responded, the witness apologised to the court for using crude language and said he answered “What the fuck?”.

“And C said ‘that’s just Alan, that’s his behaviour’,” he told the court, adding that C said Jones was “a very powerful man within 2GB”.

C’s father-in-law did not give evidence but his police statement was read out in court.

He said his son-in law occasionally told anecdotes about working for Jones, including one occasion when Jones invited him into his Circular Quay apartment and “when Alan sat down in his chair he was only wearing a dressing gown with nothing underneath” and C said “his undercarriage was hanging out”.

His father-in-law told police that C in 2023 disclosed to him that Jones had “pushed him up against the wall and kissed me” and he had “not previously told me about the hurt it caused”.

Another witness, a school friend, told the court C alleged that Jones would say inappropriate things about genitals in text messages to him.

Another colleague told the court that when C was at his house and they were watching horse racing, C commented on a presenter on Sky Racing “who was dressed very flamboyantly” and C asked “do you want to know if he is gay’”?

The witness said yes he did and C replied: “He said he was ‘as gay as Alan grabbing me on the cock day’”.

Another pupil at the same school who became friends with C as an adult said he would make reference to things that happened to him while working for Jones, like “being grabbed on the cock” and “that he would be kissed”.

Another colleague, who worked with C for a politician, said C said: In the office “he said when he drove Mr Jones he would put his hand on his leg and go the grope”.

Another former school mate who later became a colleague said at a lunch with friends C adopted a joking tone and said: “Did anything happen with you when you were working with Alan? He tried to kiss me in the lift once. And I said what do you mean?” They never discussed it again.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

The Canning MP says the cartoon, first posted by Hanson on social media over a month ago, calls him a traitor eight times

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie has called Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce “lying cowards”, after he claimed a One Nation cartoon portrayed him as a traitor for providing evidence in court against Ben Roberts-Smith.

Hastie further escalated his fight with One Nation on Wednesday, a day after the Canning MP used a letter to supporters to promise to take on Hanson and her chief strategist, James Ashby, directly – even hinting at costly court action.

Hastie told News24 the One Nation cartoon, first posted by Hanson on social media over a month ago and now pinned to the top of her X account, called him a traitor eight times.

“I would say that Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are lying cowards, and I’ll say it again, so there’s no ambiguity,” he said.

“They are lying cowards … when you start calling me a traitor to my own country, then we have a big, big problem.”

The animated video, called “Don’t be Hastie”, depicts Hastie asking Anthony Albanese for help after people called him a traitor online. When Albanese asks Hastie why people are calling him a traitor, Hastie responds: “I don’t know, all I did was testify against Ben Roberts-Smith and support your evil hate speech legislation.” It has had more than 145,000 views on YouTube.

Hastie served in Afghanistan twice and has attracted the ire of One Nation and Hanson’s billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart, after he gave evidence against Roberts-Smith, the Victoria Cross recipient, in Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation case against Nine newspapers.

Hanson and Rinehart, as well as the former prime minister Tony Abbott, say Roberts-Smith is being unfairly targeted over war crimes allegations related to his service in Afghanistan, between 2009-2012.

The 47-year-old has been charged with five counts of the war crime of murder but strongly denies the allegations.

“Are they saying the same thing of the other 20 SAS combat veterans who gave evidence under oath in the federal court?” Hastie asked.

“Are they also traitors to their country?

“I gave evidence under oath, before God. For that, I’ve been called a rat, a traitor, a dog c—, and many other things. People I trusted have walked away from me or failed to defend me.

“Now I’m calling time on cowards who have never served a day in the Australian Defence Force attacking my service record, my integrity, and my loyalty to Australia.”

Hastie pointed out than Hanson and Joyce had “never, ever served a day in our uniform overseas on operations”.

“They don’t get to define Anzac Day, or Anzac, or the values that underpin our defence force.”

Hanson denied ever calling Hastie a traitor, telling the Nightly: “I will call him a wanker.”

Joyce told Guardian Australia he has never called Hastie a traitor, “nor ventured anywhere close to any such narrative about him”.

“In fact I have never said a bad word about him,” he said.

“This morning in a press conference at Canberra I spoke in support of Mr Hastie and his family. When asked, I noted the fact that Ms Hanson stated she had never called Mr Hastie a traitor. This is now apparent as a fact.

“There has come to my attention now a satirical cartoon that made the claim. I had not seen it nor was aware of it.”

Hastie, the shadow minister for industry and sovereign capability, has spoken publicly about a campaign of threats and abuse targeting him and his family. The federal government boosted security around his home and office earlier this year.

One Nation won this month’s state byelection in the Western Australian seat of Secret Harbour, which overlaps Hastie’s federal electorate of Canning.

The party has flagged a major challenge to oust Hastie at the next election. Hastie is considered the leading alternative to opposition leader, Angus Taylor, but opted not to contest a leadership race earlier this year.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Drinking very hot drinks could triple risk of oesophageal cancer, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Research finds temperature and amount of hot drinks consumed heightens possibility of developing disease

Drinking very hot tea and coffee triples the risk of developing cancer of the gullet, the world’s largest study of the link between them has found.

The findings show that people should let very hot cups of tea and coffee cool down until they are comfortable to drink, in order to reduce their risk of the disease, cancer experts said.

The temperature of the drink and the number of very hot drinks someone consumes increase the chances of getting oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the research found. However, hot drinks do not heighten the risk of getting adenocarcinoma (AC), the other form of oesophageal cancer.

“Consumption of drinks at a ‘very hot’ versus ‘warm’ temperature was associated with a threefold greater SCC risk but not with AC risk, after adjustment for consumption frequency”, according to the study, which was published on Wednesday in the International Journal of Cancer.

“After controlling for drink temperature, daily consumption of six or more versus fewer than six hot drinks was associated with a 71% increase in SCC risk, with little association with AC risk”, said researchers. The study was led by Dr Keren Papier, a senior nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford’s population health department.

The findings are based on analysis of the consumption of hot drinks by almost 980,000 people in the UK – the largest number of people globally in any related studies to date. It followed participants over 14 years to give a long-term picture of their habits and health.

They were asked how they preferred to consume hot drinks. Available answers included “very hot”, “hot”, “warm” and “do not drink hot drinks”. The conclusions were based on people’s estimation of how hot the drinks were that they had consumed rather than their exact temperatures.

The study produced conclusions for a western European population that mirrored similar findings already seen in studies conducted in Asia, Africa, South America and the Middle East, which found that drinking tea or mate – a caffeinated herbal drink popular in South America – at or above 70C increased the risk of oesophageal cancer.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, said in 2016 that hot drinks were “probably carcinogenic to humans” and “one probable cause of oesophageal cancer”. They are thought to heighten the risk of the disease by causing heat damage to the cells which line the oesophagus, which is also known as the body’s foodpipe. Alcohol and smoking are other major risk factors for that type of cancer.

Health authorities could use these latest findings to encourage the public to consume cooler drinks and fewer very hot drinks to help ensure that fewer people are diagnosed with that form of oesophageal cancer, the study team said.

For example, one in seven cases of SCC in the UK “could be avoided if individuals who reported consuming their drinks at a ‘very hot’ temperature instead consumed them at a temperature more representative of the temperature range described as ‘hot’.

The researchers said: “The fact that we observed a clear trend in risk across self-reported temperature categories suggests that further limiting the temperature at which individuals consume their drinks to something well below average for this population may well avoid an even greater proportion of SCC cases.

“This large UK study of middle-aged adults, amongst whom hot drinks are widely consumed, provides clear evidence that temperature and frequency of hot drink consumption represent useful targets for SCC prevention.”

Fiona Osgun, the head of health information at Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, said: “It’s difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool. But if you’re worried, we’d suggest just waiting until it’s comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it’s still very hot.”

However, the charity does not believe that cafes, coffee shops and restaurants should start serving tea and coffee at a lower temperature in order to reduce the risk of SCC.

Muy-Teck Teh, a professor of molecular oral oncology at Queen Mary University of London, said the research’s reliance on self-reported temperatures may have affected the findings.

“A key limitation, however, is that perceived drink temperature is inherently subjective, and it remains unclear whether individuals who tolerate or prefer very hot drinks have altered thermosensation or mucosal sensitivity that might itself reflect underlying biological predisposition to squamous cell carcinoma and lead them to prefer hotter drinks.

“This possibility cannot be excluded and complicates interpretation of causality”, he added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/9/.title: Why Nepal is demanding climate justice and compensation after deadly floods
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/9/.author: Priyanka Shankar
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/9/.text:
Nepal is demanding “climate justice” and $20m in compensation after the recent devastating floods in the country and China’s Tibet region, which led to the deaths and disappearances of thousands of people.

The catastrophe, which scientists say was caused by the effects of climate change, was triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed and a torrent of water and mud flooded down into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions, as well as into China’s Tibet region on August 26. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,000 remain missing.

“We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create,” Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said last week.

“Support for Nepal should not be seen from an angle of aid or charity, but should be seen from the perspective of climate justice,” he told the AFP news agency.

On Monday, the country’s President Ramchandra Paudel made a similar demand during an address to the nation.

“I make a heartfelt appeal to the international community not only to listen to the voices of ecologically vulnerable countries, including Nepal, but also to take concrete and effective steps to ensure climate justice for them,” he said.

Nepal’s Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Environment have written a joint letter to the United Nations, which set up a fund to respond to loss and damage caused by climate change in 2022 in line with the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate, with a request for $20m in damages.

The UN’s Loss and Damage Fund is, however, facing a $2.8bn funding gap as it prepares to approve its first climate recovery projects.

Nepal’s leaders may have a point.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions and generates most of its electricity from renewable sources of energy. Yet its geographical location in the Himalayas makes it particularly vulnerable to severe climate and weather events.

Last month’s catastrophic flooding in the country comes against a backdrop of rapid global warming and glacial loss across the Himalayas.

Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya mountain range – which spans Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan – lost ice 65 percent faster between 2011 and 2020 than during the previous decade.

Nepal’s glaciers, which are sandwiched between two major carbon emitters – India and China – have lost close to one-third of their ice volume in roughly three decades due to global warming, the United Nations said in 2023.

Tanuja Pandey, a Nepal-based climate activist and lawyer, said there is collective frustration behind Nepal’s demand for climate justice.

“People here feel the world often pays attention to Nepal only when a climate disaster becomes impossible to ignore. It is deeply painful to people here that global attention intensifies when headlines report thousands of people dead or missing and in the end, their suffering does not generate any urgency to fight climate change,” she told Al Jazeera.

Shreya KC, a 28-year-old Nepali climate activist, said there is profound anger and sadness among people in Nepal who say that they must no longer continue to suffer the impact of climate change, which, as they see it, other countries are responsible for.

“My hometown is in Solukhumbu in eastern Nepal,” the activist told Al Jazeera. “It is a district of mountains and is also home to the world’s highest mountain, Mount Everest, and my home is also downstream. After the glacial collapse happened two weeks ago, people in my region have realised that this can now happen anywhere in Nepal since the Himalayas are warming and glaciers are melting faster.”

While Nepal has been actively fighting climate change, Shreya KC said she herself has been involved in projects in the country that focus on clean hydropower generation, forestry and other such climate advocacy programmes.

“Because of other countries,” she said, “today Nepalis are the ones most impacted by climate change. So people want justice.”

According to preliminary estimates from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the country’s property, housing and infrastructure losses in the floods amount to some $2.56bn.

But claiming compensation under a notion of “climate justice” won’t be straightforward, according to Joyeeta Gupta, a professor of Environment and Development in the Global South at the University of Amsterdam.

According to the United Nations, “‘climate justice’ is the moral and ethical principle that seeks to address the disproportionate impact of climate change on vulnerable communities and future generations”.

“I define it as a system of justice where others’ perspectives are taken into account, and no harm is caused to others,” Gupta told Al Jazeera.

Nepal is a country that has very low emissions, she said, but is facing the brunt of climate issues which it never created. “That is reason enough for Nepal to claim climate justice,” she noted.

But, practically speaking, can it? In the pre-1990 period, there was a lot of discussion among nations about the need for large emitters to compensate those that would be harmed, Gupta noted. But soon after that, the term “compensation” disappeared from the agenda of international climate treaties, which turned more to discussions about providing assistance to developing countries that need to tackle climate change instead.

In a July 2025 advisory opinion on climate change, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) declared that “all nations have binding legal duties under international law to prevent significant climate harm”.

The ICJ’s advisory opinion on climate change also says that states breaching their international climate obligations can be required to make full reparations, including financial compensation to “injured states” or countries impacted by climate change caused by the actions of other countries.

While the ICJ’s opinion is not legally binding, Gupta said, it is a statement in international law that could support Nepal’s government’s international appeal for climate justice and compensation.

Nepal’s rapper-turned-prime minister, Balendra Shah, is scheduled to travel to New York on September 22 to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on September 24. His country’s appeal for climate justice is expected to be a key part of his address.

For climate activist Shreya KC, while UN meetings and international conferences on climate change may hold some weight when it comes to discussing climate disasters, right now, what Nepal needs is money.

“So much of our money allotted for healthcare, education and to transition into a more developed nation is now being spent on fighting climate change. So countries who are causing emissions, especially from the global north, need to commit more money to the UN’s Loss and Damage Fund,” she said, adding that money from that fund should be disbursed to vulnerable communities in need, not as a loan but as compensation for bearing the brunt of climate change.

Pandey noted that this is not the first time a climate disaster has occurred in Nepal and said that the new government, which came into power in March this year on the back of Nepal’s Gen Z protests last year, has also failed to make climate a priority in its budget.

While it is a good sign that Nepali politicians are appealing for international climate justice, she said, they also need to address the country’s internal development model to fight climate change in the first place.

“There is no climate justice without internal justice within the country itself,” she said.

“I hope that even in our development, partners and investors stop treating climate resilience as an optional addition to development in Nepal just because we are economically vulnerable.

“Investing in Nepal without investing in sustainability is simply a bad investment.”

On Monday, Nepal declared a national day of mourning to remember the more than 1,300 people who are known to have died in last month’s catastrophic floods. Thousands more are still missing.

The country’s President Paudel used the opportunity to call on people to unite.

“This is not a time for division. Nor is it a time to blame one another or become entangled in political disputes and confrontation,” he said.

“This is a time to demonstrate national unity and solidarity. It is also a time for reconstruction, rehabilitation and economic recovery.”

But Gupta says Nepal’s biggest challenge right now is establishing a precedent for compensation for climate change-related disasters.

“It was recently a glacial collapse in the country, but soon, it will become a bigger issue as time goes on because the monsoon patterns will change, the sea level will rise,” she said.

As many other developing countries – notably island states that face being submerged altogether – are also likely facing similar climate change challenges, the damage could become huge.

“That is going to be a very big reason why many rich countries will probably be unwilling to pay compensation, because that would set a precedent for future issues,” Gupta said.

“But the issues countries like Nepal are facing are a very strong argument to try and convince the whole world to accelerate action to phase out fossil fuels and fight climate change.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/9/.summary: More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,000 remain missing. The catastrophe was triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed. Nepal's prime minister is scheduled to address the UN General Assembly on September 22.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/9/.title: Asian Games athletes forced to evacuate amid record rainfall in Japan
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/9/.text:
Hundreds of Asian Games athletes in Japan were briefly evacuated from their accommodation as record rainfall lashed host city Nagoya, officials have said.

About 104mm (4 inches) of rain fell in an hour in Nagoya on Tuesday, prompting municipal officials to issue an evacuation order for parts of the city.

Competition is set to begin on Thursday, with rainwater leaking into some competition venues and more wet weather forecast for the coming days.

Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of weather events in Japan and elsewhere.

This year’s Asian Games has no dedicated athletes’ village, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden containers and hotels.

An official with Nagoya Port Authority said “hundreds” of athletes staying at the city’s Garden Pier area, where the wooden container huts are located, were told to move to safety.

The athletes returned after the evacuation order was lifted about two hours later. Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said the extensive flooding left the athletes unharmed.

“We are not worried about the conditions of the venues, and we believe there is no problem holding the Asian Games as planned,” he told reporters on Wednesday.

Hirosawa said about 400 athletes and staff members staying in converted shipping containers — remodelled to serve as temporary housing units for the Asian Games — were briefly evacuated to higher ground during the heavy rain.

He said there were a number of leaking roofs but nothing more serious around the dozens of games venues.

The Asian Games officially begin with an opening ceremony on September 19, but several events get under way earlier, with the basketball competition beginning on Thursday.

Rainwater was found in several competition venues, but Mayor Hirosawa said the facilities were not seriously affected and that events would go on as scheduled.

“There has been limited impact, like rainwater leaking from the roofs of some buildings, but the situation is not so serious that the opening on the 19th is in jeopardy for now,” he said.

“Given the current circumstances, I believe there will be no obstacles to holding the Asian Games.”

More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected at the games – a bigger number than the Olympics.

Subway and bus services in Nagoya were temporarily halted on Tuesday, and the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its highest flood warning for a major river in the area.

Local media reports said about 3,500 people took shelter at emergency evacuation centres.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/9/.summary: Hundreds of athletes evacuated from their accommodation in Nagoya as record rainfall lashed host city. About 104mm (4 inches) of rain fell in an hour in Nagoyan on Tuesday. Competition is set to begin on Thursday, with rainwater leaking into some competition venues.
