https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.title: Eiffel Tower row over Hindu sect BAPS unites French politicians – but divides Indian diaspora
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.author: Leela JACINTO
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.text:
On Saturday, September 5, as members of a Hindu sect were set to make a splash visit to the Eiffel Tower, an organisation of progressive Indians living in France held a public meeting in Paris to shed some light on the religious group and the international spread of Hindu nationalism, which has been turbocharged during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s tenure.

The French press was invited to the event organised by the Indian Alliance Paris (IAP) and co-hosted by three other organisations, including France’s CGT union. Speakers at the public meeting included activists and researchers from France, as well as the US and India, who joined via video link. They focused on the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a sect that it set to open a large new temple in a Paris suburb. Issues were raised and addressed, a documentary was screened, and a press statement was released after the event.

But there was not much coverage in the French press of a weekend meeting held by one of many diaspora groups in Paris.

That changed on Monday, when the Eiffel Tower was closed after staff went on strike over female workers being removed and replaced by men during a private tour by a BAPS delegation of the Paris landmark.

READ MORE
Eiffel Tower closes due to strike over exclusion of female staff

Suddenly, BAPS and its giant temple in Bussy-Saint-Georges, an eastern suburb located between the French capital and Disneyland Paris, was all over the news. Audiences got a crash course on a sect practicing a “very conservative form of Hinduism” with “close links” to the Modi administration.

WATCH MORE
‘Was this a state visit?’ Indian opposition leader raises serious questions over Paris BAPS temple

“We tried to highlight this issue. We tried to tell them that these people are very conservative and they are very misogynistic. But it didn’t really come into the spotlight,” said IAP secretary Joy Banerjee, listing the many ways his organisation attempted to reach out to left-leaning French political parties and raise awareness of the BAPS agenda. “Suddenly, the mask was dropped on Monday because of the strike.”

The Eiffel Tower reopened to the public on Tuesday. BAPS released a statement noting that, “To our knowledge, at no time was access to the Eiffel Tower denied to anyone. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused.”

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

By then, every French politician worth their salt – and with an eye on the 2027 election – had commented on the fracas. Socialist Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire promised an investigation. Valérie Pécresse, president of the Île-de-France Paris metropolitan area and member of the conservative Les Républicains party, expressed her “shock” on X. French far-right leader Marine Le Pen also got into the act, noting that, “In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be limited."

Just days after many diaspora Indians in France opposed to Modi’s policies got together to raise awareness of BAPS, some were worried about a French far-right, anti-immigrant backlash. On Tuesday morning, the IAP took to X to warn that, “the Eiffel Tower story must not become fodder for more racism,” adding, “BAPS does not represent all Hindus and it certainly does not represent India.”

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

It was not the first time a progressive diaspora group in the West has tried to raise awareness of the inroads far-right ideologies from their homeland were making in their new countries. Many of them have spent months and years watching as Western leaders, driven by economic or geopolitical interests, ignore their warnings and lay out the red carpet for nationalist demagogues without raising human rights concerns. Now, as the far right extends its reach across Western Europe, many fear the awareness amounts to too little, too late.

Founded in 1907 with the consecration of a mandir, or temple, in the village of Bochasan in the western Indian region of Gujarat, BAPS is a denomination of the Swaminarayan Sampradaya, a Vaishnavite sect of Hinduism.

From a little-known village temple, BAPS has grown into a global organisation that manages more than 1,300 temples and more than 5,025 centres across India, North America, Europe, West Asia, Africa and Australia.

The BAPS temple on the outskirts of Paris – believed to be the biggest in Europe built in the traditional style – was inaugurated on Sunday with a video message delivered by the Indian prime minister.

The private Eiffel Tower visit was part of the events from September 3-14 marking the opening of the BAPS temple, billed as a 13-day “festival of culture” that included a procession of boats gliding down the Seine River last week.

In his inauguration address, Modi hailed the temple was as a symbol of bilateral cooperation. "A magnificent temple stands ready today in France and it will not only enrich France's diversity but also energise the cultural relations between India and France," he said.

Under the Modi administration, the construction of temples has been a potent emblem of Hindutva, or Hindu nationalism, propagated by India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the political wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a vast volunteer paramilitary group founded nearly a century ago.

The RSS is an umbrella organisation that includes trade unions, youth groups, prayer associations and women’s groups that are collectively known as the “Sangh Parivar”, or Sangh Family. In addition to the Sangh Parivar, there are also several Hindu right-wing groups and independent actors that follow and spread the Hindutva ideology without formal RSS connections, enabling BJP administrations to maintain plausible deniability when necessary.

“Since Modi came to power, when many BJP politicians do their world tours, they often stop and do a photo-op at a BAPS temple somewhere in the world. So somehow BAPS, even though it isn't traditionally considered part of the Sangh Parivar as such, has become an institution that has very openly been a place for the Indian government to kind of show off because these temples tend to be very big and opulent,” said Sunita Viswanath, co-founder of Hindus for Human Rights, a US-based NGO advocating for pluralism and social justice from a Hindu faith perspective.

On Saturday, for instance, as the IAP was holding its public awareness meeting in Paris, RSS Supreme Leader Mohan Bhagwat was visiting a BAPS temple in London’s Willesden area. Bhagwat was in London after a visit to the US, where he was the keynote speaker at a jam-packed event at New York’s Madison Square Garden. It was followed by a stop in Canada, where he addressed a major gathering in Toronto.

At a media briefing in New Delhi on Tuesday, Indian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked about the Eiffel Tower incident. “We are aware of the opening of the temple of BAPS in Paris. As to the particular issue, this is a matter purely between the entities concerned,” he said.

When asked whether India was now distancing itself even though Modi had participated in the inauguration, Jaiswal stated, “It is a common practice for [the] prime minister to convey his good wishes on such occasions. In this case it was done virtually. There is no cause for any comment in this regard.”

The Eiffel Tower incident is not the first controversy BAPS has faced abroad.

In May 2021, following an FBI raid on a BAPS temple construction site in Robbinsville, New Jersey, six Indian stone workers filed a lawsuit alleging that the sect “weaponised India’s caste system” by coercing men, mostly Dalits from the lowest rungs in India’s social hierarchy, to work under “abysmal” conditions.

Following reports by the New York Times detailing forced labour allegations, the lawsuit was later expanded to include BAPS temple construction sites across the US.

In September 2025, months after President Donald Trump’s second inauguration, the US Department of Justice closed the case without providing a cause.

BAPS North America welcomed the move, noting in a statement that the US government’s “decision to end this investigation sends a clear and powerful message” that their temple is “a place of peace, service, and devotion”.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Critics however say organisations promoting Hindutva overseas attempt to mobilise Hindu communities abroad to provide support to the RSS and BJP. Indian researchers, activists and journalists in the diaspora critical of Hindutva project face trolls, threats and accusations of promoting "Hinduphobia".

In their press statement following Saturday’s public event, the IAP noted that Hindutva groups overseas “also present a deceptive face of their politics by coating it in the language of multiculturalism and pluralism in order to broaden their appeal”.

Given the controversies and numerous reports of work conditions at BAPS temple sites, diaspora Indians opposed to far-right Hindu nationalism say they are surprised the sect got the green light from French authorities for the Paris temple project.

Viswanath, whose US-based NGO has closely monitored the BAPS case in New Jersey, said she was particularly dismayed by French authorities. “The case [in New Jersey] was only dismissed because we have Trump in power. Of course, he's going to dismiss this case. But France, I would think, would be different, since it’s not being run by a far right-wing party. I would think there are different ethical standards,” she said.

In 2023, when Modi made high-profile visits to the US and France, Viswanath was one among many activists calling on the Biden and Macron administrations to raise human rights issues. Their calls fell on deaf ears in Washington and Paris. Three years later, the co-founder of Hindus for Human Rights says she is not surprised by the BPS controversy in France. “It's not a surprise, but it’s certainly very disappointing that they weren't paying attention,” she said.

READ MORE
Arms, not democratic values, on parade as Macron hosts India’s Modi on Bastille Day

BAPS has a history of controversies over its gender policies. At a 2024 event in the eastern Indian city of Kolkata, women seated in the front rows of a gathering of chartered accountants were asked to move away before a speech by a religious leader affiliated with BAPS.

During BAPS religious ceremonies, the “enforcement of strict separation of men and women” has been described as one of the “distinctive features” of the sect, reported the Indian Express, quoting an academic study.

Given its history, Banerjee is particularly irked about conservative French politician Pécresse’s posts denouncing the gender discrimination at the Eiffel Tower. “She's the president of Île-de-France. She didn't inquire about BAPS?” he asked incredulously.

Pécresse, who presided over the temple’s inauguration in Bussy-Saint-Georges on Sunday, stated that the BAPS temple was part of the “strategic partnership” between India and France. “Have French authorities, at all levels, naively or deliberately turned a blind eye to the promoters of this temple construction project?” questioned an IAP statement released Tuesday.

“The French political parties, even the left parties, have not been very interested,” said Banerjee, admitting that economic interests, such as the sale of French Rafale fighter jets to India, enables politicians to celebrate “cultural exchanges” without careful scrutiny.

The one-day Eiffel Tower strike may usher in a change at long last, Banerjee says. “What is happening now is very interesting," he said. "Maybe they understand that they made some mistake rolling out the red carpet to this organisation which is really linked to the Hindutva programme.”
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.summary: The Eiffel Tower closed after staff went on strike over female workers being removed and replaced by men. BAPS is a sect of Hinduism that set to open a large new temple in Paris suburb.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Rubio hails Colombia's new pro-Trump leader De la Espriella on first stop of Latin American tour
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday he hoped to see the US security relationship with Colombia rebound under the country's newly inaugurated far-right president, as Rubio began a tour of Latin American countries whose leaders are closely aligned with US President Donald ​Trump's administration.

Washington is ‌stepping up security engagement with the region on issues including migration and drug trafficking as the US pushes to reassert its influence ⁠across Latin America.

Under the second Trump administration, the US military has carried out deadly strikes on small boats in the Caribbean accused of carrying drugs, seized Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in an armed raid and enforced a crippling fuel blockade on Cuba.

At their meeting in the coastal city ‌of Barranquilla, Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella said he and Rubio discussed security cooperation against drug trafficking, improved economic ties and ⁠an expanded role for Colombia in what he called "bulletproofing the hemisphere". He said Colombia would be an ally to the US on neighbouring Venezuela.

"Colombia wants to newly consolidate itself as the principal hemispheric partner for the United States on security," said De La Espriella, who took office on ​August 7.

READ MORE
Government air strikes kill 20 alleged guerrillas in Colombia, president says

Rubio told reporters that the Pentagon and Colombia's security forces were discussing new cooperation and Colombia's equipment requests. He ‌attributed fraught ties in recent years to De La Espriella's predecessor, the left-wing Gustavo Petro, who frequently clashed with Trump.

Rubio said Washington hoped to restore the cooperation and "perhaps to ‌build upon it".

"And I think you have a president here now that is very interested in making that happen," he said

De La Espriella said Colombia sought US help in the form of aircraft including drones, radar, anti-money-laundering efforts and ​other security tools for its fight against drug gangs.

Rubio agreed Colombia needed help with equipment, intelligence and training but did not specify what the US would provide.

The top diplomat lavished praise on De la Espriella as "a man of strength", joking he had known the Colombian leader long before he "lost his mind and went into politics".

He said it was unusual to visit a country and meet a head of state he had known personally long before reaching office.

Rubio will travel later this week to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa and then to Peru for talks with President Keiko Fujimori, who was inaugurated on ​July 28.

The visit comes at a moment of growing US ideological alignment with all three nations, which Rubio hailed as part of a trend in Latin America toward support for Washington's goals.

"I think it's part of a trend that you're seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with the US and US interests," he said.

The US also hopes to conclude trade ​deals with Colombia, Ecuador and Peru in the near future, Rubio said before departing the US on Tuesday.

Colombia is seeking relief from US tariffs of 12.5 percent that took effect in July, which officials have said could affect Colombian exports.

De La ​Espriella, a millionaire former criminal defence lawyer and businessman who refers to himself as "The Tiger", was endorsed by Trump, and has asked the US leader to suspend the tariff after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck the west of the country in August.

READ MORE
Who is Abelardo de la Espriella, the far‑right Trump fan who could lead Colombia?

De La Espriella said on Tuesday he hoped to cooperate with Washington on what he called a new "Plan Homeland", a reference to "Plan Colombia", a joint programme against drug trafficking that began in the late ⁠1990s under which the US provided billions of dollars to Colombia.

Colombia will fumigate plantations of coca, the base ingredient in cocaine, destroy cocaine laboratories and go after drug bosses, De La Espriella added.

His country ⁠is willing to meet annual ​targets in the fight against drug trafficking, he said, an apparent reference to Trump's spats with De La Espriella's left-wing predecessor over cocaine production.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is visiting Colombia and Ecuador. He is visiting Latin American countries with President Abelardo De La Espriella. Colombia's president says he and Rubio discussed security cooperation against drug trafficking. De La Espriella said Colombia would be an ally to the US on neighbouring Venezuela.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.title: Travellers in UK face ongoing disruption after air traffic control glitch
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
UK travellers faced more misery on Wednesday with more than 150 flights scrapped across the country, as Britain's air traffic control service scrambled to recover from a technical glitch that sparked chaos.

Aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24 said 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday had already been axed, following 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports a day before.

Nearly all the latest affected flights were at Britain's busiest airport Heathrow in London, FlightRadar24 wrote on X.

The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said it was still working to resolve disruption following a "system issue".

"This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover," said NATS in an X post late Tuesday.

READ MORE
European airports scramble to get back online after cyberattack on check-in systems

UK news outlets reported that British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander will meet NATS boss Martin Rolfe on Wednesday.

Rolfe told UK outlet Sky News he accepted "full responsibility" but declined to say if he was considering quitting his job.

Transport Secretary Alexander said earlier on X she was "seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job".

But Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for Rolfe to be fired, accusing him of having again "failed UK travellers".

"Enough is enough, it's time for the UK government to intervene ... and put somebody in charge who can do the job."

Heathrow said late Tuesday that departures had resumed, after the "technical issue" forced the airport to suspend arrivals.

But it warned that "disruption is expected to continue", asking passengers in an X post to check with their airline before travelling to the airport.

British Airways also warned of a "significant knock-in impact" from the cancellations, which had affected tens of thousands of its customers.

NATS said earlier it had "resolved" the glitch that caused the disruption and was "working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights".

"We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly," the organisation wrote on X.

The air traffic chaos follow a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled, prompting anger from airline chiefs.

Britain suffered its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.

Healthcare worker Josie Donoghue said it was "an absolute nightmare" at Gatwick after leaving the airport, having had to disembark her flight to Ireland after three hours stuck on the runway.

"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz," she told Britain's domestic Press Association news agency.

Gatwick announced Wednesday morning that flights had resumed from the airport, though it warned that it would take time for operations to return to normal.

Liverpool, Birmingham and Edinburgh airports were also affected, while Dublin Aiport in Ireland said it had cancelled dozens of flights.

Irish no-frills carrier Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and it had cancelled more than 50 flights.

Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League Wednesday in the southern Italian city, were forced to cancel a news conference ahead of the match after the team's flight was delayed.
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.summary: More than 150 flights cancelled across the country after technical glitch in Britain. Heathrow says departures resumed after "technical issue" forced airport to suspend arrivals. Ryanair COO Neal McMahon calls for NATS boss Martin Rolfe to be fired.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.title: SA government backed a risky horse in LIV Golf — lucky it hedged its bets
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

In 2025, there were cheers when the SA government announced LIV Golf would be held in Adelaide until at least 2031. (ABC News)

Spending at least $45 million to upgrade a golf course so it can host a tour that's filed for bankruptcy is a hard sell.

But that's the position the Malinauskas government would have been lumped with had it not secured hosting rights to the Australian Open golf tournament from 2028.

The announcement in May that the prestigious, traditionalist golf event would be coming to the redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course has taken some of the sting out of what would otherwise have been a nasty political headache surrounding LIV Golf's financial demise.

The acquisition of LIV Golf until 2031 was the impetus for a controversional redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course., (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

The breakaway tour filed for bankruptcy in the US overnight, four months after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund announced it would be pulling its billions in funding.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said the move was intended to keep the league in business while transitioning to a player-first ownership model. It hopes to exit bankruptcy in early 2027.

But the optimism of the press release doesn't quash the uncertainty about what LIV Golf will look like next year and whether it can hold onto the top talent — and party-like atmosphere — that made it such a success in Adelaide.

The tour owes huge sums to creditors, including its star players. Jon Rahm is owed more than $10 million, Bryson DeChambeau nearly $8 million, and Australian Cameron Smith about $6.5 million.

They could all walk away if not convinced by LIV's new model.

Premier Peter Malinauskas went all in on the LIV Golf vision back in February 2025, announcing a six-year contract extension until 2031 and that it would be moving to a new Greg Norman-designed championship course at North Adelaide in 2028.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas announced the six-year LIV Golf contract extension in 2025. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The government has been consistent that there was more to the course upgrade than just LIV Golf, pointing out it will be used by the public outside of events.

But it's also hard to imagine a world where the $45 million upgrade gets green-lighted without LIV Golf in the picture; indeed, the premier indicated as much at the time, saying the 2031 extension "justifies the investment".

"We didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it [LIV Golf] being lost from South Australia," he said in February 2025.

As the negative headlines about LIV Golf's finances piled up, so too did the questions about the justification for the course upgrade.

The development and its loss of 585 trees was always going to spark opposition from parklands advocates, the Greens and elements of Adelaide City Council.

Trees were cut down at the course in May. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

But the prospect of spending $45 million on an upgraded course without a major event connected to it risked a much broader backlash.

If you wanted a sense of the political importance of securing the Australian Open, you only have to look at how prominently it featured in the government's talking points about LIV Golf's bankruptcy today.

The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

"We've been focused on not just LIV Golf but other opportunities," Labor minister Clare Scriven said, "which is why we've been so keen to secure the Australian Open."

Cabinet colleague Nick Champion — who in April said the prospect of LIV Golf ceasing to exist was "just speculation" and "not a question we would ask ourselves" — said today that the state government was not "over-reliant" on one event.

"I appreciate that we're going to have endless media speculation about LIV Golf, but we're upgrading the golf course so that we can have a world class golf course next to a world class [Adelaide] Oval in a world class city," he said.

"And we've got the Australian men's and women's open."

The fight over the North Adelaide course upgrade appears to have largely moved on.

That's partly due to the Australian Open announcement, but also because attention has shifted to the government's controversial MotoGP circuit in the eastern parklands, which will require the felling of at least 377 trees.

The government recently unveiled designs for the MotoGP redevelopment affecting another part of the parklands. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn was today asked whether LIV Golf filing for bankruptcy raised questions about the need for the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade.

"It does, but I think that we're kind of past that point really when you look at how many trees have now been pulled out," she said.

Liberal leader Ashton Hurn says LIV Golf was the primary reason for the North Adelaide redevelopment. (ABC News: Isabella Carbone)

Ms Hurn was more focused today on questioning whether South Australian taxpayers had any exposure in LIV Golf's demise — something the government denies.

"We are good at writing events contracts," Mr Champion said, "we don't provide support for events that aren't held."

If LIV Golf can get out of its current predicament, it is next due in Adelaide in March 2027 at the Kooyonga Golf Club.

The western suburbs club has been waiting on an advanced payment from LIV Golf to help prepare.

The status of that fee remains unclear.

Adelaide's next LIV event is scheduled for March. (ABC News: Will Hunter)

But Australian golf commentator Jimmy Emanuel believes LIV Golf will put on a tournament next year, even if it looks a little different.

"The cost of putting on a tournament in that scale to attract music acts like Fisher is a lot," he said.

"Just building grandstands, building hospitality, those are big commitments financially — the scale of the investment is not going to be the same as it was from Saudi Arabia.

What happens beyond next year is a matter of anyone's guess — but the government remains certain of one thing.

Even if LIV dies, the North Adelaide course upgrade is set to survive.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/j.title: Trial hears woman repeated 'no' to footballers before alleged rape
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/j.author: Giselle Wakatama and Courtney Yeandle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Hayden Topliss (left) and Ryan Hawkshaw are on trial for allegedly raping a woman in 2023. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Ryan Hawkshaw and Hayden Topliss have pleaded not guilty to multiple counts of having sexual intercourse without consent.

Their alleged victim said she was raped by both men in 2023.

The trial is due to run up to 10 days.

A New South Wales jury has been told a woman repeatedly said "no" and "stop" before she was allegedly raped by two country rugby league footballers.

Warning: this story includes details of alleged acts some readers may find distressing.

Ryan Matthew Hawkshaw, 27, and Hayden Charles Topliss, 37, are facing a joint trial in Newcastle District Court after pleading not guilty to a series of charges.

The men are facing four counts of aggravated sexual intercourse in company regarding the alleged rape in Scone in the early hours of the morning in 2023.

The complainant, who cannot be named, continued her evidence on Wednesday before being cross examined.

The woman said she knew of Mr Hawkshaw "as a footy boy" before meeting him.

At the time, both men played for the Scone Thoroughbreds in the Hunter Valley Group 21 Rugby League competition.

Under cross examination the woman denied being interested in Mr Hawkshaw because he was a footy player.

"I knew he was on the [footy] team, I knew he was on the Scone team, I guess," she said.

Ryan Hawkshaw outside Newcastle Courthouse. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

In her opening address on Tuesday, Crown prosecutor Charisse Hodgeman told jurors the woman had exchanged prior Instagram messages with Mr Hawkshaw.

The messages talked about giving lifts and sex.

The court heard on the night before the alleged assault Mr Hawkshaw messaged saying "oi pick us up" to give the two defendants a lift.

Ms Hodgeman told jurors the woman picked the men up from a local RSL club that night, driving them to "Toppers" [Topliss's] house, as requested.

Once there the court heard she had consensual sex with Mr Hawkshaw before he asked if she wanted "Topper" to join.

The Crown said the woman said "no" before Mr Topliss came in naked.

Ms Hodgeman told the jury the woman repeatedly said "no" and "stop" as she was forced down, repositioned and assaulted.

She "repeatedly said she did not want to have threesome" when Mr Hawkshaw said "come on, we'll get Topper in".

The prosecutor told jurors she confided in a relative the next day.

Both men said all sexual acts were consensual and reject claims they operated as part of a joint criminal enterprise.

In her opening address barrister Sharyn Hall, representing Mr Topliss, told jurors they had probably all heard "far too much about footballers and their sex lives".

The men are on trial in Newcastle District Court. (ABC Newcastle: Robert Virtue)

Ms Hall said it might be easy to "assume the worst" in relation to what footballers got up to on their weekends.

She then paused and said if they made assumptions they would be in breach of the promise they had made to the court.

"Hayden Topliss maintains that each of the sexual acts that happened in that spare bedroom were consensual," Ms Hall said.

Barrister Caitlin Akthar, representing Mr Hawkshaw, questioned whether they could rely on the complainant.

While under cross examination of the complainant Ms Akthar took her through some Instagram messages, including one on the night of the alleged rape.

Ms Akthar put to the woman that Mr Hawkshaw had messaged her that night saying he wanted to have sex with her. The woman agreed that was the exchange.

It was then put to the complainant that she had replied asking whether he was sure "because what about the other chick". The woman confirmed that she sent the message.

Mr Topliss is facing a fifth charge of sexually assaulting the woman on the same night and a sixth charge of sexual touching the complainant in 2024.

The trial is due to run up to 10 days.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

SA Police arrested an 18-year-old driver after he allegedly performed a Nazi salute during a traffic stop. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

A driver accused of performing a Nazi salute during a traffic stop in Adelaide's north is also facing possible drug driving charges, police say.

The 18-year-old man was pulled over by police on Tuesday after he allegedly began driving aggressively behind an unmarked police vehicle on Main North Road at Smithfield.

After stopping the Davoren Park man's Toyota sedan in a nearby car park about 5pm, police conducted drug and alcohol testing.

Police allege the driver returned a positive roadside drug test to cannabis.

The man was arrested and charged with making the gesture and was handed an immediate three-month loss of licence.

Police said he could also face drug driving charges "pending the results of forensic analysis".

They said he would appear in the Elizabeth Magistrates Court at a later date.

A ban on the public display of Nazi symbols came into effect in South Australia in 2024.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.title: How thieves stole paintings worth millions in Renoir heist
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.author: Daniela Pizzirani
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (left) and a portrait of Madame Pichon were targeted by the thieves.   (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

Thieves sliced through a fence, grabbed 9 million euros ($14.5 million) worth of art, dumped half of it in a garden and escaped in under three minutes.

That's what went down when two thieves targeted the most valuable works of the famous impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir at a museum on the French Riviera.

The theft conjured up painful memories of the crown jewels heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and triggered a national search for the perpetrators.

Here's how they pulled it off.

A half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir's last home before he died aged 78 in 1919, lies the Renoir Museum.

On Tuesday, two "well-equipped" thieves cut through the garden fence of that home using an "electric knife or saw", the Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson said.

The thieves broke into the museum by cutting a hole in the outer fence. (Reuters: Manon Cruz)

Shortly before 6am in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, they entered the museum on the ground flood via the garden and climbed through a window before cutting the clips securing the frames of four Renoir paintings.

This triggered the museum's alarm system.

And within three minutes, the thieves had fled the scene through a garden, abandoning two of the artworks in the dirt.

Five minutes later, the police arrived.

"The museum and police sirens forced the burglars to hurry, stealing only four works from the Renoir Museum," the mayor said.

The thieves targeted the museum in the early hours of Tuesday.    (AFP: Valery Hache)

Renoir's art has fetched dozens of millions of dollars at auctions due to his pioneering portrait technique, particularly of women.

The French artist was one of the leading painters in the Impressionist movement.

Some of his more famous works are on display at the Musee d'Orsay in Paris, as well as in London and New York.

Of the four works stolen, two were left behind in the museum gardens, Portrait of Madame Pichon and Coco Reading, the prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Coco Reading, known as Coco Lisant (1905) by Renoir, was one of the paintings reportedly stolen. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

The two still missing are Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well.

At least two of the works targeted during the heist had a troubled history.

Young Woman at the Well is believed to have been looted by the Nazis during World War II, and was recovered in Bavaria in 1949 and brought back to France, according to the French Culture Ministry database.

A German officer in Paris gave Coco Reading to a German soldier at the end of the war under orders to take it to Germany, according to the database.

Young Woman at the Well was stolen from the Renoir Museum. (Reuters)

The soldier later gave it to a German priest, who handed it over to a Berlin museum in 1972.

Germany's government returned it to France in 1994.

Art theft expert James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register said unlike the Louvre heist targeting gold or jewels that could be melted down or recut, the Renoir theft left the thieves in a predicament.

''Although the [paintings] are valuable, and will have probably seven figures attached to them in terms of the financial value, trying to find a buyer who will pay that is going to be almost impossible for them,'' Mr Ratcliffe told AP.

''Unless they have a plan for that in advance, they're not going to be able to just go to an art dealer and say, 'Look, I've got these two nice Renoirs, would you like to buy them?'"

He said that underfunding was the main problem facing museums everywhere, not just in France, and smaller museums were especially exposed because of their limited finances.

''The theft of the Louvre has demonstrated to everybody with criminal intent that museums are potentially soft targets,'' he said.

"People are looking at museums differently.''

There are revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France's landscape.

The Marseille prosecutor opened an investigation into theft by an organised gang.

Bryan Masson speaks to the press outside Musée Renoir, which was closed on Tuesday.   (AFP: Valery Hache)

"This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums," the mayor said.

The museum was closed Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.

https://www.dw.com/en/brics-leaders-gath.title: BRICS leaders gather in India, but does the group have a clear purpose?
https://www.dw.com/en/brics-leaders-gath.text:
The 18th BRICS summit takes place in India this weekend. Unlike last year, the leaders of China and Russia are coming. But does the expanded group have a clear common mission and purpose?

In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.

For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.

"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."

Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi Jinping is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.

"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.

She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.

However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.

"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".

However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.

"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the west as a whole.

"India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"

Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."

BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.

The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.

"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.

"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."

Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."

He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.

"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Trump administration to confront Australia over Labor’s social media algorithm plan
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Luca Ittimani
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
White House warns trading partners against ‘imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion’ on US tech sector

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Trump administration will confront Australia over its plan to force digital platforms to take down harmful content and let users opt out of algorithm-generated “for you” feeds.

Big tech companies would be fined more than $100m for breaching the proposed laws and the Australian government is under pressure to raise those fines even further.

A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said the US administration would raise its concerns with “trading partners”, in a statement released less than 24 hours after Australia’s announcement on Tuesday.

“President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector,” Desai said.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, downplayed the statement as “broad” and told News24 she had not directly received any such warning from a US representative.

“We’re a sovereign nation,” Wells said. “We have the right to defend Australian parents and kids and we’ll do that.”

If passed, the digital duty of care laws would require platforms to protect children from harmful content around eating disorders, misogyny, pornography, glorifying crime, abuse and cyberbullying. Adults and children would need to be protected from illegal material.

They would also require platforms to send users a notification or “pop-up”, giving them a choice between a main feed that shows personalised content from across the platform or one that shows only content shared by their online connections.

The Greens party has demanded the government make the latter option the default setting and force platforms to let users opt in to having personalised feeds.

The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young repeated calls for higher fines to be pegged to companies’ global revenue, speaking to ABC radio on Wednesday.

“Big tech is going to spend a lot of money fighting these laws in the first place and finding every which way to get around them,” Hanson-Young said.

“You need to hit them really where it hurts, and that’s their revenue.”

Big tech companies Meta, Google and TikTok have not publicly commented, though their representative lobby group, Digi, has said the law’s definitions of harmful content and impact on user experience would be crucial.

OpenAI, owner of ChatGPT, said it planned to engage with the government on its laws to ensure they were “protecting Australians while enabling them to benefit from AI”.

Sign up to Politics, really

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

after newsletter promotion

Australian businesses have warned the rules could hurt their own revenue, as Australians who opt out of algorithms may stop seeing advertisements and buying from companies that sell via online platforms.

The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia has asked the government to model the costs to small businesses and their visibility in feeds.

The Labor government is also facing backlash from local conservatives, with the Coalition accusing Labor of using the bill to censor free speech.

The proposal would give the communications minister the power to set new definitions for harmful content that would have to be taken down.

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said this could extend to political speech that opposed the government.

“I don’t trust big tech, but I trust the Labor party a lot less,” Canavan said.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Canavan’s comments were “disingenuous” as the Senate would be able to reject the minister’s definitions.

Wells has repeatedly committed to leaving political content and misinformation outside the scope of the laws.

“Your right to be wrong on the internet remains preserved in the digital duty of care,” Wells said. “If you want to believe that the moon landing was fake, it is in no way impacted by the digital duty of care.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/anthropi.title: Anthropic researcher says AI has more than 10% chance of 'killing all humans' after colleague quits
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/anthropi.author: Arjun Kharpal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/anthropi.text:
Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger said there is a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

Another Anthropic researcher said he has resigned, accusing leading AI labs of racing toward superintelligence without adequate safeguards.

The warnings add to growing concerns over AI safety, including whether advanced systems could become difficult for humans to control.

There is more than a 10% chance that artificial intelligence could “kill all humans,” an Anthropic safety researcher said on Tuesday, hours after another employee said he was quitting the company over concerns that AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”

The comments underscore growing concerns among those at the heart of AI development that the technology could get out of control and pose a threat to humanity, even as Anthropic and OpenAI continue to raise large sums of money and head toward expected public listings.

Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, said on Tuesday he resigned from the company. Coxon said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is acting responsibly.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said in a post on X.

Self-improvement is the idea that AI systems can improve themselves without much human intervention. Recursive self-improvement, as it is often called, is not yet possible, but AI labs are working toward the goal.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing,” Coxon said.

He added that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

That comment prompted a response from Evan Hubinger, an alignment science lead at Anthropic, who said that not only was Coxon’s statement “correct,” but also that Anthropic has no plan for this scenario.

“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger said on X.

Anthropic and OpenAI were not immediately available for comment when contacted by CNBC.

In June, Anthropic had noted that “full recursive self-improvement also might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems.”

“If systems are capable of fully building their own successors, the ways we secure them, monitor them, and shape their behavior all grow much more important,” Anthropic said in a blog post.

Concerns over out-of-control AI are not new. Tesla
 and SpaceX
 CEO Elon Musk has warned over the past few years that AI could pose a threat to humanity. Major researchers and academics have also sounded the alarm over companies losing control of AI systems.

Those worries have grown after an OpenAI model went rogue in July and breached Hugging Face, a major platform for open-source developers.

Coxon cited the Hugging Face incident as an example of “warning shots” that have made agreements between U.S. labs more viable, making him more optimistic about the potential for coordination. But Coxon warned a global AI race would be unavoidable.

“I don’t feel like we’re on track to prevent a global race, which may require costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities,” Coxon said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/daily-op.title: CNBC Daily Open: Gulf strikes jolt oil toward triple digits
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/daily-op.author: Leonie Kidd
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/daily-op.text:
Iran’s military claims it has hit two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf.

It marks a fresh retaliation after the U.S. said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers.

Oil is driving higher towards $100 a barrel for Brent.

China’s wholesale inflation tops estimates in August, while the Bank of England warns of another inflation burst.

U.S. futures are flat after the Dow falls 600 points.

Taken from CNBC’s Daily Open, our international markets newsletter — Subscribe today

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd coming to you from London. Welcome to another edition of CNBC’s Daily Open.

Markets seem trapped in a cycle of Iran tensions leading to higher oil prices, which leads to stocks moving lower and ultimately inflation concerns rising.

Wednesday is no different, with crude prices marching back towards triple digits and inflation sirens ringing from Beijing to London to Washington.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed it has struck two U.S. vessels and a further eight oil tankers in the Gulf. The move comes in response to American military attacks on five Iranian crude oil tankers, which U.S. Central Command said it had destroyed on Tuesday.

The strikes from both sides mark an escalation in military hostilities as the Trump administration continues its pressure on Tehran via economic sanctions.

The developments are keeping oil prices sharply higher. In early Wednesday trade, U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures for October delivery are holding around $94 a barrel, while futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark, are within cents of $100 a barrel.

Speaking on “Squawk Box Asia,” Daan Struyven, Goldman Sachs’ co-head of global commodities research, said that prices driving above $120 “is definitely plausible.”

The inflationary fallout is being felt across the globe. Data for August shows Chinese wholesale inflation topping expectations, pushed higher by commodity costs.

Meanwhile, in the U.K., Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned that inflation risks are on the upside. Addressing the Commons on Tuesday, he said, “we have higher energy prices, and they could be higher still.”

The negative sentiment is playing out in stock markets, with the Dow closing 600 points lower in back-to-back losses. Asian equities are mixed in Wednesday’s trade, while U.S. and European futures are lacking direction.

It’s a tough day on the fairway for LIV Golf. The sporting venture has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection after its key backer — Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund — indicated it would pull funding. The group is now searching for new investment.

Hit TV show ‘South Park’ becomes ‘South America’

Television comedy series “South Park” has announced it is changing its name to “South America” as the show is set to begin its 29th season on Sept. 16.

The show’s creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone said, “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA. We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount
 — a Skydance Capitulation.”

Oil is driving higher towards $100 a barrel for Brent crude, the international benchmark, for Brent. The Bank of England warns of another inflation burst.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.author: Clare Armstrong
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Andrew Hastie is taking issue with a cartoon published on Pauline Hanson's X account. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Andrew Hastie has called Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce "lying cowards" in an escalating dispute over a One Nation video describing him as a "traitor".

Mr Joyce said he had not used the term and backed Ms Hanson's similar denial, but confirmed the claim had appeared in a "satirical cartoon" he had not previously seen.

Mr Hastie has vowed to fight to retain his West Australian seat, which is being targeted by One Nation at the next federal election.

Opposition frontbencher Andrew Hastie has called Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce "lying cowards" in an escalating stoush over a One Nation video that repeatedly describes him as a "traitor".

Mr Hastie has challenged Senator Hanson and Mr Joyce to "own" the accusation or delete the video, which took aim at his involvement in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case.

Mr Hastie, a former SAS officer who served in Afghanistan, was subpoenaed to give evidence in the 2022 trial and has defended doing so as consistent with the rule of law and standards expected of Australian soldiers.

In an email to supporters on Tuesday, Mr Hastie said One Nation had "picked a fight with the wrong veteran".

In response, Senator Hanson told The Nightly she had "never called him a traitor" but would "call him a wanker".

One Nation's Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce both denied calling Mr Hastie a traitor. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Joyce on Wednesday stood by this denial and suggested Mr Hastie was being "emotional" due to the electoral threat One Nation posed to his West Australian seat of Canning.

"I spoke to Pauline this morning about this, and she never called him a traitor," Mr Joyce said.

But Mr Hastie fired back, calling Senator Hanson and Mr Joyce "lying cowards" and presenting screenshots of a video as a "receipt" to support his claim.

He said the One Nation leader posted the cartoon to her X account in which he was described as a "traitor" eight times as well as a "gutless maggot".

"I am proud of my service to this country, in uniform and in this parliament," Mr Hastie said.

Mr Hastie said One Nation must either delete the video or "own" the accusation made against him.

"Your choice," he said.

Mr Joyce responded to this challenge on Wednesday afternoon, telling the ABC he had never called Mr Hastie a traitor or "ventured anywhere close to any such statement about him".

"Paradoxically, this morning in a press conference at Canberra I spoke in support of Mr Hastie and his family," Mr Joyce said.

"When asked, I noted the fact that Ms Hanson stated to me she had never called Mr Hastie a traitor.

"This is now apparent as a fact, she hasn't."

Mr Joyce said it had since come to his attention that a "satirical cartoon" had made the claim.

"I had not seen it nor was I aware of it," he said.

Mr Hastie has been the target of One Nation criticism over his decision to testify in the defamation case brought by Mr Roberts-Smith, a former SAS soldier and Victoria Cross recipient who is now fighting war crimes charges.

Mr Roberts-Smith lost his case against the Nine papers in 2023 after the Federal Court found, on the civil standard of the balance of probabilities, that allegations he was involved in unlawful killings in Afghanistan were substantially true.

He has since been charged with five counts of the war crime of murder over the alleged killings of five Afghan men between 2009 and 2012, which he has denied.

Former SAS corporal Ben Roberts-Smith has been charged with five counts of the war crime murder, which he denies. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Senator Hanson has repeatedly vocalised her support for Mr Roberts-Smith, vowing not to "abandon" him.

Her party has also campaigned with posters declaring "One Nation stands with him".

Mr Hastie has accused One Nation of politicising the case.

"I stand with a lot of Australians who believe in the rule of law, who believe that Australian soldiers should be held to high standards of battlefield conduct," he said.

"Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce have never, ever served a day in our uniform overseas on operations.

"They don't get to define Anzac Day or Anzac or the values that underpin our defence force."

Earlier this week, Mr Hastie vowed to make the fight for his seat a "costly exercise" in time, money and political capital for One Nation, declaring the party would at best achieve a "Pyrrhic victory".

The shadow industry minister's seat of Canning covers a large part of the state electorate of Secret Harbour, which One Nation won in a by-election last month.

Senator Hanson has made no secret of her desire to win Mr Hastie's seat at the next election, prompting a WA paper to splash "I'm Canning for you next" on its front page over the weekend.

The former girlfriend of Ben Roberts-Smith has been asked about her pregnancy and miscarriage in court, while sobbing in the witness box

Speaking on Wednesday, Mr Hastie said he was going to fight "exceptionally hard" to hold onto Canning against both One Nation and Labor at the next election in 2028.

"I'm not worried about losing my seat; I'm worried about being called a traitor after serving my country," he said.

Mr Hastie said One Nation had "picked a fight with the wrong veteran".

"They thought I'd just lie down and cop it; guess what, you've unlocked an achievement, and I'm going to fight all the way," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/e.author: Isobel Roe

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Alan Jones denies all allegations against him. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

A former politician giving evidence at Alan Jones's trial says he did not see the broadcaster kiss a prominent athlete at an event a decade ago.

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.

The trial has been discussing evidence related to one alleged victim, who has not yet given evidence.

A former politician giving evidence in broadcaster Alan Jones's criminal trial has been questioned about an event where Mr Jones allegedly kissed a prominent athlete on the mouth.

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching relating to six men, and has been standing trial in the NSW Local Court.

An ex-politician, who had been called to give evidence about another complainant, has also been asked about what he saw at an event a decade ago, which he attended.

Mr Jones allegedly kissed a prominent athlete, known as Complainant M, on or near his mouth during that evening, and has been charged with one count of indecent assault.

Mr Jones allegedly kissed an athlete on the mouth at an event.  (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

The former politician was shown several photographs of the event, and under cross-examination by Mr Jones's barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, he said he did not see anything inappropriate.

"You did not see Alan Jones kissing [Complainant M] on any part of his mouth that night did you?" Ms Bashir asked.

"No," the politician replied.

"If you had seen Alan Jones kissing [Complainant M] on any part of his mouth that night you would remember seeing it, wouldn't you?"

"I would remember that," the politician replied.

The prosecution has told the court that Complainant M, who is yet to give evidence in the trial, received weekly flowers from Mr Jones for more than a year and regularly received text messages with declarations of love and affection.

The former politician said he could not say how often he observed the complainant on the night of alleged offence.

The witness had been called to give evidence about Complainant C, a former colleague of Mr Jones, who has alleged Mr Jones kissed and touched him multiple times in 2008.

He told the court Complainant C worked for him for a period of time, and he took the complainant to a work meeting with Mr Jones in his Circular Quay apartment, in about 2018.

The politician told the court the complainant appeared uncomfortable at the meeting, but he chose not to ask his employee why.

"My recollection of that meeting was C was sunken and diminished," he said.

"I've spent quite a bit of time with [Complainant C], his behaviour was quite different to his normal behaviour."

Gabrielle Bashir is Mr Jones's barrister. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Another witness, a man who took over Complainant C's job after he left, has told the court Mr Jones never behaved inappropriately towards him.

The witness said Complainant C recommended the job to him, and he did it for a number of months before moving on.

"Did [Complainant C] tell you anything that made you think you had to be on your guard?" Defence barrister Claire O'Neil asked.

"No," the man replied.

"Did he tell you Alan might try to touch your penis in the car?"

The witness said it was some years after he had finished the job, that Complainant C asked him "in a jovial tone" at a social lunch whether Mr Jones had ever "tried to do anything", and said that Mr Jones had "tried to kiss him in a lift once".

The witness said he was confused by the question, and responded with words like, "What do you mean?"

But he said the conversation moved on.

He said he was then contacted by Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) journalist Kate McClymont in 2023, while she was researching a story about Mr Jones.

"I told her words to the effect of, 'Mr Jones has never done anything to me in that way.' I've told every journalist that who's ever called me," he said.

A statement from the complainant's father-in-law was also read to the court, and described the complainant telling him stories about his time working with Mr Jones, including that Mr Jones "pushed him up against a wall and kissed him".

He said another story involved the complainant going to Mr Jones's apartment known as 'The Toaster', where he said Mr Jones was wearing a robe and nothing underneath, so that when he sat down "his undercarriage was hanging out".

The father-in-law said Complainant C also discussed suing Mr Jones around 2018 or 2019, and that he warned the complainant that he should be "careful of the flow on effects" of being involved in such legal action.

Several friends of Complainant C have also given evidence about things the complainant told them about Mr Jones's behaviour.

One man told the court he was on a work trip with Complainant C and talking about Mr Jones, when the man said that the broadcaster had "reached into his crotch and squeezed it" while driving.

"Did you say anything in response?" crown prosecutor Emma Curran asked.

"I said… 'What the f***'," the man said.

"His response was to me, 'That's Alan, that's just his behaviour.'"

Other friends recalled to the court that Complainant C would "joke" or speak in a "light-hearted" way about Mr Jones's alleged assaults in social settings.

One friend said Complainant C described watching horse racing on the TV, and commenting on a "flamboyantly" dressed presenter.

He said Complainant C said the man was "as gay as Alan grabbing me on the cock gay".

The glass roof collapsed at a construction site near Curtin University's medical school.

A steel fabrication company that provided the supports for a roof that collapsed at Curtin University's medical school in 2020, has admitted responsibility in court.

An apprentice carpenter was killed and several others injured in the incident.

The company will be sentenced in October.

A company that provided steel supports for a roof that collapsed at Perth's Curtin University, killing a worker and injuring another, has admitted responsibility in court six years after the incident.

Apprentice carpenter Jonathan Hartshorn, 23, died in the 2020 roof collapse while Rikki Issitt suffered serious injuries which have prevented him from working.

Steel fabrication company Elsdon had pleaded guilty to failing to ensure workers' safety.

Perth Magistrates Court was shown two sets of CCTV footage of the incident, from different angles, with the two workers standing on the roof and then falling as it gave way.

The confronting video showed men running to the scene after the collapse.

Several workers were injured in the collapse.   (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Two other workers who were under the canopy were also injured.

The court heard that the welding for trusses was not done to specification, nor was it overseen by a qualified supervisor.

Mr Hartshorn and Mr Issitt were not directly employed by Elsdon at the university site, which was a Lendlease project.

Limping to the witness box, Mr Issitt told the court how he fell more than 20 metres, thinking he was going to die. He suffered multiple injuries, including to his spine and pelvis.

Rikki Issitt, who fell 20 metres in the accident, told the court he had suffered both physically and psychologically. (ABC News: Davi Weber)

In an emotional statement, Mr Issitt said the accident had taken away his career and subjected him to years of almost constant pain and psychological distress.

Mr Hartshorn's mother Susan Chappell also read out a statement through tears, saying her son "had a right to go home at the end of that day".

Mr Hartshorn's mother, Susan Chappell, gave an emotional statement to the court. (ABC News: David Weber )

She said he was a hardworking apprentice whose "future was torn from underneath him".

In a statement read to the court,  Mr Hartshorn's partner, Kylie Galende, said she thought she was going to spend the rest of her life with him, but was now learning to live without him.

Prosecutor Eric Heenan said the majority of the welds inspected after the incident had defects.

He told the court that Elsdon, in its defence, said it did not know it was sending inadequate welds to the site, but there had been "no procedures, no qualified welder, no supervisor, no test".

Mr Heenan said there was no adequate testing procedures. (ABC News: David Weber)

The maximum penalty under the legislation in force at the time is a $2 million fine.

Elsdon's lawyer Alex Mossop said the company accepted the welds at the trusses were meant to be "full penetration" and were not, and it did not know that its workshop "was not achieving".

Elsdon is due to be sentenced in October.

Stantec Australia, which was charged with failing to ensure the safety of workers, had both charges discontinued in May due to insufficient evidence, and had costs awarded.

The court heard separate civil proceedings had been initiated.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.title: 'Taking away my rights': Resident to fell giant tree before council rule change
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.author: Samantha Goerling and Nadia Mitsopoulos
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Melville resident Susan plans to cut down a mature tree in her backyard before the council introduces a tree retention policy. (ABC News: Kenith Png )

A home owner in Perth’s south plans to cut down a 20-metre tall “beast” of a tree in order to beat the introduction of a local council policy to protect large trees, despite the dwindling tree canopy across the city.

City of Melville resident Susan said she would fork out $10,000 to remove the Norfolk pine from her backyard while the council worked on a draft policy designed to retain trees on private property.

Susan, who asked for her surname to be withheld, said she promised the former owners she would keep the tree when she bought the block nearly two decades ago, but has now changed her mind.

“I understand the argument for, and I understand the argument against, but I cannot have a council take away my rights,” she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

The 20 metre Norfolk Pine stands tall at the edge of Susan's backyard.  (ABC News: Kenith Png )

Of all the Australian capital cities, Perth has the lowest tree canopy — shade that can lower temperatures by several degrees Celsius on days of extreme heat.

The state government has set a target to increase Perth’s tree canopy cover from 16 to 30 per cent by 2040.

The state government aims to plant one million trees in Perth by 2035.  (ABC News: Kenith Png)

The City of Melville's draft policy aims to protect medium and large trees where reasonable and practical.

Approval would need to be obtained to remove or damage a tree taller than 8 metres, with a tree canopy of more than 6 metres in diameter or a trunk circumference of more than 1.5 metres.

Despite neighbours complaining about the tree's roots and leaves encroaching on their property over the years, Susan said she previously had no intention of removing the Norfolk pine.

And although she was not planning to subdivide, she said she wanted to avoid potential complications if development opportunities arose for future owners.

“If I moved out, I can tell you that it would pass to someone else, so my child, and I don't want to feel like I'm robbing her of a development opportunity,” Susan said.

Susan said she had promised the previous home owners she would not cut down the tree.  (ABC News: Kenith Png )

The draft policy is based on a model Tree Retention policy developed by the WA Local Government Association, which has so far been adopted by 11 local governments.

Western Australian Tree Canopy Advocates community engagement lead Ester Cole said it was not a radical policy.

“This is pretty standard now and the sky hasn't fallen in,” she said.

The WA government is facing renewed questions over its plans to boost Perth's tree cover, with experts saying current funding will not come close to delivering on Labor's election promises.

She said the policy did not preclude development, but "gives a pause".

“What the council will do when there's a subdivision application is they'll ask, ‘is there a way we can keep the mature trees we've got?’

“Now maybe in Susan's case that's not possible, but maybe in another case it is.”

Local Planning Minister John Carey said Susan’s concerns typified the debate on trees as the state government looks to boost infill with an overhaul of residential design codes.

“Everyone wants to ensure that we increase our tree canopy but at the same time, when local governments are bringing in local planning policies - which I'm not criticising - but I am saying they are complex and it can affect development ... and it can affect someone's choice about what they're doing on their property,” he said.

“It's not black and white where the location of the tree can affect a residential development and it's not always easy while we want it [to be] for people to design around that.”

John Carey said local planning policies can be complex and affect development.  (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

The proposed changes to the residential design codes, which would allow about 50,000 extra residential properties to be built in Perth, are expected to be released for public comment later this year.

The City of Melville has been contacted for comment.
