https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/openai-n.title: OpenAI claims to have solved the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes math problem in 88 hours
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/openai-n.author: Katrina Bishop
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/openai-n.text:
OpenAI said 10,000 of its agents solved the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours.

The company, which is behind ChatGPT, said it used a system of 10,000 “coordinating agents” powered by its internal AI model to solve the equation.

But OpenAI’s work drew questions from Tristan Buckmaster, a professor of mathematics at New York University.

OpenAI says it solved the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes mathematics problem in 88 hours, using 10,000 agents and a new artificial intelligence model.

In a release published Tuesday, OpenAI — the company behind the ChatGPT AI chatbot — said it was “sharing a solution” to the problem, which relates to how fluids move.

It said it used a system of “coordinating agents” powered by its internal AI model.

“The agents had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code. Agents were subdivided into groups with the ability to communicate within the group,” OpenAI said. “The groups varied in size, and the group that produced the Navier–Stokes resolution involved on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents.”

“The agents arrived at their resolution on Saturday, September 5, about 88 hours after the first agents were launched,” the company added.

Navier–Stokes is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, considered to be among the most difficult mathematical problems at the start of this century.

The Clay Mathematics Institute of Cambridge, Massachusetts, which founded the Prize Problems, has not yet commented on OpenAI’s proposed solution.

OpenAI’s work drew questions from Tristan Buckmaster, a professor of mathematics at New York University, however.

In a statement on his website, Buckmaster explained that he had been working with fellow mathematician Levent Alpöge, who works at OpenAI rival Anthropic, in a “personal collaboration” on math problems including Navier–Stokes.

He said Alpöge received “tips” that information about the pair’s progress had been passed to OpenAI. He said the tech giant’s route to the solution was similar to their own work, which is “not the direction one arrives at in a few days by giving a model the problem statement.”

Buckmaster also raised questions over whether OpenAI models had been trained on, or had access to, their sessions in OpenAI’s Codex. He said the mathematicians had used several large language models as part of their work.

“I would like to be clear about what I am not claiming. I have not seen OpenAI’s proof. I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used,” Buckmaster added.

In its statement, OpenAI said its effort to solve the Navier–Stokes mathematics problem began on Sept. 1 after “hearing a rumor” about progress on the puzzle that it later found out related to Alpöge and Buckmaster.

“We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem. While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠,” the company added.

The Clay Mathematics Institute established the Prize Problems in 2000, putting up a $1 million prize for the solution of each problem.

“The Prizes were conceived ... to elevate in the consciousness of the general public the fact that in mathematics, the frontier is still open and abounds in important unsolved problems; to emphasize the importance of working towards a solution of the deepest, most difficult problems; and to recognize achievement in mathematics of historical magnitude,” the institute says on its website.

Other problems include the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture, which relates to elliptic curves, and the Riemann Hypothesis, which relates to prime numbers.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/iceland-.title: ‘This is not a joke’: Iceland condemns Trump’s post showing island under American flag
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/iceland-.author: Sam Meredith
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/iceland-.text:
Iceland summoned the U.S. ambassador after Trump posted a map showing Iceland under the American flag.

Reykjavik said the image was unacceptable, while reaffirming its support for Greenland amid Trump’s annexation threats.

Denmark and Mexico also objected, underscoring the diplomatic backlash to Trump’s territorial ambitions.

Iceland has sharply criticized U.S. President Donald Trump’s social media post of a map that appears to show the island and several other countries covered by the American flag.

Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, depicting the U.S., Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean under the Stars and Stripes flag.

The map was published without comment and came after a flurry of preceding posts suggesting that the U.S. state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America.”

Iceland summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long over the incident, with Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir saying the meeting was necessary to “make it absolutely clear that, from our perspective, this was completely unacceptable.”

Speaking at a news conference, Gunnarsdottir said that the Nordic nation of nearly 400,000 stood with Greenland over Trump’s annexation threats and would not soften its position on the matter.

“It is absolutely clear that this is a fundamental principle. In my view, this is not a joke, and if it is meant to be a joke, it is a very poor one,” Gunnarsdottir said, according to Iceland’s national broadcaster RÚV.

A White House spokesperson was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Wednesday morning.

The U.S. president has long advocated for control over Greenland, a self-governing Danish territory, on national security grounds. Notably, Trump appeared to repeatedly mix up Greenland and Iceland during a special address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier in the year.

More recently, Iceland voted to reject restarting talks to join the European Union as domestic issues such as control over fishing appeared to take priority over geopolitical security concerns.

Danish and Mexican government officials also took exception to Trump’s post.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen reportedly described the post as “disturbing and, in many ways, completely inappropriate.”

In comments made to national broadcaster DR, Rasmussen added: “It’s obviously a sign that the U.S. president still harbors some kind of maximalist vision in his own mind. We need to rein that in.”

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, meanwhile, said Monday that the country “is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country.” She added: “Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/iceland-.summary: Iceland summoned U.S. ambassador after Trump posted a map showing Iceland under the American flag. Iceland has sharply criticized the image, saying it was unacceptable. Denmark and Mexico also objected, underscoring the diplomatic backlash to Trump’s territorial ambitions.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/us-canad.title: U.S. reveals import ban on slew of Canadian goods as trade war escalates
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/us-canad.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/us-canad.text:
Washington announced it would ban imports of Canadian motorbikes as well as many dairy and alcohol products from Sept. 29.

Canada on Monday brought in what it called “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs on CA$27.6 billion of U.S. imports, targeting hundreds of products including furniture, household appliances, beauty products, clothing, agricultural equipment and more.

Tensions between the countries continue to mount, with representatives from both sides accusing the other of discriminatory practices and saying they are standing up for domestic workers.

The White House said it would ban imports of Canadian motorbikes and a slew of other products starting later this month as diplomatic and trade relations with Ottawa continue to fray.

U.S. President Donald Trump used a string of executive orders late Monday to announce bans on Canadian whey products and molasses, non-alcoholic beer, and a slew of alcoholic drinks including malt beer, wines, cider, whiskies, vodka and other spirits. Larger-capacity motorcycles and mopeds will also be banned.

The import restrictions, which largely replace tariffs of 50%, are due to take effect on Sept. 29, 2026.

The U.S. also announced that tariffs on other Canadian products would be modified and extended from Sept. 15, including the addition of all-terrain vehicles and animal hides, and the removal of rock salt and cement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the moves were a “natural consequence of Canada’s continued discriminatory treatment of crucial American exports.”

It was announced on the same day that Canadian tariffs on CA$27.6 billion of U.S. imports came into effect, targeting more than 700 goods across steel, dairy, farm equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and more.

Ottawa previously said those tariffs were a “dollar for dollar” response to the 50% tariffs imposed by the U.S. on its own goods in August, after trade talks collapsed spectacularly just before the Aug. 21 deadline.

The two sides have continued to blame one another for the failure to reach a deal, and accused the other of unfair practices that harm their domestic workers.

Trump has accused Canada of disadvantaging U.S. exports through its policies in the auto, alcohol and dairy sectors, highlighting the U.S.′ trade deficit in goods, and threatening to hit cars, trucks and auto parts with a 50% tariff from Jan. 1, 2027.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an August address that the “narrow merchandise trade deficit only exists because the U.S. buys so much of its energy from us,” and flagged that Canada is the biggest consumer for U.S. cars and steel.

He also said that the U.S. “asked too much” in its trade negotiations and that retaliation was needed to protect Canadian workers and companies, even if there is an economic hit and reduced choice for consumers.

The existing tariffs apply to a relatively small portion of the $715.5 billion trade in goods between the countries, but economists have warned of an immediate blow to small- and medium-sized businesses and of the risks to growth from further escalation.

“Companies on both sides of the border will need to wait to see if these tariffs hold, more measures are enacted, or each country decides to de-escalate. In the meantime, those businesses will realize both tariff-, compliance-, and uncertainty-related costs,” said Justin Angotti, associate in the International Trade and National Security Group at law firm Reed Smith.

Ottawa is meanwhile eyeing closer trade and security ties with the European Union as its relationship with Washington deteriorates, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

Beer and spirits sales have emerged as a political flashpoint as relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated.

Stores in several Canadian provinces have removed U.S. alcohol from their shelves, public campaigns have called for boycotts, and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in August announced a 50% tariff on American ‌imports.

Moe’s team told CNBC this week that the alcohol levy was a “reciprocal measure” intended to support local businesses and encourage progress toward a fair and balanced trade resolution.

U.S. spirits exports to Canada fell more than 70% year-on-year from the start of the retaliatory ban in March 2025 through December 2025, according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States.

Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the trade association, said American distillers had “shouldered the brunt of this trade dispute.”

“We appreciate President Trump’s recognition of the significant harm these sales bans have caused U.S. distillers and urge leaders on both sides of the border to reach a negotiated solution that restores U.S. spirits to retail shelves throughout Canada and returns the spirits sector to a permanent zero-for-zero tariff framework,” Swonger said

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/mitsui-c.title: Volatile yen risks ‘confused’ global markets, chairman of Japanese shipping giant says
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/mitsui-c.author: Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/mitsui-c.text:
A weak yen benefits Mitsui O.S.K. Lines because much of the Japanese shipping giant’s revenue is earned in U.S. dollars, Chairman Takeshi Hashimoto told CNBC.

He said sharp currency swings risk creating a “confused situation” in financial and global markets, and that a range of 150 to 155 yen per dollar would be “comfortable.”

Hashimoto also said it is “almost impossible” for the company to resume normal services through the Strait of Hormuz for now.

While the weak yen is favorable to Japanese companies doing business elsewhere, the huge swings in the currency can be a problem, according to a top shipping executive.

Mitsui OSK Lines
’ revenue is mainly in U.S. dollars, so the company benefits from a depreciating yen, according to Chairman Takeshi Hashimoto. Mitsui OSK is the largest tanker owner and operator globally, and one of the largest shipping lines.

“We had some concern that the [weak yen] would create a confused situation in the financial market,” he told CNBC’s Lisa Kim in an interview.

What he wants to see is a stable currency market, Hashimoto told CNBC, adding that a range of 150-155 yen to the greenback would be “comfortable.” The yen was recently trading around 153.

Japan’s currency has swung sharply in recent months, hitting multi-decade lows over the the course of 2026, before multiple interventions by Tokyo — with a joint intervention by Washington — strengthened the currency for a period of time.

When asked about his outlook for the Strait of Hormuz, Hashimoto said that he was pessimistic about a quick recovery for shipping in the waterway.

“For the time being, it is almost impossible for us to resume the normal service [in the] Strait,” he said. Data from analytics firm Kpler released on Monday showed that an average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest number since May.

He hopes that a “reasonably good situation” will emerge from the talks between Iran and Persian Gulf countries like Oman and Qatar, but also said that it would “take some time.”

https://grist.org/culture/wendell-berry-.title: Wendell Berry’s life on Earth
https://grist.org/culture/wendell-berry-.author: Katie Myers
https://grist.org/culture/wendell-berry-.text:
Wendell Berry made his choices and stuck to them. He did not have a computer or a smartphone. He wrote more than 50 books of poetry, fiction, and essays, mostly with a pencil and paper, from his farmhouse in Henry County, Kentucky. By the time of his passing last week, the 92-year-old had lived many lives — as a farmer, teacher, philosopher, environmental activist — and inspired several generations of writers, farmers, and advocates in turn. From these varying perspectives, Berry grappled with humanity and the natural world.

His answer to the fundamental question of how to live right was to start small — to revere the Earth’s endless beauty, and to work a little, each day, to reverse the harm we’ve caused.

“There is no public crisis that is not also private,” Berry wrote in his essay “Think Little.” Written in 1972 as the environmental movement emerged, the piece marked a conflict of Berry’s: Despite strong environmental convictions, he sometimes despaired of the movement’s focus on bending the ear of politicians, without individuals healing the rupture between modern life and the land. “The changes that are required are fundamental changes in the way we are living,” Berry wrote.

He extolled this approach in one of his most well-known poems, “Manifesto: Mad Farmer Liberation Front”: “Invest in the millennium. Plant sequoias. / Say that your main crop is the forest / that you did not plant.”

The language of activism was often at odds with Berry’s worldview. It seemed to warn of a coming apocalypse, but to Berry, the world had no end and no beginning. To move in nature’s time meant to think in cycles of death and rebirth, not a straight line leading toward destruction or salvation.

That didn’t stop Berry from engaging with activism even when it frustrated him, said Jeffrey Bilbro, an English professor at Grove City College in Pennsylvania, who’s written several books on Berry.

Berry was arrested in 1979 for protesting a nuclear plant in Indiana. In 2011, he was arrested again during a sit-in inside Kentucky state government offices while protesting mountaintop removal coal mining. He remained active in the fight against coal throughout the 2010s, helping to block the gates to a coal-fired power plant in Washington, D.C., and pulling his papers from the University of Kentucky after the school accepted a $7 million donation from Alliance Coal.

After Berry wrote his essay in Harper’s Magazine, “Why I am not Going to Buy a Computer” in 1987, some called him a Luddite. As a Grist article in 2014 pointed out, he was, in perhaps the truest sense, taking after that early 19th century movement, when textile workers at the advent of industrialization destroyed machinery to protect the dignity of their work. Berry refused, as much as he could, to let technology alienate him from his work. For this, he was sometimes criticized or called a curmudgeon.

His views didn’t fit neatly into modern politics. He believed that marriage and family strengthened community ties, but didn’t believe the government had authority to legislate such things. The law of nature, he said in one essay, was universal kinship and kindness, and Biblical stories and Psalms supported that. Berry was religious, but didn’t always like church, calling himself, according to Bilbro, a “bad weather church-goer” because he preferred to spend nice Sunday mornings walking in the woods. He hated dualisms — between humanity and the natural world, between body and soul, between person who believes x and person who believes y. This lent him broad appeal across the political and class spectrum, especially to those who felt that capitalism and industry had moved humanity away from a more honest way of life, whether through agriculture or other means.

“For an uncompromising person or a person of convictions, I think he recognized the need in a fallen world,” Bilbro said. “Our hands are all dirty, and we’re making these compromises, and it’s better to be honest about the necessity to do so and try to do what we can to live right, even if we can’t attain the purity that we might wish.”

The environmental crisis, according to Berry, takes hold in our lives and evinces itself as a sort of social decay. But living isn’t an unforgivable sin in itself, if we can only leave things better than we found them, knowing that the strip-mined mountaintop where we plant spruce, aspen, and wildflowers might not become a lush forest again until long after we’re gone.

In the poem, “A Discipline,” Berry imagines apocalypse: “it approaches / on every side, there is no other place / to turn.”

And yet, the poem continues, nothing ever really goes away: “It is the time’s discipline to think / of the death of all living, and yet live.”

Only the hard work of tending the land and learning its rhythms again can heal it, he believed. In coming into relationship with the smallest handful of earth, you can understand what it means to fight for change almost too enormous to fathom. To Berry, by tending a sprouted seedling in the ground, you can recognize you are it, and it is you.

https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.title: OpenAI says its models solved one of math's hardest problems as researchers cry foul
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
OpenAI said Tuesday that one of its unreleased artificial intelligence models had solved a mathematical puzzle that has eluded mathematicians for generations, in a claim which also drew a fight with rival researchers over credit.

Researchers at OpenAI said it took just days – and millions of dollars in computing power – to crack what is known as the Navier-Stokes problem.

Navier-Stokes is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a list of the hardest open questions in mathematics drawn up by the Clay Mathematics Institute.

It concerns the equations describing how fluids such as air and water move, which are used in aircraft design, weather forecasting and the study of blood flow.

OpenAI said its work showed that these equations are fatally flawed, answering the question as set out by the Millennium Prize.

"This is a significant milestone for AI research, and its promise for the world is that even more of our hardest questions would become possible to answer," Mark Chen, OpenAI's chief research officer, told reporters.

In a blog post describing the breakthrough, OpenAI said it began training a new model in late August, more capable than anything it had released publicly.

READ MORE
OpenAI begins rollout of GPT-6 amid growing scrutiny over safety

Days later, seeing online rumours that a competitor had solved Millennium problems, OpenAI turned the system loose on all six that remain open.

Work on Navier-Stokes showed unexpected promise, and the company poured its computing power into it.

By the final stage, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck said, 10,000 AI agents – programs that operate on their own – were working on the problem at once, passing messages back and forth.

Chen said the computing costs ran "emphatically in the millions of dollars", with Bubeck adding this was roughly 1,000 times what the company spent on earlier mathematical results.

According to OpenAI's account, the agents reached a solution Saturday, about 88 hours after launching the project.

The claim arrived hours after Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, and Levent Alpoge, who works at OpenAI competitor Anthropic, released their own AI-assisted work on three related equations.

In a statement published alongside his papers, Buckmaster said OpenAI had taken up the problem only after word of his research spread, and pursued the same unusual approach he and Alpoge had spent months developing.

WATCH MORE
Artificial intelligence in Europe: Does advanced AI have a glass ceiling?

OpenAI's researchers denied having had any access to the rival team's work and said they proposed sharing credit before realising that Buckmaster and Alpoge had fallen short of solving the problem.

"To be clear, we did not use their prompts or proofs to prompt our models or direct our agents," Bubeck said.

However, in a later post on X, OpenAI said "while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."

Each Millennium Prize Problem carries a $1 million reward, and only one has been solved since the list was published in 2000. OpenAI says it will not claim money if its finding is confirmed.

According to the prize rules, a solution has to be published in a peer-reviewed journal and survive two years after gaining acceptance in the mathematical community before the institute will even convene a committee to consider the work.

"The process of evaluation is deliberately unhurried, and we shall ensure that it is absolutely rigorous," Professor Martin Bridson, President of the Clay Mathematics Institute, told AFP.

ChatGPT-style AI is revolutionising the world of high-level math by quickly solving famous, long-unsolved problems that stumped experts for decades.

But it has also sparked debate over whether machine-generated answers truly count as real human understanding.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/b.author: Madeleine Rojahn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Organised Crime

In the past two weeks police executed searches at seven premises and on two vehicles, resulting in the arrests of seven people. (ABC News)

ACT Policing has arrested seven men it alleges are part of the Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gang involved in the illicit drugs trade in ACT.

One of the men is accused of recruiting people for offending, and was in possession of precious gems and a ledger detailing assets owned by him and liabilities of more than $3.3 million.

Police say the investigation began in early 2025 and is ongoing.

Seven alleged members of the Bandidos motorcycle gang's newly-formed Canberra chapter have been arrested as part of a long-running investigation into the group's activity.

It is alleged the group helped traffic more than 70 kilograms of cocaine with an estimated street value of over $10 million.

Over the past two weeks police said they seized quantities of cocaine, guns and drug trafficking equipment, precious gemstones, Pokémon cards and glass-sealed comic books from homes and cars connected to the accused.

Police say they began investigating the group in 2025.

Police said they would continue targeting organised crime gangs involved in the illicit drugs market. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

At 1:30am on Wednesday August 26, police said officers executed a search warrant at a home in Taylor in Canberra's north, where they arrested a 36-year-old man.

In the home, they allege they discovered drugs believed to be cocaine, $500,000, a glock-style handgun and ammunition, along with drug trafficking items.

Later that day at 2:15pm, a home in Throsby was also searched, where police allegedly found and seized several vials of what is believed to be GHB and anabolic steroids.

A handgun that police allege was seized from one of the Canberra homes. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Around three hours later, they then stopped a white Mitsubishi Triton in Belconnen, and arrested the driver, a 31-year-old man who was allegedly driving while disqualified.

A search of his vehicle returned a gel blaster firearm, suspected cocaine, and a mobile phone, police said.

The two men were charged with a range of offences including drug trafficking and firearms-related crimes.

That afternoon police also stopped another car in Lyneham, a white Toyota Landcruiser, and arrested a 36-year-old suspected gang member they allege has been recruiting people for criminal activity.

From his car they allegedly seized numerous Pokémon cards, diamonds, opals and other precious gems, and four vintage glass-sealed comic books.

The Bandidos recently formed a Canberra branch but have clubhouses across Australia. (ABC News: Henry Zwartz)

Police said they also found an accounts book detailing his assets and liabilities of more than $3.3 million.

ACT Policing later searched his home in Yarralumla, finding and seizing more vials of believed anabolic steroids, an extendable baton, and a white Volkswagen Golf.

Police say they charged one other person after he allegedly tried to smuggle evidence from a search warrant.

Over the following days, three more people were arrested in relation to investigation.

Since the investigation began in early 2025, police say they have seized four vehicles as proceeds of crime and weapons including batons, tasers and knuckle dusters.

Detective Acting Inspector Mark Battye said the arrests were "positive" and "in the interests of community safety". (ABC News: Toby Hunt)

"Outlaw Motorcycle Gangs are not harmless groups riding motorcycles," ACT Policing Detective Acting Inspector Mark Battye said.

"They use greed, intimidation and violence to fuel the commercial trafficking of harmful drugs and weapons, making large amounts of money in the process that goes towards more offending.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.title: Grief-stricken family recalls 'beautiful' mum killed in drunken crash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.author: Andrew Mangelsdorf
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Andrew Mangelsdorf

Lance O'Brien, 31, pleaded guilty in the Shepparton County Court. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

45-year-old Nathalia mother of four Vilia Sutherland has been remembered as a selfless, beautiful woman as her heartbroken family recalled the fateful day she was killed by drunk driver last October.

Lance O'Brien, 31, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions.

The case will return to court later this month.

A loving mother of four has been remembered as a selfless woman who has left an unimaginable void in the hearts of her children and family after she was killed in a head-on crash at Kaarimba in Victoria's north.

October 2, 2025, was a Thursday like any other for 45-year-old Nathalia mother Vilia Sutherland.

That afternoon, Ms Sutherland had just purchased groceries and was heading home in her Renault Captur SUV with the family's three dogs, two border collies and a labrador, when tragedy struck.

About 4:40pm while heading north on the Barmah-Shepparton Road at Kaarimba, about 25 kilometres north of Shepparton, a Toyota Corolla driven by 31-year-old Nathalia man Lance O'Brien veered into her lane, crashing into her car.

Ms Sutherland died at the scene and one of the border collies was later euthanased after sustaining critical injuries.

The then 30-year-old P2 driver O'Brien was hospitalised with serious injuries as a result of the crash.

Subsequent blood analysis found O'Brien had a blood alcohol content of at least 1.43 and the drugs methamphetamine, amphetamine and nordiazepam in his system.

According to prosecution documents presented to the Shepparton County Court, Jason Schreiber from the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine estimated O'Brien had a BAC more than three times the limit for fully licensed drivers, and possibly just below four times the limit.

The court heard after impact, O'Brien, who was trapped in his vehicle, asked a witness who had stopped to render assistance, "Did I kill someone?"

He then said, "I'm an idiot, I'm a f*****g idiot."

He was arrested on November 6, 2025, and charged with culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions.

On Wednesday he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Police charged Lance O'Brien with culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

Ms Sutherland's eldest sister Annie Koopmans addressed the court, recalling how her sister's death had broken her heart.

"My life has never been the same since that October day," she said.

"There's a huge hole in my heart and it hurts so much, my family is broken.

"I'm her eldest sister; it's my job to protect her and I failed to keep her safe."

Ms Sutherland's elder daughter Tammy Woods told the court she recalled receiving a notification alerting her to a crash while over 3,000 kilometres away in Darwin.

She said despite contacting emergency services she could not find out anything else about what had happened.

"I'd never known hopelessness until this," she said.

Eventually, she heard from a brother that their mother was in a crash and did not survive.

Ms Woods said despite several months now passing since the crash, life had become harder and she missed being able to share special moments with her mum.

"Our lives will never return to the way they were, for my family and it will always be life before October 2 and life after," she said.

She said she kept wondering if her mum had time to react or was frightened in her final moments.

Addressing O'Brien in court, she said he had taken so much away from the family.

"You took [away] the opportunities for her to grow old surrounded by the people who loved her," she said.

Prosecutor Angela Liantzakis read out a statement from Tammy's younger sister Emily, who recalled turning 21 without her mum by her side.

"Every birthday I have after this one will be a reminder … every milestone I reach will have someone missing from it," she said.

She described her anger that her mother had been taken from her and said it impacted her sense of security and her outlook on life.

"I struggle to trust [that] people I love will be there tomorrow," she said.

"I feel guilty when I am happy, I have fear of phone calls after receiving a call from [my brother] … who said mum's been in an accident and didn't make it."

The County Court heard O'Brien was on a P2 licence and was subject to a zero BAC condition.

He was also on bail at the time of offending with requirements not to drive a motor vehicle, consume alcohol or use a drug of dependence without lawful authorisation.

Prosecutor Angela Liantzakis told the court that analysis from the Collision Reconstruction Unit found O'Brien was driving at a minimum speed range of 115km/h -122km/h at the time of the crash.

During a Koori Court sentencing conversation, held in conjunction with Wednesday's hearing, O'Brien read from a statement saying how "deeply sorry" he was for the pain he had caused Ms Sutherland's family.

"I understand there's nothing I can do to undo the pain [from the] actions I have caused," he said.

The court heard he was "struggling" with drug and alcohol issues and recent trauma from losing two close relatives at the time of the crash.

"I know I can't change the past … I will carry away what has happened for the rest of my life," he said.

Judge Carolene Gwynn adjourned the matter for a further plea to appear in the Melbourne County Court later this month.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Immigration agency considering aviation category for foreign worker programs
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Japan is considering adding airport ground handling to the new Employment for Skill Development program, Immigration Services Agency officials said at a briefing Tuesday.

The government would shift 300 foreign workers from the Specified Skilled Worker program to the new system, which is scheduled to begin in April 2027, rather than increase the overall intake, officials said.

The shift would leave the combined projected intake under the two programs unchanged at about 1.23 million workers. The government estimates that the aviation sector needs 4,900 foreign workers in total, with 300 potentially moved into the new Employment for Skill Development category.

Agency officials said the proposed aviation expansion would cover airport ground handling, not aircraft maintenance.

The government is also considering changes to principal skills and industrial classifications in several other existing sectors, such as product manufacturing, construction and fishery, while keeping overall intake projections unchanged where additional demand is already reflected in existing estimates.

Separately, officials gave more details on the suspension of Certificates of Eligibility for Specified Skilled Worker applicants in the food-service sector. The number of workers had approached the 50,000-person ceiling, prompting the government to halt new certificates from April 13.

About 8,500 applications filed before the suspension remain under review. Applications to change one’s residency status are being prioritized, while certificates will be issued in filing order when departures or status changes create room below the cap.

The new system is scheduled to begin in April 2027, officials say. The shift would leave the combined projected intake under the two programs unchanged at about 1.23 million workers.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Africa’s informal economy: A burden and lifeline
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
ABIDJAN, COTE D'IVOIRE – Across the pavements, residential areas and public spaces of African cities, the informal economy is booming under the noses of authorities, who are often powerless to stop it.

Poverty, unemployment and bureaucratic red tape force tens of millions of Africans into work that is not regulated, taxed or protected by the government.

From Abidjan to Dakar and Abuja, mechanics, scrap dealers, motorcycle taxi drivers and street vendors make the most of the tiniest corner to set up their business activity.

In several African cities, the affordable prices offered by informal-sector workers make them indispensable to daily life for many.

“Life starts somewhere, so I’ve started here,” said Lohbip El-Pius Binyir, who runs a money transfer point and also sells bread, biscuits and drinks from a small pavement stall in the Nigerian capital, Abuja.

The 35-year-old has managed to set himself up in a fashionable district, even though informal businesses such as his are mostly confined to poorer neighborhoods.

He puts the authorities’ leniency down partly to the tidy and spartan way he operates his business: a bench, umbrella, card reader and table that he folds up and carts away each evening.

On a street in Cote D’Ivoire’s economic capital, Abidjan, municipal officers were in pursuit of informal vendors who had set up their stalls on the pavements and, in some cases, the roads.

It’s a common occurrence in megacities across the continent, where kiosks, carts, containers, tables and stalls laid out on the ground are part of the urban landscape.

Yacouba Sylla has been forced to move his informal garage several times because of demolition operations in Abidjan but has always found another place to resume his business.

If it were up to him, the 44-year-old mechanic would choose something better: a fully compliant workshop with modern facilities on which he would pay taxes and bid for contracts.

But all that requires “a lot of resources” or “support from the state,” which he does not have, he said as he repaired an engine laid out on the floor, his hands covered in oil.

In the early 1970s, more than 60% of employment in Africa was estimated to be informal, but it has surged to nearly 83% in recent years, according to the International Labour Organization.

In Cote D’Ivoire, Senegal, Mali and Nigeria, the figure is more than 90% of the active population.

The United Nations says the informal economy is a burden that limits the impact of growth.

Many African countries’ development is shaped by the weight of the informal sector, the absence of enterprises capable of scaling up and too few opportunities for creating decent jobs, the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) said in a report in July.

Governments have stepped up an array of measures to counter the informal sector, ranging from the more repressive, such as demolition and seizure of merchandise, to supporting workers through training or moving services online.

But they have not stopped it expanding.

“It’s not an easy task,” acknowledged Yaya Doumbia, the first deputy mayor of Yopougon, Abidjan’s biggest district and a hotspot for informal enterprise, where authorities have created a “sanitation brigade.”

“The pavements and public spaces are occupied. It’s a real challenge,” he said.

Economist Guillaume Liby said African countries were “tackling the problem from the wrong end: coercion.”

He also blamed a heavy tax burden and administrative hurdles facing those wanting to work legally.

Fruit, juices, clothes, shoes, peanuts — Lobe Sarr has turned her hand to various wares over the last 15 years, finally settling on a small street eatery in the Senegalese capital, Dakar.

“Running a shop in the street is difficult,” she said.

“At least it gives us something to do and allows us to earn money to cover our daily needs,” the aproned woman in her 30s said.

She, like others interviewed for this story, said they had no option but to work informally.

Beyond small vendors, the informal sector also includes large numbers of people employed without a contract or social security coverage in artisanal trades, security, the restaurant industry or cleaning, who face a precarious existence.

“It’s a survival economy, the only door left open” for many Africans, said Liby, the economist, pointing to a failing institutional environment and strong population growth.

The informal sector is a major part of the economy, accounting for up to 65% of the continent’s gross domestic product, according to the International Monetary Fund.

But, while the sector remains untaxed, it represents a considerable loss of revenue for African governments, economists say.

Countries must implement policies that encourage informal-sector workers to register with the tax authorities, facilitate access to financing and create infrastructure needed to accommodate small entrepreneurs.

In Cote D’Ivoire, reducing the “significant weight” of the informal sector with notably the creation of a status for small entrepreneurs is one pillar of an ambitious national development plan, unveiled in July.

Benin’s efforts have already borne fruit after it introduced a policy based on building new, modern markets and reorganizing large commercial areas.

Formerly at 97%, its informal economy now accounts for 85% of jobs.

The Beninese authorities vaunt a strategy that has enabled the state to hike its tax revenues while providing better working conditions and combating unsanitary practices.

In the early 70s, the figure was estimated at 83% of the population in Africa. In Cote D'Ivoire, Senegal, Mali and Nigeria, the number is more than 90% of active population.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Hiroshima’s governor promotes prefecture’s oysters and sake in London
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
LONDON – Hiroshima Gov. Mika Yokota promoted the prefecture’s oysters and sake at an event in London on Tuesday, expressing her desire to boost exports to Britain and deepen friendship and business relations between the two through the culture of food.

Yokota, who took office last November, made her first overseas sales promotion trip for the prefecture’s products.

About 20 people, including officials of British food importers and influencers, attended the event held at a Japanese restaurant.

Guests savored cuisine including a cold dish featuring fresh oysters in the shell harvested in Mitsu Bay in Hiroshima and shipped frozen from the prefecture.

Seven sake products from four breweries were served with the dishes, including nigori, or cloudy sake, from Kamoizumi Shuzo in the city of Higashihiroshima and junmai sake made only from rice, water and kōji mold, then brewed 38 years ago by Hanayoisyuzo in the city of Shobara.

Influencer Aiste Miseviciute praised the pairing, saying sake and the umami of oysters blended well.

“I am encouraged by our guests’ responses to the collaboration between Hiroshima’s sake and food,” Yokota said.

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.title: Gunman shoots and kills kindergarten teacher in Thailand
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.text:
The shooting occurred at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten in Chonburi province. Three other teachers and 44 students were evacuated safely

A gunman shot and killed a kindergarten teacher on Wednesday inside a school building in eastern Thailand, where 44 children and three other teachers were evacuated safely, authorities said.

The shooting took place about 11am inside a building at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten in Chonburi province, about 150km (93 miles) southeast of the capital Bangkok.

All 44 students were unharmed and evacuated along with the other teachers after the shooting, according to the Chonburi provincial government.

The shooter, who is believed to be the victim’s husband, fled the scene. His accommodation was surrounded by police, officials said.

Chonburi Governor Narit Niramaiwong ordered the school to be closed and mental health experts to be available to support the students and school staff, his office said.

School safety and gun violence in Thailand have come under scrutiny after a 14-year-old student opened fire at his high school and family home in August, killing eight people and injuring more than 20 before apparently taking his own life.

Earlier this month, a 14-year-old student was arrested after he fired several shots but failed to injure anyone at his school in Kamphaeng Phet province, 200km north of Bangkok.

Calls for tighter controls on firearms have intensified and the national government has ordered a review of gun regulations, including suspension of new permits to purchase firearms and a review of existing permits.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia despite fairly restrictive gun laws. While mass shootings are still rare, the country has seen an uptick in high-profile attacks in recent years.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.title: Australians question US commitment to Aukus submarine deal in crowdfunded inquiry
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.author: Maria Siow
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.text:
Under the Australia-UK-US security pact, Canberra will get eight nuclear-powered submarines at an estimated cost of up to US$266 billion

At an Aukus public inquiry in Canberra last week, one of Australia’s leading submarine experts, retired Rear Admiral Peter Briggs, called the plan “flawed and undeliverable”.

Australia scrapped an agreement for France to supply Attack-class submarines in favour of the Aukus sale in 2021. Briggs said the French deal was the better option, arguing that US shipyards, already struggling to meet the domestic demands, could not deliver the promised nuclear-powered submarines on time.

At the same inquiry, former civil servants dealing with national security Michael Keating and Jon Stanford said joining Aukus meant Australia was significantly more likely to be dragged into a conflict with China and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons. Australia had “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the US while leaving the country vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net, they said.

Canberra has said that, apart from protecting Australia’s vast ocean trade routes, acquiring such capability is also aimed at countering China’s growing military presence in the region.

The 12-week inquiry, which ended on Thursday, was crowdfunded as Canberra refused to hold a formal parliamentary inquiry. It was led by former ministers, parliamentarians, senior officials, public servants and retired military officers.

Demand for the inquiry showed the lack of transparency and public debate surrounding Aukus, according to Manoj Harjani, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

“Uncertainty regarding the US’ commitment to Aukus, particularly since Donald Trump took office, has been a thorny issue,” he said. “This will not be the last time you hear about a review of Aukus. It is a substantial commitment in more than monetary terms and deserves the level of scrutiny it is receiving.”

Questions about US commitment to the pact stem mainly from the slow pace of production in US shipyards and American policy reviews questioning if transferring high-end military assets abroad aligns strictly with US interests.

Troy Lee-Brown, a research fellow at the University of Western Australia’s Defence and Security Institute, said with the strategic environment in the region deteriorating, Canberra should do a better job in explaining Aukus to Australians.

Aukus, he said, was delivering results. The Submarine Rotational Force-West, an Aukus initiative where Australia will host a rotational presence of UK and US nuclear submarines at HMAS Stirling near Perth in Western Australia, will start operations next year.

“But the timeline of the Aukus project is measured over multiple decades, with the eventual delivery of SSN Aukus from the early 2040s,” he said.

The inquiry was long overdue, said Nishank Motwani, senior fellow at The Alliance Futures Institute think tank in Washington. Since Aukus was launched in September 2021, there has not been a public debate about the pact and its wide-ranging effects on the economy, workforce, waste management and use of taxpayers’ money.

“If one word captures why the Aukus public inquiry is taking place now, it would be ‘frustration’,” he said, adding that government information so far had been “top-down, drip-fed, and highly controlled”.

One reason why Canberra did not want to open Aukus up to public debate was the fear of backlash, he said. A public inquiry would “expose [the government] to hard questions, legitimate concerns, and difficult choices they are unprepared to meet because in some ways, Aukus is billed as ‘too big to fail’”.

The inquiry attracted significant interest across Australia. Over 700 written submissions were made and all the public hearings were reportedly packed. Last week’s hearings in Canberra even had to be extended by a day due to strong interest.

“It will be hard to ignore the momentum the inquiry has generated,” Motwani said. In the longer term, it could harm future governments if they dismissed the inquiry and its recommendations.

“It exposes the reality that the inquiry is doing the job the government should have done all along: explaining Aukus to the Australian people in a trusting, transparent and accountable manner,” he said.

This was an opportunity for the government to learn about public thinking on Aukus, without having to put political stakes on the line, he said, adding that “sidestepping or dismissing the inquiry’s findings would be costly for the government, as these represent real voices it has not yet reached”.

In a written statement to the inquiry on August 31, Motwani recommended the appointment of an Aukus special envoy with decision-making power.

“The appointment must sit within the national security apparatus, reporting directly to the prime minister, with an explicit mandate to drive Pillar I and Pillar II delivery against defined timelines, public accountability measures, and counter threats,” he wrote.

Pillar I is the delivery of the nuclear-powered submarines to Australia while the second pillar refers to the sharing of advanced technology and capabilities among the three allies.

The inquiry, Harjani said, should be seen as an example of the challenges facing defence policymaking regarding major acquisitions.

“Who should ultimately decide, and whose opinions should be given weight to?”

https://www.dw.com/en/the-billion-euro-t.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
https://www.dw.com/en/the-billion-euro-t.text:
Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, in suitcases on planes or by exploiting legal loopholes to end up on dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?

In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in  illegally caught eels.

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said  Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.

"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from  European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've  transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: so far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market.

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."

International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.

"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

Still, Stein, who did his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.

"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he said. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.

"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-5-baby-orang.text:
Five young orangutans, not native to India, were found in an Odisha forest, sparking suspicion of an international smuggling operation. Meanwhile, India said it was not involved in the BAPS-Eiffel Tower row.

Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India from Wednesday, September 9.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia.

The animals, not native to India, were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match.

He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia.

"I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said.

Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine.

Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India.

"We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata.

Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.

The Tapanuli orangutan is critically endangered, with fewer than 800 animals thought to be left.

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from across India.

When forest officials in India's Odisha state found five baby orangutans on a patrol, thousands of kilometers from their natural habitat, the officials suspected they were trafficked into the country from Southeast Asia.

In other news, the Indian government has steered clear of controversy in the row over Hindu group BAPS's visit to the Eiffel Tower.

Finally, New Delhi is gearing up to host the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13. With security protocols being heightened and hotel prices skyrocketing, the non-high-profile Delhi visitors may be in for a hit to their pockets.

For this and more, follow our live blog.

https://www.dw.com/en/trafficked-into-fr.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis situation in Cambodia
https://www.dw.com/en/trafficked-into-fr.text:
Cambodia is cracking down on scam operators, with the effects being felt mostly among young Africans: Thousands of trafficking victims are now stuck in the Asian country with no money, no passport, and no prospects.

Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren't the only victims of these criminal rings; the scam industry in Southeast Asia alone is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries, who are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse, and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.

In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles for facilitating any return is the fact that many African countries like Uganda, Liberia, Ghana, of Nigeria have no consular representation.

"But also because some countries have zero interest," says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who finds equal blame for the situation in many of the countries of origin.

"They're not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork for the money for them to go back."

Ferrer believes that keeping the situation unchanged has also been in the interest of the Cambodian government for a long time:

Many trafficking victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.

"They don't allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them," Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the US, the UK, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.

According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.

Many who have sought in Cambodia help have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.

Instead of being given protection, many of the trafficking often victims now face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.

Emmanuel David is one of many of the trafficking victims stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there last year after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.

"My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work," David explained.

The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia, according to the Civil Service Agency of Liberia.

The reality hit quite differently: Once there, he was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.

But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.

In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages, and later even confiscated his belongings — including his passport.

David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.

Eventually, he left "with no documents and no money," and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.

His story, however, is far from unique.

Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was "beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks."

The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and is now unable to pay his medical bills.

Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that "despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt."

She also confirmed that more and more of the trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, "because there is clearly a recruitment industry that's built around Africa, targeting African nationals."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.

"Once you're inside there's no way out," an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.

He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.

The police, he says, just turns a blind eye — at best.

Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims.

"They shouldn't be punished for crimes they were forced to commit," Oberoi highlights, though her pleas appear to land on deaf ears.

Several of the victims contacted by DW said their governments were "slow" to help with their repatriation.

DW attempted to contact several African foreign ministries to hear their side, but has not received any response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.

However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW's direct request for further information.

The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) meanwhile said it's trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide "limited, prioritized support."

Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked, even for those who have managed to return to their countries of origin.

In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — "a situation that is really unbearable," says Ferrer.

Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success. When asked about his little daughter, he says that "daddy can't go home without money."

To his mind, he hardly is the victim of his circumstances.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-tra.title: Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-tra.text:
At least four people were killed, and 29 others were injured, in a Ukrainian attack on a Russian Black Sea port. Meanwhile, Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border, killing two.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk overnight killed at least four people, including a child, Russian officials said Wednesday.

Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region in southern Russia, said 29 others were injured in the drone attack.

Ukraine has frequently targeted Novorossiysk, a port city that is a major outlet for Russian oil and grain exports.

Earlier on Wednesday, the mayor of the city, Andrei Kravchenko, had said the debris from a Ukrainian drone fell onto several businesses and nearly landed on a residential building, sparking fires.

In the nearby town of Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three homes and a kindergarten, Kondratyev said, adding that there were no casualties.

Russia's Defense Ministry said nearly 600 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight.

Russian drone strikes overnight on a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, meanwhile, killed at least two civilians, the regional governor Oleh Kiper said on social media.

Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.

The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.

Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.

Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.

At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Russia also said President Vladimir Putin had had an "extremely frank" phone call with his US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday, as Washington continues to press Ukrainian and Russian officials to hold face-to-face talks to end the war.

Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.

Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.text:
Alice Weidel and Friedrich Merz are facing off in the Bundestag days after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt has put new pressure on the German chancellor. DW has the latest.

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sharply attacked the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) over its migration policy during Wednesday's Bundestag debate.

He described the party's concept of "remigration" as "nothing other than ethnic cleansing based on skin color and origin."

Merz said such a policy would also have severe consequences for Germany's labor market, where many people with migrant backgrounds are employed.

"If things were to happen the way the AfD wants, the skilled trades in Germany could no longer function, not a single care home would be able to operate, not a single hospital would be able to operate, and not a single restaurant could be run," Merz said.

"That would be the result of your remigration policy," he told AfD lawmakers.

Merz said there was agreement within his governing coalition that many people without a right to remain permanently in Germany should be deported.

"But we distinguish carefully between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, who are welcome in Germany, and those who do not have a permanent right to remain and who must leave our country again," he said.

The government made that distinction carefully "in contrast" to the AfD, Merz added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the German parliament, the Bundestag, gave a barbed response to opening remarks from the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) co-leader Alice Weider, who lambasted Germany's ruling coalition as a "failure."

The Bundestag debate comes days after the AfD's after its strong showing in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, warning the party against assuming it was on course for broader majorities.

"Ms Weidel, today you can barely contain yourself," Merz told AfD co-leader Alice Weidel during the Bundestag's general debate on Wednesday. "But you do not have an absolute majority, and you will not achieve one in Germany."

"Nowhere in Germany will you win majorities with this politics," Merz said. "You are, and you remain a destructive force."

Merz acknowledged that the AfD had achieved "a remarkable election result in every respect" in Saxony-Anhalt.

"The voters spoke pretty clearly. They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," he said.

However, he stressed that the AfD had failed to achieve its stated goal of securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Merz accused the AfD of showing "contempt for our democratic institutions" and of repeatedly denigrating representatives of the state.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," Merz said.

He said there was a "deep divide" between the AfD and the other parties in foreign, European, social and peace policy.

Merz also accused the AfD of damaging German interests through its friendly stance towards Russia.

"The only thing that really threatens Russia and Putin is the appeal of democracy," he said. "And yet you are obviously still standing on Russia's side."

"You are part of the problem we have in Germany — and we will resist that with everything at our disposal."

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), said Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing coalition had been rejected by voters after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking in the Bundestag's general debate in her first direct encounter with Merz since Sunday's state election, Weidel said voters wanted a change of political direction rather than "more of the same."

"The voters in Saxony-Anhalt have made it absolutely clear to you, in the language of democratic choice: black-red is over," Weidel said, referring to the traditional party colors of the conservative CDU/CSU and center-left Social Democrats within the governing coalition.

Weidel also attacked the government's fiscal policy, accusing Merz of pursuing unprecedented levels of borrowing.

She said Germany's public finances had been "shattered" and accused the chancellor of leaving behind "scorched earth."

"You are driving Germany towards national bankruptcy in record time," Weidel said.

She described the government's draft budget as a "declaration of surrender" by the coalition and claimed it was unconstitutional.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmr.title: 'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmr.text:
The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.

His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours.

"When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month.

The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal.

The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand.

Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.

Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go".

Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged.

The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term.

In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs.

"Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said.

The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency".

"I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October.

He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month.

A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given.

"For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added.

The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week.

Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages.

He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network.

"We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience."

Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.
