“I don’t think there is seafood competitiveness without conservation so if they’re making short-term decisions that undermine conservation, that will undermine our fisheries and fishing communities,” added Moore.

Though environmentalists see some positives in the mix—such as modernizing NOAA’s data systems or deploying eDNA studies—much of the policy looks like it’s “going backwards,” according to Moore.

The announcement was welcomed by industry insiders. The National Fisheries Institute (NFI), the largest commercial seafood trade group, said in a statement: “Calls for modernization and a return to a true risk-based regulatory structure, rather than the inertia of persistent bureaucratic expansion, could go a long way to mitigating the operational and administrative burdens the agency has committed to reduce.”

“We congratulate NOAA Fisheries and the Trump Administration for these new efforts and stand as a resource as the agency begins implementation,” said Lisa Wallenda Picard, president and CEO of NFI.

Geographically, the most significant proposal is to fast-track the expansion and introduction of new commercial fishing operations at the Mariana Trench, Papahānaumokuākea, Rose Atoll and Pacific Remote Islands national monuments.

These four protected areas currently shield “some of the last remaining relatively pristine ocean ecosystems,” according to NOAA.

Covering over 1.1 million square miles—an area almost double the size of Alaska—these habitats are home to millions of acres of coral reef and endemic species found nowhere else in the world, such as the Mariana snailfish and the Hawaiian pigfish.

Other backsliding includes applying new Endangered Species Act reforms that rescind longstanding interpretation of “harm,” and reducing the use of the conservation standards of Habitat Areas of Particular Concern in regulatory actions to “ensure protections are balanced with economic interests.”

“Regulation is the backbone of sustainable fisheries management,” said Janet Coit, the former director of NOAA Fisheries under President Joe Biden. “I worry about what [circumventing science-based limits] will do to the fish populations that future generations are counting on us to steward responsibly.”

When asked for comment on these issues, a spokesperson for NOAA told Inside Climate News that “the best available information” could be found in the press release. “We are moving away from regulations that treat domestic harvesters like a problem to be managed, and toward a science-based, common-sense system,” NOAA Fisheries assistant administrator Eugenio Piñeiro Soler wrote in the announcement.

The agency did not respond to direct questions regarding what scientific protections will be kept in place and whether NOAA Fisheries now prioritizes commercial profits over environmental stewardship.

For Coit, who directed the previous administration’s seafood strategy and believes “100 percent” in supporting and promoting U.S. seafood, short-term efforts to roll back protections miss the mark: “With climate change impacts reshaping our ocean ecosystems, now is not the time to avert our eyes and just go fish.”

https://grist.org/transportation/georgia.title: Georgia bet big on EV manufacturing. Trump pulled the plug.
https://grist.org/transportation/georgia.author: Emily Jones
https://grist.org/transportation/georgia.text:
For years, Georgia Governor Brian Kemp has been working to make the state a welcoming home for clean energy manufacturing — EVs, solar panels, batteries for storage. The state went all out with tax breaks and a worker training program to attract EV and battery makers — and for a while it was working.

Georgia-based bus manufacturer Blue Bird started selling electric buses commercially in 2018 and built an expanded factory for electric buses in 2023. In 2022, Hyundai built a plant near Savannah that it said would be dedicated to making EVs. In 2024, Kia started making EVs at its West Point plant. And in 2025, Rivian broke ground on its manufacturing plant near Atlanta. The Hyundai and Rivian operations are two of the biggest economic development projects in Georgia history. The state has also worked to attract other parts of the EV and clean energy manufacturing sector, including battery makers and recyclers and solar panel companies.

Under the second Trump administration, the economic outlook for these companies has been destabilized. In addition to ending federal EV tax credits, the Trump administration has imposed tariffs on battery packs, charger hardware, and other components; loosened rules around emissions from gas-powered cars; and ended the Biden administration’s push to make government vehicle fleets electric. And a year ago, federal immigration agents raided an electric vehicle battery plant and arrested more than 400 people, most of them South Korean workers there to help get the new factory off the ground.

The past year and a half has been a grim moment for what was a booming industry in Georgia. But the EV makers are still forging ahead, even if that means making some adjustments.

At Kia’s plant in West Point, a long and constantly varied line of vehicles moves steadily forward on the assembly line, step by step gaining all the trimmings that turn metal shells into driveable cars. But this plant functions more like a short-order cook than a traditional assembly line. Instead of producing big, uniform batches, Kia has designed the plant to manufacture cars according to unique specifications — each one a different model, color, trim, or even drive train — that is, gas-powered, hybrid, or electric. Kia says it has done this to make more of the cars people most want to buy at any given moment. Right now, that means hybrids.

“What we’ve seen is a transition back away from maybe full EV vehicle building to this kind of a middle-of-the-road opportunity,” said factory CEO Stuart Countess.

Electric cars are still the future, he said. But for several reasons, including price and charging access, consumers just aren’t there yet. Changes to federal policy are a major factor, too.

“We had a tax incentive credit that did go away,” Countess said. “Sales were really moving in the right direction, but once it went away, it became a much different environment.”

Just as Kia has ramped up hybrid production, its sister company Hyundai has added hybrid production to the lineup produced at its massive plant near Savannah, which was originally built to make EVs.

“It’s kind of a messy period we’re in right now,” said Stephanie Valdez-Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive. “But I think the manufacturers are adjusting.”

At the same time, battery makers throughout the state have started shifting to producing storage batteries for electricity in addition to ones made to power vehicles.

“The state continues to have a lot riding on the success of both the electric vehicle but also the battery market,” said Stan Cross of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, or SACE.

Georgia leads the region in EV and battery manufacturing, but the growth has stumbled, with layoffs at SK Battery earlier this year. More than $4 billion in investment has been canceled or scaled back in the last year across the Southeast, according to SACE.

That’s dwarfed, though, by the nearly $74 billion in manufacturing investment that’s moving ahead. Still, one open question, Cross said, is whether Georgians will buy the hybrids and EVs being made in the state.

Despite actively pursuing EV manufacturing, Georgia doesn’t have incentives to encourage EV adoption like some other states. In fact, there’s an extra registration fee designed to make up for lost gas taxes. And the thorny politics may extend beyond state policy and the now-ended federal incentives. “When it comes to electric vehicles, Georgia politics remains utterly confused,” Cross said.

Private investment continues, though. Kia and Hyundai are part of a charging consortium called IONNA that has installed several charging stations around the state, including one at the Kia factory site in West Point. Electric utilities are investing more in vehicle charging too. Across the region, EV-related investment by utilities increased by 14 percent this year, according to SACE.

“Though we’re not seeing a lot of activity on the legislative side, we do see potential on the regulatory side and really are encouraging Georgia Power to step up and help kind of fill the void that policymakers in the state are creating,” Cross said.

Valdez-Streaty believes that, over time, making EVs in Georgia will likely lead to more people in Georgia buying them.

“It’s like that familiarity, right?” she said. “People have jobs at those companies and familiarity with those products.”

Though shaky for the last 18 months or so, she said the EV market is starting to stabilize — and the auto industry is still going electric, it’s just taking a little longer.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/09/ger.title: German Democracy, as We Knew It, Is Over
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/09/ger.author: John Kampfner
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/09/09/ger.text:
My FP: Follow topics and authors to get straight to what you like. Exclusively for FP subscribers. Subscribe Now | Log In

Has a small, largely elderly, left-behind pocket of Germany struck a fatal blow against its postwar liberal democracy? That is the question many are asking after Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, which saw the Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounce the mainstream parties to stand on the verge of power—the first time a far-right party would do so in Germany since the fall of the Nazi regime.

As has been the case when other tsunamis have struck—Donald Trump’s presidential election victories in the United States, Brexit in the United Kingdom, to name but two of many around the world—the response of those in the political center has ranged from fury to consternation to despair. But most of all, a sense of dumbstruck paralysis. They could see it coming; they took some action, but they were swept away. And now, as they face the consequences, so the recriminations begin.

Has a small, largely elderly, left-behind pocket of Germany struck a fatal blow against its postwar liberal democracy? That is the question many are asking after Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, which saw the Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounce the mainstream parties to stand on the verge of power—the first time a far-right party would do so in Germany since the fall of the Nazi regime.

As has been the case when other tsunamis have struck—Donald Trump’s presidential election victories in the United States, Brexit in the United Kingdom, to name but two of many around the world—the response of those in the political center has ranged from fury to consternation to despair. But most of all, a sense of dumbstruck paralysis. They could see it coming; they took some action, but they were swept away. And now, as they face the consequences, so the recriminations begin.

In Washington, the targets of opprobrium ranged from presidential nominees Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton to Democrats in Congress to the entire party establishment. In the United Kingdom, they were many and varied, from then-Prime Minister David Cameron, who called the 2016 referendum, to then-London mayor Boris Johnson, who changed his mind at the last moment to lead the calls to quit the European Union, to the ever-present right-winger Nigel Farage, to Jeremy Corbyn, the left-wing Labour leader who campaigned half-heartedly to stay while purportedly preferring to leave.

In Germany, it’s simpler. All the guns are trained on Friedrich Merz, the chancellor of the past 16 months with the ignominious distinction of historic low opinion poll ratings. He is the man who boasted when first challenging for the leadership of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party in 2018 that he would halve the popular support for the AfD, only to see it double. He is the man who promised voters an “autumn of reforms”—he meant 2025, and yet they are still spluttering their way through parliament.

Merz spent years trying to become CDU leader, criticizing former Chancellor Angela Merkel, openly and behind her back, for taking the party too much to the center, for being too generous to welfare claimants and too welcoming to migrants. What Germans wanted, he insisted, was more genuine conservatism.

They’ve now got that, but they’ve decided they would rather eat their meat rare. They’re opting in droves for the AfD, a party that promises remigration for “non-Germans,” to prioritize “German” culture, to incentivize child-rearing, to restore traditional family values: a party that is tacitly supported by the Kremlin and is openly embraced by Trump, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, and Elon Musk. A party, which in the European Parliament many other right-wing groups won’t touch and whose chapters in Saxony-Anhalt and in neighboring regions have been declared extremist by the federal office to protect the constitution.

There are some, a dwindling number it must be said, who seek to play down the consequences. After all, they say, Saxony-Anhalt is small. Its 2.2 million people constitute but one-fortieth of Germany’s overall population. It is poorer, older, more surly than other parts of the country. And it belongs to the former communist east, where support for the AfD has, throughout the party’s 13 years of existence, always been stronger.

All that may be true, but the alarm expressed by most political players in Berlin and elsewhere—words such as “seismic,” “devastating,” and “earthquake” are thrown about with abandon—is grounded in the fear of not what’s happened, but about what’s set to come for the Germany’s established postwar parties.

The number-crunching in Saxony-Anhalt points to a crisis, the depth of which cannot be overstated. The CDU failed to win a single direct mandate in the election (its paltry 15 seats in the 83-strong parliament arising from the proportionate distribution of votes). This had been a stronghold for the party more than two decades. And there are more elections to come.

On Sept. 20, the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (also in the east) and the city-state of Berlin also go to the polls. In both, the AfD is expected to perform strongly (though not to win). The CDU is likely to be trounced again.

The calls on Merz to step down are growing ever stronger. His initial response has been to stay the course until general elections in 2029, but in his first appearances after Sunday’s rout he seemed genuinely nonplussed about what to do.

The economic damage is just one of the consequences.

He would like to go harder on public service reforms and welfare cuts, make even deeper inroads into immigration numbers than he has already done—in the hope that this might bring back some of the voters that have deserted the CDU.

The problem is that the junior partner in the ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), won’t let him go further than the compromises it has already agreed to. Merz’s personal relations with SPD co-leader Lars Klingbeil, who is vice chancellor and finance minister, are said to be good. But Klingbeil’s job is also on the line; the center-left SPD is also hemorrhaging support.

Both parties are pointing in opposing directions. The SPD needs to claw back voters who have deserted it for Die Linke (the Left party), the Greens, and the AfD as well. They all want different things, but what many of them don’t want are further spending cuts that are being introduced into the Bundestag, the federal parliament, this week.

There is a more optimistic scenario. Might the two ruling parties conclude from their cataclysmic performances that they have to speed up the reforms, show more radicalism? Most commentators in Berlin are not holding their breath.

While the domestic consequences are important, the greatest danger lies further afield. The one area where Merz could be seen to have led courageously is the overhaul of Germany’s military capabilities, and the commitment to meet the NATO target of 3.5 percent in military spending by 2029, far earlier than equivalent countries such as the U.K. or France. He has been uncompromising in confronting the Kremlin; only days before the election, he openly accused Moscow of a series of drone attacks.

Many voters appeared to go along with him; the mood shifted considerably, but perhaps more in the head than in the heart in a country that has long shied away from a hard posture in defense. What is perhaps most striking in Saxony-Anhalt is that a majority of voters opted for parties that are either avowedly pro-Kremlin—not just the AfD, but also for BSW, a breakaway left-wing group—or Die Linke, which argues for peaceful engagement with Russia. As one election poster in Magdeburg, the state capital, declared, with reference to the now-closed gas pipeline to Russia: “Nordstream. Turn it Back On. Sanctions against Russia are Making Us Go Broke.”

Merz pointed to the arithmetic himself. Exactly 57.7 percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt, he said, backed parties “that question our unstinting support for Ukraine,” adding that he would “not deviate from his position one millimeter.” The pressure to shift away from his hawkish approach will only grow; within the SPD there are concerns, too, with many activists preferring the government to spend less on arms and more on public services.

For Trump and for Russian President Vladimir Putin, the events of the past few days in Germany are cause for celebration. Russian bots have been fueling disinformation for many years, particularly in the east of Germany; the number of so-called hybrid attacks is increasing. Meanwhile, last year’s U.S. National Security Strategy promised to support “patriotic” groupings across Europe to help prevent “civilizational erasure.” It came as no surprise that senior MAGA figures, not least Musk, congratulated the AfD, as did Kirill Dmitriev, one of the Russian president’s most senior officials.

The bigger immediate prize will be France’s presidential election next April and May; a victory for Marine Le Pen and the far-right National Rally is highly possible. European cohesion, within the EU and NATO, would then be extremely hard to sustain.

The AfD has now established itself as a major player, perhaps the major player, in German politics. For years, the parties of the center sought to exclude it and marginalize it through the Brandmauer, firewall, which stipulated they would not include it in any national or regional coalition. That exclusion order only added to the party’s sense of grievance and establishment stitch-up, arguably increasing its popularity among prospective voters.

Indeed, soon, the boot could be on the other foot. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel has declared that she wants her party to achieve an average 40 percent nationally and across the regions, echoing its performance in Saxony-Anhalt, thereby assuming the mantle as the one and only party of the right. In some countries, this takeover has already taken place. Sometimes the far right subsumes the traditional center-right party, as has happened with the Republicans in the United States. In others, it shoves its rival aside by being more attractive, such as in France. The battle for the soul of Germany is on.

John Kampfner is the author of Braver New World: The Countries Daring to Do Things Others Won’t.

Hundreds of employees from leading tech firms in July urged the US government to support an international effort to develop tools for managing the pace ‌of advanced AI development.

Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has quit the AI company, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Mr Coxon said he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at Anthropic and OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he posted on X.

"They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Superintelligence is considered to be the stage of AI when machines surpass human performance in every field.

Anthropic Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger posted a reply on X saying Mr Coxon was correct.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade," he wrote.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

Mr Coxon is one of a growing number of AI experts to call on the industry to slow down.

In July more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies signed a statement saying there was a "real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems".

The letter called on the US government to support an international effort to develop tools that can "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

CEO and co-Founder of Anthropic, Dario Amodei. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

Responding to the initiative, called Pacing the Frontier, Anthropic said in an X post: "Our own research on recursive self-improvement, published last month, points to the need for tools to deliberately pace the frontier of AI development ⁠so society can prepare".

OpenAI also responded to the letter, posting on X: "We believe that, at some point in the future, AI acceleration ‌for ⁠frontier model development may be so high that the world will need to pace the rate of AI advancement."

The "alignment problem" for superintelligence is that an AI system may not share human values.

UN-rights chief has addressed a council in Geneva saying AI posed a threat to humanity.

On Monday, United Nations rights chief Volker Turk also warned that artificial intelligence could pose a threat to humanity and pledged to press AI firms to reduce risks that his office said included disruptions to services, communications and democratic systems.

He called for "cast-iron guarantees" to secure AI in a speech ahead of the start of his unprecedented second term.

"I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity," Mr Turk told the body in Geneva.

"I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI before it is too late."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The Tachikawa branch of Tokyo District Court on Wednesday sentenced swimmer Tomoru Honda, who won a silver medal at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, to one year in prison, suspended for three years, for dangerous driving resulting in injury.

The prosecution had demanded a one-year sentence, arguing that Honda, 24, drove dangerously out of a selfish desire to catch up with a sports car in front of him, which was “reckless and vicious.”

During his trial, Honda admitted that he could not make a calm judgment because of his poor competition results at the time. “I feel sorry for causing trouble to many people,” he said. “I will never drive again.”

According to the indictment, Honda was driving between 88 and 108 kilometers per hour on an ordinary road with a legal speed limit of 30 kilometers per hour when he crashed into an oncoming car around 8:30 a.m. on Nov. 21 last year. The car’s driver, in his 60s, was left with serious injuries including a fractured sternum.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Alcaraz falls to Shelton in epic latest-ever U.S. Open finish
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
NEW YORK – Carlos Alcaraz tumbled out of the U.S. Open quarterfinals at 3:34 a.m. Wednesday, falling to Ben Shelton in an epic five-set thriller that broke the record for latest finish ever at Flushing Meadows.

The big-hitting American claimed his first career win over Alcaraz, 6-7 (5/7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10/7), ending the Spaniard’s hopes of retaining his title in his first tournament back after a four-month injury absence.

It took a brutal four hours and 28 minutes, finishing long past the previous latest finish in New York of 2:50 a.m. — Alcaraz’s five-set quarterfinal win over Jannik Sinner in 2022.

Shelton matches his semifinal run at the U.S. Open three years ago and booked an all-American semifinal against Frances Tiafoe, who came back from two sets down to beat Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10/6).

“That was a war, epic match, so physical,” Shelton said. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old.

“It’s always fun being on the court against him. It’s ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes — the most enjoyable match that I’ve had in my career, for sure.”

Alcaraz had gone from strength to strength through his first four matches, but Shelton posed his biggest test and finally proved too much.

Shelton, pumped up by the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd, reeled off nine straight games bridging the second and third sets to seize control, capitalizing on Alcaraz’s flagging serve and getting the better of him in rallies that left him winded.

Alcaraz stopped the rot, mustering a break chance as Shelton served for the third set before the American closed it out.

It was a sign that Alcaraz was far from a spent force, and he roared back to take the fouth set in just 36 minutes.

The margins in the fifth set were razor thin. Alcaraz had a break chance at 2-2, then it was Shelton’s turn at 4-3, but the match was destined to go all the way, to a 10-point match tiebreak that Shelton capped with an ace on match point.

After the first three matches of the day all went the distance, Alcaraz and Shelton didn’t get under way until after 11 p.m. — and both exploded out of the gate.

Neither man faced a break point through the first 10 games, although Alcaraz came under some self-inflicted pressure with back-to-back double faults that made for a complicated hold for 4-4.

Alcaraz put together his first love hold for 5-5 then grabbed the first break in the next game, forcing a forehand error from Shelton as the American was feeling the pressure at 0-40 down.

That left the Spaniard to serve for the set, but two errors to start the game were all the opening Shelton needed.

He broke to force the tiebreaker and siezed a 5-3 lead only for Alcaraz to win the last four points and pocket the set after 61 minutes.

But Alcaraz couldn’t maintain the pace and as his struggles on serve increased Shelton roared away, two of his three service breaks coming courtesy of double faults from the Spaniard, including one on set point.

“I knew that my serve was only going to get better, and if I had already dialed in the return to the point that I could break him, I thought my chances were good to get that second set,” Shelton said. “Once I got rolling the second set, broke him three times in that set, it was a lot easier to just play and swing more freely.”

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.title: Quartz deposit purity in central China ‘highly similar’ to US Spruce Pine standard: study
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.author: Victoria Bela
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.text:
Geologists identify Xiaohuaguo site in central Hubei, unlocking potential silica resources for solar panels and semiconductor production

The high-purity quartz from the Chinese deposit is described as having “highly similar” properties to the resources produced at North Carolina’s Spruce Pine, which is crucial to the global production of solar panels and semiconductors.

In the US, there is a growing call from the industry to use high-purity quartz as a weapon against China’s rare earth export ban.

“This discovery of the Xiaohuaguo high-purity quartz deposit provides a new prospective area for the exploration of hydrothermal vein-type high-purity quartz resources in China,” the team wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language journal Earth Science last month.

“Furthermore, the particle size, morphology and residual fluid inclusion characteristics of the purified quartz sand were highly similar to those of Unimin’s IOTA-CG type high-purity quartz sand, demonstrating significant potential for application in high-end technology fields.”

Researchers from the China University of Geosciences, the Wuhan Centre of China Geological Survey and the Hubei Geological Bureau conducted the exploration and purification of the Xiaohuaguo quartz.

While quartz is the second most abundant mineral in the Earth’s continental crust, high-purity quartz is a rare form characterised by silica purity above 99.9 per cent.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.title: Hong Kong, Kazakhstan sign MOU on transport lab, discuss low-altitude economy
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.author: Lam Ka-sing
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.text:
Kazakh vice-minister Bakhtiyar Mukhametkaliyev says his country envisions connecting mainland tech companies with Hong Kong financial tools

Kazakhstan has signed a memorandum of understanding with Hong Kong’s transport authorities to establish a laboratory and discussed low-altitude economy initiatives to help manage traffic jams.

Bakhtiyar Mukhametkaliyev, Kazakhstan’s vice-minister of artificial intelligence and digital development, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday about discussions with the team of Hong Kong’s Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan on the sidelines of the Belt and Road Summit in the city.

“In Hong Kong, I signed the memorandum agreement about launching the ... laboratory with the [Transport and Logistics Bureau] of Hong Kong,” Mukhametkaliyev said.

“We discussed the low-altitude economy … we tried to exchange knowledge about the management of traffic jams.”

He noted that Hong Kong actively implemented low-altitude economy initiatives, such as drone delivery and autonomous taxis.

Mukhametkaliyev added that Kazakhstan aimed to connect mainland Chinese technology companies with Hong Kong financial tools.

“Hong Kong has good financial tools, good experience,” he said, adding that if his country cooperated with mainland big tech firms, for example, the country could use Hong Kong’s financial tools to realise projects in Central Asia.

“Because in Central Asia we’re the leader, it’s not just only one country; it’s a Central Asian market.”

Mukhametkaliyev added that Kazakhstan wanted to work with mainland Chinese artificial intelligence companies including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Huawei Technologies, after two supercomputer clusters were launched in the country last year. Alibaba owns the SCMP.

Organisers of the 11th Belt and Road Summit, the Hong Kong government and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, said the event brought together global political and business leaders to explore Central Asia cooperation and emerging market opportunities.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led the city’s first business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June to open up bilateral trade opportunities.

Mukhametkaliyev said Kazakhstan offered land, electricity infrastructure and a flexible tax regime to attract technology investors.

He said he met a robotics company in Hong Kong in April, which launched manufacturing operations in the country in September.

“We give the land, we give the conditions, we give the special tax regime. No problem,” he said.

Mukhametkaliyev added that Kazakhstan had adopted a digital code and launched more than 1,300 government services online.

“It’s like your official document, your driving licence, your passport. It’s only online,” he said, referring to a QR code on an application.

https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.title: US-China trade, tariffs in 2026
https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.author: Fan Hou
https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.text:
With domestic demand sluggish, China’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is being sustained by exports, prompting protests from trading partners over its economic imbalances.

The value of China’s exports to the United States rose by 34.4 per cent in August from a year earlier, more than twice the 17.1 per cent increase in July, while growth in the value of shipments to the European Union slowed to 6.6 per cent from 16 per cent a month earlier, the customs data showed. Exports of semiconductors surged by 129.8 per cent in August and the overall value of shipments of hi-tech products rose by 56.9 per cent.

The value of car shipments was 43 per cent higher than a year ago, with global demand for Chinese EVs rising as disruption to shipping due to the US-Israeli war on Iran keeps oil prices high.

Growth dampened: China’s robust August trade shows the global AI expansion continues to drive strong demand for hardware. Manufacturing competitiveness in many areas across the AI supply chain has provided a tailwind for China’s exports this year, offsetting the drag from higher US tariffs. For GDP growth, though, the simultaneous surge in tech imports damped the impact. Much of the strength in tech-related trade reflects soaring prices of key components such as memory chips, not just volumes. The net export contribution to growth fell to 0.8 percentage points in 1H26 – with roughly half driven by AI-related demand by our estimates – down from 1.7 ppt in 2025. (Bloomberg Economics)

Easing space: Economists see room for further monetary easing this year. Shan Guo, a partner at China-focused Hutong Research, expects one or two interest-rate cuts by year-end, with the pace tied to the [US] Federal Reserve’s policy moves, the Ministry of Finance bond issuance, and the yuan’s pace of appreciation. The more the yuan appreciates, the more room the PBOC has to cut interest rates, even if the Fed keeps hiking, Guo said. (CNBC)

Irreplaceable role: Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit US battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on US soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. (Foreign Affairs, opinion)

Not imminent: “The latest trade data do not materially strengthen the case for an imminent interest rate cut,” said Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities. “While further policy support cannot be ruled out, the combination of resilient external demand, steady industrial momentum, and increasingly targeted fiscal measures implies that the timing and necessity of additional monetary easing will require further observation.” (Reuters)

Big player: “China is very competitive in its tech goods exports,” said Chi Lo, a senior market strategist for Asia-Pacific at BNP Paribas Asset Management. In recent years, rising exports of electric vehicles, industrial machinery and semiconductors have helped fuel China’s robust shipments globally. China has moved aggressively up the value chain and has become a major player in AI infrastructure and industrial automation,” he said. (Associated Press)

Another month, another blistering export performance that feeds China’s ballooning trade surplus.

Overseas shipments in August grew by a quarter from a year ago to push the surplus so far this year past US$800 billion, keeping China on course to match last year’s US$1.2 trillion surplus that so rankled the United States and European Union.

Demand for semiconductors and the buildout of AI infrastructure in Asia fuelled a sharp rise in technology shipments.

The latest trade data will provide more fodder for China hawks in Washington ahead of President Xi Jinping’s expected summit on September 24 with his US counterpart, Donald Trump, and could cause fresh grumbling in Brussels.

Unless progress is made by next month on measures to reduce China’s trade surplus with the European Union, the bloc’s leaders will consider steps to counter the flood of cheap, well-made Chinese goods that threatens its industries.

China’s trade surplus with the US grew by 44 per cent from a year earlier, the biggest monthly increase since Trump returned to the White House last year. At the same time, the 6.6 per cent rise in shipments to the EU was the smallest since October.

Alarm about China’s trade surplus spilled out of the meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the US state of North Carolina last week. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in a draft statement backed by all G20 members except China, urged countries with excessive and persistent external surpluses to remove distortions constraining domestic consumption that result in an over-reliance on exports.

Unnamed but clearly the target, China opposed the language of the joint statement and blocked its release. The governor of China’s central bank, Pan Gongsheng, argued that countries with trade deficits should reduce their fiscal deficits and increase domestic savings rates, while those with a trade surplus should appropriately promote consumption and investment growth.

With consumption, the property sector and investment all flagging, China needs exports to thrive for it to reach its GDP growth target this year of 4.5 to 5 per cent.

Despite continuing frictions over China’s trade surplus with the US, both sides appear to be adhering to a consensus reached when Xi and Trump met in May to pursue a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”, as the Chinese leader put it.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer echoed that sentiment just last week, saying he was optimistic the leaders’ upcoming talks would produce progress on setting up the US-China Board of Trade agreed at the May summit, and incentives for US agricultural sales.

“The Chinese very much want to have a stable relationship. That’s the word they use: stability,” Greer said. “We’re in favour of that as well.”

On the board of trade, both sides are identifying sectors and products in non-sensitive areas – for example, toys, games and fireworks – that would be eligible for reduced-tariff trade worth up to US$30 billion for each side. There has been little progress on an investment board, also agreed in May.

It’s been clear where the sensitive areas are. Most are related to US efforts to maintain its technological lead over China, often by invoking national security. In August alone, the US imposed tariffs of 15 per cent on polysilicon, used in semiconductors and solar panels, and blocked imports of new drones and robots. In addition, Chinese ships and businesses were among the targets of US sanctions imposed to tighten its economic noose around Iran after six months of inconclusive war.

The US is also planning to levy 7.5 per cent duties on Chinese imports to punish the country’s perceived overcapacity in manufacturing. These would come on top of the 12.5 per cent tariffs slapped on in respect of China’s purported use of forced labour, and would bring the tax US importers pay on Chinese goods to 20 per cent, hitting a ceiling agreed in trade talks according to China’s Ministry of Commerce.

If the US and China are now managing their relationship after a fractious trade war last year, Europe and China appear to be doing the opposite.

Beijing and Brussels are holding talks to manage their ties now in order to avert the threat of a trade war starting in October. So far, neither side has said much publicly about their negotiations yielding positive results.

Denis Redonnet, the bloc’s top trade enforcement officer, was in Beijing last week for three days of talks. The European Union’s top trade official, Ditte Juul Jorgensen, is due in late September and EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will continue the parade next month. EU leaders meet to discuss possible trade barriers on October 15.

Sefcovic has warned the bloc will take defensive measures if the trade talks make no progress. A Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesman last week responded that the talks “cannot be driven by one-sided demands” and should instead address concerns on an equal footing.

Perhaps August’s easing of the flood of exports to Europe will take some of the tension out of the air.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c05r.title: Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c05r.text:
A South Korean court has ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay his ex-wife 2.55tr won ($1.87bn; £1.38bn) in assets, marking the largest divorce settlement in the country's history.

Kwon, who founded South Korea's third-largest video game company Smilegate, is one of the country's richest men. Bloomberg puts his net worth at $3bn.

Smilegate was wholly owned by him until Wednesday when a court ruled that a 35% stake, valued at about 2.5tr won, be transferred to his wife Lee Hwa-jin. He was also ordered to pay her an additional 65bn won in cash.

This settlement is more than double the previous record of 944bn won which tech titan Chey Tae-won was ordered to pay his ex-wife.

In filing for divorce with Kwon, Lee had sought a 50% stake in Smilegate. Her lawyers argued that she had helped finance the company at its founding, according to Bloomberg.

Kwon and Lee got married in 2001, a year before he founded Smilegate. Its best-known titles include the first-person shooter game CrossFire and the action role-playing game Lost Ark.

Lee also said she spent more than 20 years raising their children and caring for their household.

Kwon in turn argued that Lee neither invested nor worked for the company. Earlier this year, Smilegate published a statement saying all of the company's initial capital came from Kwon.

A Smilegate spokesperson declined to "comment on the major shareholder's personal matters".

"We will continue to faithfully perform our duties as usual," they said in a statement cited by The Chosun Daily.

Both parties can still challenge the ruling.

In July this year, Chey Tae-won, the chairman of the corporate giant SK Group, was ordered to pay his ex-wife 944bn won which, prior to today's ruling, was the largest divorce award in Korean history.

However, this was later struck down by the Supreme Court who cited a miscalculation that increased the value of the couple's assets. It has ordered the case to be reviewed.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.title: Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text:
Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.

Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong.

Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.

Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.

The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials.

They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored.

Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road.

"The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said.

"The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway."

The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry.

Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days.

A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said.

Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old.

Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said.

Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years.

The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha.

There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN.

Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting.

International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws.

Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors.

This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India.

In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas. The critically endangered apes are not native to India. They are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgw.title: Antropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgw.text:
A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he personally believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger said in a post on X the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might become able to improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

It comes after the Financial Times reported Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

The BBC has approached Anthropic for comment.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".

Neil Lawrence, Professor of Machine Learning at University of Cambridge, told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4 that the report was credible.

"I suppose it's unsurprising against a background where there's a perception where the United States very much sees AI as a race between themselves and China and is moving more towards isolationist positions, that it might be that the administration is saying that they should reduce cooperation with some of their allies," he said.

In his post, which has been viewed more than 10 million times, Hubinger said "we really do earnestly believe" AI poses a species-ending risk to humans.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," he added.

Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.

But those warnings have become much more stark in recent weeks, as evidence emerges that firms may be struggling to control AI.

Over the summer, there were a string of incidents where AI agents - AI systems that are allowed to operate autonomously - carried out cyber-attacks.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all disclosed hacks carried out by their AI tools.

And in September, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for "extreme caution" over AI's progress, warning more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".

Major figures in the space have been calling for AI development to be slowed in recent months, including Anthropic bosses Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan.

In an open letter signed by 1,300 staff members of AI firms, they called for the US government to "support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.title: Learner drivers still waiting 20 weeks to book tests
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text:
Learner drivers have to wait an average 20 weeks before booking a practical test, according to new figures, despite attempts to reduce delays.

The data from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) for August is only a marginal improvement from an 20.2 weeks in July.

The average wait time between booking and sitting a test is unchanged at 11.1 weeks.

The DVSA initially had a target of reducing the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible.

The DVSA made a number of changes to its practical driving test booking system earlier this year.

Only the learner driver themself is now able to book their driving test, blocking an instructor or third parties from booking using the learner's details.

There is also a geographical restriction which means a learner can only book a test at their three local test centres, rather than one at the other side of the country if they found a test available.

The number of times a would-be driver can swap a test date has also been restricted.

Lucy Rend is 19 and lives in south east London and has been learning to drive for two-and-a-half years. She has a driving test on Thursday and feels under pressure to pass because getting a slot has been so difficult.

It meant getting up at 5.45am everyday to get on the DVSA for 6am. "Then I'd be 21,000 in the queue," she said. "It was very hard but randomly one popped up."

Rend: "I feel lots of pressure to pass because if I don't pass I will have to go through all that again and try find another test, so would rather pass this one and then it is done."

Her friends are also struggling to book a test and "most of them have given up and not going to bother anymore".

The DVSA said on Wednesday that more than 2.13 million practical driving tests took place in the 12 months to August 2026 – the highest rolling 12-month figure on record.

DVSA chief executive Beverley Warmington, said: "There's more to do and we're not going to stop until every learner can get a fair test slot when they need one but today's figures show our plan is working."

The long wait times have been frustrating for driving teachers too.

Adem Veli, who has been an instructor for 16 years and runs his driving school Passman in Sidcup, said: "Before Covid we had the luxury we could pick the test date and work towards that date."

But he said learners having to wait so long can have a huge impact on their confidence.

"It's about a six month wait," he said. "Can you imagine if you did fail your driving test, you're test standard and ready to go [but] have to wait another six months to get back in?"

Veli said that some of the changes the DVSA has made have been positive, such as limiting the number of swaps a learner can make.

However, while the DVSA has made changes to stop third parties booking tests, Veli said: "I get messages weekly, they're trying to sell them to me.

"I've had students ask me about this site or that site, but I tell them don't bother with it now as there's so many scams."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c790.title: Nicolas Cage's driveway collapses as sinkhole opens up at his Malibu home
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c790.text:
A large sinkhole has opened up up outside a house in Malibu reportedly belonging to Hollywood actor Nicolas Cage.

The sinkhole, estimated to be 30ft (9.1m) by 30ft, appeared after the driveway collapsed and follows heavy rain in southern California over recent days.

Local media said that no injuries had been reported. BBC News has asked representatives for Cage for comment.

The actor bought the home in 2024, according to a report in the New York Times shortly after the sale.

Cage won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas and is also known for films such as Gone in 60 Seconds, Face/Off and Con Air, as well as Pig, Moonstruck and The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent.

Nearby residents said they were informed that an 8ft sinkhole had begun forming on Monday.

"At that point, the homeowners were not overly concerned," one resident told Los Angeles magazine.

"We thought it could be fixed pretty quickly." But then, he continued, "all hell broke loose".

Further ground gave way in the early hours of Tuesday morning, leaving a 30ft crater.

The collapse was said to swallow up much of the home's driveway, and left broken asphalt, concrete and construction debris inside the hole.

Emergency services responded in the early hours of Tuesday morning when the structural failure caused a gas leak. SoCalGas later confirmed the leak had been secured.

Traffic cones have been placed around the crater, and AFP reported that waves pounding the sea front can be seen "lapping in the hole and rushing out again under the stanchions that support the home".

The damage occurred after a Los Angeles coastal flooding warning was issued linked to Tropical Storm Marie, which was previously a hurricane.

While the hurricane had remained offshore, it was said to have brought rain and high waves to Southern California.

Malibu City officials have declared at least five homes on the street unsafe for entry and warned residents that emergency access is "severely constrained", and that the area "may be impassable due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c790.summary: Sinkhole appeared after driveway collapsed in Malibu, California. Actor Nicolas Cage bought the home in 2024, according to a report in the New York Times. The sinkhole is estimated to be 30ft (9.1m) by 30ft.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m.title: Family of slain teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m.text:
The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter.

D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder.

In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses.

The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple US media outlets, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.

Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.

In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.

Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".

In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.

Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.

Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.

In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.title: Cargo jet tried to abort unsteady landing before Miami crash, flight data indicates
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/g-s1-1424.text:
An Amazon cargo plane sits at Miami International Airport after overshooting a runway on Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, in Miami.

MIAMI — Flight data suggest an Amazon cargo plane tried to abort an unsteady landing at Miami International Airport before smashing into a van and killing five people inside, according to information investigators released Tuesday.

National Transportation Safety Board investigators will interview the pilot and co-pilot on Wednesday as they try to determine why the jet overran the runway while landing Sunday.

NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said at an evening news conference that they are reviewing flight data and cockpit recordings to figure out what happened in the seconds before the aircraft slammed into the van on airport property, careened through a fence and then smashed an SUV on a city street.

Homendy said investigators want to talk to the pilots before releasing anything from the cockpit voice recorder about why they appeared to briefly attempt to perform a go-around to retry the landing approach before abandoning that and trying to stop the plane. She said the data showed the thrust reversers were never used to help stop the plane.

The five people killed were all inside a van used to shuttle crews that clean planes, authorities said.

Five other people were injured. The pilot and co-pilot have been released from the hospital, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said Tuesday. Two people remain in critical condition, while a third is in stable condition, she said.

Both the mangled white van, its entire front end crushed, and the SUV — so badly damaged it was nearly unrecognizable — remained at the crash site Tuesday, along with the jet, which sat nose-down with a large soot mark near the P in "Prime Air."

The Amazon jet was landing after a two-hour flight from Puerto Rico as storms brewed around the Miami airport. The NTSB said the plane barreled roughly 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the end of the runway.

Former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said Tuesday the fact that the plane landed on its nose and right landing gear first demonstrates this was an unstable landing. He said the pilot might have been attempting a go-around.

Officials stand near a destroyed wing and engine as they inspect an Amazon cargo plane two days after it overshot a runway at Miami International Airport, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Miami.

"A go-around probably should have been executed sooner than that. And it seems like they hesitated," O'Donnell said.

O'Donnell said that by the the time the crew tried to abort the landing, it may have been too late if there wasn't enough runway left. But the interviews investigators scheduled with the pilots for Wednesday will reveal more about what they were thinking at that moment.

Aviation attorney Mary Schiavo, who once was the Transportation Department's Inspector General, said "it almost seems like there was a disagreement between the pilots on what to do."

The weather could have also been a factor because experts said it appeared a strong tail wind propelled the plane far past the point where it was supposed to land. Investigators will want to know what the pilots were told about the weather and why air traffic controllers had not flipped the approach to the runway to allow the plane to land into a headwind.

Amazon said in a statement that it is cooperating with the investigation and the company's deepest sympathies go to the victims and their families.

The five people killed were all in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company that cleans planes. The company said it wouldn't comment on the crash out of respect for the families who lost loved ones.

"Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved. Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed," the company said in a statement Tuesday.

An NTSB investigator works near a damaged van at the site where an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway two days earlier while landing at Miami International Airport, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Miami.

The Miami-Dade sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

Homendy said the crash raises safety concerns for workers at airports. "This is certainly very tragic. You would not think riding in a van to clean an airplane, that this would happen," she said.

Homendy has said that investigators will look at whether the lack of a special system to slow and stop speeding jets at the end of Miami's runways could have been a factor in the crash. But other experts say the airport complied with FAA requirements to provide a cleared buffer space of at least 1,000 feet (305 meters) past the end of the runways.

Miami is not one of the more than 120 airports in the U.S. with lightweight, crushable material that the Federal Aviation Administration says has saved around 500 lives.

Homendy said her agency's goal is to prevent tragedies, but thousands of runway excursions have continued to happen. The NTSB's final report will identify the cause and make recommendations to prevent it from happening again, but that likely won't be complete until a year or more from now.

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines in foreign countries for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

The Miami airport regained the use of a third runway Tuesday evening after the NTSB released it, but investigators are still documenting the evidence around the wreckage at the end of the runway the jet landed on.

More than 225 flights were canceled Sunday and Monday, and hundreds more were delayed, officials said. But that should improve now that the airport can use three of its four runways.

Homendy said the NTSB will try to release the runway back to the airport as quickly as possible after investigators document the scene.

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.title: COMIC: If we fight, is our love doomed? And other honest questions about conflict
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.author: Navied Mahdavian
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-596.text:
Should we argue with the people we love? For Priya Parker, author of a book published in September, The Art of Fighting: The Transformative Power of Conflict, the answer is yes.

While many people dread conflict, it's not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, it's necessary if we want to be in close, authentic relationships, says Parker. So when you have a moment of misalignment with someone, try thinking of it as a signal. There's something here to talk about.

"We assume if the heat is rising, this must be bad. But the reframe is that there's something relevant here. I should pay attention," she says.

Parker, who has been a conflict resolution facilitator for 20 years, shares advice about common questions you may have about getting into fights — whether that's with a partner, a family member or a friend.

Navied Mahdavian is a New Yorker cartoonist and the author of the graphic memoir This Country: Searching for Home in (Very) Rural America.

Still cringing about that awkward moment? Here's what to do about it. Experts demystify the science of awkwardness — and explain how to reduce the emotional intensity of mortifying flashbacks (like that one time you called your teacher "Mommy").

To raise a confident little talker, learn to speak 'parentese'. So you've got a baby in your life. How do you talk to them, exactly? In this comic, experts explain why conversing with your baby is important — and share ways to help them develop their language skills.

Don't panic! 6 strategies to keep you calm in a crisis. House fires, mass shootings, emergency medical procedures and mental health crises. Emergencies can happen at any time — and knowing how to overcome feelings of panic, stress and indecision can be a matter of life or death.

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-595.title: Citing the 'Deep State,' Trump overhauls the intelligence community
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-595.author: Greg Myre
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-595.text:
President Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Venezuela with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (left) and CIA Director John Ratcliffe (center) at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Fla., on Jan. 3. U.S. forces captured Venezuela's leader Nicolas Maduro and brought him to New York where he faces criminal charges.

John Sipher spent nearly three decades at the CIA focused on the Russians, a core part of the agency's mission. That changed dramatically after the al-Qaida attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

"Frankly, tracking and hunting terrorists, finding people, finding a needle in a haystack was not something that we trained for," said Sipher, who served in Moscow and later ran the agency's Russia operations at CIA headquarters.

The CIA and the larger intelligence community had to adapt quickly.

"We did that by by learning, and actually even developing new technologies, computer power, data collection, drones, communications, means to defeat networks, terrorist networks."

There were real successes, such as locating Osama bin Laden in 2011 and destroying his group, al-Qaida, and later, dismantling the Islamic State.

More broadly, the Department of Homeland Security was created, and now has a quarter-million employees, making it the second-largest government agency, trailing only the Pentagon. Military and intelligence budgets soared.

By most all accounts, the U.S. is safer at home. The country has not been hit on U.S. soil with anything remotely comparable to the 9/11 attack, which killed nearly 3,000 people.

CIA officer Johnny Michael Spann, 32, was the first American killed in Afghanistan after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in the U.S. Spann's widow, Shannon Spann, and their 6-month-old son Jake follow Spann's casket to the grave site at Arlington National Cemetery on Dec. 10, 2001. The CIA's paramilitary force grew substantially as the agency joined the fight in Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks.

Yet 25 years later, U.S. national security industry is undergoing another dramatic change.

President Trump is waging an ongoing campaign against the so-called "deep state," which he describes largely as national security officials trying to undermine him.

"We will clean out all of the corrupt actors in our national security and intelligence apparatus, and there are plenty of them," Trump said in announcing his plans for his second term.

Critics say Trump is tearing down the national security infrastructure with no clear vision of what comes next, aside from protecting the president's personal interests.

"Since the re-inauguration of Donald Trump, the architecture of American national security is being destroyed, just like the east wing of the White House," said author Tim Weiner, who's covered the U.S. intelligence community for decades. This includes a book last year, The Mission: The CIA in the 21st Century, that examines the CIA since 9/11. "Trump has deliberately swung a wrecking ball through American national security and has in great part worked to dismantle the systems set up after World War II to protect the United States.

Weiner said Trump consistently selects loyalists with limited experience to lead national security agencies.

"The people he has put in charge, [Pete] Hegseth at the Pentagon, Kash Patel at the FBI, John Ratcliffe at CIA, are sycophants," said Weiner. "They will tell the president what he wants to know rather than what he needs to know."

While many officials have been dismissed under Trump, some left on their own.

Steven Cash held multiple national security posts — at the CIA, the Senate Intelligence Committee and the Department of Homeland Security.

He resigned when Trump began his second term.

"I could not in good conscience keep working for a president who was going to take what I was working on and what others had spent careers working on, and turning it against Americans, which is exactly what he has done," Cash said.

Cash now leads the Steady State, a private group of more than 400 former national security officials. They were career officials who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, but are now highly critical of Trump's policies.

Cash believes the intelligence community made important advances over the past quarter-century, particularly in information sharing. But he acknowledges it's been an imperfect process.

The post of director of national intelligence, or DNI, was created to coordinate the work of what are now 18 separate intelligence agencies.

"The original idea was it would be very small," Cash said. "We sort of joked that the new DNI would get a deputy, he'd get a big conference table with 18 chairs, and the biggest, best coffee machine he could find. And other than that, he'd get nothing."

The office quickly swelled and is often criticized for not functioning as intended. There are periodic calls for the office to be abolished.

Trump cut back the office, along with other national security agencies, as part of his larger government reductions.

Cash said these moves have gone way too far.

"We took a dive off the cliff in 2025. All the gains, I think, are gone, and we are in the process of destroying our intelligence community," he said.

U.S. successes in fighting terrorism have made it less of a priority these days, leading to cutbacks, according to Marc Polymeropoulos, a former CIA officer who spent much of his career in the Middle East.

"Counterterrorism is getting second fiddle to the threats from China and Russia, and the current administration's focus on the border and narco-trafficking means a shift of resources to the Americas," said Polymeropoulos. "I am afraid that counter-terrorism will not be a priority until a mass casualty event, and then it very much will be once again."

John Sipher says one of the most damaging ideas that's taken root is that career intelligence officials actively take sides in partisan politics.

"We have allowed our partisan anger, and specifically the Trump administration, to create this narrative that there's a deep state and that the intelligence services work for one party or another. I think it's a real danger," he said.

Tim Weiner said the damage has also been inflicted abroad as Trump repeatedly antagonizes U.S. allies.

"The CIA in particular relies or depends on intelligence sharing with friendly and not so friendly foreign intelligence services," Weiner said. "It it is still only 20,000 people, and they cannot cover the entire world. They need the British. They need the Dutch. They need the Saudis. They need help."

That help, he says, is much harder to come by today than in the aftermath of 9/11.
